title: Kenyan World Marathon Champion Peres Jepchirchir Suspended For Doping
body: In a fresh hammer blow for Kenyan athletics, world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended for doping, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced Friday. The highly decorated 33-year-old Kenyan, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for banned blood booster EPO. An athlete is provisionally suspended while their case is investigated. Jepchirchir joins more than 140 Kenyan athletes, including current women’s marathon world record-holder Ruth Chepngetich, who have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017. The AIU said Jepchirchir’s out-of-competition sample had been collected in Kenya prior to her recent Sydney Marathon victory. Jepchirchir’s lauded career has also seen her as a former world record-holder in the half-marathon while she is a four-time World Marathon Major winner having captured the Sydney Marathon (2026), the London Marathon (2024), the Boston Marathon (2022) and the New York Marathon (2021). The decision of World Athletics to award Nairobi the 2029 world championships is likely to increase the scrutiny of the east African nation’s anti-doping policies. Barnabas Korir, Athletics Kenya Youth Development Director and National Olympic Committee of Kenya vice president, said he was left feeling shocked by the news of the suspension. “It’s a big disappointment coming soon after we were awarded the World Athletics Championship in 2029,” Korir told AFP. “We are in shock, especially in the calibre of Peres Jepchirchir after a stellar career. “We don’t know what is happening with our athletes.” Kenya played host to a three-day visit from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) earlier this month, the body’s chief Witold Banka telling the country that it had to strive for zero tolerance on doping. “Kenya proudly calls itself the Home of Champions. But for that home to remain respected and credible, it must also be clean,” Banka said. “That is why Kenya needs a strong culture of clean sport, zero tolerance for doping, and a more determined approach to preventing and fighting doping.” Banka said that joint cooperation with Kenyan authorities would help lay the foundations for a cleaner sport. “WADA or ADAK (Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya) alone cannot achieve its vision if we do not cooperate with those who have the power to go against those who are producing, smuggling and trafficking dangerous steroids to your athletes,” he said. “We’ve found a common understanding and we are on the same track and there’s a clear goal within Kenya for zero tolerance for doping policy and it has to be established immediately with joint actions and a more aggressive approach to those who are destroying the image of the country and the reputation of the athletes.” The post Kenyan World Marathon Champion Peres Jepchirchir Suspended For Doping appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Terrorism: FG secures 653 convictions, prosecutes 1,060 suspects
body: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri The Federal Government has secured a total of 653 convictions of persons arrested across the federation for their involvement in various acts of terrorism. The convicts, some of whom were found guilty of aiding insurgents or concealing information about their operations from security agencies, were among the 1,060 persons brought before the court in the third phase of the ongoing mass trial of terror suspects. Speaking to newsmen shortly after stepping out of the courtroom on Friday, the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, who led the prosecution, disclosed that a total of 880 cases had been heard, out of which the court convicted 653, acquitted seven and discharged 27 of the defendants. He said the exercise would continue and the final figures would be announced after the conclusion of the trial. Describing the current phase of the mass trial as the largest since the FG commenced the special court sessions for the prosecution of terror suspects, the AGF attributed the success of the exercise to judicial cooperation, effective prosecution and inter-agency collaboration. He expressed appreciation to the judges handling the cases, particularly Justice Binta Nyako, who has been acting on behalf of the Chief Judge of the Federal High Court, Justice John Tsoho. The AGF also commended the prosecution team, the defence counsel and the security agencies for contributing to the smooth conduct of the proceedings. Among the agencies he acknowledged for their contributions were the Office of the National Security Adviser (NSA), the Department of State Services (DSS), the military, the police, correctional centres and the Legal Aid Council of Nigeria (LACoN). According to the AGF, collaboration among the institutions has been critical to advancing the prosecution of terrorism, terrorism financing and related offences in the country. On the representation of the defendants by lawyers from the LACoN, the AGF explained that the council was fulfilling its responsibility of providing legal assistance to eligible defendants. He clarified, however, that private legal practitioners were also representing some of the suspects. He said the defence lawyers were not only given the opportunity to interact with their clients before the court proceedings, but were also granted access to the detention facilities to enable them to prepare the defendants’ defence effectively. On the issue of deradicalisation of suspects recommended by the court, the AGF said the process remained an important component of the overall exercise. He maintained that rehabilitation and reintegration were necessary to complement the judicial process and reduce the risk of individuals returning to extremist activities. The post Terrorism: FG secures 653 convictions, prosecutes 1,060 suspects appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: My Word: When Europe fiddles and burns - opinion
body: It was a searing image. The sight of the historic city hall in Limoges, France, going up in flames, and the spire collapsing into the blazing building was haunting.Two different news clips captured two sides of the story: In one, the crowd of onlookers could be heard cheering as the tower fell; in the other, someone called out in a shocked voice: “It's fallen!” I wondered whether he was referring just to the spire or to French civilization in general.According to Smithsonian Magazine, the city hall first opened its doors on Bastille Day in 1883, and “has been celebrated as an architectural wonder. Well-known for its tall spire and ornate metal belfry, the 143-year-old building gained historic monument status in 1975 as a prime example of late 19th-century French architecture and civic pride.”There's something sadly symbolic in the beautiful building that opened on the French National Day all those years ago being burned down in the 2026 French riots. Beautiful architecture and civic pride are being willfully destroyed.For the masked assailants, arsonists, and looters rampaging throughout France – and elsewhere in Europe – this is a modern version of Bastille Day. The mobs are ruling through fear and violence.Whatever initially triggered the riots – ostensibly highschoolers complaining about their conditions – the flames are being fanned from other directions. This is not about the cost of living, the price of fuel, or crowded classrooms.News footage showed shocked storekeepers along the iconic Champs-Élysées helplessly looking on as their stores were looted and trashed. Not only were their livelihoods being stolen, but their very way of life.It's not by chance that symbols of the government, and of France itself, were attacked. The Statue of the Republic was defaced in Paris; the marble bust of Marianne was damaged in an attack in the historic Marseilles City Hall building; and the tourist office in Lyon, housed in a 19th-century architectural gem, was also destroyed – not that the city can expect an influx of tourists any time soon.France has seen demonstrations before, even violent ones, but “vive la difference” – these were not French students holding philosophical discussions as they marched in May 1968; nor were they “the Yellow Vests,” protesting fuel prices in the mass rallies that petered out with COVID 19 restrictions; and today's rioters are not the workers who took to the streets three years ago to protest the planned rise of the retirement age.The Yellow Vests have made a comeback, but these riots are not quintessentially French. Thanks to immigrants and illegal migrants, and their children and grandchildren, foreign flags of former colonies like Morocco and Algeria rival the French tricolor, and Palestinian flags and keffiyehs are prevalent. I couldn't help but note the guest appearance last week by keffiyeh-clad, omni-activist Greta Thunberg. She is now absorbed by the global political climate rather than the world's weather.More than ever, when protesters chant, “From the river to the sea,” the question is which river and sea they are referring to. Anarchists and jihadists are agents of chaos and destruction – they create a lethal combination.In some French cities, the lingua franca of the rioters was Arabic. There's a word for it: “Intifada.” The Intifada has been globalized, and the results can be seen on the streets of France, where hundreds of protesters and police officers have been injured, and damage could reach a billion euros.The current conflagration in France is not (yet) specifically an attack on Jews, but the writing was spray-painted on the wall years ago, along with the slogan “Free Palestine.”When French President Emmanuel Macron last year declared his unconditional recognition of a State of Palestine, he did not strengthen France and French values; he rewarded terrorism and violence. No wonder there are jokes and memes about first implementing a “Two-state solution” in France.Newsweek and other media noted the appearance of protest videos featuring the song “MRH” by rapper BORO700, which refers to jihadist Mohamed Merah, who murdered 30-year-old teacher Rabbi Jonathan Sandler and his two young sons along with eight-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse in 2012, as well as killing French soldiers in other attacks.The lyrics also praise a perpetrator of the November 2015 jihadist assault in Paris, in which 130 people were murdered, including those at a concert at the Bataclan hall, at a football stadium, and at cafés and bars. The victims were not chosen specifically, but the targets were carefully selected to include all that the young, carefree, French way of life represents.What's causing the French riots?As Abe Greenwald put it in Commentary, trying to explain “the real cause” of the riots in France is “kind of like trying to determine the official cause of death in someone who suffered from multiple fatal conditions at the end of his life. That someone is Europe, and the conditions are progressive, in more than one sense of the word. “There are the real crises: welfare-state failure, education collapse, the disappearance of community, an unsustainable old-age dependency ratio, and unassimilated immigration. Then there are the isms, the activist theologies ensuring that solutions remain out of reach: socialism, anarchism, Islamism, Palestinianism, and antisemitism…“This indecipherable convergence of radical pursuits is now everywhere in the West, and it's been with us for a while…“In the years since 2011, the storm has been fueled by Black Lives Matter, Antifa, gender radicalism, anti-Israel mania, and jihad fandom… The riots in France will add something new, too.”Macron had his “let them eat cake” moment last week, attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte as the riots worsened. Perhaps it was more like Nero fiddling as Rome burned. The French president is quacking like the lame duck he is ahead of the scheduled April 2027 elections.Both far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon  and far-Right front-runner Marine Le Pen are hoping to gain from the current protests. Neither bodes well for the Jewish community.  Marseilles-born rector of Bar-Ilan University Prof. Cyrille Cohen, speaking on Reshet Bet's “International Hour” radio show, pointed out that polarization is not a byproduct of the riots but an aim.Whether the Right or the Left wins, there is likely to be a wave of aliyah. Bar-Ilan, like other Israeli universities, is already absorbing more French-speaking students, he noted. Cohen quipped about a French cartoon ahead of the presidential elections showing Jews “undecided how to vote: whether to choose Jerusalem or Netanya.”Those Israelis threatening to leave the country if next week's general election doesn't bring about their desired results, should keep in mind that there is no guarantee of a safe haven and a warm welcome for Jews anywhere in the global village, no matter which camp they belong to. Israelis also need to be aware that outside forces – including Iran, Russia, Turkey, and Qatar – are happy to foster Israeli divisions and foment unrest as a way of weakening the Jewish state.The attacks on Israel have long morphed into an assault on Judeo-Christian values. Ahead of November 11, the British Commonwealth's Remembrance Day for its war dead, it is customary to wear poppy pins. Indeed, November 11 is also known as Poppy Day. This year, the Palestinians and their supporters have hijacked that too, selling a poppy badge in Palestinian colors while claiming the poppy-anemone is the Palestinian national flower. It's not; it's Israel's national flower, and the red anemones that carpet the Negev in the spring have come in particular to symbolize the 1,200 slaughtered in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led invasion and mega-atrocity.Europe is discovering that the nightmare wasn't a bad dream but reality of its own making. It needs to wake up and smell the burning buildings. Violent riots are not demonstrations of free speech and democracy. This is war. But the world has yet to internationalize the message of the French maxim, “En la guerre comme en la guerre.”

title: Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
body: Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two U.S. researchers who analyzed more than a year of commercial satellite images. More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters. But they risk fueling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the U.S. Congress to a U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation. Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the U.S., took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 125 miles west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026. The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits — wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden. The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organization in Philadelphia. A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said. The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote. Militaries favor solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems. Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organization told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology. Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics are also similar to Chinese missile plants. Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a YouTube video and photographs of the event. The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile. Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile. Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems. The Chinese embassy and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The CIA declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Missiles would alter the balance of power Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its U.S.-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defenses. “You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran ... if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to U.S.-made satellite-guided bombs. “Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.” Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles. Janes, the defense intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.” Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment. “This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said. “You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.” The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation. Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan. Work began last year The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said. A December 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet. A Sept. 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures. The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.” Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year.

title: Dubai sends winter relief supplies to Gaza through new air bridge
body: Dubai Humanitarian has launched a new air bridge to deliver winter relief to Gaza. The first flight, carrying essential humanitarian supplies including thermal blankets for Unicef, arrived in Al Arish, Egypt, before being transferred to Gaza. The initiative is being carried out under the directives of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai . The air bridge involves multiple flights operated by the Dubai Royal Air Wing using C-130 aircraft, each carrying approximately nine metric tonnes of humanitarian supplies. At least three more flights are scheduled in the coming days to deliver blankets for children and other vulnerable groups as families prepare for the approaching winter. Marwan Ahmed bin Ghalita, chairman of the Dubai Humanitarian Authority , said the winter months pose additional challenges for families already enduring difficult conditions, particularly children. “The first facilitated shipment of this new air bridge arrived in Al Arish , ahead of its onward transfer to Gaza. This operation reflects Dubai Humanitarian’s long-standing role as a trusted global hub that brings humanitarian partners together, supports their efforts and enables aid to reach those in need,” he said. The shipment also represents the first co-ordinated sourcing order under the UN80 Integrated Supply Chain Approach, which brings together UN agencies to strengthen joint sourcing and delivery of humanitarian supplies. Enabled by Dubai Humanitarian in collaboration with its partners, the initiative aims to improve co-ordination, speed up relief operations and make aid delivery more efficient. Since 2023, Dubai Humanitarian has supported relief efforts in Gaza through air bridges, land convoys, and sea shipments, working with international humanitarian partners to keep essential supplies flowing through multiple transport routes.

title: Rivers Boat Tragedy: Fubara vows probe as 10 reportedly die
body:
Ten people were reportedly killed after a boat capsized during a confrontation over the removal of an oil vessel in Kula Kingdom, Akuku-Toru Local Government Area of Rivers State.
The Police Command in Rivers State confirmed the incident but said investigations were ongoing to establish the exact number of casualties and the circumstances surrounding the tragedy, The Guardian reported on Friday.
The incident reportedly occurred on Tuesday evening amid tensions over the planned removal of the Anambra Basin FSO, a floating storage and offloading vessel owned by Max Shipping Services Limited.
Community members had opposed the vessel’s removal, citing an alleged oil spill and demanding environmental remediation and compensation.
Sukubo Sara-Igbe, a Kula indigene and president of the National Youth Council of Nigeria, told Guardian that six gunboats arrived during the operation and that a boat conveying community members capsized during the confrontation.
Mr Fubara promised that anyone found responsible for the “death of 10 persons” would face the law, according to a statement issued by the Rivers State Government House and emailed to PREMIUM TIMES on Thursday night.
Represented by his Chief of Staff, Sunny Ewule, the governor gave the assurance when Kula residents staged a peaceful march to Government House in Port Harcourt to seek government intervention.
“We want to sympathise with the Kula Community and the bereaved families.
“Anybody who is involved in this incident or found culpable for whatever happened will definitely pay for it according to the law. We are not going to sit by and allow Rivers indigenes to go through this type of unnecessary death,” he said.
The governor urged residents to remain calm and avoid taking the law into their own hands.
Earlier, community delegation leader Anabs Sara-Igbe said they approached the government because they wanted justice without resorting to violence.
“It is proper we inform him (Fubara) because we don’t want to take the law into our hands. We have the capacity to react, but we don’t want to react,” he said.
Max Shipping Services Limited, the vessel’s owner, expressed sadness over the reported deaths but denied responsibility for the oilfield operations, according to a Guardian newspaper report .
The company said the vessel had been hired to Menal Technical Services Limited under a marine equipment hire agreement and that the contractor had specific contractual responsibilities concerning operations, community settlements, security and demobilisation.
It said it initiated the retrieval of the vessel after prolonged outstanding hire payments and unsuccessful efforts to secure settlement. The company also maintained that the crude oil previously stored in the vessel had been discharged before the retrieval exercise.
The circumstances surrounding the confrontation and the boat’s capsizing remain under investigation.
The latest incident adds to a history of fatal boat accidents in Rivers State.
In January 2025, police confirmed that three people, including a toddler, died after a passenger boat travelling from Port Harcourt to Bonny capsized during a storm. Nineteen passengers were rescued.
In January 2024, 11 people, including five infants, died after two boats capsized in Rivers State, PREMIUM TIMES reported.
The latest tragedy differs from those incidents because it reportedly occurred amid a confrontation linked to an oil vessel’s removal and community grievances over alleged environmental pollution.
Authorities are expected to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, confirm the casualty figure and determine whether anyone should be held responsible.

title: Russian forces attack enterprise in Chernihiv, leaving one killed, 25 injured
body:
This was reported by Head of the Chernihiv City Military Administration Dmytro Bryzhynskyi on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
“Unfortunately, the number of injured has risen to 25. One person has been killed. According to preliminary information, 16 people sought medical assistance from ambulance crews at the scene, while another eight were taken to hospital,” Bryzhynskyi said.
Earlier, Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, Head of the Chernihiv City Military Administration, reported that Russian forces had attacked two enterprises in Chernihiv.
The official reported that the Russian strike caused damage to the enterprise. Preliminary reports indicated that people were trapped under the rubble.
Bryzhynskyi also said that Russian forces had attacked a Nova Poshta terminal in the northern part of the city.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces previously attacked Chernihiv’s transport infrastructure.

title: Military takeover of New Mexico borderlands challenged in court
body: A group of nonprofits alleges the federal government illegally transformed more than 100,000 acres of public land along the New Mexico-Mexico border into a military installation so U.S. troops could assist in immigration enforcement. In a federal lawsuit , the New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Battalion Search and Rescue and Southern Border Communities Coalition argue the Trump administration is misusing so-called “national defense areas” to circumvent longstanding restrictions on military participation in civilian law enforcement. In a statement , Brian Netter, legal director at Democracy Forward, one of the teams representing the plaintiffs, called the “national defense area” designation “an extraordinary abuse of power with devastating consequences for the people who live, work, worship, recreate, and carry out lifesaving humanitarian work along the border.” “Public lands do not become military installations simply because the president says so, and the military cannot be handed sweeping new authority to police civilians by drawing a line around land that belonged to the public,” he said, adding, “Our Constitution and laws impose clear limits on the use of the military for civilian law enforcement for a reason.” The Trump administration began sending troops to the area in March 2025 to support border security and has since expanded the military’s presence along the border in other states. By April of that year, the Defense Department assumed jurisdiction over the 109,651 acres from the Department of the Interior . The designation made the land, officially named the New Mexico National Defense Area , an expansion of Fort Huachuca for three years. The Defense Department said the designation allowed troops to detain people accused of trespassing in the military area after crossing the border illegally. However, the lawsuit argues that the federal agencies exceeded their authority to transfer public land through emergency powers. “No statute authorizes the creation of ‘national defense areas,’ let alone permits carving one out of formerly public land,” the lawsuit says. The lawsuit adds that the Defense Department has historically used such land restrictions only temporarily to protect people or property during accidents or emergencies. “Creating a semi-permanent military zone along the southern border for purposes of immigration enforcement is directly contrary to the agency’s longstanding practice,” the lawsuit says. Beyond alleging violations of federal law, the plaintiffs say the military zones are disrupting their work by limiting access to public lands used for recreation and conservation; supporting border communities; and providing humanitarian aid. James R. Holeman, founder of Battalion Search and Rescue, said his organization leads volunteers who search for people in distress in remote areas and recover the remains of migrants who died crossing the border. Over the past three years, he said, the group’s monthly searches along the Arizona and New Mexico border have uncovered more than 100 death sites. “Imagine how many more people could be found if we had the access, resources, and support to search systematically. Instead, we’re being locked out,” he said, adding that vast stretches of borderlands are “virtually inaccessible to humanitarian searchers” because of federal designations. “Now the government is closing off even more territory. We don’t find weapons or drugs. We find Bibles, prayer cards, love notes, and the belongings of people simply trying to survive,” Holeman said. “There is no meaningful, systematic government effort to search for the missing and the dead. They don’t search, and now they’re preventing us from searching.”

title: Precedent-setting human trafficking sentence handed down in Saskatchewan
body:
A case Saskatchewan Crown prosecutors are calling precedent-setting for human trafficking convictions in the province has concluded with a judge’s sentencing decision. Judge Miguel Martinez handed down prison sentences of four years for Sohel Hadiar for human trafficking offences and 14 years for Muhammad Musam on charges of human trafficking and sexual assault.
Senior Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning said this case will be used to inform future human trafficking cases in Saskatchewan.
“We didn’t cite any Saskatchewan human trafficking cases, all of what we cited mainly came out of Ontario. So this is one of the precedent-setting cases for human trafficking in the province,” said Dunning.
The judge found the Bengali men, Hadiar and Musam, took advantage of a Bengali woman’s vulnerability. She is referred to as S.K. to protect her identity.
Court heard the men withheld S.K.’s citizenship documentation and threatened to break her work permit in an effort to exploit her. The judge determined the men forced the victim to work up to 12 hours a day, six days a week with very little pay.
The two moved S.K. between the Saskatchewan communities of Gull Lake, Elrose and Tisdale for jobs at their restaurants.
Both men will have to pay restitution to S.K. of more than $17,000.
The courtroom also heard the victim impact statement from the woman, in which she said the abuse ruined her life.
S.K. wrote about feeling stuck in her life and feeling scared of being trafficked again if she tried to improve her situation.
“I don’t think much about my future anymore and focus on keeping my head down,” said S.K.
“How could they do this to a Bengali sister for just a little money?”
S.K. also said her family in Bangladesh know about the abuse and are facing intense public scrutiny.
She said her mother sometimes asks her why she had to try to come to Canada. S.K. said she asks herself the same question.

title: France in flames: As Paris lectures Israel, riots leave its Jews fearing for their safety - opinion
body: France likes to speak in the name of the human conscience. It lectures other countries, hands out moral grades, and proudly invokes its national promise of liberty, equality, and fraternity.But when its streets are burning, stores are being looted, and Jews fear for their safety, the disgraceful gap between France's international posture and its domestic reality is exposed. A world power that seeks to teach others how to manage conflicts is struggling to protect its citizens' storefronts.This is more than a governance crisis. It is an indictment of French President Emmanuel Macron and a leadership that has replaced responsibility with empty rhetoric.The student protests and anger over the cost of living may have originated in genuine hardship. Precisely for that reason, allowing them to become a pathway to arson and looting is a betrayal of the public that came to protest.No shortage of classrooms justifies burning businesses, and no electricity bill justifies attacking police officers. Anyone who wraps criminality in the flag of social justice is not a revolutionary. He is granting legitimacy to lawlessness.A government that cannot protect both the right to protest and the victims of violence has failed in its most basic duty.Amid the chaos, the question arises once again: Why are Jews expected to pay the price?Rioters vandalized a synagogue in Paris' 19th arrondissement. The Torah ark was forced open, and religious items were thrown to the floor. There is no moral path leading from student hardship to attacks on Jews. When such a path emerges, protest has become a refuge for hatred and antisemitism.There is no reason to condemn all the protesters. But the Palestinian flags and chants of “Free Palestine” provide ample evidence of what parts of the demonstration became. Once again, French Jews are expected to answer for the actions of the IDF and the Israeli government.The citizenship of French Jews has been subjected to racist tests before, during the infamous Vichy regime. Nor should anyone forget the Dreyfus affair.The figures on antisemitism demolish the excuses offered by the French leadership. France recorded 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025. The synagogue in La Grande Motte was attacked, and a police officer was injured in an explosion.These are not isolated incidents. They constitute a reality demanding national introspection. When the state must place security around Jewish institutions, it should begin examining its own failures. Jews do not need another emotional speech after the next attack.Evasion is not tolerance when confronting Islamism. According to a survey conducted in 2025, 44% of Muslim respondents said they placed the rules of their religion above French law, while some expressed a preference for Sharia law.A country cannot accept a situation in which its laws become recommendations and a minority seeks to dictate the legal rules. There must be no street where the law retreats in the face of threats or where police officers fear to enter certain areas. A Paris whose streets are in flames is the victim of state failure.In France, as in Britain, politicians fear losing the Muslim electorate. When politicians exchange principles for electoral calculations, and when a leader softens his opposition to extremism for fear of losing support, he also abandons moderate Muslims.A leadership that purchases temporary calm through moral ambiguity is selling its country's future.Macron's presidency will be remembered with disgrace. The riots, the burning of stores, and the resurgence of antisemitism are the consequences of his failed leadership and that of the government he heads.The importance of the presidencyMacron has forgotten that the presidency is more than a title, a palace and a flag. The images coming from France are a political humiliation for the president and the French leadership.Anyone seeking to embody European leadership must explain why citizens in his own country are forced to pray that the next protest will pass over their businesses.Israel remembers French moralizing all too well. On the eve of the Six Day War, France imposed an arms embargo and withheld Mirage aircraft ordered by Israel. Fifty Mirage 5 jets ordered in 1966 were never delivered under the agreement and instead entered French service.From an Israeli perspective, this was a betrayal of trust by a major supplier at a moment of danger. Behind the lofty language of balance and responsibility stood a decision demonstrating how friendship can become conditional on diplomatic convenience.France does not enter this debate with clean hands.In Algeria, France operated a system that enabled torture and disappearances, as Macron himself acknowledged in the case of Maurice Audin. In Paris in October 1961, police killed dozens of Algerian demonstrators, including victims who were thrown into the Seine and drowned.The colonial stain and hypocrisy did not end in Algeria. In Madagascar, France brutally suppressed the 1947 uprising, killing thousands. President Francois Hollande later acknowledged the brutal repression and its victims.Behind the slogan of a civilizing mission stood a reality in which demands for independence were answered with military force. The liberty France presented as a universal value ended when people under French rule sought to exercise it themselves.It is difficult to imagine a sharper contradiction between declaration and action: liberty for the ruling nation and subjugation for the people it ruled.The depth of that betrayal was also exposed in Senegal. In December 1944, French forces opened fire on African soldiers at the Thiaroye military camp after those men had served France and demanded the pay owed to them.Men who had risked their lives for France discovered that their service did not guarantee equal treatment. Macron recognized the incident as a massacre in 2024, 80 years after it occurred.That recognition was important, but the delay remains painful. It took decades to call the killing by its proper name. This was not only colonial brutality. It was also state-sanctioned ingratitude.The philosopher and author Maarten Boudry published a powerful monologue on X/Twitter about the riots in Europe:“Before long, we will all know what it feels like to be Jewish. In France, they already know. This will be the punishment we deserve for abandoning the Jews, ignoring their warnings, turning against them, and even marching alongside their oppressors.“For three years, you useful idiots marched with Palestinian flags, wore keffiyehs, screamed 'From the river to the sea,' and recognized a fictitious Palestinian state as a reward for the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7. You boycotted the world's only Jewish state, defamed the Jewish people's right to self-determination, and spread the blood libel of 'genocide in Gaza.'“Did you think that if you fed the crocodile enough Jewish flesh, it would eventually be satisfied? All you did was strengthen the monster and further stimulate its appetite.“The Palestinian flag has become a flag of victory, proudly raised among the ruins of historic buildings that were looted and vandalized. It is a symbol of hatred toward our culture and everything it represents. It never ends with the Jews.”France is paying, and will continue to pay, the price of its arrogance. Human rights were presented as a noble promise but were repeatedly subordinated to the interests of those in power.There is now a simple demand of France's leaders. Before presenting yourselves as judges of the world, acknowledge your own responsibility. Open the archives and give the victims a place more dignified than a footnote in a ceremonial speech.Even if France eventually withdraws its support for the forces of evil represented by Palestinian terrorists who murdered, raped, mutilated, and abducted approximately 1,500 innocent Israeli and foreign civilians, history will not forget.The writer is the CEO of Radios 100FM, an honorary consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israeli Radio Association, and previously served as a monitor for Israel's Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

title: Gas prices unlikely to drop below $4 before midterms, some experts say. Here's why.
body:
Gas prices usually fall at a slower pace than they rise, experts say.
High gas prices continue to weigh on wallets as voters list affordability as a top concern ahead of early November's midterm elections .
The national average price of a gallon of gas stands at $4.27, marking an increase of nearly $1.30, or 43%, since the outbreak of the Iran war in February, AAA data showed.
Fuel prices are unlikely to ease significantly before Election Day on Nov. 3, some analysts told ABC News, predicting gas prices would all but certainly remain above $4 a gallon.
Analysts attributed elevated gas prices to ongoing fighting in the Middle East, which has damaged oil infrastructure and forced firms to take up costly means of transporting crude. The Russia-Ukraine war has also crimped fuel exports from Russia, they said, compounding the supply shortage.
There is little indication of an imminent resolution of either conflict, the analysts said. Even in the event of a peace deal in the Middle East and a drop in oil costs, for instance, gas prices would likely fall at a delayed pace as retailers sell through refined product purchased while oil prices were at higher levels, they added.
"It's weeks before the election and we’ve got a ramp up of what’s happening in the Middle East, as opposed to some type of calming and a sign energy prices are coming down," Tom Seng, a professor of energy finance at Texas Christian University, told ABC News.
GasBuddy Petroleum Analyst Patrick De Haan ruled out the possibility of a fall below the $4 a gallon threshold by early November. "Gasoline will not fall below $4/gal prior to the midterms," De Haan said in a post on X.
The Brent crude futures price, a benchmark for global oil trading, climbed above $112 a barrel on Thursday. Until this week, oil prices had last reached that benchmark in May. The latest reading amounts to a rise of nearly 60% since the start of the Iran war.
Oil prices climbed earlier this week after Iran and its Houthi allies claimed attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy claimed on Thursday to have attacked four vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, accusing the ships of navigating an "illegal route" and "transferring oil cargoes from one ship to another."
The ships were hit while in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf, the IRGC Navy claimed, in a statement published by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The IRGC Navy also reported that three vessels hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night.
The reports came days after Yemen-based Houthi militants claimed a wave of strikes on Saudia Arabia, including the Shaybah oil field as well as Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a port city near a key transport corridor on the Red Sea.
Despite continued fighting, crude oil exports from the region had improved in recent weeks, according to tracking firm Kpler . Even so, heightened transport costs and damaged refinery infrastructure have disrupted the supply of refined product necessary for auto gasoline, Denton Cinquegrana, chief oil analyst at Dow Jones Energy, told ABC News.
The U.S. -- the world's largest oil producer -- imports a small amount of fuel from the Middle East. Since oil and gas are sold on a global market, however, the unrest has sent prices rising for everyone, including U.S. drivers.
"I’m sure you've seen everything about crude oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz at pre-war levels. The simple fact is that refined products are not," Cinquegrana said. "If prices are going up in one place, the chances are they will pull up prices in another place."
A resolution of the war would eventually ease gas prices, but it is unlikely that significant relief at the pump would materialize within days or weeks, some analysts said. Some key oil infrastructure in the region would still require lengthy repairs, they said, while retailers may prove reluctant to slash prices.
Gas prices usually fall at a slower pace than they rise, since retailers prefer to keep prices elevated as they sell through inventory acquired at high cost, Ramanan Krishnamoorti, a professor of petroleum engineering at the University of Houston, told ABC News.
"It's usually a pretty slow downward trajectory for gas prices," Krishnamoorti said.
Even if gas prices are likely to remain high within the coming weeks, some analysts acknowledged reason to be hopeful about the general outlook for costs at the pump.
Seasonal fluctuations typically provide price relief for drivers in the fall.
A slowdown in travel has eased demand for gas as families have returned from summer vacation and resumed routine driving associated with work and school commutes.
Refineries, meanwhile, have begun shifting toward a less-expensive blend of winter fuel. Refineries contend with fewer regulations from the Environmental Protection Agency in the cooler fall and winter months, allowing for a cheaper blend of fuel.
"Demand tends to go down at this time of year. That's seasonality at play," Cinquegrana said.
For now, however, a supply shortage will likely keep gas prices above $4 a gallon over the next couple weeks.
When asked about whether U.S. gas prices could fall below that benchmark by Election Day, Cinquegrana said, "Short answer: No."
ABC News' Nasser Atta, Othon Leyva and Desiree Adib contributed to this report

title: Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 23 (MNA) – Iran’s mission to the Vienna-based UN organizations has criticized the IAEA's continued failure to condemn the US and Zionist regime's attacks on its nuclear facilities.
The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna PRESS RELEASE On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute 23 October 2026 Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document.
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute.
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility.
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States.
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special needs of developing countries.
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires due observance of the sovereign rights of States.
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically motivated action.
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non- proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective scrutiny and unequal expectations.
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without discrimination.
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the prohibition of aggression. They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold.
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly.
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability.
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests.
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit from nuclear science and technology.
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate rights of all its members.
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception.
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

title: Works and Housing Minister gives Ghana Hydrological Authority 3 months to report progress on key challenges
body: The Minister for Works, Housing and Water Resources, Ahmed Ibrahim, has directed the Ghana Hydrological Authority (GHA) to submit a comprehensive report on its operational challenges, with progress on key issues expected to be assessed within three months. The directive covers staff attrition, recruitment, approval of conditions of service, outstanding regulations and the operationalisation of the Authority’s statutory fund. It was issued during a working visit to the Authority, where Mr Ibrahim expressed concern that the challenges could persist without clear follow-up and accountability. A report by the GHA highlights several challenges affecting the agency, including severe staff shortages. The Authority has an established workforce of about 230 positions but currently has only 89 staff members. Mr Ibrahim warned that continued staff departures could result in the loss of institutional knowledge built up by experienced hydrological specialists. The Ministry also wants the report to outline progress on the regulations needed to implement the law establishing the Authority, as well as the proposed statutory fund and staff conditions of service. The Minister said he had asked the Authority’s Chief Executive Officer to update the institution’s presentations to include all outstanding concerns and submit them for consideration. The directive comes as the Ministry engages agencies under its supervision to assess their operational challenges and identify measures to improve performance. Mr Ibrahim said the Ministry would work with the relevant institutions to address the issues, including engaging the Ministry of Finance on financial clearance for additional recruitment. The Ghana Hydrological Authority provides services including flood forecasting, early warning systems, desilting and coastal protection.

title: 82-yr-old US senator charged with drug trafficking, money laundering
body: An 82-year-old Democratic state senator in Virginia, L. Louise Lucas, has been indicted alongside six others, including members of her family, over an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving the illegal sale of marijuana and money laundering. According to the indictment, Lucas, president pro tempore of Virginia’s Senate, allegedly operated several businesses that bought and sold illegal quantities of marijuana in the state to build her family’s wealth. The indictment also accuses her of using her political influence to protect the alleged operation from criminal scrutiny and influence legislation for financial gain. In a statement on the charges, FBI Director Kash Patel alleged that Lucas worked with “a close-knit group of family members and associates” to build a “criminal marijuana enterprise”. Patel further accused the senator of using her “position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves.” Lucas faces charges including racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to possess and distribute marijuana, and conspiracy to launder money. A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed that she had surrendered to law enforcement. Responding to the indictment on Thursday, Lucas criticised the federal government’s actions against her. “Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother,” Lucas said in a statement. “I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now.” Lucas has long advocated for the legalisation of marijuana in Virginia, including through legislative efforts. However, prosecutors allege that she and her co-conspirators spent years selling and maintaining illegal quantities of the drug through various businesses and shops. Virginia recently passed a law permitting regulated retail marijuana sales from July 1, 2027. The indictment comes weeks before Election Day, although Lucas is not seeking re-election this year. Her daughter, Lisa Lucas-Burke, who was also charged in the case, is running for City Council in Portsmouth, Virginia. Virginia Democratic Governor Abigail Spanberger said she had reviewed the charging document and maintained that Lucas and her family should be allowed to defend themselves against the allegations. “They deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented,” Spanberger said. She also criticised the timing of the indictment, arguing that it could undermine public confidence in the Justice Department. “The timing of this indictment undermines the U.S. Department of Justice’s previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions — to include indictments or significant investigative steps — close to an election and sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice,” Spanberger said. Earlier this year, FBI agents executed search warrants at two of Lucas’s marijuana shops as part of an investigation that began under former President Joe Biden. According to the indictment, investigators recovered marijuana and firearms from both locations. Lucas, who was elected to the Virginia State Senate in 1991, is also accused of paying $750,000 for a 100 per cent stake in a shell holding company that prosecutors allege was established to help a co-conspirator obtain a state licence to sell marijuana. Prosecutors further allege that Lucas subsequently received what the Justice Department described as a “bribery payment” from the co-conspirator in connection with her efforts. The department also alleged that Lucas “failed to report the interest obtained in this entity on her required Statement of Economic Interests forms” as a legislator. In a statement announcing the charges, the Justice Department alleged that Lucas met with the co-conspirator at her office in the Capitol complex to receive a partial repayment. “Lucas allegedly met with the co-conspirator at her office at the capitol complex to receive a partial repayment and spoke with other officials, including legislators, about the co-conspirator’s qualification for a recreational marijuana license depending on her receipt of a bribery payment from the co-conspirator,” the department said. Investigators also alleged that Lucas spoke with an unidentified co-conspirator by phone in February about obtaining a recreational marijuana licence and sharing the proceeds. “This is our last chance at generational wealth,” investigators quoted Lucas as telling the co-conspirator. “I’ve got too old to not be greedy.” Vanguard News The post 82-yr-old US senator charged with drug trafficking, money laundering appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Many feared trapped as a tall building collapses in Kenya
body:
A multi-story building has collapsed in a busy commercial area of Kenya’s capital, and many people could be trapped beneath the rubble
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Many people were feared trapped as a tall building collapsed Friday in Kenya’s capital, leaving a huge mound of concrete and more than a dozen floors stacked like pancakes, with little space between them.
The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1 p.m. along a busy commercial street in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 upper floors under construction. Rescue operations were complicated, with police firing tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops, as officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams.
The Kenya Red Cross said its teams were on their way and urged people at the site to give responders space to work safely.
There was little in the way of heavy equipment immediately available. Hours later, a group of rescuers in hard hats were using poles stripped from trees to poke at the huge pile of rubble.
One excavator arrived on site and started moving the concrete bound with steel away so that the rescuers might reach the ground-level and basement floors that were said to have been rented out as shops while construction continued on the upper floors.
Residents said some of their loved ones who were trapped had made phone calls calling for help immediately after the collapse, but that their phones later became unreachable.
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi. County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with safety guidelines and construction standards.
