title: Von der Leyen: Attack on civilian vessel off Romanian coast marks another Russia’s escalation in Black Sea
body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has expressed concern over an escalation by Russia in the Black Sea following an attack on a civilian vessel, manned by a Ukrainian and Azerbaijani crew, off the coast of Romania. The incident resulted in the death of one sailor, while three other crew members remain missing.
" Deeply alarmed by yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea. A civilian vessel carrying Ukrainian and Azerbaijani crew has been struck off the coast of Romania. These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen said on X.
She expressed condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased sailor, as well as to the families of the three crew members who remain missing, and thanked the rescue teams involved in the search.
As earlier reported, a merchant vessel flying the flag of the Comoros sank in the Black Sea, approximately 24 km from the port of Constanța (Romania), likely after being struck by a drone.
Coast Guard officials stated that units from the Romanian Ministry of Internal Affairs are participating in a search-and-rescue operation for those who went missing following the incident.
"The merchant vessel sustained severe damage and capsized, creating an imminent risk of sinking. Of the 13 people on board, ten were rescued by another merchant vessel in the area: nine survived, while one person died. Three others remain missing," the Coast Guard representatives stated.

title: Russian troops liberate 13 communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 13 communities in the Kharkov, Dnepropetrovsk and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of October 17-23 in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better positions and established control of the settlements of Palamarevka and Kovalevka in the Kharkov Region through decisive operations. <…> Last week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and liberated the settlement of Alekseyevo-Druzhkovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic. <…> During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Dobropolye, Pervomaiskoye and Sergeyevka in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active operations," the ministry said in a statement.
"During the past week, Battlegroup East units continued advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlements of Omelnik, Timoshevka, Chervony Yar and Mirovka in the Zaporozhye Region and took control of the settlement of Velikomikhailovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region. <…> During the past week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and liberated the settlements of Malokaterinovka and Yulyevka in the Zaporozhye Region," it said.
Russian troops delivered three massive and 11 combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, energy and transport sites over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 17-23, 2026, the Russian Armed Forces delivered three massive and 11 combined strikes, hitting military-industrial enterprises, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, sites producing, assembling and storing medium-and long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, materiel depots, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, the strikes degraded Ukraine’s port infrastructure facilities used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, it said.
"During the week, 14 dry cargo ships and a container ship involved in the delivery of armament, military hardware and dual-use products for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,505 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units have completed the destruction of the surrounded enemy in the northeastern part of the Kharkov Region and continue carrying out measures to eliminate the adversary’s single groups," the ministry said.
Over the week, Battlegroup North units "improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two assault brigades of the Ukrainian army, two territorial defense brigades and a border guard detachment of Ukraine’s Border Guard Service," it said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,505 personnel, seven armored combat vehicles, 124 motor vehicles, two field artillery guns and 10 electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,560 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 19 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, <…> Battlegroup West units inflicted losses on formations of three mechanized brigades, two assault brigades of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,560 personnel, 19 armored combat vehicles, 130 motor vehicles, 12 field artillery guns and seven electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,275 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 16 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup South units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two airmobile brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,275 personnel, 16 armored combat vehicles, 221 motor vehicles, 10 field artillery guns and three electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,405 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 44 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, an assault brigade, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade, five National Guard brigades and the Azov special operations brigade [outlawed as a terrorist group in Russia]," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,405 personnel, 44 armored combat vehicles, 53 motor vehicles, 16 field artillery guns and 15 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,380 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 22 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, three air assault brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,380 personnel, 22 armored combat vehicles, 38 motor vehicles and two field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 215 Ukrainian troops and destroyed four enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 215 [Ukrainian] military personnel, four armored combat vehicles, 127 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and eight electronic warfare stations were destroyed," it said.
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,593 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and seven Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down five guided aerial bombs, three rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, seven Flamingo long-range cruise missiles and 5,593 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet destroyed five Ukrainian naval drones in Black Sea waters over the week, the ministry reported.
"The Black Sea Fleet’s forces destroyed five uncrewed boats of the Ukrainian Navy in Black Sea waters," the ministry said.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 268,828 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,363 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,792 multiple rocket launchers, 36,794 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,380 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

title: Obuasi SHTS Sexual Abuse Allegations: Otiko Djaba urges Vice-President to visit alleged victims
body: Former Minister for Gender, Children and Social Protection Otiko Afisah Djaba has urged Vice-President Prof Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang to visit students allegedly sexually abused at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), saying that calls for the law to take its course are not enough to address their immediate needs. Speaking in an interview with JoyNews about the allegations against the school’s headmaster, Ms Djaba questioned what was being done to protect the affected girls while investigations continued. Her comments follow a statement by the Vice-President describing the allegations as a serious national concern and calling for the law to take its course. Ms Djaba said the Vice-President should demonstrate her commitment to the welfare of the students by engaging directly with them and ensuring they receive the necessary support and protection. “While the law is taking its course, what’s happening to the children?” she asked. “I would have expected by now that she herself would go there,” she added. Ms Djaba said her appeal was not about restricting the Vice-President’s responsibilities to women’s issues because of her gender. Rather, she said, the country’s first female Vice-President had an opportunity to demonstrate leadership on matters affecting women and children. Recalling the Vice-President’s appeal for women’s support during the election campaign, she said the significance of having a woman in the country’s second-highest political office should be reflected in action on issues affecting their welfare. “It’s not about gender boxing,” she said. “Nobody is saying that because you are a woman and you are a vice; only focus on women.” She added: “When you have been given this huge opportunity, to whom much is given, much is expected.” Ms Djaba also questioned the handling of the allegations, arguing that an earlier intervention could have prevented further harm to students. Read also: Let the law take its course in Obuasi SHTS abuse exposé – Vice-President Opoku-Agyemang Referring to April 2025, she said the failure to address the matter decisively at the time had allowed the situation to worsen, with the number of alleged victims reportedly reaching 19. “The law, as we have seen, has failed us. The system has failed the girls,” she said. “If this thing had been addressed in April of 2025, do you think we would be talking about 19 girls? No, it wouldn’t have gotten to that. It wouldn’t have.” She further argued that an earlier intervention by the Vice President could have prevented other girls from allegedly being assaulted. “If she had interfered, intervened in 2025, would we be talking about 19 girls? We would have avoided all these other girls being assaulted,” she said. “And that is my pain,” she added. Ms Djaba also criticised what she considered an inadequate public response from President John Mahama, urging him to speak clearly on the allegations and demonstrate that protecting children and upholding the law take precedence over political considerations. “And the President of Ghana, what has he said? He’s the father of all of us,” she said. Acknowledging that the person at the centre of the allegations was a member of the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC), she said political affiliation should not prevent the President from addressing the matter. “Yes, the person is a member of his party. But even if it is your child who has committed a crime against Ghana, you must speak up and let the people of Ghana know,” she said. “If you spoke, I don’t think the police and these other institutions would be dilly-dallying and fooling around with what they are doing,” she added.

title: Inflation expectations close to two-year highs — Central Bank
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Despite a certain decline in inflation expectations this October, they are close to two-year maximums in recent months, the Bank of Russia said after the Board meeting.
"High inflation expectations impede a slowdown in inflation. Despite a slight decrease in the expectations of households and businesses in October, they have generally remained near two-year highs in recent months. Expectations of financial market participants and analysts have increased," the regulator said.
"According to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace" in the second half of this year, the Central Bank added.
The Bank of Russia made a decision earlier today to keep the key rate at 14% per annum after its Board of Directors’ meeting.

title: Rogers reports Q3 revenue edges higher
body:
TORONTO – Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees.
While Rogers reported a year-over-year increase in overall revenue during its most recent quarter, primarily due to growth in its media division, the company said wireless service revenue decreased one per cent.
During its third quarter, Rogers’ mobile phone average monthly revenue per user was $55.22, down from $56.70 in the same quarter of the prior year.
Chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the “largest impact” to that closely watched figure came from the CRTC’s move in June to prohibit telecoms from charging customers when they activate, change or cancel plans.
“The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday.
“The charge disappeared (due to) the CRTC decision. The costs don’t.”
He said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.”
“We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs, shipping costs, for example … so that effort remains ongoing.”
The CRTC has said the new rules are meant to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected charges.
The regulator is in the midst of a review into whether Rogers, along with rivals Bell Canada and Telus Corp., violated the ban by introducing new fees around the time it took effect.
It said Rogers began charging customers a $40 device setup fee, $25 shipping charge, and an unspecified SIM card fee in mid-June that “would not appear” to qualify for an exemption under the rules for optional services or products that consumers consent to purchase.
Rogers has argued the device setup fee is related to an optional purchase. It also said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation.
Overall, the quarter saw a “less active telecom market,” said Rogers president and CEO Tony Staffieri said, as the company reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $482 million.
“In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” he told analysts.
The company reported 17,000 total mobile phone net subscriber additions, including 6,000 postpaid — those who pay a monthly bill for their wireless services after charges have accumulated. That was down from 62,000 postpaid additions in the same quarter last year.
Rogers’ monthly churn — a measure of those who cancelled their service — for net postpaid mobile subscribers was 1.03 per cent, up from 0.99 per cent during its previous third quarter.
Retail internet net additions totalled 10,000, down from 29,000 a year earlier.
The company said its profit amounted to 88 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.
The result compared with a profit of $5.71 billion or $10.54 per diluted share a year ago when it saw a $5-billion non-cash gain related to its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment and $151-million gain on the redemption of long-term debt.
On an adjusted basis, Rogers said it earned $704 million in net income, or $1.29 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of $1.37 per diluted share a year ago.
Revenue totalled $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year.
“Financial results were in line with our forecast while subscriber growth was a little lighter than our forecast,” said RBC analyst Drew McReynolds in a note.
“We view the results as largely neutral for the shares at current levels.”
Earlier this month, Rogers completed its $4.35-billion purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in MLSE it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts.
Staffieri reiterated Rogers’ plan to sell a minority interest in its consolidated sports, media and entertainment portfolio to third-party investors, adding he remains “bullish about our plan to unlock shareholder value and drive long-term growth.”
Rogers is targeting the first half of 2027 to close that minority interest sale.
“Investor interest in these assets is substantial as sports franchise valuations continue to rise,” Staffieri said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

title: Edo Community Leader Defrauded of N5.4m in Fake Appointment Scam
body: Operatives of the Delta State Police Command have arrested three suspected members of a fraud syndicate for allegedly defrauding a community leader of N5.4 million in the state. The suspects, identified as Aghogho Okpogbodu 51; Moses Exist, 48; and Benjamin Owah 49; were arrested by the police attached to the Effuru Area Command division following an investigation. The command’s spokesperson, Bright Edafe, said preliminary findings revealed that the suspects allegedly used SIM cards purportedly registered under the identities of prominent public officials, including the Secretary to George Akume, the Secretary to the Government of the Federation; Chief Hon. Onoriode Sunday, Director of Protocol to the Governor of Delta State; and Hon. Prince Johnson Erijo, identified as Chief of Staff to the Governor of Delta State, among others. He said the suspects also allegedly exploited a caller-identification application on mobile phones, which displays names associated with incoming telephone numbers, to create the false impression that their calls originated from the officials being impersonated. INEC: Results with discrepancies won’t be uploaded on IREV 11 killed as trailer rams into vehicles in Gombe He said in one of their alleged operations, the suspects impersonated the Director of Protocol to the Governor of Delta State and defrauded a community leader from Otu-Jeremi of ₦5,475,000 million, under the false pretence of facilitating his appointment as President-General of the community. Edafe said a search of the suspects’ premises led to the recovery of seven mobile phones, 17 SIM cards, 12 ATM cards bearing different account holders’ names, one Point-of-Sale (POS) terminal and documents containing financial and identification information belonging to different individuals. He said investigation was ongoing to identify other possible victims and accomplices and bring them to justice.

title: UAE petrol prices expected to rise again in November
body: Petrol prices in the UAE are expected to rise again in November, as the recovery in Middle East oil supplies does not immediately translate into a return to normality for the energy market, according to analysts. Costs at the pump rose for a third consecutive month in October due to lingering uncertainty around a potential US-Iran truce . At present, Super 98, Special 95, E-Plus 91 and diesel cost Dh4.40 ($1.20), Dh4.28 ($1.17), Dh4.21 ($1.15) and Dh4.80 ($1.31) per litre, respectively – up by more than 70 per cent since March, the first full month of the war in Iran. They are still significantly lower compared to markets such as Britain. The Petrol Prices UK website shows that this week unleaded petrol and diesel cost an average of £1.75 (Dh8.61) and £1.99 (Dh9.79) per litre, respectively. In the US, petrol prices, which vary by state, are mostly higher than in the UAE. AAA Gas Prices shows that petrol ranges from $4.29 to $5.20 per gallon, which is equivalent to $1.13 to $1.37 when converted to litres. Diesel is at $6.32 per gallon, or $1.67 per litre – markedly higher than in the Emirates. Oil prices also recorded a sharp rise this month, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia, causing crude to hit five-month highs this week . On Friday, Brent was trading 1.65 per cent higher to hit $115 a barrel at 5.26pm UAE time, while West Texas Intermediate climbed 1.89 per cent to $101.30 a barrel. With Brent this month exceeding September's peak, “the risk of another increase in UAE petrol prices for November is elevated”, said Jordan Lawrence, chief executive and co-founder of London-based financial services firm Damisa. “October’s fuel rates already rose significantly, and the committee’s end-of-month review will reflect the full month’s international averages, refined-product prices and costs,” Mr Lawrence told The National . Oil movements across the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, are gradually picking up, according to ship tracking data. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week that up to 14 million barrels of oil a day were moving through the strait, with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels. However, while October has shown a recovery in Middle East oil exports, that does not necessarily mean the market has returned to normal, said George Pavel, general manager at Naga.com Middle East, a capital markets firm operating in Abu Dhabi's ADGM. “Ongoing threats to shipping and persistent uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz continue to support prices. The key change is that the market is increasingly pricing the risk of further disruptions, instead of simply assessing current production and export volumes,” he told The National. “ Even when supply flows recover, the cost and reliability of transporting crude remain important constraints … if exports remain resilient and diplomatic progress reduces the threat to shipping, prices could retreat quickly. “The next decisive factor will be whether October's security risks translate into lasting physical supply losses.” Ahmad Assiri, a research strategist at financial services firm Pepperstone, noted that even if barrels continue reaching markets through the Strait of Hormuz, uncertainty over the reliability of future deliveries gives buyers a reason to pay a significant premium for now. “Many buyers have become price-insensitive due to elevated uncertainty … a diplomatic breakthrough could provide some ease and a pullback,” he told The National . “However, a sustained decline would require confidence that infrastructure and shipping routes can operate securely, which is a hard thing to see in the current environment,” he said. “October has strengthened the conviction that the geopolitical premium will be persistent, and this in turn makes the eventual growth and inflation consequences more concerning.”

title: Tselliny HIMOYA Exhibition: Women’s Memory, Protective Amulets, and Colonial Legacies
body: Kazakh protective amulets incorporating family photographs are among the works on display at HIMOYA: Matrilineal Energies, Oracular Kin at the Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture in Almaty. Elsewhere, a pregnant bird-woman stands at the boundary between life and death. Artists from Central Asia and beyond explore how inherited beliefs and women’s experiences help preserve cultural identity. The exhibition opened on October 15, 2026, and runs through April 4, 2027. It features more than 20 artists and is curated by Natasha Ginwala, who has previously worked on international projects, including the Gwangju and Sharjah biennials. From Natasha Ginwala’s personal archive. The title HIMOYA evokes protection across several linguistic traditions. In the participating artists’ works, that includes preserving ancestral memory. Speaking at the center, Alima Kairat, Tselinny’s artistic director, said the exhibition’s concept had developed over several years. “For Tselinny, HIMOYA is the culmination of a conversation that began in 2021. We gradually explored questions of maternal memory, rituals, protection, inherited ideas about shame, and care. These themes are deeply rooted in life in Kazakhstan and Central Asia, where ancestral knowledge continues to influence the present and helps us imagine the future in new ways,” she said. Female Figures and Ancestral Memory Ginwala’s curatorial concept centers on women’s experiences and knowledge passed down through generations. The artists draw on folk narratives and religious practices, including pre-Islamic steppe beliefs, to reconsider ideas about women’s roles and power. “During conversations with the artists as we prepared the project, different female figures emerged – nurturing and powerful figures, as well as ‘monstrous’ beings from folk tales, steppe mythology, and pre-Islamic cosmologies,” Ginwala said. In Kazakh tradition, genealogy is closely linked to the concept of zheti ata , the knowledge of seven generations of ancestors on the paternal side. The custom also served as the basis for prohibitions on marriage between close relatives. HIMOYA turns to another line of inheritance: the maternal one. The grandmother holds a particularly important place as a guardian of family memory. This theme intersects with the history of colonial and Soviet pressure on local beliefs. The artists explore how traditions once dismissed as backward or superstitious have survived through family practices and acquired new meanings in contemporary art. The Bird-Woman Between Two Worlds One of the exhibition’s central works is Gatekeeper by Rajni Perera, an artist born in Sri Lanka and based in Toronto. Her work draws on South Asian folklore and fantasy to explore migration and motherhood, including questions of reproductive rights. “Gatekeeper” by Rajni Perera. Image: Theo Frost. The life-size sculpture was first presented at the 2025 Sharjah Biennial in the United Arab Emirates. It depicts a pregnant woman with features of a hornbill and a crow. Its surface is decorated with motifs inspired by azulejos, painted ceramic tiles widely associated with Portugal and shaped by Islamic decorative traditions. “When I was creating this figure, I was thinking about the umbilical cord because she is pregnant. She seems to pull life out of nonexistence and into being. She is a kind of superheroine, a goddess standing at the boundary between life and its absence,” Perera explained. Through the hornbill, the artist explores birth and motherhood, while the crow represents ancestral memory. Water is another important element. When the installation was shown in Sharjah, it stood on the grounds of a former hospital. Wells at the site had once supplied water to the maternity ward. Perera saw this coincidence as adding another layer of meaning to her work. Prayer Beads and the Colonial Gaze Sudanese artist Ahmed Umar, who lives in Norway, explores tensions between religious traditions and personal faith. “Glowing Phalanges” by Ahmed Umar. Image: Max Belech. His series, Glowing Phalanges, grew out of a memory from his school years in Mecca. “Its story began at school in Mecca, when a teacher told us that we should never use prayer beads to count our prayers. Instead, we should use our phalanges, or finger bones, because Allah would reward us by making them glow on Judgment Day,” Umar recalled. The teacher’s instructions conflicted with the artist’s family traditions in Sudan. His relatives used large prayer beads associated with Sufism, a mystical tradition within Islam. Such beads can be used during dhikr , the repeated recitation of God’s names and devotional phrases. Umar transformed this contradiction into an exploration of religious authority and an individual’s right to determine the form of their own spiritual practice. In other works, the artist uses souvenirs and objects made from animal remains collected during his years in Norway. He transforms them into objects resembling prayer beads and talismans, drawing attention to colonial attitudes toward nature and culture. Another installation focuses on Sudanese amulets that were described as inauthentic in British colonial accounts. Beneath an enormous suspended amulet, visitors hear sounds from the artist’s family mosque, spanning the day from fajr, the obligatory dawn prayer, to isha , the night prayer. The work contrasts colonial judgments about these objects with the religious experiences of the people for whom they held spiritual significance. Tumar as Resistance to Imposed Gender Roles Kazakh artist Radina Yasueva draws on the tumar, a traditional protective amulet intended to ward off misfortune and evil forces. Such amulets were made from leather, fabric, or metal, often in a triangular shape. They could contain written prayers or other objects believed to offer protection. Tumars are found in the traditions of various Central Asian peoples. “The Unconquered” series by Radina Yassuyeva. Image: Max Belech. For the exhibition, Yassuyeva created the series Tumar Power (2026), continuing her exploration of themes introduced in The Unconquered. In that earlier project, she examined women’s resistance to prescribed family roles. “For me, the tumar is more than an amulet that protects against the unseen. It is a form of memory in which protection takes on a physical body. At the heart of my Tumar Power are phallic images that were once part of the visual language of The Unconquered series. Now, they return transformed: complex, intricately beaded, restored, and assembled as if from fragments of personal and collective memory. Woven into them are photographs of my parents, my grandmothers, and myself. The faces of those who lived before me become part of my own talisman,” Yassuyeva said. Her work also addresses motherhood and the figure of the female horse rider, as well as bride kidnapping. Known in Kazakhstan as alyp qashu , bride kidnapping can describe an arrangement agreed upon by a couple or the forcible abduction of a woman for marriage. Coercive abduction has become a focus of criticism in contemporary art and public debate. “I think of protection as an inheritance passed down through the maternal line. It is an attempt to give form to the invisible power of a mother’s love – a love that outlasts time, distance, and life itself. Protection here does not mean a promise that misfortune will never touch us. It is the presence of those who love us, those who lived before us, and those whose strength we carry forward,” Yassuyeva said. In the works presented at HIMOYA, protective amulets, devotional objects, and mythological figures become more than elements of traditional heritage. Through them, the artists examine women’s place in society, the right to define one’s own identity, and ways of preserving memory in the aftermath of colonial and ideological pressure.

title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet set to continue
body:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police is set to resume this afternoon after adjourning early on Thursday.
The inquest into the death of 29-year-old Regis Korchinski-Paquet was paused roughly an hour into Thursday’s proceedings after her mother made a new allegation against police.
Claudette Beals testified that she saw officers push her daughter toward the balcony.
The presiding coroner, Dr. David Cameron, told jurors Thursday counsel were strategizing on how to best have them hear evidence related to the circumstances of Korchinski-Paquet’s death “in a clear and fair manner.”
As the inquest reconvened this morning, Cameron said counsel had worked “very late into the evening to reach a consensus on how to proceed forward” but weren’t “quite there yet.”
He encouraged jurors to review and discuss the evidence until 3 p.m., when he would provide an update on the situation.
Beals is expected to continue her testimony when the inquest begins hearing evidence again.
Earlier Thursday, she said that the family struggled at times to deal with Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures and would have benefited from support and education regarding epilepsy.
The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet experienced seizures from epilepsy and had two on May 27, 2020, the day she died.
Her seizures were often followed by periods of erratic and aggressive behaviour, the inquest has heard.

title: Russia and Ukraine Exchange 540 POWs
body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged 270 prisoners of war each in the second consecutive repatriation effort in as many days, the Russian Defense Ministry said Friday.
“On Oct. 23, 270 Russian servicemen were returned from territory controlled by the Kyiv regime,” the military said. “In exchange, 270 POWs of the Ukrainian armed forces were handed over.”
The swap took place at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus, according to Belarusian state media.
While in Belarus, the Russian soldiers are being provided with mental health and medical support, after which they will return to Russia for further treatment. Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova is accompanying them, the Defense Ministry said.
On her Telegram channel, Lantratova said that 12 families were also reunited across the border, with seven civilians returning to Russia and seven others departing for Ukraine. She did not mention the POW exchange.
Lantratova said the family reunification was a joint effort with her Ukrainian colleague Dmytro Lubinets. She also thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for helping mediate the initiative.
Friday’s exchange comes a day after Russia and Ukraine repatriated the remains of 277 fallen soldiers at the same Belarusian border crossing.

title: Kazakhstan and China Plan Cross-Border Driverless Truck Trials
body: Driverless trucks could eventually carry freight between Kazakhstan and China, with the two countries planning to test them on international routes. The Kazakhstan Road Research Institute (KazdorNII) and Chinese technology company China TransInfo Group signed an agreement in Astana on October 16 to develop the trials and establish a joint center for autonomous transport. The partners plan to establish a testing ground and introduce systems that can weigh trucks while they are moving. They are also considering a joint center to coordinate transport operations and share data. KazdorNII will work to adapt the Chinese company’s technologies to Kazakhstan’s roads and technical requirements. At the NEW SILK WAY transport forum in Astana, China TransInfo Group signed a separate memorandum with Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport on cooperation in autonomous vehicle technologies. Kazakhstan has already conducted a similar trial with Russia. In May 2026, two Russian-made KamAZ trucks traveled in opposite directions between Astana and Moscow, crossing the international border. However, only parts of the roughly 3,000-kilometer journey were completed autonomously. Kazakhstan and China also launched the Smart Customs project at the Bakhty–Pokitu border crossing in 2025, with plans to use driverless electric shuttles to transport cargo between the two countries. The new initiative envisages testing autonomous trucks on an international road route rather than limiting their operation to border infrastructure. Separately, Kazakhstan plans to begin producing Chinese SITRAK autonomous semi-trucks by 2028, as The Times of Central Asia previously reported .

title: Ruble slowing down amid Russian regulator’s decision to keep key rate
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The ruble slowed down in its growth amid the decision of the Bank of Russia to keep the key rate at 14% per annum, according to the trading platform.
The yuan fell to 12.037 rubles (down 12.8 kopecks) before the release of the regulator’s decision but slowed down in the decline to 12.05 rubles (minus 11.45 kopecks).
The Russian stock indices also dropped against such a background. The MOEX Russia Index lost 0.45% to 2,418.68 points. The RTS Index declined by 0.5% to 939.21 points.

title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really? In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come. Check out our stories on how they all stacked up . Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned! In the biotech world, you can’t see everything —Jessica Hamzelou Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything. The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science . This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. Help choose our next Roundtables topic Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about? Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs Warhound says the dogs will detect explosives and protect troops. ( Wired $) + It’s raised $200 million from investors, including Sequoia. ( TechCrunch ) + Colossal Biosciences will help clone and gene-edit the dogs. ( Bloomberg $) + The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Donald Trump says Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s Starlink access But Zelensky says Starlink speeds remained capped. ( Reuters $) + Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift the speed limits. ( WSJ $) 3 The newly disclosed PHP flaw is yet to yield successful attacks Experts say the vulnerabilities are harder to exploit than expected. ( NBC News ) + Officials urged patches after the flaws forced websites offline worldwide . ( BBC ) + But publicly disclosed fixes can help hackers. ( The Economist $) 4 Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death by 42% The vaccine reduced melanoma patients’ risk of recurrence. ( Ars Technica ) + Federal health agencies are abandoning mRNA. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 A powerful new gene editor has reached its first human patient The prime editing technique rewrites DNA in liver cells. ( Nature ) + Companies are planning gene-edited babies. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Google will pay customers to free up power for data centers Its virtual power plant will reward people for adjusting energy usage. ( NYT $) + It’s also illegally felled 250,000 trees in Finland for a data center. ( Guardian ) 7 Dutch spies reportedly hacked Jared Kushner’s iPhone The report alleges financial links to foreign officials. ( Vanity Fair $) 8 Fossil fuels may have stopped the next ice age Modern warming reversed 2,000 years of ice growth. ( Wired $) 9 Scientists have recreated solar flares to explain the corona’s mystery They hope to explain why it’s so hot. ( New Scientist $) 10 A road trip with America’s cheapest EV shows charging is much improved Fast chargers kept the journey manageable despite sparse coverage. ( WSJ $) + And bigger EVs aren’t always better. ( MIT Technology Review ) Quote of the day “If anything happens to this guy, that’s just it. Everyone is screwed.” —Software developer Ian Landsman says on X that volunteer Ondřej Surý’s work on patching PHP vulnerabilities makes him an unsung hero of the entire internet. One more thing STUART BRADFORD How sounds can turn us on to the wonders of the universe For decades, astronomy has relied on visual information to make sense of the cosmos: images, charts, and graphs. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe. Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education. Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing . —Corey S. Powell We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A team of domino experts broke a Guinness World Record with a 29,193-piece 3D pyramid. + Scientists suspect that pigeons sense Earth’s magnetic fields using specialized immune cells in their livers . + See inside cells like never before with these vivid microscopic images from the Nikon Small World competitions. + Cuddly capybaras and playful penguins joined 10,000 animals on the scales for London Zoo’s annual weigh-in .

title: UAE art guide: 15 exhibitions to see, from Indian Ocean history at Louvre Abu Dhabi to Paul Guiragossian
body: Galleries and institutions across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah are presenting a diverse programme of exhibitions as the UAE's autumn art season gathers pace. Current highlights include Provisional Sanctuaries at Tashkeel, where Malaysian artist Shamin Sharum explores the overlooked prayer spaces that offer a sense of belonging in the UAE; Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve at NYU Abu Dhabi, which brings together eight women artists using ceramics to explore emotion and lived experience; and Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean at Louvre Abu Dhabi, tracing 1,000 years of maritime trade and cultural exchange. Elsewhere, exhibitions examine memory, migration, identity and environmental change, with works spanning painting, photography, sculpture, textiles and moving image. Here are 15 exhibitions to see across the UAE. 1. Unseen Script at Rizq Art Initiative In Unseen Script , curated by Meena Vari, works by 10 artists explore the patterns people form through repetition, from familiar journeys and domestic objects to changing landscapes and gestures that become so ingrained they often go unnoticed. The exhibition brings together art by Najat Makki, Nujoom Alghanem, Nasir Nasrallah, Abdulla PA, Ana Escobar Saavedra, Fadi Balhawan, Ismail Al Rifai, Joanna Barakat, Neveen Abu Samra and Simrin Mehra Agarwal. Across painting, sculpture, assemblage and mixed media, the artists return to recurring subjects within their practices, revealing how personal habits and ways of seeing become a kind of visual script. Several works draw on the relationship between people and their surroundings. Abdulla reflects on abandoned homes and the ways nature reclaims human-made spaces, while Saavedra transforms seashells into delicate assemblages. Nasrallah draws on memories of his grandfather’s antique shop, Makki extends her abstract practice into steel and Alghanem examines the cityscape as a contemporary horizon. While the exhibition touches on the way technology can identify and predict human patterns, its focus remains on subjective experience, asking what memory, consciousness and observation can reveal that data cannot. Until October 28; Abu Dhabi 2. Taking Form at The Third Line Taking Form is Rana Begum’s fifth solo exhibition at The Third Line, bringing together new works across textile, linen, wood and paper that continue her exploration of light, colour, geometry and material. Large wool tapestries suspended from the ceiling form the centre of the exhibition. Woven with geometric patterns, their appearance shifts as visitors move around them. Elsewhere, diluted acrylic has seeped into linen, while smaller works on paper and wooden panels explore interactions between colour and surface. The exhibition introduces a greater sense of softness to Begum’s practice while retaining the abstraction and geometric structures that have long shaped her work. Until November 10; Dubai 3 & 4. Between Land and Sea, and Between a Fold and a Memory at Leila Heller Gallery Two exhibitions at Leila Heller Gallery consider Emirati identity and heritage through the work of Azza Al Qubaisi and Karima Al Shomely. Al Qubaisi’s Between Land and Sea, curated by Aysha Al Hemeiri, surveys a multidisciplinary practice spanning intimate jewellery and large-scale public works. Her use of natural resources and materials connects the UAE’s desert and coastal environments with ideas of memory, identity and place. In Between a Fold and a Memory, Al Shomely turns to the clothing, textiles and objects associated with Emirati women. Photography, sculpture, textile and video explore how materials such as the burqa and traditional fabrics can carry memories of labour, social change and cultural knowledge across generations. Until November 10; Dubai 5. Sojourner: The Difference is the Same at Efie Gallery Kenyan artist Maggie Otieno transforms reclaimed materials into vessels of memory in Sojourner: The Difference is the Same, her first solo exhibition with Efie Gallery. Otieno’s practice has centred on distressed and discarded materials for almost three decades. The exhibition includes works made from 150-year-old railway sleepers, whose histories are tied to East Africa’s colonial railway network, alongside sculptures incorporating fragments of wooden canoes produced during a residency at El Anatsui Studio in Ghana. By cutting, assembling and reconfiguring these materials, Otieno shifts objects once associated with movement and infrastructure into forms concerned with stillness, memory and passage. Until November 13; Dubai 6. The Horizon We Inherit at Iris Projects Emirati artist Eman Al Hashemi examines the changing rhythms of urban life in the UAE in The Horizon We Inherit, her first solo exhibition with Iris Projects. Working across ceramics, printmaking and mixed media, she considers how cities shape attention, memory and everyday routines. The sun, street lights, buildings and roundabouts recur throughout the works, turning familiar features of the UAE cityscape into forms that can appear both recognisable and strange. Al Hashemi is particularly interested in the routes people repeatedly travel and the traces left behind as places are altered through construction and redevelopment. Rather than treating the built environment as a backdrop, the exhibition considers it as an active force in daily life and asks what remains when familiar places survive only through photographs, maps, memories or repeatedly travelled routes. September 26 to November 26; Abu Dhabi 7 . Provisional Sanctuaries at Tashkeel Dubai-based Malaysian artist Shamin Sharum explores the overlooked prayer spaces found across the UAE in Provisional Sanctuaries , his solo exhibition at Tashkeel. Drawing on the small, often temporary musollas established in warehouses, industrial areas and workplaces, the exhibition examines how modest architecture can provide a sense of familiarity and belonging in a city shaped by migration. The exhibition grew from Sharum's experience of encountering a makeshift prayer room shortly after moving to Dubai. Working across painting, drawing, architectural models and axonometric studies, he reconstructs these spaces through memory, focusing on improvised minarets, hand-painted signs, prayer mats and other details that reflect the communities using them. Trained as an architect, Sharum considers how temporary structures can acquire lasting emotional significance through shared rituals and everyday use. One model recalls a prayer space he encountered during his first days in Dubai that has since been demolished, turning an architectural study into an act of remembrance. Developed following his participation in Tashkeel's Critical Practice Programme, the exhibition connects the impermanence of these spaces with wider experiences of displacement, identity and belonging. Until November 27; Dubai 8. Vantage Point 13 at Sharjah Art Foundation Vantage Point 13 marks a new chapter for Sharjah Art Foundation's long-running photography platform as it moves into the institution's dedicated photography gallery. Selected through an international open call, six artists present commissioned photographic series developed with the foundation's curatorial and production support. The exhibition features work by Adam Rouhana, Guanyu Xu, Latifa AlBokhari, Luisa Dorr, Maheder Haileselassie and Sathish Kumar. Together, their projects demonstrate the breadth of contemporary photography, reflecting the programme's evolution from a platform for UAE-based photographers into an international exhibition embracing diverse approaches. Introduced in 2013, Vantage Point has become one of the UAE's key photography initiatives. This edition also reflects the foundation's expanded commitment to supporting new work, with participating artists receiving production funding to create original projects specifically for the exhibition. Until November 29; Sharjah 9 . Fellow Travellers at Tabari Fellow Travellers brings together six artists whose practices span Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas, exploring themes of movement, memory, kinship and cultural exchange. Conceived and curated by artist, author and cultural historian Professor Omar Kholeif, the exhibition draws on nearly two decades of research, writing and personal relationships with artists. The exhibition features works by Sonia Balassanian, Jai Chuhan, Luísa Correia Pereira, Lalitha Lajmi, Irene Scheinmann and Kholeif himself. Bringing together landmark pieces and rarely seen works, it traces artistic journeys across different geographies, considering how experiences of migration, cultural encounters and personal histories shape creative expression. Accompanied by a limited-edition publication featuring original poetry and a curatorial essay, the exhibition also reflects Kholeif's longstanding interest in the relationships between artists and the connections that emerge across generations and borders. Until November 30; Dubai 10. Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve at NYU Abu Dhabi Project Space Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve brings together eight UAE-based women artists whose practices are rooted in the Global South, exploring how ceramics can give physical form to emotions and experiences that are difficult to express through words. Curated by Shafeena Yusuff Ali, founder and executive director of Rizq Art Initiative, the exhibition examines the relationship between the body, clay and emotional expression. The exhibition features sculptures by Nujoom Alghanem, Mirna Bamieh, Moza Al Falasi, Malavika, Parneet Pahwa, Zahra Shafie, Laiba Sherin and Haseena Suresh. Working on an intimate, domestic scale, the artists use processes of pressing, building, breaking and firing clay to explore memory, grief and lived experience. Presented at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery's Project Space, the exhibition also considers the long-standing relationship between ceramics, women's labour and practices of care. By focusing on the physical act of making, it positions clay as a medium through which personal experiences and emotions can take shape. October 22 to December 13; Abu Dhabi 11. The Sky Held It, The Earth Remembered at Ishara Art Foundation The exhibition brings together works by Shahana Rajani, Rohini Devasher and Sarker Protick to explore how land, water and the cosmos can act as archives of memory and history. Through photography, moving image and installation, the exhibition considers how ecological change and human intervention leave traces on the environment that can persist across generations. Rajani’s three-channel film Lines That World a River focuses on communities displaced from the Indus Delta, where paintings and murals reconstruct villages submerged following the construction of dams and barrages. Devasher turns towards the cosmos with Latent Fields , monumental silk panels inspired by sunspots and other solar phenomena, while Protick’s Dhaka 1217 documents 15 years of transformation around the neighbourhood in Dhaka where he was born and continues to live. Drawing together perspectives from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, the exhibition considers ecological decline across national borders, and the ways landscapes can preserve histories of displacement, destruction and resilience. Until December 15; Dubai 12. Revelation at 421 Arts Campus Emirati artist Juma Al Haj explores seclusion, reflection and personal transformation in Revelation, his first institutional solo exhibition. Developed through 421 Arts Campus's Artistic Development Programme, it brings together painting, engraved glass, text, light, shadow and installation to consider how moments of uncertainty can lead to greater self-understanding. The exhibition unfolds as a physical journey, beginning with Balaa , a painting concerned with trials and the ways people measure their lives, and Traces , a series of engraved glass panels whose inscriptions shift with light and shadow. It culminates in Hijr , a darkened, carpeted space centred on a water feature, where visitors remove their shoes and are encouraged to slow down and contemplate. Al Haj's approach draws on journaling, philosophy and spiritual texts, extending the layered marks of his paintings into an environment visitors can move through. Rather than presenting revelation as a final answer, the exhibition treats it as one stage in an continuing process of reflection and discovery. Until January 10, 2027; Abu Dhabi 13. Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art celebrates the centenary of the Lebanese artist's birth, bringing together significant works from his estate at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation in Abu Dhabi. Developed in collaboration with the Paul Guiragossian Foundation, the exhibition offers an overview of the life and legacy of one of the leading figures of modern Lebanese and Middle Eastern art. Known for his expressive use of colour and distinctive depictions of the human figure, Guiragossian (1926–1993) developed a visual language concerned with family, identity and the human condition. His paintings frequently explored themes of displacement, belonging and everyday life, reflecting both personal experiences and the wider history of the region. Drawing primarily on works from the artist's estate, the exhibition traces the development of his practice and considers his enduring influence on modern Arab art. October 17 to January 17, 2027; Abu Dhabi 14. Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean at Louvre Abu Dhabi Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean explores 1,000 years of maritime trade and cultural exchange, tracing the routes that connected communities across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, India, China and South-East Asia. Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders. The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's pearl trade and the movement of spices, precious stones, textiles and religious artefacts. Highlights include six detailed models of historic vessels, objects recovered from shipwrecks, ancient navigational instruments and a third-century Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan. Through specially created maps and immersive displays, the exhibition examines how sailors navigated using stars and coastal landmarks, while merchants and pilgrims carried goods, beliefs and artistic traditions between distant societies. Its historical narrative concludes in the 17th century, drawing attention to the extensive trading networks that existed before European powers came to dominate Indian Ocean commerce. Until February 14, 2027; Abu Dhabi 15. A Board Game Adventure at Louvre Abu Dhabi A Board Game Adventure transforms Louvre Abu Dhabi into a giant playground, using some of the world's oldest games to explore how people have connected across cultures for thousands of years. Designed for children but engaging for all ages, the exhibition traces the journey of games including chess, Mancala, Ludo and Carrom as they travelled between ancient civilisations and evolved into the games still played today. The exhibition combines immersive installations with rare artefacts borrowed from international museums, including some of the earliest known board game objects from ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Iran and India. Highlights include centuries-old chess pieces carved from ivory and rock crystal, engraved backgammon pieces, ancient six-sided dice and one of the earliest known predecessors of Ludo. Interactive displays encourage visitors to solve puzzles, challenge artificial intelligence, play on oversized game boards and discover how strategy, chance and storytelling have always been part of human play. Throughout the exhibition, historical figures ranging from Queen Nefertari and Achilles to samurai Hatakeyama Shigetada are reimagined through playful “player profiles”, linking games to the personalities and cultures that shaped them. Rather than presenting games as simple entertainment, A Board Game Adventure reveals them as cultural objects that have crossed borders, adapted to societies and brought people together for millennia. Until April 25, 2027

title: Show HN: I gave my AI eyes for YouTube tutorials
body:
When you ask ChatGPT or Claude about a YouTube video, it only reads the spoken transcript—it cannot see the screen. FrameCap snaps the key visual moments so your free AI can see the exact settings, recipes, formulas, and slides.
FrameCap (also written Frame Cap) is a free Chrome extension that lets AI "watch" a YouTube video. One click captures what is said (a timestamped transcript from the video's captions) and what is shown (sharp frames of the screen, each with a timestamp). It then sends both to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity as a PDF, or downloads them as a ZIP for AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Everything runs inside your browser, with no account and no API key.
Click the FrameCap button on any YouTube video—whether it's an Excel guide, terminal commands, or deeply technical work.
FrameCap captures a sharp frame every few seconds (you choose 1 to 30) and reads the captions as a timestamped transcript, right inside your browser.
ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity opens with a PDF of the frames and a ready prompt. Or download a ZIP for Claude Code, Codex or Cursor.
When someone in a video says "click right here," regular AI has no idea where "here" is. See the difference:
Most tutorials are 20 minutes of talking and 5 seconds of the thing you actually need. Instead of squinting and pausing, FrameCap lets your AI look at the screen and give you the answer right away.
The person types a formula on screen and hits Enter, but never reads out the brackets, commas, or symbols out loud.
FrameCap shows your AI the screen, so it reads the exact line directly off the video for you.
No manual downloading, no screenshots, and no file uploads. FrameCap bridges YouTube directly to your favorite AI.
FrameCap captures the important moments from the video and links them with the speaker's words. You click once, and your AI opens with the complete picture ready to chat.
