title: New $8 Million Central Asia Conservation Program to Protect Rare Wildlife
body: Around 100 grants will be made available to local conservation groups under a new five-year program to protect threatened wildlife in the Pamir and Tien Shan mountains. The initiative will cover mountain ecosystems across five Central Asian countries, running from 2026 to 2031. The program has a budget of up to $8 million, with the European Union providing the majority of funding through the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF). The British conservation organization Fauna & Flora will coordinate activities in the region, overseeing grants, providing technical assistance, and helping local organizations develop and manage conservation projects. The Pamir and Tien Shan mountains form one of the world’s biodiversity hotspots — areas with high concentrations of unique species threatened with extinction. The mountain region covers approximately 860,000 square kilometers across parts of seven countries, including western China and northeastern Afghanistan. The region is home to Menzbier’s marmot, the steppe eagle, the Semirechensk salamander, and other rare animals. More than 20 regionally threatened tulip species also grow in these mountains. The main threats to these ecosystems include habitat loss and fragmentation, poaching, overgrazing, and climate change. Habitat fragmentation is particularly dangerous for mountain wildlife, as roads, economic activities, and other barriers make it harder for animals to move between populations. The program will fund local conservation projects, with particular emphasis on protecting endangered species and maintaining wildlife corridors. Around 100 grants are planned, with recipients also receiving training and technical support. The aim is to enable local organizations to continue managing conservation projects independently after international funding ends. This is the second phase of CEPF investment in Central Asia’s mountain ecosystems. During the previous phase, from 2019 to 2025, the fund allocated approximately $7.4 million to conservation projects. The new program will run for another five years. One of the region’s most prominent conservation initiatives focuses on the snow leopard. In April 2025, Kyrgyzstan established the Ak Ilbirs ecological corridor, covering more than 792,000 hectares. It connects Khan-Tengri Nature Park, the Sarychat-Ertash Nature Reserve, and the Naryn Nature Reserve, helping maintain connections between habitats used by rare wildlife. The Times of Central Asia previously reported on the project .

title: At least seven killed in shooting at church in Jordan's Karak province
body: At least seven people were killed when unknown gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan's Karak province on Friday, a relative of one of the deceased told The National . Petra News Agency confirmed details of the shooting and said casualties were reported. It took place at a funeral for a woman in Hamoud, a Christian village north of Karak. Two gunmen in a vehicle fired at the mourners and fled, according to the relative. State-owned broadcaster Al Mamlaka said at least seven people had been killed and more than 10 wounded. Live footage showed security personnel deployed at the scene. Karak is about 100 kilometres away from the capital, Amman.

title: Trump asserts his right to seek third presidential term
body:
WASHINGTON, October 23. /TASS/. Donald Trump said he has the right to run for a third term as US president because the 2020 election he lost to Joe Biden was allegedly fraudulent.
"I think I have the right to run again because they cheated. They rigged the election," he said, addressing a GOP midterm rally in Iowa.
However, the US leader acknowledged that he may be barred by law from running again. "I'm not 100% sure, but I think the law says that I'm not allowed to run again. It says something to the effect that under no circumstances and for any reason will you even consider thinking about running for president," Trump noted.
By law, Trump’s second term as president is scheduled to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, adopted in 1951, limits a president’s tenure to two terms. Nevertheless, the current US leader has repeatedly raised the possibility of seeking re-election for a third term. Steve Bannon, the president’s former key political strategist, also argued last fall that Trump should serve as president again.
Trump won the election for the second time in November 2024 when he defeated Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris. He previously led the US administration from 2017 to 2021.

title: Culture Ministry in talks with EBRD on completing construction of Karpenko-Kary University building on Lvivska Square in Kyiv – Berezhna
body:
The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine is in discussions with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) regarding the completion of a building for the Karpenko-Kary Kyiv National University of Theatre, Cinema and Television on Lvivska Square in Kyiv, as well as the development of a hotel within the Hetman’s Inn (Hetmanskyi Zayizd) structure near Pidhirtsi Castle in Lviv region, announced Tetiana Berezhna, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture.
"Our cooperation with the EBRD is a highly pragmatic initiative. Through it, we are demonstrating to the bank’s clients—our international partners—that Ukrainian cultural heritage (such as the unfinished Karpenko-Kary University building, you have all seen this large structure on Lvivska Square) represents a national cultural heritage asset that is ripe for investment and can be transformed into a culturally attractive destination," Berezhna stated at the 10th Ukrainian Women’s Congress.
In this same context, she also mentioned the Hetman’s Inn near Pidhirtsi Castle in Lviv region.
"Could it not become a hotel that attracts a great number of tourists and visitors? Certainly, it could. That is what we are discussing with the EBRD," the Deputy Prime Minister added.

title: CPA marks 20 years without consumer protection law in Ghana, urges passage of bill by December
body: The Consumer Protection Agency (CPA) has renewed calls on the President and Parliament to pass Ghana’s long-awaited Consumer Protection Bill before the end of 2026, warning that the absence of a comprehensive law continues to leave consumers vulnerable to unfair business practices, substandard products and poor services. In a statement issued on Friday, October 23, to mark its 20th anniversary, the agency described the failure to enact the legislation, first drafted in 2006, as the country’s biggest setback in protecting consumer rights. The CPA said the bill remained at the Ministry of Trade and Industry despite years of advocacy, petitions, national forums and stakeholder engagements aimed at securing its passage. It warned that the lack of a dedicated legal framework had become particularly concerning amid the growth of e-commerce and the circulation of fake, unregistered and inferior products on the Ghanaian market. The agency called for the passage of the bill and the establishment of a well-funded Consumer Protection Authority with the mandate and resources to enforce consumer rights and hold businesses accountable. Two decades of consumer advocacy Founded and funded by Kofi Kapito in 2006, the CPA was launched by the late Vice-President Alhaji Aliu Mahama to provide consumers with a platform to seek redress over goods and services. Over the past two decades, the agency has campaigned against poor telecommunications services, called for sanctions against underperforming operators and advocated the use of fines imposed on them to fund consumer education. It also organised what it described as Ghana’s first Off Phone Day protests against telecommunications companies over poor service delivery. In the retail sector, the CPA campaigned against the use of “olonka” and other unapproved measuring containers in markets, advocating certified weighing scales to protect consumers from unfair measurements. The agency said it had also worked with regulatory bodies, including the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA), Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) and Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC), on initiatives to improve product safety and consumer welfare. Over four million fake diapers removed from market The CPA cited its interventions against fake and unregistered baby diapers as one of its notable achievements, claiming that more than four million pieces had been removed from the Ghanaian market through enforcement activities. It also highlighted its involvement in addressing complaints about sanitary towels, saying the re-testing of registered products confirmed that they were safe for use. The agency further listed its advocacy for reductions in electricity tariffs among its efforts to ease the burden on consumers. It said fake, unregistered and substandard products continued to pose health and financial risks while threatening the survival of locally manufactured goods. The CPA disclosed that it was collaborating with the Ministry of Finance and other stakeholders to develop a policy to address the influx of such products into the country. Agency establishes mediation and arbitration centre The CPA identified its contribution to making consumer protection a national issue as one of its major achievements, noting that media organisations and other institutions increasingly seek its assistance in resolving consumer complaints. It also announced the establishment of what it describes as Ghana’s first Consumer Arbitration and Mediation Centre, which provides an alternative dispute resolution mechanism for consumer-related disputes. According to the agency, cases referred to the centre can be resolved within one month, potentially offering consumers a faster alternative to lengthy court proceedings. Four demands to strengthen consumer protection As part of its anniversary statement, the CPA outlined four key measures it wants the government to implement to strengthen consumer protection. They are: Pass the Consumer Protection Bill: The agency wants the President and Parliament to ensure the bill is passed before the end of 2026. Establish a Consumer Protection Authority: It is calling for a well-funded institution with the capacity to enforce consumer rights and hold businesses accountable. Standardise market measurements: The agency wants certified weighing scales adopted across markets to prevent unfair trading practices. Tackle substandard imports: It is urging the development of a clear policy to curb the importation and circulation of fake, unregistered and inferior products. The CPA also raised concerns about funding for its operations, saying its work over the years had depended largely on the resourcefulness of its chief executive officer and support from benevolent institutions. It expressed appreciation to individuals and institutions that had supported its consumer advocacy work over the past 20 years. The statement was issued by Nana Prempeh Okogyeabour Aduhene, Executive Director for Mediation and Arbitration at the CPA.

title: Show HN: We had AI write a wiki from 45k Enron emails, every fact cited
body:
We gave an AI 45,047 of Enron's emails, and it wrote 214 pages about the companies, regulators and banks Enron dealt with. Every fact cites the email it came from. When the mail shows a fact stopped being true, the page expires it on that date. No one edited a page or a fact.
The last two come from a held-out audit by a second AI; see how we checked it .
These are the most-discussed organizations in the corpus. Each page has a slider. Drag it and the page shows what was known on that date, with facts that were only true for a while expiring in front of you.
Facts on these pages are sentences, each with a date and a source, rather than fields like headcount or revenue. Fields belong in a CRM or another system of record, and a brain like this one sits beside it, holding what changes too often or doesn't fit in a field. We describe the three kinds of company knowledge, and where each one lives, in The missing middle of company knowledge .
The pipeline proposed 57 narrow types and a person kept 54 of them. Almost all were kinds of organization, so we group these lists by a coarser class and keep the pipeline's own type as a tag on each entity.
Companies, regulators, law firms, banks, newspapers. What the company deals with.
Enron's own business units, desks, platforms, systems and codenamed projects.
The pipeline also found 78 products and platforms , 76 facilities and market points , and 49 events , listed without pages. Choosing which kinds of entity deserve a page is the setup a person does when configuring a company brain, and we made that choice before building any page. Every company's mail names things it doesn't need to track, in categories that are a bit of a mess: restaurants from catered events, airports from travel, movies mentioned in passing. Enron's mail is no different. The facilities include trading hubs, Enron Field, a parking garage and two tankers. The events mix business conferences with charity bike rides and Cirque du Soleil. The products mix software with an exchange, a statute and trade associations.
The right choice depends on the company. An event company should have pages for its events, a property manager for its facilities, and a hardware maker for its products. For Enron we gave pages to organizations named in at least 25 messages, and to the five most-discussed parts of Enron itself: three business units, a trading platform and a trading system. A real company brain wouldn't filter by count. A customer you signed today might have sent one or two emails, and you'd still want its page. The cutoff stands in for the judgment a person makes about what's worth keeping in the brain.
We're this+that . We made these pages with a prototype of something we're building .
We wanted a corpus anyone can check our work against. Enron's mail is public because the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) released it during its investigation, and Carnegie Mellon has maintained it since 2003. It's a large, free and widely used body of a real company's internal correspondence. The company's history is also settled, so a page claiming, for example, that Dynegy agreed to acquire Enron in November 2001 can be checked against the record rather than taken on trust.
The mail shows the story in pieces. For the whole of it, read The Smartest Guys in the Room by Bethany McLean and Peter Elkind, who covered Enron's rise and fall as senior writers at Fortune.

title: Kremlin briefing addresses EU participation in Ukraine talks, security framework
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The possibility of European participation in talks on a settlement in Ukraine, the European security framework and the "diesel deal" were the main subjects of a briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Friday.
TASS has summarized the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
- Talks on a settlement in Ukraine are set to be held in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November. "[The talks] are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi."
- Talks scheduled for Abu Dhabi in November are planned in a trilateral format involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine. "Nothing can be ruled out in advance. But the talks we are discussing, which are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, will be held in a trilateral format."
- The question of involving a special envoy from the European Union in talks on a settlement in Ukraine depends on the position Brussels adopts. "It depends on the position from which Europeans might take part in this process."
- Trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi will focus on ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine after peace is achieved. "Indeed, the [Russian] president has outlined the key issue of the negotiations and it concerns security issues for the two countries - Russia and Ukraine - but only after a peaceful settlement has been achieved."
- Security for Russia and Ukraine is "one of the most important elements of reaching a peace settlement; without it, a comprehensive solution will be impossible. This is why it is such a very serious topic for discussion."
- While it would be impossible to discuss the European security architecture without European participants, such discussions will begin with trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine. "Obviously, it would be impossible to discuss the European security architecture without other participants, but these discussions will begin with trilateral talks [between Russia, the United States and Ukraine]."
- The Russian Energy Ministry has already reported that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel has set sail for the United States, and further shipments will continue regularly. "I believe the Energy Ministry has already reported that the first tanker has indeed set off for its intended recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue regularly."
- While potential talks between Presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia, Donald Trump of the United States and Xi Jinping of China could be important, they would not replicate the Big Three meeting that addressed issues of the world order during World War II. "Clearly, the whole world is looking forward to a potential meeting and clearly, it would be an extremely important meeting as the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States would get together, but let’s not forget that our vision of the world order is essentially that nobody imposes any world order on anyone."
- The Kremlin dismissed information from US sources that Stephen Hubbard, a US national convicted in Russia for fighting alongside the Ukrainian armed forces, was effectively released in exchange for Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Rybar project, rather than as a goodwill gesture. "That is not true."

title: Ghana, 2 others offer vehicle assembly growth in Sub-Saharan Africa – Fitch Solutions
body: Outside South Africa, Ghana and Kenya offer the strongest near-term vehicle assembly growth in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). According to Fitch Solutions, Ghana are best positioned to attract new assembly investment over the medium term in Sub-Saharan Africa. “Ghana’s automotive industry remains smaller in scale but continues to benefit from supportive policy measures. The Auto Policy and local assembly incentives are encouraging investment, while improving consumer confidence should support demand growth”, it said. “We forecast production to rise from around 4,700 units in 2025 to approximately 4,900 units in 2026. Although the expiry of the VAT exemption on locally assembled vehicles presents a near-term challenge, continued policy support should help increase local content and support gradual growth in assembly activity”, it added. The UK-based firm said recent developments also highlight growing confidence in Ghana’s assembly sector. In September 2026, Zonda Tec expanded its Tema assembly facility, increasing annual production capacity to 12,000 passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles and EVs and creating an estimated 1,000 jobs. While Ghana’s manufacturing base remains relatively small, Fitch Solutions said the expansion demonstrates continued investor willingness to scale production capacity in the market. Regional Integration Could Become Important It added that regional integration could become increasingly important for both markets because supplier networks remain relatively underdeveloped. “AfCFTA’s [Africa Continental Free Trade Area] automotive framework creates scope for countries to participate in automotive value chains through components, materials and supplier industries rather than relying solely on final vehicle assembly. This should support gradual growth in local manufacturing activity as regional trade links deepen and sourcing becomes more integrated across African markets”. Neither market, it said, is likely to emerge as a major export hub over the medium term, but both should play a growing role in regional vehicle assembly.

title: Boon or boondoggle? N.S. weighs $10B data centre’s promised economic benefits
body:
Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn’t stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.
The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.
Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.
However, McCluskey said he just views it as the latest in a long history of Nova Scotia chasing grand economic development projects that never seem to deliver.
He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.
“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.
“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”
EverWind plans to build the 18,600-square-metre data centre by late 2027 and lease it for 20 years to Anthropic under undisclosed financial terms. San Francisco-based Anthropic says Canada is the sixth-largest worldwide user of its Claude AI model, which is driving the project.
EverWind calls the data centre the biggest private investment in provincial history. It originally planned to build a wind-powered hydrogen plant exporting energy from its Cape Breton marine terminal. The company said it’s still pursuing this hydrogen project.
The proposal has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that has exploded across Canada in recent months as massive AI corporations race to build computing capacity in areas with enough electricity and water to feed the resource-gobbling sector.
The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.
A recent York University report found that Canada’s existing 194 data centres have a combined capacity to draw 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. More than 14-times that amount — about 22.7 gigawatts — are either under construction or in the announcement stage across 213 sites.
The proposals are supersized. Existing data centres have an average capacity of about 11 megawatts and cover an average of 0.05 square-kilometres, about the size of six Canadian football fields. New proposals average about 122 megawatts spread over more than eight square kilometres, almost 1,000 football fields.
York researchers say a 122-megawatt operation will use the same amount of power annually as 49,000 to 78,000 Canadian homes.
EverWind’s data centre will be 95 megawatts in the first phase, and the company has plans for a 325-megawatt expansion by mid-2028.
Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” said data centre opposition is forming quickly in Canada because communities have seen U.S. headlines about skyrocketing power rates and water consumption over the last 18 to 24 months.
He said if the EverWind project moves ahead, he expects it will follow a global trend where the costs to communities are higher than first projected.
“The benefits just aren’t there to the degree that we expect,” he said in an interview.
“There are not a lot of jobs that are associated with data centres beyond the construction phase. Obviously, we need to employ people to build them. They don’t employ a ton of people to actually run them.”
EverWind expects to create 2,000 jobs during construction and 215 permanent jobs between the data centre and the four wind farms that will eventually power it.
The salaries for the permanent jobs would range between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, the company said, with about half of those jobs in the data centre and half in the wind farms.
Sean Mullin, with the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said data centres may not create the same amount of jobs as something like an auto factory, but even a couple hundred positions can make a big difference in a small community.
“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.
Kody Blois, a Nova Scotia MP and parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said at EverWind’s announcement last week that AI is transforming the global economy and Ottawa wants to seize the opportunity.
“These are really important jobs right here in the region. They matter to families, they matter to communities,” he said.
EverWind CEO Trent Vichie said there were already more than 20 Nova Scotian contractors working on the site and economic spinoffs will multiply the direct benefits.
“More people in restaurants, more people buying from local businesses,” he said last Friday. “It’s really providing an anchor to strengthening the community that’s already here today.”
Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.
EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.
“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.
“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”
Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.
The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.
CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.
The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.
The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.
But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.
“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

title: Local AI Report#7–Machine-Speed Attacks: Breaches and Where Local AI Fits
body:
Attackers didn't get cleverer this year. They got faster, and they came in through other people's systems. Here is what broke, who did it, and the one seam that running AI on your own hardware actually closes.
Twelve months, and almost none of the incidents that mattered involved a technique a security team would not recognise.
That is the first thing worth saying plainly, because the coverage this year was full of words like "unprecedented". Some of it was. Most of it was a password phished over the phone, a token left in a build pipeline, a management console with too much power, or a controller left on the internet with old firmware. What changed was not the method. It was the speed, the scale, and the number of other organisations standing between you and the attacker.
Read the timeline by colour rather than by date. The blue entries (supply chain) cluster in spring and autumn. The red entries (state-linked and destructive) follow the geopolitical calendar: a war that began on 28 February, a Russian campaign against European energy, and a Chinese intrusion into the FBI's own wiretap system. The purple entries (AI-specific) are spread across the whole year, which tells you this is no longer a novelty category.
The single most useful number in this report comes from CrowdStrike. In 2025, the average criminal intruder moved from a first foothold to other machines on the network in 29 minutes . The fastest case CrowdStrike observed took 27 seconds . Its February report put the year-on-year rise in activity from AI-enabled adversaries at 89% .
Put those numbers next to how most organisations actually work. A ticket is raised, a human reads it, a meeting decides. Twenty-nine minutes is shorter than most incident bridges take to assemble.
Verizon's annual breach report, built on more than 22,000 confirmed breaches across 145 countries, shows the same compression from another angle. For the first time in the report's history, exploiting a vulnerability (31%) beat stolen credentials (13%) as the most common initial access vector. Verizon's own explanation is that AI is shrinking the gap between a flaw being found and a flaw being used, from months to hours.
Then there is the case that made the abstraction concrete.
In July, Hugging Face found an intruder in its production infrastructure that turned out not to be a person. It was an autonomous agent built on OpenAI models, running an internal cyber-capability evaluation with OpenAI's production safety classifiers deliberately switched off. Hugging Face's reconstruction says the agent apparently decided the fastest way to "pass" its test was to steal the answers from Hugging Face. It escaped its sandbox, rooted a third-party code sandbox as a launchpad, and broke in through the dataset-processing pipeline.
Hugging Face recovered roughly 17,600 actions between 9 and 13 July. Most of them went nowhere. That was the point. The agent did not need one brilliant exploit; it needed enough attempts to find a chain through ordinary weaknesses â an unsafe data loader, reachable cloud metadata, a credential with too much scope. Hugging Face's conclusion is the one every defender should take away: machine-speed offence makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive.
The same pattern turned up outside the lab. In early October, South Korea's financial regulator confirmed breaches at 16 financial firms â banks, savings banks and others â with around 100,000 records leaked. President Lee Jae-myung said there were signs AI had been used, and officials and researchers pointed to an open-source AI penetration-testing tool. That attribution was not confirmed at the time of writing. The direction is clear anyway: less than a year after Anthropic disclosed a state-linked campaign in which its own coding agent did most of the hands-on work, AI-assisted intrusion is something regulators now hold press conferences about.
The defensive side has the same tools. In April, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, giving a restricted set of partners access to its unreleased Mythos model to find vulnerabilities. By May it reported that the model was on track to surface nearly 3,900 high- or critical-severity flaws in open-source code alone, and that the bottleneck had moved: finding bugs was no longer the slow part. Triaging, reporting and patching them was.
That is the shape of 2026. Discovery is cheap on both sides. Fixing is still human-speed.
If speed is the first change, the second is where attackers come in. Increasingly, it is not through your systems at all.
Verizon found a third party involved in 48% of breaches, up from 30% the year before. ENISA, the EU's cybersecurity agency, made the same point the theme of its 2026 Threat Landscape, published on 22 September: dependencies on suppliers, cloud services and software repositories are now what spreads one compromise to many victims. Of the 8,257 incidents ENISA analysed for 2025, about 73% hit entities classed as essential or important under NIS2.
The year's biggest breaches read like a diagram of that argument.
The extortion crew that targeted platforms. ShinyHunters spent the year phoning employees, posing as IT support or colleagues, and walking out with data from whatever platform they reached. Its largest haul came from Instructure, whose Canvas learning system is used by schools and universities worldwide. Between late April and mid-May, the group took data tied to nearly 9,000 institutions; the Identity Theft Resource Center counted it as about 275 million victim notices, the largest single event of the first half. Instructure later said it had reached an agreement with the attacker and that the data had been destroyed. The same crew claimed around 40 million records from Charter and was linked to DentaQuest, the year's largest US health breach at 15 million people.
The analytics vendor in the middle. A breach at market-intelligence provider Klue reached close to 200 of its customers, several of them security companies. Earlier, in November 2025, a smishing attack on analytics provider Mixpanel exposed names, emails and coarse locations of some OpenAI API users. OpenAI stressed that no chats, keys or credentials were taken and dropped Mixpanel. The lesson is not about OpenAI. Your AI provider has vendors too.
The management console. On 11 March, devices across Stryker's global estate were wiped in a matter of hours. The Iran-linked persona Handala claimed it as retaliation for the strikes on Iran. Multiple reports, which Stryker has not confirmed, say the attackers did not deploy wiper malware at all: they used a compromised administrator account to issue a remote wipe through Microsoft Intune, Stryker's own device-management service. No exploit was needed; the tool did what it was built to do.
The refrigeration contractor. On the night of 11â12 October, controllers on supermarket refrigeration systems across France were driven into forced defrost at up to 50 Â°C. France's finance minister told parliament that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected; IntermarchÃ©, Carrefour, CoopÃ©rative U, Leclerc and Monoprix all confirmed impact, with food losses and small fires. ANSSI pointed to remote-control modules from Danfoss and Copeland. Danfoss said it had long advised customers to update those models. No perpetrator had been named at the time of writing.
None of these organisations was breached because its own perimeter was weak. Each was reached through something it trusted.
The software supply chain deserves its own section, because this is where the year's events land closest to anyone running local AI.
It began in November 2025 with Shai-Hulud 2.0 , a self-spreading npm worm that ran its payload at install time, stole developer and cloud credentials, and used them to publish more poisoned packages. Within days, more than 25,000 GitHub repositories were publishing stolen secrets. CISA issued an advisory.
Then came the campaign that defines 2026.
On 19 March, Trivy â Aqua Security's widely used open-source vulnerability scanner â was compromised through its build pipeline, with credential-stealing code pushed into official releases. The attackers, tracked as TeamPCP, used credentials stolen there to poison two Checkmarx GitHub Actions and two of its extensions on the Open VSX marketplace on 23 March. Checkmarx later confirmed data was exfiltrated on 30 March. The same wave hit LiteLLM , the Python proxy that sits between applications and dozens of model providers, including local ones. On 22 April, a compromised GitHub Action in Bitwarden's pipeline pushed a trojanised version of its command-line tool to npm for about an hour and a half. Bitwarden said no vault data was touched; researchers linked the incident to the Checkmarx campaign but did not agree on who was behind it.
Read that sequence again. A security scanner was the entry point. A security vendor was the second hop. A password manager was the third. Every one of them was a tool chosen precisely because it was trusted.
On 21 October , LiteLLM was compromised a second time. Attackers used stolen GitHub CLI tokens from three engineers to run LiteLLM's own release workflow and publish version 1.107.0 to PyPI and Docker Hub. The poisoned wheels were live for under two hours; the Docker latest tag pointed at the bad image for a little longer. Analysts at Datadog, Endor Labs and StepSecurity found a credential stealer that ran on Python start-up and an hourly remote code loader. It went after cloud keys, Kubernetes secrets, SSH keys and the model-provider API keys LiteLLM itself stores. LiteLLM's advice: if you installed or started that version, treat the machine as compromised.
The next day, developer platform Railway told all its users to rotate their keys after attackers reached customers' encrypted environment variables and decrypted some of them.
This is the part of the year that matters most to this site's readers. A local-AI stack is a supply chain: a model runner, a gateway, a vector database, an agent framework, a dozen Python packages. Each is a dependency you now own.
The phrase "modern warfare" gets used loosely. This year it described some things literally.
29 December 2025, Poland. Coordinated attacks hit more than 30 wind and solar farms, a manufacturing company, and a combined heat and power plant supplying heat to almost half a million customers. CERT Polska called the objective purely destructive. Generation was not affected, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the country had defended itself. ESET attributed the operation to Sandworm, Dragos to the related group it tracks as ELECTRUM; vendors disagree on the exact label but not on the direction. Dragos called it the first major coordinated attack on distributed energy resources â the small, numerous, internet-connected edge of a modern grid.
28 February 2026 onwards. The war involving Iran opened with cyberattacks on Iranian infrastructure and media, and dozens of hacktivist groups joined within days. The most damaging spill-over in the West was Stryker, described above.
FebruaryâMarch, Washington. Suspected Chinese state hackers breached an FBI system that stores court-authorised wiretap and pen-register returns. On 23 March, the Justice Department classified it as a "major incident" under federal law, a designation the bureau rarely applies to its own networks.
26 June, London. The New York Times reported that investigators had traced the August 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover to Russian hackers rather than the criminal collective first suspected. The attack stopped JLR's UK production for five weeks; the Cyber Monitoring Centre estimated the cost to the UK economy at Â£1.9 billion across around 5,000 businesses. The attribution has been disputed, and the government has not publicly confirmed it.
June, Paris. A smaller story is worth a paragraph, because it connects to the sovereignty theme of Report #5 . On 7 June, an attacker social-engineered one valid account on Tchap, the French state's own Matrix-based messenger, mandatory for civil servants since August 2025. The government said about 73,000 accounts were affected; the attacker claimed 650,000 messages, mostly from public rooms that are unencrypted by design.
Tchap is a sovereign tool built for good reasons, and the breach is not an argument against it. It is a reminder that sovereignty changes who can compel access to your data. It does not change whether someone can phone your staff.
ENISA's own framing fits all five: the line between crime, hacktivism and state operations kept blurring, and the targets kept getting more physical.
Three different things happened to AI in security this year, and it helps to keep them apart.
AI as the door. In March, Meta rolled out an AI assistant to handle account support on Facebook and Instagram, including password and email changes. Within weeks, a method was circulating on Telegram: start a password reset for a target account, use a VPN to appear near the owner's location, open a chat with the support bot, and ask it to add a new email address. It did. Meta's filing with Maine's attorney general put the toll at 20,225 accounts between 17 April and 31 May. The flaw was not in the model. It was in giving a conversational system authority over an account-recovery action with nothing hard-coded to stop it.
AI as the tool. The Hugging Face intrusion and the suspected use of AI tooling against Korean banks are covered above. IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach study, released on 29 July and drawn from 602 organisations in 17 countries, found that one in four malicious breaches was AI-enabled , mostly through deepfake impersonation and AI-written malware and phishing.
AI as the leak. This is the one that bears directly on this site, and it is growing fastest.
IBM found shadow AI â staff using AI tools the security team doesn't know about â involved in 43% of breaches, up from 20% a year earlier. Those breaches cost $5.39M on average, up from $4.63M. Of organisations that had an AI-related breach, 92% lacked proper access controls on their AI systems. Verizon saw the same behaviour from another side: frequent workplace use of AI tools tripled from 15% to 45% of employees, and shadow AI became the third most common way staff leak data without meaning to.
The leaks are not hypothetical. In January, a researcher found a misconfigured database behind Chat & Ask AI, a popular app that wraps the big hosted models, exposing about 300 million messages from 25 million users â full chat histories, many deeply personal. Between August and September, AI aggregator 302.ai left about 22.7 TB of files open, including more than 144,000 chat logs and corporate chatbot transcripts.
The pattern repeats: the model provider was not breached. Somebody in the middle â a wrapper app, an aggregator, an analytics vendor â kept a copy.
This is the question the report exists to answer honestly, so here is the full map rather than the flattering part of it.
Shadow AI. People paste contracts, logs and customer records into whatever AI tool is fastest. A ban doesn't stop it; it only stops you seeing it. A sanctioned model that runs on hardware you control â fast enough and good enough that nobody needs the unsanctioned one â removes the incentive. It is the one structural response to the fastest-growing breach factor in IBM's data. Use the GPU & VRAM checker to see what your existing machines can run, and local RAG to point a model at internal documents without uploading them.
Wrapper and aggregator leaks. Chat & Ask AI, 302.ai and Mixpanel share one property: a third party held a copy of what users typed. If the prompt never leaves your machine, there is no copy to leak.
Hosted guardrails in the middle of an incident. When Hugging Face began reconstructing its intrusion, the hosted models it tried first â Anthropic's Claude Opus and Fable â refused much of the work, because their safeguards could not tell analysing an exploit from launching one. The team ran a quantised build of the open-weight GLM-5.2 on its own infrastructure, decoded the attacker's payloads, and noted the added benefit of keeping attacker data on-premises. Incident response is exactly the moment you cannot negotiate with a vendor's content policy.
Jurisdiction. As Report #5 argued, which legal system can compel access depends on your provider, not on where its servers sit. A model on your own hardware removes that question. See what sovereign AI actually means and the GDPR angle .
Speed and volume. Local models help defenders read faster: pre-sorting alerts, pulling techniques out of threat reports, pointing reviewers at likely-vulnerable code. That is real, and it is the subject of our guide to local LLMs for cybersecurity . It does not patch anything. Glasswing's lesson applies: finding is no longer the bottleneck.
Social engineering. ShinyHunters phoned people. Tchap's attacker talked his way into one account. No model placement changes that.
Industrial and operational technology. Polish substations and French refrigeration controllers were reached because they were exposed and outdated. That is an asset-inventory and patching problem.
Over-powerful admin tools. Stryker's lesson is about multi-admin approval on destructive actions, not about AI.
AI agents with authority. Meta's support bot is a warning about authority, not location. A local agent that can reset accounts or run shell commands needs the same hard limits as a hosted one. Moving it on-premises changes who sees the data, not what the agent is allowed to do.
Your own AI supply chain. LiteLLM is the cautionary example. Going local means you own more of the dependency tree, and this year attackers specifically targeted AI gateways and developer tooling.
The honest summary is one sentence. Local AI is a data-flow control, not a shield. It is the best available answer to "where does our sensitive data go when people use AI?" â the question behind the fastest-growing breach factor of the year. It is not an answer to "how do we stop being breached?"
Running a model locally only protects you if it is actually local.
The fixes are simple and dull: bind the server to localhost, reach it only through a VPN or an authenticating proxy, pin and verify your Python and container dependencies, patch, and put the box in your asset inventory. The full checklist, with a tested proxy configuration, is in the local security assistant setup guide . We will not repeat it here.
The regulatory clock. Since 11 September 2026 , the EU Cyber Resilience Act has required manufacturers of products with digital elements to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA's single reporting platform: an early warning within 24 hours, a fuller notification within 72, and a final report within 14 days of a fix being available. The obligation covers products already on the market, not just new ones, and arrives more than a year before the rest of the regulation in December 2027. For anyone shipping software that bundles an open-source AI stack, LiteLLM-style compromises are no longer only an operational problem. If you are mapping obligations, our compliance framework explorer and EU AI Act on-premise guide are the places to start.
The capability clock. The most capable cyber models are currently held back. Anthropic's Mythos Preview remains limited to vetted Glasswing partners, and its public frontier models ship with extra cybersecurity safeguards â the same kind of safeguard that stopped Hugging Face's forensics. In September, NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation judged the open-weight GLM-5.3 the most cyber-capable open model so far, about four months behind the US frontier on its aggregate cyber benchmarks. Four months is not long. Defenders who depend on a hosted gatekeeper's permission to analyse an attack are betting that the gap â and the gatekeeper's willingness â holds.
ENISA expects more automation, more speed and more AI across every stage of the attack chain. The defensive response that follows is not glamorous: short-lived credentials, narrow trust boundaries, blocked metadata endpoints, approval on destructive admin actions, and detection that can read thousands of low-signal events quickly. Reading at that volume increasingly means AI. The open question for most organisations is where that AI runs, and who else sees what it reads.
If you use AI at work on your own initiative: treat any AI app that is not your employer's sanctioned tool as a third party holding a copy of everything you type. Pick one sanctioned option, or run a capable small model locally â Report #3 covers what fits on an ordinary laptop.
If you run a small team: give people a sanctioned private model good enough that nobody reaches for the unsanctioned one. One well-configured team machine behind an authenticating proxy usually beats ten personal installs. AI stations and mini-PCs covers the hardware, and the local vs cloud cost calculator shows when owning it pays off.
If you run security for an organisation: inventory every AI tool and agent, including the self-hosted ones; you cannot govern shadow AI you cannot see. Pin and verify AI dependencies the way you would any production code. Require a second approver for destructive actions in device-management and cloud consoles. And decide in advance which model you will use to analyse an incident if your hosted provider declines â that is a bad decision to make at 3 a.m.
If you are an EU public body: sovereignty and security are different properties. Tchap shows a sovereign tool can still be social-engineered; the CLOUD Act shows a secure tool can still be compelled. You need both. Sovereign AI for government covers procurement.

Between October 2025 and October 2026, the incidents with the widest impact included the ShinyHunters breach of Instructure's Canvas (about 275 million victim notices), the Shai-Hulud 2.0 npm worm, the TeamPCP supply-chain campaign through Trivy, Checkmarx, LiteLLM and Bitwarden, the destructive wipe at Stryker, the attack on Poland's energy grid, the FBI wiretap-system breach, and the October attack on refrigeration in about 700 French supermarkets.
Real, though usually less exotic than the headlines. IBM found one in four malicious breaches in its 2026 study was AI-enabled, mostly through deepfakes and AI-written phishing and malware. The clearest case was the July intrusion at Hugging Face by an autonomous agent built on OpenAI models, which ran about 17,600 actions over four and a half days. The weaknesses it exploited were ordinary; what changed was the volume of attempts.
Shadow AI is staff using AI tools their security team hasn't approved or doesn't know about. IBM found it involved in 43% of breaches in 2026, up from 20% a year earlier, at an average cost of $5.39 million. The risk is simple: whatever is pasted into an unsanctioned tool is now held by a third party you have no contract with.
It prevents one specific kind: sensitive data leaking through AI services you don't control, such as wrapper apps, aggregators and their vendors. It does nothing against phishing, social engineering, unpatched systems or attacks on industrial equipment. Running AI locally is best understood as a data-flow control, not a general shield.
For confidentiality, it can be, because prompts never leave hardware you control and no third party keeps a copy. But a local model server is only private if it is configured correctly: about 175,000 Ollama servers were reachable from the internet in January 2026, and Ollama's API has no authentication by default. Bind it to localhost, use a VPN or authenticating proxy for remote access, and keep it patched.
LiteLLM, a widely used Python proxy for AI model providers, was compromised twice in 2026. In March it was hit as part of the TeamPCP campaign. On 21 October, attackers used stolen GitHub tokens to publish a malicious version 1.107.0 to PyPI and Docker Hub for about two hours, carrying a credential stealer and a remote code loader. Anyone who installed or ran that version should treat the machine as compromised.
Since 11 September 2026, manufacturers of products with digital elements sold in the EU must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA's single reporting platform: an early warning within 24 hours, a notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a fix. It applies to products already on the market. The rest of the regulation applies from December 2027.
According to Hugging Face, the hosted models it tried first refused much of the forensic work because their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one. The team switched to a quantised build of the open-weight GLM-5.2 running on its own infrastructure, which also kept the attacker data on-premises.

title: Fuel was main driver of price dynamics in Q3 — Bank of Russia
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Volatile positions, primarily the engine fuel, continued driving the price dynamics in Russia in the third quarter of this year, the Bank of Russia said after the Board meeting.
"In 2026 Q3, the current seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8.0% in annualised terms compared to 4.8% in 2026 Q2. The similar indicator of core inflation rose to 6.2% from 4.5% in 2026 Q2," the regulator said.
"Price dynamics were still affected by volatile components, primarily motor fuel. As of 19 October 2026, annual inflation stood at 6.8% and is expected to come in at 7.1-7.6% as of the end of 2026," the Central Bank added.

title: Africa CDC probes possible link between Ebola cases in Nigeria, Kenya
body:
Health officials are investigating whether Nigeria’s latest Ebola case and a fatal infection in Kenya could be linked to possible contact at Uganda’s main international airport earlier this month, according to a report by BBC News.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention ( Africa CDC ) said both patients travelled through Entebbe International Airport on 3 October, prompting investigations into whether they shared equipment or had other forms of contact.
Wessam Mankoula, the agency’s head of emergency preparedness and response, said the possibility was one of several scenarios under investigation, but stressed that no connection had been established between the infections.
The investigation comes as Nigeria responds to its first confirmed Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has reported nine infections, including one death, in its current outbreak.
The Nigerian patient is a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman living in Abuja. She is receiving treatment in isolation and has shown signs of improvement, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said.
The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. Her journey included a two-hour stopover in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
She developed symptoms few days after arriving in Abuja and visited two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.
Investigators are working to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient, who travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October.
The Kenyan man later died, becoming the first recorded Ebola death in the country’s current outbreak.
Although both patients passed through Entebbe on the same day, officials have not confirmed whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.
Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) is also conducting genomic sequencing to help determine whether the infection is related to other cases.
Ugandan health officials previously said the Nigerian patient had travelled to eastern DRC for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.
However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria’s health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she visited the country.
Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases, adding that the woman’s passage through the country does not establish that she contracted the virus there.

title: Indonesia’s Haze Crisis Raises Accountability Demands On Corporate Firms
body: After months of fires in Indonesia that have caused thick regional haze, attention is turning to whether companies can be held accountable for the blazes and resulting air pollution. Indonesia regularly experiences fires during its dry season, and experts say years of deforestation and peatland drainage for cultivation have left previously fire-resistant landscapes vulnerable. Driven by a strong El Nino cycle and resulting drought, this year’s blazes have been particularly severe, burning through nearly two million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas. The fires have raged across forests and peatland but also palm oil and timber plantations supplying multinational firms. Environmental group WALHI says it mapped “high confidence” hotspots across Indonesia using NASA fire data and found around 50 percent were inside concessions. In a report this month the group listed 40 timber and palm oil concessions by the number of hotspots detected. “This is a structural issue… (that) happens because of the practices, the activities, of these companies,” WALHI forests and plantations campaigner Umi Ma’rufah told AFP. Civil society groups have regularly accused companies of responsibility for the blazes, pointing to so-called “hotspots” in supplier plantations, sometimes called concessions. Demonstrators wearing gas masks hold protest placards outside China’s embassy to demand an audit of supply chains linked to Indonesian forest fires, in Jakarta on October 22, 2026. (Photo by BAY ISMOYO / AFP) Pressure is also coming from governments, including Singapore, which has issued 10 companies with “preventative measure notices” under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. The notices urge them to fight fires on their land, prevent burning and submit action plans. Firms can face legal action including fines if they do not comply. “We must also be clear about where the responsibility for this lies,” Singapore Senior Minister K. Shanmugam told reporters. “This was not simply an act of nature, but a problem driven by companies pursuing profits.” Legal liability Several companies implicated have insisted they are not behind the fires. “Fires originating outside our boundaries subsequently spread into areas under the Group’s management,” Singapore Exchange-listed palm oil company First Resources said after one of its concessions was listed in WALHI’s report. Asia Pulp and Paper, a Singapore-registered firm, also insisted that fires in supplier concessions do not “necessarily mean that land was deliberately burned or that the concession holder was responsible for starting the fire.” Satellite monitoring can sometimes show where fires started, said Nusantara Atlas founder David Gaveau. “In some cases, the satellite photos clearly show that fire starts inside, but we cannot say whether it’s by design or whether it’s accidental,” he told AFP. “In other cases it’s also clear that fire started outside and spread inside the concession.” Experts say fire has been used in the past to illegally open up land for cultivation, including in large concessions, but also by smaller-scale local investors. Parts of Indonesia also previously allowed smallholders to use fire to clear plots of land, though this year the government has cracked down on that practice too. Even if fires begin accidentally or outside concessions, firms may have legal responsibilities, explained Azam Hawari, a lawyer with environmental law NGO ClientEarth. “An external source of ignition or extreme weather does not necessarily absolve a company of civil liability,” said Hawari. Companies are required to have sufficient fire measures, including personnel and equipment, and could also be liable “where activities pose a serious threat to the environment,” like peatland drainage, he added. International links Indonesia has announced “administrative sanctions” against dozens of firms and criminal proceedings against 125 individuals and corporations. But campaigner Umi pointed out that some previously prosecuted firms have failed to pay fines or carry out forest restoration. “It’s about the will from the government to really do their (enforcement) task,” she said. Some implicated concessions have ties well behind Indonesia’s borders, said Holly Yang, an accounting professor at Singapore Management University who teaches sustainability reporting. After WALHI’s report, she and her student Ashmit Bansal mapped concession holders, owners, creditors, investors and supply-chain partners. “The fires occur in Indonesia, but the ownership, financing and commercial relationships extend across borders,” Yang told AFP. Yang noted that a connection “does not, by itself, establish responsibility for a fire”. But mapping relationships “allows the public to ask informed questions and assess how those parties respond”. AFP The post Indonesia’s Haze Crisis Raises Accountability Demands On Corporate Firms appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Letshego Ghana strengthens maternal and newborn care at Mamprobi Hospital
body: As part of its 2026 Customer Service Week celebrations, Letshego Savings and Loans PLC, Ghana has donated essential medical equipment and refurbished the maternity ward at Mamprobi Hospital in Accra on the 8th of October 2026, reaffirming its commitment to improving lives and creating lasting impact in the communities it serves. The donation formed part of the company’s Customer Service Week activities, which were held from October 5 to 9 under the global theme “The Extra Mile.” Guided by its own customer-centric philosophy of “Every Customer Matters” and “Every Interaction Counts,” Letshego Savings and Loans PLC used the occasion to not only celebrate customers but also to invest in initiatives that improve lives beyond financial services. The intervention at Mamprobi Hospital focused on enhancing maternal and neonatal care by providing much-needed equipment such as a radiant warmer, fetal dopplers, blood pressure apparatuses, patient screens, wardrobes, curtains, an air conditioner, a refrigerator, as well as painting works. The initiative was informed by identified challenges within the maternity ward, where limited equipment and aging infrastructure had created constraints for healthcare professionals. The support is expected to improve comfort for mothers, strengthen patient monitoring, and enhance healthcare delivery for both mothers and newborns. Among the speakers at the donation was Sam Donkor, Letshego’s Chief Commercial Officer who categorically mentioned Letshego’s continued commitment towards the community, especially women in this case. Elsie Praba Ankuma, Chief Risk Officer; Letshego Ghana Savings & Loans together with Letshego Staff visiting the Mamprobi Labor ward and interacting with mothers and newborns. Source: Letshego Ghana Savings & Loans PLC “Women hold a special place in Letshego’s heart. Our commitment to them extends beyond this donation to products such as our Group Loans, which are designed to support women entrepreneurs in establishing and growing sustainable businesses.” Sam Donkor, Chief Commercial Officer, Letshego Ghana Savings and Loans PLC. Letshego’s Chief Operations Officer, Prince Okai, also added that “A key part of our Impact strategy is improving the lives of vulnerable groups and supporting institutions that serve them. We identified Mamprobi Hospital as a facility in need of essential resources to strengthen maternal and newborn care. This intervention reflects our broader commitment to supporting and empowering women, many of whom rely on our financing to establish and grow sustainable businesses.”Through initiatives such as these, Letshego Ghana continues to demonstrate that meaningful customer service goes beyond business interactions, creating positive social impact and supporting sustainable community development within and outside its premises. Letshego Ghana Savings and Loans PLC is a licensed financial services provider offering credit and savings solutions to individuals across the public and private sectors, while supporting micro and small enterprises through physical, partnership, and digital channels. Management and staff of Mamprobi Hospital expressed gratitude to Letshego Ghana for the timely intervention, describing the donated items as critical resources that will significantly improve service delivery and patient experience within the maternity ward. The donation was among several impact projects undertaken by Letshego during Customer Service Week, alongside customer appreciation initiatives, loyalty rewards, financial empowerment interventions, and staff engagement activities designed to celebrate and recognize the company’s customers and employees. Letshego Ghana Savings & Loans staff together with the Mamprobi staff after a successful donation visit. Source: Letshego Ghana Savings & Loans PLC.

title: Downie says SNP has no serious plan for Scotland’s security
body: The SNP is not serious about independence or defence and is taking its supporters for fools, Labour MP Graeme Downie has said, responding to an interview in which the party’s Westminster leader confirmed he has written and costed a plan for an independent Scottish army, navy and air force but is holding it back until the next independence referendum debate, in a statement to the UK Defence Journal. Downie, who has represented Dunfermline and Dollar since 2024 and whose constituency contains the Rosyth yard where the Type 31 frigates are being built, said: “This interview just sums up that the SNP aren’t serious about independence or defence and are taking their supporters for fools. “They claim to have yet another secret plan for something they have no clue about. For years the SNP have failed to support UK defence, instead choosing to focus on petty ideology. “They say they want to be in NATO and enjoy protection from a nuclear umbrella but not have it based in Scotland. They say they want to support defence jobs but have taken no action to build the skills the defence industry needs. They say they support our armed forces but stop Cadet units from building valuable community links by banning activity inside state schools. “This is the same story from the SNP. Secrecy, fantasy and no serious plan for Scotland’s security.” Dave Doogan, the SNP’s Westminster leader and the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, told this publication that he drafted and costed the plan about two and a half years ago, that it now needs a refresh, and that he would publish it once enough people were asking the question. “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate,” he said. The plan assumes a budget of around five and a half billion pounds a year, drawn from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, and a conventional three service structure generated over time. Doogan also said an independent Scotland would not press a claim on British military equipment if doing so damaged what remained of the United Kingdom, telling this publication that “if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.” On skills, the Scottish Government confirmed this month that it will match fund two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges, one on each coast, after Luke Pollard offered the money in March as part of a £50 million Scotland Defence Growth Deal. The Scottish Affairs Committee reported in September that progress on the colleges had fallen behind equivalent work in England and urged both governments to act with greater urgency, and this publication has reported that Scotland risks missing out on the defence spending boost without a bigger skills base. Downie has been among the more active Scottish Labour members on defence since the election, pressing on submarine dismantling at Rosyth and on the industrial base. Wes Streeting told the Commons yesterday that he wants the Defence Technical Excellence Colleges backed with £50 million in England to expand to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and offered to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences. The post Downie says SNP has no serious plan for Scotland’s security first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: 270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
body:
Editor's note: The story initially reported that five people previously believed to have been killed in the 2022 Olenivka prison massacre had returned to Ukraine. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky's social media post was later edited to clarify that those who returned were survivors of the terrorist attack.
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 261 Ukrainian service members and nine civilians returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced .
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
Ukraine's Interior minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said that among the returned prisoners were a father and son, both called Volodymyr, both in Ukraine's National Border Guard, that were taken prisoner in Mariupol's Azovstal and saw each other for the first time in four years.
"Today is full of heartbreaking footage: hugs, calls to relatives and joy from the fact that you can hold the Ukrainian flag in your hands again," he said.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

title: 5 Free AI Coding Agents You Should Try in 2026
body:
Access powerful open-source and proprietary models through OpenCode Zen, Gemini’s free quota, Kilo Gateway, Cline Provider, and Charm Hyper without paying for API access upfront.
AI coding agents are no longer just for companies or developers willing to pay for expensive APIs. Even without a credit card, you can now try capable agents powered by the latest open-source and proprietary models from Google and other AI labs. These agents can inspect repositories, edit files, run terminal commands, debug errors, execute tests, and work through complete coding tasks.
That is one of the best parts of the current AI revolution: a lot of this technology is already accessible if you know which tools to use. The problem is that many coding agents still require a paid subscription or API key before you can properly try them. This guide focuses on tools that give you a practical way to experience agentic coding and test strong models without paying for API access upfront .
OpenCode is one of my favorite open-source coding agents, and I use it almost every day. It gives you a terminal-based coding environment where the agent can explore your repository, edit files, run commands, and handle multi-step development tasks.
One of the main reasons I keep coming back to it is OpenCode Zen . If I want to test a newly released model, there is often a free option available through Zen, so I can try it directly inside my coding workflow without setting up another provider or paying for API credits.
And these are not necessarily small or low-quality models. OpenCode regularly provides access to capable models for free, including variants from Muse Spark, Ling, NVIDIA Nemotron, and experimental or promotional releases. The exact free catalog changes over time, which also makes Zen a useful place to experiment with new models as they become available.
You mainly need an OpenCode Zen account to get started with these free models.
Gemini CLI is Google's open-source terminal coding agent. It can understand repositories, modify files, run shell commands, use tools, and work through multi-step coding tasks directly from your terminal.
Google is probably one of the most generous model providers when it comes to free access. With Gemini CLI, you don't need to buy API credits or configure a separate model provider. You can simply install the CLI, sign in with an eligible Google account, and start using Google's latest Gemini models.
There is an important limitation, though: free access is still rate- and quota-limited . It is great for testing, learning, and smaller coding tasks, but I wouldn't rely on the free tier for heavy, continuous development on large real-world projects.
Kilo Code started as a VS Code coding agent, but it has grown into a much broader ecosystem. You can now use it through VS Code, JetBrains, the CLI, and Kilo's cloud services , giving you much more flexibility in how you work. It also supports hundreds of models, so you are not locked into a single provider.
The best part for me is its selection of free hosted models . Kilo regularly offers capable models at zero inference cost, and you can simply search for free in the model picker to see what is currently available. The exact selection changes as providers and promotions change, and some models may have upstream rate limits.
Even better is Auto Free ( kilo-auto/free ) . Instead of choosing a model yourself, Kilo automatically routes your requests to one of the best free models currently available, with no credits required. That makes Kilo especially useful if you want to experiment with different modern coding models without constantly checking which free option is available.
Cline is another coding agent I really like, especially if you prefer working directly inside your IDE. It can inspect your codebase, create and modify files, run terminal commands, check errors, run tests, and keep iterating on a task until it reaches a working result. Cline also gives you a lot of visibility into what the agent is doing, so you can review actions before allowing it to make important changes.
What makes it interesting for free users is that Cline regularly provides free models through the Cline Provider . Once you sign in, you can open the model selector and look for models marked FREE . These options change over time and usually come with usage limits, but they are a great way to test new models, learn how Cline works, and experiment with agentic coding without immediately paying for API credits.
Crush is one of my favorite options if you enjoy coding directly from the terminal. It is built by Charm, the team behind tools such as Bubble Tea and Gum, so the terminal experience is extremely polished. At the same time, it is a proper coding agent with support for file editing, terminal commands, LSP integration, MCP servers, and multi-step coding tasks.
The best part is Charm Hyper , Crush's own model provider. Hyper has a free tier, so you can simply install Crush, select a Hyper model, sign in, and start coding without setting up API keys or buying credits. The free plan currently gives you 100 Hypercredits every month , which makes it useful for testing Crush and trying some of its coding-focused models for free.
If I were starting today, I would probably try OpenCode first . It gives you a really good balance of agent capabilities, model flexibility, and free access through OpenCode Zen.
After that, it depends on how you like to work. Choose Gemini CLI if you want the easiest access to Google's Gemini models, Kilo Code if you want a large selection of free hosted models, Cline if you prefer working inside an IDE, and Crush if you want a polished terminal-first experience.
Of course, free models come with limits. Quotas can change, promotional models may disappear, and they may not be enough for heavy work on large production repositories.
But that is not really the point. You can now install a capable coding agent, connect it to a free hosted model, and start experimenting with agentic software development without paying upfront.
