title: Canva launches Craft, its first in-house image model
body:
Design platform Canva has released Canva Craft, its first in-house image generation model. The company says it can compete with comparable models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. According to Canva, its internal lab Canva Research trained the model from scratch, relying mainly on millions of design templates rather than photos.
Craft first plans out image composition, proportions, and text, then generates images at up to 2K resolution across more than 30 aspect ratios. The model can render text in 55 languages, Canva says. Users can break results into editable layers using Magic Layers. On the DesignArena platform's ranking, Craft placed fourth overall and first in portraits and landscapes, according to Canva.
Craft is available to all users through Dream Lab and the public API , with MCP integration for chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini planned for later. Beyond lower costs, the in-house model gives Canva more control over quality and speed. Researchers from Leonardo.ai, which Canva acquired in 2024, also contributed to the project. Two cheaper variants called Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast are expected soon. Ad Ad

title: Iran 'deliberately undermining Iraq’s security', says Al Zaidi adviser
body: Iran is committing serious violations against Iraq, including security breaches, economic disruption and drug trafficking, said an adviser to the Iraqi Prime Minister, as Baghdad closed some border crossings over security issues. Abdelamir Taiban, a senior adviser to Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi , told local media that Iran had “deliberately undermined Iraq’s security”, alleging that Iranian-linked people were entering the country without authorisation and causing “chaos” along the border. Mr Taiban said Tehran must take “strict legal measures” against those responsible. His remarks this week appeared to be an unusually direct public criticism by an Iraqi government official of Iran’s influence over Iraqi state affairs. Iraqi citizens had been kidnapped after crossing into Iran, particularly near the Shalamcheh and Al Sheeb border points, he said. The government must expand new electronic monitoring and automation systems to all crossings with Iran, he added. Mr Taiban said Iraq’s most serious border problems involved Iran. One of the biggest challenges was the flow of drugs and counterfeit currency from Iran, which he said had inflicted economic damage “greater than what ISIS caused”. The terrorist group has been responsible for widespread violence and human rights abuses. Mr Al Zaidi, who took office in May, has sought to maintain balanced ties with both Tehran and Washington while moving to bring armed factions under state control. Some Iran‑aligned groups have complied, while others have resisted. Mr Taiban said the government’s efforts to tighten border controls were part of a broader push to stabilise the economy and strengthen state authority. In September, Iraq closed the Shalamcheh crossing as a precautionary security measure after drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. His comments came as protests erupted in the southern city of Maysan over the closure of Al Sheeb crossing. Dozens of lorry drivers and workers demonstrated on Thursday, calling on the government to reverse its decision to shut the crossing, a strategic land route used by commercial and civilian vehicles. Protesters said their livelihoods depended on cross‑border traffic. The shutdown has disrupted trade and daily activity in the province. It is expected to impact the prices of basic goods, especially fresh produce and Iranian building materials that dominate southern markets. Mr Al Zaidi called on security forces to ensure a safe environment for demonstrators. The Prime Minister chaired a meeting of the Ministerial Council of National Security that underscored the need to “secure peaceful demonstrations” and to treat protesters with respect, his office said in a statement. All security agencies must prioritise humane treatment and guarantee a safe space for citizens to voice their demands, he said. Iraq and Iran share a 1,599km border and there are nine official border crossings linking Iran to Iraq and the Kurdistan region.

title: Kalashnikov starts assembly of Ratnik combat gear under new contract
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Central Scientific-Research Institute for Precision Machine Engineering (TsNIITochMash), a subsidiary of Russia’s Kalashnikov Group, has started assembling the Ratnik combat gear under a new contract, the company’s press service told TASS.
"Under the new contract, specialists of the Central Research Institute of Precision Engineering (JSC TsNIITochMash, part of the state tech corporation Rostec and managed by the Kalashnikov Group) have begun assembling the Ratnik combat gear. The contract for the gear manufacturing will be in effect during 2026-2027," the statement said.
The Ratnik combat gear is designed to outfit military personnel and consists of a set of interconnected modular elements.
Under the terms of the new contract, the tactical gear includes a reversible camouflage suit, a modular load bearing vest with a patrol backpack, elbow and knee pads, protective goggles, a helmet-mounted flashlight, and web gear.

title: Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Perm Region Chemical Plant
body:
A Ukrainian drone strike damaged an industrial plant in the Ural Mountains region of Perm, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said Friday.
Makhonin said air defense systems intercepted 20 drones over the Perm region overnight, with falling debris shattering windows in residential buildings in the city of Berezniki and the nearby town of Solikamsk.
“An industrial facility also sustained minor damage,” he wrote on Telegram without identifying the site.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of rising smoke from the purported area of the attack to identify the targeted facility as the Azot chemical plant in Berezniki. Azot is part of Uralchem, a corporation controlled by billionaire Dmitry Mazepin.
The facility is Russia’s sole producer of higher aliphatic amines, sodium nitrate and crystalline sodium nitrite, and manufactures ammonium nitrate, liquid ammonia, urea, nitric acid and nitrite-nitrate salts.
Ammonium nitrate is widely used as fertilizer and is also a component in explosives.
The Azot plant, which employs around 2,500 people and is located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from the border with Ukraine, was previously targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks in September 2026 and October 2025.
Russian civil aviation authorities issued airspace restrictions during the air raid alert in the Perm region on Friday.
The Defense Ministry said it intercepted 443 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

title: Fake business listings: How Ghanaians can check who they are paying
body: A customer searches for a business online, finds a phone number, discusses a booking and sends a deposit. Later, the business says it never received the money. The person who answered the call was pretending to work there. Ghana’s Cyber Security Authority (CSA) has warned that fraudsters are placing fake business listings on search engines and online maps. In an alert issued in April, it said 54 such cases had been reported between January 1 and April 26, 2026, with losses totalling GH₵266,195. Cybersecurity governance and risk specialist Valerie Arko-Adjei says customers should verify who they are dealing with before sending money. Finding a business online, she explains, does not mean the contact number beside its name belongs to it. The scam works because the first steps feel ordinary. Many people use a search result or a map listing to find a phone number without giving it much thought. A fraudster can use the name and address of a real business, then substitute a number they control. Once a customer gets in touch, the conversation may sound much like a genuine booking or sale. Knowing the price of a service does not prove that the person answering is legitimate. Prices, photographs and descriptions may already be public. Before agreeing to pay, customers should check whether the number they called appears on the business’s own website or on a social media account they know belongs to it. If the details do not match, they should contact the business through a different, independently verified channel. Arko-Adjei also urges customers to pay attention to sudden changes in payment instructions. Someone might say the usual mobile money number is temporarily unavailable or ask for a deposit to be sent to a personal account. There may be innocent reasons for a change, but customers should confirm it with the business using contact details they found separately. Calling the number that sent the new instructions only takes them back to the person whose identity they are trying to establish. The CSA says some people responding to fake listings have been directed to forms asking for their phone number, mobile network, transaction amount, and mobile money PIN. A request for a PIN, one-time code, or banking password should end the conversation. Customers should leave the form or chat and contact their payment provider or the business through a number they have verified themselves. If a payment has already been made, acting quickly matters. Contact the payment provider, explain what happened, and ask what steps are available for that transaction. Keep screenshots of the listing and conversation, along with the phone number and payment reference. Anyone who shared a PIN or code should secure the affected account immediately and report the incident. These records may help the provider and authorities investigate. Arko-Adjei says businesses must make it easier for customers to check they are dealing with the right people. Those that accept online bookings or deposits can make their official contact numbers and payment channels easy to find. A clear notice explaining how payments are requested, and stating that staff will never ask for a customer’s mobile money PIN or one-time code, gives people something to check against when a message feels wrong. Business owners should also search for their own names and check the phone numbers shown in map results. If they find an impersonator, they can report the listing to the platform and warn customers using their genuine accounts. Staff should know how to handle a report from someone who may have paid a fake account, including gathering the listing details and directing the customer to their payment provider. The warning comes ahead of Ghana’s National Cyber Security Awareness Month in October. At the campaign’s September launch, the CSA said it had recorded 3,876 cybersecurity incidents between January and July 2026, with online fraud making up about 47%. That figure covers online fraud generally; it is not a count of fake business listings. Arko-Adjei says the answer is to pause when a search result turns into a request for money: check the contact number, confirm any change in payment details, and keep PINs and security codes private. A short check before paying could spare a customer a far more difficult conversation afterwards. Suspicious listings and cybercrime incidents in Ghana can be reported to the CSA by calling or texting 292, sending a WhatsApp message to 050 160 3111, or emailing report@csa.gov.gh . Valerie Arko-Adjei is a cybersecurity GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) Professional with a background in behavioural science, focused on helping businesses and individuals understand risk and build stronger security habits through human-centred cybersecurity. She can be reached via adjeiv2@yahoo.com .

title: Seven dead, 11 injured in Gombe road crash
body:
Seven people, including three children, have died, while 11 others sustained injuries in a multiple-vehicle accident at Kumo in Akko Local Government Area of Gombe State.
The crash, which occurred at Tashan Magariya Junction along the Gombe–Billiri road at about 5:30 p.m. on Thursday, involved a heavy-duty truck, two Volkswagen Golf cars and five motorcycles.
An incident report by the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) attributed the accident to suspected brake failure, which reportedly caused the truck driver to lose control while travelling from Gombe towards Yola.
The truck subsequently collided with the two cars and five motorcycles, bringing the total number of vehicles involved to eight.
According to the report, the deceased comprised four adult men, two boys and a girl.
The 11 injured victims included four adult men, three adult women and four girls. They reportedly suffered various injuries, including severe fractures, cuts and bruises.
Although the FRSC recorded 25 people as being involved in the accident, the report did not provide details about the condition of the remaining seven individuals.
The agency said its personnel received an emergency call at 5:32 p.m. and reached the scene two minutes later.
The injured victims were taken to the Federal Medical Centre in Kumo for medical attention, while 11 people reportedly received first aid.
The vehicles involved in the crash were subsequently handed over to the Motor Traffic Division of the Nigeria Police Force in Kumo for further investigation and necessary action.
The identities of the deceased and the latest medical conditions of the injured victims were not immediately known.
The suspected mechanical failure that triggered the crash highlights the dangers faulty vehicles pose to motorists, motorcyclists and other road users.

title: Government pays over GH¢4.40bn to SSNIT and for second-tier pension obligations
body: Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson has announced that the government has paid over GH¢4.40 billion to the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT) and for the settlement of Second-Tier Pension obligations. According to him, the payments would help protect workers’ pensions and demonstrated the government’s commitment to managing public money responsibly and meeting its obligations. “Government has paid over GH¢4.40 billion to SSNIT and for Second-Tier Pension obligations,” Dr. Forson stated. “This helps protect workers’ pensions and shows our commitment to managing public money responsibly and meeting our obligations.” The announcement follows a similar disclosure by the Minister that the government had released GH¢24.8 billion to statutory funds since January 2026. Those payments were made on time and in full to support schools, healthcare, roads and local development. The Minister said timely releases ensure that the funds have the resources needed to deliver essential services to Ghanaians.

title: Anthropic's Claude now writes code and proves it safe automatically
body:
Anthropic used Claude to mathematically prove that existing code is correct. The approach tackles a core problem with AI-generated software but comes with strict practical limits.

Proving that software runs error-free under all circumstances has always been prohibitively expensive. A team of specialists needed 20 person-years just to formally verify the small operating system kernel seL4, so the method was reserved for extreme cases like Airbus avionics software.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with partner Theorem, let Claude take over the proof work instead. The model produced roughly 180 million lines of mathematical proof code in just a few weeks, drawing on test programs from 123 open-source libraries in Google's OSS-Fuzz security project.

Rather than writing new code, Claude verified existing software by translating crash tests into mathematical problems, analyzing the compiled machine code, and producing extensive proofs. An independent verification program called Rocq automatically checks those proofs, and according to Anthropic, the process needs almost no human reviewers. The researchers call it "fully autonomous" proof generation, though the tools and formal foundations were built by humans at Theorem.
Claude catches bugs that years of testing missed
While generating proofs, Claude ran into hundreds of bugs and was allowed to fix them itself. Many would have slipped past conventional testing because they only show up under very specific conditions, like unusually large input files or a particular sequence of accesses, the researchers say.

During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, for example, the team found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported for that software in an entire year. In another application, Claude caught a logical error that had gone undetected for over a decade. Even when a complete proof ultimately fails, Anthropic says, the attempt still surfaces real bugs.
What formal verification can and can't do
Anthropic acknowledges that "formally verified" doesn't mean "error-free." The proofs only hold under strict conditions: a specific processor architecture, single-threaded programs, and inputs under 64 MB. In practice, these libraries run on different hardware and in different configurations.

The compute cost is steep, with individual proofs running up hundreds of millions of tokens. Anthropic doesn't report total project costs. But if AI can verify its own code, developers can trust AI-generated software more and spend less time reviewing it. That saves costs not just on verification but on the entire coding process. A smaller test run also showed that proofs are reusable, and newer models are getting more efficient: Opus 5.5 solves half the proofs with about 40 percent fewer tokens than Opus 5.

The project strengthens the case for software automation. If AI can write code and guarantee its correctness under defined conditions, the question shifts from "Can AI program?" to "Can AI prove that the code it writes is safe?" If the answer is yes, the consequences could go well beyond today's coding tools.

Case in point: Anthropic expects formal verification with AI will soon become as practical as standard testing, and Theorem's roadmap already targets critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

title: Commercial vessel carrying Ukrainian sailors sinks off Romania's coast; drone attack not ruled out
body:
This was reported by the Romania Journal , according to Ukrinform.
The vessel was located 13 nautical miles from the Romanian port of Constanța. According to preliminary reports, it may have been struck by a drone.
There were 13 crew members on board the Khoryv, which was sailing under the flag of the Comoros: 10 Ukrainian citizens and three Azerbaijani citizens.
Romanian authorities received a distress signal, prompting a rescue operation to save the crew members on board the vessel.
The Romanian Maritime Transport Authority stated that nine sailors were rescued, three are missing, and one died.
It is noted that this 43-year-old vessel is an ore/oil carrier. According to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder, it was en route from the Turkish port of Ereğli to Sulina, Romania, where it was scheduled to arrive on Saturday.
As reported by Ukrinform, last week eight people went missing after a fire broke out on a San Marino-flagged tanker in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania, where a series of drone attacks has recently been recorded.

title: Text-to-Diagram for AI Systems: Designing a DSL an LLM Gets Right
body:
I have worked on sensor design, e-commerce, airlines, medicine and CAD software, in several countries. The domains could not be more different, yet one problem kept coming back: people do not understand each other. Not because they are careless. Everybody simply looks at the same system from a different side. Legal sees data, the CEO sees cost, DevOps sees uptime.
Take one sentence from a kick-off meeting:
âWe are building an agent to fix invoices.â
What does fix mean? Who uses it? Does it see customer data? Where does it run, and who owns it? Nobody asks, because everybody thinks they know. A year later the project has five different answers to each of those questions.
Large language models make this more urgent, not less. Anybody can now describe a system in a paragraph, and a model will happily draw it. The open question is whether that drawing is the architecture, or just an architecture.
Gnomon is my attempt at an answer. It is a small language, gnomocode, and a compiler that checks every statement against an ontology. A language model translates what people say into gnomocode; the compiler decides what is allowed; and the result can be drawn, queried and read back as prose. The compiler is written in Python, on top of Lark, rdflib and pySHACL.
I presented it as a keynote at DevAI by Data Science Summit in Warsaw on 20 October 2026, under the title of this article. This is the written version of that talk: why I built Gnomon, how it works, and what the measurements say about it.
Work in progress, October 2026. A public repository is being prepared. Until it exists, this article is the best description of what is built and why it looks the way it does.
Draw the invoice agent and you are done in five seconds: invoices go in, an agent does something, fixed invoices come out. The box is easy. The questions around it are the architecture: who owns the data, where the model runs, whether personal data is involved, who reviews the edge cases. That gap between words and a diagram somebody can be held to is what I wanted to close.
It has to work in both directions. Forward, from a conversation to a model that a developer, or an agent, can build from. Backward, from existing code and diagrams to text that people can read. The forward direction is the harder one, and it is what this article is mostly about.
Before writing any code, I wrote down what a language sitting in the middle has to offer:
The last one turned out to matter more than I expected.
I did not start with a language. I started with the cheapest option and let it fail.
Just ask the model. âDraw an architecture for an agent that fixes invoices.â The answer is fluent, plausible and different every time. It invents words, gives no errors and no line numbers, and there is nothing to diff. When it is wrong, nothing tells you where.
Objects. Pydantic [12] classes, filled in by the model through structured output. Validation is real and every provider supports it. But an architecture is a graph , not a tree. A missing fact is either an error or a null , and a conversation with a client is mostly missing facts. Two statements cannot be merged, nor can they contradict each other, and every new term means a new class and a new release. The vocabulary ends up cemented in code.
Existing notations. UML, BPMN, C4 [10] , ArchiMate and SysML v2 [11] are standards, and people understand them. They come with fixed symbols and a fixed depth, none of them has a âmaybeâ, and only some of them check whether a diagram makes sense , as opposed to whether it is drawn correctly.
A language of my own, with a compiler. This is the one that stayed. The idea is old and boring, which is how I like my ideas: let the model talk, let the compiler decide.
The translator, text2gnc, turns natural language into gnomocode. The compiler, which is plain rules with no model inside, checks each statement and builds a graph. When it finds errors, it sends them back to the translator with line numbers and hints. Everything else, diagrams for different audiences, recommendations, even prose, is drawn from the graph.
Two consequences matter to me. The script is the source of truth, not a single call to a model: the same script always compiles to the same graph. And errors are located and readable , so a person and a model can both act on them.
Before designing a single keyword, I went looking for who had already described this world. Plenty of people had. A taxonomy says what is a kind of what: a language model is a machine learning model. An ontology goes further and adds relations and rules: an agent uses a model, a model runs on an environment, and a dataset cannot run on anything at all. Such vocabularies have been written in RDF [1] for years, and some are widely used: SKOS [3] for taxonomies, PROV-O [2] for provenance, DCAT [4] for data catalogues, DPV [7] for privacy, QUDT [8] for units and schema.org [9] for the web. OWL [6] defines the classes and SHACL [5] checks the graphs.
So the rule became: take terms, relations, types and hierarchy from what exists, and add the minimum. The result is a kernel of 57 terms and twelve modules (systems, deployment, integration, data, ML, agents, processes, operations, security, legal, cost and service levels) that a script imports only when it needs them. From day one there was also a licence rule: nothing copyleft goes in, so that the whole thing can later be distributed freely and commercially.
Why call the ontology the key? Because every other part of Gnomon is generated from it or checked against it. Take a single word that a script writes, runs_on . In the ontology it has three layers: a lexicon entry that gives the word and its inverse reading, a property with a definition, and a shape that says what may stand on either side of it.
That one definition feeds the whole tool chain. The lexicon decides which words a script may use, and therefore which words a model may generate. The shape becomes the compilerâs error message, word for word. The labels become the English sentences in which a script is read back. The concerns attached to each term decide which audience sees it on a diagram. And because Gnomonâs classes are declared as subclasses of the borrowed ones (a gn:Dataset is also a dcat:Dataset and a prov:Entity ), the compiled graph is readable by tools that have never heard of Gnomon.
The grammar of gnomocode is generated from the kernel alone. Words come from the lexicon, so adding a module adds vocabulary without changing the grammar. Extending the language is a matter of editing data, not releasing code.
Why not let the model write RDF directly and validate it with SHACL? RDF is precise, but it is not something I want to read in a review. Here is the invoice agent as gnomocode, 23 lines:
It compiles to 76 lines of RDF. Three forms carry almost everything: name: Type declares an element, property = value states a fact about it, and action(object) says what it does. Flows connect steps ( >> ) and data ( -> ). The notation borrows from places people already know: front matter from Markdown, indented blocks and assignments from Python, arrows from graph query languages. Even the case of a word tells you its kind: Type , property , CONSTANT .
The front matter pins the release of the ontology the script was written against, says whether it describes the current state or a target, and imports only the modules the text needs. An old script therefore compiles against the same release, or gets migrated to a new one on purpose.
Look at the ~0.5 on the runs_on line. It means âI think so, but I am only half sureâ, and it is part of the language. Confidence has a few reference points: 1 is confirmed in a system or a document, 0.8 is stated by someone who does the work, 0.5 is second-hand, 0.2 is a guess. Below 0.7 a fact is not an error, but it is reported as a finding. In the graph it becomes an annotated statement, so you can query for everything that still needs confirming:
The invoice script uses only part of the language. Here is most of the rest in one script that compiles, with a comment on what each line does:
A few things are worth noticing. A declaration inside a block makes the element a part of its parent, so nesting is how you say âconsists ofâ. An action such as reads(product_catalogue) does not need a name: the compiler creates an unnamed activity of the right kind, with the agent as its performer and the catalogue as its input, and numbers it so that later lines can refer to it. And | in a flow means exactly one branch is taken, while & means all of them are.
The compiler is plain Python 3.14, managed with uv. Parsing is done by Lark [20] , a parsing toolkit for Python under the MIT licence. The grammar is not written by hand: gnomon grammar generates it from the kernel of the ontology, with one slot per class of words. A new module adds words, never grammar rules. An excerpt:
Indentation works exactly as in Python, because Lark ships a post-lexer for it. Subclass Indenter , name the tokens, and the LALR parser receives _INDENT and _DEDENT like any other token:
LALR keeps parsing fast and deterministic, which matters when the studio rechecks the script after every pause in typing. propagate_positions keeps the line and column of every node, so each diagnostic can point at the exact span of the source. A Lark Transformer turns the parse tree into statements; rdflib [21] builds the graph from them; the rules of the release derive further facts; and pySHACL [22] validates the result against the shapes of the ontology. Every violation is mapped back to the line it came from.
Mistype a word and the compiler answers like a linter, with the line, a caret and a suggestion taken from the lexicon:
Syntax errors look the same. Indent a block by three spaces instead of four and you get:
A script that compiles still gets its findings. For support.gnc above the verdict is compiles (0 errors, 12 warnings, 18 infos) , starting with lines such as:
With --format json the same diagnostics come as records. This is what the translator receives in the repair loop:
Each line of the script answers something somebody said. Suppose the kick-off meeting went on a few minutes longer. This is how its sentences map onto the script, and how the compiler reads each line back, in its own controlled English ( gnomon explain , no model involved):
The read-back matters more than it looks. A person who will never learn gnomocode can still check, sentence by sentence, whether the script says what they meant. And a language model that turns the script into prose works from these sentences, so it has nothing to guess.
The same lines are also a picture. The process line becomes the process view, with the branch, its condition and the performer of the review:
This is the principle I am most attached to. A real conversation is full of gaps and guesses. A language that rejects every incomplete statement will never be used; a language that accepts everything is useless. So the compiler draws a different line: it accepts vagueness and rejects contradictions.
invoice_agent: AIAgent is valid. It is vague, but it is true. The statements below are not, and the compiler says why, with the line and the reason taken straight from the ontology:
Diagnostics have three levels. Errors block; warnings and infos pass. The useful side effect is that the missing information turns into questions. The invoice script compiles, with 11 warnings and 15 infos, and those read like the agenda for the next meeting:
These are the questions nobody asked at the kick-off. The same messages, with their line numbers and hints, are what the translator receives in the repair loop. In practice that is what makes a language model usable here: it gets an error it can act on, not a shrug.
A diagram is a projection of the graph, not the model itself. Gnomon draws three views of a script (architecture, process and data lineage), filters them for an audience (executives, architects, legal and compliance, security, operations) and folds them to a level of detail. A lawyer sees the personal data and where it is kept; an architect sees every part.
The drawing itself is replaceable too. The same compiled graph goes to Gnomonâs own isometric canvas, to Mermaid, or to LikeC4, and nothing in the script changes:
Each renderer makes its own choices. The canvas sets the ERP on the slab of the cloud it runs on and marks personal data with a red lock. Mermaid labels every edge. LikeC4 stacks the same edges top-down. The facts underneath are identical, which is the point: you can argue about the picture without arguing about the system.
From the same graph, the rules of the ontology also recommend where an agent could take over work, ranked by effort, with the facts still missing to decide.
I did not want to show only a demo, so I built a way to measure the translation.
There are three measures. Coverage says how much of the original the prose still says. Faithfulness says how much of the prose the original supports. Graph F1 counts the facts two graphs share, and it is computed by code, with no model involved. The first two use a language model as a judge [13] : it extracts claims from a text, each with a quote of the original that code then verifies, and gives a verdict per claim.
The test set is 54 texts about architectures, agent systems, data pipelines, processes and audits, all from public sources that allow reuse: 40 from the Azure Architecture Center [18] , 5 from the GDS Way [17] and 9 algorithmic transparency records of the UK government [19] . Each has a golden script written for it.
With Claude Sonnet 5.5 as the translator, all 54 texts ended up as scripts that compile. 29 compiled at once, 23 needed one repair round, and 2 needed two or three.
Of 100 claims in an original text, 58 survive the round trip. The interesting part is where the other 42 go. Splitting the loss into layers shows that about 40 are lost because the language, and my golden scripts, cannot say them yet. The translator loses only 7.
I find this the most useful result of the whole project. The bottleneck is the language, not the translator. That is a very different to-do list from âuse a bigger modelâ, and it tells me which words to add next.
Not blindly. The judge finds every claim of a text in the text itself, and 99.7 of 100 in a text with a fifth of its sentences removed. But when asked to notice the removed claims, it caught only 57 of 100. Two different judges (gpt-oss-120b and Claude Haiku 4.5) gave the same verdict on 73% of 6,054 claims, a Cohenâs kappa of 0.55, which counts as moderate [14] .
The graph measure needs no judge. Against its own golden graph, a generated graph scores an F1 of 0.56 on average; against the golden graph of a different text, 0.29.
So the graph is clearly about the right text, and only about half of its facts match. Part of that is the translator choosing different relations and levels of detail for the same fact: two translations of one text agree with each other at an F1 of 0.74. This is enough for a demo, not yet proof, and I would rather say so here than have you find out.
All of this sits behind a local web page, Gnomon Studio: the chat on the left, the script in the middle with live diagnostics and its description in plain English, and the diagram on the right. You describe a system, a script appears, compiles or repairs itself, and the picture updates. Every later message extends the script instead of starting again.
What is next: separating the public repository (the ontology, the compiler and the studio); conventions that narrow the ways of writing one fact, since the same text still gives different scripts; words for the 40% the language cannot say yet; and the backward direction at scale, from existing code and diagrams to text.
If you work on architecture descriptions, agent systems, or on making language models and rules cooperate, I would be glad to hear from you. Gnomon is also meant as a working tool for audits: mapping the processes and data of a company before anyone builds an agent for them. The project page collects the scenarios I have translated so far.

title: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 23 (MNA) – IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi said the United States has suffered strategic defeats in the war with Iran, including damage to its claims of ensuring regional security and protecting energy flows.
In remarks published by Iranian media on Friday, Mohebbi said the enemy initially sought to change Iran’s political system and disintegrate the country, before dividing its objectives into 13 smaller goals, none of which it achieved.
He said the war has undermined Washington’s claim that its military presence in the region guaranteed security, noting that despite its large naval fleet and numerous regional bases, the United States had faced challenges in ensuring security and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC spokesman described the situation as a contradiction in US military doctrine, saying bases intended to provide security had instead become sources of insecurity.
He also said the war had called into question Washington’s claims of intelligence superiority and exposed the vulnerabilities of its intelligence centers and bases.
The targeting of US fighter jets, destruction of air defense systems and operations against American naval equipment, he added, had dealt a blow to the country’s claimed technological and military superiority.
Mohebbi further stated that the United States had suffered damage to its international standing, saying its reputation had already been affected by the Jeffrey Epstein case and had been further tarnished by the targeting of the Minab school and the killing of children.
He also pointed to the economic consequences of the war for the United States, citing rising fuel prices and the country’s need for raw materials, including aluminum, as signs of mounting economic difficulties.
Concluding his remarks, the IRGC spokesman praised the Iranian people’s resilience, saying their achievements during the period of resistance had been remarkable and deserved recognition.

title: Russia, US managing to build constructive and pragmatic dialogue — Foreign Ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Moscow and Washington are currently managing to rebuild constructive and generally pragmatic dialogue at various levels, Russian Foreign Ministry Department of North Atlantic Affairs Director Alexander Gusarov said in an interview with the International Affairs magazine.
"It is encouraging that, following US President Donald Trump’s return to power, we have been able to rebuild constructive and generally pragmatic dialogue both between the leaders of our countries and between our foreign ministries," he noted.
At the same time, Gusarov stressed that the restoration of "constructive elements in Russia-US dialogue does not mean the automatic resolution of the numerous, deeply rooted and fairly systemic problems and disagreements that accumulated over the years under previous administrations."

title: Witkoff Meets Putin: the Upshot?
body:
Following the meeting between Vladimir Putin and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are set to resume. However, Witkoff describing Putin as a “humanitarian” during the meeting has drawn criticism even from US Republicans. The press looks at who stands to benefit from Trump’s attempts at mediation .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Der Standard (Austria) takes issue with the American special envoy’s fawning praise of Putin:
“No one has ever called him that before. That’s a first. How will Vladimir Putin react to Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, calling him a ‘humanitarian’? Witkoff is a property developer and Trump’s golfing buddy, and together with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he keeps meeting up with Russian envoys and Putin himself in a bid to end the war in Ukraine. Two wheeler-dealers with no clue about foreign policy who have achieved absolutely nothing so far.”
The US’s haste risks rewarding Russia for its patient strategy, La Stampa (Italy) warns:
“Putin can already derive political advantages from the negotiations, without having to halt the war. Winter will put this strategy to the test. Moscow will seek to weaken Ukraine while the Ukrainians try to protect their cities and hold the front line. In the meantime, acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and disinformation aim to undermine European unity and the consensus on aid to Ukraine. Putin is banking on wearing down Ukrainian resistance and the West’s willingness to support Ukraine.”
Ukraine is not about to throw in the towel, says Aamulehti (Finland):
“Even if the United States were to side fully with Russia, the war in Ukraine would not end. The massacre in Bucha has shown what happens to Ukrainians at the hands of the Russians, which is why Ukraine will not give up the fight. How long would the war last, and how would it end? Recent history answers that question. France waged war in Indochina for eight years. The US fought the Vietnam War in that region for 20 years, ten of which with its own troops. The Soviet Union waged war in Afghanistan for ten years, and the US for twenty. Each of these wars ended in defeat for the major power waging the war.”
Writing on Facebook, author Carina Cockrell-Ferre (Russia) discusses the possibility of a Russian attack on Europe:
“The greatest danger facing Europe is that Putin could form a full alliance with Trump, who then assures him that he will not honour the terms of Article 5 of the Nato Treaty. ... This could indeed lead to a Russian attack on Europe. This is the common ground over which these two diabolical old men have joined forces. ... While Europe may be able to block a bad deal for Ukraine, it is powerless to push through a good one. All it can do is delay a Russian attack on Europe by supporting Ukraine and its armed forces.”
Kremlin giving no sign of being ready to negotiate
Future meetings are also unlikely to yield any tangible results, The Spectator observes (Germany):
“There has been nothing to suggest yet that the Russian president is genuinely ready to make a deal or concede on his war aims. ... Facing the prospect of brutal midterm results for the Republicans in two weeks’ time, Trump is desperate for a win with Russia. Putin can sense this and appears to be using this to play for time ahead of a winter in which he hopes to make substantial progress on subjugating Ukraine. Not for the first time, it is Zelensky who is being forced to jump through hoops and show willing in the hope that doing so will save his country from a stitch-up by an enemy and supposed ally.”
The US’s policies of recent weeks are having repercussions across the world, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) points out:
“Putin and his inner circle are convinced that in the war against Ukraine and their struggle against the West as a whole, they will firstly have the greater staying power, and secondly be able to play the Americans and Europeans off against one another. Everything the American leadership has done in recent weeks confirms this belief. Consequently, the prospect of a ceasefire, not to mention peace in Ukraine, has become even more remote. Instead, the Kremlin is likely to feel emboldened to escalate the conflict even further. ‘Restoring justice of Russians’ takes place above all on the battlefield, Putin’s foreign minister has said.”
Unlike Trump, Putin is not in a hurry, notes Corriere della Sera (Italy):
“For five years now, Vladimir Putin seems to have been applying the old Russian proverb ‘The slower you go, the further you’ll get’ to a war that he originally thought would last no more than two weeks. … So Putin is biding his time, waiting to see how events unfold and what happens with the elections in the US and Europe – and taking whatever he can get without making any concessions. He has the chance to achieve in Washington what he is unable to achieve on the front line; but he also knows that this window of opportunity could be closed again by a single social media post in the middle of the night. ... What the Russian president needs to work out now is whether the path available to Trump will be long enough.”
The US President’s supposedly new stance on the war in Ukraine is not really new at all, argues Dagens Nyheter (Sweden):
“Some interpret this as the US changing sides with regard to Ukraine, and it’s easy to understand why Zelensky feels betrayed. Yet this development is nothing new. The difference is that Trump is no longer making a secret of what he has wanted all along: for Russia and his friend Vladimir Putin to win the war. ... Trump’s eagerness to help Putin now is particularly good news for the Kremlin. Russia is in a bad way, both on the front line and at home, where all its oil depots are burning. So it’s good that it has an ally in the White House.”
Experts will continue to puzzle over the US president’s policy on Ukraine, says Ilta-Sanomat (Finland):
“A clear intention can certainly be discerned behind Trump’s confused remarks on Ukraine and Russia. He wants to take credit for bringing about peace. But does anyone still believe he could actually achieve such a thing? After all this, can anyone still trust Trump’s word when it comes, for example, to security guarantees for Ukraine, which are a key safeguard for peace? ... When the war in Ukraine eventually ends and Trump is no longer president, a lot will be written about current events. Perhaps the most important question then will be: what on earth was going through Trump’s mind? It won’t make for pleasant reading.”

title: A Tale of Three Months with AI: Guardrails, and How We Are More Alike Than We
body:
As I prom­ised in A fresh leaf , I want to share my ex­per­i­ences with us­ing LLMs for agen­tic de­vel­op­ment in the last three months. Sum­mar­ised: I star­ted as an ini­tial scep­tic, be­came quite en­thu­si­astic, and am now mod­er­ately en­thu­si­astic and guarded for the fu­ture. Al­low me to take you through my jour­ney.
Com­ing from a back­ground of rig­or­ous en­gin­eer­ing with up-front think­ing about pro­gram struc­tures, al­gorithms, and types, it seemed in­com­pre­hens­ible to me how a jumped-up neural net could gen­er­ate work­ing code, let alone sens­ible sys­tems. How to write un­der­stand­able soft­ware has been hotly de­bated for dec­ades, con­tinu­ously shift­ing as new lan­guages, type sys­tems, and eco­sys­tems in­tro­duce dif­fer­ent trade-offs.
Early in my ca­reer, com­ing from aca­demia, I was fix­ated on find­ing the “just-right” solu­tion: el­eg­ant ab­strac­tions, strict cor­rect­ness, and formal sound­ness. As prob­lems grew lar­ger and messier, and time be­came scarce, hold­ing out for per­fec­tion be­came an obstacle. I found far more sat­is­fac­tion in achiev­ing some­thing func­tional, with el­eg­ance as a wel­come second. Hav­ing both over­lap is fant­astic; achiev­ing the ac­tual goal re­mains both a pri­or­ity and a ne­ces­sity.
This shift in per­spect­ive ex­plains why LLMs, and agen­tic de­vel­op­ment, even­tu­ally proved so at­tract­ive to me. Ex­pect­ing a model to gen­er­ate a “just-right” ar­chi­tec­ture, code, or text only causes frus­tra­tion. Con­versely, it acts as an en­gine to reach con­crete mile­stones in areas I was al­ways curi­ous about without hav­ing the time to do things “prop­erly”, or simply elim­in­at­ing the toil of writ­ing boil­er­plate when I can de­scribe my in­tent with less mech­an­ical pre­ci­sion.
If your goal is simply to achieve some­thing con­crete, they are re­mark­ably ef­fect­ive. That spans from some­thing as simple as in­teg­rat­ing an un­fa­mil­iar lib­rary to break­ing ground in an un­fa­mil­iar prob­lem do­main where you lack the tools and vocab­u­lary.
My cata­lyst was a device sit­ting in my liv­ing room. After re­ports emerged that its suc­cessor was ag­gress­ively hos­tile to user pri­vacy, I wanted to verify whether my own hard­ware be­haved the same way. Since I had no back­ground in firm­ware in­spec­tion or packet ana­lysis on em­bed­ded devices, I was ini­tially dis­cour­aged. Luck­ily, I no­ticed right then that I had a free trial month of Co­dex ly­ing around, so I de­cided to see how far these so- called “amaz­ing fron­tier” mod­els could carry me.
I star­ted out by talk­ing in ChatGPT and ask­ing ques­tions on how to solve my prob­lem.
This quickly be­came us­ing Co­dex to work on my laptop, let­ting it down­load im­ages, and run­ning local scripts. The way of work was very in­ter­act­ive, prompt-based, and re­l­at­ively un­struc­tured and un­guided.
I was amazed by how well the model worked when told to achieve a very spe­cific goal and even more so when giv­ing the con­text and con­straints in a single prompt: as long as the prompt wasn’t too big.
When I poin­ted out er­rors, the mod­els com­pli­men­ted me lav­ishly on the dis­cov­ery and apo­lo­gised pro­fusely for the de­fect. 1 Yet that con­tri­tion yiel­ded no dur­able change in their sub­sequent be­ha­viour. It was just text, learned from reams of doc­u­ments.
As soon as the code­base and pro­gram to de­tect any ne­far­i­ous be­ha­viour was grow­ing, I no­ticed the per­form­ance of the mod­els de­grade. 2 Re­sponses lost their ini­tial speed, pre­ci­sion, and cor­rect­ness. The model began over­look­ing in­ter­de­pend­ent up­dates that re­quired lock-step co­ordin­a­tion, shed­ding con­text es­tab­lished in earlier turns. In other words, it re­quired more hand-holding, for which I had neither time, nor pa­tience, nor ap­pet­ite.
At that point, I also star­ted work­ing on some other ideas that had been ly­ing dormant in my head. I used an agent to cre­ate a Ter­ra­form pro­ject to spin up a small timeseries- db backup in Google Cloud con­strained such that it would stay within the free tier. Cre­at­ing the pro­vi­sion­ing scripts was the work of mere mo­ments. It checked the ex­act siz­ing re­quire­ments for stay­ing within the free tier in­clud­ing some caveats, whipped the Ter­ra­form code to­gether, and ad­ded the Tails­cale in­teg­ra­tion. All from a simple prompt of what I wanted to achieve and the fact that I wanted to be able to re­con­struct the VM from a single com­mand. That was awe­some.
It was here that I first star­ted sus­pect­ing a deeper link between mod­els and hu­mans: it all came down to how bounded the task was. Over the years, I no­ticed that when you ask a per­son an open-ended ques­tion, their an­swer is mostly in­flu­enced by their re­cent his­tory, their emo­tional state, and whatever prob­lem they were just wrest­ling with. Mod­els work al­most identic­ally. Ask them a broad, open-ended ques­tion and you get a gen­eric re­sponse shaped by their pre-trained weights and im­me­di­ate con­text win­dow. Get­ting either a hu­man or a model to think out­side that de­fault box re­quires tight, ex­pli­cit con­straints, and care­ful prod­ding (or prompt­ing).
One of the of­ten touted best-practices I en­countered in the be­gin­ning was to have a three- phase ap­proach. Use one agent to plan the work in­ter­act­ively, pro­du­cing a han­dover doc­u­ment. Then task a second agent with im­ple­ment­ing that han­dover doc­u­ment un­at ­ ten­ded. Fi­nally pass the con­trol to a re­view agent, which gets the diff and the plan, and re­views it. The ob­vi­ous im­prove­ment is to make the last two com­mu­nic­ate and work in a loop un­til no more find­ings are es­tab­lished.
I first tried auto­mat­ing this di­vi­sion of work (plan­ning, im­ple­ment­a­tion, and re­view) by writ­ing con­ven­tions as prose in AGENTS.md . As code grew and threads grew longer, how­ever, prose in­struc­tions be­came less ef­fect­ive and eas­ily ig­nored by the model. To take this work­flow fur­ther, I wanted to com­bine the spe­cial­ised strengths of dif­fer­ent mod­els: Co­dex as the fast, local work­horse for writ­ing code, and Gem­ini as the thought­ful re­viewer for ar­chi­tec­ture. To let them talk dir­ectly to each other, I built gemini-mcp .
Here I hit an­other quirk of model psy­cho­logy: autonom­ous mod­els pos­sess such su­preme self-certainty that re­view trig­gers re­quire ex­pli­cit pro­gram­matic con­di­tions. A loose prose dir­ect­ive like “Ask Gem­ini for help when un­cer­tain” gen­er­ated pre­cisely zero in­voc­a­tions; the model was never un­cer­tain. Con­versely, a de­term­in­istic cir­cuit breaker (“At­tempt to solve each prob­lem a max­imum of three times; if still fail­ing, con­sult Gem­ini via MCP, im­ple­ment its re­com­mend­a­tions, and re­peat”) re­li­ably promp­ted Co­dex to es­cal­ate for second opin­ions.
This put me with an im­me­di­ate se­cur­ity chal­lenge: be­cause I was us­ing this setup to as ­ sess the pri­vacy of the TV, I needed a clas­si­fier to pre­vent prompts between mod­els from look­ing like of­fens­ive se­cur­ity probes, which could get my Google ac­count sus­pen­ded.
Scaf­fold­ing the clas­si­fier was quick work. Mak­ing it func­tion re­li­ably, how­ever, in­volved dozens of subtle ar­chi­tec­tural choices that flew past too fast for me to prop­erly eval­u­ate. Steer­ing the model through prose in AGENTS.md simply wasn’t giv­ing me the con­trol I needed. That was the mo­ment I turned to sys­tem­atic, de­term­in­istic tool­ing, start­ing with a simple dir­ect­ive: run make check after every modi­fic­a­tion to verify that the pro­ject was still co­her­ent.
This worked so well that ever since I have been ex­tend­ing what is be­hind this check con­tinu­ously. Re­ly­ing on what I already knew worked well in lar­ger pro­jects with mul­tiple con­trib­ut­ors, I de­cided to use strict tools to check as much as pos­sible. This meant auto­matic lint­ing, format­ting, and up­grades of the dif­fer­ent types of files in the pro­ject: Mark­down, code, YAML files, ADRs, format­ting, mod­ern­isa­tion of Go, and de­pend­ency up­grades. Moreover, I de­cided to take more out of the hands from the agents and not even bother them with format­ting and easy to fix lint­ing er­rors by auto­mat­ic­ally run­ning format­ting, auto­matic im­ports, and adding --fix to golangci-lint already as part of the check step to en­sure all easy fixes were im­ple­men­ted be­fore the agent even saw the res­ult. 3
I in­tro­duced this rig­or­ous track­ing in my first big vibe-coded pro­ject, semantic-editor . The whole point of the pro­ject was to let the agent worry about in­tent while del­eg­at­ing the nitty-gritty edit­ing work to de­term­in­istic AST tools. I ap­plied that same mind­set to the re­pos­it­ory it­self, us­ing strict checks for the mark­down, the ADRs, and the schemas. This ap­proach worked pretty well, and the pro­ject was pro­gress ­ ing smoothly.
Around that time, an­other per­sonal pro­ject came into my head. I had al­ways felt sad that in this age of search en­gines and lately om­ni­scient (and of­ten wrong) LLMs, my kids didn’t have the ex­per­i­ence to just browse an en­cyc­lo­pe­dia, guided by in­terest. For me the con­crete ex­ample of this was Mi­crosoft En­carta ‘97. It gave me end­less brows­ing, learn­ing of all kinds of things, and im­port­ant to my par­ents (and now me), re­l­at­ively safe be­cause it was cur­ated con­tent.
As you may have guessed, I de­cided to vibe code the an­swer to this prob­lem as well and make a viewer of En­carta data. Be­cause in-repository de­cision track­ing had op­er­ated sat­is­fact­or­ily, I re­lied on that es­tab­lished har­ness to guide de­vel­op­ment.
How­ever, be­cause this was my first GUI app, I sensed it needed an­other layer of con ­ straints and de­cision track­ing which I dubbed “GUI-invariants” as a spe­cial­ised form of ADR for GUI de­cisions such as lay­out on a more gen­eric level in­stead of spe­cific de­cisions. Get­ting the agent to con­sider the in­vari­ants proved re­l­at­ively simple by just adding it to the agent in­struc­tions. Let­ting it in­ter­pret them in a way was harder, be­cause in­vari­ants are in­her­ently gen­eric. So they needed more con­crete pos­it­ive and neg­at­ive ex­amples and be more pre­script­ive.
For some reason I had a quirk that I wanted all text to be “prop­erly” type-set such as in TeX. And why not? We are cus­tom cod­ing this pro­ject and I have tokens to burn, so let’s have at it. The agent was very help­ful in this bounded con­text. A simple as­sign­ment, a start­ing ex­ample al­gorithm, the spe­cific con­straint of the SwiftUI in­fra­struc­ture, and an or­acle to de­term­ine whether it did it right. This al­lowed me to set a simple goal and I could walk away from it.
These three main pro­jects and sev­eral side pro­jects, all shared one im­port­ant prop­erty: they were green­field pro­jects where I in­di­vidu­ally was the sole owner and de­cision maker.
In urban plan­ning terms, green­field land is ef­fort­less to tra­verse and de­velop, pre­cisely be­cause it is vir­gin ground: un­touched, open, and un­en­cumbered by his­tory. Brown­field sites, by con­trast, are con­tam­in­ated swaths of land burdened by bur­ied found­a­tions, un­doc­u­mented pipelines, and wrapped in a ven­eer of toxic leg­acy waste. Left un­at­ten ­ ded, soft­ware tends to fol­low an identical tra­ject­ory. When pro­jects ex­pand without dis­cip­line, the vir­gin meadow rap­idly de­teri­or­ates into a muddy, haz­ard­ous swamp that en­gin­eers dread to touch.
Yet that de­cay is avoid­able. Long-lived sys­tems like the Linux ker­nel sur­vive dec­ades of churn not through bur­eau­cratic up­front plan­ning, but through un­com­prom­ising main ­ tainer gate­keep­ing: strict sub­sys­tem bound­ar­ies, re­lent­less re­view against es­tab­lished pat­terns, and clear com­mit ra­tionale. 4 We should learn the les­son and ap­ply it to agen­tic pro­gram­ming. Be­cause gen­eral pur­pose mod­els lack this in­her­ent in­sti­tu­tional memory and in­trinsic mo­tiv­a­tion, we must co­dify that gate­keep­ing dir­ectly into the en­vir­on­ment: track­ing ar­chi­tec­tural de­cisions, en­for­cing in­vari­ant suites, and main­tain­ing de­term­in ­ istic mech­an­ical guard­rails.
Handled with that dis­cip­line, a code­base avoids be­com­ing a toxic brown­field. In­stead, it be­comes a cul­tiv­ated glass­house : a struc­tured, highly pro­duct­ive en­vir­on­ment where auto­mated checks sup­ply con­tinu­ous nour­ish­ment, and re­cor­ded con­text al­lows de­vel ­ op­ment to con­tinue to flour­ish at speed.
While agents seem to shine on green­field pro­jects that they man­age them­selves, which is why vi­be­cod­ing works so well, they start fall­ing flat when pro­jects be­come lar­ger or they need to be used in es­tab­lished pro­jects. This is be­cause the struc­ture agents use to loc­ate where to make changes mir­rors the lat­ent pat­terns in­grained dur­ing train­ing. 5 What a co­in­cid­ence, this is also the same for hu­man en­gin­eers.
My ex­per­i­ence cre­at­ing the ini­tial draft of the dynamic-fault-injection fil­ter for an open-source “Built on En­voy” pro­ject ex­posed this bound­ary. I had the found­a­tional dis­tri­bu­tion for­mula and prior ex­per­i­ence run­ning it in a JVM-based side­car; dir­ect­ing an agent to scaf­fold the ini­tial Go plu­gin was straight­for­ward. The fric­tion began when in­teg­rat­ing it up­stream. Un­like self-owned pro­jects where you can in­vent your own short­cuts, I needed to fit cleanly into the project’s es­tab­lished dis­cip­line: ad­her­ing to its battle-tested test pat­terns, doc­u­ment­a­tion con­ven­tions, and re­pos­it­ory lay­outs.
Any­one can staple a quick fix onto a code­base, and just that quickly an­other wart is ad­ded. The ac­tual chal­lenge is fig­ur­ing out where the change truly be­longs, and do­ing the painstak­ing re­work so it looks like it was de­signed that way from the start. Oc­ca­sional con­trib­ut­ors face this con­stantly: de­cid­ing when to live with an ex­ist­ing pat­tern, and when to roll up your sleeves and re­write sur­round­ing code to make it fit prop­erly.
Nav­ig­at­ing that fric­tion suc­ceeded primar­ily be­cause I re­ceived gen­er­ous, pre­cise guid ­ ance from the lead main­tainer. That hu­man feed­back sup­plied the un­spoken re­pos­it­ory con­text and ar­chi­tec­tural in­tent that neither I nor the model could ex­tract from the code alone.
I could then feed those main­tainer in­sights dir­ectly back into prompts, giv­ing the agent the con­crete bound­ar­ies it needed to shape the im­ple­ment­a­tion cor­rectly.
How­ever, sit­ting down quietly with a cup of tea and look­ing over the code, I real­ised the code or­gan­isa­tion was still a bit off. That in­tu­ition was only avail­able as lat­ent skill in my head based on code scattered across the re­pos­it­ory, and ad­mit­tedly not ap­plied con­sist­ently enough for an un­trained eye like mine on the pro­ject. This is where con­crete ADRs and con­trib­ut­ing guides earn their keep: they turn what is locked in maintainers’ heads into ex­pli­cit rules agents can ac­tu­ally read.
When tack­ling big­ger pro­jects, and more-insufficient us­age lim­its, I star­ted look­ing into other mod­els and no­ticed that the model fam­il­ies tend to have sim­ilar be­ha­viour.
To me these are the qual­i­fic­a­tions of the model fam­il­ies, that I have per­sonal ex­per­i­ence with. Even though they are a math­em­at­ical prob­ab­il­istic bag of para­met­ers, they seem to have emer­gent per­son­al­it­ies:
Hy­per­act­ive Ju­nior En­gin­eer Qwen : The Qwen fam­ily (both 3.6 dense, MoE, and 3.8) gen­er­ates code at blis­ter­ing speed, rarely paus­ing to ask ques­tions. It de­mands highly gran­u­lar guid­ance. The 2-bit Sa­luki quant­isa­tion dis­plays this im­puls­ive­ness even more acutely.
Ex­pens­ive easily-distracted CS Pro­fessor Gem­ini : Ex­tremely strong at re­du­cing a prob­lem de­scrip­tion to its core and find­ing the aca­demic con­sensus on the solu­tion fit. It is par­tic­u­larly strong in Go and machine-learning top­ics, and great at ex­plain­ing why mod­els be­have in cer­tain ways. Es­pe­cially at the ar­chi­tec­ture level.
How­ever, it is ex­pens­ive for routine cod­ing, not that fast or good , and gets stuck in re­pet­it­ive read loops, end­lessly in­spect­ing files without mak­ing changes:
Gem­ini 4.0 Ar­gon is even worse for every­day work: a re­view of a small piece of text burns through 50% of my weekly Pro al­low­ance. No mat­ter how good it is, it is un­us­able in this way.
De­pend­able, rabbit-holing work­horse GPT : This is the fam­ily that is ac­tu­ally in­ter­est ­ ing, es­pe­cially given the pri­cing strategies. In gen­eral, I found GPT to rabbit-hole into a par­tic­u­lar solu­tion dir­ec­tion faster and re­fuse to get out of it, where Gem­ini could step back. Sol 6.1 (and prior with 5.6 Terra) is the per­fect re­viewer and Luna (both 5.6 and 6) is the per­fect work­horse. Luna is de­cently smart, but es­pe­cially be­cause it is vir­tu­ally free. Both Sol and Luna have the tend­ency to double down on a chosen path and are very hard to get to think out­side the box or take a step back.
Across all these model fam­il­ies, one shared quirk emerged: an al­most in­furi­at­ing de­fault bias to­ward Py­thon for writ­ing quick scripts. In­struct­ing an agent ex­pli­citly not to use Py­thon in­vari­ably yiel­ded TypeScript. This is clearly the grav­it­a­tional pull of pub­lic train ­ ing data, where Py­thon and TypeScript ex­amples dwarf everything else. 6 It con­stantly left me long­ing for some­thing like goshell : a single stan­dalone Go file de­clar­ing its de­pend­en­cies in­line, ex­ecuted dir­ectly without scaf­fold­ing an en­tire mod­ule.
AI com­pan­ies love to shout about break­throughs at the ab­so­lute peak of their fron­tier mod­els. Yet what ac­tu­ally changed my day-to-day ex­per­i­ence was not a dra­matic leap in the raw in­tel­li­gence of the top tier. The real shift was the surge in qual­ity among the af­ford­able mod­els: the ones ac­tu­ally in reach for every­day work. A model like Sol 6.1 brings reas­on­ing that used to be­long ex­clus­ively to flag­ships, but at a price where you can af­ford to keep it run­ning con­tinu­ously in tight feed­back loops. It is not that the ab­so­lute Pareto fron­tier has moved, but that the af­ford­able Pareto fron­tier has moved. In that sense, prac­tical agen­tic de­vel­op­ment has be­come far more of an eco­nom­ics game than a sci­ence game. 7 Slash­ing the price of a mon­ster flag­ship like As­tra or Ar­gon would be an easy way to win the “smartest model” con­test, but sub­sid­ising those gar­gan­tuan in­fer­ence costs would burn through cash at a stag­ger­ing rate. The pro­vider that wins the prac­tical de­veloper eco­sys­tem won’t ne­ces­sar­ily be the one with the cleverest pa­per, but the one that de­liv­ers re­li­able reas­on­ing at a price where hun­dreds of daily it­er­a­tions don’t break the bank.
Choos­ing the right model for the task at hand is an im­port­ant part of be­ing able to work in large code-bases. How­ever, more is needed.
Look­ing back at my ca­reer on what made suc­cess­ful teams achieve their suc­cesses be­sides their so­cial skills and trust among them­selves, was the fact that they spend time on great tool­ing. Even the best of minds have a limit to how much they can keep in their RAM, how fast they can write new code, and how fast they can di­li­gently re­view code.
They use tools to pre­vent dis­cus­sions about code style by ap­ply­ing lin­ters and auto format­ting rules, any­where from in a check com­mand, a git hook, or in the PR re­views. This avoids noise.
They have an in­teg­ral test-suite, that lets them move fast ahead with ideas, while mis­takes are still caught. This in­teg­ral test suite goes fur­ther than mere unit tests and in­cludes tools that have been around in vari­ous vari­ations.
No­tice how far away this is from reams of prose. Hu­mans with a lim­ited span of at­ten­tion and lim­ited brain ca­pa­city can­not map their every ac­tion against a book­work of ar­chi ­ tec­ture and pro­ced­ural rules, it would be too time con­sum­ing. They use heur­ist­ics to drive their “on­line” work, and “off­line” guard rails to pre­vent their over­sights from hit­ting cus­tomer im­pact. These same meas­ures ap­ply with agen­tic cod­ing.
Be­cause agents are LLMs with ex­tra rules, as long as you have com­pute power, and suf­fi­cient sup­ply of well thought out jobs / is­sues, the agents can pro­duce code faster and without bot­tle­necks. This in­creases the lever­age, arm, or mul­ti­plier of how much agents be­ne­fit from hav­ing these guard­rails in place.
Guard­rails in the form of rig­or­ous auto­mated test suites, as in­tro­duced above, carry us only so far. They can­not re­mem­ber the WHY : why do we have a cer­tain test, why do we im­ple­ment a fea­ture, why did we choose a par­tic­u­lar lib­rary.
In smal­ler, one-person green­field pro­jects, re­cord­ing the de­cisions in simple ADRs was good enough to keep the agent bounded and give me a mech­an­ism for manu­ally point­ing out to ad­here to the ADRs. In sprawl­ing brown­fields and cul­tiv­ated glass­houses alike, de­cisions come from many dif­fer­ent dir­ec­tions; the in­sti­tu­tional ex­per­i­ence of the en­gin­eer­ing corps is het­ero­gen­eous and in con­tinu­ous flux.
This is what or­gan­isa­tional the­or­ists and soft­ware ar­chi­tects also refer to as “In­sti­tu­tional memory”. 8
In hu­mans this know­ledge is gradu­ally in­grained into the en­gin­eer through ex­per­i­ence. If you are lucky they stay on the pro­jects long enough to provide con­tinu­ity.
Agents have no such con­text at all. Ac­tu­ally, en­gin­eers are also fal­lible. They can for­get. (Con­text com­pac­tion and fresh ses­sions) They can have a lapse of fo­cus or be­ing dis ­ turbed. (The “lost-in-the-middle” ef­fect 9 .) They can move on to a new pro­ject. (Start­ing brand new chats.)
With agents, that de­par­ture hap­pens con­stantly: every time you open a brand-new chat thread, every un­re­cor­ded in­sight simply evap­or­ates into /dev/null (un­less you count the pro­vider re­train­ing on your prompts ;-) ).
Thus we need a sys­tem that ac­tu­ally be­ne­fits both en­gin­eers and agents and so I ex­ten­ded the har­ness in two ways:
First: I in­tro­duced Re­search Ques­tions , cap­tur­ing the in­tent of any change or fea­ture. Ba­sic­ally it rep­res­ents the in­box to the pro­ject. Be­fore an im­ple­ment­a­tion starts, stake ­ hold­ers and en­gin­eers dis­cuss goals, trade-offs, and ex­plore al­tern­at­ives. This leads to what to build and more im­port­antly what not to build. This is con­text that very rarely sur­vives into is­sues, pull-requests, and/or com­mit mes­sages and is there­fore lost. By re­cord­ing these de­lib­er­a­tions in the re­search ques­tions, it re­tains this in­form­a­tion while at the same time also al­lows ADRs to stay small, con­crete, and fo­cussed, to stay kind to the lim­ited con­text win­dows of Agents.
Secondly: Even with this mech­an­ism in place, I no­ticed that there was still drift so I ad­ded a rule to check nightly or weekly to do a full re­con­cili­ation of changes against es­tab­lished ADRs and of code against Re­search Ques­tions to see whether new data had come in or we ac­tu­ally already made de­cisions.
This now closes the loop in the har­ness:
This high­lights a fun­da­mental par­al­lel: the core en­gin­eer­ing dis­cip­line re­mains identical for hu­man en­gin­eers and autonom­ous agents; only the ex­e­cu­tion ve­lo­city dif­fers. Im­prove­ments in­tro­duced for en­gin­eers be­ne­fit agents even more dra­mat­ic­ally. We must heed what soft­ware en­gin­eer­ing has demon­strated over the past half-century.
This en­tire har­ness stems from a core con­vic­tion: let the neural net fo­cus on high-level reas­on­ing and in­tent, while let­ting de­term­in­istic CPU tools handle the mech­an­ical veri­fic­a­tion.
Com­pilers (es­pe­cially with strong type check­ers), lin­ters, and test suites ex­ecute in mil­li ­ seconds with ab­so­lute cer­tainty. Burn­ing ex­pens­ive, prob­ab­il­istic tokens on veri­fic­a­tion that a local bin­ary handles in mi­cro­seconds is waste­ful in the ex­treme.
This same con­vic­tion also drives my pref­er­ence for dense lan­guages such as Haskell. Strict types, pur­ity as a first prin­ciple, and a dense syn­tax help to keep func­tions small, isol­ated, and fo­cused. It al­lows an en­gin­eer to hold a func­tion in their work­ing memory, reason about its be­ha­viour, and en­sure its cor­rect­ness. From the out­side it is enough to know that the types match. Af­ter­wards, type sig­na­tures alone dic­tate how to com­pose func­tions, rarely re­quir­ing sub­sequent re­pairs due to un­fore­seen de­fects.
With de­term­in­istic guard­rails gov­ern­ing both code qual­ity and in­sti­tu­tional memory, a curi­ous dy­namic emerges. The bot­tle­neck shifts up­wards from code gen­er­a­tion to co­ordin­at­ing con­cur­rent, sens­ible streams of work.
Ad­di­tion­ally, with the ap­proach of us­ing ADR and Re­search Ques­tions as out­lined in this art­icle, the in­sti­tu­tional memory re­mains siloed in a single re­pos­it­ory, whereas ar­chi­tec ­ tural prin­ciples, designs, and or­gan­isa­tional con­ven­tions span the en­tire or­gan­isa­tion and there­fore mul­tiple pro­jects. The cur­rent ap­proach still lacks a clean mech­an­ism to un­lock that higher-level in­sti­tu­tional memory to the agent without flood­ing its con­text win­dow with (po­ten­tially) ir­rel­ev­ant his­tory.
These two chal­lenges are where an act­ive body of re­search is cur­rently dir­ec­ted, and what I will fo­cus on next. 10
I like to end with some­thing that has been cyc­ling in my head all along and my AI quoted back to me when re­view­ing this con­clu­sion:
soft­ware en­gin­eer­ing has never been about syn­tax; it has al­ways been about man­aging fal­lible, context-bounded in­tel­li­gence, whether made of car­bon or sil­icon.
(Gem­ini, when re­peat­ing back what I told it above.)
Soft­ware Pro­gram­ming has tra­di­tion­ally centred on syn­tax, al­gorithms, and code gen­er ­ a­tion. In that nar­row do­main, mod­ern mod­els ex­cel: they pro­duce func­tional routines, wire up lib­rar­ies, and spit out syn­tax with as­ton­ish­ing ve­lo­city. On that level, pro­gram ­ ming as we know it has be­come very niche.
Con­versely, Soft­ware En­gin­eer­ing has al­ways be­gun where raw pro­gram­ming ends. 11 It en­com­passes es­tab­lish­ing ar­chi­tec­tural bound­ar­ies, align­ing tech­nical trade-offs with busi­ness pri­or­it­ies, and man­aging fal­lible, context-bounded in­tel­li­gence across time.
Al­though agents are tire­less pro­gram­mers, they pos­sess zero busi­ness con­text. They lack the know­ledge whether a re­pos­it­ory is a throwaway pro­to­type that needs to ship by Fri­day or a core pay­ment en­gine where a subtle edge case cre­ates legal li­ab­il­ity. En­gin ­ eer­ing tran­scends syn­tax be­cause it de­mands com­mer­cial judge­ment : know­ing when to ac­cept tech­nical debt, how to bal­ance el­eg­ance against com­mer­cial dead­lines, and which prob­lems ac­tu­ally mat­ter to the busi­ness. In­sti­tu­tional memory (cap­tured in our ADRs and Re­search Ques­tions) is simply the dur­able re­cord of those busi­ness trade-offs. The agent can gen­er­ate the syn­tax, but the en­gin­eer must sup­ply the stra­tegic con­text: the ar­chi­tec­tural bound­ar­ies, the busi­ness pri­or­it­ies, and the long-term in­tent that code alone can never ex­press.
Ul­ti­mately, in the con­text of soft­ware en­gin­eer­ing, hu­man en­gin­eers and autonom­ous agents are far more alike than we might care to ad­mit. Both are fal­lible, context-bounded in­tel­li­gences prone to lapses in at­ten­tion, re­cency bias, and un­stated as­sump­tions. The hard-won dis­cip­lines of dec­ades of soft­ware en­gin­eer­ing (clear bound­ar­ies, ex­pli­cit con­tracts, auto­mated in­vari­ant test­ing, and dur­able re­cords of in­tent) were al­ways meant to safe­guard us from our own lim­it­a­tions. It turns out nicely that these ex­act same dis­cip­lines are also what al­low AI to suc­ceed. Hope­fully this marks the time where we are able to bring these prac­tices in daily use.
What we need to fig­ure out next is how to lever­age the im­mense speed gains agen­tic pro­gram­ming gives us while stay­ing sane as en­gin­eers ourselves.
This blog post is it­self an ex­ample of that dy­namic: mak­ing some­thing of higher qual­ity in the same amount of time. I spent about a day writ­ing this post. Us­ing LLMs in a tar­geted way al­lowed me to test dif­fer­ent phras­ing and let the model hunt for in­con ­ sist­en­cies in my ar­gu­ments. All text was hand-written (or rather, typed), then re­viewed along­side Gem­ini to re­fine lo­gical flow, prune me­an­der­ing thoughts, and source primary ref­er­ences. I hope you en­joyed the jour­ney.
