title: Russian Diesel Tanker Heads to New York After Trump-Putin Deal
body:
A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel has set sail for New York under a deal between Washington and Moscow, with the shipment set to arrive on Nov. 7 – four days after the US mid-term elections.
The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded ultra-low-sulfur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on Thursday, Oct. 22, Reuters reported, citing LSEG shipping data. It added that the shipment’s due in the US on Nov. 7.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
US President Donald Trump has sought to reduce diesel prices before the Nov. 3 midterms to help his party win the by waiving parts of a new sanctions law against Russia. He also threatened to ban US diesel exports unless European countries release more emergency reserves.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that the first tanker under the Kremlin’s diesel agreement with the White House would sail in two to three days .
The shipment is about 13 percent of the initial 300,000 metric tons (about 330,700 US tons) Trump said Russia would release immediately under the agreement.
Trump announced the arrangement on Oct. 9 , saying larger volumes would follow in November and afterward. He claimed the deal would bring down fuel prices for US farmers, truckers and consumers.
Putin said Russia was preparing several tankers, suggesting the first cargo would be part of a wider series of shipments.
The timing he gave refers to departure, rather than delivery to a US buyer. Shipping and unloading would still have to take place after the vessel sails.
While Trump initially boasted of up to 2 million tons of Russian diesel to the world market upon announcing the deal, a Russian minister raised the figure to 3.5 million tons by year-end in a later remark.
Kyiv Post recently estimated that the planned 300,000-ton shipments to the US would last a bit over half a day , based on known consumption data. Ukraine’s sanctions envoy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, said the 40,000-ton shipment would last less than two hours.
The diesel agreement has become a source of friction between Washington and Kyiv.
After Trump announced the deal, the US Treasury authorized transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027, easing restrictions imposed over Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump later signed an Oct. 16 executive order waiving sweeping new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were scheduled to take effect.
The suspended measures included additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized the diesel arrangement and broader sanctions relief, arguing that additional energy revenues would help Russia finance its war rather than persuade Putin to stop it.
Opposition has also come from US lawmakers. A bipartisan group of 12 senators urged Trump to rescind the diesel agreement , warning that it would reward Moscow while offering limited relief to Americans.
The senators called for stronger enforcement of economic pressure on Russia as attacks on Ukraine continued.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Ukraine Still Recording Starshield Connectivity Losses at 161 Kph, Defense Ministry Source Says
body:
Ukraine is still recording satellite connectivity losses at speeds of 161 kph (100 mph), with no confirmation that restrictions on Starlink and Starshield have been lifted, a source in Ukraine’s defense ministry told Kyiv Post on Friday, Oct. 23.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces and defense ministry specialists are continuously monitoring Starlink/Starshield connections and recording the results. As of this morning, cases of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 kph are still being observed,” the source said.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted,” the person added.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, also said in a Facebook post that there was no evidence the restrictions had been removed.
“We are not currently seeing the restrictions on Starlink being lifted. There are occasional cases when Starlink can move somewhat faster than the limit, but these are likely the result of SpaceX’s algorithms or specific operating conditions, rather than the removal of the restriction,” Beskrestnov wrote.
The latest assessment comes a day after US President Donald Trump said Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s satellite service , but did not confirm whether he had personally intervened to lift the restrictions.
“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that he had called Musk and asked him to restore the service.
It remains unclear whether the reported restoration has significantly improved Ukraine’s satellite communications capabilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN’s Christiane Amanpour in an interview published Thursday that restrictions were still affecting Ukraine’s military satellite communications.
“Now it’s still limited,” Zelensky said.
CNN reported that some Ukrainian military units saw higher connection speeds after the reported restoration, but improvements were uneven, and restrictions remained.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN that the available speeds were “clearly not enough to intercept jet-powered drones.”
On Oct. 17, Zelensky said Starlink speeds in Ukraine had been capped at 161 kph , making the system unusable for some interceptor drones designed to destroy Russian jet-powered Shahed attack drones and endangering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attacks.
“When an Iranian drone goes with a speed of 450 or 500 kph [280 to 311 mph], and you limit [the speed] one night to 70 or even 100, you cannot intercept anything,” Zelensky told CNN. “And this is terrible.”
Zelensky said Ukraine does not use Starlink to attack Russian military or energy targets inside Russia.
“We don’t attack Russian military targets or energy targets using Starlink. Never,” he said. “That’s why it was strange they limited us in Ukraine. It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves.”
The inability to intercept Russian drones effectively has become a major threat to Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Ukraine’s acting chargé d’affaires in the United States, Denys Senik, previously said Kyiv was awaiting an official response from the Pentagon and SpaceX on the full restoration of Starshield services. The system’s performance remained unstable, he said.
According to The Telegraph , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk proposed that Trump restrict Starlink speeds in Ukraine.
The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the speed restrictions imposed by the SpaceX chief.
Asked who ordered the restrictions, Zelensky said he did not know whether the decision came from SpaceX or US government institutions.
“I don’t know,” he said. “Technically, I think SpaceX can do it. But whether the decision comes from them or from some institutions, I don’t know.”
Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service, is controlled by the US government .
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Starlink is a commercial product whose operating decisions are made by SpaceX , while saying Ukraine’s request for broader access to Starshield remained under discussion.
The Pentagon has denied issuing instructions to slow the system.
Alisa is the Head of News and a correspondent at Kyiv Post, where she leads the newsroom’s coverage of breaking events and global developments. With over seven years of experience in TV journalism, Alisa has reported on international and Ukrainian politics, making complex stories easier to understand. Back in September 2022, Alisa joined the Kyiv Post team.
Kateryna investigates today's most important topics, from geopolitical challenges and defense strategies to stories that change the course of events. She explores the secrets of Ukraine's intelligence services and shows the hidden side of global events. Her passion is uncovering secrets that change history. Born and lives in Kyiv.

title: SP Hutzler Warns Delayed Referrals and Blocked Records Hinder Prosecutions
body: By: Eoghan Olkeriil Ngirudelsang KOROR, Palau — Special Prosecutor Tamara Hutzler told senators on October 21, 2026, that Palau’s fight against financial crime and other government misconduct is being weakened by delayed referrals, restricted access to records, and poor coordination between her office, the Office of the Attorney General, and the Ministry of Justice. Hutzler said the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) is meant to operate independently and have access to government information, but that authority is increasingly being limited in practice. “Some of the complaints that should come to my office are not coming to my office,” she said during the Senate hearing. “A lot of our complaints also involve financial crimes,” Hutzler said. “When amendments to the PGST law were enacted, it did not allow my office to get any tax records.” She argued that the restriction undermines the purpose of the OSP. “The point of the SP’s office is to be an independent office that has access to any and all government records. So that we can look at anything we need to look at,” Hutzler said. “The problem is that it is being slowly whittled away, and it sounds like there is not an appetite to fix it.” Access to records Hutzler told lawmakers that several government entities have resisted providing information her investigators requested. “Social Security Administration says they don’t have to comply. AG’s Office doesn’t have to comply,” she said. “Now people are also telling me that they don’t have to give information because of the Privacy Act.” “It feels like people don’t want to give us access, and it’s really handcuffing our ability to do our job and prosecute cases,” she said. The Special Prosecutor also described an incident regarding obtaining street-camera footage during an investigation that began in July. “We did a surveillance on somebody for a long time, both of my investigators were involved and we had pictures and videos, and we went to try and get footage of one of the cameras -one of the cameras on the streets,” she said. “It took a couple of weeks, and we got some footage, but when it was reviewed by my investigators, it became very clear that there was something wrong with the time and date on the camera because the vehicle and person that we know were at this place at this time because we have pictures and videos that were not on the footage of the camera,” Hutzler said. She said the OSP reported the issue to the Bureau of Public Safety (BPS), but that her staff continued to encounter resistance when seeking a corrected recording. Hutzler said that when her investigators offered to review the footage directly, they were again met with resistance. She said the episode illustrates how record-access problems can delay or complicate criminal investigations. Case workload Despite those obstacles, Hutzler told senators that the OSP’s work is successful. She said the office inherited 45 open cases from prior years, of which only three had been closed. When she took office, there were five litigation cases, all but one of which have since been closed. “We opened 52 cases in 2025, and we have closed 41 of those,” Hutzler said. “There were 11 cases carried over into 2026, and we have closed 7 of those 11 and opened 19 cases this year.” She also said the OSP has recovered more than $300,000 in fines and restitution payments to the national treasury over the past two years. Hutzler emphasized that cases are not discarded simply because they cannot be prosecuted at first. “We have a lot of cases that we close because we do not have sufficient evidence of a crime, but they stay on our radar,” she said. “Every complaint gets investigated.” Referrals and coordination A central concern Hutzler raised was that major cases involving government employees or public agencies are not consistently referred to the OSP. She said the Attorney General’s Office issued a legal opinion to the tax office stating that it could not provide information to the OSP under current statutes. Hutzler said her office could not obtain a copy of the opinion because of attorney-client confidentiality. Hutzler cited the Palau Housing Authority case and a theft case at the Bureau of Agriculture as matters she believed should have been referred to her office. “In my opinion that should have come to my office,” she said of the Palau Housing Authority matter. “Big crimes involving government employees should be coming to my office like the Palau Housing case and the Bureau of Agriculture,” Hutzler said. “I don’t know what the resistance is to sending things to my office. I don’t know,” she added. Hutzler said the problem extends to basic investigative materials, including police reports. “I believe that the AG’s office and my office both work for the ROP and I feel like we should be a team. I can’t get police reports,” she said. “I ask for police reports, and I can’t get them,” Hutzler said. “I will give you an example. The AG is a dear friend of mine, but being friends does not mean we can’t say the truth of what is going on business-wise.” She referenced a November oversight hearing on the Ministry of Justice, during which allegations emerged that a police officer had entered the jail and beaten an inmate. “You had an oversight hearing last November of the MOJ where it came out that there was a police officer going into the jail and beating up an inmate,” Hutzler said. “That’s how my office heard about it; that’s how everybody heard about it because it was kept on the down low.” Hutzler said she wrote directly to the BPS director requesting the police report. According to Hutzler, the director told her: “I was told no, the AG has told me not to give them to you, and if you want them you need to talk to her.” She said she then raised the matter with Whipps, “The SP will have to sue the AG’s and it’s a terrible look for the ROP,” Hutzler said she told the president. “Within a few hours she was able to get the report,” she said. Call for teamwork Hutzler said the OSP, the Attorney General’s Office, and the Ministry of Justice must function as partners in serving the Republic, rather than as agencies operating in isolation. “There has been this direction for us to work together so we’ll see how that goes,” she said. The post SP Hutzler Warns Delayed Referrals and Blocked Records Hinder Prosecutions appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Defense Forces strike drone launch site near Donetsk and Russian warehouses
body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
“Unfortunately, there have been instances of communication losses in the Starlink/StarShield system at certain speeds. However, the Ukrainian military continues to inflict damage on the enemy,” the statement reads.
According to the General Staff, among the targets struck was a storage, training, and launch site for Russian strike drones in the area of the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk. The military emphasizes that striking such targets reduces the enemy’s ability to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure using various types of drones.
In the Donetsk region , Ukrainian forces successfully struck a Russian ammunition depot near Hirnyk, a drone depot near Sverdlove, and logistics depots near Berdiansk. Depots containing the invaders’ logistical supplies in the Balkove and Orikhivka areas of Zaporizhzhia Oblast were also struck.
“The destruction of depots containing weapons and logistical supplies makes it more difficult for the Russian aggressor to supply its units and reduces their ability to conduct combat operations,” the General Staff emphasizes.
Other targets struck include a command post of a Russian military unit in the area of the temporarily occupied town of Hromove (Crimea) and a concentration of personnel from the enemy’s “Rubicon” drone unit in the Kamianka area of Zaporizhzhia region.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Defense Forces struck an electronic warfare station in the Bryansk region of the Russian Federation and an invaders’ military depot in the Luhansk region.

title: Is this the new cyber normal?
body:
The last week has seen a flurry of severe and critical software vulnerabilities affecting thousands of major sites and sending people into a panic. What’s going on here, and what can we do about it?
If we want to understand what’s going on in the world of software security at the moment, we need to understand what’s going on with all these bugs. I’m not a cybersecurity expert, so I’m going to link to external explanations instead of going into the gory technical details myself as these people are always going to do a better job at that.
Two different security teams, one from California security company Calif (as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program) and another from Israeli-U.S. cloud security company Wiz (they’re part of Google Cloud, apparently), both found these two Remote Code Execution (RCE) bugs in PHP. They were both using frontier AI models (a.k.a. LLMs, specifically GPT-5.6 Sol/Gemini 4 Argon) to find these vulnerabilities and build the exploits.
Interestingly, one of the bugs (CVE-2026-109618) was found by a security audit the PHP Foundation did in 2024 (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency which is coincidentally one of the most interesting things happening in the open source space at the moment) but they basically ignored it because they had bigger concerns and couldn’t agree on a fix. The reasoning behind it was that no-one could really figure out how to create an actual exploit based on the theoretical issue.
One thing LLMs are very good at is taking a theoretical security vulnerability, even if that vulnerability is a vague description of what the issue could be, and building it into a full exploit. This has become a major issue in recent months as any notice of a security patch will immediately result in people pointing their LLMs at the codebase, whereupon the agents can very quickly read through diffs until they find something that looks like a security patch, then go backwards to the vulnerability it covers, and follow this all the way to an exploit.
This happens so fast, in fact, that at this point I think it is a reasonable that the moment you announce a security patch should be taken as a last possible date that the full exploit is not being publicly or privately distributed.
This PHP2Shell (as it’s being marketed, vulnerabilities seem to come bundled with their own marketing departments now) is estimated to affect upwards of 70% of the internet, with thousands of websites from Wikimedia Foundation to DeviantArt to much of the UK government and Japanese banking systems to The Traitors BBC programme website . Vulnerabilities do get found, but they don’t normally cause half the internet to shut their servers down, so what’s going on?
To understand this, let’s look at the original post from the PHP Group :
Someone called petecooper posted on Hacker News about the CVEs , apparently unaware that there even was an embargo. This (and other apparent leaks) prompted this hurried statement from the PHP Group and bringing the patch forward from Thursday 22nd to Wednesday 21st. However, the patch still wasn’t going to be available till the next day. This unintentional leak included CVSS scores of 10.0 (i.e. bad , although weirdly the actual scores were 9.2 instead).
Pretty much immediately, this news spread like wildfire and people started panicking. Even though this was found by “responsible security researchers” at “respectable companies” , by the time the security patch actually got released, it was already being exploited in the wild 1 . The PHP Foundation blamed Calif and a company called Chainguard by saying that Calif leaked a video of the exploit in action (with weird background music and a dancing anime girl) while Chainguard published fixes 6 hours before the embargo was due to lift, both allowing attackers to beat the systems administrators to the punch. The timeline is confusing, but it seems like multiple interconnected things have gone wrong here, all within the space of about 17 hours.
There’s been lots of discussion about whether AI really is the game changer that completely revolutionises computer security or not. The big AI companies (and they are big ) obviously want you to think that it is. Some people argue that PHP2Shell is overblown because LLMs tend to be paranoid about vulnerabilities and come up with “exploits” that make bad assumptions (like that the server will run PHP code you upload yourself via some existing file inclusion vulnerability) or cheat in some way. As LiveOverflow points out , LLMs make it very easy to create exploit slop that proves nothing and doesn’t work, but that doesn’t mean that the vulnerability isn’t real and easy to exploit using AI. You can have 10,000 bad slop exploits that don’t work but if there’s one that does, that’s all that matters. Maybe we just need to get used to wading through slop to find the important stuff now.
Others point out that lots of governments ( UK 2 , EU , Japan , USA ) got overexcited and released urgent announcements saying everyone had to unplug their computers immediately, so people panicked. I think the reason everyone panicked is that everyone kind of knows that PHP is intensely insecure and they use it anyway, so they’re kind of primed for bad news and to overreact. Also, it actually is really quite bad, so maybe panicking is kind of the correct reaction?
The big takeaway for me from this is that – because of LLMs – the time from “hey I heard there’s a bad RCE in this project” to “there are sophisticated, automated, and concerted attacks using an exploit targeting this vulnerability” has gone from weeks/months to hours/minutes. The fact that there’s loads of non-working exploit slop just shows how genuine expertise is still required to make these things – if you don’t know what you’re looking at, you can’t tell whether the AI has cheated or made bad assumptions.
On the exact same day (20th October 2026), Mozilla announced that they were blocking 8 intermediate certificates signed by Indian certificate authority eMudhra. This happened after a pseudonymous security researcher known only as “Wayne” reported to several big tech firms (such as Mozilla, Apple, Google, Microsoft, etc.) that the certificate authority were using laughably poor quality private keys for their intermediate certificates. Where a secure key might be a 100 digit number, eMudhra were using keys like “115”, “56”, and “4”. They must’ve been following RFC 1149.5:
There are no indications that this was found or exploited using AI or LLMs, although researcher Scott Helme notes that given a single prompt, Claude was able to recover the private keys of the intermediate certs.
At the time of writing (23rd Oct), eMudhra has announced that it will be retiring from the certificate authority space. In unrelated news, a farmer has announced that he has shut his stable door, following reports of an escaped horse.
The next day, cloud provider Railway announced that they found evidence that hackers had accessed and even decrypted environment variables from their platform, which often hold secrets such as database credentials, API keys, etc. In their statement, they said that they believed that this was part of a concerted effort aimed at compromising companies that provide AI inference.
What would the end goal be here? At the time of writing (23rd Oct), we have very little information to go on. Is this “unauthorized third party” (official announcements of “some randos got into our computers” always find a way to make it seem like a terms of service agreement, maybe that way they think people won’t pay attention to it) trying to spy on people using AI inference to see what they’re doing, even stealing new models or research? Or maybe they’re trying to build a network of compromised inference providers for their own nefarious generative AI purposes (like finding more PHP bugs).
On 12th October 2026, GitLab warned of a max severity bug in GitLab CI/CD’s regular expression parsing that could enable attackers to execute arbitrary code (another RCE) using a specially crafted regex. This is a CVSS score of 10.0 which is the maximum possible, meaning “this is pretty much as bad as they come” 3 . This was followed on 21st October 2026 by yet another regex integer overflow RCE , another 10.0.
This follows hot on the heels of yet another 10.0 CVSS CVE from last month ( CVE-2026-85706 ), that time related to path traversal . All three of these bugs were reported through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. When it became clear that LLMs could research vulnerabilities and write exploits, there was a lot of talk about shutting down bug bounty programs because they didn’t make sense anymore. I’m sure GitLab are glad they didn’t do that now.
Although GitLab is used very widely across academia, government, and private companies, this doesn’t seem to have got as much attention. CVEs in GitLab are obviously very serious, especially for private companies, as a lot of their vitally important intellectual property is stored in there, and having that leak could be disastrous. Often, companies put their GitLab instance behind a VPN/firewall so that they aren’t publicly accessible, which greatly reduces the risk associated with this. It’s also not entirely clear whether these CVEs require specific conditions like publicly accessible projects, user self-registration, etc. It does seem like CVE-2026-110264 requires at least one public project, but I can’t find any information on the conditions around the earlier CVE.
There’s no indication that these were discovered using AI or LLMs. They may have been, but there’s no reason at this point to think they were.
On 21st October, a bug in musl’s libc related to regex (libc has regex? Apparently…) was announced that leads to denial of service at least, if not code execution. As far as I can tell, this is entirely coincidental in timing and not related to the GitLab bugs, which both also seem to be integer overflows when parsing untrusted regular expressions, one reported on the exact same day. Who knew a regex engine was such a security issue – is regex the new font rendering? The GitLab bugs were both found by a Swede called Johan Carlsson (joaxcar) while the musl bug was reported by Julien Voisin , a French self-proclaimed “open sourcerer”.
Ah, hello my old friend LiteLLM. Proving that, when you’re made of metal and 200 feet tall, lightning can in fact strike twice. It’s not a good sign that when someone asks whether you’ve heard of the big 2026 LiteLLM compromise, you have to ask “which one?” In a piece of good fortune, the whole PHP2Shell and all the others have cannibalised much of the attention, meaning this isn’t getting quite the same traction as last time in March, despite being similarly bad.
This time, it’s a malicious version on the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images. For those who don’t remember, LiteLLM had a very similar thing happen back in March, where a malicious package was uploaded to the litellm package on PyPI that used the .pth files to autoload malicious code (yeah, it was bad).
This compromise again took advantage of .pth files and this time also the sitecutomize.py file for autoloading malicious payloads, running in the preload step as soon as the Python interpreter starts up. According to the analysis from Wiz , the payload has “strong indications of LLM-aided development” – things like overly verbose variable names, overly defensive error handling, brittle edge cases, and all the comments saying “this is where it really bites”, “it’s worth sitting with that”, “lean into that”, and “that stays yours” repeatedly 4 .
According to LiteLLM, the incident occurred because the attacker had access to credentials for GitHub CLI which allowed them to run CI jobs. LiteLLM note that Claude Code will apparently sometimes embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into response bodies which could cause them to appear in LiteLLM logs.
On October 19th 2026, an enterprise software company called “PingCAP” that develops a database called “TiDB” revealed “unauthorised access to PingCAP” with “no evidence that data stored in TiDB was impacted”. At the same time, a cyber extortion group called “FulcrumSec” (a.k.a. the “Threatspians” 5 ) said they had exfiltrated 10.6 TB of data from PingCAP and publicly released a torrent with 200 GB of data, as a “stage one release” (you’ve gotta get people invested in the sequel).
They also posted full details of what they took and some of the excellent security practices of PingCAP, including putting client AWS secret access keys inside Jira tickets and attaching massive unredacted logs to Jira tickets including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI API keys . Yikes. If you’re willing to visit the cyber extortion group’s website, they do a pretty interesting write-up of it. Gone are the days of shoddy broken English back when the Russians had to write these things up without LLMs to do it for them and remind them of definite and indefinite articles. 6
The good news for PingCAP is that not finding evidence of data extraction is actually incredibly easy. In fact, I’m doing it for thousands of companies right now, for free. I’m sure there’s a business proposal in there somewhere. All you have to do is not look (see also: U+1F648). To be fair, I think their argument is that no data inside TiDB instances was compromised. 10.6 TB seems like a lot of data if that’s the case. There’s clearly still tons of customer data.
Linux kernel development all happens through mailing lists. Naturally, some of those are about security sensitive things, so these are private. Over the night of 21st-22nd October 2026, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), a software vulnerability initiative owned by Trend Micro, reported a bunch of high severity (upwards of 9.0 CVSS) CVEs to the public mailing list, instead of the private one. Naturally, the assumption is that anyone with an LLM and a heart full of dreams will then be able to take those reports and turn them into active exploits within a matter of minutes. This isn’t quite as bad as that time Pete Hegseth accidentally texted details of upcoming military strikes in Yemen to The Atlantic 7 , but it’s still interesting how seriously people take this now.
I think it’s fair to say these last few days have been abnormally active in terms of all of these cyber incidents and security disclosures. There are many commenters on the Hacker News discussions for these incidents that say that this is nothing and it’s only going to get worse. Honestly, I’ve not decided yet. To be honest, if you’d asked me 4 years ago how far LLMs would go, I’d never have guessed they’d get as good as they are right now. Even so, people do tend to get overexcited by these announcements and suggest that we are going to live in a world where no software is secure and everyone is vulnerable.
It’s worth noting that while a lot of the online discussion around this focusses on AI and LLMs, only some of these disclosures were researched or created with LLMs. We don’t know about some of them like the PingCAP one, but there’s clear evidence that many criminal and state-sponsored groups are using AI to do more hacking and faster. Why wouldn’t they? It seems to be pretty good at it. Many of these vulnerabilities were good old fashioned software vulnerabilities found and written using human meat fingers, but the online conversation focusses on the exciting, scary new thing. Why wouldn’t it?
You can see why organisations like NHS England decided to take all of their open source code private (even though that was a silly decision). When these LLMs are so good that anyone can point their agent at some open source code and find tons of vulnerabilities, then write full exploits for them, that is concerning for many. So what’s the solution here?
The NHS approach: close source everything . (A.k.a. the Madagascar approach )
The AI-embracer approach: if you can’t beat ‘em, join ‘em . In other words, they can’t use LLMs to find vulnerabilities if we’ve already run our better LLMs on our code faster and with more money and better models.
The optimist approach: universally better, standardised approaches to reporting, handling, and mitigating security vulnerabilities followed by all companies having top-notch security postures, well-understood risks, well-documented processes, and so on .
There are some easy wins we could get from this moving forwards, like “never announce details of a critical vulnerability before the patch is ready to install”, but in this case unintentional leaks meant everyone knew about the vulnerabilities even before the official announcement. Maybe even that’s asking too much. In this case, it was a series of mistakes from multiple people and companies that led to or accelerated the exploit being in active use hours before the patch was available, hence everyone taking their servers offline. AWS have since said they saw someone trying out this vulnerability from 17th October, before any of these leaks happened.
Even something like minimum release age which gained popularity after shalk/debug , Shai-Hulud , & March LiteLLM incidents, as it means big updates that fix widely exploited vulnerabilities don’t get patched for a few days, giving attackers ample time to hack you to pieces. At the very least, we could maybe do with some better client management to avoid everyone panicking and taking all their servers offline.
Maybe we just need to accept that if you expose something to the wider internet, it will get hacked, and plan accordingly. Maybe it’s our expectations that are at fault.
There’s definitely a story about AI and security here. It’s changing the world of software, and it’s not yet clear whether that’s for the better or the worse. Money has a way of warping truth like matter warps spacetime, and there’s enough money in AI to cause whatever the truth equivalent of a medium-sized black hole is. There’s an incredible amount of money being spent on AI and it all wants you to think that it’s going to change everything about your life, including software and security. That doesn’t mean it’s not true, of course.
Some people say automated analysis tools led to loads of new bugs being found back in the ’10s, and now the same thing is happening again. It feels categorically different to me, but perhaps there will be an initial period of escalating bug reports before it all settles down and goes back to how it was. I suspect not. Some people say this is only happening because humans wrote all the dodgy code in the first place – once AI is writing all of the code to start with, there’ll be no vulnerabilities because LLMs are better at writing secure code than humans. I am not convinced by this argument.
While I’m not making many predictions about the future (because I don’t want to look like an idiot in 12 months’ time when I’m inevitably proven wrong), I will say that the software industry is going to change, and open source is going to change, and it is our collective responsibility as members of the software community to make sure that this change is for the benefit of all of us, not special interests and private corporations.
This is a developing story – I’ll note any updates in here. I wrote this in somewhat of a hurry, so I may also make some incremental improvements to the wording and evidencing behind some bits.
There is some discussion and disagreement about whether any real, working attempts at exploiting this were made before the patch was released. ↩
Disclaimer: I kind of work for the UK government. ↩
GitLab is using CVSS 3.1 while PHP is using CVSS 4.0 here, which means they’re following slightly different metrics to calculate the CVSS score, meaning you can’t directly compare them. ↩
If these reprehensible criminals are ever brought to justice, I propose their longest sentence be for crimes against wordplay. Truly atrocious. ↩
To clarify, there’s no evidence that this group are Russian hackers. They seem to be primarily financially motivated, so they could be from anywhere and everywhere. You get my point though – back in the day, you could tell the Russian phishing campaigns from their grammatical peculiarities. Nowadays it’s lost all of its charm, all because of AI. ↩
Fortunately, being the upstanding and trustworthy citizen that he is and someone who bases his administrative recruitment decisions on what’s best for the country as opposed to personal loyalty and piety to the president’s personal agenda of emolument, the president ensured that all those responsible were swiftly removed from his administration, never to be seen in Washington again. ↩

title: Abu Dhabi talks are set to take place in trilateral format — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Talks due to be held in Abu Dhabi in November are planned in a trilateral format involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
However, the possibility of European participation cannot be excluded beforehand, he noted.
It was reported earlier that the talks would address guaranteeing the security of Russia and Ukraine after peace is achieved. In this context, the framework of European security could also be discussed.
"Nothing can be ruled out in advance. But the talks we are discussing, which are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, will be held in a trilateral format," Peskov said.

title: Energy winter to be difficult but not catastrophic, no worse than last – CER director
body:
The upcoming winter of 2026-2027 in terms of energy supply will be difficult, but not catastrophic and no more difficult than the last one, and it will be successfully navigated, believes Oleksandr Kharchenko, Director of the Center for Energy Research (CER).
Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Ukraine on threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality
"I am absolutely certain that we will get through the season. Despite all the challenges, there is an understanding of how to proceed. There are a sufficient number of scenarios, people who are ready to execute these scenarios, and the means with which they will be carried out (...) And I do not think that the winter will be more difficult than the last one. Rather the opposite," he said during a discussion on "Ukraine on the Threshold of Winter: Energy, Defense, and the New Diplomatic Reality" at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Friday .
According to the expert, the main factor of uncertainty for the energy sector right now is the weather. At temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius, scheduled power outages can reach 10-12 hours. In energy-deficient regions such as Kyiv, Odesa, and parts of Sumy and Chernihiv regions, scheduled outages may be quite long. At the same time, with milder weather, the restrictions will correspondingly be softer.
"Another truly risky component is heating. There are high risks that there will be attacks on large thermal facilities in Kyiv; they will undoubtedly happen, they happen constantly," Kharchenko emphasized.
However, according to him, a significant part of the capital's heat infrastructure is protected, and power engineers understand how to act after facilities are damaged.
"Whatever we could protect, we protected; whatever we couldn't – well, let's say, we know how to maneuver with that," he added.
At the same time, in those cities where there are actually only two or three boiler houses, if they are destroyed, a significant threat to heat supply will arise, and much in critical conditions will depend on how these cities prepared for winter.
In turn, as Kharchenko explained, energy engineers have more or less come to terms with the factor of Russian missile and drone attacks and understand that the intensity of these attacks will neither increase nor decrease cardinally.
"That is, they are not capable of inflicting more massive strikes than they are currently inflicting," he believes.
The expert added that these strikes have their own periodicity and a certain rhythm, and energy engineers understand how to respond to them, how to restore power supply to consumers as quickly as possible, and how to return core municipal infrastructure systems to operation as soon as possible.

title: Ship sinks off Romania, one sailor dead, three missing after suspected drone strike - media
body:
A Comoros-flagged merchant vessel sank in the Black Sea approximately 24 km from the Romanian port of Constanta, possibly after being hit by a drone, Digi24 reported.
The crew sent an SOS signal, prompting Romanian authorities to launch a rescue operation. Nine crew members survived, one died and three remain missing, the report said.
Romanian Coast Guard officials said units of the Interior Ministry were taking part in search-and-rescue operations to locate the missing crew members.
"The merchant vessel suffered major damage and capsized, creating an imminent risk of sinking. Of the 13 people on board, 10 were rescued by another merchant vessel in the area: nine were alive and one person had died. Three people are still missing," the Coast Guard said.
The nine survivors were subsequently transferred to a Coast Guard vessel. The Coast Guard and a vessel operated by the Romanian Agency for Saving Human Lives at Sea (ARSVOM) were continuing search-and-rescue operations.
A helicopter operated by the Interior Ministry's General Inspectorate of Aviation had been placed on standby to support the operation if necessary, but weather conditions were preventing an air operation, the report said.
The response team at the port of Constanta had been reorganized and included four SMURD ambulances, a mobile intensive care unit, two special vehicles for transporting personnel and multiple casualties, and an advanced medical post, Coast Guard representatives said.
Digi24 noted that the incident was the latest in a series of attacks on merchant vessels in the region in recent weeks. Drones have attacked 11 vessels in the Black Sea, seven of them near Romania, the report said.

title: Ukraine returns seven more civilians from Russia, incl 90-year-old woman, mother with her child – Lubinets
body:
Ukraine has brought seven more civilians back to Ukraine-controlled territory as part of an agreement on the mutual return of individuals. Simultaneously, seven Russian citizens were transported to Russia for family reunification, with the support of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), reported Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman).
"Through my humanitarian communication channel with the Russian Commissioner for Human Rights, Yana Lantratova, we reached an agreement on the mutual return of civilians," he wrote on Telegram.
Among those returned to Ukraine are a 90-year-old woman with limited mobility and a 50-year-old Ukrainian woman who has suffered a myocardial infarction and a stroke, among other health conditions. Given their medical status, specific arrangements were made to ensure appropriate transport conditions for both women.
Also returned to Ukraine were a young woman and her child, who had been unable to reunite with their family since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. At the time, the woman was staying temporarily in Mariupol. Due to the hostilities and the subsequent occupation of the city, she was unable to return to her relatives. A particular obstacle to their return was the process of obtaining documentation for the child.
According to Lubinets, the mother and her child are now in Ukraine and are in need of psychological support. The ombudsman thanked Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Lantratova and stated his intention to continue humanitarian efforts aimed at the return of Ukrainians.

title: Crackdown urged after attacks on defence workers’ homes
body: Police Scotland, the Ministry of Defence and the Scottish Government should be brought together to protect defence industry staff after a run of attacks on manufacturing sites and on the private homes of workers, according to a letter sent to the Home Secretary by the Shadow Scotland Secretary. Harriet Cross, the Conservative member for Gordon and Buchan, warned of a “dangerous escalation” in attacks on the Scottish defence sector, citing incidents at Leonardo UK in Edinburgh, Bruntons Aero Products in Musselburgh, Ultra I&C in Aberdeenshire and Kelvinside Electronics in Kilsyth, all of which she described as having links to Israel. The pro-Palestinian group The List has claimed responsibility for vandalising the homes of two defence workers in Dunfermline and South Queensferry earlier this month, and has threatened to target more employees. Cross told the Home Secretary that the attacks form part of a wider rise in antisemitism across the United Kingdom, pointing out that the Community Security Trust recorded 1,926 antisemitic incidents in 2026, up 21 per cent on the previous year. She has asked ministers for an urgent meeting to discuss what can be done to protect the industry, its workforce and the wider Jewish community in Scotland. Cross said: “These criminals have gone from attacking defence manufacturers to targeting innocent employees in their own homes. “This is not peaceful protest. It is blatant criminality and intimidation, and those responsible must face the full weight of the law. “These attacks cannot be viewed in isolation, nor as relating solely to the defence sector. They form part of a wider climate of a rising tide of antisemitism across the United Kingdom. “The Home Secretary needs to work with Police Scotland, the Ministry of Defence and the SNP government to protect the defence industry, its employees and the wider Jewish community in Scotland.” Scottish defence sites have been targeted repeatedly over the past two years, and a van was driven into the Leonardo plant in Edinburgh by activists who then damaged the building. Leonardo’s Edinburgh site produces targeting and laser systems, and employs around two thousand people in the city. The post Crackdown urged after attacks on defence workers’ homes first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
body:
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.
In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?
What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.
Meta has limited how many hyperlinks Facebook Pages can post through a subscription Tony Avelar/AP Photo hide caption
Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."
What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!
How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.
It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.
Tom Kloza is the chief energy advisor for Gulf Oil Screenshot of a post on X by @tomkloza/X hide caption
What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history , that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.
If you HAVEN'T listened: We keep hearing about the AI boom that's propping up the U.S. economy. Well, Oracle is a part of that story. The enterprise software company has moved into building out data centers to serve the AI industry. Now, they have a huge deal with OpenAI worth $300 billion over five years. Here's the problem. Oracle has been spending freely with the assumption that this OpenAI deal will deliver. But what if it doesn't? Oracle already has $169 billion in total debt and a growing credit risk. They're one link in an interconnected chain of enormous tech companies. If that link breaks, it could spell trouble for the economy.
If you HAVE listened: Lindsay Tyler, credit analyst, explains in the piece that Oracle is making a bet on data centers. "The analogy might be you have 10 apartments, you've pre-signed leases with, for those 10 apartments, and you're thinking, 'Should I build another floor?'"
On the surface, this doesn't seem plausible. Isn't computing demand insatiable right now? Yeah, right now. But…
Some economic historians like to compare the AI buildout to the railroads, but this one is different. Rails last longer than one to three years. The cost of shipping does not plummet 13x per year. And maybe Oracle is at the center of these economic forces colliding: a railroad-type investment boom building castles made of sand .
Rest of the Week We can inflate away the national debt… at a cost
Piercing the American taboo of talking about income and class
Can a "Moneyball" system work for campaign funding?
Context: Last week, we ran an episode full of consumer rage stories. One included a story about someone charged for damage to a rental car that was impossible to disprove. Stay to the end for a surprising twist.
Listener Jim Zerefos sent in a response from Colorado.
I share the frustration of the person who complained about dubious damage claims from a rental car company. I've been fighting Alamo for nearly a year now over a $1,600 damage claim. Alamo sent me photos of very minor damage taken AFTER our rental, but never provided photos from BEFORE our rental. [The car] had some 23k miles so seems possible (likely?) the scratches occurred some time before our rental.
My spidey sense here smells a scam: "rental companies now scan cars for damage and so are trying to find scapegoats for all prior damage"? Alamo's reaction to me (and my insurance company) has been to ignore us - never sending the "before" pics and never acknowledging that's an issue. They just keep sending us invoices. They now are threatening collection action and have banned me from renting from the Alamo rental family (as if I would). So, the story on the broader scam? Or story on which credit cards still offer primary rental damage coverage (which we THOUGHT we had)?
By the way, here at The Indicator, we reached out to the car rental company and they responded in a statement through a spokesperson from Enterprise Mobility: "Customer satisfaction is our top priority, and we are always open to further conversations with customers regarding damage claims. Our team is actively reviewing this matter through our escalation process and will reach out to the customer to share an update today."
And we already have an update: Jim tells us Alamo has since dropped the claim and will make no further collection efforts. Alamo's "risk" department instructed the Cleveland manager to drop the claim, according to Jim.
Jim's response: "Sad to see that you got more action in a day than my insurance company and I got in nearly a year."
Co-host Wailin Wong is reading Under Story
This fall has yielded a bumper crop of big new fiction releases. My favorite from the last couple of weeks of reading is UNDER STORY by Chloe Benjamin. This novel is about a fungi expert who goes to Antarctica after a family tragedy. She's hoping to anonymously wash dishes at a research station. However, a strange light phenomenon and the arrival of her physicist ex-husband pull her back into the scientific world. This was an exciting, imaginative, and beautiful story about grief, family, parallel universes, trees, and mushrooms. (Bonus rec: This book also makes for a good pairing with Emily St. John Mandel's new novel, Exit Party .)

title: Terror investigation launched after drive-by shooting near Paris
body: One person was killed and ⁠at least four others were injured in a shooting west of Paris , ​the French Prime ⁠Minister Sebastien ‌Lecornu said on Friday. A suspect has been arrested. Firefighters were called to a petrol station where the shooting took place. Ali Rabeh, the ​mayor of the Yvelines town of Trappes, told BFMTV that a man had fired shots from his car and "appeared to be firing at random and seemed intent on carrying out a massacre". He said one of those injured was a 12-year-old girl, adding that the shooter lived in a nearby town. There is no information so far ​about his motive, he ‌said. Mr Lecornu wrote ⁠on X that security ​forces had been fully mobilised. "The ​national ‌anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office has announced that it is ⁠monitoring the situation," he added. Representatives for ⁠the prosecutor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the prefecture declined to comment. The anti-terrorism prosecutor's ​office confirmed it was monitoring the case.

title: The Taliban’s Road Reaches China, but the Border is Closed
body: After several years of slow progress, the road connecting Afghanistan to China is finally ready. On October 4, Taliban officials inaugurated the 121-kilometer road through Afghanistan’s remote and arid northeastern Wakhan Corridor. China, however, has not been too keen on the project, and, according to one report, when the Taliban reached the Chinese border, the way was barred, with Chinese border guards ordering the Taliban to leave the area. The Hard Road The Wakhan Corridor was part of ancient trade routes through Asia, but was clearly only used by hardy merchants. The area is one of the most isolated regions on the planet. Nearly all of it is 4,000 meters or more above sea level, mostly bare stone mountains with some grass and a few trees and bushes growing on hillsides and in the valleys. The Wakhan Corridor officially appeared on maps as part of Afghanistan at the end of the 19 th century. It was a buffer zone agreed to by representatives of the British and Russian empires. Today, the far eastern section of the Wakhan Corridor is the only place where Afghanistan directly borders China. That 74-kilometer border was easy to ignore due to the remoteness of the area, but not long after the Chinese revolution in 1949, officials in Beijing still ordered it closed. The harsh climate and rugged mountains make most of the corridor virtually unhabitable, but that did not stop some from believing a modern trade route could be opened through Wakhan that would connect Afghanistan to China. Dirt roads reached a few of the larger settlements in the western part of the corridor, villages of, at most, several hundred people. The Taliban just finished building a gravel road and four bridges that finally make it all the way to the Chinese border. By itself, this is far from sufficient to qualify as a legitimate trade route. There is no infrastructure to serve traffic through the region, no petrol stations, no accommodation, no places to buy food or drink, and temperatures are well below freezing for at least half the year. China’s Big Objection The bigger obstacle is that China has no strong interest in opening this route, and in fact, would prefer the Afghan border to remain closed. The East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) is still present in Afghanistan. ETIM is comprised mainly of ethnic Uyghurs from China’s western Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, the same Chinese region that borders Afghanistan. ETIM’s goal is to topple Chinese rule in Xinjiang. ETIM fighters have been in Afghanistan for at least 25 years, and were allies of the Taliban during the years foreign troops were in Afghanistan. The Islamic State of Khorasan Province is active in northern Afghanistan, and that group has also made specific threats against the Chinese government. The Taliban have promised that they will not allow any group to use Afghan territory to plot or carry out attacks on neighboring countries. However, the Wakhan Corridor is part of Afghanistan’s Badakhshan Province, and the Taliban have been battling several groups there this year. None of those groups are connected with ETIM, but the current unstable situation in Badakhshan probably raises concerns in China about security along its Afghan border. These security concerns extend to Tajikistan, which borders the Wakhan Corridor to the north. Elsewhere along the Tajik-Afghan frontier, two attacks from Afghan territory killed five Chinese nationals in November 2025. Chinese workers later returned under armed protection to work on a highway project in eastern Tajikistan. The violence has shown that threats from Afghanistan can also affect Chinese projects in neighboring Central Asia. The Chinese Response China has never shown much public support for the road through the Wakhan Corridor. China started construction of a road to its border with Afghanistan in 2009 or 2010 in order to be able to reinforce its border guards there, but it is unclear whether that road ever reached the border. The proposed crossing point at the Afghan-Chinese border is the Wakhjir Pass, with an elevation of about 4,920 meters. One indication of China’s views on the project was the absence of any Chinese official at the Afghan inauguration ceremony for the road on October 4, despite the Taliban having extended an invitation. Then, a video was posted on October 20 that purports to show the Afghan-Chinese border, where there is a long strip of two barbed fences running up a hillside with a guard tower in the distance. The video also shows monitoring equipment placed along the border. Most interesting is the claim in the video, subsequently picked up by the Afghanistan International media outlet, that when Taliban fighters recently approached the border, Chinese border guards warned them to leave the area immediately. It is not clear when the video was recorded, and neither government has mentioned the alleged encounter. If this incident did occur, it would not be surprising. The South China Morning Post reported nearly three years ago that if the Afghan road was built through the Wakhan Corridor, it was likely “Beijing [would] be cautious about giving its war-torn neighbor full access to its land border because of security concerns over terrorists and separatist militants.” So, a gravel road is completed on the Afghan side of the border, leading to a mountain pass at an elevation of nearly 5,000 meters, where two fences still bar passage to the Chinese side, where there is no connecting road.

A new Texas-based defense startup has a plan to improve military and police dogs in the US: it’s going to genetically modify them and equip them with Anduril’s military technology. Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm, co-founder of Colossal Biosciences (the company that says it’s trying to resurrect extinct animals ), and it’s already secured $200 million in funding from investors.
Warhound plans to use Colossal’s work in genetics, cloning, and animal biology to “produce healthier dogs with characteristics suited to demanding missions,” with Anduril then equipping them with its “advanced cybernetic Augments.” That includes eye and ear protection and EagleEye military technology to provide the dogs and their handlers with “greater awareness and protection in the field.”
“Man’s best friend deserves man’s best tech,” Luckey said in the press announcement. Bloomberg reports that despite having helped with the company’s conception, Luckey has no equity or ongoing role in Warhound.
The goal is to reduce dependency on Europe, where 80 percent of US military dogs are currently sourced, and improve the success rate of training the animals for specialist work. According to the startup’s press release , less than half of the dogs procured from overseas are typically deemed fit for service following the current three-year acquisition-and-training pipeline.
In a statement to TechCrunch , Lamm said Colossal is looking to enhance the animals by editing their genes to remove problems like poor eyesight and cancer likelihood, while adding new genes to improve performance “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot.” High-performance working dog breeds like the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd are the base of their studies, but the plan is to create “a new type of dog.”
These dogs don’t exist yet, but when (or if) they do, Warhound says they’ll be deployed for elite working roles in US military forces, emergency first response teams, and law enforcement. The American Humane Society will help to guide the company and certify its training programs. Marine veteran and intelligence specialist David Spirk has been named as Warhound’s CEO, and said the company’s goal is simple: “healthier dogs, better-prepared teams, and more service members and first responders coming home safely.”

title: Russia believes in Trump’s sincere intention to resolve Ukrainian conflict — diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Moscow has no doubts at all about US President Donald Trump’s sincere intentions to find mutually acceptable parameters for a long-lasting and sustainable settlement of the Ukrainian conflict, a senior Russian Foreign Ministry official said on Friday.
"We have no doubts whatsoever about President Trump’s sincere commitment to finding mutually acceptable parameters for a long-lasting and sustainable political and diplomatic settlement around Ukraine," Alexander Gusarov, director of the ministry’s department of North Atlantic, said in an interview with the International Affairs magazine.
"We appreciate the efforts that he personally and our teams are steadily making to achieve this goal," he added.

title: Rosoboronexport to unveil 'Anti-Drone Dome' UAV defense concept
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the Rostec State Corporation) will showcase for the first time its latest air defense system designed to protect the population, troops, and facilities from drones, called the Anti-Drone Dome, the company’s press service reported.
The Anti-Drone Dome is designed to shield the civilian population, as well as strategic and infrastructure facilities, bridges, buildings, fuel and energy complex enterprises, and troop deployment sites from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks. "Options are also available for protecting convoys and vehicles transporting VIPs or sensitive cargo," the press service stated. It said that the project will be presented at the third Russia-Africa Summit, which will be held at Moscow’s Gostiny Dvor fairground on October 28-29.
The project was developed by specialists from Rosoboronexport in collaboration with leading Russian manufacturers of counter-UAV systems and representatives of specialized law enforcement agencies. It draws on practical experience in countering UAVs gained during military and counterterrorism operations in recent years.
"Protecting critical infrastructure from unmanned aerial vehicles has today become the cornerstone of national and economic security, as well as the foundation for further technological development. The proper design and implementation of such a system makes a significant contribution to demonstrating the effectiveness of government and business operations, maintaining supply chains, and signaling to investors that their investments are secure. Rosoboronexport offers the implementation of reliable site-specific protection against UAVs, tailored to each specific partner and facility. All the equipment and solutions used in this system have proven their effectiveness in real conditions," said Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheyev, quoted by the press service.
It added that the project is a multi-layered system comprising airspace reconnaissance capabilities, firepower capabilities, and electronic countermeasures against UAVs, a geoinformation system based on an automated control system, as well as engineering (physical) protection measures.
The company said that during the third Russia-Africa Summit, Rosoboronexport will present the concept itself to its partners, along with solutions designed for the development of the Anti-Drone Dome. These include physical UAV destruction systems such as the Pantsir-SMD-E air defense missile system and the Pantsir-S1M air defense missile and gun system developed by the High Precision Systems Holding Company, the Verba man-portable air defense system (MANPADS) and the TKB-1167 air defense system, as well as the Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system with programmable-detonation ammunition, developed by Rostec.
The company is also showcasing the Silok, Repellent-Patrol, Sky-Hunter 4PC, and Radescan (in its anti-drone version) systems for detecting and electronically jamming the control and navigation channels of unmanned aerial vehicles.
The Anti-Drone Dome is a comprehensive system whose configuration and functionality are adapted to a specific customer, taking into account the characteristics of the protected facility.
All of its components are developed and manufactured at facilities in Russia.

title: Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine's Cabinet has opened the construction of underground arms production space to private investors, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on 22 October, saying the rule applies from that day. A second decision eases imports for partner-funded weapons production. Koretskyi said the change would add more of the space arms makers need, especially as Russian strikes intensify. On 9 December 2025, the Defense Ministry reported that more than UAH 1.5 billion (about $36 million) in budget support had let war-damaged defense firms restore operations. At the time, the ministry planned to relocate or duplicate the most critical plants, and underground complexes were under construction. The new model puts no additional burden on the state budget, Deputy Defense Minister Hanna Hvozdiar said . The bill still lands somewhere, though. Defense firms will buy, lease, or take the space for use, and companies working on state contracts are among those eligible. If they pay developers out of state-contract revenue, part of the cost could come back to the budget. Developers build, arms makers move in The changes to Cabinet resolution No. 1494 give private investors a simplified route to construction and permits, the ministry said. Developers can build protected facilities with their own or raised funds. Deadlines, terms of use, and the handover are set in a contract between investor and defense firm. The mechanism covers new sites as well as moving or expanding existing production. If a firm gets only part of a facility, that part must be at least 25% of the facility's total area and fit for production. Explore further One year of Ukrainian arms exports, and industry has questions: how much army gained, where Berlin office is, who joins joint ventures Developers must sign deals with, among others, residents of Defence City, Ukraine's special legal regime for arms makers, holders of state defense contracts, and firms the ministry designates as critical. Tax break for partner-funded arms production Components for weapons production that international partners pay for will enter Ukraine free of import duty and VAT, Koretskyi said. He added that customs inspection and clearance would be simplified and sharply shortened through a "single window."
