title: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
body: Switzerland’s foreign ministry has confirmed that the woman who has tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria is the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national who lives in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, tested positive for the virus on 20 October, becoming the country’s first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade. They both travelled to Uganda earlier this month. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, according to the Swiss foreign ministry. The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The ministry said the woman had spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja with symptoms before her diagnosis. It believes she contracted the virus while travelling in Uganda, although health authorities have yet to establish the source of her infection. Uganda borders Democratic Republic of Congo, where some 4,600 have died in the country’s most deadly outbreak of Ebola. Two people died in Uganda shortly after the outbreak began in May but it has been declared free of Ebola since August. The ministry said the decision not to isolate the embassy’s eight Swiss and 17 local employees was taken in consultation with Nigeria’s Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO). It added that the embassy remained open and operational, with health and safety measures in place. The woman is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the WHO. She returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. The patient did ​not travel to DR Congo, the Swiss ‌government told Reuters news agency on Friday, contradicting accounts from Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October. Health officials are now investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died from Ebola and had travelled through Uganda’s main airport on the same day. Investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday. Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency’s head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was “one of the possible scenarios”, but stressed that no link had been established. “One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport,” he told journalists. The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died shortly afterwards, becoming Kenya’s first recorded Ebola death. Kenya has since confirmed nine infections, including the fatal case. Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact. Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source. The WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria became infected. “The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together,” said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official. He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital. Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. “The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority,” said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO’s representative in Nigeria. Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business. However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria’s health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country. Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman’s travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there. Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing more people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially identified. Kenya’s Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant and not panic but warned: “We are not out of the woods”. He said the remaining eight patients were still in isolation and responding well to treatment. The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands cross daily for trade, work and family visits. Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points. The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for “regional vigilance” and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers. Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu. The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms. Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

title: Tusk: Zelenskyy does not back Lviv Regional Council decision that could hinder Ukraine's integration
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy does not support the decision of the Lviv Regional Council, which, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, could complicate Ukraine's integration due to an insufficient consideration of Polish sensitivity regarding shared historical issues, Tusk stated during a conversation with journalists in India.
"I received a signal from President Zelenskyy that, if further actions depend on him, he will in no way support this decision. He was very unhappy with what happened," Tusk said.
According to him, he made considerable efforts to explain to the Ukrainian side why it is important to take Poland's position into account on matters of a shared tragic history. "Ukraine will simply have very serious problems with integration if it does not also respect our sensitivity. We are not demanding anything extraordinary," the Polish prime minister stated.
At the same time, Tusk noted that it is difficult for him to answer for the decisions of individual district or regional deputies. He described the event in Lviv as resembling a planned provocation by one of the local nationalists.
As reported, on October 20, the Lviv Regional Council voted in favor of a decision to declare 2027 Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, and Oleh Olzhych. The corresponding decision was approved at a meeting of the regional council's commission on culture, information policy, and promotion on July 6, shortly after Polish President Karol Nawrocki announced his decision to strip Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle due to his conferring upon the Separate Center for Special Operations North of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine the honorary name "Named after the Heroes of the UPA."
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized this decision by the Lviv Regional Council on October 20, noting that it helps Ukraine's enemies, and Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that the decision harms relations between the two countries.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski signed a motion to add Lviv Regional Council deputy Svyatoslav Sheremeta to the list of persons persona non grata on the territory of Poland.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine issued a statement emphasizing the importance of developing friendly bilateral relations with Poland and considering the recent decision of the Lviv Regional Council to be counterproductive to current efforts.
On October 21, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki stated that the Ukrainian side had promised to repeal the decision of the Lviv Regional Council.

title: UK government advises stockpiling water and food
body: The UK government has published guidance urging households to “be ready” in the event of a national emergency by stocking up on essentials and signing up for government support. The new advice that households should ensure they could be self-sufficient for three days in an emergency was posted on a government website on Thursday, along with a written ministerial statement to Parliament by Security Minister Dan Jarvis. He also posted on social media about the campaign. The UK has been facing threats from bad weather, drought and flooding, as well as AI and hostile activity from Russia and Iran. The campaign for Britons to step up their preparations had been planned for earlier in the year by Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer. However Mr Burnham delayed the launch due to concerns that it could be seen as an overly pessimistic start to his premiership, Bloomberg reported. Mr Burnham has spent his first three months in office trying to build optimism across the UK. Policy announcements have focused more on feel-good steps such as bus fare caps and greater devolution than on thorny issues such as defence spending and the threats facing the UK. But the decision to publish guidance telling households to “take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted” suggests the government is now seeking to build voter awareness of the difficult decisions facing John Healey in his budget next week. The Chancellor is weighing the need to increase defence expenditure against other government spending priorities. “Individual households can play their role in making sure that they’re more resilient, but government has a role in making sure we’ve got the right defences,” Paymaster General James Murray told Sky on Friday morning. “The big focus, rightly for many years and into the future, is on our military capability, our defensive capability.” The online checklist advised Britons to stock up on three days’ supply of bottled water and non-perishable foods, as well as hand sanitiser, a torch and batteries, and a radio. It also advised them to keep cash at hand, copies of important documents, and blankets and warm clothing. “The storms last winter and the wildfires this summer have shown how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, like phones, power, water and the internet,” Mr Jarvis said in his statement. They “are a reminder that we can all play our part to keep ourselves, our loved ones and our communities safe in times of emergency.” Ministers are under pressure to take significant steps to modernise infrastructure and prepare for the future. Hotter summers and plans for data centre construction are increasing demand for water, but the UK has not built a reservoir since 1992, shortly after the privatisation of the water sector. Britain has also been warned by leading defence experts that it needs to invest heavily in its military, as it is unprepared to defend itself in the event of a full-scale war. Mr Healey quit as defence secretary under Mr Starmer in a row over military spending. Now, as Chancellor, he faces the challenge of getting defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035. The way the advice has been rolled out highlights the government’s determination not to overdo the worries, with memories of supermarket shelves being emptied in the early days of the Covid pandemic still relatively fresh. Mr Jarvis said the move “brings the UK into line with many of our European peers who also have the three-day message at the heart of their campaign”. No government ministers had been scheduled to speak on the launch of the resilience campaign this week. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting only revealed that the launch was imminent when questioned by journalists at the opening of weapons factory in the West Midlands on Thursday. He said the public needed to be prepared for supply chain disruption caused by “hostile state actors or terrorists” and later added, in an appearance on BBC’s Question Time , that he wanted “people to be alert but not alarmed”. Speaking in front of the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee last week, Jim Bligh, corporate affairs director of the British Retail Consortium, said he was concerned about being too alarmist. “Panic buying is quite easy to generate, particularly if you tell people to buy a particular type of product – they will go out to buy it,” he said. “If the government were to say to you, ‘Go and buy x litres of water,’ would we run out of water? I do not know.” UK shoppers rushed to stockpile essentials in March 2020 as the Covid-19 pandemic stoked fears of lockdowns and shortages. Toilet paper, pasta and cleaning products vanished from shelves in many stores, forcing supermarkets to step up restocking. Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons joined the BRC that month in urging shoppers to buy only what they needed, warning that panic buying risked leaving others without essentials.

title: The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); US President Donald Trump said Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starshield speeds, but the restrictions remained in place on 23 October, according to Ukrainian officials. The cap, in place since 14 October, has disrupted interceptor drone missions against jet-powered Shaheds flying above 400 km/h for more than a week. On 16 October, Trump told reporters that, from what he understood, nothing had changed with the service. His latest claim that Musk restored it appears to acknowledge the restriction, even as he denies ordering it. Ukraine says restrictions remain “At the moment, there is no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted, ” a Defense Ministry official told LIGA.net on the morning of 23 October. The official said connections continued to drop at above 161 km/h. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on 23 October that no lifting had been recorded. He said occasional operation above the limit could result from SpaceX algorithms or usage conditions. A day earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had promised to return with information in “48 plus hours,” according to his remarks to reporters in Kyiv. A Ukrainian official separately told The Kyiv Independent that reports of restored speeds were “all false.” A senior European official told the Associated Press that the cap remained at about 160 km/h and that Ukraine had no clear explanation of who ordered it or why. Conflicting reports of a lift Trump said Musk had restored the speeds but declined to clarify whether he had contacted him. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said. Meanwhile, AP reported that the Wall Street Journal said Musk had agreed to lift the restrictions. The Ukrainian drone and mapping channel Kartohraf posted on the evening of 22 October that the cap had been lifted. The Economist’s Oliver Carroll said that frontline drone commanders thought it had likely been lifted but were still testing, according to his post on X. Who ordered the cap? The order came from inside the White House, according to a Reuters report on 15 October. Days later, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered the slowdown. Rubio denied White House involvement, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on 20 October that the US had not ordered the restriction. Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal announced an inquiry into how the service was slowed, AP reported. Ukraine’s gains in Donetsk Oblast rely on drones the cap slows The 3rd Army Corps’ Operation Vivaldi retook ground north of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast with drones, many of which rely on Starlink or Starshield, and those gains could erode if the cap stays. At the same time, Radio Svoboda reported that Ukraine needs a limit of at least 450 km/h and that Germany pays for the service under a contract running until April 2027.
