title: Abu Dhabi F1 concert and clubbing guide, from Andrea Bocelli and Imagine Dragons to Jennifer Lopez
body: The Abu Dhabi Grand Prix has become one of the UAE's busiest weekends for live music, with entertainment extending beyond the after-race concerts to clubs, restaurants and parties across Yas Island. This year's programme begins a day before the Formula One action with a selection of stirring arias from Italian opera star Andrea Bocelli. From Thursday to Sunday, pop and rock headliners will take over the newly renamed Etihad Live, while international DJs perform at glitzy venues overlooking Yas Marina Circuit. Here is what to expect. Wednesday, December 2 Andrea Bocelli at Etihad Arena The Italian tenor will open the inaugural Yasalam Classics series with his Romanza 30th Anniversary World Tour, accompanied by the Armenian State Symphony Orchestra. The concert revisits the 1997 album that helped establish him internationally, with songs including Con te Partiro and Vivo Per Lei . Bocelli, who has sold more than 90 million records, also performed at this year's World Cup opening ceremony in Mexico. Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295 Thursday, December 3 Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson at Etihad Live Scottish singer Lewis Capaldi returns less than a year after his sold-out Saadiyat Nights concert in January. Best known for Someone You Loved and Before You Go , he is back on the road after a two-year break, with newer songs including Survive and Something in the Heavens . Swedish pop star Zara Larsson will perform a separate set featuring Lush Life and Never Forget You , alongside material from her fifth album, Midnight Sun , which earned her first Grammy nomination. Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders Friday, December 4 Jennifer Lopez and Alex Warren at Etihad Live Jennifer Lopez is to return to Abu Dhabi to headline the second night of the Grand Prix after-race concert series. It will be her third concert in the capital in less than two years, following a sold-out performance at Saadiyat Nights in February 2025 and a show at Etihad Arena five months later that attracted more than 14,000 fans. The latter show was part of her Up All Night international tour and comprises a 90-minute set with elaborate choreography, costume changes and new arrangements of songs spanning her career. Ranked among The National's best UAE concerts of 2025 , the performance included a mash-up of Jenny from the Block and Queen's We Will Rock You , as well as a flamenco-inspired rendition of her debut single If You Had My Love . This night of the after-race series will begin with a set by American singer-songwriter Alex Warren, who will make his UAE debut after the international success of his hit single Ordinary . Warren first found an audience through social media and his music draws on grief, family and relationships in songs including Carry You Home and Burning Down . His second album, Wildchild , was launched in August. Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders Anyma at Yas Gateway Park The Italian-American DJ, also known as Matteo Milleri, brings his melodic techno and elaborate visual production to the official Grand Prix after-party. One half of electronic duo Tale of Us, he has developed a solo show featuring towering digital figures and science-fiction imagery. The production has taken him to the Sphere in Las Vegas and Egypt's Pyramids of Giza . Doors open 9pm; show starts 10.30pm; tickets from Dh495 Shimza at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit The South African DJ brings his percussion-heavy Afro-tech sound to the trackside hospitality venue. Known for lengthy hypnotic sets, Shimza has performed at clubs and festivals across Europe and Africa and collaborated with fellow South African artist Black Coffee, who takes to the stage here on Sunday. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 Mont Rouge and Moojo at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi Swiss duo Mont Rouge will share the Friday bill with French DJ Moojo at Bagatelle's rooftop pop-up. Mont Rouge are known for their Afro-house version of Voyage Voyage, recorded with Francis Mercier and Coco, and their remix of Axwell and Sebastian Ingrosso's More Than You Know . Tables from Dh7,000 Saturday, December 5 Imagine Dragons at Etihad Live The American pop-rock band return three years after selling out Etihad Arena in 2023. Fronted by Dan Reynolds, their concerts feature heavy percussion and singalong hits including Radioactive , Believer and Thunder . Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders CamelPhat at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit British electronic duo CamelPhat, comprising Dave Whelan and Mike Di Scala, broke through with the Grammy-nominated 2017 single Cola, recorded with Elderbrook. They followed it with club favourites including Panic Room with Au/Ra and Breathe with Cristoph and Jem Cooke, combining house, techno and melodic electronic music. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 Gordo at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi Formerly known as Carnage, the Nicaraguan-American DJ plays a blend of hip-hop-infused house music and contributed to Drake's 2022 album Honestly, Nevermind . He followed it with his solo album Diamante in 2024, featuring collaborations with Drake and Maluma. Tables from Dh10,000 Sunday, December 6 The Chainsmokers and The Script at Etihad Live American electronic duo The Chainsmokers and Irish band The Script will close the after-race concert series with separate sets. The Chainsmokers, comprising Andrew Taggart and Alex Pall, are behind hits including Closer and Something Just Like This with Coldplay. Their latest work includes Love Is Kind , a five-track EP released in May with Swedish singer Oaks. The Script return with their eighth album, The User's Guide to Being Human , released in August. Led by Danny O'Donoghue, the band are known for Breakeven and Hall of Fame. Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders Black Coffee at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit The Grammy-winning South African DJ will bring his blend of deep house, African percussion and soulful vocals to the trackside venue. His 2021 album Subconsciously , featuring Pharrell Williams and David Guetta, won Best Dance/Electronic Music Album at the 2022 Grammy Awards. He is also a regular fixture on Ibiza's club circuit. His interest in racing extends beyond the DJ booth through Carl Cox Motorsport, which he founded in 2013. Tables from Dh10,000

title: Sultan of Sokoto Advocates Intelligence-led Policing
body: Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto The Sultan of Sokoto, His Eminence, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, has called for a paradigm shift toward robust, intelligence-led policing to tackle evolving security challenges in the country. The Sultan made the call recently when the new Assistant Inspector-General of Police (AIG) in charge of Zone 10, Ahmed Musa, paid him a courtesy visit at his palace in Sokoto. He said modern policing requires proactive intelligence gathering, community partnership and professionalism to sustainably address insecurity in the North-west and the country at large. Alhaji Sa’ad Abubakar commended officers and men of the Nigeria Police Force serving across Sokoto State for their dedication and sacrifices in safeguarding the region. The Sultan warmly congratulated AIG Musa on his posting as the 25th AIG in charge of Zone 10 Headquarters, Sokoto, and expressed optimism for his success in the new assignment. He expressed hope that the AIG would return to the Seat of the Caliphate in an even greater leadership capacity, having distinguished himself in service. The religious leader assured the police leadership of the Sultanate Council’s sustained institutional support and deepened relationship with the Nigeria Police Force. The Sultan also underscored the importance of the forthcoming general elections, offering prayers for peace, stability and decorum throughout the campaign period and the polls. Earlier, AIG Musa told the Sultan that the visit was part of his familiarisation tour and to formally announce his assumption of duty at the Zonal Command. The AIG, who was accompanied by the Commissioner of Police, Sokoto State Command, and other senior officers, said the visit was to identify with the traditional institution. He disclosed that before his posting to Zone 10, he served as AIG in charge of Community Policing at the Force Headquarters, Abuja. Musa said that, with his background in community policing, he was committed to enhancing community policing efforts to tackle insecurity within Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara States. The visit, according to the Zonal Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Faruk Abdallah Ambursa, ended with mutual assurances of collaboration between the traditional institution and the police.

title: Russia prepares new provocations to destabilize Europe – GUR
body:
Russia is intensifying its hybrid destabilization strategy against the European Union with the aim of reducing or depriving Ukraine of external support. This involves attempts to discredit the Defense Forces, as well as intimidate European governments and societies, reported the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (GUR).
"According to military intelligence estimates, this may involve carrying out provocative sabotage actions on the territory of Central and Eastern Europe, in particular the Baltic states. Various scenarios feature in Moscow's plans – including conducting 'false flag operations' with subsequent blame placed on Ukraine through Russian propaganda channels and international platforms accessible to the Kremlin," reads the statement on Telegram.
According to GUR, potential sites for Russian provocations could include critical infrastructure facilities, the border area with Russia, the Kaliningrad enclave, regions in EU states with a present "Russian-speaking population" and structures controlled by the Kremlin, particularly the network of Russian Orthodox Church facilities and historical sites associated with Russia.
Earlier, in early October 2026, GUR reported orders to Russian special services to step up activity on the territory of the EU and NATO – Ukraine warned its partners about the corresponding threats.

title: Russia, US need to move forward in eliminating bilateral irritants — Russian MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Moscow and Washington must make progress in eliminating bilateral irritants, the director of the North Atlantic Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, Alexander Gusarov, said in an interview with the International Affairs Journal.
"It is the directive impulses emanating from our presidents that set the vector and content of our bilateral contacts, including on the topic you mentioned of so-called irritants in our relations," he said. "Specifically, in relation to this topic, these impulses were set by the presidents at the very dawn of their communication at the beginning of last year, when the heads of state agreed to move towards the normalization of our diplomatic relations."
"Since then, quite significant results have been achieved in the form of agreements to improve the operating conditions of our diplomatic missions. This, of course, is not the ultimate dream, we understand that. We need to keep trying to move this cart. For its part, Russia is very ambitious in assessing the range of what is possible on this track," Gusarov said.
He also drew attention to the priorities of the Russian side: first of all, the return to Russia of diplomatic property in that country illegally confiscated under previous US administrations, as well as the resumption of direct air traffic between the two countries. At the same time, according to him, there is not yet sufficient political will on the part of American colleagues, who often try to link these matters with far-fetched regional and international issues.
"As for future rounds [of talks concerning irritants], we assume that before the end of the year, probably another such round could take place. Its specific dates will be agreed upon through channels," he said.

title: Media reports: Fire breaks out near military airfield in Voronezh after missile alert
body:
This was reported by the ASTRA Telegram channel, according to Ukrinform.
Alexander Gusev, governor of the Voronezh region, stated that “dry grass caught fire as a result of falling debris from downed targets.”
“ Air defense forces on duty detected and destroyed several aerial targets in the sky over Voronezh. According to preliminary data, there were no casualties. Debris from the downed targets caused a fire in dry grass in the suburbs; the fire has already been extinguished,” he wrote on social media.
Earlier, Gusev had reported a missile threat in the region.
According to publicly available data, the 47th Guards Bomber Aviation Regiment is stationed at the “Baltimore” airfield.
The airfield has been regularly used by the Russian Air Force to launch airstrikes against Ukrainian territory since February 24, 2022.
A fire near the “Baltimore” airfield in Voronezh was previously reported on September 2. Prior to that, the airfield had been attacked on May 27.
As reported by Ukrinform, just last week, the Ukrainian Navy, using the “Neptune” coastal missile system, struck six Su-34M bombers at the “Borisoglebsk” military airfield in the Voronezh region of the Russian Federation.
The first photo is for illustrative purposes only

title: Job Loss and Cortisone Mania
body:
Losing my job, getting sick, and searching for meaning. Written at 06:45, 2026-10-20 .
On the morning of 18th August, I got invited at short notice into a 1:1 meeting by my manager, which was unusual . I think I knew what was coming, and I was right: The company is restructuring, and I’m being let go (among a lot of other people). I had time until lunch to say my goodbyes to my colleagues as I would be logged out of my account after that. Because I was still in my six-month probation period, I was put on paid leave for two more weeks; after that I’d be out of a job for the first time since I started working roughly 10 years ago.
I’ve seen it happen to other people and entire departments, but it had never happened to me — I guess I’m a real tech worker now!
Shortly after, I got sick. I believe it was a Covid infection; I didn’t have any respiratory symptoms, but low energy, joint pain and general feelings of stiffness. Every move was a show of strength. I developed a cough that is now — 2 months later — still subsiding but present.
I’m not sure if it was Covid, but being sick triggered the autoimmune condition I have. I mostly got out of bed, watched shorts, videos and movies, and then I went to bed again. I had to take some trips into the city by bike, and hours later it would hit me like a brick wall, leaving me even more exhausted on the next day. I lost my appetite and some weight, which is not good since I rarely moved and I’m fairly lean to begin with.
This state dragged on for three weeks until I went to see a specialist and got all the blood work and tests done, so that my medication could get adjusted. Being sick for a couple of days is something I can bear, but not being able to perform even the smallest tasks for such a long time was a disheartening experience.
I was put on cortisone treatment, which relieved my symptoms immediately. Cortisone essentially lowers your body’s immune response — which is great when your body tries to defend itself against itself, like mine did. On the other hand, cortisone is not meant for long-term or permanent treatment, and it has a lot of potential side effects.
After one or two days, I was back to my normal self, energised, vital, with no signs of inflammation. I now fully realised that I was out of a job, and had the chance to fill my time meaningfully. Job searching doesn’t take up your 16 waking hours.
In some phases of my life, I can take a giant step back, and look at it like from a bird’s eye view. I’m approaching 30, but how will I live when I’m 40, 50, 60, 70 years of age? Will I be healthy? Will I still pursue my hobbies? Will I have children, or grandchildren even? Who will be close to me? I can’t force my fate, but I can make conscious decisions every day to aid this transition. I felt mindful, present in the moment, and free. Lucid.
So I researched a sleep routine. Cleaned the entire apartment. Discarded useless stuff. Created lists and overviews. Organised. Shopping lists. Meal plans. Jotted down recipes. Fixed broken things. Impulse-bought some personal items for my living room.
I addressed tiny things that stuck out to me more than once, like a mark on the wall that I painted over, or re-seasoning my cast-iron pan since it was in a bad state. Every time I looked at these, I felt remorse or the need to do them, but never followed through.
I did all of this, and it felt incredible. Focusing on something, and realising it (as in putting it into reality). Self-efficacy. While I can’t vouch for the movie, it surely felt like this scene from Limitless .
I didn’t realise right away, but I was feeling strong signs of restlessness. My heart felt like it was racing, even though I wasn’t doing anything exhausting. I couldn’t sit still for an extended time. My mind was jumping from thought to thought. I felt like a wound-up toy, manic. I used this frenzy to tackle all the chores and tasks and projects and minuscule things, and yet I still kind of liked it. 110% productivity.
Other side effects I noticed: My face swelled up a bit, making it look more full (which looks good on me tho). My knee joints feel weird. My sleep is basically broken: I go to bed at 23:00–00:00 every day, and try to wake up at 8:00. The routine is there, but falling asleep actually takes some time, and I usually wake up at 5:00 or 6:00, completely awake. Not necessarily fully rested, but not sleepy anymore.
Right now, I feel healthy and great. As I’m tapering off the cortisone, the side effects will cease, but all the work I put into improving my daily life will still be there.
Maybe this post can inspire you to take a step back from your own life, and assess your priorities. I can rarely get into this mindset, but when I do, it makes me feel serene, in control. Every day life can get to you in so many ways.

title: Chalenko: Russia, partners try to use winter factor to pressure Ukraine in talks
body:
The winter period could become an additional instrument of pressure on Ukraine in the context of the negotiation process, while Kyiv must maintain diplomatic resilience and not retreat from its baseline positions, believes political scientist and Head of the Center for Analysis and Strategies Ihor Chalenko.
Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Ukraine on threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality
Speaking during the discussion "Ukraine on the threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality" at the press center of the Interfax-Ukraine information agency on Friday , Chalenko noted that the energy, security, and diplomatic dimensions are currently inextricably linked.
"The winter factor is being used not only by our Russian enemy, but obviously also by our partners to exert certain elements of pressure on the Ukrainian side in order to soften Ukraine's position," he said.
According to the political scientist, Ukraine has recently faced difficulties in obtaining certain defense capabilities, in particular Patriot interceptor missiles, as well as delays in the implementation of certain decisions by partners. At the same time, he emphasized that in the energy sphere, a positive effect from previously reached agreements with allies remains, which should facilitate getting through the heating season.
Chalenko believes that Russia shows no readiness for a compromise settlement of the war, but instead attempts to use the diplomatic track to increase pressure on Ukraine. In his opinion, the most realistic scenario remains a difficult winter without reaching comprehensive agreements on ending the war, while new opportunities for fruitful negotiations could open up after the winter period ends.

title: Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters
body: The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say. Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department. Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?” Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.” Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.” Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.” Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems. Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve. Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk. The post Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Opinion: A friendly frigate and a lesson in choosing partners
body:
On Monday 19 October I stood on the deck of INS Tarkash in False Bay as the ship’s Chetak helicopter hovered overhead. Brazil’s BNS Barroso steamed nearby, and South Africa’s submarine SAS Manthatisi was in the same waters – as well as SAS Amatola. The Indian crew were impressive: professional, welcoming, and friendly. They were keen to talk about all kinds of things, from their ship to naval strategy and tactics, to cricket. The weather was perfect for the exercise, and I came away thinking about a different naval exercise held in the same waters nine months earlier.
IBSAMAR is a maritime co-operation forum that brings together the navies of India, Brazil and South Africa. It has run every second year since 2008, with this latest edition the ninth. South Africa is an ideal host because of where it sits on the sea route between the Atlantic and Indian oceans. The lead nation changes, and this time it was India’s turn. The exercise ran from 8 to 20 October, with a harbour phase followed by a sea phase in False Bay. The South Africa navy contributed the Valor Classs frigate SAS Amatola, two inshore patrol vessels of the Warrior Class, SAS King Sekhukhune and SAS Adam Kok III, and the submarine SAS Manthatisi. Brazil sent the corvette BNS Barroso, while India sent INS Tarkash, which carries a Chetak helicopter and a special forces team. The theme was “Stronger Together Towards a Shared Future in the Maritime Domain”.
Exercise Will for Peace ran from 9 to 16 January 2026, with China being the exercise lead. Russia and Iran joined, and the United Arab Emirates sent a corvette. The exercise was first planned as Mosi III, the third in a series South Africa has held with China and Russia. By the time it started, it had morphed into something else.
Ukrainians protested outside the Simon’s Town base. The Democratic Alliance objected to the presence of Russia and Iran. On 16 January, the United States embassy called Iran a “destabilizing actor and state sponsor of terror” and said its inclusion in any capacity undermined maritime security. Reports also said the presidency had ordered Iran excluded, yet Iranian ships were anchored in False Bay. A probe was launched to investigate what happened. Brazil and India, both BRICS members, stayed away. India’s foreign ministry said the drill was a South African initiative and not a regular BRICS activity.
The two exercises can be compared on what South Africa’s navy gained, and what South Africa’s government (read: the taxpayer) paid for it.
On the first measure, they look alike. Both gave the SA Navy time at sea with foreign ships. Both offered practice in vessel boarding, escort and search-and-rescue drills. SAS Amatola, took part in both. A navy with a small fleet needs that practice from whoever will provide it.
But on deeper reading, they differ sharply. IBSAMAR is an exercise between three democracies that have worked together for eighteen years. Nobody must explain who is on the guest list or why. Will for Peace needed days of explanation. The government had to defend it to Washington, to its own coalition partners and to a public that wanted to know why Iranian warships were in South African waters. Pretoria spent diplomatic capital that IBSAMAR, by contrast, does not draw down.
The lead nation sets the tone. IBSAMAR passes the lead from one partner to the next, and every edition has the same three members. Will for Peace had China in the lead and a guest list that changed as the politics changed. A rotating lead among three fixed partners gives South Africa a predictable exercise. A single dominant lead with an open guest list leaves the host answering for other countries’ choices.
India shows how this can be handled. Tarkash was built in Russia, and India also sent INS Sahyadri to Vladivostok for a separate exercise with the Russian navy from 13 to 18 October. On the way to South Africa, Tarkash held a passage exercise with the Kenyan navy at Mombasa, and India and Kenya held their first staff talks. In June the same ship called at Port Victoria in the Seychelles. India builds each of these partnerships separately, with its own rules and its own guest list. Nobody asks India to choose between them, because New Delhi never presents them as a bloc.
The Indian Navy is also growing rapidly, currently operating more than 140 ships. It commissioned 12 warships and one submarine in 2025, and its defence minister said on 29 September that the navy would commission 18 warships this year, the largest single-year addition in its history. The navy has said it will have more than 200 ships by 2035. About 45 to 50 ships are under construction, and every one is being built in an Indian yard. Tamal, a sister ship of Tarkash, was commissioned in Russia on 1 July 2025. She was the last warship the navy took from a foreign yard.
The orders create work and skills at home. The Indian government’s 70 000 crore rupee (R120 billion) shipbuilding package was meant to lift production, jobs and supply chains in steel and electronics. One recent frigate, INS Dunagiri, was reported to carry 75% indigenous content, with more than 200 small suppliers and more than 14 000 jobs behind it. India’s defence ministry reported record defence production of 1.78 trillion rupees (about R300 billion) in the 2025-26 financial year, up 15.6% on the year before, and record defence exports of 384 billion rupees (about R65 billion).
Technological innovations and progress, with benefits for other economic sectors, follow the orders. India took delivery of its own aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, in 2022, builds Kalvari-class submarines at home, and commissioned its third nuclear-powered submarine, INS Aridhaman, on 3 April 2026. A navy that builds at home also pays wages and trains engineers at home.
Simon’s Town’s strategic location and value explain why South Africa’s choice of partners matters. The base sits on False Bay, next to the Cape Sea route that links the Atlantic and Indian oceans. Ships carrying oil, grains, containers and cars between Asia, Europe and the Americas pass it every day. Since the Red Sea became dangerous in late 2023, more of that traffic has gone round the Cape. The US, Israel-Iran war that erupted in February has forced yet more traffic around the Cape.
South Africa also carries a heavy responsibility at sea. It runs the search-and-rescue service for a very large stretch of three oceans. It has to protect its fishing grounds, its offshore resources, and its ports. No other country will do this for South Africa. The job needs ships that can stay at sea for weeks, aircraft that can see and reach a long way, and submarines, to protect undersea infrastructure and deter aggression. It needs a navy and an air force that train together and can be sent wherever they are needed. That ability to project capable forces far from home and keep them there is vital.
What I saw on the water showed how little South Africa has available to do that job. The sailors on SAS Amatola did what they could with what they have. So did the air force crews flying an Oryx helicopter and a Gripen fighter in support of the exercise. The effort is there, but the equipment is perilously little and thin.
The submarine in my photograph, SAS Manthatisi, is the only one of the navy’s three submarines that can go to sea. She returned to sea in July, nearly three years after a training accident off Kommetjie in September 2023 that resulted in three deaths. The navy said it cleared her after safety inspections and crew certification. The other two, SAS Charlotte Maxeke and SAS Queen Modjadji I, are in the midst of an unfunded refit programme. Manthatisi’s own midlife refit, planned for 2022, has not taken place. She can sail, but she is not in the condition a modern submarine should be.
Amatola is one of four frigates. The CRA Macro Review, Under Siege, found that she was the only one of the four that was serviceable, and able to go to sea. She spent years out of service for maintenance and returned to the fleet in 2024. In January she sailed for India, the navy’s first long-range foreign deployment in about ten years. The navy’s sea-hour record shows the strain. In the 2024/25 financial year, it spent 3 717 hours at sea, less than half its planned target.
A claim to sovereignty over the sea gets tested by other countries – and in increasing numbers, non-state actors. The claim holds only as far as the state can enforce it. A country that cannot patrol its waters, escort its trade or respond to an incident depends on others to do those things, and those others have interests of their own. The world is more uncertain than it was a decade ago. South Africa cannot treat its navy and air force as an afterthought and still call itself sovereign.
South Africa could do the same as India. Pretoria says it is not aligned. To be credible – and useable – non-alignment means that no single partner decides who comes to Simon’s Town. A sensible rule would be that South Africa publishes the participant list before any exercise it hosts and sets out the exercise’s purpose in plain terms. The navy would then train with whoever fits that purpose. IBSAMAR already follows that rule in practice.
Exercises such as IBSAMAR matter greatly. A navy, air force, or army can look great in theory and on paper, but things become harshly different when equipment and troops must be deployed – and if they haven’t had the time to actually practice, theory will only carry them so far. With one working submarine and very few working frigates, every week at sea with a capable partner builds skills that cannot be learned in harbour. Spending that time on a drill that costs goodwill with major trading partners wastes a scarce resource. Spending it with partners who bring seamanship, a clear purpose and no controversy builds the capability that sovereignty needs. IBSAMAR shows what that looks like. The harder question is whether the budget will give the navy and the air force the ships, aircraft and crews to match the coastline South Africa has to defend.
I owe thanks to Captain Rohit Mishra, the commanding officer of INS Tarkash, and to his crew. They hosted me with warmth and courtesy, and they were happy to answer questions on any subject. A visitor on a warship is an extra burden in the middle of an exercise, but they never made me feel like one.
I left Tarkash with a pleasant memory of the crew and a clear view of the contrast. Both exercises cost South Africa fuel and sailors’ time. Only one of them also cost South Africa friends.
Chris Hattingh, Executive Director of the Centre for Risk Analysis, for CRA Defence & Geopolitics.
Republished with permission from The Daily Friend. The original article can be found here .

title: Merchant vessel sinks in Black Sea, one dead — media
body:
BUCHAREST, October 23. /TASS/. A merchant vessel sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania, killing one person, the Realitatea Plus television channel reported, citing sources.
According to the television channel, the Romanian Navy received a distress signal at 10:00 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT). There were 13 people on board, including 10 Ukrainian nationals and three Azerbaijani citizens. Nine people have so far been rescued from the water alive, and one fatality has been reported. Search and rescue operations are continuing and are being hampered by adverse weather conditions.
The cause of the vessel’s damage remains unknown. The vessel may have been carrying petroleum products, the report said.

title: Top EU diplomat looks to strengthen defence, peace and security ties with SA
body:
Unrest and armed violence in the Middle East has seen a rethink of European Union (EU) partnerships. This saw the diplomat heading the Peace, Partnerships and Crisis Management apparatus of the bloc’s External Action Service talking regional stability and African-led peace efforts in Pretoria earlier in October.
Speaking to DefenceWeb, Director Cosmin Dobran noted increased shipping on the Cape of Good Hope route with its added – and unwelcome – addition of potentially more piracy and criminality along the lower eastern continental seaboard. “This was one of a number of discussion points,” he said, at the first ‘Peace, Security and Defence Dialogue’ between South Africa and the European Union, which was agreed during the South Africa–EU Summit in March 2025. He added that Africa’s Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa along with Gaza and the Ukraine were also agenda items.
With maritime security in the Mozambique Channel expected to become a higher priority, Dobran hopes for more involvement from the Southern African Development Community (SADC). He pointed to the ongoing EU naval tasking Operation Atalanta and said expanding the SADC maritime commitment “made sense”. He would not be drawn on whether this meant additional assets deployed under the EU Atalanta banner or more patrols by South African Navy hulls (under the Operation Copper banner).
The dialogue between the Dobran delegation and South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Co-operation (DIRCO), led by Deputy Director General Xolisa Mabhongo, was a first marking what is termed “a new step in the EU/South Africa strategic partnership”. The partnership is seen as a platform to identify common priorities and deepen co-operation in support of peace and security.
Discussions centred on approaches to peace, security and defence as well as how the EU/South Africa partnership can support efforts in this regard. Also on the table were an exchange of views on, among others, conflict prevention, mediation and peacebuilding as well as multilateral co-operation and crisis management. Counter-terrorism, cybersecurity and hybrid threats, maritime and space security and tackling transnational organised crime were also on the agenda with closer exchanges between relevant institutions, including on threat analysis and information sharing, identified as necessities.
Acknowledging the importance of African regional blocs, specifically SADC in the case of the Mozambique Channel, Dobran said South Africa’s stature on the continent made it an obvious choice as a partner. “We want to work with like-minded countries and representative bodies in the best interests of all for peace and security.”
Apart from Atalanta, the EU has two other maritime security taskings operating in and around African waters – Irini in the Mediterranean Sea focussed on ensuring the UN (United Nations) arms embargo on Libya is enforced, and Aspides, safeguarding maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Gulf under the EU Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP).
On land, one of the bloc’s two military assistance missions (MAMs) is in Mozambique where training quick reaction forces (QRFs) of that country’s defence forces is priority.

title: Armscor and Unisa link up for cyber defence education
body:
South Africa’s defence procurement and project management specialist, Armscor, is partnering with the country’s major distance learning tertiary facility to boost education and skills capacity in the cyber defence field.
Additionally, Pretoria headquartered Unisa (University of South Africa) will support students in development, training, research and innovation for defence and national cyber security requirements as per a memorandum of understanding (MoU).
The partnership, an Armscor statement has it, will see Armscor’s defence sector expertise and understanding of operational requirements link with Unisa’s academic capabilities, research expertise and technological resources. The collaboration will support development of solutions to emerging national and defence security challenges and contribute advancing the specialised skills needed in cybersecurity.
The ODeL (Open Distance e-Learning) or CODeL (Comprehensive Open Distance and e-Learning) institution will be complementary to Armscor’s in-house Defence Cyber Academy with the partnership leading to opportunities for defence requirements to be integrated with academic knowledge and technological capabilities to strengthen cyber defence capacity.
Armscor Chief Executive Solomzi Mbada sees the partnership as an important step toward building sustainable cyber defence capabilities through collaboration between government, academia and the defence sector.
“Cybersecurity has become an integral component of national security and defence capability. As the nature of cyber threats continues to evolve we must ensure our defence capabilities are supported by the right skills, knowledge, research and technological solutions. This partnership with Unisa provides an opportunity to bring together complementary strengths in pursuit of that objective.”
Additionally, he sees the Armscor/Unisa partnership bridging the gap between academic research and industry’s practical skills requirements for the defence environment.
“The value of research is ultimately realised when knowledge can be translated into practical solutions. Through the Armscor Defence Cyber Academy, we want to create an environment where academic expertise, research and technological innovation can respond directly to real world defence requirements. Our collaboration with Unisa strengthens our ability to develop capabilities that are relevant, sustainable and responsive to cyber threats facing our country,” he said.
The MoU makes provision for initiation and support of collaborative research and development projects in mutual interest areas relating to defence, cybersecurity and associated technologies. The partnership will further facilitate information sharing sessions, seminars and related initiatives to promote professional development, knowledge exchange and innovation.
The Armscor/Unisa partnership, as per the statement, reinforces Armscor’s commitment to partnerships with academic and research institutions to support development of innovative defence solutions and strengthen the broader national defence ecosystem.
The implementation of the MoU will be overseen by a Joint Steering Committee, which Armscor and Unisa will create. This committee will coordinate, and track the progress (against agreed targets) of, the implementation plan.

title: Patriot interceptor shortage driven by politics, allies' limited stockpiles – Popovitch
body:
The shortage of interceptor missiles for Patriot systems is connected not only with the political decisions of Ukraine's partners, but also with limited global stockpiles of these strike assets and growing demand for them, believes military-political observer Denys Popovitch.
Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Ukraine on threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality
According to him, repelling massive ballistic attacks requires a significant number of interceptor missiles. Popovitch noted that during one of the recent strikes on Kyiv, the enemy used more than two dozen ballistic missiles, to intercept which, under ideal conditions, twice as many Patriot missiles might be needed.
"Even if the United States were maximally favorable toward Ukraine, they would not be able to transfer an unlimited number of such missiles to us because they are physically not produced in sufficient quantities globally," Popovitch said during the discussion "Ukraine on the threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality" at the press center of the Interfax-Ukraine information agency on Friday .
He also emphasized that European countries are in no hurry to transfer their own stocks of missiles and air defense systems, as they view them as an important element of their own security against the backdrop of the Russian missile threat. According to the observer, this winter Ukraine will continue to face intense missile and drone attacks, and the key challenge will remain ensuring a sufficient number of air defense assets to protect cities and critical infrastructure.

title: Dubai Fashion Week opens with dazzling couture by Yousef Al Jasmi, Sara Pedram, Pallavi Puri and Kresha Bajaj
body: Dubai Fashion Week opened its spring/summer 2027 season with a reminder that the region’s fashion ambitions extend well beyond the runway. Before the first models took their places on Thursday, a showroom in Dubai Design District previewed emerging talent from around the world and introduced several designers to the UAE market. Among them was Bahrain’s Touchless, whose 3D-printed handbags have already attracted the attention of British Vogue , Selfridges, Level Shoes and Fashion Trust Arabia, as well as making an appearance in the Bridgerton universe. Egyptian jeweller-turned-eyewear designer Amr Saad brought a precious touch with bespoke gold and silver frames finished with jewellery-like detailing along the arms and bridge. Tunisian footwear label Balga drew on traditional metalworking techniques for its sculptural heels. Leather mules featured hand-hammered metalwork, including a tapered heel etched with graphic lines reminiscent of baklava. Kuwaiti designer Kochylia, whose name means seashells in Greek, offered a considered take on wardrobe classics, from reworked trench coats to tuxedo jackets finished with handmade porcelain buttons fashioned from Kuwaiti mud. Yousef Al Jasmi The evening’s runway programme opened with Kuwait’s Yousef Al Jasmi, a designer well-versed in dressing for the spotlight. Having created looks for Lady Gaga, he understands the appeal of theatrical excess, and this collection delivered it in abundance. Crystal-encrusted dresses skimmed the body, long strands of crystals cascaded from shoulder to floor, and sculpted bodices were paired with sheer, close-fitting skirts. Moving from barely-there nude to dramatic black, the collection was designed to catch the light from every angle. Sara Pedram Next came self-taught designer Sara Pedram, whose collection, Simurgh, drew inspiration from The Conference of the Birds , the 12th-century epic poem by Attar of Nishapur. Exploring transformation, spirituality and Persian cultural heritage, Pedram translated the story into a series of sculptural silhouettes. A ballerina opened the show, followed by sheer creations with wing-like extensions at the shoulders. A richly embellished burnt-umber column gown gave way to a shimmering cascade of swaying paillettes, while a Prussian-blue velvet gown featured a Swarovski-crystal Tree of Life traced across its train, symbolising growth and renewal. Most arresting was a voluminous, full-skirted creation in rough hessian, hand-painted with a scene inspired by Persian poet Hafez , whose work, Pedram explained, was “close to my heart”. “Simurgh is a legendary bird that represents rebirth, transformation and rising again,” Pedram explained backstage. “This collection is very personal to me, especially this year. Fashion is more than a beautiful dress; I love to explain the story behind each piece.” Pallavi Puri Indian designer Pallavi Puri followed with Beyond Borders, a collection exploring cultural exchange through a wardrobe designed for women across the region. Drawing inspiration from family and friends, their tastes and the way they dress, Puri reworked traditional Indian beadwork for a contemporary audience, citing Emirati, Asian and Moroccan women among her most inspirational clientele. Horses were another recurring motif, reflecting both the designer’s long-standing fascination with the animals and Dubai’s enduring equestrian culture. Indian model Lisa Haydon opened the show, while Lebanese actress Cyrine Abdel Nour closed it wearing an embellished bridal look. “Did you realise one is from India and one is Arab?” Puri said, highlighting the collection’s cross-cultural message. “My show is Beyond Borders, so it is about mixing and coming together.” It was Haydon's first appearance for Puri and a return to opening a runway show after a lengthy break. “When you open a show, you set the tone, so I was extra nervous,” she admitted. “This is [Puri’s] debut show [at Dubai Fashion Week], so it was quite a special moment to be part of. I have walked in Dubai Fashion Week before, but today was a lot of firsts.” Kresha Bajaj Closing the evening was Kresha Bajaj, who returned with a collection showcasing the designer’s signature beadwork. Applied to daywear, it trailed across delicate crocheted tops, framed the necklines of street-style tank tops and formed striking zebra-skin patterns. As the collection moved into evening wear, the embellishment became increasingly elaborate, forming latticework across torsos, looping around hips and swaying across legs with every step. It was glamour with an edge.

title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad as top Republicans call for taking it down
body:
Trump said he himself would run such an ad: 'it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"
President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad from Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her daughter a "liar," with the president on social media calling it "powerful" and saying that he himself would run such an ad.
"Who wouldn't use such an Ad? I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt,'" Trump wrote in a social media post on Thursday afternoon.
Trump also said that Ramaswamy should keep the ad up -- despite several Republicans' calls to take it down.
The president attacked those Republicans -- including GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," according to audio provided by Cleveland ABC affiliate WEWS.
Trump called DeWine "disloyal to the Republican Party."
"He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing," Trump wrote on social media.
DeWine, earlier Thursday, had said it's "wrong to run this ad," adding that even though the midterms are fast approaching, he "would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down."
Iowa Republican Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson also condemned the ad, telling ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl in an exclusive interview for "This Week" that Ramaswamy should take down the ad. Hinson is one of the most high-profile Republican women running for office this year in a key battleground state that could determine control of the upper chamber.
"I think about it as a mom, and you think about childhood having to relive that trauma. I think it's absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down,” Hinson told Karl in Iowa.
The ad, which circulated on social media late Monday, shows Acton's long-estranged mother, Donna Arthur, saying that her daughter has lied about her past and her struggles growing up.
Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother, whom she says she has not spoken to since she was 12 years old. Acton alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004.
In his post, Trump called Acton's mother "brave" for speaking out against her daughter.
Ramaswamy, on Tuesday, confirmed his campaign had made the ad, which has drawn bipartisan backlash for bringing up his opponent's childhood trauma.
Acton has criticized the ad, calling it "horrible and hideous" during a campaign event on Wednesday, adding that the ad is "despicable" and "an exploitative thing to do."
DeWine invoked his own past as a prosecutor of several rape cases, saying "I think we all have an obligation to speak out for the victims."
"It's one of the reasons I'm doing this today. We need to speak out. We need to send the message to children that we are here to protect them and that there are people who will in fact protect them, and we just have to make sure we always try to do that," DeWine said.
The ad came nearly two weeks out from the high-stakes midterm elections where Ohio is home to not only a gubernatorial race, but also key Senate and House races.
DeWine had endorsed Ramaswamy for governor -- and indicated he would still back Ramaswamy and the whole Republican ticket in the state, according to WEWS.
"Today is about the ad. But ... I'm not changing my endorsement," DeWine responded to a question about his support for Ramaswamy.
DeWine joins several other Republicans in the state who have recently spoken out against the controversial ad.
Former Ohio Rep. Jim Renacci -- who also ran for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022 -- on Thursday called on Ramaswamy to "pivot quickly" away from the attack ad.
Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who is running for reelection for the seat, said on Wednesday, "I would not have run that ad."
Ohio Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose told ABC Affiliate WSYX earlier this week that his office is reviewing complaints about the Ramaswamy ad to see if it violated any state laws after he said he has received "complaints from various people." He later added, "I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."
Vice President JD Vance defended Ramaswamy's use of the ad during a campaign event in Ohio on Wednesday.
"Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said.
Vance also told reporters on Wednesday that he was "a little bit disgusted" by seeing "Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
Hinson called those comments from Vance "ridiculous."
"It's absolutely the wrong tone,” she told Karl. "It sends absolutely the wrong message."
DeWine, who was Acton's boss when she was head of the Ohio Department of Health, said he knew her to be truthful.
"My experience with her and working closely with her every single day was she certainly told the truth," he said.
ABC News' Benjamin Siegel contributed to this report.

title: ‘Keep this team for the future’ – Kassim Ocansey tells GFA
body: Black Starlets head coach Kassim Ocansey has urged the Ghana Football Association (GFA) to keep the current U17 squad together, stressing that consistency and continuity will be crucial to developing a strong foundation for the senior national teams. Ocansey believes the young players have demonstrated significant potential at the 2026 WAFU Zone B U17 Championship in Burkina Faso and should be given the opportunity to develop together rather than being disbanded after the tournament. “I will say we should not do away with the team. We must keep this team together for the future. There are a lot of potential players in the team and if we can keep them, they can be the foundation for the future of our senior national teams.” The coach’s appeal highlights the importance of long-term planning in Ghanaian football, where promising young players need a clear pathway from youth football to the senior level. Maintaining the core of a squad over time can help players build stronger partnerships, gain valuable international experience and adapt to the demands of competitive football. Ocansey’s call goes beyond preserving a single squad. It is a plea for a consistent development strategy that gives talented youngsters the time and support they need to mature into senior internationals. With the right investment and continuity, members of the current Black Starlets team could form an important part of Ghana’s future at the highest level.

title: DOJ probing Trump ally Corey Lewandowski's actions at DHS after IG referral: Sources
body:
The probe is examining contracting activities at DHS, sources said.
Justice Department prosecutors are investigating the Department of Homeland Security's contracting activities in the first year of the second Trump administration and scrutinizing Corey Lewandowski, a longtime Trump ally who served as ousted DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's top aide, two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to ABC News.
The investigation is in its early stages, sources said, and followed a referral to the department regarding Lewandowski's conduct from DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari.
"Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity," said Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski in a statement provided to ABC News.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment.
The probe marks a rare instance of Trump's Justice Department examining conduct of an ally of the president.
When asked by reporters Thursday about the probe into Lewandowski, President Donald Trump said he did not know about the specifics of the investigation.
"All I know is I want my people to be honest," Trump said. "And if they're not gonna be honest they have to be prosecuted. I don't know about specifically, but -- because I view if people are not honest they're stealing from me."
Lewandowski served as a special government employee during Noem's tenure effectively acting as her chief of staff as the department came under scrutiny for its controversial spending practices through costly government contracts.
Noem and Lewandowski were ousted in March following a congressional hearing where Noem claimed President Trump knew of her decision to launch a $220 million digital ad campaign for the department with videos that featured her prominently.
Both have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the DOJ's probe of Lewandowski.

title: US Reportedly Proposes Nord Stream Revival in Ukraine Peace Talks
body:
The United States has proposed restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe, including reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system, as an economic incentive for Moscow to agree to a settlement of its war against Ukraine, The Economist reported on Thursday, Oct. 22 .
The magazine described the proposal as Washington’s latest prospective concession to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, some of the benefits under discussion would require decisions by European governments and institutions, rather than an agreement between Washington and Moscow alone.
EU countries adopted a legally binding phaseout of Russian gas imports in January.
Under the phaseout timetable , imports under remaining long-term Russian liquefied natural gas contracts must stop from Jan. 1, 2027. The corresponding ban on long-term pipeline supplies takes effect on Sept. 30, 2027, with a possible postponement until Nov. 1 if winter gas-storage targets are at risk.
Restoring Russian supplies on a lasting basis would therefore conflict with the bloc’s existing legal framework.
Nord Stream faces additional obstacles. As Kyiv Post previously reported , Germany’s government opposes reopening the pipelines, which are also subject to US and EU sanctions.
Nord Stream 1 stopped operating in 2022, while Nord Stream 2 never entered commercial service. Three of the system’s four lines were damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022. Any revival would require regulatory approval, alongside decisions about the damaged infrastructure.
The gas proposal forms part of a broader package of potential economic and political benefits for Russia, according to The Economist. These include commercial agreements with American companies, sanctions relief and normalized political relations.
Ukraine would reportedly be offered an investment package and EU membership in exchange for abandoning its ambition to join NATO. The proposals also envisage a demilitarized zone in the Donbas, the eastern Ukrainian region comprising Donetsk and Luhansk.
These remain reported negotiating proposals, rather than an agreed settlement. EU membership, like access to Europe’s energy market, cannot be guaranteed by Washington.
For Ukrainian negotiators, a key concern is the order in which concessions would take effect. They fear US representatives could pursue profitable economic agreements with Russia before Moscow ends the war, according to the magazine.
Earlier this month, Reuters reported discussions about bringing an American investor into Nord Stream . At the time, a White House official said there had been no recent Nord Stream discussions, while another US official described a deal as unlikely in the medium term.
The renewed diplomatic effort follows US special envoy Steve Witkoff’s Oct. 21 meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg .
Witkoff traveled to Russia after talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo . The discussions covered security guarantees, territorial questions, sanctions and Ukraine’s postwar economy.
On Tuesday, Oct. 20, Zelensky said proposals discussed in Norway would be presented to Russia, after which Kyiv would await Putin’s response.
He also confirmed that US intelligence sharing for early warnings of Russian attacks was working again . At the time, he said he expected progress within 48 hours on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions; that statement did not itself confirm deliveries or the removal of restrictions.
Hours after the Oslo talks, US President Donald Trump said Ukraine “has to want to make a deal” , claiming that Washington and Europe had spent “a fortune” supporting Kyiv and that Europe was tired of the conflict.
European governments, meanwhile, have been weighing additional support for Ukraine as Washington eases pressure on Moscow , underscoring the differences between the prospective benefits US negotiators are discussing and the decisions Europe is prepared to make.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.
