title: AI Is Changing Everything About Hacking. No One Knows What Happens Next
body:
For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs.
The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to vagueposting about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the internet was nice while it lasted,’ to outright prepper-level terror .
To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, posted “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper , suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios.
And all those posts came before people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in eMudhra (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), Node.js (an alternative to PHP), Gitlab (a software development platform), Plex (media server software), Railway (a cloud provider), OpenCode (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers from Wiz , Calif , and OpenAI discovered using AI.
Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet , posted , “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”
So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this.
But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something.
Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models.
In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no.
AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation , said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. In a LinkedIn post, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said that his company independently found the same bugs by typing “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP” into a frontier AI model. Amazon, meanwhile, said that it saw exploit attempts before the official disclosure. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning.
After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the National Security Agency , the Prime Minister of Japan , and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. 4chan , several Wikimedia services , and Archive.org were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated.
As The Atlantic has already suggested , one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost.
For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Various low-effort, LLM-developed exploits have been dropped online; many of them will not work. A blog post called “There isn’t an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability,” written by Elias Taylor, quickly went viral and was dissected on Hacker News , especially by people pointing out that the website eliastaylor.com had been recently registered and that it wasn’t clear who Elias Taylor was. 404 Media reached Taylor by Signal; he said “I am real and on a delayed train.”
“Lots of people are being tricked by AI into thinking they have an exploit when they don't, because they can't read or understand what the LLM gave them,” Taylor told 404 Media. “It doesn't appear to be anywhere near as exploitable as the other ‘stop the world’ vulnerabilities i.e log4j, heartbleed. But patch your servers, it’s still a vulnerability. Please do not paraphrase me as saying ‘there is no vulnerability’ for any reason. There is, and people should patch.”
Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI on the Patch the Planet initiative, posted that his company had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.”
It should also be noted that Taylor’s other blog post is called “Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces,” which includes the lines “software engineers have spent the past 40 years writing vulnerable, dogshit software. LLMs are easily above the bar needed to break into said software.”
It remains unclear, at the moment, what the ultimate impact of all of this is going to be, or where we’ll be in one hour, one week, one year, or 10 years. But AI is changing how cybersecurity and hacking works. It is making finding and exploiting bugs faster and easier. We’re about to find out how insecure the internet really is.

title: Russia develops advanced Titan robotic demining system
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian specialists have created the Titan advanced robotic demining system, the system’s developer told TASS.
"To address the challenge of clearing mine and explosive obstacles using robotic systems amid the enemy’s widespread use of anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices in the special military operation zone, the latest robotic demining system, Titan, has been developed. The use of electric motors, a low-profile design, and all-round fragmentation protection against all known performed fragments of anti-personnel engineering munitions ensure stealth during missions and the necessary survivability. The system has increased blast resistance. According to our information, there are no counterparts with comparable quality of equipment and protection being used on either side of the line of contact," a company representative stated.
The system is designed to clear a continuous route through anti-personnel minefields by sweeping away the main types of anti-personnel mines. "The Titan enables the sweeping of mines equipped with pressure-action, pull-action, and break-wire target-sensors," he noted.
He specified that the system has successfully completed testing and is expected to be deployed in the special military operation zone. "Work is currently underway to improve the level of protection, add new controls, and refine the design of the sweeping equipment," he added.
The system’s total weight is 2.3 metric tons, and its payload capacity is one ton. "The Titan’s maximum speed with the sweeping equipment is seven km/h, and without it - 14 km/h. The system is capable of operating autonomously for at least 3.5 hours. The sweep width is two meters. If necessary, the Titan can be equipped with electronic warfare capabilities. The system’s control range depends on the type of communication used but is at least 500 meters," the developer added.

title: Russia recognizes importance of maintaining stable, predictable ties with US — diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia completely recognizes the importance of maintaining stable and predictable relations with the United States, a senior Russian Foreign Ministry official said on Friday.
"Russia’s approach to relations with the United States is well known, and it remains unchanged," Alexander Gusarov, director of the ministry’s department of North Atlantic, said in an interview with the International Affairs magazine.
"We fully recognize the indispensability of maintaining stable and predictable relations between Russia and the United States, which remain the main guarantors of international strategic stability," he noted.
In this regard, Gusarov pointed out that Moscow is "interested in working together with US colleagues to form precisely such relations that rest on equality, mutual respect, consideration of each other’s national interests and non-interference in internal affairs."

title: Philadelphia Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss NFL season with blood clots in lungs
body: In short: (ABC-Australia) Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected miss the rest of the NFL season due to blood clots in his lungs. According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of a game earlier this month. What’s next? The Eagles host the Dallas Cowboys, a division rival, next Tuesday AEDT. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-20/philadelphia-eagles-qb-jalen-hurts-blood-clots-in-lungs/107286260 Share article Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in both lungs, according to his team and his agent, with media reports saying the former Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season. Hurts was clinically stable but his treatment would involve blood thinners, which would rule him out of contact activities, the Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said in a statement. The 28-year-old was initially diagnosed with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis after an ultrasound in London before Philadelphia’s 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which Hurts played in. The current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bilateral pulmonary embolism is where a blood clot travels from a deep vein in the body, often the leg, and blocks an artery in both lungs. “Jalen’s prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery,” the statement said. “We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners.” It said no long-term effects were expected. According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of the game and did not sleep the night before the contest as a health precaution. Speaking at a press conference on Monday, local time, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said the team cared about its players and he trusted the medical staff. “I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them,” Sirianni said. “We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players’ health first and foremost in every situation. And, you know, that’s where we were there.” The Eagles said in a statement on Thursday that their medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the ultrasound results and concluded that “activity and mobility were important” and that Hurts could safely play in the game against the Jaguars, adding that he “played without limitation”. Hurts guided the Eagles to the Super Bowl title in February 2025, throwing for two touchdowns and running in another against the Kansas City Chiefs to earn the game’s Most Valuable Player trophy. Reuters The post Philadelphia Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss NFL season with blood clots in lungs appeared first on Island Times News .

title: When a Good Base Becomes a Bad One: Battlefield Disposition and the Operational Campaign
body:
Israel’s renewed military presence in southern Lebanon puts an old military problem back in view: Where should a force establish bases?
No matter the operational context—years-long counterinsurgency commitments, high-intensity ground combat, long-range strike campaigns, or forward deterrence—basing combat power and support infrastructure somewhere is a requirement. Bases give ground forces access, protection, reach, and staying power. Advantages like these can justify large troop and resource commitments, especially when no other posture can produce the same effect. But the more difficult problem, and the one that the Army hasn’t taught well, is knowing when a useful base has stopped earning its place in an operational campaign.
Army doctrine recognizes this connection—in part. It describes basing as an indispensable part of operational art and ties it directly to operational reach. Doctrine further says that basing can determine a force’s reach, endurance, depth, and ability to generate combat power. The guidance is strongest on why commanders establish bases; it offers less description of how they should judge positions whose value changes as the campaign develops.
Commanders need to keep basing tied to the campaign they are fighting. Khe Sanh, eastern Afghanistan, southern Lebanon, and Henderson Field show how the value of a position can change over time and why the same problem can produce very different decisions.
Khe Sanh and a Changing Operational Campaign
A base at Khe Sanh in Vietnam made sense in early 1968. General William Westmoreland had strong operational reasons to hold Khe Sanh. The base sat near important approaches from Laos and gave American forces another way to observe and threaten North Vietnamese movement, so Westmoreland viewed the position as important to operations in the area, both near Laos and in western Quang Tri. He argued that, with enemy forces concentrating around it, abandoning Khe Sanh would hand the enemy a major psychological and propaganda victory. He also warned that a broader retreat to enclaves would return violence to populated areas.
By summer, the Marines changed their operational approach. The 3d Marine Division was operating beyond the range of Khe Sanh–based artillery and relying more heavily on mobility and forward fire-support positions. The official history of the Marine Corps in Vietnam described the base by this time as “more of a liability than an asset” because it tied down division troops that could be used in mobile operations.
The value of Khe Sanh changed as the division adopted a more mobile way of fighting. The Marines had developed other ways to reach, support, and maneuver forces in western Quang Tri, reducing how much the campaign depended on the base.
Holding Khe Sanh in early 1968 made sense; leaving it months later did too. The campaign had changed enough to alter the position’s value.
Sunk costs can bias commanders toward keeping a base after its campaign value has changed. Once a force has fought to hold a position, invested in its defenses, built infrastructure, and accepted casualties to sustain it, leaving can feel like wasting those investments. But those costs are already paid. The relevant judgment is whether the base continues to justify the forces and options required to hold it. Eastern Afghanistan posed a related problem: whether continued access and influence still required permanent presence.
Eastern Afghanistan and Permanent Presence
American operations in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, tied security to access, roads, reconstruction, and government presence. Coalition projects in and around the Pech and Korengal valleys connected communities to the Afghan government and opened the Korengal to economic activity. Forward positions gave US forces persistent access to terrain that was difficult to reach and sustain.
By 2010, the campaign placed greater emphasis on populated areas. The brigade commander in the area said the Korengal had once been operationally important but that US forces could continue operating there without a permanent base. The valley could remain accessible without requiring a permanent commitment.
Closing a base altered where forces lived and how quickly they could act, but it did not necessarily eliminate their ability to patrol, strike, reinforce, collect intelligence, support partners, or return when required. That gave commanders another way to think about the value of permanent presence.
Major General John Campbell took the same approach as commander of Regional Command–East. His command closed some positions, transferred others to Afghan forces, reinforced some, and kept selected coalition bases. Campbell described those adjustments as a continuing command responsibility. He also observed that troops in remote combat outposts could become highly static because much of the force was required to protect the positions themselves.
The burden Campbell described was more than logistical. Soldiers committed to defending an outpost were unavailable for other missions. Aviation, intelligence, fires, and command attention carried opportunity costs.
The 2011 Pech realignment makes the choice even clearer. Campbell and a battalion commander argued that the US presence in the remote valley no longer fit the population-focused campaign. Operation Pech Realignment closed bases in the valley, but the command did not treat every base in the valley the same way. Combat Outpost Honaker-Miracle, for example, was left in place to help protect nearby Asadabad from insurgent pressure.
One position could be transferred, another reduced, another reinforced, and still another closed. The decision depended on what each position contributed to the campaign rather than on preserving a basing network intact because it once made sense.
The eastern Afghanistan experience showed that permanent presence was only one way to preserve access and influence. Commanders could adjust the basing network as campaign requirements changed. Southern Lebanon presented a harder version of the same problem, where the value of forward presence had to be weighed against growing costs, enemy adaptation, and the risks of withdrawal.
Israel’s security zone in southern Lebanon began with a clear military purpose. The Israel Defense Forces have described the zone as a buffer intended to protect northern Israeli communities from attacks originating in Lebanon. Israel maintained a military presence in southern Lebanon for that purpose until its withdrawal in May 2000.
The arrangement gave Israel distance from its border and placed much of the fighting inside Lebanon. It also reduced the number of Israeli forces required for a full occupation.
Hezbollah changed the character of the fight. Israeli and South Lebanon Army (an Israeli-aligned militia) positions became persistent targets, and the Israel Defense Forces adjusted surveillance, outpost protection, and force employment in response to Hezbollah’s improved methods. Tactical adaptation helped preserve the positions but could not settle whether the larger posture remained worth the commitment.
Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak eventually concluded that the security zone no longer served Israel’s military needs. In 2000, he said the zone had ceased to be a military asset and had become a liability. His argument went beyond the immediate casualty count. Barak also questioned whether the continuing military effort remained worth the human and operational cost.
Senior Israeli officers had substantial reasons to resist Barak’s conclusion. Chief of Staff Shaul Mofaz and other senior leaders warned that unilateral withdrawal might encourage Hezbollah attacks inside Israel and force Israeli troops to reenter Lebanon under international criticism and without the South Lebanon Army’s assistance.
Barak and his military critics were weighing different risks. One side saw a forward posture that consumed more effort for a declining benefit. The other side feared the military consequences of surrendering terrain, partners, deterrence, and the ability to shape events north of the border.
Enemy adaptation can reduce the value of a position even when the position remains defensible. A base intended to deny infiltration may become less useful when the adversary develops other ways to attack. A network built to impose costs can also become a predictable set of targets that draws more forces into defending the network itself.
Israel’s current positions in southern Lebanon should be judged by what they continue to provide as the campaign changes. They may offer advantages that cannot be reproduced from Israel’s border, and those advantages may justify substantial costs. Their value will depend on how Hezbollah adapts, what Lebanese forces can assume, what other Israeli capabilities become available, and how Israel’s objectives change. The earlier security zone offers no automatic answer. But it does show why commanders need to keep reassessing what a forward posture provides to the campaign.
Henderson Field provides the counterpoint to southern Lebanon, illustrating when a costly forward position still deserves to be held. American forces accepted severe costs because the airfield provided capabilities the campaign could not readily reproduce elsewhere.
Henderson Field and the Case for Staying
Henderson Field on Guadalcanal during World War II imposed extraordinary costs on American forces. The Navy avoided slow transports in contested waters and instead used fast destroyers to carry aviation fuel, bombs, and Marine ground crews to the airfield. The fight to sustain the island drove repeated naval engagements because neither side could securely maintain its forces on Guadalcanal.
American commanders kept paying those costs because Henderson Field provided capabilities the campaign needed. Completing and operating the airfield allowed US forces to interdict Japanese reinforcements and supplies, while American aircraft controlled the surrounding waters during daylight. Japan planned to land roughly ten thousand additional troops while battleships suppressed Henderson Field. The naval Battle of Guadalcanal limited the reinforcement to about two thousand of this intended number.
Henderson gave American forces an advantage they could not readily reproduce elsewhere. Its aircraft threatened Japanese shipping, supported the Marines ashore, and made daylight movement around Guadalcanal far more difficult for Japan. Losing the airfield would have weakened the campaign at its core.
Henderson is useful because it highlights why cost should not inevitably become the deciding factor. Some bases need large commitments precisely because they generate effects the campaign cannot afford to lose.
Khe Sanh eventually reached a different point. The Marines had developed other ways to support mobile operations, while holding the base increasingly tied forces to a position the division no longer needed. Henderson continued to provide capabilities American forces could not readily reproduce elsewhere.
Taken together, these cases show that base value depends on what a position provides to the campaign, what the force gives up to maintain it, and whether those effects can be produced another way.
As campaigns change, commanders and their staffs should reassess base value in four ways.
First, assess whether the position continues to serve the operational campaign. Khe Sanh’s value changed as the 3d Marine Division changed how it fought, even though the position remained defensible and useful for local operations. A base has value because of what it contributes to the campaign, not because of its location, history, or past importance.
Second, assess what capability disappears if the force leaves. Henderson Field provided capabilities American forces could not readily reproduce elsewhere. By 2010, American commanders believed they could continue operating in the Korengal without maintaining a permanent presence. Some bases provide access, fires, protection, intelligence, or logistical support that cannot be replaced. Others provide effects that commanders can generate from another location or by another means.
Third, assess what the force gives up by maintaining the position: the opportunity cost of keeping the base. Fuel, construction, and transportation impose costs, but the larger burden may fall on combat power. Bases consume maneuver forces, aviation, fires, intelligence, engineers, air defense, and command attention. Campbell’s concern about static forces in eastern Afghanistan centered on what troops could not do while committed to protecting remote positions. Commanders should compare the value produced by a base with what those same forces and resources might accomplish elsewhere.
Finally, assess whether the position supports the next stage of the campaign. Some bases create options for what comes next. Others preserve a disposition built for an earlier phase. As the main effort shifts or commanders gain other ways to produce the same effects, a base that once supported the campaign can begin to constrain it.
These assessments can lead to retention, adaptation, transfer, realignment, or closure. They can also produce different answers for nearby positions, as the Pech experience demonstrates.
Keep the Base Tied to the Operational Campaign
Bases acquire permanence easily because forces build routines, infrastructure, command relationships, and history around them. Units learn the surrounding terrain, logisticians build systems to sustain the position, engineers improve it, and headquarters begin planning around its continued existence. These investments can make reassessment harder, but they do not determine the military value of the position.
Much has changed since World War II. The technologies available to commanders are more sophisticated. The speed and reach of modern fires have increased dramatically. The character of conflict has evolved. But the fundamental problem remains: Commanders must judge whether a position continues to justify its costs.
Commanders and their staffs should preserve the military advantages a forward posture was built to create. When those advantages change, basing decisions should change with them. The hard lesson from seventy years of campaigns is that permanence is the enemy of relevance. A commander who waits for the reduced value of a position to become undeniable will have waited too long.
Michael Carvelli is a US Army lieutenant colonel and engineer officer who writes from an operational planning, protection, and engineering perspective.
The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

title: Tema Development Corporation steps up digitalisation, security and customer services
body: The Tema Development Corporation (TDC) says it is introducing digital systems and strengthening security at its facilities as part of efforts to improve service delivery and make its operations more accessible to clients. The corporation says it has begun implementing an enterprise resource planning (ERP) programme to digitalise its internal processes and reduce reliance on manual files and paperwork. The initiative was outlined during a working visit by the Minister for Works, Housing and Water Resources, Ahmed Ibrahim, as management briefed him on measures being taken to improve the corporation’s operations. The measures form part of a broader effort to improve the experience of clients and other people who visit the corporation’s offices. Head of Corporate Planning and Communications at the agency, Dorothy A. Asare-Kumah Adolf, speaking during the visit by the sector Minister, says it was pursuing strategic land acquisitions to expand its operations beyond the Greater Accra Region, with locations mentioned in the Volta Region and Kumasi. The expansion plans form part of the corporation’s broader real estate development agenda, which includes residential, commercial and other supporting facilities. The Minister’s visit comes as the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources reviews the operations of agencies under its supervision to identify challenges and explore ways to improve their performance.

title: FACTBOX: What we know about Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian regions, 443 drones downed
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed a total of 443 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.
Falling drone debris injured three people in the Nizhny Novgorod Region.
TASS has compiled key details of the aftermath.
- Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed a total of 443 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.
- The Defense Ministry said the drones were shot down over the Smolensk, Nizhny Novgorod, Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Oryol, Lipetsk, Tambov, Voronezh, Ryazan, Vladimir, Rostov, Volgograd, Perm and Krasnodar regions, as well as over the Moscow Region, the republics of Tatarstan, Udmurt and Crimea, and the Black and Azov Seas.
- More than 150 drones flew toward the Moscow Region overnight, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Max messenger.
- On-duty air defense systems destroyed most of the drones at long range and intercepted five as they approached Moscow.
- Air defense forces shot down 20 Ukrainian drones over the Smolensk Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Vasily Anokhin said on Max.
- The Defense Ministry forces and the Bars-NN unit (a regional volunteer defense unit) repelled an attack by 19 drones in the Nizhny Novgorod Region in western Russia overnight and during the morning, regional Governor Gleb Nikitin said on Max.
- Air defense systems destroyed 12 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev said on Max.
- Air defense forces brought down drones overnight over the Sholokhovsky, Kamensky, Verkhnedonsky and Millerovsky districts of the Rostov Region in southwestern Russia, regional Governor Yury Slyusar said on Max.
- Falling drone debris injured three people in the Gorodetsky municipal district of the Nizhny Novgorod Region, according to preliminary information, regional Governor Nikitin said on Max.
- The injured were hospitalized and are receiving the necessary medical care.
- The attack also damaged several residential buildings, an educational facility and infrastructure.
- Schools in the Gorodetsky municipal district have shifted to remote learning, Nikitin said.
- Emergency response teams are operating at the affected sites, and the extent of the damage is being assessed.
- Traffic on the dam of the Nizhny Novgorod Hydroelectric Power Station in Zavolzhye was temporarily suspended due to the drone threat.
- The municipal administration said emergency services are taking all necessary measures to ensure safety at sites where drone debris fell.
- Public transportation was temporarily suspended on some routes due to road restrictions but later resumed in localities across the district.

title: Wesley So tops 2026 US Chess Championship, bags P3.55 million
body: MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-born Wesley So recovered from a hard fall in the last round to clinch the 2026 US Chess Championship on Thursday, October 22 (Friday, October 23, Philippine time). Shrugging off a harrowing last round loss, the 33-year-old pride of Bacoor, Cavite, beat top seed Fabiano Caruana in the rapid playoffs, 1.5-0.5, to bag the $56,000 (P3.55 million) champion’s purse at the Saint Louis Chess Club in St. Louis, Missouri. With the crown for his taking, So faltered against cellar-dweller Sam Sevian in the 11th round, allowing Caruana to catch him at 7.0 points following a victory over Awonder Liang in the 12-man, all super-Grandmaster tournament. After a see-saw draw in the first tiebreaker, So pounced on a dubious pawn sacrifice by Caruana to win the second and secure his fourth US national title, having prevailed in 2017, 2020, and 2021. The champions and their trophies! 🏆 Congratulations, Wesley So and Rachael Li! 🇺🇸 📸 Lennart Ootes pic.twitter.com/IYDA4WP4zC — Saint Louis Chess Club (@STLChessClub) October 23, 2026 Enjoying a strong season, So — a three-time Philippine champion before transferring to the US Chess Federation in 2014 — also ruled the Americas Cup in March and the Sinquefield Cup in August. So bested Sam Shankland in the first round, drew with Jeffery Xiong, Liang, Levon Aronian, Grigory Oparin, Abhimanyu Mishra in succession; trounced Ray Robson and Andy Woodward; and drew with Caruana and Hans Niemann in the ninth and 10th rounds. In the post-interview, So admitted he barely slept after that defeat to Sevian, napping only two to three hours, but willed himself to victory as Caruana wasn’t in his best form. Caruana had ruled the annual event since 2022, but So ended his reign. WIM (Woman International Master) Rachel Li snared the US women’s crown, where 13-year-old Fide Master Megan Paragua, born of Filipino parents in New York, shared fourth place. Li scored 8.5 points, IM Alice Lee 8.0 points, GM Irina Krush 7.5 points, and WGM Thalia Cervantes and Paragua, niece of US-based Filipino GM Mark Paragua, 6.0 points. – Rappler.com

title: Taiwan vows to remain Palau’s ‘most reliable partner’ at first Independence Day celebration in Taipei
body: By: Eoghan Olkeriil Ngirudelsang Taipei, Taiwan — The Embassy of Palau in Taipei held the first official celebration of Palau Independence Day in Taiwan on Tuesday, October 20, bringing together Taiwanese partners from the health-care and education sectors, business leaders, students, and Palauan citizens living in Taiwan for an evening of speeches, dinner, and cultural performances. The event marked Palau’s 32nd anniversary of independence and drew Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr. and First Lady Whipps, along with Taiwan’s Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim. It followed another Independence Day celebration this month by the Palauan diaspora in Guam and marked the first time the embassy, Palauan students, and Taiwanese partners from government agencies and the private sector marked the anniversary in Taiwan. Speaking at the event, Hsiao said Taiwan would continue to stand beside Palau. “Taiwan will remain Palau’s most reliable partner. In turbulent waters, we will stand firmly with Palau like family, just as Palau has resolutely stood with Taiwan,” she said. Hsiao described Palau as a staunch and vocal ally of Taiwan, saying the two countries’ partnership extended beyond words. “It paves roads, it builds vital infrastructure, and directly improves lives,” she said. In his remarks, President Whipps highlighted Taiwan’s assistance to Palau and the close ties between the two nations in areas including health care, education, trade, and travel. “Our direct flights, our students, our investments, we create an unbreakable bundle,” he said. Whipps also emphasized the mutual commitment underpinning the relationship. “We give each other strength, we protect each other’s sovereignty, and we lift each other up,” he said. Taiwan and Palau established formal diplomatic relations in 1999. The Taipei celebration underscored the enduring partnership between the two Pacific allies, with both leaders framing their relationship as one built on shared values, practical cooperation, and mutual support. The post Taiwan vows to remain Palau’s ‘most reliable partner’ at first Independence Day celebration in Taipei appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Creatives Connect Afrika returns to Accra to drive entertainment-led tourism
body: Creatives Connect Afrika will return to Accra from 30th November to 3rd December 2026 for its second edition, focusing on how entertainment can drive tourism growth and economic opportunities across Africa. The AfCFTA Tourism, Creatives and Cultural Industries Forum and Festival will bring together policymakers, tourism leaders, creatives, investors, entertainment executives and entrepreneurs from across Africa and the diaspora. The 2026 edition is planned to take place at Alisa Hotel North Ridge in Accra under the theme “Entertainment-Led Tourism: Transforming Pan-African Creative Wealth into Global Economic Influence”. The event is convened by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat in collaboration with Africa Tourism Partners (ATP) and the Black Star Experience (BSE). From creative industries to entertainment-led tourism The second edition broadens the conversation beyond individual creative sectors to examine the growing relationship between entertainment and tourism. Across the world, music festivals, film productions, sporting events, fashion weeks, cultural festivals, wellness experiences and digital content increasingly influence travel decisions and shape destination perceptions. Africa is well positioned to capitalise on this trend, with its music, film, fashion, sports, cultural and digital creative industries attracting growing international audiences and commercial interest. The Forum and Festival will examine how this momentum can translate into increased tourist arrivals, stronger destination brands, new investment opportunities, employment and greater participation in continental trade in services. By bringing tourism and entertainment stakeholders together, the gathering aims to identify opportunities for developing marketable experiences that connect Africa’s creative output with destination promotion, hospitality, transport and other tourism services. The event builds on the inaugural 2025 edition, held under the theme “Lights, Camera, Trade: Unlocking Africa’s Film, Fashion and Music Creative Industries under the AfCFTA”. That gathering brought together policymakers, tourism authorities, filmmakers, musicians, fashion designers, investors, development partners and creatives, generating recommendations on market access, mobility, investment, intellectual property protection, financing and regulatory cooperation. Four days of policy, business and culture The 2026 programme will combine high-level policy dialogue with business, investment and cultural experiences. The opening day will feature an AfCFTA Trade in Services Masterclass, closed-door technical sessions and a Tourism Boards and Regulators Roundtable. The second and third days will focus on high-level policy dialogues and panel discussions. Alongside the policy programme, a Film, Animation and Creative Content Festival will showcase animation and stop-motion productions, creative storytelling and digital content, while providing opportunities for discussions on film tourism, location marketing, content distribution and networking among filmmakers and producers. A Music, Sports and Entertainment Tourism Showcase will explore the role of live entertainment, sporting events and music in destination development. Wellness activities will highlight opportunities in wellness and lifestyle tourism, including yoga, mindfulness, fitness and related experiences. The programme will also feature exhibitions, cultural and entertainment showcases, business matchmaking and an investment forum designed to connect destinations, businesses, creatives, investors and development partners. By strengthening the links between tourism, hospitality, transport, sports, film, music, fashion, events, digital services and cultural industries, the Forum and Festival will seek to promote integrated African value chains and expand opportunities for intra-African trade. Addressing barriers to growth Despite the rapid growth of Africa’s entertainment ecosystem, significant barriers remain. These include limited access to finance, fragmented markets, restrictions on the movement of creative professionals, inadequate infrastructure, skills gaps and the limited commercialisation of cultural and creative assets. The Forum and Festival will focus not only on celebrating Africa’s creative excellence but also on identifying practical solutions relating to investment, mobility, market access, regulation, intellectual property and cross-border collaboration. The AfCFTA provides a continental framework for advancing trade in services and strengthening cooperation between African markets. Through policy dialogue, business engagement and cultural showcases, Creatives Connect Afrika aims to help stakeholders identify ways to translate the continent’s creative potential into sustainable economic opportunities. Expected outcomes include new partnerships between tourism and entertainment stakeholders, enhanced investment prospects, increased visibility for African destinations and practical recommendations to strengthen tourism and entertainment services under the AfCFTA. Ahead of the main event, continental roadshows and promotional launches will be held in selected African cities to build participation, strengthen partnerships and raise awareness of the opportunities presented by entertainment-led tourism. About Creatives Connect Afrika Creatives Connect Afrika is the AfCFTA Tourism, Creatives and Cultural Industries Forum and Festival, a continental platform convened under the AfCFTA Protocol on Trade in Services to advance entertainment-led tourism, trade in services, investment, cultural exchange and collaboration across Africa. The inaugural edition was held in 2025 under the theme “Lights, Camera, Trade”. The second edition expands the platform’s focus to explore how entertainment can become a strategic driver of tourism growth, destination development and economic transformation across the continent.

title: Train Scots workers to seize defence billions, says Marra
body: Billions of pounds of defence investment heading for Scotland will only translate into skilled jobs if colleges, employers and councils are handed the power to decide what training their local economies need, according to the Scottish Labour leader. Michael Marra made the argument during a visit to Babcock’s Rosyth yard, where the Royal Navy’s five Type 31 frigates are being built, and said the centralised approach taken at Holyrood had failed. He called for regional leaders to be given greater powers to bring colleges, employers and training providers together so that people are equipped with the skills industry actually wants. He said: “Scotland has world-class shipyards, outstanding engineering expertise and the talent to lead the next generation of British industry. “Here at Rosyth, Babcock is building the next generation of Royal Navy frigates. Across Scotland, billions of pounds of defence investment offer a huge opportunity to create skilled jobs, strengthen our industrial base and open up new careers for young people. “But investment alone is not enough. We must make sure people in our communities have the skills to take advantage of these opportunities. “In this area Holyrood’s centralised approach to skills has failed. We need to hand over power to local people and communities. “Local colleges, employers and councils can work together to train people for the jobs their local economies actually need. “Decisions about the skills needed in our shipyards, our energy industry and our advanced manufacturing sector should be shaped by the people who understand those industries best. “There are billions of pounds of investment on the table here. Scottish workers should be given the skills to grab it. Let’s turn that investment into opportunity: good jobs, stronger local economies and a new generation of skilled workers building Scotland’s future.” The figures published alongside the visit show apprenticeship starts by people aged sixteen to twenty four in Scotland falling from 20,506 in 2015/16 to 13,891 in 2025/26, a drop of more than six thousand, or 32 per cent. Starts in the twenty to twenty four bracket are down 41 per cent, from 7,669 to 4,491, and the sixteen to nineteen bracket is down 27 per cent, from 12,837 to 9,400. Starts by people aged twenty five and over more than doubled over the same period, rising from 5,312 to 10,958. Scottish Labour took the numbers from Scottish Government modern apprenticeship supplementary tables for the fourth quarter of 2025/26, and said one in six young people in Scotland is not in education, training or employment. The Type 31 programme supports around two and a half thousand skilled jobs across Scotland and the wider United Kingdom supply chain, including four hundred apprenticeships. A shortage of trained welders in Scotland has meant Babcock using workers from overseas, the party said. Marra’s call follows the commitment of £6 billion to three new floating docks for the submarine service at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, work that has been reserved for British shipyards , alongside wider investment in maritime industries. Babcock is building five Type 31 frigates at Rosyth under a contract worth around £1.25 billion, based on the Iver Huitfeldt design, with the first of class named HMS Venturer. The post Train Scots workers to seize defence billions, says Marra first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Energy facilities across Ukraine targeted as Russian attacks kill at least 8, injure 67 over past day
body:
Russian attacks killed eight civilians and wounded 67 across Ukraine over the past day, as strikes on the country's energy infrastructure triggered emergency power outages on Oct. 23, local authorities said.
Power cuts were reported in Zhytomyr, Donetsk , Khmelnytskyi, Volyn, Kharkiv, Poltava, Rivne, and Mykolaiv oblasts, state grid operator Ukrenergo said, adding that energy workers were already working to restore damaged facilities.
Ukrainian private energy company DTEK said one of its thermal power plants had halted generation following a Russian attack. The company did not disclose the plant's location.
The attacks come as Ukraine braces for what could be its most difficult winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, with Moscow continuing to target power generation and other critical infrastructure.
According to Ukraine's Air Force , Russia launched 176 long-range drones at Ukraine overnight, including 92 jet-powered drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 140 drones, including 68 jet-powered ones.
Drone impacts were recorded at 19 locations, while falling debris was reported at another 13, the Air Force said.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, a total of eight civilians were killed and another 67 wounded in Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three civilians were killed and a total of 46 injured, the majority coming from an attack on a market in the city of Lozova in the southeastern corner of the region, according to governor Oleh Syniehubov.
Three people were killed and one injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia Oblast, according to regional authorities , as 940 Russian attacks of various kinds were reported in 46 settlements.
Russian attacks killed two civilians and injured nine more in front-line Donetsk Oblast, said oblast governor Vadym Filashkin.
Six people were injured in three separate Russian attacks on Sumy Oblast, including on the capital Sumy, the regional administration said.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , two people were injured in Russian attacks: a 44-year-old man in the Nikopol area, and a 26-year-old woman in the Shakhtarsk area, near the front line.
Two people were injured, including a child, in Russian attacks across the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, regional authorities said.
A 51-year-old man was injured in a Russian attack in the Bashtanka District of Mykolaiv Oblast, Governor Heorhii Reshetilov reported .

title: Closing the Sea: Lessons from Ancient Mediterranean Blockades
body:
Nearly a century ago, Rear Admiral William A. Moffett, U.S.N., wrote in the foreword to Arthur M. Shepard’s seminal work, Sea Power in Ancient History , that “Readers of this work cannot but be impressed by the similarity between the problems of sea power in ancient times and problems of sea power which are engaging the attention of maritime nations today.” 1 Practitioners of naval power have long looked to the past for warnings, lessons, and insights that might inform the challenges of the present and future. This post follows in that tradition by considering what antiquity might offer for understanding one of the most enduring applications of naval power, the blockade.
The British naval theorist Julian Corbett distinguished between commercial blockade, intended to restrict an enemy’s maritime trade, and naval blockade, directed against an enemy’s fleet. The latter could itself serve different purposes, either keeping an enemy fleet confined to port or watching it closely while encouraging it to put to sea, where it could be brought to battle. 2 Although Corbett developed these categories from the experience of more recent naval warfare, their basic purposes would have been readily recognizable in antiquity. Ancient fleets likewise sought to restrict maritime commerce and supplies, contain hostile naval forces, or compel an adversary’s fleet to come out and fight.
The relevance of these forms of blockade is hardly confined to the past. At the time of writing, the United States is enforcing a blockade against Iran, restricting maritime traffic to and from Iranian ports as part of the ongoing conflict. 3 At the same time, across the Indo-Pacific, the possibility of a Chinese blockade of Taiwan remains a central concern in discussions of a potential cross-Strait conflict. Chinese military planning considers blockade operations as one means of isolating and coercing Taiwan, alongside the considerably more demanding possibility of an amphibious invasion. 4 Despite enormous differences in political circumstances, technologies, and scale, these situations underscore a common problem. Establishing control of the sea is one thing, but maintaining that control long enough to achieve a political or military objective is another.
There are, of course, many examples of naval blockade in the ancient Mediterranean, but four cases highlight particularly well the different challenges such operations presented: Samos in 440–439 BCE, Syracuse in 413 BCE, Rhodes in 305–304 BCE, and Roman operations around Lilybaeum and Drepana in 250–249 BCE. Each exposes a different problem associated with blockade, including maintaining forces on station, preserving or contesting command of the sea, restricting or sustaining access to supplies, and protecting the forces involved.
Samos, 440–439 BCE: The Challenge of Maintaining a Blockade
The Athenian campaign against Samos in 440–439 BCE provides a clear example of both the effectiveness and fragility of naval blockade. After an earlier Athenian intervention on the island, a group of Samian exiles returned, overthrew the Athenian-backed government, and revolted. 5 Athens responded by sending sixty ships under the command of Pericles and other generals. After defeating a Samian fleet of seventy vessels near Tragia and receiving additional ships from Athens, Chios, and Lesbos, the Athenians landed troops and surrounded Samos with three walls while simultaneously blockading the city “from the sea at the same time” (ἐκ θαλάσσης ἅμα). 6
The blockade quickly revealed a problem that remains fundamental to such operations, as forces maintaining a blockade may also be required to respond to threats elsewhere. Reports reached Pericles that a Phoenician fleet was approaching to assist the Samians. He therefore took sixty ships from the force stationed around Samos and sailed toward Caunus and Caria to meet the anticipated threat. 7 His departure weakened the blockade at precisely the moment the defenders needed.
The Samians exploited the opportunity. They attacked the inadequately protected Athenian naval station, destroyed the guard ships, and defeated the vessels sent against them. For fourteen days they “controlled the sea in their area” (τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς καθ᾽ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκράτησαν) and, as Thucydides puts it, “brought in and carried out whatever they wished” (ἐσεκομίσαντο καὶ ἐξεκομίσαντο ἃ ἐβούλοντο). 8 When Pericles returned, however, the Athenians reestablished the blockade by land and sea. Further reinforcements arrived from Athens, Chios, and Lesbos, and after a nine-month siege the Samians surrendered, demolished their walls, surrendered their fleet and hostages, and agreed to repay the costs of the war. 9
For fourteen days, the diversion of part of the Athenian fleet was enough to reopen Samian access to the sea, demonstrating the importance of persistence in maintaining a blockade. For those under blockade, even a temporary weakening of the forces on station could provide an opportunity to restore maritime access.
Syracuse, 413 BCE: The Reversal of a Blockade
When the Athenians arrived at Syracuse in 415 BCE, seeking to conquer the city and extend their power into Sicily, their overwhelming superiority at sea was one of the expedition’s greatest advantages. Over the course of the campaign, however, they gradually lost that advantage and ultimately found themselves trapped in the Great Harbor. 10 By 414 BCE, the campaign had developed into an effort to isolate Syracuse by land and sea. The Athenians occupied Plemmyrium at the entrance to the Great Harbor, using it to protect their ships and store equipment, while their army attempted to complete a wall of circumvallation around the city. Thucydides emphasizes how far the Athenian works had progressed by the time Spartan support for Syracuse arrived under the command of Gylippus. Much of the wall toward the Great Harbor was already complete, while materials had been prepared to extend the line toward the opposite coast. 11
Gylippus’ intervention changed the strategic situation. Syracusan counter-walls prevented completion of the Athenian circumvallation, while the capture of Plemmyrium deprived the expedition of its principal position at the mouth of the Great Harbor and cost it substantial stores and naval equipment. 12 The Syracusans also refused to remain blockaded within the Great Harbor, continuing to contest Athenian control of its waters. In 413 BCE, they modified their triremes for its confined waters, strengthening and shortening their prows for direct, head-on, prow-to-prow attacks (ἀντιπρῴροις), rather than the maneuvering attacks (ἐκ περίπλου) for which the more lightly constructed Athenian prows were designed. 13
After defeating the Athenians at sea, the Syracusans closed the mouth of the Great Harbor with merchant vessels, warships, and other crafts moored across the entrance. The fleet that had arrived with overwhelming maritime superiority now had to fight its way out of the harbor it had once helped control. In the final naval battle, the Athenians attempted to break the Syracusan blockade, attacking the barrier across the harbor entrance, but the Syracusan and allied fleet prevented their escape. 14 The surviving Athenians abandoned their ships and attempted to retreat overland, ending in the destruction of the expedition.
Syracuse demonstrates that a blockade depends on continued control of the surrounding maritime space. As Athenian control weakened through setbacks ashore, the loss of key positions, Syracusan tactical adaptation, and defeat at sea, the Athenians went from attempting to cut off Syracuse to being trapped themselves. For a force under blockade, contesting control rather than simply accepting isolation can fundamentally alter the strategic situation.
Rhodes, 305–304 BCE: The Limits of a Blockade
Few commanders in antiquity possessed a reputation for naval siege warfare comparable to Demetrius Poliorcetes, yet his enormous effort against Rhodes in 305–304 BCE failed to isolate the city completely. Maritime commerce was fundamental to Rhodian wealth and strategic power. Diodorus Siculus describes Rhodes as possessing considerable naval strength (ἰσχύουσα ναυτικαῖς δυνάμεσι) and notes its particularly close economic relationship with Ptolemy I of Egypt. 15 When Antigonus and Demetrius attempted to force Rhodes away from its relationship with Ptolemy, separating the city from outside support became a central part of the campaign.
Demetrius arrived with a formidable fleet. He attacked the Rhodian harbor defenses from the sea, deployed ship-mounted artillery and siege machinery, and later shifted much of his effort ashore. 16 Yet his fleet could not make the waters around Rhodes impermeable. Rhodian warships continued to operate, and outside powers repeatedly sent assistance. Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus supplied the city, with Diodorus describing major shipments of grain and other provisions. 17 Their importance was reflected in the honors Rhodes later granted its benefactors.
Every successful entry weakened the coercive purpose of Demetrius’ effort to isolate the city. So long as Rhodes retained sufficient maritime access to receive supplies and outside assistance, time did not necessarily favor the attacker. After roughly a year of fighting, Demetrius accepted a settlement. Rhodes preserved its autonomy and its relationship with Ptolemy, while agreeing to support Antigonus except in conflicts against Ptolemy. 18
Rhodes illustrates the difficulty of maintaining a fully effective blockade. A blockade does not need to stop all traffic to exert pressure, nor does every successful passage render it ineffective. Its effectiveness ultimately depends on whether enough traffic is restricted to achieve its strategic purpose, while even limited access may be sufficient for the defender to sustain resistance.
Lilybaeum and Drepana, 250–249 BCE: The Costs of Maintaining a Blockade
By 250 BCE, during the First Punic War, Roman successes in Sicily had narrowed the Carthaginian position to a handful of strongholds in the west, but the effort to blockade Lilybaeum exposed the Roman fleet to risks that would ultimately threaten the operation itself. Polybius notes that the Romans believed its capture would open the way for attacks against North Africa, while Carthage resolved to hold it at virtually any cost. 19 The Romans therefore invested Lilybaeum by land and sea.
The harbor proved exceptionally difficult to blockade effectively. Carthage exploited local knowledge, favorable winds, and skilled seamanship to penetrate the Roman blockade. A force under Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, carried approximately 10,000 troops and supplies into Lilybaeum despite the Roman presence. 20 Hannibal “the Rhodian” later repeatedly sailed between Carthaginian territory and Lilybaeum, running the Roman blockade until the Romans captured a sufficiently fast Carthaginian vessel to intercept him. 21 These episodes demonstrated the difficulty of transforming naval superiority into complete control of a contested area.
The blockade also imposed costs on the Romans. Combat, siege operations, and disease depleted the fleet’s manpower, requiring 10,000 replacement sailors. 22 In 249 BCE, the Roman consul Publius Claudius Pulcher used the reconstituted fleet to strike the nearby Carthaginian naval base at Drepana, apparently hoping to surprise the Carthaginian commander Adherbal and eliminate the threat to Roman blockade operations around Lilybaeum. 23 Instead, Adherbal brought his ships into open water. The Romans, caught close to the coast with less maneuverable ships and inexperienced replacement crews, suffered a devastating defeat. Polybius reports that ninety-three Roman vessels were captured while Claudius escaped with about thirty. 24 Carthaginian forces subsequently returned to the vicinity of Lilybaeum and attacked Roman ships there. 25
Lilybaeum and Drepana reveal the sustained costs of blockade. Maintaining pressure exposes the forces involved to attrition, crew exhaustion, enemy action, and competing operational demands. As these pressures accumulate, they can create opportunities for the opposing force to challenge the blockade and reshape the balance at sea.
Ancient Blockades and the Problem of Sea Power
Ancient and modern blockades operate with radically different technologies. Samos, Syracuse, Rhodes, and Lilybaeum offer no tactical prescriptions for fleets operating with submarines, aircraft, missiles, satellites, or unmanned systems. Their relevance lies instead in the strategic problems they expose.
Taken together, the four cases suggest that blockade should be understood as a continuing contest rather than a condition established simply by achieving maritime superiority. Samos demonstrates the demands of persistence, as even the temporary removal of part of the blockading force created an opportunity to reopen access to the sea. Syracuse shows how control can be reversed, as the Athenians went from attempting to isolate the city to being trapped within the Great Harbor themselves. Rhodes demonstrates that a blockade need not be broken completely to fail; sufficient access may allow a defender to continue resisting. Lilybaeum and Drepana show how the accumulating costs and vulnerabilities of maintaining a blockade can create opportunities for it to be challenged.
These cases raise several enduring strategic questions about blockades. How difficult is a blockade to impose, sustain, resist, or break? How much force does it require, and for how long? How complete must it be to achieve its political or military objectives? How much traffic can continue to pass through before its effectiveness is undermined? What outside powers might intervene or provide support? And what forces, bases, or geographic features might strengthen, weaken, or threaten a blockade?
The central question is therefore not simply whether a blockade can be imposed, but whether it can be maintained long enough to achieve its purpose in the face of resistance, changing circumstances, and the costs of sustaining it.
That broader lesson returns us to Moffett’s observation nearly a century ago. The instruments of sea power have changed beyond anything an ancient commander could have imagined. The underlying strategic problem has not changed. Control of the sea is only valuable insofar as it can be translated into lasting political or military results.
Dr. Stephen DeCasien is the Henry A. Kissinger Visiting Scholar Postdoctoral Fellow at Yale University’s Jackson School of Global Affairs. His research integrates archaeological and historical evidence to examine ancient warships, naval warfare, and the exercise of maritime power. He is currently co-editing, with William M. Murray, “The Naval Rams from the Battle of the Egadi (Aegates) Islands in 241 BCE”, a volume presenting archaeological evidence from the first securely identified ancient naval battlefield and examining Roman and Carthaginian naval warfare, technology, and logistics.
