title: Yambio infant attacked by baboon needs specialized surgery
body: A three-month-old baby girl who was attacked by a baboon, which severely damaged her nose, in the Western Equatoria State capital, Yambio, is in stable condition but in need of specialized reconstructive surgery, health officials said. Dr. Kinawo Richard, a health worker at the Western Equatoria State Ministry of Health, said the infant was brought to Yambio State Hospital on Thursday morning, prompting medical staff to mobilise emergency treatment. “The attack severely damaged the infant’s nasal tissue, leaving only small openings through which she could breathe,” he said. Despite the severity of the injuries, Dr. Richard said the child remained stable after treatment. “However, she requires specialized surgery to reconstruct her nose and repair the damaged tissue, a procedure that cannot be performed at the hospital because the necessary expertise and facilities are unavailable,” he said. The doctor explained that medical staff had inserted a nasogastric tube to help feed the infant breast milk as she continues receiving treatment. A family member, whose identity is being withheld to protect her privacy, said she was sweeping the compound when a neighbor alerted her that the animal had disappeared. She said she went inside and found that the baby’s face had been severely injured. The family member said the animal belonged to her husband’s grandfather and had reportedly left its feeding area before entering the house and attacking the child. The exact circumstances of the incident remain unclear. Meanwhile, Joseph Dau Deng, Director of wildlife in the state, said his office had received a report about the incident and urged residents to stop keeping dangerous wild animals in towns and residential areas. “The person who brought the baboon and tied it at home is at fault. Wild animals cannot be domesticated and must be left to live in the bush,” he said. “You cannot bring a wild animal home where there are children and people. It is illegal, and we will legally deal with such people.” He warned that such animals pose a risk to children, women and other members of the community. Western Equatoria State Police Commissioner Brigadier Justin Waiwai condemned the incident, saying wild animals should not be kept in residential areas where they could endanger people. He said the owner of the baboon will be held accountable under the law. The post Yambio infant attacked by baboon needs specialized surgery appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Meet Trump’s favorite House Republican candidate
body: President Donald Trump and his allies are mounting a last-minute mission to shore up his longtime personal friend in a battleground Arizona district. GOP groups have spent more than $22 million to boost Jay Feely against Democrat Amish Shah, with much of that spending coming in the final weeks of the race. The president has known Feely for decades as a friend and golf partner, and he sees the former Arizona Cardinals kicker as a formidable candidate, according to two Trump officials familiar with their relationship, who were granted anonymity to share details about it. The ferocious support for Feely appears to mark a rare instance of personal friendship and loyalty shaping political strategy in the close of the midterm campaign — especially after Trump personally intervened to clear a pathway for Feely to clinch the nomination. Trump and his allies have largely taken an unsentimental approach to political spending, including backing away from high-profile Senate races in Georgia and North Carolina where Trump loyalists are on the ballot. Trump, in public and private, maneuvered other Republicans out of the way so Feely could switch races and defend one of the premier battleground districts in the country, according to the two Trump officials. Still, Feely has been forced to navigate Trump’s deep unpopularity on the campaign trail. Shah has been working to tie Feely to Trump in a flurry of ads, in the district where the president has an approval rating around negative 13 points, according to Democratic internal polling viewed by POLITICO. Feely, a star GOP recruit, also attended a meeting with Speaker Mike Johnson and tech billionaire Elon Musk in Texas this August as top Republicans worked to secure Musk’s help in defending the House GOP majority alongside the Senate, according to two people with direct knowledge of the meeting, granted anonymity to share private details. Musk has donated $20 million to the top House GOP super PAC, though he’s focused much of his attention this midterms season on the Texas Senate race. The Trump team appears to be taking a pragmatic view of Feely’s campaign, giving him some room to distance himself from the White House — even if that means avoiding the president’s rallies and breaking with him on other matters, according to the two Trump officials and two other people with direct knowledge of the matter who were granted anonymity to speak candidly. Feely posted on social media this week: “I will stand up to anyone including the president if it is not in the best interest of this district and this state.” He and another battleground Arizona Republican, Rep. Juan Ciscomani, didn’t attend a rally Trump held in their state Oct. 14. Brian Seitchik, Feely’s general consultant and a former 2016 and 2020 Trump campaign staffer, would only say Feely "regrettably could not attend” the event. Feely’s run is a rare case this cycle where the Republican candidate is a well-known figure in his own right — and who has been personal friends with Trump for decades. He’s running in a wealthy GOP-held district that includes Scottsdale and part of the Phoenix suburbs that the president only narrowly won in 2024 and Democrats are eager to flip. Trump officials are keenly aware if they lose the seat, Democrats could hold it for several elections to come. “Both parties know how important the seat is,” Feely told POLITICO at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas this September. “It'll be one of three to five seats in the country that'll determine who wins the House,” he said, predicting it would “probably be the most expensive race in the country.” “I'm honored to have a relationship with President Trump for the last two decades and to have his support at the same time,” Feely added at the time. Internal polling on both sides show Feely locked in a tossup race against Shah, who was a physician with the New York Jets during Feely’s tenure on that team. Feely noted the importance of winning over independent voters in the district. That’s an even harder task now given the growing unpopularity of the war in Iran and high fuel prices hitting voters. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. “In a race that’s going to come down to potentially hundreds of votes, Jay is doing the hard work required to win this battleground seat,” Seitchik, Feely’s general consultant, said. Trump and Feely, who went on to have a career in broadcasting, have known each other for several decades. They’ve golfed together in recent years: Feely posted a photo of himself with Trump in August of 2020 after a round of golf with the president at his Bedminster, New Jersey, club. “What an epic day!!” he wrote. Trump-aligned super PACs have poured north of $9 million into the race to boost Feely on the airwaves against Shah. The top House GOP super PAC, Congressional Leadership Fund, is highly focused on defending the seat and has also dropped nearly $7 million on the race. And the National Republican Congressional Campaign has spent $2.6 million on coordinated ad buys with Feely’s campaign. Feely was originally running in the redder 5th District to replace Andy Biggs, who is now competing to be the state’s next governor. But Trump urged Feely to switch races to the battleground 1st District after retiring GOP Rep. David Schweikert announced he would also run for governor. Trump’s encouragement helped draw Feely into a GOP primary fight with Gina Swoboda, a longtime Trump ally and former state party chair. The president initially expressed support for both Feely and Swoboda, but soon he posted only in support of his personal friend . “I know Jay well, and he is a TOTAL WINNER, on and off the field!” Trump wrote.

title: Poll: Trump is mobilizing more Democrats against him than Republicans for him
body: President Donald Trump is asking voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot. That might backfire. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Democratic midterm voters are more motivated to oppose the president than Republican voters are to support him. Many Republican voters also aren’t looking for blind loyalty to Trump in the midterms: Half say they’d rather their local candidate aim to win, even if it means speaking out against the president. It’s not uncommon for voters in the party out of power to be more motivated in a midterm year. But the lopsided findings are an ominous sign for Trump, who has fundamentally reshaped the GOP over the past decade and has once again staked his brand — and political capital — on delivering wins for Republicans in November. With less than two weeks before the election, the poll suggests Republicans are pragmatic, and care more about preventing a blue wave than standing by Trump. And in a year when voter frustration over high prices appears poised to play a major role, that distinction could prove consequential. The poll, conducted by London-based firm PF Global, reveals the extent to which frustration with Trump is driving Democrats: Nearly half of Democratic midterm voters say they will be voting “mainly to oppose President Trump,” compared to just 38% of Republican voters who say they will be voting mainly to show support for Trump. Instead, a plurality of Republican midterm voters — 48% — say their main motivation when casting a vote is to show support for a local candidate. Only 37% of Democratic voters agree. “[Trump is] 100% motivating Democrats more than Republicans,” said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist. “That may have been the case regardless, but it’s even more true with words like ‘diesel’ and ‘Iran ’ now a part of everyday political discussion.” Half of Republicans think candidates have a better chance of winning if they align themselves with Trump rather than breaking from him, compared to just 30% who believe candidates would have a better chance of winning if they break away. But half of Republicans also accept their candidates speaking out against the president if that’s what they need to do to win their own election. That’s compared with 37% who say candidates should remain loyal to the president and support his agenda, even if it means risking a loss. On top of that, majorities of Republican voters say Trump himself should give candidates some room to break with him on specific policy issues to win elections. If it helps GOP candidates’ chances of winning, they said, the president should allow for disagreement on the speed of AI development, the cost of living, and whether the war in Iran was a good decision. That holds true for pluralities or even majorities of Trump 2024 voters who self-identify as part of the “MAGA” movement across each policy area, suggesting that even his most loyal voters want the president to let candidates distance themselves if it can help them win. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said "POLITICO didn't need to conduct a poll to know that Democrats are motivated by their hatred for President Trump and Republicans.” She added that the GOP is "running on actual accomplishments like cutting taxes and securing the border," while saying Democrats have made "investigations, obstruction, and impeachment" their campaign platform. Still, the tension is playing out in real time as Republican candidates locked in competitive races walk a tightrope between maintaining Trump’s support — and that of his MAGA base — without alienating critical moderate and independent voters. They’re especially under pressure as Trump hits the campaign trail in battlegrounds and red states, with several candidates having to quietly make calculations whether it will hurt them politically to appear next to him. “I think Republicans ... are stuck choosing which finger to cut off,” said a national GOP operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the midterm landscape. "There is no good answer." In Iowa, where voter frustration over some of Trump’s marquee policies, including tariffs and rising costs stemming from the Iran war, has mounted, Republican candidates have sought to create some distance from the president. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate nominee, has said the war needs to be “ brought to a successful and immediate end .” She also skipped a rally Vice President JD Vance held in the state last month. Several other GOP candidates have also skipped Trump rallies in their home states, and many have grown increasingly wary of mentioning Trump in ads , including in red states that over the last few months have suddenly started to look competitive. In battleground Georgia, GOP gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson has carefully navigated his relationship with Trump, avoiding public breaks with the president on policy but still limiting direct references to him in campaign ads and on the debate stage. “I don’t know that Trump coming [to Georgia] helps Republicans more so than it excites Democrats, especially in a wave election year,” said Jason Shepherd, a former Cobb County GOP chair who is supporting Jackson. That leaves Republican candidates in a tricky position: Their voters are willing to accept breaking from Trump if victory is on the line, but voters — and candidates — won’t know what will cost them their race until it's too late. "There's no reason to gratuitously attack the White House and make an enemy,” the national GOP operative said. “But the end game here is to get reelected, and if they have to get reelected, but the president's annoyed at them for a period of time, they'll get over it.” While Republican candidates balance loyalty to Trump with the possibility of breaking away on certain issues, Democratic midterm voters remain highly motivated to vote against Trump’s agenda. Even Trump’s endorsement of a Republican candidate seems to influence Democrats more than Republicans: Roughly 70% of Democratic midterm voters say his endorsement would make them less likely to support a candidate, compared to 55% of Republican midterm voters who say the endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate. “The midterm elections are about anger management and failed expectations,” said North Carolina based GOP strategist Paul Shumaker. “A lot of Republicans and swing voters feel like their expectations have not been met in helping address their economic concerns.” Alec Hernández and Alisa Vasquez contributed to this story.

title: Brazil's runoff: Lula's legacy vs. Bolsonaro's dynasty
body:
A combination of file photos shows Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brasília on Oct. 1, 2026, and presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro at a rally in Belo Horizonte on Aug. 17, 2026. The two face off in the Oct. 25 runoff. Evaristo Sa and Gledston Tavares/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
RIO DE JANEIRO — Sunday's presidential runoff in Brazil could prolong the career of a political giant—or usher in a new generation of a political dynasty.
Voter energy has surged ahead of the runoff, with rallies for each candidate drawing tens of thousands of people in major cities and packing plazas and university campuses nationwide
Many polls show a race within the margin of error between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Flávio Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula in the first round of voting on Oct. 4 and currently leads polls, though some surveys show the gap narrowing in recent days .
A Bolsonaro victory would extend his family's influence over the Brazilian right, which in previous decades was dominated by more moderate figures. A close ally of President Trump, Flávio Bolsonaro would, if elected, reinforce a broader rightward shift across much of Latin America, where conservative candidates have made gains in recent elections.
"We have a new feeling of urgency," said 40-year-old corporate event planner Camila Sixel, referring to Bolsonaro's first-place finish earlier in the month. Sixel has been campaigning for Lula in Rio de Janeiro.
"I'm really worried about the future for women, the fight against racism and social inequality, and the protection of vulnerable people," Sixel said.
Lula, 80, is running for his fourth nonconsecutive term and says this will be his last election. He has been at the center of the Brazilian left for a generation, first taking office in 2003 and falling out of favor with many voters in the 2010s when he was embroiled in a corruption scandal and jailed. His convictions were later annulled on procedural grounds .
Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro to win the presidency in 2022. The elder Bolsonaro is under house arrest while serving his sentence for plotting to overturn that election result, but his son, who is 45, has pledged to pardon him if elected.
The younger Bolsonaro's other proposals include trimming the size of the Brazilian state to boost economic growth. Those economic proposals became one of many points of contention in the election's first televised debate last Sunday night.
"Have you seen how things are going in Argentina, and are you going to keep saying that Milei is your model?" asked Lula, referring to Argentine President Javier Milei's austerity program and the country's rising poverty rate.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, promised an aggressive crackdown on organized crime, telling voters that "I will give you back the streets so that you can walk in safety."
It's a message that's attractive to many Brazilians, who rank crime as a top election issue. "Security is awful," said Rio de Janeiro prison worker and Bolsonaro voter Marli Alves, 63. "You can be at an outdoor event and someone sweeps through and robs you of everything."
Beyond campaign rallies, the final days of Brazil's election have also seen protests outside Meta's São Paulo offices. Lula's campaign has accused Meta of unfairly restricting his content, potentially giving his rival, an advantage — a claim the company denies. Meta's Oversight board and a group of U.N. experts have also raised concerns about the handling of political content.
Meta acknowledged technical issues in handling election-related content in Brazil, but said in a statement , "We do not suppress content to harm one side, nor do we give preferential treatment to any side."
In a race this tight, small factors — from distortions on social media to voter turnout on Election Day—could make a difference.
And while polls have for months suggested a fairly even division of the country into Lula and Bolsonaro supporters, a survey released Wednesday found that 10% of voters were still open to changing their minds, leaving space for a last-minute surprise.

title: With jet fuel prices near a record, holiday airfares soar higher
body:
A worker fuels a United Airlines plane at Salt Lake City International Airport in April, 2026. The price of jet fuel, one of airlines' biggest expenses, is close to an all-time high in the U.S. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
BALTIMORE — Herb and Latasha Williams flew from Dallas to Baltimore/Washington International Airport this week for a quick vacation to celebrate his birthday.
But their plane tickets cost hundreds of dollars more than they expected. And Latasha Williams is now wondering if they can afford to travel for the holidays.
"I kind of wanted to go somewhere warm. Florida, I'm thinking," she said.
"Maybe next year. Maybe," she said with a laugh. "Fingers crossed."
Those planning to fly this holiday season, should be prepared to pay more than they did last year. Experts expect airfares for this holiday travel season will be the highest in years as airlines scramble to cover the rising cost of jet fuel, which is one of their biggest expenses.
The average price of jet fuel in the U.S. reached $4.90 per gallon on Thursday, according to the tracking firm Argus. That's the highest single-day average the firm has ever recorded, and more than twice what the price was a year ago.
"Airfares right now are at what we see as a 10-year high because of the high cost of jet fuel," said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. "Airlines have to pass on these super high jet fuel prices in the form of higher fares to consumers."
Airfares for Thanksgiving are up about 30% compared to last year, according to Berg. Tickets for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20%.
But so far, Berg said, travelers seem willing to pay, at least for their big holiday trips.
"We're at the time of year where travel is really sticky. Even with higher prices, travelers are unlikely to make major changes to their traditional holiday home for the holiday trips," Berg said in an interview with NPR.
U.S. airlines say demand is holding steady even as fares have gone up. In an earnings call this month, Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said consumers have put up a "limited amount of resistance" and still view airfare as "reasonably affordable" even after fare increases.
"I think that's a very good sign for the future," Bastian said.
Some in the industry think fares will go even higher next year.
"You could see airfares rise next year in Europe. I think by 10, 15, maybe 20 percent," Michael O'Leary, CEO of the European low-cost carrier Ryanair, said this week in Belgium. "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months."
The picture may be slightly better in the U.S., which has more oil-producing and refining capacity than Europe. Still, higher fuel costs are hurting U.S. carriers, too.
"The airlines themselves are eating most of that cost," Chris Sununu, the head of Airlines for America, a trade group representing the big airlines, said in an interview this week with CNBC. "And some of it unfortunately has to be passed on to the customer and so you see that 20 to 30 percent increase as we go into the holidays."
Consumers are shopping around more in search of better deals, Berg said, and booking their tickets earlier to try to lock in reasonable prices.
"Usually I am shouting from the rooftops in the middle of October, 'Book your holiday travel by the end of this month, prices will not go down from here,'" Berg said. "But we actually saw an increase in customers booking holiday travel in September already."
At the airport in Baltimore, some travelers say they're priced out of flying for the holidays this year altogether.
"I'm gonna have to drive," said Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland. "I'm from Chicago originally, so I'm gonna drive. For me and my kids, just too much to get tickets."
But others said they're resigned to paying more for their holiday tickets. Mary Haller of Bethany Beach, Delaware is planning a trip to Europe.
"Literally I looked at the economy tickets two weeks ago and they have gone up," Haler said. "It was significant and I sort of had shell shock."
Still, Haller said she has little choice but to buy the tickets anyway.
"I feel bad for people who don't have the means to pay the extra money," she said.

title: Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students
body:
"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," says Zyearre Amoah, who works to recruit students in the Black Honors College at Sacramento State. Andri Tambunan for NPR hide caption
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
When Zyearre Amoah was a student at Sacramento State in 2023, there were times when he felt like the only Black student.
"There were African-American students on our campus," he recalls. But at a sprawling state university with more than 30,000 students, "it just felt like we had to look for each other."
Amoah graduated in 2024, just as his university was launching its Black Honors College, a school within a school with a special focus on Black history, life and culture. He's now a staff member at the BHC, as it's called, helping recruit students.
"Unfortunately I didn't have the luxury to be part of it as a student," he says, but the university's effort to elevate, and celebrate, the scholarship of Black students has changed how he perceives his alma mater.
"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," he says, laughing. "That is really helpful for everyone here. We're finding each other relatively easier. "
The initiative at Sacramento State, formally known as the California State University, Sacramento, began just months before the Trump administration began its widespread assault on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs on college campuses. In the last two years, dozens of colleges and universities have rolled back or eliminated such offerings to avoid accusations of racial discrimination that have led to loss of research funding and other sanctions.
"Historically, the campus struggled to create an environment of success" for Black students, says Luke Wood, Sac State's president, who helped create the BHC. "So we created an intervention that was designed to meet their needs while also serving any student who was interested in being part of it."
Wood sees this as a vital part of his, or any university's, mission. "I think that more institutions could be easily doing the same."
There are more than 800 students currently enrolled in the BHC, and while the majority of them identify as Black, African, African-American or mixed race, Wood insists it's not exclusive and that it complies with federal and state laws.
"It's nondiscriminatory because you can be a white student, an Asian student or Latino and be in the Black Honors College," he says, "and we have non-Black students who apply who want to have an elite, specialized experience."
Being part of the Black Honors College has helped Naomi Thrower, a junior, get in touch with her black identity. She runs a natural hair business on campus and says it's helped her develop a creative expression. Andri Tambunan for NPR hide caption
All of the college's courses are taught from a Black studies perspective. A math class, for example, also includes stories of famous Black mathematicians.
Faculty are chosen based on their track record of educating Black students. Among the criteria are low withdrawal and failure numbers for those students.
Now in its third year, women make up a majority of the BHC's enrollment, according to the college's dean, Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe. That's the case on most U.S. campuses . She says one of her priorities is to change that. To do so, she plans to provide more male role models and mentors: not just to convince more men to enroll, but to support them when they do.
Following the Supreme Court decision in 2023 banning affirmative action , the Trump administration has launched civil rights investigations targeting programs that single out a specific race — such as a scholarship program for Black students or an office designed to celebrate multiculturalism.
In September, the Treasury Department proposed a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide help to students based on their race.
At President Trump's State of the Union address in February, he declared, "We ended D-E-I in America!"
Around the country, many students have felt increasingly isolated, and let down, as diversity programs have disappeared.
"I was pretty sad just at the fact that our university would comply with those federal guidelines," says Hayden O'Neill, a senior at the University of Michigan. She was part of a scholarship program that was shut down last year.
"It definitely feels disheartening," she says, "I don't feel as comfortable as I thought I would at a school like this."
O'Neill is one of the many students around the country who say that understanding their identity – especially as it relates to their race – is a high priority in college. And while O'Neill feels like she is losing some of that opportunity, students in the Black Honors College say they're being given that chance.
The bell above the door to the Black Honors College headquarters – housed on the first floor of Sac State's library – rings often:
A sophomore arrives to meet with an advisor. A first-year student has a question about tuition. Over in the corner, a professor has come to ready his notes before class. It's a hub, a home within a home.
On a recent day, one of the students in the office is Naomi Thrower, a junior majoring in Deaf Studies and American Sign Language.
She wanted to attend a historically black college, but California doesn't have any. So, she says, Sacramento State with its BHC felt like the closest alternative.
Growing up in the East Bay, she had what she calls a very multicultural experience, going to school with kids of all different races. While she gained a lot from that, she also felt she was missing a deep understanding of Black culture and identity.
"The kids used to bully me in middle school and say I was whitewashed," Thrower says. "So when it came time for college, I wanted to be surrounded by students who looked like me and also had that same academic drive."
She runs a natural hair business on campus as a side hustle, and says it has helped her develop a creative expression. "In high school, when I'd say I have to do my hair, my friends wouldn't understand it's an all day thing. They'd be like, 'Why does it take so long to wash and brush out your hair?'"
But when she made friends in the honors college, it seemed everyone understood. "Two of my friends helped me take down my hair. We detangled it, washed it. We were just listening to music and hanging out, and that was the community that I was longing for, just someone who understood."
She and others NPR talked with often quoted the saying, Ubuntu , which comes from South African philosophy. It describes an interconnected way of living, often translated as, "I am because we are."
Many students said this concept is central to their educational experience.
And at Sacramento State, Wood says, the efforts to build that identity and sense of community are paying off: Enrollment of Black students is up – and those students are doing better – with more of them re-enrolling, and graduating.

title: What if you gave yourself a day to cancel all the plans you dread?
body:
To free up more time in your life, writer Caroline Sylge proposes a creative idea: Give yourself a "say no" retreat. It's a day to look at your calendar and thoughtfully decline obligations in the next few weeks and months. Juan Moyano/ Moment RF/ Getty Images hide caption
This story is adapted from Life Kit's weekly newsletter. Sign up here to get expert advice on lifestyle topics like health, money, relationships and more.
How is your to-do list looking for the next few weeks? If it's already full of obligations and tasks you've been dreading, and ramping up toward the holidays, you might need a "say no" retreat.
That's one of dozens of creative ideas in Caroline Sylge's book, How to Retreat: A Guide to Stepping Away from the Everyday to Find Space for Yourself , published this spring.
A "say no" retreat is a day to brainstorm all the things you want to say no to in your life in the coming weeks and months, she says. Then, you'll spend the last part of your day saying no to a few of those things.
Sylge, who has spent the last 30 years attending and organizing health and wellness retreats around the world, developed this exercise to help people reclaim their time.
"We often say yes for reasons that have nothing to do with what's good for us, because we feel like we should, don't want to seem difficult or fear missing out," Sylge says. "Saying 'no' is uncomfortable, but is a brave act of self-respect."
Devoting a whole day to saying "no" may seem like a wild idea, but with the holidays on the horizon, it may make room in your life for the things that matter. Here's how to do it.
Before you start: Pick a day on your calendar to do your "say no" retreat. That might mean calling out of work or moving obligations. Then find a comfy place in your home to reflect.
Right when you wake up, make a list of things you want to say no to in your life. What immediately comes to mind? Name anything obvious you don't want to do. For example, coordinating a big potluck for your book club or making a complicated dish for that dinner party on Saturday.
Then eat some breakfast and get yourself into nature to give yourself some time to think about your list. Maybe take a bike ride or a walk.
After your break, come back to your designated retreat space and build on your list. Add to that initial "say no" list by thinking about your upcoming days, weeks and months. Look at your digital calendar if you need to, but make sure your notifications are turned off, Sylge writes in her book.
Review all your requests, appointments, volunteer work, scheduled phone calls, work and social commitments, and memberships.
Is there anything you've planned that you're dreading? Are there tasks you've given yourself that you don't actually have to do or even want to do?
That might be sitting at a time-consuming hair appointment, hosting a playdate at your house, traveling to spend Thanksgiving with your husband's family or moderating a panel discussion for a work event.
Jot down notes — and if you'd like, reasons why you are saying no to a task.
Take lunch, then spend the afternoon reviewing your list — and take action. It's time to start saying no. You probably won't be able to get to all the nos on your list today, but you can pick a small, easy win, Sylge says. Maybe you just cross the arduous task of planting tulip bulbs off your to-do list … forever. You can just enjoy your neighbor's tulips next spring.
Now, you'll also need to start thinking about the harder nos — the ones that involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.
Sylge says instead of saying no outright, you can try delaying your yes. For example, "I'd love to, but can we plan it for a few weeks later?" You could also suggest alternatives. Instead of cooking for your friends, could you order takeout?
Don't underestimate the power of "crafting a kind decline," Sylge says. It "takes effort, but it saves time in the long run."
How to say 'no' and stop being a people-pleaser . Constantly saying 'yes' to everything and everyone drains us of time and energy. This episode helps explain the roots of people-pleasing behaviors and how you can say no more often.
How to set boundaries with family — and stick to them . Maintaining healthy boundaries is a way of taking care of your closest relationships, but setting those boundaries with family can be hard. The process starts with asking yourself what you need.
Could you give up shopping for a year? Try the 'no-buy challenge'. The goal is to save money, cut back on overconsumption and be more mindful of wasteful and unsustainable shopping habits. This guide can help you start a challenge of your own.
5 ways to resist the urge to keep looking at your phone . So you want to spend less time on your phone. How do you do that when it's designed to suck you in? Life Kit spoke to experts in behavioral science, psychology and technology for real-world advice.
This story was edited by Clare Marie Schneider. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify , and sign up for our newsletter . Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit .

title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
body: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried. Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything . In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood. Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old. Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015 . Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong. In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023. It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film. As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her? I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie? But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022 . I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all? One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers. Except that sometimes you can’t. Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn— 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 . At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews. I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have? I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review . I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim. But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think! This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here .

title: Georgia opposition party ban case: Day two of court proceedings
body: On 22 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court continued hearing a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party in Batumi, seeking to ban (declare unconstitutional) five opposition parties: the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Below are the key developments from the second day of hearings. The proceedings remained at the preliminary motions stage, with none of the opposition’s motions granted. The hearings continue today, 23 October, and are being broadcast live by the Georgian Public Broadcaster. The court has until 24 June 2027 to issue its final ruling, meaning it still has plenty of time. Unprecedented case The main issue raised by the opposition on the second day of hearings was that the lawsuit sought to ban all five parties in one go. Lelo leader Badri Japaridze told the court that the case was unprecedented, as the parties had no links to one another. He argued that this was particularly true of Lelo, which was founded in late 2019. Court begins hearing case to ban opposition parties in Georgia: first-day developments The court rejected all the opposition’s motions on the first day of hearings. Badri Japaridze described a statement by a Georgian Dream leader that the parties would be dissolved within days as disrespectful to the court. He argued that this meant the “verdict had already been delivered”. Presiding judge Revaz Nadaraya responded that the court could not comment on statements made by politicians and that no-one would be able to exert any influence over it. Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze partially agreed with Japaridze’s argument. He acknowledged that there was indeed no precedent for dissolving five parties in a single proceeding, but argued that there was equally no precedent for five closely linked parties jointly violating Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits parties aiming to forcibly change the constitutional order. Venice Commission The Lelo party asked the court to invite three experts from the Venice Commission to the hearing to assess whether banning the parties would comply with European democratic standards. Other opposition parties supported the motion, while Georgian Dream opposed it. However, Revaz Nadaraya dismissed the motion as unfounded, saying that the European legal experts could be heard elsewhere. Nika Gvaramia , co-chair of the Coalition for Change, argued that the Venice Commission was an association of European constitutional courts and that the right to consult it was enshrined in the Organic Law. The court’s full bench then held consultations and rejected the motion. Should state have right to ban political parties? Tbilisi street poll – Video Most respondents said that banning political parties was unacceptable in a country that claims to be a democracy. The court also rejected another motion by Lelo, requesting that its lawsuit No. 1907, filed on 28 October 2025, be admitted for consideration on its merits. The lawsuit challenges provisions of the Organic Law on Political Associations of Citizens which, according to the party, restrict freedom of association, freedom of expression and political pluralism. “Lack of trust is not enough reasoning” Another Lelo representative, Giorgi Sioridze, requested that the Constitutional Court seek an advisory opinion from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on five questions: the criteria under which a political party may be banned, the evidence required, whether a party’s stated objectives or its actual actions should carry greater weight, whether less restrictive measures are available, and what standards should apply when examining a case involving several parties simultaneously. One of the arguments put forward in support of the motion was a lack of trust in the Constitutional Court. Revaz Nadaraya dismissed this argument as unfounded. He said that although the case was important and unprecedented, this was not sufficient grounds for seeking an advisory opinion from the ECtHR. Nadaraya also added that a national court should not have to ask the European Court whether five parties could be named as co-defendants in the same proceedings. Evidence and one month to review case materials The Coalition for Change, meanwhile, requested that evidence be obtained from the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Government Administration, that witnesses be identified and that consideration of the case on its merits be postponed. The coalition also requested that the defendants be given one month to review the case materials. The court’s full bench unanimously rejected the motion. Nadaraya explained that, at this stage, the court was not convinced of the need to obtain additional evidence, as the requested materials relied on the same opinion already included in the case file. Georgian Dream representatives accused the opposition of attempting to delay the proceedings. According to Archil Gorduladze , the defendants were filing motions that had no legal basis or relevance to the case. Tornike Cheishvili argued that the parties were expressing the same arguments using different terminology and that their motions were virtually identical. Meanwhile, outside the courtroom… – Georgia’s Public Defender (ombudsman) has yet to submit a legal opinion (amicus curiae) to the Constitutional Court, despite Lelo calling on him to do so on 19 October. According to First Deputy Public Defender Tamar Gvaramadze, the ombudsman’s office is holding internal discussions and no decision has yet been made. – Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili said it was unacceptable for international actors to make statements intended to put pressure on the court. He argued that such statements served harmful political purposes. Reactions after the hearing Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, compared the proceedings to Franz Kafka’s novel The Trial, saying that no-one really knew who was being accused of what. Badri Japaridze also said that, by the end of the second day of hearings, none of the parties understood exactly what Georgian Dream was accusing them of. Ana Tsitlidze , a representative of the United National Movement, accused the judges of behaving like Georgian Dream activists. According to Lelo representative Irakli Kupradze , the proposed ban would affect not only the parties but also nearly a million Georgian voters. Ana Buchukuri , a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, suggested that the third day of hearings would also begin with procedural motions. She argued that the court’s refusal to grant any of the motions indicated that a decision had already been made.

title: TinyFish Breaks Down Agentic Search Architecture for Production AI Agents
body:
An AI search agent can work in a demo but fail under production workloads when retrieval returns incomplete evidence, retries repeat unsuccessful actions, or execution exceeds time and cost limits. TinyFish , which provides web infrastructure for AI agents, has published two technical guides addressing these challenges. The first defines a production agentic search architecture , while the second shares lessons from building a deep research system . Together, they examine how an autonomous search agent can plan retrieval, evaluate evidence, handle failures, and manage the boundary between model reasoning and deterministic execution. TL;DR TinyFish introduced its agentic search architecture and key engineering lessons from building deep research systems. Built on four web primitives ( TinySearch, TinyFetch, TinyBrowser, and TinyAgent ), the system operates via a seven-phase control loop around the base model. On OpenBenchmarks, TinyFish achieved a 79.0% completion rate on coding tasks while delivering the lowest median task cost ($0.050) and token footprint, highlighting the importance of rigid control loops, failure-specific retries, and unified reasoning over standalone planners. What is Agentic Search Architecture? Agentic search architecture enables an AI agent to plan retrieval, access sources, evaluate evidence, and adapt its approach as new information becomes available. The model provides reasoning, while the surrounding application manages state, tool execution, evidence handling, runtime policies, and output validation. Together, these components allow an agent to handle incomplete results, recoverable failures, and changing information requirements. TinyFish’s architecture draws foundational concepts from a February 2026 architecture preprint , which decouples reasoning from execution through typed tool interfaces. The paper establishes essential system guardrails, including detailed tracing alongside strict caps on tokens, execution time, overall cost, and tool invocations. How does a production search run work? TinyFish splits a run into 7 phases: Define the task: Turn the goal into an “evidence contract”: required fields, sources, freshness and completion rules. Plan retrieval: Separate independent needs from dependent ones. Dependent queries wait for earlier answers. Pick the first route: Choose a tool based on what the system knows about the evidence. Discover, select, retrieve: Treat search results as candidates until the page content arrives. Evaluate: Label evidence as sufficient, incomplete, conflicting, inaccessible or budget exhausted. Recover or escalate: Revise the query, retry, change sources or change access method. Stop and validate: Return completed, incomplete, failed, cancelled or human review required. Phase 2 addresses a known failure. ChainRAG (ACL 2025) calls it the ‘lost-in-retrieval’ problem, where key entities disappear during multi-hop question decomposition. Phase 6 draws on Search-R1 , which demonstrates how models can learn to generate additional search queries during reasoning when earlier retrieval is insufficient. Across 7 QA datasets, its learned multi-turn search beat RAG baselines by 41% (Qwen2.5-7B) and 20% (Qwen2.5-3B). How should a search agent route tools? Routing should follow the information gap, not a fixed ladder. Starting condition Primitive What the app still owns Source location unknown Search Query planning, source policy, stopping URL known and readable Fetch Completeness checks, claim validation App must control page actions Browser Every action, retry and checkpoint Decisions across several pages Web Agent Business rules, budgets, validation Escalation is not always the fix. Weak results need a better query. Conflicting sources need stronger evidence. A heavier tool fixes neither. Retries should be based on the failure type and remain within defined limits. Transient errors may justify repeating a request, while incomplete or conflicting evidence requires a different approach. The deep research agent searches, browses, and generates comprehensive, cited reports. Most engineering challenges centered around context management, system orchestration, and product design. Lesson #1: Removing the separate planner Initial iterations used a standalone planner called fresh each time. Only structured state crossed into it. On follow-up queries like “focus only on pricing risks in Southeast Asia,” the agent drifted back to broad market research. TinyFish subsequently moved planning into the orchestrator’s own unified reasoning loop. Lesson #2: Removing subagents: TinyFish initially assigned a separate subagent to each search query, increasing context-switching overhead, latency, and cost. The team later replaced these subagents with tool calls for repeatable tasks such as ranking search results, classifying sources, and extracting evidence. This reduced the information passed back to the orchestrator, allowing it to focus on research planning and deciding what to investigate next. Lesson #3- Matching researchers: TinyFish initially optimized its research system for source coverage, but users placed greater importance on the quality and relevance of supporting evidence. The team adjusted source ranking to account for the research objective and added controls for prioritizing, excluding, or restricting domains. It also developed an internal evaluation harness using an LLM judge to assess reports for relevance, evidence strength, citation trust, and source diversity. How do cost and latency add up? TinyFish budgets the full task, not single calls: Task latency = planning + search + retrieval + evaluation + retries + interactive steps + queueing. Task cost = tokens + tool calls + page or browser usage + retries + infrastructure. SearchAgent-X (ICLR 2026) shows why. Exact retrieval added overhead, and coarse retrieval forced extra reasoning. Its fixes reached up to 3.4x throughput and 5x lower latency versus tested baselines. How does TinyFish compare on search and fetch? OpenBenchmarks fixes the model (gpt-5.6-sol), 100 tasks and budgets, and varies only the provider. Scores are means of 3 runs. Metric TinyFish Exa deep Perplexity Firecrawl Search + fetch completion 79.0% ± 2.0 83.0% ± 1.0 77.7% ± 1.5 76.0% ± 1.0 Median task time 24s 37s 22s 34s Median task cost $0.050 $0.127 $0.083 $0.082 Median task tokens 12,844 23,660 20,062 17,379 Search-only completion 59.3% 66.3% (Exa fast) 77.3% 70.3% Search list price $0 $0.012 $0.005 $0.005 Source: OpenBenchmarks board , updated 26 Sept 2026. Tasks cover enterprise documentation only. OpenBenchmarks also reports search-only results separately. In that configuration, TinyFish achieved 59.3% task completion, compared with 77.3% for Perplexity, 70.3% for Firecrawl, and 66.3% for Exa Fast. These results should not be directly compared with the search-and-fetch scores because the available retrieval capabilities differ. Key Takeaways Control the whole trajectory, not 1 search call. Route by information gap; escalate only when access fails. Keep planning and execution in 1 reasoning loop. Move deterministic steps into tool calls, not subagents. Rank sources by research objective, not one quality score. Read the architecture guide , the deep research lessons and the TinyFish docs . title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $US25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
body: In short: (ABC-Australia) A judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $US25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook. This marks the biggest fine ever against the tech giant. What’s next? Meta’s chief legal officer says the company is confident it will win on appeal. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-22/meta-ordered-to-pay-new-mexico-us25-billion/107294964 Share article A judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico US25billion(35.6 billion) after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant. Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J Mathew wrote in his ruling on Wednesday local time. “Facebook promised users that they [the users] controlled their data. This was false,” he said. Jurors in September found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users’ personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season. The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney-General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference. “This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said. Meta said the ruling and Mr Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico”. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” CJ Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. Meta also reported on Wednesday better-than-expected quarterly revenue of US64.6billion(92 billion) , ahead of Wall Street estimates of US63.37billion(90.32 billion) . New Mexico goes it alone In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay US18billion(25.6 billion) and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms. The settlement ended a trial over teenage social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention. New Mexico did not join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own. During the trial, prosecutors cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed from Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in which he wrote that the company did not sell user data. “You have control over how your information is shared,” Mr Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.” Attorneys for New Mexico had sought US35billion(49.8 billlion) to US40billion(57 billion), arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price. Meta’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation harmed New Mexicans. They contended that the company should pay no more than US3.4billion(4.8 billion), saying an award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up on appeal. Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable. The US25billion(35.6 billion) award far exceeds the US5billion(7.1 billion) fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019. Villanova University associate law professor Peter Ormerod said he was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower. “It comes out to about US12,000[17,000] per person in New Mexico, and that’s just a very large number. It’s quite unlike anything else we’ve seen,” Mr Ormerod said. Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending. But it could take years before the state sees any of the money while the company appeals. Company argues that the state failed to prove harm The state’s case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from about 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm’s clients included Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign. Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population, not just Facebook users, was deceived by the company. They also said Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate. Meta attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company’s content moderation policies were robust and that freedom of speech must be considered. They argued that the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. In one of the tech giant’s few wins, jurors found that the state did not prove Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic. During a video deposition, Mr Zuckerberg denied the state’s claims that Facebook profited off harmful content. He said the company had to balance freedom of speech with content moderation. Attorneys for the company said it had changed its policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it caught and removed an estimated 99 per cent of the content that violates its standards.
