title: Vanity Fair: Trump son-in-law received $750m from Azerbaijani bank
body: Kushner’s links to Azerbaijani bank Reports have emerged of hundreds of millions of dollars being transferred through Azerbaijan to a secret bank account that Jared Kushner, the son-in-law and former senior adviser to US President Donald Trump , allegedly had access to. However, no evidence has been presented that the money belonged to the Azerbaijani state or that Azerbaijani authorities were involved in arranging these transactions. The name of the Azerbaijani bank through which the transfers were allegedly made has also not been disclosed. According to an investigation published in Vanity Fair , Dutch intelligence, while monitoring Kushner’s phone, discovered that a large sum of money had been transferred from an Azerbaijani bank to an account in the United Arab Emirates. The claims were detailed in an article by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole, published on 22 October. The article is an excerpt from his new book, Princes and Thieves. The investigation refers to a bank account holding approximately $750m, as well as an additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan. The author links these financial transactions to unofficial diplomatic negotiations involving the United States, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel. Ex-German intelligence chief arrested as investigators probe links to Azerbaijani intelligence Hanning has also served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum for many years. How did Dutch intelligence gain access to Kushner’s phone? According to Matthew Cole’s investigation, the Netherlands’ Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) gained access to data from Kushner’s phone in late 2017 through a hacker linked to Russian military intelligence. Dutch intelligence officers initially discovered screenshots from Kushner’s iPhone on Russian military intelligence servers. Then, exploiting the same technical vulnerability, they were able to monitor activity on his phone screen in early 2018. The intelligence officers’ attention was drawn to Kushner’s use of a bank account in the UAE. According to the investigation, hundreds of millions of dollars had previously been transferred to this account from an Azerbaijani bank. Dutch intelligence initially suspected that the bank account from which the funds originated might have been linked to the Azerbaijani government. However, the article does not provide any banking documents confirming this connection. Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice Azerbaijan has drafted a law to encourage and protect people who report corruption. $750m and possible intermediary role of Azerbaijani bank The account, referred to in the investigation as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, one of the UAE’s largest banks. According to the author, the Saudi and UAE leadership transferred around $750m into the account from 2017 onwards. The funds were allegedly intended to finance unofficial foreign policy initiatives. The account did not legally belong to Kushner. It was held by Watani Al Emarat, a charitable organisation funded by the UAE government. However, according to the investigation, Kushner had signing authority over the account, allowing him to carry out certain banking transactions. The section of the investigation concerning Azerbaijan focuses particularly on the mechanism used to transfer the funds. According to Cole, all the funds deposited into the account monitored by Dutch intelligence arrived in US dollars from an Azerbaijani bank. The author claims that some Azerbaijani banks acted as intermediaries in transferring large sums of money abroad. They accepted funds in Saudi riyals and UAE dirhams before transferring the equivalent amounts overseas in US dollars, charging a commission of 6–7%. Under the arrangement described, a client would transfer funds in local currency to an Azerbaijani bank, which would then send the equivalent amount in US dollars to a recipient abroad from a separate internal account. The author notes that such transactions could make it more difficult to trace the original source of the funds. Tourism support package: can Azerbaijan reach its target of 3.8 million tourists? In 2026, arrivals from the Gulf states fell by 31.4%, hotel overnight stays by 8.3%, and hotel revenues by 3.8%. Additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel The investigation also describes a second major financial transaction allegedly carried out through Azerbaijan. According to the author’s sources, by spring 2018, UAE leader Mohammed bin Zayed had transferred around $1bn to Israel through Azerbaijan, allegedly intended for Kushner. The second account, referred to by Cole as Beta, was reportedly held at the Bank of Israel. The article claims that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was to be informed of any potential transfers from this account. According to the author, former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman acted as an intermediary between Kushner and Netanyahu. Friedman categorically denied these allegations. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client was unaware of the accounts in question, had no involvement with them and had not broken any laws. $94.3m in violations: What Azerbaijan's mid-year audit reveals During the reporting period, the chamber carried out 20 compliance audits, two financial audits, eight performance audits and three analytical reviews. Kushner’s financial ties have previously come under scrutiny The new allegations come amid ongoing debate in the US over Kushner’s business ties with Gulf states. In March 2026, US Senator Ron Wyden and House Representative Robert Garcia launched an investigation into Kushner’s continued efforts to raise funds from foreign governments for his investment firm while simultaneously engaging in diplomatic activities. The members of Congress sought to establish whether investments received by Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, from Middle Eastern governments could have influenced his involvement in US foreign policy. An investigation published by The New Yorker in September reported that Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund had invested $2bn in Kushner’s firm in 2021. The UAE and Qatar also invested in Affinity Partners. These were separate financial arrangements, not directly linked to the alleged secret banking transactions of 2017–2018 described in the Vanity Fair article. In addition, on 1 October, CNN published an investigation into investments made by Kushner’s firm in Israeli financial group Phoenix Financial. According to CNN’s analysis, Phoenix Financial had invested in at least nine companies supplying equipment to the Israeli military. However, CNN said it had found no evidence that Kushner’s diplomatic decisions had directly influenced these investments. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client had not been involved in the companies’ investment decisions. On 8 October, Kushner published a detailed response on his website to the earlier New Yorker article, rejecting allegations that he had used his diplomatic activities for personal financial gain. Millions reported stolen from safe of president of Azerbaijan’s Academy of Sciences’ daughter in Germany According to the investigation, over €1 million in cash and valuables stored in a rented German bank safe were fraudulently stolen. Which previous investigations have implicated Azerbaijani banks? Azerbaijan’s role in international financial transactions has previously been the subject of journalistic investigations. In 2017, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), together with its partners, published a major investigation titled The Azerbaijani Laundromat . The investigation documented financial transactions totalling around $2.9bn, carried out between 2012 and 2014 through various companies and bank accounts. According to OCCRP, around $1.4bn of this amount was transferred through Baktelekom LLC, a company that held an account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan. The investigation highlighted the role of Azerbaijan-linked financial entities in international money transfers. However, there is no confirmed link between this scheme and the recently reported accounts allegedly connected to Kushner. Meanwhile, in January 2026, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Experts on the Evaluation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures and the Financing of Terrorism (MONEYVAL) reported progress by Azerbaijan in this area. The committee upgraded Azerbaijan’s compliance ratings against international standards in seven areas, including money transfer controls, identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of legal entities and banking supervision. However, the country remained subject to enhanced monitoring. Azerbaijan: selective punishment for financial violations – what “culture of corruption” looks like. Opinion

title: Radiance 2026: NsromaMusic delivers a memorable night of worship
body: Some events entertain you. Some impress you. Others leave you asking questions, humming songs you barely knew, and wondering when the next edition will happen. Radiance 2026 did all three. Organised by NsromaMusic, the event was an unforgettable experience that stirred hearts, celebrated musical excellence, and left many of us counting down to next year. Honestly, I am still trying to find the right words to describe what happened. And trust me, that is saying something! The production was speaking before the music did From the moment I walked into the auditorium, it was clear that serious thought, creativity and hard work had gone into putting Radiance together. The lighting was excellent. The sound was on point. The stage design, auditorium arrangement, ushering and protocol all contributed to an atmosphere that felt intentional, polished and worthy of the occasion. Nothing about the experience suggested that the organisers had simply gathered a few musicians, hired a sound system and hoped for the best. There was a vision, and the execution reflected it. One moment that particularly caught my attention was the cinematic audio introduction of NsromaMusic. The creative presentation explained the meaning of Radiance and connected it beautifully to NsromaMusic’s identity and musical journey. It was more than an introduction. It was storytelling, branding and artistic identity rolled into one brilliant moment. Whoever conceived that idea deserves serious applause. That was how you introduce an artiste, not simply announce a name and wait for the crowd to scream! Then NsromaMusic took over! And then came the moment we had all been waiting for. NsromaMusic stepped on to the stage, and the atmosphere changed. From the first song, her passion, confidence and spiritual intensity were unmistakable. The initial ministers laid a beautiful foundation, but what followed took the experience to another level. This was not the kind of performance you politely applaud while checking your phone under the cover of darkness. No! This was the kind that demanded your attention, engaged your spirit and made sitting still feel like an unnecessary suggestion. It was more than music. It was an encounter! What impressed me just as much was the quality of NsromaMusic’s catalogue. At several points, I caught myself wondering how songs of such quality could exist while so many people were only just discovering the artiste. The songwriting was impressive. The melodies were memorable. The arrangements were thoughtful, and her delivery carried both conviction and energy. The band also deserves enormous credit. Those musicians did not come to play around. They came prepared, and they delivered! Akesse Brempong, Perez Music and the surprises we did not see coming Every memorable concert needs moments that catch you off guard in the best possible way. Radiance had its fair share. The reggae ministration featuring Akesse Brempong was one of my personal highlights. The chemistry, rhythm and energy made the collaboration a delight to watch. It was one of those performances that reminded you that gospel music has room for variety, creativity and infectious grooves without losing its spiritual essence. Then Perez Music made a surprise appearance. Just when you thought the evening had already delivered enough, another musical treat arrived. His appearance alongside NsromaMusic added another layer of excitement to an already impressive night. But let us talk about the real business! That Ga song! Somebody, please release it! If you ask me for the highest point of the night, I will answer without hesitation: that Ga song featuring Perez Music! Oh, my goodness! I do not speak Ga. I suspect I was not the only person in the auditorium who could not translate every lyric. Yet, somehow, we were all singing along! Explain that! The melody was infectious, the rhythm was irresistible, and the connection between the two artistes was beautiful. The language barrier stood no chance against the power of a good song. You did not need to understand every word to feel every emotion. The music did the translating. And that is the magic of great songwriting. It makes strangers participate in something they may not fully understand but instinctively enjoy. That song has been living rent-free in my head ever since. I want it released, promoted, distributed and given the opportunity to find its audience. If the live performance is anything to go by, NsromaMusic and Perez Music may have something very special on their hands. Dear team, please do not let us suffer unnecessarily. Release the song! A turnout that deserves recognition The attendance was another impressive feature of the evening. Considering the distance from central Accra, ongoing road construction that made access to the church challenging, and the fact that Pastor Isaiah had a major programme on the same day, the turnout was remarkable. Both the upper and lower sections of the auditorium were filled with people who came ready to participate. Yes, access was difficult. Yes, the programme started later than scheduled and eventually extended to around 9 pm. Those challenges were real, and future editions could benefit from better traffic guidance, clearer access information and tighter time management. Nevertheless, the audience showed up, remained engaged, worshipped, celebrated and left with memories worth discussing. That level of commitment says something about the appeal of the event and the experience it offered. When excellence meets the presence of God Perhaps what I appreciated most about Radiance 2026 was that it did not feel like another concert where technical perfection and recording the songs were the only priorities. The production was excellent, but it did not overshadow the purpose. The music was beautiful, but it was not merely a showcase of vocal ability. There was a genuine spiritual atmosphere that gave the evening its deeper meaning. Radiance brought musical excellence and heartfelt worship into the same room without making either feel secondary. After the event, I heard several attendees express their excitement about hearing the songs again when they are officially released. I completely understand. When a song connects with you in a moment like that, you want to relive it. You want it on your playlist, in your car, during your quiet moments, and perhaps on repeat until everyone around you starts singing along too. That is the opportunity before NsromaMusic now: to turn the magic of the live experience into lasting musical connections. NsromaMusic, there is something special here Radiance 2026 reminded me that NsromaMusic has something worth paying attention to. She has a strong stage presence, a compelling catalogue, the ability to connect with an audience, and a musical identity that deserves wider recognition. The next step is to ensure that the excellence witnessed in the auditorium reaches people who were not fortunate enough to attend. Strategic releases, consistent promotion, strong digital distribution and continued audience engagement can help transform the excitement surrounding Radiance into sustained growth. To NsromaMusic and the entire team, congratulations! The vision was beautiful, the execution was impressive, and the experience was unforgettable. May God continue to strengthen the team, expand NsromaMusic’s reach, and take the music to greater heights. As for me, I am already looking forward to the next edition.

title: Nollywood actor Francis Duru dies at 57
body: Veteran Nollywood actor Francis Duru has died at the age of 57 following a brief illness, his family has announced. The family announced his death in a statement posted on the actor’s official Instagram page in the early hours of Friday, expressing appreciation to fans and well-wishers for their prayers and support. “We, the family of Francis Duru, regret to announce his passing following a brief illness. “We appreciate your prayers, love, and understanding. May his soul rest in perfect peace. Amen,” the statement read. Duru is survived by his wife, Adokiye, and children Duru, who began his acting career in 1989, became widely known for his role as Ahanna in Rattlesnake, the 1995 film produced by the late filmmaker Amaka Igwe. His death came months after he dismissed reports that he was battling a life-threatening illness, describing footage circulating online in June as false. In a video posted on Instagram in response to the reports, the actor rejected claims about his health and criticised those circulating the footage. Born on July 27, 1969, in Cameroon to Nigerian parents from Imo State, Duru completed his primary and secondary education in Cameroon before moving to Nigeria for university studies. He studied Theatre Arts at the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1996. Duru made his film debut in Missing Mark in 1989, in a production directed by the late Ndubuisi Oko. His performance in Rattlesnake later established him as a recognised face in Nollywood. Over his decades-long career, he featured in several Nigerian films, including Blood Money (1997), Stigma (2013) and Mboputa (2020). In 2020, he won the Best Actor in a Leading Role (Igbo) award at the Best of Nollywood Awards for his performance in Mboputa. He also received the United Nations Ambassador of Peace award in 2007 in recognition of his influence on young people. Duru served as interim president of the Actors Guild of Nigeria in 2010 and was nominated for Best Actor in a Supporting Role at the Africa Movie Academy Awards that year.

title: Kesewaa Kessy releases debut EP’s lead single ‘Jesus Endorsement’

title: UAE's G42 signs pacts to explore AI infrastructure in Greece
body: Abu Dhabi-based G42 has signed an initial pact with public and private partners in Greece to explore artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country. The deal was part of the 18 memorandums of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships valued at €12.75 billion ($14.3 billion) signed between the UAE and Greece during an official visit to the European country by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. The pacts were signed at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum in Athens. G42 and five of its portfolio companies also signed initial agreements with Greek entities for government services, life sciences and smart cities, the company said in a statement on Friday. The agreements “mark an important milestone in expanding G42’s intelligence grid across Europe, bringing together advanced compute infrastructure and proven AI platforms for government and industry”, said Mansoor Al Mansoori, chief executive of G42 International. The intelligence grid covers the full AI value chain, from data centres and advanced compute to cloud infrastructure and industry-specific applications. Under agreements with Greece's Copelouzos Group, Khazna Data Centres and Core42 will explore the development of an AI factory in Greece, G42 said. Khazna will lead the development of the physical infrastructure, while Core42 will provide cloud and AI compute capabilities to support organisations in sectors including banking, telecoms, shipping and government. Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Prime Minister of the Hellenic Republic, have attended the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum in Athens and witnessed the announcement of 18 MoUs, agreements and commercial partnerships valued at €12.75bn. pic.twitter.com/BlVL1bvpwV — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 22, 2026 The deal “strengthens the country’s position as a strategic digital and energy hub in South-east Europe”, said Christos Copelouzos, chief executive of Copelouzos Group. The factory will support the digital transformation of the Greek economy, attract new investment and create highly skilled jobs, he added. G42 has been working to help countries build domestic AI capabilities. In February, G42 signed a framework agreement with a Vietnamese consortium to develop sovereign AI capabilities and cloud infrastructure across the South-East Asian country. Urban planning and life sciences G42 said its subsidiary Presight will also collaborate with Greece’s Ministry of Digital Governance to explore the use of AI-powered analytics and real-time intelligence capabilities focusing on urban mobility and municipal operations. The collaboration will initially focus on using agentic AI to support municipal waste management and water network monitoring through analytics, G42 said. “Cities generate enormous volumes of data every day, but their real value comes from turning that information into intelligence that improves how cities function and how people live,” said Thomas Pramotedham, chief executive of Presight. Meanwhile, Inception42 will work with Greece’s Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence to use agentic AI across government and education. Areas of focus include using AI-powered tools to support cabinet meetings and monitor progress against government priorities, training government officials to work with AI agents, and developing AI tutors and learning platforms to enhance educational outcomes. Tech-enabled health care company M42 has also signed an initial pact with Athens LifeTech Park (ALTP) for a partnership spanning life sciences research, genomics sequencing infrastructure, population genomics, clinical development and connecting institutional biobanks. The deal is aimed at supporting biomarker research in priority areas including oncology, rare genetic diseases and neuroscience, the statement said. The pact also covers a bilateral programme offering UAE life sciences start-ups a base at the ALTP Incubator for European market entry, and Greek and European ventures access to the UAE through M42’s network.

title: Russia Strikes Odesa Energy Facility, Claims Naval Drone Sites Hit as Attacks Injure 2 Elsewhere
body:
Russian forces attacked energy and civilian infrastructure in Odesa region overnight, damaging a facility belonging to DTEK Odesa Electric Networks.
Oleh Kiper, head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration (OVA), said Russian forces had targeted energy infrastructure and civilian facilities in the southern part of the region, including a recreation area.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The fires that broke out have now been extinguished. There have been no reports of casualties,” Kiper said .
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) later reported that four defunct recreation centers were destroyed in the Russian attack. The attack also damaged energy infrastructure and sparked a fire at the impact site.
Emergency crews extinguished the fires at all affected locations. No fatalities or injuries were reported.
Russia ’s defense ministry, meanwhile, claimed its forces had struck facilities in the Danube port of Vylkove in the Odesa region, including two temporary deployment sites for operators of unmanned boats, a boat parking area, a storage facility for unmanned boats, and port infrastructure used to store and prepare them for operations.
The ministry also claimed that a cargo ship was hit while sailing toward the port of Odesa with cargo allegedly intended to support the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU). The claims have not been independently verified.
Separately, DTEK reported that Russian forces had severely damaged one of its thermal power plants , completely shutting down generation capacity.
The company said the plant’s equipment had sustained significant damage but did not specify its location.
Russian forces also attacked railway infrastructure in central Ukraine’s Poltava region, according to the DSNS . The strike sparked a fire, which emergency crews later extinguished. No casualties were reported.
An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) also fell in an open area in the Poltava community, with the resulting blast wave damaging nearby private homes, buildings and power lines, said Vitaliy Dyakivnych, head of the Poltava OVA.
Local authorities reported that at least six households in one residential neighborhood sustained damage, including shattered windows and damaged roofs.
Russia’s defense ministry claimed that its forces had struck a railway depot in the Poltava region, alleging that the site was used by AFU to store and repair military equipment. The claim has not been independently verified.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian attacks injured two people overnight, according to the DSNS.
The attacks targeted four districts and sparked several fires. A man was injured in Nikopol district and a woman in Synelnykove district.
In the city of Dnipro, infrastructure was damaged, while strikes in Pavlohrad damaged an administrative building and a residential property. Emergency crews extinguished all the fires, the service said.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: NAF Air Mishaps: Of Aircraft Maintenance and Operational Safety
body: The recurring aviation mishaps involving Nigerian Air Force aircraft raise troubling questions about aircraft maintenance, operational safety and accountability, making it imperative to address the underlying causes before more lives are lost, writes Linus Aleke . Over the past decade, the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has experienced a series of aviation mishaps involving transport aircraft, fighter jets, helicopters, training aircraft and unmanned aerial platforms. Media reports have identified at least 16 incidents during the period under review. The latest and deadliest incident occurred on 5 October 2026, when an ATR-42 aircraft, designated NAF 931, crashed near the naval base at Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, while undertaking a routine flight from Benin City to Lagos. All 25 people on board, comprising 20 passengers and five crew members, reportedly died. As of 10 October 2026, the cause of the crash had not been officially established, and an investigation had been ordered. Barely 24 hours later, an NAF helicopter made a precautionary landing in Benue State following an air interdiction mission near the Benue–Enugu boundary. The helicopter subsequently returned safely to base. Other recent incidents included an Alpha Jet emergency at NAF Base Kainji, Niger State, on 6 December 2025, during which both pilots ejected safely, and the reported loss of a CH-4B unmanned aerial platform in Niger State in January 2026, which did not result in human fatalities. Earlier incidents included a Super Mushshak trainer aircraft mishap near Kaduna Military Airfield on 7 March 2024, from which both pilots emerged uninjured; the crash of an FT-7NI training aircraft at Makurdi on 14 July 2023, with both pilots reportedly ejecting safely; and the crash of an Mi-171E helicopter at Chukuba, Niger State, on 14 August 2023, during a casualty-evacuation mission. Reports differed on the death toll from the latter incident. On 1 December 2023, an Mi-35P attack helicopter crashed shortly after take-off at NAF Base Port Harcourt, although all five crew members reportedly survived with minor injuries. In 2022, a Super Mushshak trainer aircraft crashed at NAF Base Kaduna, killing Flight Lieutenant Abubakar Muhammed Alkali and Flight Lieutenant Elijah Haruna Karatu. The year 2021 witnessed several major incidents. On 21 February, a Beechcraft King Air 350i, designated NAF 201, crashed while returning to Abuja, killing all seven personnel on board. On 31 March, an Alpha Jet disappeared over Borno State, with both pilots presumed dead. The NAF rejected claims that the aircraft had been shot down, stating that a video circulated in connection with the incident did not establish enemy action. On 21 May 2021, a Beechcraft King Air 350 crashed near Kaduna Civil Airport, killing all 11 occupants, including the then Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Ibrahim Attahiru. A joint investigation by the NAF and Nigeria’s Accident Investigation Bureau subsequently produced an interim report containing 27 initial findings and eight immediate safety recommendations. Another Alpha Jet incident occurred near the Kaduna–Zamfara boundary on 18 July 2021, with the pilot surviving after ejecting. Earlier accidents included the crash of an Mi-35M helicopter at Damasak, Borno State, on 2 January 2019, with five reported fatalities; an RV-6A Air Beetle trainer aircraft crash in Kaduna State on 17 August 2019, which killed one person; and a training helicopter crash in Enugu State on 14 November 2019, with no reported fatalities. On 28 September 2018, two F-7NI fighter jets collided during rehearsals for Nigeria’s Independence Day celebrations at Katampe Hills, Abuja, resulting in one reported fatality. In July 2017, an Agusta 109 utility helicopter came down in the Borno River following a reported technical problem, without loss of life. Collectively, these incidents encompass fatal and non-fatal crashes, mid-air collisions, emergency ejections, precautionary landings and the loss of an unmanned platform. They underscore the importance of distinguishing confirmed facts from preliminary reports and awaiting the findings of official investigations before attributing causes. Although the NAF has institutionalised civilian harm mitigation through intelligence-driven targeting, collateral damage assessments, adherence to international humanitarian law and measures to protect civilians during air operations, concerns persist about the adequacy of its preventive policies and programmes. Public outcry from communities affected by collateral damage, amplified by international human rights organisations such as Amnesty International (AI), has further intensified scrutiny of the service. Meanwhile, questions about the effectiveness of existing aviation safety safeguards remain. The persistence of mishaps has fuelled public criticism, with some detractors disparagingly likening NAF aircraft to overripe mangoes that fall from trees at the slightest breeze. Against this backdrop, security experts and public affairs analysts have called for more transparent investigations, improved maintenance, better training, stronger civil-military cooperation and a long-term strategy for developing Nigeria’s indigenous aerospace capabilities. Speaking on the recurring mishaps, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Beacon Security and Intelligence Limited, Dr Kabir Adamu, described the recurrent loss of NAF aircraft as a national tragedy that extends beyond the substantial financial cost to taxpayers. More significantly, he said, these incidents represent the irreversible loss of highly trained and patriotic personnel whose expertise takes years and considerable financial resources to develop. The crash of NAF 931 in Igbokoda on 5 October 2026 has, he noted, understandably reignited public debate about military aviation safety. However, he argued that addressing the crisis requires moving beyond speculation to examine the underlying systemic factors and develop evidence-based solutions. According to Adamu, aviation disasters rarely result from a single point of failure. The Swiss Cheese Model of accident causation illustrates how incidents occur when multiple underlying vulnerabilities align. He identified several factors that could contribute to recurring NAF mishaps. The first is operational tempo and environmental stress. The NAF operates across multiple theatres, from counter-insurgency operations in the North-East to maritime surveillance in the Niger Delta and internal security missions nationwide. Such demands increase flying hours, accelerate wear and tear, and heighten the risk of crew fatigue. Operating in challenging weather conditions, including dense Harmattan haze and sudden tropical storms, also requires exceptional pilot proficiency and reliable instrument systems. Adamu identified maintenance practices and supply-chain constraints as another concern. While cautioning against blanket accusations of poor maintenance, he observed that sustaining an ageing fleet in a challenging economic environment presents considerable difficulties. Even when aircraft undergo major overseas maintenance, their continued airworthiness depends on local technical capacity and the availability of spare parts. He cited the crashed ATR-42, which, he said, had undergone maintenance in Germany before returning to Nigeria in late 2024, as an example of the importance of sustained maintenance beyond major servicing. Delays in procuring genuine original equipment manufacturer (OEM) parts, he added, can sometimes result in workarounds or deferred maintenance, potentially compromising airworthiness over time. Aircraft age is another consideration. Although older aircraft can remain safe with rigorous maintenance, many NAF platforms have reportedly been in service for 15 to 20 years or longer. As aircraft age, inspections become more frequent and expensive. Without a robust, adequately funded lifecycle-management plan, the risk of mechanical failure may increase. Adamu also highlighted human factors and training gaps, noting that pilot decision-making, air traffic control and maintenance errors can contribute to aviation accidents. Although NAF pilots are highly skilled, he argued that recurrent training must evolve to address emerging operational challenges. Simulator training should adequately reproduce region-specific hazards, including sudden microbursts, instrument failures and spatial disorientation, to prepare pilots for critical situations. To address these challenges and restore public confidence, Adamu called on the NAF and the Federal Government to adopt a proactive, transparent and systemic approach to aviation safety. First, he advocated independent and transparent investigations, urging the NAF to strengthen its collaboration with the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) and aviation safety experts. While acknowledging legitimate operational security concerns, he argued that declassified interim and final investigation reports should be made public. Transparency, he maintained, would promote accountability, dispel speculation and enable the wider aviation community to learn from previous incidents. Second, he recommended comprehensive, independent safety and airworthiness audits covering the entire fleet, maintenance facilities and operational units. Such audits should examine not only aircraft condition but also spare-parts supply chains, maintenance engineers’ certification and compliance with technical manuals. Third, he called for greater investment in simulator-based and recurrent training for aircrew and maintenance personnel. Pilots should undertake mandatory training in emergency procedures, navigation in adverse weather and crew resource management to reduce the risk of human error. He also recommended a non-punitive, confidential safety-reporting system, or Just Culture, that would encourage pilots, engineers and ground crew to report near misses, minor technical faults and procedural violations without undue fear of disciplinary action. Identifying and correcting such problems early could prevent them from developing into serious accidents. Furthermore, Adamu advocated stronger alignment between military aviation safety practices and the standards of the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Although military aviation has distinct operational demands, he argued that greater civilian regulatory input into safety reviews could strengthen oversight and improve standards. He also called for accelerated fleet modernisation and comprehensive lifecycle planning. Government, he said, should develop a clear, adequately funded plan for the phased retirement of obsolete aircraft and their replacement with modern, reliable platforms. Continued reliance on ageing aircraft, he warned, could prove a false economy by increasing maintenance costs, downtime and the risk of further loss of life. Adamu emphasised that the NAF operates in a demanding security environment and that its personnel deserve the highest possible standards of safety and support. Addressing systemic vulnerabilities, he said, should not be interpreted as an indictment of the service’s bravery or competence, but as a necessary step towards operational excellence. Through transparency, rigorous auditing and modern safety-management systems, Nigeria could honour fallen aviators by improving the prospects of their colleagues returning safely from every mission. On his part, Head of the Department of Political Science at Benue State University, Makurdi, Professor Atah Pine, expressed concern over the persistent aviation mishaps involving military aircraft in Nigeria. He argued that whenever an aviation accident occurs, the relevant authorities should promptly institute an investigation to establish its cause. Given the number of mishaps recorded over the years, he questioned how many investigation findings had been made available to the public. Pine said the apparent lack of transparency made it difficult to draw empirically sound conclusions or develop evidence-based projections. He also highlighted the importance of flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, commonly referred to collectively as black boxes, in establishing an aircraft’s performance and the circumstances leading up to an accident. He questioned what these recorders had revealed about the incidents under scrutiny, observing that the public remained largely unable to access such information. Pine called on the NAF authorities to conduct, as a matter of urgency, a comprehensive technical and mechanical audit of their aircraft and implement the necessary corrective measures to prevent a recurrence of accidents that had claimed numerous lives and caused profound trauma, pain and sorrow. Also, former Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson, Ambassador Ogbole Amedu-Ode argued that the recurring aviation mishaps could be attributable to several factors, including inadequate funding, insufficient pilot training, poor maintenance practices and the procurement of used aircraft whose operational suitability might be compromised. He maintained that addressing these challenges required adequate budgetary allocations, continuous personnel training, rigorous maintenance regimes and a shift towards acquiring new, fit-for-purpose aircraft. Beyond immediate procurement requirements, Amedu-Ode called for a long-term national strategy to develop indigenous aerospace manufacturing capabilities. Nigeria, he noted, possesses relevant natural resources, including iron ore and aluminium, but requires sustained investment, technological advancement and the political will to translate these resources into industrial capacity. He suggested that Nigeria could draw lessons from countries such as China, India, Brazil and Singapore to gradually develop its capacity to manufacture, maintain and sustain military aircraft. Such an approach, he argued, could improve flight safety, protect human lives, preserve valuable military assets and reduce long-term dependence on foreign suppliers. Similarly, Chairman of the Guild of Public Affairs Analysts of Nigeria, Enugu State Chapter, Dr Ambrose Igboke, expressed concern over Nigeria’s numerous military aviation accidents, arguing that they raised serious questions about airspace management, operational safety and accountability. He said the apparent disparity between civilian and military aviation safety warranted closer scrutiny, particularly regarding the sophistication of military navigational equipment and the extent of information-sharing between the military, the NCAA and other relevant agencies. Igboke also emphasised the importance of training and capacity development, advocating stronger collaboration and personnel exchange programmes between the Ministry of Aviation and the military hierarchy. He welcomed the meeting between the Chief of the Air Staff and the Minister of Aviation as an initial step towards greater cooperation. Accountability, he added, remained essential. He questioned what previous military aviation accident investigations had revealed about the causes of the incidents, including possible human error, mechanical failure or negligence, and whether anyone found culpable had faced disciplinary action, dismissal, prosecution or other sanctions. He maintained that these questions required transparent, evidence-based answers if Nigeria was to strengthen aviation safety and prevent future tragedies. Military aviation mishaps are not peculiar to Nigeria but remain a persistent hazard worldwide. A review of available records from October 2016 to October 2026 indicates that air forces in countries like the United States, Brazil, Egypt and Morocco have also experienced aircraft accidents and losses involving different aircraft types and operational circumstances. The United States Air Force publishes mishap summaries and investigation reports, while Brazil maintains an established aviation accident investigation system through its Centre for Investigation and Prevention of Aeronautical Accidents (CENIPA). These examples demonstrate that aviation accidents remain a concern even among countries with extensive military aviation capabilities and formalised safety-investigation systems. Nigeria’s experience should therefore be examined within the realities and inherent risks of military flying rather than portrayed as an exclusively Nigerian phenomenon. Military aviation involves complex training exercises, demanding operational missions, low-level flying, adverse weather, mechanical challenges and operations in environments where the margin for error can be limited. Such conditions expose military aircrews and aircraft to risks that cannot be entirely eliminated, even with rigorous maintenance and operational procedures. Nevertheless, recognising the global hazards of military aviation should not diminish the need to investigate every mishap, establish its causes and implement measures to prevent recurrence. The crucial distinction lies between acknowledging that accidents occur across air forces worldwide and determining whether particular incidents could have been prevented. Nigeria’s experience should consequently be assessed through verified accident investigation reports, casualty records, aircraft serviceability data and evidence of the implementation of safety recommendations. International comparisons must also account for differences in fleet size, flying hours, mission profiles and public disclosure practices, as raw accident totals alone cannot establish which air force operates more safely. Ultimately, military aviation mishaps constitute a global operational risk requiring continuous vigilance, professional training, effective maintenance, rigorous investigation and institutional learning. The objective should not be to portray Nigeria as uniquely susceptible to aircraft accidents, but to examine its experience within an informed international context while ensuring that every aircraft loss and every life lost contributes to improved aviation safety, greater accountability and the prevention of avoidable tragedies.

title: Oyebanji’s Industrialisation Blueprint for Ekiti’s Economic Transformation
body: Governor Biodun Oyebanji of Ekiti State has unveiled his agenda to transform the State acclaimed as the ‘fountain of knowledge’ from a largely agrarian state to an industrial hub. Gbenga Sodeinde writes. For years, the development story of Nigerian states has largely been measured by the roads constructed, bridges completed and public infrastructure delivered. But as fiscal pressures mount and states are compelled to build more productive economies, the real test of leadership is increasingly shifting from infrastructure delivery to wealth creation. It is against this changing economic landscape that Governor Biodun Oyebanji is redefining the next phase of Ekiti’s development. Having spent his first term laying the physical foundation for growth through road expansion, electricity projects, agricultural interventions and improved connectivity, Oyebanji says his second term will focus on converting those investments into industries, stronger businesses and sustainable economic opportunities. In an interview, the governor unveiled an economic blueprint anchored on industrialisation, local processing of agricultural products, private-sector investment and support for small businesses, declaring that the state’s next major priority is to build an economy driven by productivity. “Our next major focus, therefore, is industrialisation and support for small businesses. That is the only way we can deepen our shared prosperity agenda,” Oyebanji said. The declaration marks a significant shift in the administration’s development strategy — from building the infrastructure required for growth to ensuring that those assets begin to generate jobs, expand enterprises and improve the livelihoods of Ekiti residents. At the heart of the blueprint is the conviction that infrastructure, however essential, cannot by itself deliver prosperity. Roads, electricity connections, farm access routes, water systems and an upgraded airport must ultimately serve as platforms for production, investment and enterprise. For Oyebanji, the next phase of governance will therefore be judged not merely by the scale of public works completed, but by the economic activity those projects unlock. During his first term, the administration constructed and rehabilitated roads, connected previously underserved communities to electricity, improved township and farm roads, and strengthened the foundations of agricultural production. By the end of the year, the governor said, the state would have completed close to 400 kilometres of roads. Those interventions, he argued, were necessary to create the conditions for a more productive economy. The second-term agenda is designed to build upon that foundation. Oyebanji wants agricultural commodities produced in Ekiti to be processed within the state rather than exported in raw form, thereby creating additional value, expanding local supply chains and generating employment. The objective is to move from production without sufficient value addition to an integrated economic system in which farmers, processors, manufacturers, transport operators and small businesses participate in a shared cycle of growth. “Our farmers must also be able to produce at scale and have reliable off-takers who can purchase their produce and supply it to companies that will add value through processing,” he said. That ambition is already reflected in the state’s emerging agro-industrial landscape. The Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone has attracted significant investment, with businesses committing billions of naira to agricultural production and processing. Companies such as Arog Agro-Allied and Agbeyewa Farms are part of this expanding ecosystem, while the latter’s large-scale cassava operation has been described as one of the biggest of its kind in the world. The administration is also seeking to improve access to these investment corridors. The award of the Ayetoro-Iyemero Ekiti road project is intended to open up the area, facilitate the movement of goods and strengthen the connection between agricultural production zones and markets. Ekiti’s selection by the African Development Bank as a Tier-2 state under the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone programme further reinforces the government’s strategy. Studies are being conducted on Itapaji Dam to assess the possibility of developing irrigation facilities, an intervention that could improve year-round farming, raise productivity and make the state more attractive to agro-processors. Yet, the governor recognises that industrialisation cannot be achieved through agriculture alone. It requires a broader investment ecosystem supported by efficient institutions, predictable regulations, accessible land, reasonable taxation and reliable infrastructure. To this end, the administration is reforming its investment promotion agency and establishing a one-stop shop for investors. The initiative is expected to simplify the process of obtaining approvals, accessing information and navigating government procedures. Land administration is also being reformed, while taxation is being streamlined to prevent excessive burdens on businesses and residents. “Capital will flow to any place where it is treated well,” Oyebanji said, stressing that the responsibility of government is to create the conditions in which private investment can thrive. The governor’s approach reflects a deliberate preference for enabling private enterprise rather than placing the state at the centre of industrial production. Government, he explained, is not necessarily expected to establish industries itself; its primary responsibility is to provide the infrastructure, security, policies and institutional support that encourage investors to commit capital and create jobs. That philosophy extends to the transportation sector, where the administration is attempting to balance the need for affordable mobility with the survival of existing operators. Rather than displacing members of transport unions and other associations, the government plans to introduce fair competition through a pilot mass transit scheme. If the pilot succeeds, more vehicles will be procured to expand the programme. But the governor believes that a lasting reduction in transport costs will require a transition away from petrol-dependent vehicles towards Compressed Natural Gas-powered buses, electric vehicles, tricycles and motorcycles. Such a transition, however, will require more than the procurement of vehicles. It will demand conversion centres, refuelling stations, charging points and a supporting energy infrastructure capable of sustaining the new transport system. The administration is therefore engaging private companies to develop the necessary facilities and roll out cleaner, more affordable mobility options across the state. The airport is another critical component of the economic blueprint. Oyebanji wants the facility to operate around the clock, rather than close at 6 p.m. or remain inaccessible to aircraft during adverse weather conditions. The installation of an Instrument Landing System is being assessed by a certification team, while contracts have been awarded for airport lighting infrastructure. Once completed, the interventions are expected to enable night operations and improve the airport’s reliability. The commissioning of a private-sector fuel depot will further strengthen its commercial potential by allowing aircraft to refuel in Ekiti, making the facility more attractive to airlines and improving the viability of scheduled operations. For the governor, these projects are not isolated infrastructure schemes. They are components of a wider economic strategy intended to connect Ekiti to regional markets, reduce logistical constraints and support the movement of people, goods and capital. The same productivity-centred philosophy informs the administration’s plans for small businesses. Oyebanji identified welders, tailors, hairdressers, barbers and other small-scale entrepreneurs as essential participants in the state’s economic transformation. These businesses, he said, must have access to affordable financing if they are to expand, employ more people and contribute meaningfully to shared prosperity. The challenge is to ensure that the benefits of industrialisation do not remain concentrated among large investors. A productive economy must also create opportunities for informal operators, women traders, artisans, farmers and young entrepreneurs. This is why the administration’s economic agenda is linked to its gender policy and its broader commitment to reducing discrimination and expanding women’s access to markets and enterprise opportunities. Oyebanji also acknowledged that development cannot be sustained without effective urban planning and environmental management. The recent flooding in Ado-Ekiti, he said, was largely man-made, worsened by indiscriminate refuse disposal and the construction of buildings on waterways. The government has directed the Ministry of Environment to conduct a comprehensive inventory of structures obstructing waterways, with illegally constructed buildings facing removal. The decision is politically sensitive, particularly where property owners claim to have obtained official approvals. But the governor insists that decisive action is necessary to prevent more severe flooding in the future. The administration intends to distinguish between buildings that received formal approval and those erected illegally, with compensation considered where applicable and unlawful structures removed. Water supply remains another major challenge. Although Ekiti has four functioning dams and has benefited from World Bank intervention, the governor said the difficulties extend beyond the dams and pumping equipment. Ageing asbestos pipes, high energy costs, inadequate reticulation and consumer resistance to paying for water have all weakened the distribution system. The administration has replaced pumps, procured generators and begun replacing obsolete pipes. It has also established water consumers’ committees to improve community participation and accountability. In the second term, the focus will be on rehabilitating the distribution network so that water pumped into reservoirs can reach households and businesses efficiently. Taken together, these initiatives reveal an administration attempting to move Ekiti from a phase of foundational construction into one of economic activation. The roads, airport, dams, agricultural zones and electricity projects are being repositioned as instruments of production rather than ends in themselves. The governor’s re-election, secured with 85.45 per cent of the votes cast, has given the administration a strong political mandate. But it has also raised expectations. The central question now is whether the infrastructure delivered during the first term can translate into factories, processing plants, stronger small businesses, lower transport costs, expanded agricultural value chains and more jobs. Oyebanji’s answer is that the state’s future depends on productivity. His second-term agenda is therefore not simply a continuation of the first, but an attempt to convert public investment into private enterprise, agricultural output into industrial value and infrastructure into broad-based prosperity. “We will do everything possible to ensure that our economy becomes more productive,” he said. For Ekiti, the success of that promise will be measured not only by what government builds, but by what the people are able to produce, process, sell and earn from the economic foundations now being laid.

title: Ododo Tasks Kogi’s New LG Chairmen on Rural Security, Accountability
body: Governor Ahmed Ododo of Kogi State has tasked the newly elected 21 Local Government Chairmen in the state on the need to prioritise rural security and ensure accountability. Kogi State Governor, Alhaji Ahmed Usman Ododo, has charged the newly sworn-in chairmen of the 21 Local Government Areas of the State to strengthen rural security, ensure accountability in the management of public funds and prioritise grassroots development. Ododo represented by state deputy governor, Comrade Joel Salifu, made this call recently during the swearing-in ceremony of the council chairmen at the Glass House, Government House, Lokoja. The Governor urged the council chairmen to work closely with security agencies, traditional rulers and community leaders to protect lives and property, stressing that no community in the state would be abandoned to criminal activities. He also called on them to prioritise rural roads, primary healthcare, basic education, environmental sanitation and programmes that create opportunities for youths and women. Congratulating the chairmen on their election, Ododo thanked the people of Kogi State for their support for the All Progressives Congress (APC), which won all chairmanship and councillorship seats across the local government areas and two hundred and thirty-nine wards. He described the victory as a call to greater service and urged the elected officials to justify the confidence reposed in them by delivering on their campaign promises. The Governor expressed confidence in the state’s continued support for President Bola Tinubu and APC candidates ahead of the 2027 general and state Assembly elections, while commending the President for his leadership and commitment to development through his Renewed Hope Agenda. Ododo further charged the chairmen to manage public funds transparently and responsibly, remain humble, accessible to the people and govern fairly without discrimination based on political differences. The Governor wished the chairmen success in their tenure, while assuring them of the state’s government support for more development at the grassroots. The swearing-in according to stakeholders is indeed the start of a new chapter in Local Government administration in the Confluence state, with a call on the chairmen to improve security, use public funds wisely and ensure government presence is felt at the grassroots.

title: Kano Promotes over 18,000 SUBEB Staff
body: No fewer than 18,984 teaching and non teaching staff of Kano State Universal Basic Education Board were promoted between January and July, 2026. Kano State Governor, Alhaji Abba Kabir Yusuf, has approved the implementation of promotions for 18,984 teaching and non-teaching staff of the State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB) for January and July 2026. The approval followed a request submitted by the Executive Chairman of SUBEB, Yusuf Kabir, seeking the release of ₦235,116,339.09 for the implementation of the promotions across the 44 Local Government Education Authorities (LGEAs). In the letter dated 2nd September 2026, SUBEB said the affected staff comprised eligible teaching and non-teaching personnel whose promotions for the January and July 2026 cycles had been processed, including the corresponding salary adjustment calculations. The Board said timely implementation of promotions was essential to staff motivation, career development, capacity strengthening and improved service delivery within the basic education sector. It noted that SUBEB, one of the largest public institutions in the state, has approximately 60,000 teaching and non-teaching personnel serving across the 44 LGEAs. According to the Board, the administration inherited outstanding promotion backlogs, including arrears spanning seven years and another backlog of one-and-a-half years. It said Governor Yusuf had previously approved and ensured the implementation of the outstanding promotions. SUBEB said the intervention had significantly boosted staff morale, restored confidence in the service and demonstrated the administration’s commitment to the welfare of public servants. The Board explained that it had completed all necessary arrangements and processes for the January and July 2026 promotions, including staff eligibility verification and salary adjustment computations. Governor Yusuf approved the request, which was ratified at recent State Executive Council paving the way for the release of the approved funds for the implementation of the promotions.

title: Thousands of unclaimed forces pensions now being paid
body: Tracing and claims activity has brought 11,201 previously unclaimed armed forces pensions into payment, with a total value of £29,446,443, according to an answer given in Parliament. Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what progress his department had made on expanding communications to better reach those with unclaimed and deferred armed forces pensions. Calvin Bailey, the Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has continued its approach to identifying and contacting individuals with unclaimed and deferred Armed Forces pensions. “As part of an ongoing contractual requirement, regular tracing activity is undertaken for deferred pension members whose pensions have become payable but remain unclaimed. New cases are reviewed each month and, where updated contact details are identified, individuals are contacted and invited to claim their pension entitlement. “These activities form part of the Department’s wider efforts to ensure members receive the pension benefits to which they are entitled. As a result of tracing and claims activity, 11,201 previously unclaimed Armed Forces pensions have been brought into payment, with a total value of £29,446,443. “The MOD also continues to support the development of the Pensions Dashboard programme, which is intended to make it easier for individuals to identify pension entitlements they may have across multiple pension schemes.” A service leaver with sufficient qualifying service earns a preserved pension that becomes payable at sixty or sixty-five, depending on the scheme. The figures give an average of around £2,630 for each pension brought into payment, and arrears are paid from the date the pension first became payable. The post Thousands of unclaimed forces pensions now being paid first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Hiplife, azonto, physical sales: Why the future may lie in the past
body: There was a time when Ghanaian music did not need to explain where it came from. You could hear it, see it and feel it. It had an accent. It had a swagger. It had a dance. It had a physical product you could hold in your hand. Most importantly, it had a story. Today, as Ghana searches for its next great musical export, perhaps the answer is not entirely ahead of us. Perhaps part of it is sitting in our history. Hiplife. Azonto. Physical music sales. These were not simply trends. They were pieces of a Ghanaian music ecosystem that demonstrated how sound, identity, culture and commerce could work together. Reintroducing the principles behind them could help position Ghanaian music for another serious run at the world. When Hiplife Changed the Conversation Hiplife was revolutionary because it answered a simple but important question: What happens when Ghanaian culture meets a global sound on Ghana’s own terms? Emerging in the 1990s, Hiplife fused hip-hop with highlife, local rhythms, Ghanaian languages and the everyday Ghanaian experience. Reggie Rockstone became one of its most important pioneers and popularisers, particularly following his 1997 album Makaa Maka and the hit “Choo Boi”. But Hiplife’s greatest achievement was bigger than creating another genre. It made it cool to be Ghanaian. Young people could rap in Twi, Ga, Ewe or Pidgin and still sound contemporary. They could borrow from American hip-hop without becoming American rappers. Ghanaian language became an asset rather than a barrier. That was the magic. Hiplife essentially told the world: we can take what you know and turn it into something that belongs to us. Its influence travelled beyond Ghana and helped shape subsequent generations of Ghanaian artists and sounds. Grammy’s retrospective on Ghanaian Hiplife describes the genre as having significantly influenced music from Ghana and across Africa. That is not just musical history. That is a blueprint. Then Azonto Happened If Hiplife established Ghana’s musical identity, Azonto turned that identity into a cultural phenomenon. Azonto was not merely a genre. It was a movement. Suddenly, Ghanaian music came with choreography. People could participate even if they did not understand every lyric. The dance mimicked everyday activities and became an instantly recognisable expression of Ghanaian life. By 2012, Azonto had spread across Africa, Europe and the United States, appearing in clubs, schools, fitness classes and popular culture. Academic research later described Azonto as an embodiment of Ghanaian identity in a mobile, digital world. That is precisely what makes Azonto worth revisiting. It demonstrated that the global music business is not only about songs. Songs can create movements. Movements create culture. Culture creates influence. Influence creates markets. Azonto gave Ghana something every ambitious music market needs: a recognisable cultural export. The lesson is not that Ghana should manufacture another Azonto and call it a day. That would be missing the point. The lesson is that Ghana must deliberately create, support and commercialise cultural phenomena that are unmistakably Ghanaian. The next global Ghanaian movement may not be a dance. It could be a sound, fashion movement, slang, visual language or lifestyle. But we should be looking for it. And Then There Were CDs Before streaming turned the phone into the record shop, music was something you bought. You walked into a shop. You asked for an album. You paid money. You walked out with a CD. Simple. But behind that simple transaction was an entire commercial ecosystem involving artists, producers, distributors, retailers, marketers and investors. Physical music sales gave music a tangible economic value. Albums were products. Music businesses could invest in recording, production, packaging, promotion and distribution because there was a visible route from creativity to cash. That commercial muscle matters.Streaming has opened remarkable global opportunities, but Ghana should not confuse digital availability with a complete music economy. There is room for physical music to return, not as a replacement for Spotify, Apple Music or Audiomack, but as another revenue stream. And the CD does not have to carry the entire burden. Give me a pendrive. A beautifully packaged USB album containing an artist’s music, videos, photographs, lyrics, behind-the-scenes material and exclusive content could become a viable Ghanaian music product. Add a signed photograph, T-shirt, collectible card or limited-edition packaging and suddenly the music becomes an experience. For Ghana’s diaspora market, tourists and serious music collectors, this could be particularly attractive. The global resurgence of interest in CDs also demonstrates that physical music has not completely disappeared. In 2026, CDs are increasingly being treated as collectible merchandise rather than simply a means of listening to music. The Opportunity Is Bigger Than Nostalgia The argument, therefore, is not bring back the past . It is bring back what worked . Bring back Hiplife’s confidence in Ghanaian identity. Bring back Azonto’s ability to turn music into culture. Bring back physical sales’ direct relationship between music and commerce. Then connect all three to today’s digital world. Imagine a Ghanaian artist launching a new sound with a signature dance, fashion collection, streaming campaign, international collaborations, touring strategy and limited-edition physical release. That is no longer simply releasing a song. That is building an intellectual property ecosystem . Ghana does not need to choose between tradition and technology. We need to make tradition technologically relevant and make technology commercially useful to Ghanaian creativity. Hiplife showed us how to create identity. Azontoshowed us how to export culture. Physical music sales showed us how to turn music into a product. Perhaps the next chapter of Ghanaian music’s global story begins by putting those three lessons back on the table. Because the world does not need another country trying to sound global. The world needs Ghana sounding unmistakably Ghanaian, and building a business around it.

title: Russian forces attack Rivne region overnight, leaving parts of region without power
body:
According to Ukrinform, Rivne Region Governor Oleksandr Koval said this in a Facebook post .
According to him, a small settlement in the northern part of the region came under seven consecutive Russian attacks.
Parts of the Rivne region are currently without electricity.
