title: Russian forces attack energy infrastructure and homes in Zhytomyr region overnight
body:
Vitalii Bunechko, Head of the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration, reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
He said six private households were damaged.
No casualties or injuries have been reported.
As of 7:00, more than 900 settlements remained without electricity.
Critical infrastructure facilities in the region are using backup power sources. Points of Invincibility have been set up.
Energy workers are working around the clock to restore electricity to consumers. Their efforts are being hampered by the constant threat of further attacks.
“All services continue to work in an enhanced mode to deal with the aftermath of the enemy attacks and assist those in need,” the head of the Regional Military Administration noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces launched a massive attack on one of DTEK’s thermal power plants, forcing it to halt electricity generation.

title: Poland Probes Plot to Torch Drone Factory Supplying Ukraine
body:
Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into a suspected plot to set fire to a factory producing military drones for Ukraine, after a Russia-linked recruiter offered to pay $30,000 for an arson attack.
The suspected sabotage attempt targeted a Flytronic facility in Gliwice , southern Poland, owned by WB Group, the country’s largest privately owned defense manufacturer.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Prosecutors in Gliwice said on Thursday that an investigation had been launched into an attempt to recruit someone to carry out sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.
The case has been handed to Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW), the country’s main domestic intelligence service.
The plot was exposed earlier this month by Vot Tak , TVP World’s sister channel, after one of its journalists posed as a Belarusian looking for work and made contact with a recruiter on the Telegram platform.
The recruiter, using the pseudonym Joker, initially offered money to set fire to cars with Ukrainian license plates before proposing a much larger attack on the drone factory.
Vot Tak traced the recruiter’s Telegram account to a Russian telephone number registered in the Saratov region in southwest Russia.
Flytronic manufactures FlyEye reconnaissance drones used by Ukrainian forces to direct artillery strikes, while its parent company also produces Warmate attack drones, which are designed to crash into targets and explode.
The alleged plot comes after a fire at another WB Group facility in Skarżysko-Kamienna, south-central Poland, in late August.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk described that incident as “ an act of sabotage ,” while prosecutors launched an investigation into whether the blaze had been deliberately started on behalf of a foreign intelligence agency.
Poland, a key military supporter of Kyiv, has repeatedly warned of Russian sabotage operations on its territory since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: Calling US-Israeli aggression ‘Iran conflict’ moral evasion
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 23 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has criticized the use of the term “Iran conflict” for the US and Israeli aggression as an attempt to evade moral responsibility by obsecuring truth.
In a post on X pub;ished on Thursday night, the spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Esmaeil Baghaei, said that the refusal to call aggression by its name is not neutrality but moral evasion.
“If we lack even the courage to identify the aggressor and name the aggression, how can we claim to have the moral courage to confront injustice, propose workable solutions, or contribute meaningfully to peace?” he said.
“Peace cannot be built by appeasing aggressors, legitimizing aggression, condemning the victim, or sacrificing fundamental principles,” the spokesperson added.

title: Gasps as Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
body: The Prince of Wales made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show as part of a special edition marking the Earthshot Prize. During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, all of whom are involved with the prize. As Norton spoke with the trio about the initiative, he surprised the audience by inviting the prince to join them on the sofa. They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. William founded the prize to “celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet”. The guests also chatted about William’s long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films. William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, inspired by US President John F Kennedy’s Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to send astronauts to the Moon and back safely. The prize has five Earthshots, or goals, for which it awards prizes: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m. The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year’s winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November. Last year, the prize ceremony drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro. The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for “transforming one of the world’s most wasteful industries” by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability. At last year’s ceremony, William said the winners were “proof that progress is possible”.

title: Drones Hit Occupied Luhansk, Disrupting Communications as Russia Strikes Ukrainian Power Plant
body:
Drones hit Russian-occupied Luhansk in eastern Ukraine early Friday, Oct. 23, disrupting communications in parts of the city, while Russian forces struck a Ukrainian thermal power plant, forcing it to halt electricity generation.
According to the monitoring channel Exilenova+ , explosions were heard in Luhansk at around 4 a.m. The blasts were followed by disruptions to communications and electricity supplies.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Footage circulating online appears to show an impact on infrastructure near a communications tower. Communications were subsequently lost completely in parts of the occupied city.
Later, Exilenova+ clafiried that the Marshal plant in Russian-occupied Luhansk had been attacked overnight.
The large machine-building enterprise specializes in producing industrial shut-off valves for the oil, gas, chemical, and energy sectors.
In 2024, the plant increased its product sales by more than 20%. It also received new equipment as part of a modernization program supported by the Russian-installed occupation authorities.
Luhansk has been under Russian occupation since 2014, and the Russian-installed administration has not yet reported the consequences of the attack.
The attack follows a series of recent strikes on telecommunications infrastructure in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. On the night of Oct. 21, drones targeted a building belonging to telecommunications operator Lugakom and a telecommunications service center in Luhansk.
On Oct. 20, a data center belonging to Ugletelekom in Russian-occupied Donetsk was also targeted.
Meanwhile, Russian forces attacked one of the thermal power plants operated by Ukrainian energy operator DTEK on Friday, forcing it to stop generating electricity, the company reported . The strike caused significant damage to the plant’s equipment.
Russian forces have repeatedly targeted DTEK’s thermal power plants since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. The company said its facilities have come under attack more than 230 times.
Explosions were also reported overnight in western Ukraine’s Lutsk and the Rivne region, which faced sustained attacks.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force , Russia had launched 176 attack drones since 6 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 22. The drones included Shahed-type unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), 92 of which were jet-powered, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones.
The Ukrainian military responded using aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
As of 8 a.m. Friday, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 140 Russian drones, including 68 jet-powered Shahed-type UAVs, as well as Gerbera and other drone types.
“Ten strike drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing!” the Air Force said in a report published at 8:04 a.m.
Russian drones were reported to have struck 19 locations, while debris from intercepted UAVs fell at 13 other locations.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Kpandai: One reportedly killed in Kumdi farmland dispute
body: One person has reportedly been killed following a clash between two communities over a farmland dispute at Kumdi in the Kpandai District of the Northern Region. The confrontation occurred on Thursday, October 22, with reports indicating that gunfire was exchanged during the dispute. The disagreement is said to have centred on farmland used for farming, with the matter reportedly having been taken to court before the latest incident. A resident who spoke to Citi FM said the land dispute had been the subject of legal proceedings. “It is because of land for farming. The issue was even sent to court,” the resident said. Security personnel have since been deployed to the area to restore calm and prevent further violence. The circumstances surrounding the reported killing, as well as the identities of the deceased and those involved in the clash, remain unclear.

title: Water shortage: GWCL targets 3-4 days’ supply as residents demand answers
body: Ghana Water Company Limited (GWCL) is targeting three to four days of water supply per week in affected communities in parts of Greater Accra, after weeks of unreliable flow forced some households to buy water from alternative sources. The company is re-engineering its distribution system and working to restore the Teshie Desalination Plant to ease the shortages, while longer-term plans include expanding treatment capacity. During a tour of affected communities in the Tema East region, residents welcomed recent improvements but called for sustained supply and better communication about interruptions. At Community 22 Junction, resident Alhaji Ali Ayornu reported a significant improvement in water pressure over the past few days, after periods of low-pressure nighttime flow. “Water is our source of life. We are urging GWCL to sustain their efforts,” he said. Alhaji Ali Ayornu, Resident, Community 22 Junction In Ashaiman’s Moni Obaanye, residents also endured difficulties over the past three weeks, although water has begun flowing again in recent days. According to Juliana Tetteh, after contacting Ghana Water Company Limited, they learnt water was being rationed amid distribution challenges. “The past few weeks have been difficult for residents, some of whom have had to carry gallons in search of communities with running water or pay for supplies from water tankers,” she recounted. At Bethlehem, resident Stephen Kweku Kemevor also recounted nearly three weeks without water, forcing residents to buy supplies elsewhere. He was also frustrated by the lack of information about the interruption. “You can’t just shut off the water like that without any information. You have to update us so we can prepare. We pay our taxes and water bills, so you guys have to keep us informed. Your customer relations need improvement. It’s very, very bad,” he criticised. Stephen Kemevor, Resident, Bethlehem GWCL’s Head of Public Relations and Communications, Stanley Martey, attributed the challenges partly to the shutdown of the Teshie Desalination Plant, which serves eastern Accra, including Teshie-Nungua and Spintex. Last year’s shutdown forced the company to redirect water from the Kpong Treatment Plant to affected communities, even though Kpong was already struggling to meet demand in its existing service areas. Mr Martey said engineers spent the past two weeks reconfiguring the distribution system after discovering that some communities were not receiving water despite the network having supplies. However, he cautioned that the interventions would not immediately restore round-the-clock supply. “We are not promising that we are going to get water flow 24/7, but at least between three and four days in a week most of the areas are going to get it,” he said, adding that elevated communities could continue to face difficulties. GWCL plans to divide the affected areas into three zones and publish a water rationing timetable within one to two weeks to help residents know when to expect supply and store water accordingly. On restoring the desalination plant as a key priority, he said President John Mahama had directed that efforts be accelerated, with GWCL negotiating with the plant’s private owners under a build, own, operate and transfer arrangement. According to him, restoring the facility could resolve between 80 and 90 % of the problem. Longer-term plans include a proposed treatment plant at Aveyime in the Volta region to serve the corridor towards Tema’s industrial area, alongside the Kpong Phase Two project, which is expected to add between 40 million and 60 million gallons of water to the system.

title: UAE tackles oil spill, Yemen warns of Houthi child recruitment and Oman strengthens UK investment ties
body: In today’s episode of Trending Middle East , UAE authorities work to contain an oil spill from a supertanker in the Arabian Gulf after reports of a strong fuel smell. Beaches in Umm Al Quwain have been closed temporarily as clean-up operations continue. Yemen’s internationally recognised government warns citizens against attending Houthi-organised gatherings, accusing the group of recruiting children and young people as fighters. Oman and the UK pledge to strengthen trade and investment ties during Sultan Haitham’s historic state visit, with agreements involving more than £1 billion ($1.3 billion) in investment. Meanwhile, the UAE announces plans to invest a further €15 billion ($16.8 billion) in Greece during an official visit by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. And a UAE-led international crackdown on digital fraud results in more than 960 arrests and uncovers $39 billion in illicit funds and assets. The three-month operation, involving law enforcement agencies from 30 countries, has also thwarted more than 123 million online fraud attempts. Trending Middle East is AI-assisted, using original reporting published in The National and curated and edited by humans.

title: Ghalibaf reiterates warning to US about heavy costs of war
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 23 (MNA) – Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has warned US policymakers and the American public that a war with Iran would carry heavy economic and military costs for the United States.
In a post on his account on X, Ghalibaf shared an image inspired by American popular culture, stressing that the belief that a war with Iran would benefit the United States was mistaken. He said such a decision would bring at least 10 negative consequences for the country.
Among the potential consequences, he cited a stock market crash, downed fighter jets, rising government debt, higher inflation and an increase in the number of US military personnel killed.
Ghalibaf also said that choosing the path of war was not inevitable, but warned that if the United States made that choice, it would have to bear all the consequences.
He concluded his message by urging Americans to “break this artificial Matrix” and walk away from what he described as a bitter and fruitless course of action.

title: Analysis: Ukraine, Russia set stage for climax of Battle of Donbas
body:
Ukrainian soldiers "Mahura" and "Hrek" of the 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade return to their battalion command post after visiting forward infantry positions near the Russian border in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 28, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images)
This autumn, as Russia escalated its total-war-style strike campaign against Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and economy, and relations between Kyiv and Washington hit an all-time low , the daily battles along Ukraine’s vast battlefield have faded into the background of the information space.
Despite the reduced attention in international media — often spawning misleading perceptions that both sides are bogged down in some kind of stalemate — the attritional fighting in Ukraine’s east remains as intense and brutal as ever, with both sides looking to establish a clear upper hand going into winter.
In simple terms of territory taken and lost, 2026 has been a year of relative success for Kyiv on the front line.
Net Russian territorial gains have largely flatlined despite consistently heavy casualties, while Ukrainian forces also managed to conduct two successful counterattacking operations, each carrying strategic importance.
Though other parts of the front line have largely stabilized, Russia’s main goal continues to be the capture of the remainder of Donetsk Oblast.
Slowly but surely, Russian forces inched closer to the gates of the last remaining Ukrainian cities in the region, largely driving out what was left of any normal civilian life in the area.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s defending forces, reorganized under a new command structure, have looked to create the conditions to grind down and stop whatever offensive power Russia can muster in its tracks.
With the Trump administration tightening the screws on Kyiv, while Moscow refuses to budge on its demand that Ukraine hand over the rest of Donetsk Oblast as a bare minimum for ceasefire discussions, the strategic and political weight of this slowly shrinking and increasingly ruined patch of land is as great as ever.
Since the full-scale invasion, the backbone of Ukraine’s defense of Donetsk Oblast has been the so-called fortress belt, made up of four industrial cities running north to south: Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka.
For about a year, all of these cities have been within range of Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones.
But over 2026, incremental advances on the ground, combined with improved technology extending the range of these drones, have made Ukrainian logistics anywhere in the area noticeably more difficult while also driving many of the remaining civilians out from their homes.
Since the Ukrainian army’s corps reform last year, the direct approach to the fortress belt has been defended by two army corps: the 11th and 19th.
Over May and June, while Ukraine was riding the high of successive positive developments in the war, Russian forces entered and overran much of Kostiantynivka , following a model of mass infiltration backed by heavy support from drones, artillery, and glide bombs that was used to take Pokrovsk last year.
Simultaneously to their frontal attacks, Russian forces have attempted to achieve a double envelopment of the fortress belt, with two large pincers pushing north and south of the fortress belt, respectively.
The northern pincer, bearing down on the liberated city of Lyman, was famously the site of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi: a slow but ingenious series of counterattacks conducted by the country’s 3rd Army Corps under commander Andrii Biletskyi.
On the southern flank, Russia has concentrated immense offensive pressure for over a year on the mining city of Dobropillia.
After a mass infiltration of Russian soldiers in August 2025 pushed up to 20 kilometers deep behind Ukrainian lines, Kyiv redeployed the 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard, commanded by Denys Prokopenko, leader of the Mariupol garrison, to the area, where it stands to this day.
After years of brutal fighting across the front line, the defense of any area is often only as good as its weakest point.
With Russian forces learning to aggressively target potential weak links in Ukraine’s overstretched defense, raising the base level of Ukraine’s brigades has been just as important as the placement of more elite units.
While the 1st and 3rd Corps were able to gather their units in a coherent sector and lead the fight as a truly unified formation, other corps like the 11th and 19th, commanding a mixed bag of exhausted and inexperienced brigades without extra resources and assigned units, struggled.
To rectify this, in August, under new Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, Kyiv decided to divide the defense of Donbas between two newly formed task forces, built up by Biletskyi and Prokopenko from the staff of their respective corps.
Task Force Azov would expand west, covering the frontage recently vacated by the 7th Air Assault Corps, while Biletskyi took the 11th and 19th Corps — and with them most of the fortress belt — under his wing with a new Task Force Center.
The most strategically important part of the front line was now being led directly by the military’s two most high-profile field commanders.
Operation Vivaldi was already well underway when Andrii Biletskyi was given command of the defense of the fortress belt.
His 3rd Corps was probably the best example of success in Ukraine’s corps reform , bringing up other mechanized brigades to elite standards of training and command, despite a dire manpower shortage.
Now, the general has been given the challenge of doing something similar with the brigades of the 11th and 19th Corps, some of which have been fighting high-intensity battles in their sector for years without rotation.
Over autumn, Russia’s attempts to push and probe through the hilly terrain immediately east of the fortress belt have gotten bogged down, while even Kostiantynivka — which looked likely to fall by the end of summer — is still hanging on.
The brigades fighting in this area have their work cut out for them, facing daily Russian infiltrations, a kill zone that only gets deeper and deadlier with time, and very thin, if not empty, infantry ranks.
But none of these are new problems, and over time, even with limited resources, the brigades have adapted.
All logistics to infantry positions in this area are handled by heavy bomber drones, while the revolution in unmanned ground vehicles has been key to keeping Ukrainian drone teams supplied.
Inside Kostiantynivka, the difficulty that Ukraine has had over the past year defending cities against Russian infiltrators has been turned on its head, thanks to the dogged heroism of Ukrainian infantrymen still in the city.
By now, control of one neighbourhood or another is almost impossible to accurately portray, as the positions of Ukrainian and Russian soldiers in the residential and industrial areas of Kostiantynivka heavily overlap.
While Russian forces try to push onwards towards Druzhkivka, Ukrainian troops remain entrenched in the city center of Kostiantynivka, and even on the eastern outskirts, occasionally moving around and rotating, and making it difficult for Russia to deploy its drone teams in the city.
Many of these men have been inside the city for the better part of this year and have little prospect of being evacuated if wounded.
But nonetheless, they hold on, buying Ukraine precious time to prepare the defense of the next fortress.
It is on the southwestern flank of the fortress belt, around the city of Dobropillia, where Russia’s most intense offensive continues.
Unlike the north of Donetsk Oblast, where the Siverskyi Donets River provides a natural defensive barrier, advancing in the Dobropillia area would give Russian forces a direct back door into the fortress belt.
According to Prokopenko , Russia enjoys a six to one personnel advantage in the Dobropillia area, and has deployed a third of its elite Rubicon drone unit — around 400 teams — in the narrow sector.
For the past year, the mining city of Dobropillia has provided shelter for much of the 1st Corps’ work, including many of the drone teams stopping Russian forces approaching the outskirts of the city.
But this convenience has also made Dobropillia a particular target for Russian glide bombs , launched in groups of three or four indiscriminately, but with a real chance of burying a Ukrainian drone team with every direct hit on a building.
On the ground, although a spectacular and well-coordinated attempt at a mechanized assault in summer failed, Russian forces, through sheer strength of numbers, have been slowly saturating the area around Dobropillia with small infiltration groups.
This process gained pace over autumn, and in the last few months, more videos have emerged of Russian soldiers raising flags in the city, though they are often quickly eliminated and do not indicate any certainty of territorial control.
But that nuance clearly hasn’t reached Moscow, as the Russian defense ministry claimed in October that the city had already been captured completely, a statement quickly denied by Kyiv.
A video released on October 21 by the Azov Corps argues that Russia’s increasingly outlandish claims about capturing Dobropillia are a direct result of the same culture of lies in the Russian high command chain — much the same as what helped facilitate the success of Operation Vivaldi for the Third Corps.
As well as Ukraine can organize its defense of Donbas, much in the coming half-year will depend on Russian plans and resources.
The coming weeks and autumn weather are likely to provide the last favorable conditions for Russian infiltration for the rest of the year.
If, under cover of fog and rain they can entrench themselves in and around Dobropillia before winter, Ukraine will have a lot more trouble smoking them out.
Another challenge is the looming prospect of Russian forced mobilization , which some Ukrainian commanders have argued has already started, just without a public announcement.
With a new flow of hundreds of thousands of bodies to augment those already voluntarily signing contracts, Russia could have more options, whether that means further increasing the intensity of its offensive in Donbas or attacking somewhere else and creating major strategic dilemmas for the Ukrainian defense.
Crucial could also prove to be the future of Ukraine’s ability to use Starlink , something now in the hands of Elon Musk and Donald Trump, two men who have shown consistent contempt for Ukraine’s fight for survival.
Both the 1st and 3rd Corps have made extensive use of middle-strike capabilities in offensive and defensive operations over the last year, not to mention the work of top brigades of the Unmanned Systems Forces in the area.
If Starlink is further restricted in one way or another, Ukraine’s forces and their drone-based defense could be severely hampered in their ability to spot and destroy advancing Russian troops in good time.
With that, Ukraine’s strongest card, a solid defense along the front line and a strong military uninterested in capitulation, could itself be further undermined by those who believe Ukraine has no cards.
Hi, this is Francis Farrell, the author of this piece. We are entering a new phase of the war, where once again the daily, brutal fight on the front line to hold Russia back is drowned out by geopolitical noise. Despite the difficult winter ahead of us and the effect that will have on the work of our newsroom, we will continue to report from the field wherever necessary. If you want to help us do that, please consider supporting our journalism by becoming a member.
Francis Farrell is a senior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is the co-author of War Notes, the Kyiv Independent's weekly newsletter about the war. For the second year in a row, the Kyiv Independent received a grant from the Charles Douglas-Home Memorial Trust to support his front-line reporting for the year 2025-2026. Francis won the Prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandy for war correspondents in the young reporter category in 2023, and was nominated for the European Press Prize in 2024. Francis speaks Ukrainian and Hungarian and is an alumnus of Leiden University in The Hague and University College London. He has previously worked as a managing editor at the online media project Lossi 36, as a freelance journalist and documentary photographer, and at the OSCE and Council of Europe field missions in Albania and Ukraine.

title: Ukraine’s air defenses down 140 out of 176 Russian drones overnight
body:
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
According to the military, starting at 18:00 on Thursday, October 22, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 176 Shahed-type strike drones (92 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The launches were carried out from Bryansk, Shatalovo, Oryol, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea.
The enemy attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
As of 8:00 on Friday, October 23, air defenses had reportedly shot down or jammed 140 Russian Shahed-type drones (68 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and UAVs of other types.
Hits by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 19 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at another 13 locations.
Ten Russian strike drones remain airborne, and combat operations are ongoing.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces launched a massive attack on one of DTEK’s thermal power plants, forcing it to halt electricity generation.

title: Booking.com Faces EU Investigation Over Fake Hotels and Payment Scams
body: European regulators are investigating whether the travel booking giant is doing enough to protect customers from fraudulent accommodation listings, phishing scams and misleading search rankings. The European Commission has launched a formal investigation into Booking.com over concerns that travellers could be exposed to fraudulent accommodation listings, fake payment requests and scams involving their personal booking information. Announced on 21 October, the investigation will examine whether the world’s leading online accommodation booking platform has failed to meet its obligations under the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires major online platforms to identify and address risks to consumers. At the centre of the investigation is a growing concern about how criminals exploit the trust travellers place in established booking platforms. Fraudulent listings can advertise properties that do not exist, while phishing scams can use genuine reservation details to convince customers that an additional payment is required to secure their accommodation. The latter is particularly concerning because fraudulent requests can appear to come from legitimate accommodation providers. Messages may reference actual booking dates, property names and reservation information, making them considerably harder to distinguish from genuine correspondence. European regulators are examining how Booking.com shares guest information with accommodation providers and whether sufficient safeguards exist within its messaging system to prevent criminals from exploiting those details. “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed,” said Henna Virkkunen, European Commission Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy. “The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.” The investigation follows a separate security incident earlier this year. In April, Booking.com notified some customers that unauthorised third parties may have accessed personal information associated with their reservations, including names, contact details and booking information. The company said it had taken steps to contain the incident, changed affected reservation PINs and informed customers. It also maintained that financial information had not been accessed. The incident attracted attention in Australia, where travellers were warned to be vigilant about suspicious messages requesting payment details. Beyond fraudulent accommodation and phishing, the European Commission is also questioning how Booking.com determines which properties appear most prominently in its search results. Accommodation providers can increase their visibility by paying higher commissions to the platform. European regulators want to establish whether these promoted listings are sufficiently identified as advertisements, allowing travellers to distinguish between properties appearing because of their relevance and those receiving preferential placement through commercial arrangements. The distinction matters in a market where Booking.com holds considerable influence over how travellers discover and select accommodation. According to the European Hotel Distribution Study 2026, published by hospitality industry association HOTREC, Booking.com accounted for 66.1 per cent of European online travel agency bookings in 2025. Its parent company, Booking Holdings, and rival Expedia Group together controlled 85.4 per cent of that market. The figures illustrate the extent to which European hotels and travellers rely on a relatively small number of booking platforms, placing questions of transparency, security and consumer protection under greater scrutiny. The Commission’s investigation follows an earlier assessment of Booking.com’s risk reports covering 2023 to 2026, alongside formal requests for information issued in September 2025 and May 2026. Under the Digital Services Act, major platforms found to have breached their obligations can face fines of up to six per cent of their worldwide annual turnover. Booking.com has said it is cooperating fully with the investigation. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. The company also reaffirmed its commitment to working with regulators, law enforcement agencies and industry partners to combat online fraud and protect travellers. For customers, the investigation highlights the importance of verifying unexpected payment requests, even when they appear to relate to an existing reservation. Booking.com advises travellers to be suspicious of requests for bank transfers or payments outside its official platform and to verify unusual messages independently. The European Commission will continue gathering evidence and could require changes to the platform’s practices or impose penalties if violations are established. No findings of wrongdoing have been made, and the opening of formal proceedings does not determine the outcome. For millions of travellers who routinely book accommodation online, the investigation raises a fundamental question about how effectively booking platforms protect the people who depend on them. title: You.com Launches Inference Router: 12 Open-Weight Models With 99.9% Uptime SLA
body:
You.com has launched Inference Router , a managed API for running open-weight models in production. The You.com Inference Router is an OpenAI-compatible service that routes requests across 12 live models. It bundles a 99.9% minimum uptime SLA and zero data retention (ZDR). It adds 100% US hosting and server-side web search. It is pay-as-you-go, with no platform fee. TL;DR Size: 12 live models, from GPT-OSS 120B (125K context) to Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 Max (1M context). Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter model; Qwen3.8 Max is a 2.4T MoE. Runs on: Fully managed. Requests hit You.com Inference Direct first, then fail over to US-hosted partners. No GPUs to manage. Performance: On You.com’s LiveNewsBench run, open-weight models plus You.com search matched frontier models at lower cost. Best: GLM-5.3 with You.com search scored 86.53%, at $0.0485 per question versus $0.0920 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (self-reported). Worst: Per-token prices sit near market. Kimi K3 is $2.85/$14.25, only 5% below Together AI’s $3.00/$15.00. What is You.com Inference Router? It is one API for many open-weight models. The endpoint is https://api.you.com , with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible routes . Existing SDK code moves over by changing the base URL and key. You.com team frames the problem around stalled migrations. Dev teams test open-weight models on aggregators, then hit security review. Reviewers ask about ZDR, US hosting, access controls and DPAs. Dedicated providers clear those bars, but usually with a large commitment. Inference Router targets that gap. How does the routing and failover work? Every request goes first to You.com Inference Direct , the company’s own inference capacity. If it is down or full, the request fails over to a vetted partner. The official post names Parasail, Wafer, Alibaba Cloud, Meta and Inception, with Prime Intellect coming soon. All are 100% US-hosted and must meet ZDR rules. Failover does not change the bill. Each model has 1 published per-token price. You.com also offers spend caps per API key and daily usage views by model, cost and provider. Accounts run on SOC 2 compliant infrastructure, with a DPA on request. What does zero data retention cover? The ZDR policy states that prompts and outputs are processed in memory and not stored. It covers both model calls and web search requests. You.com keeps only operational metadata, such as token counts, timestamps and account IDs. Prompt hashes, de-identified text and disk-backed prompt caches are explicitly excluded. Which models are available, and what do they cost? The models page lists 12 live models, all US-hosted. Prices are per 1M tokens (input / output): Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI): $2.85 / $14.25, 1M context Qwen3.8 Max (Alibaba): $1.85 / $5.55, 1M context GLM 5.3 (Z.ai): $1.35 / $4.25, 1M context DeepSeek V4 Pro : $1.65 / $3.65, 1M context DeepSeek V4.1 Flash : $0.30 / $1.20, 1M context Mercury 3 (Inception): $0.10 / $0.35, 1M context GPT-OSS 120B (OpenAI): $0.097 / $0.73, 125K context Muse Wonder, Muse Spark 1.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash and MiniMax M3 round out the list. How does built-in web search work? Developers declare a web_search or web_extract tool, and the router runs searches for the model. The docs show up to 20 results per search and a default of 30 search rounds. Responses return a web_results object with citations. Search runs on the same server as the model. You.com says internal tests show up to 15% lower latency. Send request

title: Binance's Qafila 2026 campaign rewards Gen Z users driving digital finance adoption across the region
body: Binance has unveiled a generous regional initiative designed to rally eligible users to celebrate shared financial journeys and explore a broader range of digital financial tools. Qafila 2026 launched with US$1 million in USDC rewards, bringing together eligible users across the Middle East, North Africa (MENA) and Pakistan. New data from Binance - the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume and number of registered users - reveals that 50 per cent of users across that geography are aged 18-29. Binance says Qafila reflects its “commitment to evolving alongside its community” as user needs extend across trading, earning, payments, learning and access to global financial markets. The Qafila initiative arrives against a backdrop of growing digital financial participation in the region, supported by new Binance user data that highlights the rising influence of Gen Z and broader adoption of digital financial services across MENA and Pakistan. The 18-29 age group, representing the adult Gen Z demographic, accounts for 50 per cent of the Binance user base across MENA and Pakistan, rising to 54% in Pakistan. This underscores the importance of younger generations in shaping the region’s evolving digital financial landscape, explains Tarik Erk, head of MENAT and senior executive officer at Binance. “MENA and Pakistan are priority markets for Binance, where growing digital adoption is changing what users expect from financial services,” he tells The National. “Our focus is to evolve alongside our community, bringing greater choice, practical utility and education into one ecosystem through our vision of All Finance on Binance . Erk adds: “Qafila celebrates that community and the different ambitions driving its financial journey.” Named after the concept of a caravan, the word draws on an idea familiar across Arabic- and Urdu-speaking communities - that of people moving forward together while pursuing their own ambitions. The Qafila initiative brings that shared purpose into a regional experience, connecting users across markets through participation, discovery and rewards. Strong numbers tell a story Beyond demographic trends, Binance’s regional data also points to growing engagement across its ecosystem. It reported more than half - 52.9 per cent - of verified users across MENA and Pakistan had engaged with two or more Binance products. The UAE recorded the highest adoption rate at 69.3 per cent, followed by Bahrain (57.2 per cent), and Pakistan (52.6 per cent). The Binance ecosystem now spans services and experiences from trading and earning, to payments, Binance Square and Binance Academy, reflecting its expanding role beyond trading as it brings together financial tools, education and community engagement in one platform. The exchange says these trends reflect broader developments in digital financial participation across MENA. Previous research by Binance cited it as the fastest-growing region for stablecoin savings on Binance Earn; the area’s share of global stablecoin balances held through the platform increased from 5.53 per cent to 9.21 per cent. The region’s share of global stablecoin trading volume on Binance also rose from 7 per cent in 2023 to 11 per cent this year. This made it the fastest-growing region by trading-volume share over that period. Within MENA, the UAE was shown to account for the largest stablecoin holdings, highlighting the region’s growing adoption of digital assets for trading, holding value, and earning rewards on eligible assets. Services adoption growth These regional developments sit within a wider shift in financial participation across emerging markets. Binance’s global platform data shows that 77 per cent of its users are based in these growth economies, a substantial increase from 49 per cent in 2020. Global Binance Research findings further highlight the prevalence of a new generation of financial users. Gen Z accounts for 44 per cent of Binance Direct Stocks and bStocks users. Meanwhile, its share of new TradFi users rose from 41 per cent in January to 47 per cent in July 2026. Essentially, the global findings highlight the wider participation of younger users in traditional financial markets through digital platforms which, in turn, reinforces the importance of access, choice and financial education, says Binance. It also notes these evolving user needs reflect its All Finance on Binance vision, which brings digital assets, traditional financial markets and everyday financial tools together in one ecosystem. Rewarding younger users Qafila elevates this outlook for eligible communities across the region through shared participation and access to locally available products and services. Admissible participants can participate in activities across the Binance platform, including trading, Simple Earn and community referral activities, subject to applicable market rules. Qafila offers a total reward pool of US$1 million in USDC to support the experience, with tasks, eligibility and rewards varying by market and user. Binance says this regional initiative translates into a “shared journey” shaped by different ambitions, practical needs, and ways of participating in digital finance. This page was produced by The National in partnership with Binance

title: Finland getting wet but mild weekend weather
body:
A precipitation front is expected to approach from the southwest on Friday evening, bringing the first showers to southern and western parts of the country.
Weather conditions in Finland are set to become more unsettled over the weekend, as a low pressure system brings precipitation to some areas, according to Yle meteorologist Henriikka Heikinoja .
Conditions will remain largely dry during the day on Friday, though isolated rain showers are possible in areas of southern and central Finland. Western Lapland will see foggy conditions with possible drizzle. Cloud cover will be more extensive in the south and west, while eastern areas and parts of Lapland will also see some sun. Temperatures will range from just over 10 degrees in the south to just under 5 degrees in Lapland.
A precipitation front is expected to approach from the southwest on Friday evening, bringing the first showers to southern and western parts of the country.
The wet weather will head northward overnight, and showers will reach Lapland by the afternoon. Central Finland and some southern areas will see light showers and drizzle, but there will be occasional spells in the south. Temperatures on Saturday will be cclose to those seen on Friday — relatively milder than usual.
Winds will pick up in southwestern areas on Sunday. At the same time most of the country will see extensive overcast conditions, with drizzle and light showers possible in many areas. Conditions are likely to be drier in southern areas.
The fairly mild temperatures are set to continue all weekend, and overnight frost is not expected in most of the country, with little temperature variation at night in many places.

title: Europe's summer heatwaves 'caused 50,000 excess deaths'
body: Europe's hottest summer on record may have killed more than 50,000 people across 30 European countries, researchers have found, as they called on governments to reduce the use of fossil fuels. Scientists from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine examined excess heat deaths in 854 cities in Europe from June 1 to August 31 this year, comparing it to data for the same period dating back to the year 2000. The modelled death toll of 50,391 was the highest in the research covering the past 26 years, far in excess of the next highest in 2022, when about 29,000 excess heat -related deaths occurred and 2003, with around 18,000 excess deaths. The summers of 2022 and 2003 involved record-breaking heatwaves. This summer, late June was especially severe , with almost a third of deaths happening from June 17 to July 1, when the daily mean temperature across Europe was more than 5°C above the 1991-2020 average. The heat was a danger only for elderly people. An estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are thought to have died as a result of heatwaves during summer this year. Cities in Europe's major economies had the highest total estimated heat-related deaths. The highest was in Italy, where 13,303 excess deaths from higher temperatures were recorded, followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) and the UK (4,354). The study also analysed weather data and climate models to compare how summer temperatures have changed between today's climate and pre-industrial temperatures. They found that two thirds of the excess heat deaths could be attributable of global warming , “primarily as the result of burning fossil fuels”. The findings were published as two peer-reviewed papers in the journal Nature Health on Friday. Though the findings provide an estimate, the modelling method used has been found to produce results in line with the records of excess deaths published by national health authorities for previous heat waves. Dr Claire Barnes, a co-author of the report from the Centre of Environmental Policy at University College London, called for “target interventions” to protect people in summers to come. “These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health,” she said. “Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them.” The findings also reflected the “growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming”. The research comes as the UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, in a move opposed by environmental campaigners. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the move was needed to protect British consumers from rising energy costs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” The report's authors also called for cities to adapt to hotter weather. “It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation,” said co-author Dr Pierre Masselot of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. “This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.” The excess deaths and emergencies from heat also put additional strain on British hospitals, that was comparable to a “really bad winter virus season”, according to Prof Andrew Hartle, an intensive care consultant at the Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust. Hospital buildings and equipment have also not adapted to the heat, he added. “Here in the UK, the summer is historically the quietest time for our health service. This summer, however, saw demand and strain that was akin to a really bad winter virus season. “Patients already in hospital have also been overheating, with much of the UK’s hospital estate largely not built to withstand these temperatures, and there are serious risks to equipment from heat too,” he said.

title: Russian drone attack injures 9 people, including 2 children
body:
A Russian drone struck a residential home in Zhytomyr Oblast on Oct. 22, injuring nine people, including two children, local officials said.
"Russia continues its deliberate terror against the peaceful Zhytomyr Oblast," regional Governor Vitalii Bunechko wrote on Telegram.
Two of the injured had been taken to hospital, Bunechko added. The full extent of the injuries sustained was not immediately clear.
Zhytomyr is a city in northwestern Ukraine home to over 200,000 people. The city's energy facilities have been under repeated Russian attacks in recent weeks.
While Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian energy facilities, it has ramped up its attacks on energy infrastructure in recent weeks ahead of the winter months. Strikes on energy facilities earlier this month left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line cities with repeated energy and water outages.
Elsewhere across Ukraine overnight into Oct. 23, explosions were heard in northwestern Ukrainian city of Lutsk, local media outlets reported. Explosions could also be heard when a drone crashed in Poltava Oblast, Vitalii Diakivnych, the head of the Poltava Oblast Military Administration, wrote on Telegram. Although the blast damaged private homes, buildings, and a power line, no people were injured according to preliminary reports.
While in Sumy Oblast, a "massive attack" of Russian drones hit civilian infrastructure facilities overnight injuring two, according to Sumy Governor Oleg Grigorov .

title: Cristiano Ronaldo seeks redemption as Rodgers eyes Al Qadsiah record in Al Hilal clash
body: Brendan Rodgers will be doubly motivated for the latest round of the Saudi Pro League when Al Qadsiah face heavyweights Al Hilal on Friday. Al Qadsiah have emerged as the surprise league leaders this campaign after 10 games, one point ahead of Hilal who have played one match fewer due to the rescheduling of games. For Rodgers, maintaining their lead at the top will be the main target at the Prince Saud bin Jalawi Stadium in Dammam, mainly because Hilal have a rearranged SPL fixture later in the season (v Al Riyadh on December 19) up their sleeve. But Rodgers will have his sights on another prize. The former Celtic boss, who guided Qadsiah to fourth in the league last season, is now on the verge of becoming the most successful manager in the club’s history. Al Qadsiah’s last-gasp win over Al Taawoun took Rodgers to 26 league wins, equalling the record set by former boss Michel. Victory over Hilal will allow the Northern Irishman to occupy the top spot by himself. Qadsiah will be aiming to raise their game substantially after being held goalless for over 90 minutes by relegation-threatened Al Taawoun. They needed Tijjani Reijnders, summer signing from Manchester City , to score the winner in the sixth minute of stoppage time and maintain their top spot. Brendan Rodgers on the challenges ahead: “The fixture schedule puts physical pressure on the players, but they are dealing with it very well. The coming weeks are a very important period, and we look forward to continuing our work and delivering our best.” 🎙️ #QADABH |… pic.twitter.com/wgpqMwrwnE — AlQadsiah Saudi Club (@AlQadsiahEN) October 15, 2026 Ronaldo eyes redemption Meanwhile, Cristiano Ronaldo will be desperate for some positive news after a spate of setbacks on and off the pitch. This week, Ronaldo was given a 30-day suspension and ordered to pay a fine of €255 as punishment for walking out on the national team. Ronaldo had left Portugal's base in Copenhagen ⁠ahead of their Uefa Nations League match against Denmark earlier this month over disagreements over his role in the team. Thereafter, Ronaldo stumbled badly on the pitch as Al Nassr scraped past Neom at Al Awwal Park. The Portuguese superstar looked set to score his 982nd career goal but failed to convert a penalty just before half-time. His bad week continued as Ronaldo wasted another great chance, firing over the crossbar from close range after being set up by Sadio Mane. Nassr still managed to complete a 1-0 win but will need to up their game against Al Faisaly on Friday. Manager Ange Postecoglou tried his best to defend Ronaldo. “This is the nature of football, and it is good that we create this number of chances, and we will work on making up for the mistakes,” he said. “We work as a family, so a win will be good for everyone and a loss will fall upon the whole team, so we must support one another and move forward.” Ronaldo was in the news once again when former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag questioned his ​fitness ​and preparation during a second ⁠stint at the club. Under Dutchman Ten Hag, Ronaldo struggled in the 2022/23 season, scoring once in 10 league appearances before leaving the club in ⁠November 2022. Despite the negativity, Ronaldo will have his sights firmly set on his next big target; the 41-year-old is 19 short of the 1,000 career goals landmark.

title: George Bouzianis: Greece’s Leading Expressionist Painter
body: George Bouzianis is remembered as one of Greece’s leading expressionist painters. Born in Athens on 8 November 1885, he studied at the Athens School of Fine Arts under teachers including Nikiphoros Lytras, Konstantinos Volanakis, Georgios Roilos and Dimitrios Geraniotis. In 1907 he moved to Munich to continue his studies, later going to Berlin where he worked with Max Liebermann. By 1917 he had absorbed the spirit of German expressionism into his own style and soon became a respected figure in Germany, exhibiting with the Barchfeld gallery. A major show of his work was held in Chemnitz in 1927, and between 1929 and 1932 he lived in Paris with support from the gallery. The rise of Nazism and the decline of expressionism in Germany eventually forced him back to Greece in 1934. He was initially met with hostility from Athenian art circles and failed to secure a teaching post at the School of Fine Arts. Recognition came later, particularly after his exhibition at the Parnassos gallery in 1949. In 1950 he represented Greece at the Venice Biennale, and he later received the first Greek award in the Guggenheim competition. Bouzianis died in Athens on 23 October 1959. His house in Dafni has since been turned into a museum, and his paintings are held in the National Gallery of Athens and other collections in Greece and abroad.
