title: UFC in Abu Dhabi: 'Street Fighter' Volkanovski says Evloev has plenty, but not enough to beat him
body: Alexander Volkanovski arrived at the UFC 333 pre-fight press conference on Thursday sporting a new look. The Australian's distinctive bald head was covered by a blond wig as he dressed up as his character "Joe" in the Hollywood movie Street Fighter . Volkanovski, 38, will put his UFC featherweight title on the line against the undefeated Movsar Evloev in the headline bout at UFC 333 on Saturday. If he has his hand raised at Etihad Arena, he will surpass the legendary Jose Aldo for most title fight wins in the 145-pound division with nine. Volkanovski (28-4) said he respects Evloev, an elite wrestler and the No 1 contender. He admires the Russian's all-round game but said despite his credentials, Evloev's skills pale in comparison to his own. "I believe I've seen that puzzle before, but he's undefeated and knows how to win, but I just don't think that's enough," he said. "He's got all the skills; he can take it anywhere. I think he's the most well-rounded [fighter], but I think I get my hand raised 'And still ...' once again." Volkanovski is in his second reign as champion, and another victory will only add to his claims as the greatest featherweight in history. Evloev, dressed in a three-piece suit and flat cap in the style of Tommy Shelby's character in the hit show Peaky Blinders , has yet to taste defeat in his 20-fight career, a fact Volkanovski wants to change. "He doesn't have a loss yet. So, that's something that I want to take from him." Evloev, 32, earned his shot at gold with a victory over Lerone Murphy earlier this year. He elected to stand and trade with the Englishman before a point deduction for a low blow forced him to revert to type and grapple. Volkanovski urged his opponent to stick to his strengths but warned that it would be he who dictates where the fight goes. "I think he could have made that fight look a lot easier. You could see he was the better fighter. But like I said, just don't try that on me; come bring your best game. Try and take me down," said Volkanovski. "If it's going to be forced on the feet, it's because I'm going to make it be on the feet. And this will be the most dangerous we've ever seen Mov because he's never been forced to fight on the feet. So, he can't panic shoot. He's going to have to panic punch. Let's see how dangerous he is on his feet." Questions will be answered @alexvolkanovski vs @MovsarUFC [ #UFC333 | OCT 24 | 2pmET LIVE on @paramountplus ] @VisitAbuDhabi | @InAbuDhabi | #InAbuDhabi pic.twitter.com/JoTNBYkS1m — UFC (@ufc) October 22, 2026 Evloev said he was ready to throw down wherever the fight takes place and that he will make Volkanovski eat his words. "I don't have a game plan. I can solve everything. He brings striking, OK, no problem. If you want to be knocked out, I'll do that. But when he says I cannot take him down or something, with all respect to the champ, I can do anything I want, and I'll prove it." Fan-favourite Yan The co-main event sees Petr Yan defend the UFC bantamweight championship he took from Merab Dvalishvili last December. There has been plenty of bad blood in the build-up. Saturday will be the third meeting between two of the best 135-pounders of their generation. Dvalishvili won the first encounter and hopes to close out the trilogy with another win. If he is to do so, he will have to do it in his opponent's territory. The biggest cheer was reserved for the Russian champion, and there is no doubt he will enjoy the majority of the support from the crowd come fight night. As has been the case all week, Dvalishvili was unfazed and got a big pop of his own when he name-checked the city where he hopes to reclaim the title. "Saturday night, this is my territory. I love Abu Dhabi and Abu Dhabi loves me, right? Let's go!," said the Georgian, who has 21 wins against five losses. "I'm the king, bro. People always will be with me because I love people and they love me. They support me and I'm grateful for that. "Mentally, I'm very strong. You know, all I have to do is just bring myself in the octagon Saturday and everything will be good. I believe in myself and I believe in my style. I can beat him this time." Yan said that his recent victory over Dvalishvili will count for little this time around. "Guys, for me this is a new fight. I don't want to think about the last fight. Today I have a big goal: I want to smash this guy. I want to defend my title," said Yan. The Russian (20-5) will be fighting in Abu Dhabi for the fifth time and has fond memories of the UAE capital. He beat Jose Aldo to win the bantamweight title for the first time in 2020 and has followed that up with wins over Corey Sandhagen and Marcus McGhee. "Abu Dhabi for me is the best place. I remember 2020 when I was here and win my belt against Jose Aldo, and I have already defended my title here [against Sandhagen]," Yan said, "And on 24 October, I smash this guy one more time."

title: The Missed Opportunities of Sonic 06 (2025)
body:
Most people know Sonic 06 has cut content, but few realise just how much...
During the process of building Marathon Recompiled , weâve ended up digging deep into many of Sonic 06âs core systems, including the rendering. The appearance of 06âs various areas varies from pretty good, like in Crisis City, to utterly flat and depressing in Castle Town.
Crisis City has reflections, particle effects, dramatic lighting.
It really makes you wonder what exactly went wrong? If you look at what limited footage we have of beta content, we can see many effects that arenât present in the final game. Kingdom Valley had full bump maps, Castle Town had more complex geometry and plants, and New Cityâs collision implies a very different building layout at some point in development.
Beta Castle Town had proper lighting and shadows. Source: TCRF
It turns out, much of the cut content is actually still in the game, but is simply not enabled for performance reasons in vanilla. Even with the cut-back visuals, the game struggles to reach target FPS on real hardware. Itâs not surprising that given the crunch Sonic Team were under to get the game out the door, these features were among the first to go.
How exactly were these features disabled, though? It comes down to the many different shader variants used throughout. Most things in Sonic 06 are rendered using either the Terrain or Billboard shaders (despite the name, Billboard is not actually billboard-ed). Both of these have many variants, each with different feature levels numbered 00-07. As a general rule, the higher the number, the better the feature set. These shaders have not been entirely decompiled yet, so I canât account for every difference with 100% certainty, but here is a rough feature table for the Billboard variants. CSM here stands for cascaded shadow maps, the shadow technique used by 06.
Want to take a guess as to which is the most used shader in the game? Thatâs right, Billboard02 . Not quite the worst one, but definitely one of the worst. So yes, the most used shader in the game only has per-vertex lighting, no CSM support, and no point lights. If youâre wondering why so many things look so dull, this is why. Most of the game is not rendered with anything but the most basic albedo textures and ambient lighting.
If youâre curious about how much each shader is used and where, Iâve made a handy table , with descriptions of each shader available on HedgeDocs .
Unfortunately, because of the different I/O layouts between the variants, swapping them out is not as easy as youâd hope. My current attempts to do so have been largely unsuccessful, mostly just resulting in the various techniques breaking in one way or another. Additionally, the textures used for each material are defined in an objectâs .xno file. It may be the case that some .xno s simply do not reference their other maps like normal and bump maps, despite them still being in the game files, and so swapping the shaders would not be enough.
Castle Town with Billboard07 shader. Shadows do not apply to buildings correctly.
So about those shadow maps, theyâre not free from problems either. The game is set up for a maximum of 4 cascades. Each cascade is used for a portion of the view along the cameraâs frustum, keeping the amount of pixels used to resolve shadows relatively consistent across distances. However, it seems CSM was also the target of some last-minute performance hack-n-slashing.
The level of cascades used is defined by GenerateCSMLevels and GenerateCSMObjects . Levels generally refers to terrain/static elements, while Objects refers to wellâ¦ other objects. Most areas will use the full 4 cascades, except twn_a and a few test levels where GenerateCSMLevels is downgraded to 3 and GenerateCSMObjects to just 2, significantly shortening the distance shadows render at. Multiplayer has this reduced cascade count everywhere.
Even when shadows do render correctly, theyâre prone to severe shadow acne, a common artifact when using these sorts of techniques. This is usually resolved by adding a small epsilon value to shadow map samples, but Sonic Team didnât do this, and I donât have the knowledge of the shaders yet to attempt to add this.
Shadows are also occasionally ill-defined in vanilla. Objects can set whether they contribute to shadow maps, and they sometimes get this wrong, leading to problems like Sonicâs Crisis City snowboard having no shadow, and Eliseâs skirt missing a shadow in one of Sonicâs story cutscenes. These are not as easily patchable, as it would likely require direct edits to the objects themselves, or a complicated hook to find and correct objects in the render code itself.
This is one of the sadder cuts in my opinion. For what itâs worth, Sonic 06 in theory has a pretty flexible lighting system. Thereâs a couple of fixed ambient lights defined for every object, and then several point lights. These are meant to provide additional small details for objects like torches, they donât cast shadows, and are rather inexpensive to render.
Sonic Team limited the number of point lights per-object to 2, that means at any given time, only 2 lights literally have the space in shader inputs to be rendered. Ordinarily, this sort of limitation would be fine, most forward renderers will have this kind of limit, so long as the designers remained cognisant of the limit when designing stages. Well, uh, they didnât.
Some stages like Kingdom Valley obey the limit pretty faithfully, and then stages like Flame Core and Dusty Desert utterly blow the limit out of the water, attempting to render 8+ lights per object. Needless to say, this doesnât work out. The renderer gets confused, and lights will âfightâ for priority, causing some to appear or disappear semi-randomly.
Overloaded point lights in Flame Core. Only lights on the left side of the path render.
Sonic Team attempted to provide a general optimisation for point lights, and allocate them effectively to nearby objects, but something in this check went wrong. I suspect a combination of the limit being sharply lowered later in development, and the switching of many per-pixel lit objects to per-vertex, which can vastly alter the contribution area of a point light. The result is point lights rarely work at all in vanilla, even in stages that respect the limit.
In the recomp, we are able to patch out most of the optimisation that breaks them, allowing point lights to render much more stable than in vanilla, however we are still limited to the 2 light limit. The lighting calculations responsible for adding point light contribution are all unrolled/inlined in the final shader bytecode, which makes identifying and modifying this code tricky as it can look different from one shader to the next. This is an area I want to tackle in the future.
Did you know Sonic 06 had real-time planar reflections? Hint: We saw them earlier in Crisis City. I actually donât have much to complain about here, generally they work really well and add a lot of realism to a scene. Of course, the resolution is severely limited in vanilla to 1/4 the resolution of the framebuffer, but thatâs easily patched. There is one area where the gameâs visuals get screwed over, and thatâs in multiplayer.
Murky fixed cubemap reflection in Kingdom Valley.
To save having to render expensive planar reflections twice in multiplayer, Sonic Team opted to just remove them entirely and replace them with static cubemaps. The problem is these cubemaps are pretty meh. Kingdom Valley goes from looking awesome to more like a depressed swamp. Well no problem, we can just patch it in right? Unfortunately due to how the rendering code works this isnât so easy.
Sonic 06 uses Lua scripting to build the render graph, and different modes have different scripts. Itâs a pretty cool and flexible system, when it works. As expected, singleplayer and multiplayer have their own render scripts, render_gamemode.lua and render_gamemode_multi.lua respectively.
In render_gamemode.lua we can see that crucial RenderReflection() call, which is unfortunately entirely absent from render_gamemode_multi.lua . As a result, attempting to enable the realtime reflections in multiplayer will just leave us with a black void rather than pretty reflections.
We canât just swap out render_gamemode_multi.lua for render_gamemode.lua either. The multiplayer renderer has special steps for creating the split-screen, essentially two framebuffers, so for multiplayer to render correctly, the provided render graph needs to be able to render both framebuffers. Even if you modify the multiplayer renderer to have RenderReflection , itâs not set up to work in this split-screen environment, and will, again, not work as intended. As it stands this quickly becomes a rabbit hole thatâs not easy to resolve. If in future we have an easier way to apply Lua patches, I may revisit this.
Maybe. Several of these problems have been at least partially addressed, but Iâve yet to figure out the shader edits that would be needed to get us to that beta footage goodness. Some of these fixes are largely, out of scope for the recomp, but whether fixes make it or not, weâre still learning a ton about how this game works on the backend. That still directly contributes to future improvements and patches.
This game has much, much more to give, and itâs honestly sad that Sonic Team were not given the time to finish it. Thereâs many things that I didnât get in to in this article including the insanity of the character shader, or the lack of occlusion culling, but itâs long enough already. Have fun with this silly game and happy early 20th anniversary.
Thank you to Gordon Ramsay for fact checking.

title: Ukraine’s Defense Forces neutralize 408,000 Russian drones since start of year
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine said this.
The ministry emphasized that all strikes were recorded on video in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
According to the ministry, in the first 10 months of 2026, Ukrainian forces struck nearly 248,000 Wing type drones, about 125,000 copter-type drones and more than 35,000 Shahed drones.
Confirmation of Russian UAV strikes is carried out in the DELTA system, which the ministry described as the “digital core” for managing the modern battlefield and one of the technological solutions key to Ukraine gaining an advantage over the enemy.
The ministry emphasized that this verification mechanism makes it possible to track the specifics of each enemy drone interception and more quickly scale up solutions that prove effective.
As reported by Ukrinform, military personnel recorded more than 1.8 million completed mission results in the Mission Control system in September.

title: ‘Not Another Budapest Memorandum’ – Kyiv Seeks US Security Guarantees Backed by Congress
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday, Oct. 22, that Ukraine is negotiating detailed security guarantees with the US modeled on NATO’s Article 5, insisting that any American commitments must be backed by Congress to prevent a repeat of the failed Budapest Memorandum.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, Zelensky outlined a comprehensive security framework combining direct US guarantees, NATO membership and a European-led Coalition of the Willing with American backing, all built around a strong, adequately funded Ukrainian military.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We are discussing not the Budapest Memorandum, not a piece of paper – with all due respect to those who signed it – but detailed security guarantees from the United States, backed by a vote in the US Congress,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president was responding to a journalist who questioned whether Kyiv could trust new American security commitments after the 1994 Budapest Memorandum failed to protect Ukraine from Russian aggression.
Zelensky stressed that Ukraine needs enforceable commitments supported by concrete defense capabilities rather than political assurances that could prove ineffective in the event of another Russian invasion.
He confirmed that the proposals remain under discussion with Washington, with no final agreement yet announced.
Zelensky pointed to Ukraine’s experience under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which Kyiv surrendered the nuclear weapons inherited from the Soviet Union in exchange for security assurances from Russia, the US and Britain.
Russia subsequently violated those commitments by occupying Crimea in 2014 and launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
“We gave up everything that guaranteed Ukraine’s security,” Zelensky said.
He argued that Ukraine cannot afford another arrangement lacking clear obligations and credible mechanisms to deter renewed Russian aggression.
Zelensky outlined three complementary security arrangements: NATO membership, bilateral American guarantees modeled on Article 5, and a European-led Coalition of the Willing backed by Washington.
He stressed that these mechanisms should reinforce one another rather than be treated as competing alternatives.
“We are talking about a comprehensive set of guarantees,” he said.
The president emphasized that all three would depend on Ukraine maintaining a strong, properly equipped military capable of defending the country against future attacks.
Zelensky said Ukraine and its Western partners had already calculated the personnel requirements and financing needed to maintain a powerful military after the war.
“All these guarantees are possible on the basis of a strong Ukrainian army,” he said.
He warned that Ukraine could not finance its defense needs entirely from its own budget without sacrificing national reconstruction.
International support would therefore be essential not only for maintaining the armed forces but also for rebuilding infrastructure, restoring education, supporting veterans and helping displaced Ukrainians return home.
Zelensky also argued that Ukraine’s membership in NATO would strengthen European security and could ultimately benefit Russia by reducing the risk of another war.
“We, with our army, are important for NATO, just as NATO is very important for Ukrainian security,” he said.
“I believe that, frankly, even the Russians need Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Zelensky added. “Because it would provide them with greater security than Ukraine remaining outside NATO.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Patriarch Bartholomew Marks 35 Years on the Ecumenical Throne
body: The story should be updated for 2026, marking the 35th anniversary of Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew’s election, which took place on October 22, 1991. The original 2020 anniversary message can provide historical context, but it should not be presented as a new statement for this year. The 2026 update can also include the anniversary liturgy at the Patriarchal Church of St George in Constantinople and the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia’s commemorations, giving the article a current news angle rather than simply changing “29th” to “35th.” Orthodox Observer +2 Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew Marks 35 Years on the Throne By Bill Giannopoulos His All Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew has marked 35 years since his election as Archbishop of Constantinople and Ecumenical Patriarch, commemorating a milestone in a ministry shaped by Orthodox unity, interfaith dialogue and environmental protection. Elected on October 22, 1991, Patriarch Bartholomew has led the Ecumenical Patriarchate for more than three decades, becoming one of the most prominent voices in the Orthodox Christian world. The anniversary was marked on Thursday, October 22, 2026, with a Patriarchal Divine Liturgy at the historic Church of St George at the Phanar in Constantinople. The service was presided over by the Ecumenical Patriarch, with Archbishop Elpidophoros of America and other hierarchs concelebrating. Clergy and faithful from the United States, Australia, Europe and other regions attended the celebrations. The liturgy followed Great Vespers held the previous evening as part of the anniversary programme. https://orthodoxtimes.com/patriarchal-divine-liturgy-marking-the-35th-anniversary-of-the-election-of-the-ecumenical-patriarch-live/ “>Read more about the anniversary liturgy. A ministry focused on dialogue and the environment Throughout his patriarchal ministry, Bartholomew has become widely recognised for promoting dialogue between Christian churches and other religious traditions, while drawing attention to environmental protection as a spiritual and moral responsibility. His work has also addressed peace, religious freedom, human rights and the plight of refugees. In a 2020 anniversary message, Nikos Papachristou, then Director of the Press and Communication Office of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, highlighted the Patriarch’s contribution to inter Christian and interreligious dialogue, environmental awareness and social issues. Papachristou also called for God to grant the Patriarch strength and health to continue his service to the Church and humanity. The message reflected themes that have remained central to Bartholomew’s public ministry throughout his time on the Ecumenical Throne. Australia honours the Ecumenical Patriarch The 35th anniversary has particular significance for Greek Orthodox communities in Australia. The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia designated 2026 the “Year of Patriarch Bartholomew”, with commemorative activities planned across the country. Around 250 pilgrims from Australia travelled to Constantinople for the anniversary celebrations, taking part in events honouring the Patriarch’s life and ministry. A special commemorative event was also organised for October 22 by the Archdiocese’s Holy Eparchial Synod at the Grand Cevahir Hotel and Convention Centre in Istanbul. The programme highlighted Bartholomew’s contribution to Orthodox tradition, inter Christian dialogue, peace and environmental protection. The celebrations underscored the close spiritual ties between the Greek Orthodox faithful in Australia and the Ecumenical Patriarchate. From Imbros to the Ecumenical Throne Born Dimitrios Archondonis on February 29, 1940, on the island of Imbros , now part of Türkiye, Bartholomew studied at the Theological School of Halki before pursuing further studies in Rome, Switzerland and Germany. He was ordained a deacon in 1961 and a priest in 1969. In 1973, he became Metropolitan of Philadelphia. On October 22, 1991, he was elected Ecumenical Patriarch by the Holy and Sacred Synod. His enthronement followed on November 2, 1991. As Archbishop of Constantinople and Ecumenical Patriarch, he occupies the historic first throne of the Orthodox Church, serving as a spiritual leader for Orthodox Christians around the world. A continuing call to protect creation Environmental protection has become one of the defining themes of Bartholomew’s ministry. He has repeatedly urged individuals, governments and religious communities to recognise the moral responsibilities associated with caring for the natural world. His emphasis on the spiritual dimensions of environmental responsibility was also recognised by Pope Francis in the 2015 encyclical Laudato si’ , which highlighted the Patriarch’s calls for humanity to reconsider consumerism, waste and its relationship with creation. As the Ecumenical Patriarchate commemorates 35 years of Bartholomew’s leadership, his anniversary provides an opportunity for Orthodox Christians worldwide to reflect on his longstanding emphasis on faith, dialogue, unity and stewardship of the environment. title: The Hibernate Origin Story (Outsider Edition)
body:
I've told this story many times over the years, usually with a beer in my hand, but for some reason I've not written it down before now. As a disclaimer, the events I'm about to describe happened twenty-five years ago, and I was a peripheral, if not entirely tangential, participant, so I'm probably going to get a few of them wrong.
The root Java package for Hibernate 1.0 was cirrus.inf . Weâll get to the inf in a moment, but first letâs start with the cirrus .
Cirrus Technologies was a small IBM Business Partner. I think at its height it was about fifteen people. Four of them were called David, which embarrassingly meant the company had three more Davids than it had women. The company's core business, at least when I was there, was to get bigger companies to buy Websphere, IBM's enterprise Java server platform , then sell them access to developers who know how Websphere worked.
Which is where I came in. These days we'd have been called something exciting like Forward Deployed Engineers , but back then we were just consultants.
In the early 2000s, needing some forward-facing programmers who lived closer to certain banks (as far as I remember), Cirrus opened a three-person office in Melbourne. Two of those people were Gavin King and Daniel Bradby, both very good programmers, but Gavin had that dangerous combination of being disturbingly intelligent, with absolute conviction of his own opinions, and annoyingly, was often right.
Around 2001, us front-loading developers at Cirrus were working doggedly on a project that was rapidly going wrong, and would continue to go wrong until we agreed that even saying its name was bad luck, deploying a Shakespearean euphemism: The Scottish Project .
There were many reasons this project was going off the rails, but the biggest problem was that back in 2001, server-side Java was an absolute pain in the arse to develop. This was the era of Servlets and JSPs. Struts 1.0 and âform beansâ were considered state-of-the-art. And beneath them all like an unblinking Elder God slept the most terrifying of them all: Enterprise Java Beans.
If you don't know what EJBs were, count yourself lucky. They were a brutally over-engineered component model for Java designed to sell expensive middleware like Websphere. To get an idea of what it was like, developing an EJB required you to write two different interfaces, and then an implementation that did not implement either interface . And then add a âdeployment descriptorâ that was, at least for the first few versions of the spec, vendor-specific (and in Websphere's case, could only be generated by IBM's VisualAge for Java IDE ). And it got worse from there .
Fun fact, the earliest days of Jira development started off using EJBs. This lasted maybe a few weeks before Mike and Scott realised how much they sucked.
So Gavin, being Gavin, got hacking. Enter cirrus.inf . The inf stood for âinfrastructureâ and it was his valiant mostly solo attempt to make Enterprise Java suck slightly less. The first entry in the package had nothing to do with databases or persistence, or even EJBs. It was a lightweight replacement for Struts, an attempt to smooth some of the rough edges of web development. I have absolutely no recollection of how it worked, but my vague memory is that it took a bit of effort to get your head around conceptually, but once you had, it did the job.
With the Scottish Project staring in the face of a major missed deadline, the powers that be decided to fly the Melbourne contingent of the company to Sydney for two days of intense meetings deciding how to get things back on track. Number one issue on the agenda: what do we do about EJBs? On one hand they were slow to develop, painful to test, hard to maintain, a huge source of bugs, and offered very little actual utility to the project. On the other hand, they were the marquee feature and major selling point of the application server we had just sold to this customer, and hoped to sell to many others.
Opinions quickly divided into three camps. Management was conservative, and wanted to stay the course with the technology we had chosen. Most developers wanted to reduce our reliance on EJBs, maybe keeping session beans for transaction management and component discovery, but ditching entity beans (the strain of EJB used for managed object persistence) in favour of hand-written SQL.
The third camp was Gavin and Daniel. Gavin had a really cool idea for a persistence framework for Java, using concepts borrowed from successful Smalltalk frameworks, that could replace both entity beans and hand-written SQL with something demonstrably better.
After a long, long argument, we finally got management to compromise as far as option two, went to The Establishment , and drowned our sorrows. Gavin's persistence framework was a cool idea, it was acknowledged, but maybe not the right idea for this moment.
The next day, with not much to do before getting on a plane back to Melbourne, Gavin sat down at a CRT monitor much like the one pictured above, and stubbornly laid down the first few classes of his persistence framework. Again to be clear here, my contribution to this project started and ended with him maybe bouncing a few ideas off me over beers, and me nodding and saying it sounded cool.
The Scottish Project continued on into disaster.
And then, a few months later, to everyone in Sydney's surprise, a new Java persistence library called Hibernate was released under the Lesser GNU Public License, with the package name cirrus.inf . There was a certain amount of grumbling from management about how this was allowed to happen, and why the company didn't get any credit for a project they did nothing to support, but as they say, the rest is history.
The fantastic irony is that I didn't get to use Hibernate once during my remaining time at Cirrus: the first time I did more with it than the tutorial was after I moved to Atlassian and started working on Confluence.

title: Greece Turns Clocks Back This Sunday: What You Need to Know
body: By Bill Giannopoulos Greece will switch to winter time in the early hours of Sunday, October 25, 2026, when clocks go back one hour and residents gain an extra hour of sleep. At 4:00 am, clocks across Greece will move back to 3:00 am, ending daylight saving time and returning to standard time. The change means Sunday will effectively have an extra hour. The seasonal adjustment follows the European Union’s existing rules, which require clocks to move forward in spring and back in autumn. Why Do Clocks Change in Greece? EU Directive 2000/84/EC governs the seasonal time change and sets common arrangements for summer time across member states. The system moves clocks forward by one hour on the last Sunday of March and back by one hour on the last Sunday of October. The aim is to make better use of available daylight during different parts of the year. Although the European Commission proposed ending the twice-yearly clock changes in 2018, EU member states have not reached a final decision. The current system therefore remains in force. Source The History of Daylight Saving Time in Greece Greece first experimented with daylight saving time in 1932, when clocks were moved forward during the summer months. European countries later reintroduced the practice as they looked for ways to manage energy consumption. The modern system became part of everyday life in Greece during the 1970s, amid the energy crisis that encouraged countries to reconsider how they used daylight. Across Europe, the practice has roots in the First World War, when Germany introduced seasonal clock changes in 1916 to conserve energy resources. How the Time Change Affects Daily Life The shift to winter time brings more daylight into the morning hours but means the sun sets earlier in the evening. For some people, the extra hour of sleep is welcome. Others find the change disruptive, as their sleeping patterns, daily routines and body clocks adjust to the new schedule. The impact of seasonal clock changes continues to fuel debate over whether Europe should maintain the current system or adopt a permanent time arrangement. Will the Clocks Change Again in 2027? Under the current EU system, Greece is scheduled to move back to standard time on Sunday, March 28, 2027, when clocks will move forward by one hour. For now, residents should remember to set manual clocks back one hour before going to bed on Saturday night, October 24. Smartphones and other internet-connected devices will generally update automatically if their date, time and time-zone settings are configured correctly. Source: Greek Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport; Council of the European Union. title: Trump claims Iran is 'making up fake hits' on tankers to drive up oil costs ahead of elections
body: US President Donald Trump accused Iran of fabricating reports of attacks on oil tankers and naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections in a Truth Social post on Thursday.“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election,” Trump wrote.“They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."Trump also accused Iran's regime of killing protesters and reaffirmed his commitment that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.The post came as Trump continued to defend the US campaign against Iran and its impact on American energy prices ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump said the war had come at a political cost but maintained that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was necessary.“There's a price to pay, which I knew immediately when I did it,” Trump said. “But we can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”Asked about public reaction to the war, Trump said Americans had mixed feelings about the campaign.“In one way they love it because I'm doing what should have been done by other presidents. In another way, maybe they don't,” he said.Trump also suggested the US could carry out further military action against Iran, saying Washington had already inflicted significant damage but “may do it a little bit further.”Tensions surrounding the Strait of HormuzThe Strait of Hormuz has remained a key point of contention during the conflict, as attacks on commercial shipping and restrictions on maritime traffic have threatened the flow of oil through the waterway.Iran's IRGC Navy reported that four oil tankers were hit and caught fire overnight, according to the Iranian state media IRNA. The incidents added to concerns about a renewed escalation in the region and the potential effects on global energy supplies.Trump, meanwhile, argued that oil was moving through the strait at a higher rate than before the war, despite what he described as fabricated reports of attacks.

title: No negotiated peace possible while Putin in power – Hudson Institute President
body:
No negotiated peace is possible while Putin is in power.
John P. Walters, President and CEO of the Hudson Institute, expressed this view in an analytical article published on the institute’s website, according to Ukrinform.
“The strategy should also recognize that it is a mistake to believe Putin will agree to accept defeat. His rule depends on keeping Russia at war. Short of victory, he cannot end the attacks, return all abducted Ukrainian children, and accept credible, monitored withdrawals and security guarantees. In short, no negotiated peace is possible while Putin is in power,” Walters said.
In his view, U.S. policy toward Russia is based on the dangerous equation of Putin’s capacity for destruction with strategic strength. At the same time, Walters points out that the war has weakened Russia and undermined the ambitions of its leader: rather than subjugating Ukraine, weakening NATO and dividing Europe, it has strengthened Ukrainian national identity, contributed to Finland and Sweden joining the Alliance, and accelerated European rearmament.
The author highlights Ukraine’s extraordinary resilience, military innovation, drones and long-range capabilities, which have inflicted enormous losses on Russian forces. In his view, neither additional territorial gains nor intensified terrorist bombardments are likely to force Ukraine into submission.
“Even replacing President Volodymyr Zelensky would not fundamentally change the strategic reality. Ukraine’s military and potential successors, including General Valerii Zaluzhnyi, will not accept surrender any more than Zelensky,” Walters stressed.
The Hudson Institute CEO points out that Putin’s growing dependence on communist China risks turning Russia into a subordinate partner of Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“Maintaining Putin, not his fall, makes Xi Jinping a bigger threat to America,” Walters added.
The author warned that the inability to conquer Ukraine could prompt Putin to intensify attacks against Ukraine and Europe. He views Russia-linked sabotage, cyberattacks, intimidation and disinformation as systematic assaults on the sovereignty, critical infrastructure and national security of Western states, laying the groundwork for further escalation.
“The West needs a strategy that recognizes both the dangers of Putin’s strategic weakness and the opportunity created by those weaknesses,” he stressed.
According to the author, the cornerstone of this strategy should be strengthening Ukraine through military, economic and diplomatic assistance. This should convincingly demonstrate that continued Russian aggression will not succeed. To strengthen deterrence, he also proposes redeploying forces capable of delivering nuclear weapons.
At the same time, the Institute’s President called for expanding contacts with Russians capable of contributing to change, including representatives of the current economic elites who do not want to tie their future to Putin. In his view, Western policy should take into account the prospect of Russia after its current ruler and support those prepared to help the country emerge from the strategic failure caused by him.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian, U.S. and Russian negotiating teams will communicate to work out the agenda for a trilateral meeting that could take place in early November, although exact dates have not yet been determined.

title: Eminem’s Former Employee Pleads Guilty to Selling Unreleased Music for $50,000
body: Joseph Strange, who worked at the rapper’s Michigan recording studio for 14 years, faces up to five years in prison after admitting to selling unreleased recordings that were subsequently accessed more than eight million times online. A former employee of Eminem has pleaded guilty to criminal copyright infringement after admitting to copying and selling the rapper’s unreleased music for approximately US$50,000, bringing a significant development in a case involving recordings that were never intended for public release. Joseph Strange, 48, worked for Eminem, whose real name is Marshall Mathers, from 2007 to 2021 at his recording studio in Ferndale, Michigan. On Thursday, 22 October, he pleaded guilty in a Michigan federal court to unlawfully reproducing and selling music belonging to the Grammy-winning artist. He now faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison. According to the US Department of Justice, Strange had access to password-protected hard drives containing recordings in various stages of development. His responsibilities included helping to establish and operate the studio’s computer storage system, giving him access to material that had not been authorised for release. Between July and August 2024, Strange sold at least 10 audio files to buyers over the internet, receiving approximately US$50,000 without Eminem’s knowledge or permission. Some of the recordings had undergone professional mastering, although prosecutors said there was no certainty they would ever be commercially released. The music subsequently appeared online and on public streaming platforms, attracting considerable attention among fans. By November 2025, the illegally distributed files had been accessed more than eight million times, with prosecutors estimating the infringement amount at a minimum of US$750,000. The investigation began in January 2025, when employees at Eminem’s studio discovered that unreleased recordings were being offered for sale online. A photograph accompanying the listings appeared to show material taken directly from one of the studio’s hard drives. The FBI subsequently traced several purchasers, who identified Strange as the person who had supplied the music. He was formally charged in March 2025. Among the recordings that surfaced were previously unheard collaborations with Dr. Dre and 50 Cent, as well as an alleged diss track dating from 2003 that referenced Suge Knight and Ja Rule. The leaked material spanned different periods of Eminem’s career, offering listeners access to recordings that had remained in his private archives for years. At the time of the initial leak, Eminem’s longtime spokesperson, Dennis Dennehy, described the recordings as “demos, experiments and ideas”, stressing that they had never been intended for public consumption. The concern extended beyond the commercial value of the material to the release of unfinished work without the artist’s approval. Following Strange’s guilty plea, Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said the former employee had “abused a position of trust” to profit from music that Eminem had not authorised for distribution. Strange’s lawyer, Wade G. Fink, challenged the prosecution’s characterisation of the case, telling Billboard that the circumstances were considerably more complex than publicly suggested. While acknowledging that his client had accepted responsibility for his actions, Fink said Strange was remorseful and expressed concern about the impact of the proceedings on his family. “This is a much more complicated and nuanced matter than it is being made to seem,” Fink said. Strange was originally charged with both criminal copyright infringement and interstate transportation of stolen goods. His guilty plea relates to the copyright offence. He is scheduled to be sentenced on 27 January 2027, when a federal judge will determine his punishment after considering the applicable sentencing guidelines. title: ‘Putin Is Using Hitler’s Tactics’ – Ranking US Senator Slams Russian Attacks on Ukrainian Cities
body:
US Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, compared Russia’s intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure to Nazi Germany’s bombing campaign against Britain, warning that Vladimir Putin is seeking to break civilian morale.
“Putin’s tactics have changed from using WWI-style tactics on the front lines to attacking major metropolitan areas in the country to undermine morale,” Shaheen said.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“It’s the same tactic Hitler used in Britain before WWII, and targeting the country’s energy infrastructure.”
Her comparison evokes the Blitz, Nazi Germany’s sustained bombing campaign against British cities during World War II, which began in 1940.
The remarks come as Russia continues launching ballistic missiles and attack drones against Ukrainian residential neighborhoods, transportation networks and power infrastructure ahead of winter.
In an Oct. 19 statement following a meeting with Zelensky , Shaheen reaffirmed bipartisan congressional support for Ukraine and criticized measures she argued could provide Russia with additional war revenue.
“Putin only responds to strength,” she said, calling for greater pressure on Moscow rather than Kyiv.
Shaheen’s remarks come amid bipartisan outrage in Congress over US envoy Steve Witkoff’s description of Putin as a “humanitarian” following the release of American detainee Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had been imprisoned in Russia for more than four years.
During Wednesday’s meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard and praised the Russian leader.
“You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin.
Shaheen condemned the remarks , calling Putin a war criminal and a dictator responsible for killing thousands of Ukrainians.
She also challenged the notion that releasing Hubbard made Putin a humanitarian, stressing that the American should never have been imprisoned in the first place.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis reacted with disbelief in a post on X .
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis wrote, describing Witkoff’s praise as embarrassing and outrageous.
He urged the envoy to ask Ukrainian families whose children had been abducted or killed by Russia whether they considered Putin a humanitarian.
Republican Senator John Cornyn was equally dismissive.
“No. Putin is a stone cold killer,” he wrote.
Republican Congressman Don Bacon called Witkoff’s remarks “another embarrassment,” while Senator Joni Ernst rejected any portrayal of Putin as a humanitarian, pointing to Russia’s relentless attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets
body: The Pentagon has concluded a new agreement to buy laser-guidance kits that turn rockets into drone-killing weapons. BAE Systems and the Defense Department announced a framework deal of up to seven years for 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits annually for the U.S. military. Another 10,000 kits could be produced each year for international customers, who are increasingly interested in the system. APKWS is a laser-guidance kit that converts 2.75-inch unguided rockets into precision munitions. It is currently fielded by the U.S. Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, and Navy, as well as U.S. allies. APKWS has become the preferred method for U.S. warplanes to down drones fired by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in the Middle East over the past few years. But it is not just an air-to-air weapon. APKWS munitions can also be fitted to various platforms for air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, and surface-to-air use. APKWS is an attractive capability for the Pentagon because of its low cost—roughly $35,000, according to officials. That gives the Air Force a way to shoot down drones without expending costly air-to-air missiles. For compraison, Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000. APKWS was first tested in an air-to-air role in 2019. The Air Force did not pursue the idea heavily until a few years later, before fielding it in combat in 2024. “We were on the wrong side of the cost curve in our munitions employment,” former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The great thing about it is that there wasn’t a formal requirement set out for this. This was sort of organic. People started figuring it out without it being a big program of record,” Allvin added. “Good thing they did.” A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft takes off from a base in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Sept. 28, 2026. Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System rockets are fitted under one of the aircraft’s wings. U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Noah J. Tancer Now, just a few years later, the Pentagon is betting big on APKWS’ future. APKWS scored its first combat air-to-air kill in the fall of 2024 in the Middle East by F-16 from the 510th Fighter Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy, current and former officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. When the 480th Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East soon after, they scored dozens more aerial kills— 108 in total using all weapons during their deployment. By the spring of 2025, the Air Force began flight testing APKWS on F-15E Strike Eagles, and fielded the capability in the Middle East within roughly a week . Around the same time, U.S. Air Forces in Europe also fielded APKWS for its air-to-air training . The system has also been on A-10s to shoot down drones. The APKWS has its origins in the decades-old Hydra rocket system and was first used as precision air-to-ground weapon during the Global War on Terror, deploying in 2012. It was adapted to serve in an air-to-air role when Air Forces Central, commanded by then-Lt. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich from 2022-2024, began looking for an alternative to using costly air-to-air missiles against drones. CENTCOM and the Air Force supported the effort. The framework agreement is intended as a signal of what the Pentagon plans to buy, subject to specific contracts and the congressional funding needs for those deals. BAE says the new agreement will help expand production at its facilities in Hudson, N.H., and Austin, Texas. “This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs,” BAE Systems president and CEO Tom Arseneault said in a statement. “By securing multiyear demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, added. APKWS can also be used in a ground-to-air role, as the modifications needed to hit aerial targets are largery limited to software and the use of a proximity fuse. It can be fitted to anti-air systems such as Sierra Nevada Corporation’s BRAWLR, which is deployed overseas by the U.S. military, and L3Harris’ VAMPIRE , which is used by Ukraine and is being supplied to the U.S. It has been fitted to other nations’ fighter platforms and has been tested on the MQ-9 Reaper as well. “This drone problem is not going away,” retired Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who led Air Forces Central from April 2024-August 2026, said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers. That’s the direction that we’re going.” The post Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: 2 pilots eject from military training jet in Texas after landing gear issue
body: Two pilots safely ejected from a military training aircraft near Seguin, Texas, on Thursday after experiencing a landing gear issue, officials said.The pilots were aboard a T-6A Texan II assigned to the 12th Flying Training Wing when they conducted a "controlled bailout" at approximately 5:51 p.m. local time, according to a news release from Joint Base San Antonio.After receiving indications that the aircraft's landing gear was unsafe, the pilots consulted experts, who recommended they eject, officials said.Both pilots were being evaluated by local medical personnel. Their conditions were not immediately known.The T-6A Texan II is a single-engine, two-seat primary trainer designed to train students in basic flying skills for U.S. Air Force and Navy pilots, according to the U.S. Air Force.The 12th Flying Training Wing "develops the next generation of Air Force aviators and enlisted aircrew by providing world-class flying training and education," according to the Air Education and Training Command.Seguin is located about 35 miles east of San Antonio.

title: Petrol Supply Crashes 23% as Imports Drop 30%, Local Receipts Fall 21%
body: • Dangote refinery hits 106% production capacity in September •Nigeria supplies 80.4% of feedstock intake by local facilities • Indigenous refiners get 618,000 bpd oil, down 9% •Diesel supply slumps to lowest level in 13 months Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja Nigeria’s daily petrol supply fell 23 per cent in September despite the Dangote Petroleum Refinery operating above its installed capacity, as declining domestic deliveries and imports coincided with higher petrol prices, which exceeded N1,400 per litre in some cities. The September 2026 factsheet of the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) released yesterday showed that total petrol receipts dropped from 50.5 million litres per day in August to 38.7 million litres, although consumption rose 7 per cent to 44.4 million litres daily. Besides, local petrol receipts declined 21 per cent, from 35.9 million litres to 28.5 million litres per day, while imports fell 30 per cent, from 14.6 million litres to 10.2 million litres. The figures mean that the Nigerian market received 11.8 million fewer litres of petrol daily in September than in August. The decline occurred despite a 13 per cent increase in petrol production at the Dangote refinery, which raised its average daily output from 41.94 million litres in August to 47.22 million litres in September. The refinery’s average capacity utilisation also rose from 105.21 per cent to 105.98 per cent, above its installed capacity of 650,000 barrels per day. Yet, the volume of petrol it supplied to the domestic market fell by about a fifth, while exports increased. According to the document, Dangote supplied an average of 28.5 million litres of petrol daily to the domestic market in September, compared with 10.2 million litres from imports. Its recorded domestic deliveries were therefore almost 2.8 times the volume of imported petrol. Also, in August, domestic deliveries from the refinery stood at 35.87 million litres per day, against imports of 14.6 million litres. Although local refining remained the dominant source, its share of total petrol receipts rose from 71 per cent in August to about 74 per cent in September because imports declined more sharply. The refinery exported 15.47 million litres of petrol daily in September, up 59 per cent from 9.73 million litres in August. It also added 3.25 million litres per day to its petrol stocks, closing the month with 366.2 million litres, compared with 360.4 million litres at the end of August. The figures showed that higher production did not translate into increased domestic deliveries. While output increased, local supplies fell as exports rose and stocks accumulated. The fall in market receipts came amid high fuel retail prices. The NMDPRA’s indicative petrol price stood at N1,371.01 per litre in Lagos, N1,420.01 in Abuja, N1,447.75 in Kano and N1,464.75 in Maiduguri. The highest actual price recorded in the surveyed centres was N1,445 per litre in Abuja, while the lowest was N1,293.75 in Lagos. Beyond finished products, the report showed that domestic refineries received an average of 618,000 barrels of crude oil daily in September, down 9 per cent from 681,000 barrels per day in August. Nevertheless, Dangote processed an estimated 689,000 barrels daily, about 71,000 barrels above the volume received during the month. The regulator explained that the refinery made up the difference by drawing on its crude inventory. Its reported utilisation above 100 per cent therefore did not mean it received more crude in September. Similarly, the authority’s nine-month data showed that local refineries received 156.51 million barrels of crude between January and September. Of this, 125.85 million barrels were sourced domestically and 30.66 million barrels imported, meaning Nigerian crude accounted for 80.4 per cent of the total intake, while imported crude represented 19.6 per cent. The supply squeeze was more pronounced in the diesel market, where daily receipts fell 40 per cent, from 14.5 million litres in August to 8.7 million litres in September, the lowest level in the 13 months covered by the regulator’s data. According to the factsheet, domestic diesel receipts dropped 39 per cent, from 13.2 million litres to 8.1 million litres daily, while imports fell 54 per cent, from 1.3 million litres to 600,000 litres, although consumption edged up from 14.3 million litres to 14.5 million litres per day. Dangote’s diesel production, however, increased 35 per cent to 24.32 million litres per day. Domestic deliveries fell from 12.37 million litres in August to 8.14 million litres in September, while exports rose 82 per cent, from 8.75 million litres to 15.91 million litres daily. The refinery ended September with 232.5 million litres of diesel in stock, against 137.2 million litres a month earlier. The NMDPRA report showed that among modular refineries, Walter Smith operated at 62.25 per cent capacity utilisation, Edo at 104.24 per cent, Aradel at 31.90 per cent and OPAC at 18.43 per cent, while Duport was shut down. Their combined diesel supply was 620,000 litres per day, equivalent to 4.3 per cent of national consumption. Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) commonly known as cooking gas, recorded a more favourable trend. Daily receipts rose 9 per cent to 4.7 kilotonnes in September, with domestic supply increasing 50 per cent to 4.5 kilotonnes and imports falling 85 per cent to 0.2 kilotonnes. In the same vein, domestic sources accounted for about 96 per cent of receipts, although consumption rose 8 per cent to 5.2 kilotonnes daily. In the gas sector, total average daily supply, including volumes supplied to Nigeria LNG Limited, declined 2.2 per cent to 4.822 billion cubic feet in September. Domestic gas supply fell 6.7 per cent to 2.066 billion cubic feet daily, while supply to NLNG rose 1.5 per cent to 2.756 bcf.

title: Hydra Voted Europe’s Best Island by Condé Nast Traveller Readers
body: Hydra has been named the best island in Europe by readers of the British edition of Condé Nast Traveller, in the magazine’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards. The small Saronic Gulf island scored 98.12 to take first place. It edged out Italy’s Sardinia (98.01) by just 0.11 points, while fellow Greek island Naxos came third with 97.14. Hydra’s harbour. The island was voted Europe’s best in Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards. Photo: dronepicr / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. The results were published on 6 October 2026. The magazine said the awards, now in their 29th year, are based purely on votes from its UK readership. Israeli outlet Ynetnews reported that the survey was carried out between April and June, with participants asked to rate travel destinations and experiences. A warm welcome to ‘drifting travellers’ Condé Nast Traveller described Hydra as the island “immortalised by Leonard Cohen” that “still offers a warm welcome to drifting travellers”. The magazine said that quality was “a criterion that helped it beat six other Greek islands this year”. Cohen lived on Hydra in the 1960s and bought a house there, Ynetnews noted. The island has long drawn artists and creative figures. Hydra lies within ferry distance of Athens, and ordinary car traffic is virtually non-existent. Locals and visitors get around mainly on foot or by boat. Life centres on the picturesque harbour, which is ringed by stone houses and historic mansions, while many of the island’s swimming spots are rocky coves, some reachable only by boat. Naxos loses its crown, but Greece still dominates Hydra’s win means the top title stays in Greek hands. Naxos was voted Europe’s best island last year, and Condé Nast Traveller noted that it “lost first place and dropped to third place” in 2026. The magazine said Greece “has dominated the list once again”. Seven Greek islands made the Europe top 20: Hydra (1st) – 98.12 Naxos (3rd) – 97.14 Sifnos (6th) – 95.71 Paros (9th) – 94.01 Santorini (16th) – 90.00 Mykonos (18th) – 88.57 Crete (20th) – 87.81 That makes Greece the best-represented country on the list, ahead of Spain with four entries: Menorca (7th), Ibiza (8th), Mallorca (10th) and the Canary Islands (19th). Corsica was fourth and Sicily fifth. Some of Greece’s best-known names finished well down the rankings. Santorini placed 16th, Mykonos 18th and Crete, the country’s largest island, rounded out the list in 20th place. A strong year for Greece The island win caps a strong showing for Greece in this year’s awards. In the same Readers’ Choice Awards, Condé Nast Traveller readers named Greece the best country in the world , with a score of 98.14. In that entry, the magazine singled out “car-free Hydra” as one of the islands drawing more and more visitors. Elsewhere, the Isles of Scilly were voted the best island in the UK. Palawan in the Philippines topped Asia, Fiji led Australasia and the South Pacific, and Barbados was the favourite in the Caribbean and Atlantic. title: Oil Firms Decry Long Tender Cycles Delaying Upstream Projects Despite Tinubu’s Directives
body: • PETAN flags double-digit bank rates, 90-day payment delays stifling capacity Peter Uzoho Indigenous oil and gas service companies have raised alarm over long tender approval cycles and delayed payments by upstream producers, a situation that negates President Bola Tinubu’s Presidential Directives on Local Content introduced in March 2024. Service providers under the aegis of Petroleum Technology Association of Nigeria (PETAN) also complained that high bank interest rates was hurting them, warning that the bottlenecks are stifling local capacity and slowing Nigeria’s upstream growth. They raised the concerns in Lagos at the Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists, (NAPE) Pre-Conference Workshop themed “Navigating Nigeria’s Upstream Future: Exploration and Development Approaches vs. Energy Security Demand.” Publicity Secretary of PETAN, Dr Joan Faluyi, who spoke on execution capacity of her members, said the blames that Nigerian service providers lack capacity ignore the financial and procurement realities they face. Faluyi said the biggest problem was cycle time, with tender approval, award and mobilisation taking years to materialise, distorting pricing and execution. Curiously, the 2024 presidential directive is meant to accelerate oil and gas contract timelines, fast–track tendering process and approvals, incentivize investments in the sector and increase Nigeria’s crude oil production, bringing to question the implementation of the policy by the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB). Faluyi flagged procurement issues, long lead times, budget constraints and hostile financing environment where local banks lend at double-digit rates even for one year on a five-year project, while producers demand delivery at thin margins. She cited instances where a tender quoted four years ago becomes unexecutable due to foreign exchange shifts, price changes and geopolitical events, including situations where global shocks alter costs before mobilisation. “Our banks’ interest rates is double digit. You have a project that is five years, and they’re willing to finance one year. And these producers want you to deliver whatever service at a very small margin,” Faluyi said. “Some of them even specify your margin and say, you have to make nine percent. Someone that is producing or delivering a rig, it takes him so long to get that rig into the country? His bank is already counting. Then it takes him to mobilise, the bank is counting. Then it now takes him another 90 days in which these producers are saying they’re going to pay you whatever money they’re owing. At the end of the day, where is the profit?” She said the squeeze leaves service firms without ability to deliver, yet they are labelled as lacking capacity. She called for faster bid processing and alignment of finance and timing, noting that the same companies secure jobs outside Africa with short cycles and produce immediately. She said all members of the association share the same complaint that finance and timing must be aligned for effective production. NCDMB did not respond to the claims as its General Manager, Corporate Communications, Dr Obinna Ezeobi promised to get back to THISDAY but never did as of the time of filing this report. However, in his contribution to the discourse, Chairman of Energia Limited, Mr George Osahon, said the oil industry cannot work without service providers who hold the technology, recalling that Shell’s operating model discourages operators from owning rigs to avoid conflict of interest and inefficiency. Osahon said operators also face pressure to ensure contractors have capability and wherewithal to avoid debt and production losses, citing cases where a 25 to 30-day well takes 60 days, compared to the past when ExxonMobil drilled development wells in 10 days. He attributed part of the drop in performance to declining competencies across the industry, loss of training grounds like Shell’s Intership Training Programme (SITP) that previously built industry-wide skills, and dwindling industry-wide capacity building efforts. He also admitted that service providers bear the brunt of industry downturns, as when crude crashed to $10 per barrel, operators under financial pressure delayed payments due to non-performing loans, not out of wickedness, but due to the rollercoaster nature of the business. He noted the situation is now improving with rig count doubling in the last two years. On regulation, Osahon said regulators cannot monitor enough, contrasting Nigeria’s war room with Saudi Aramco’s real-time drilling control rooms where drill bits are steered remotely, saying Nigeria still has gaps to close. Delivering the keynote on behalf of Managing Director of Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Tony Attah, Vice President Exploration, Dr Johnbosco Uche, said energy security is not defined by resources underground but by value created above ground. He said Nigeria must sustain a continuous cycle of discovery, development and production, stressing that exploration is an act of belief in the future that replenishes reserves, while development and production solve today’s needs. According to him, Renaissance now views itself as an energy security company, with philosophy to safely receive, stabilize and grow assets, leveraging Infrastructure-Led Exploration and Near-Field Exploration to reduce time from prospect to production. “Pace matters. A resource that arrives too late cannot solve today’s energy challenge,” Uche said, adding that gas remains Nigeria’s most powerful tool for industrialisation and transformation, while people and innovation, not just technology, will determine success”, Uche said. .

title: $242m Petroleum Dispute: Court Grants UBA Interim Order Against Vitol, Four Shipping Firms
body: Wale Igbintade The Lagos State High Court has granted interim preservative orders of Mareva injunction in favour of United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc against Vitol SA, a Switzerland-based energy trading company, and four other shipping companies over a petroleum products diversion dispute involving $242 million. UBA alleged that Vitol wrongfully released cargoes of petroleum products consigned to the bank’s order under the relevant bills of lading. Addressing the court, Bode Olanipekun, SAN, lead counsel to UBA, urged the judge to grant the interim preservative orders against Vitol and the other shipping companies. In her ruling, Justice K. A. Jose granted three prayers in UBA’s application, including requests to restrain the dissipation of assets and dealings in funds up to the disputed amount by Vitol SA. “Prayers 1-3 are granted as prayed against the second respondent only,” the judge ruled. The application was brought pursuant to Order 43, Rule 1 of the High Court of Lagos State (Civil Procedure) Rules 2019 and Lagos State High Court Practice Direction No. 2 of 2019. In the substantive proceedings, UBA intends to contend that Vitol SA and the owners of the vessels are liable for alleged conversion, misrepresentation, and negligence arising from the non-delivery of the petroleum products. The bank also cited 34 financial institutions and public agencies, including commercial banks, merchant banks, microfinance banks, Nigerian Ports Authority, and Nigeria Customs Service, in connection with the application. In an affidavit supporting the application, UBA’s Group Head of Recoveries and Remedial Management, Anthony Chilaka, stated that the bank had issued a letter of credit in favour of Vitol SA to facilitate a petroleum products transaction. According to the affidavit, the cargo was transported to Nigeria, where the masters of the vessels issued several bills of lading. UBA further alleged that Vitol subsequently endorsed the bills of lading in favour of the bank and handed over the original copies to it. The bank maintained that the endorsement entitled it to take possession of the cargo upon completion of the voyage. However, Chilaka stated that UBA had not received the gasoil, despite the completion of the voyage. “The applicant has not been given possession of the gasoil despite completion of the voyage,” the affidavit stated. UBA alleged that the cargo was, instead, diverted for the benefit of another party, arguing that the failure to deliver the petroleum products amount to conversion and negligence. The bank further contended that the respondents had obligations arising from the transaction and the endorsement of the shipping documents, but failed to fulfil them. It alleged that cargoes associated with the transactions were diverted to other parties after the completion of their voyages rather than being delivered to UBA.

title: BOI Targets N1.35trn Loan Disbursement in 2027, Eyes 10-year Long Term Financing for Manufacturers, MSMEs
body: • Attained N645bn disbursement in 2025, funded 25% of manufacturing GDP, 6.5% agriculture lending Dike Onwuamaeze Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Bank of Industry (BOI), Dr. Olasupo Olusi, has announced that the bank is targeting an annual loan disbursement of N1.35 trillion to manufacturers and operators in the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in 2027. Olusi also said the bank was exploring various sources of capital that would enable it to grant real long-term loans of about 10-year tenure to manufacturers and other businesses. He stated these yesterday during the “MD/CEO BOI Meeting with Media Partners.” He said the bank disbursed N645 billion in 2025, which was the highest disbursement it had ever achieved. He also elaborated on BOI’s 2025-2027 corporate strategy that was being executed in three phases. Olusi said 2025 was “our foundation year, where we put in place the governance, the frameworks, the products and digital tools, while 2026 was the year of execution and scale, and 2027 will be the year we consolidate our results and meet our targets. He said the bank was currently at the mid-point of the strategy implementation, adding that the results so far tell that the strategy is working. He said BOI accounted for 6.5 per cent agricultural loans and 25 per cent of the manufacturing GDP. Olusi stated, “The results so far tell us that the strategy is working. In 2025, we disbursed N645 billion, which is the highest ever disbursement by the bank. This represents a 26 per cent increase on N510 billion we disbursed in 2024. “And our financing has reached 12,500 more businesses and helped to create or support 1.6 million jobs. “We disbursed over N120 billion to women-owned businesses, which again shows how much we are committed to delivering on our strategy to enhance opportunities for gender. “We are also on track across our thematic areas. MSMEs received over 41 per cent of our 2025 funding, even against our 35 per cent target. “Youths and women received 20 per cent each against our 15 per cent and 10 per cent minimum commitment, respectively. Olusi explained, “In infrastructure, we recorded N108 billion funding, including 100 mini-grids to power businesses and households, as well as broadband internet connectivity to over 700 communities. “We also achieved our disbursement targets for climate and social financing.” He stated that the bank embarked on a number of landmark capital raising activities that enabled it to deliver its disbursement targets. The capital raising activities included a landmark deal of nearly €2 billion (Euros), raised from three international banks, and in 2026, BOI was able to get five commitments from the African Export and Import Bank for a €75 million facility to support the Pharmaceutical Value Chain (PIVAC) in Nigeria. He stated, “Together, we have done more than €2.2 billion and N274 billion in new funding for Nigerian industries. “Investors have placed their money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline, our impact and our financial results. “We are already advancing new capital raising engagements with quite a number of international partners, including the likes of the African Development Bank, the Agence Française de Dévelopment and also pursuing further fundraising opportunities that are available within our domestic capital markets. “We have also expanded our financing toolkits with a non-interest banking products, which will enable us to promote financial inclusion and widen the range of financing structures available for eligible businesses who have interests in non-interest banking.” The CEO recounted that in the course of the last couple of years, the bank had managed the federal government’s N200 billion grants and loans intervention programme to the enterprise sector. He said the N75 billion MSME intervention funds and N75 billion manufacturing sector funds that were disbursed by BOI had delivered results. Olusi said, “We delivered more than 85 per cent of all these funds, reaching 957,400 grant beneficiaries, 9,000 MSMEs, and 104 large manufacturers across the country. “Through our Rural Area Program Investment for Development (RAPID) program, we have disbursed over N6.5 billion to nearly 1,000 rural enterprises across all 36 states and FCT of the country, supporting more than 8,000 jobs. “We have financed more than 100 mini-grids that have connected 11,000 households and businesses to electricity, many of them for the first time.” According to him, BOI’s strategy is dedicated to raising long term capital at a scale that would match Nigeria’s unending industrialisation needs, widening its reach to underserved segments of the economy, particularly MSMEs, women, young people, and rural enterprises. He said BOI’s target was to ensure that 35 per cent of its loans went to MSMEs, while lending to infrastructure and women-owned businesses accounted for 30 per cent and 15 per cent, respectively, of the bank’s loan book. He added that the bank would allocate 10 per cent and 15 per cent of its credit to digital and climate enterprises, respectively, while youth-owned enterprises will command 20 per cent of credits to MSMEs. Olusi stated, “Infrastructure remains a big pain on our economic development, so we have dedicated a large chunk of our finance, around 35 per cent for all of our large credits to finance infrastructure. “Women owned businesses are one of the most underserved in Nigeria. So, we have decided that we will direct at least 15 per cent of our financing to them under our strategy. “We have targeted 20 per cent of our MSMEs disbursement to youth owned businesses.” He said, “We are providing about 10 per cent of our entire portfolio to climate and sustainability. We want to finance clean energy, climate resilience investments, and of course the circular economy. “On the digital front, we are very committed also to financing technology-led businesses and digitisation of Nigerian enterprises by committing 15 per cent of our disbursement to the sector.”

title: Lubinets says upholding human rights during war is a matter of survival
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said this in an interview with RBC-Ukraine .
“If we say that human rights are not a priority right now, then how are we different from the Russians? Protecting democratic values is precisely the main argument for our partners to provide financial, military and diplomatic assistance,” the Ombudsman said.
