title: Russia Launches Massive Drone Attack on Sumy as Moscow Continues Strikes Despite Peace Talks
body:
Russian forces launched a massive overnight drone attack on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Sumy early Friday, Oct. 23, striking civilian infrastructure in three separate parts of the city, damaging residential buildings and injuring at least two people, Ukrainian authorities reported.
The attack was confirmed by Sumy Regional Military Administration chief Oleh Hryhorov, who said multiple Russian attack drones had reached their targets despite Ukrainian defensive efforts.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Tonight, the enemy carried out a massive attack on Sumy using strike drones,” Hryhorov wrote on his official Telegram channel .
“Unfortunately, some enemy drones reached their targets.”
According to the regional governor, Russian forces struck civilian infrastructure at three locations across the city, including residential areas of the Kovpakivskyi district.
At least two residents were injured, although the severity of their wounds was still being assessed.
Medical personnel were providing assistance, while emergency crews worked at the impact sites.
The damage and casualty figures were preliminary, with authorities continuing to assess the consequences of the attack.
The strikes marked another night of Russian attacks on civilian areas in Sumy, a regional capital near the Russian border that has faced repeated drone, missile and aerial bomb strikes throughout the war.
Residential buildings in the Kovpakivskyi district sustained damage, while emergency services worked to establish the full extent of destruction.
The repeated attacks have placed civilians, homes and essential urban services under continuing threat.
The latest bombardment came after another night of Russian missile and drone attacks on Oct. 22, when Ukrainian authorities reported casualties and widespread damage to civilian infrastructure across several regions.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles struck residential buildings, medical facilities, businesses and transport infrastructure, including sections of the metro system on the Southern Bridge.
The State Emergency Service reported one person killed and at least 22 injured in the capital as of Thursday morning, while emergency crews continued working at damaged sites.
Russian forces also struck parts of the Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Kherson regions during the preceding reporting period.
Russian attacks killed two civilians and injured nine in Donetsk region, while Kherson regional authorities reported one death and four injuries. Three people were killed and three wounded in Zaporizhzhia region.
President Zelensky warned that Moscow was taking advantage of slowing deliveries of Western air defense systems and an easing of sanctions pressure.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its partners for additional US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which are critical for defending against Russian ballistic missiles.
The president warned that Russia was exploiting shortages as it intensified attacks against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
He urged Ukraine’s partners to maintain economic pressure on Moscow while accelerating the delivery of air defense missiles.
In Brussels, NATO announced that Ukraine would be allowed to purchase weapons through the alliance’s central procurement agency on a case-by-case basis, potentially opening another avenue for obtaining urgently needed military equipment.
The Ukrainian government has warned that insufficient air defenses leave civilians increasingly vulnerable as Russia targets heating, electricity and other essential services before winter.
The continuing bombardment came despite Moscow’s announcement that it was prepared to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US next month.
Russia continues to demand that Ukraine withdraw from Ukrainian-controlled areas of Donetsk region and accept sweeping restrictions on its military and Western security relationships.
Kyiv has rejected those conditions, warning that they would undermine Ukrainian sovereignty and leave the country vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.
Russia’s relentless bombardment of Ukrainian cities underscores Kyiv’s concerns that Moscow is using peace talks to buy time while pressing ahead with its war.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: ‘Breast Is Best’? Ancient Greek Mothers Breastfed for Nearly Four Years
body: New archaeological research from Sicily reveals how breastfeeding continued well beyond infancy in an ancient Greek community, offering a rare insight into family life 2,400 years ago. In the ancient Greek city of Himera, breastfeeding could continue until children were approaching their fourth birthday. Yet new archaeological research suggests that while families shared certain childcare traditions, there were considerable differences in how individual children were fed. The study, published on 19 October in the European Journal of Archaeology, examined the diets of children who lived in the Sicilian settlement during the sixth and fifth centuries BC. Researchers found that breastfeeding was gradually reduced over several years, with other foods introduced from around three to four months and weaning typically completed between the ages of three and a half and four. Led by anthropologist Laurie Reitsema of the University of Georgia, alongside Abigail Shahar Gancz, Stefano Vassallo and Britney Kyle, the research offers a perspective on ancient Greek childhood rarely found in historical accounts. Rather than relying on written descriptions of how children should be raised, the team examined physical evidence of how they were actually fed. The researchers analysed carbon and nitrogen isotopes preserved in the bones of 58 children and adolescents and 27 adult women recovered from Himera’s cemeteries. These chemical markers provide evidence of diet, allowing scientists to investigate the transition from breast milk to other foods as children grew. Breastfeeding produces a recognisable chemical signature because infants receive their nutrients through their mothers’ milk. As children begin consuming other foods, that signature gradually changes. By examining these patterns and applying statistical modelling, the researchers estimated when breastfeeding was supplemented and when it eventually ended. The findings indicate that breast milk remained part of children’s diets for several years, even after other foods had been introduced. Importantly, the research does not suggest children were exclusively breastfed until the age of four. Rather, weaning was a prolonged process in which breast milk and other foods were consumed alongside one another. What makes the discovery particularly interesting is that families did not appear to follow an identical timetable. Although a general pattern emerged, the researchers identified considerable variation between individual children, suggesting that feeding practices reflected both shared traditions and decisions made within individual households. Himera provides a fascinating setting for exploring these differences. Founded by Greek colonists in the seventh century BC on Sicily’s northern coast, the city developed within a region influenced by Greek, Phoenician and indigenous Sicilian communities. Its population reflected a mixture of cultural backgrounds, raising questions about which customs families maintained and which they adapted. Archaeologists have investigated more than 13,000 burials at Himera, revealing extensive information about the city’s history, conflicts and burial traditions. The lives of its youngest inhabitants, however, have received comparatively little attention. Among the discoveries are nearly 500 small pottery vessels traditionally identified as baby bottles, known as gutti, recovered from graves. One child’s burial illustrated in the study contained such a vessel alongside a lamp and other pottery objects. Their presence is intriguing, although the researchers caution against assuming they were necessarily used for infant feeding. Similar vessels have also been discovered in adult burials, suggesting they may have carried symbolic or ceremonial significance. The skeletal evidence provides a different kind of insight. Unlike objects placed in graves, the chemical composition of children’s bones can reveal aspects of their diets during life. The researchers found that children’s diets differed from those of adults, with evidence suggesting they consumed proportionally more plant-based foods and less animal protein. These differences remained apparent until approximately nine or ten years of age, indicating that dietary distinctions between children and adults extended well beyond infancy. The findings also offer an interesting contrast with surviving ancient medical literature. Greek physicians such as Soranus and Galen, writing centuries later during the Roman period, recommended shorter breastfeeding durations than those estimated at Himera. Their advice, however, cannot be assumed to reflect the everyday practices of families living in earlier Greek settlements. The research raises broader questions about the transmission of customs across the ancient Greek world. Similar patterns of prolonged breastfeeding have been identified at Apollonia Pontica, a Greek settlement on the Black Sea coast, despite the considerable geographical distance between the two communities. For the researchers, these similarities suggest that some childcare practices may have been shared across Greek settlements, even as families adapted to different cultural and social environments. The findings cannot establish why individual mothers breastfed for different lengths of time. Household resources, maternal responsibilities, health and personal circumstances may all have influenced those decisions, but the archaeological evidence does not allow researchers to determine the precise reasons. Nor does the study establish whether prolonged breastfeeding improved children’s health or survival. The findings are based on skeletal remains from ancient cemeteries, meaning the individuals examined cannot necessarily represent every child or family in the wider population. Nevertheless, the research reveals something that conventional histories of ancient Greece rarely capture. Within a community shaped by different cultural traditions, families appear to have shared certain approaches to feeding their children while retaining considerable variation in how those practices were followed. The result is a more personal understanding of ancient Greek life, one in which the everyday decisions surrounding infant feeding offer insight into the experiences of mothers, children and families whose stories were otherwise largely absent from the historical record. title: 'Grave incitement': Heckler throws glass bottle at Netanyahu's motorcade near Mahaneh Yehuda market
body: A glass bottle was thrown toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's motorcade while driving past the Mahaneh Yehuda market in Jerusalem on Thursday night to celebrate his 77th birthday.Light rail service had temporarily been suspended to allow the motorcade to pass through unimpeded, with thousands of Israelis gathering to cheer on and watch the convoy pass.המוקד: בקבוק זכוכית נזרק לעבר שיירת ראש הממשלה נתניהו סמוך לשוק מחנה יהודה https://t.co/qmkNmtGFXJ— חדשות המוקד (@hamoked_il) October 22, 2026According to footage shared online of the incident, security personnel quickly jumped the barricade holding back the gathered crowd in attempt to locate the individual who threw the bottle. The motorcade continued undisturbed.Upon arriving at Mahaneh Yehuda, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, were greeted with celebratory birthday music.Footage online appeared to show attendees waving Likud flags, as well as the Iranian Lion and Sun flag, and Netanayhu waving a bouquet of flowers before throwing it back out to the gathered crowd.ראש הממשלה בנימין נתניהו הגיע כעת לשוק מחנה יהודה בירושלים https://t.co/PiZ8bXuP4i— כל החדשות בזמן אמת (@Saher_News_24_7) October 22, 2026National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir condemned the bottle-throwing, calling the incident "very grave.""The incitement directed against the prime minister, and the actions taken against him, have consequences and repercussions. I say to those on the Left: act responsibly. Words can kill."Netanyahu visits Tel Aviv's HaTikva MarketNetanyahu's visit to Mahaneh Yehuda followed an earlier Thursday trip by the prime minister to Tel Aviv's HaTikva Market.There, he was confronted by an angry spectator who asked "why did you send Hamas millions?" according to footage online. When the individual attempted to film the incident, Likud supporters in attendence reportedly knocked his phone from his hands and physically shoving him from the space.Israeli media reported that Michel Iluz, father of deceased hostage Guy Iluz, Gil Dickmann, cousin of deceased hostage Carmel Gat, and Einav Zangauker, the mother of former hostage Matan Zangauker, were also in attendence.The three were there to affirm to Netanyahu that those in power on October 7 must step down from government. While there, individuals at the market attacked Iluz. Netanyahu was not in the area at the time."We came to tell Netanyahu the truth, that he is one of those responsible for the massacre.  That no person who was in a position of authority on October 7 can continue, certainly not the prime minister," wrote Zangauker on X/Twitter. "They called us traitors, enemies of the state, spat on us, threw vegetables at us. title: Russian disinformation campaign targets pro-Ukraine candidates ahead of midterms, lawmakers say
body:
Russia is running a covert online disinformation campaign targeting U.S. politicians who support Ukraine, two Democratic lawmakers said on Oct. 21.
Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes, two Democrats, told reporters that a recent intelligence briefing revealed Russian efforts to undermine U.S. backing for Ukraine. The misinformation campaign was particularly targeted against Democratic and Republican candidates running in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections who have expressed support for Ukraine.
The lawmakers’ comments come amid an apparent softening of the Trump administration’s stance toward Moscow. President Donald Trump recently announced that the US would allow Russia to export diesel into U.S. markets, and on Oct. 16 waived sanctions passed by bipartisan legislation aimed at countries that purchase Russian energy.
Warner and Himes said they were given a security briefing by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. While the details of the briefing were classified, the two lawmakers said Russia was conducting a misinformation campaign targeted at Democrats running in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, Reuters reported.
The campaign uses social media to sow distrust over the integrity of U.S. elections and generate "a sense of chaos and anarchy," the lawmakers said, according to Politico . They added that artificial intelligence has accelerated these efforts, allowing Russian operatives to more effectively target Americans online.
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for re-election in Georgia, and James Talarico, a Democrat running for a Senate seat in Texas, are being especially targeted by AI-generated ads, Warner said.
Recent AI-generated videos targeting Talarico that emerged after early voting began in Texas were likely made by a Russian government-backed group, three teams of disinformation researchers said Oct. 22, according to NBC News .
Russian disinformation campaigns , which have also targeted France , Moldova and the United Kingdom , have become a common feature of U.S. elections .
In 2016, a grand jury indicted twelve Russian nationals for interfering with the U.S. presidential elections.
The Department of Justice said that the Russian operatives "engaged in a sustained effort" to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic National Committee, the Democratic Congressional Committee, and the Presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton, in a 2018 press release .

title: Dressmaker and eight simulator games that make everyday tasks surprisingly fun
body: Not every video game needs an elaborate story, a sprawling open world or enemies to defeat. Sometimes, the simple satisfaction of completing a task is enough to keep players entertained for hours. Simulation games have found creative ways to turn ordinary activities into absorbing experiences. Whether making coffee, repairing a car or painting a picture, players can explore different crafts without the expense, mess or consequences of attempting them in real life. Some reproduce the tools and techniques of their chosen activity with surprising attention to detail. Others encourage experimentation, allowing players to make mistakes and discover their own approach. The recent success of Dressmaker on Steam is a compelling example of this appeal. Here are nine games that make the seemingly ordinary entertaining. Dressmaker (2026) Released on September 21, Dressmaker has become an unlikely hit on Steam , attracting more than 11,000 purchaser reviews in less than three weeks, with an overwhelmingly positive reception. Developed by Cozy Lives, the game turns sewing into a surprisingly involved creative process. Players operate a dressmaking shop, choosing fabrics, arranging patterns, cutting material and stitching garments together using a virtual sewing machine. Every decision, down to the placement of a button or lace trim, affects the finished dress. There are customers to satisfy, commissions to complete and plenty of opportunities for experimentation. Those feeling mischievous can even deliberately produce terrible outfits. Master of Pottery (2026) Few creative pursuits are as satisfying to watch as a lump of clay being transformed into a carefully shaped vase. Master of Pottery places that process in the player's hands. Inspired by traditional Chinese pottery techniques, the game recreates several stages of ceramic production, including shaping, firing, painting and glazing. Players can experiment with different forms and decorative patterns before exhibiting their finished works in a personal showroom. Visitors have their own preferences, and successful creations can attract buyers. First available in early access in 2019 before its full release in September 2026, the game combines artistic experimentation with the pleasure of gradually building a collection of handmade objects. Espresso Tycoon (2023) Anyone who has watched a barista prepare an elaborate coffee order might have wondered whether they could do a better job. Espresso Tycoon offers the opportunity to find out, albeit with considerably more responsibility than making the occasional cappuccino does. Its 3D coffee editor allows players to experiment with ingredients and create customised drinks, while customer preferences help determine which recipes succeed. The simulation also places players in charge of running a cafe. Hiring employees, managing supplies, decorating the premises and balancing finances are all part of the experience. It is an interesting combination of culinary creativity and entrepreneurship, particularly for anyone who has entertained the idea of opening their own coffee shop. Garden Life: A Cozy Simulator (2024) Gardening requires patience, attention and an understanding that plants rarely grow according to a convenient schedule. Garden Life captures much of that process while removing some of its frustrations. Players inherit an abandoned community garden and gradually restore it by planting flowers , removing weeds, watering plants and pruning overgrown vegetation. Its gardening mechanics draw on real techniques, while a procedural growth system allows individual plants to develop differently depending on their surroundings. There are also neighbours to help, flowers to sell and new areas to unlock. For players without access to a garden or those whose real plants have a habit of dying, it offers an inviting alternative. SuchArt: Genius Artist Simulator (2022) Artistic ambition meets a wonderfully absurd premise in SuchArt , which places players in the role of a supposedly brilliant artist living in the year 2130. Working from a studio in space, they can paint almost anything using brushes, palette knives, stencils and a variety of unconventional implements. The game's physics-driven painting system allows colours to mix and different tools to produce distinct textures and strokes. It has also found an appreciative audience, with 97 per cent positive feedback among more than 2,000 English-language Steam reviews. Perhaps its greatest attraction is the absence of artistic restrictions. Players can pursue serious painting projects or cover their surroundings in increasingly chaotic experiments, with no actual studio to clean afterwards. Cooking Simulator (2019) Preparing a meal becomes considerably more complicated when every ingredient, utensil and cooking accident is governed by a physics engine. Cooking Simulator recreates a professional kitchen with ovens, grills, knives, blenders and more than 140 ingredients. Players must chop, season, cook and plate dishes while paying attention to timing and temperature. Developer Big Cheese Studio has reported sales of one million copies of the game and its add-ons, demonstrating the appetite for virtual cooking. While its career mode encourages precision across more than 80 recipes, the sandbox mode is arguably where things become most entertaining. Players can experiment freely, break equipment or accidentally set the kitchen ablaze. It is a game that rewards culinary competence while enthusiastically accommodating incompetence. Car Mechanic Simulator 2021 (2021) Modern cars can be intimidating machines, particularly for those who struggle to identify anything beneath the bonnet. Car Mechanic Simulator 2021 attempts to demystify their workings through an extensive virtual workshop featuring more than 4,000 individual parts. Players diagnose mechanical problems, dismantle components, replace damaged equipment and gradually restore vehicles to working condition. There are customer jobs to complete, garages to upgrade, and neglected cars to discover at auctions and junkyards. More ambitious projects involve rebuilding vehicles from almost nothing. The simulation offers an unusually detailed look at automotive maintenance, making it especially appealing to car enthusiasts interested in understanding the mechanical processes behind their favourite machines. PowerWash Simulator (2022) There is something strangely mesmerising about watching a filthy surface become clean under a jet of high-pressure water. PowerWash Simulator builds an entire game around that sensation, asking players to remove accumulated dirt from houses, vehicles, playgrounds and other increasingly elaborate locations. Its success has been remarkable. Developer FuturLab announced in March 2025 that the game had reached 17 million players across platforms, a milestone that helped pave the way for a sequel. Different nozzles and cleaning equipment help tackle stubborn grime, while completed jobs earn money for better tools. There are no elaborate strategies to devise. Sometimes, the pleasure of seeing a job properly finished is reward enough. Sticky Business (2023) Designing stickers sounds like a modest occupation, but Sticky Business turns it into a colourful creative enterprise. Players run an online sticker shop, combining illustrations, shapes and decorative elements to produce original designs. These are arranged into printable sheets, with efficient layouts helping to reduce wasted materials. Customer orders must then be packaged and sent, with additional decorations and little gifts available to personalise each delivery. The game also introduces a gentle narrative element through customers whose stories unfold as they return to the shop. It captures the appeal of running a small creative business, from the satisfaction of designing something original to the pleasure of seeing someone appreciate the finished product.

title: Capt Smit Machchhar is ‘more than a pilot’
body: Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week Stay blessed, Capt Machchhar This is regarding Mina Al-Oraibi’s conversation with flydubai captain Smit Machchhar (October 19): Capt Machchhar said: “It’s about moving forward, not staying stuck in the moment.” I see a courageous, honest man who has chosen gratitude over bitterness. May God bless you, captain. – Joey Habgood Capt Machchhar suffered a lot in those moments, when he was being attacked. He must have been terrified. Yet he showed the courage to fight back and ended up saving so many lives. It’s in moments like these that a person’s true character is revealed. – Divyanshi I’ve waited so much time to finally see Capt Machchhar in an interview. Thanks to The National News for this and thanks to the captain for his courage. May God bless him more, and hoping for that speedy and full recovery. I’ve been following this flydubai story ever since it happened, and I’m getting emotional watching this. – Hanna Alexandria Abordo Your courage, strength and incredible willpower in the face of danger are truly inspiring. Your calmness, quick decisions and dedication to protecting every passenger reflect the true spirit of a pilot. You didn’t just fly a plane that day; you showed the world what courage, responsibility and humanity really mean. You are more than a pilot – you are a real-life hero. We salute you. We love you, and we will always remember your bravery. – Vipin A proud moment for the UAE I write in reference to the article UAE’s Ali Alhosani becomes first Emirati to be elected executive director at IMF (October 16): an important appointment that I am confident will bring even greater prestige and recognition to the UAE. Congratulations to Ali Alhosani on this remarkable achievement. May this be the beginning of a successful journey, delivering meaningful results, strengthening the UAE’s international standing, and creating new opportunities for the country and its future generations. Wishing him every success in this important role. – Luca Barton Conti, Calolziocorte, Italy A proud moment for the UAE. Ali Alhosani is the first Emirati executive director at the IMF, and many young Arab professionals in finance will look up to this. Mabrook. – Adnan Feroz, Dubai Congratulations. This is really exceptionally and commendable for the UAE, and for Ali Alhosani. This is big. – Pratik Das, Dubai Wow, what an honour! Congratulations to Ali Alhosani and the whole UAE nation. – Marsha Lipton, Abu Dhabi Tackling obesity I read Shireena Al Nowais’s article Weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Foundayo to be packaged in UAE (October 20) with keen interest. Obesity has become a major global health concern, affecting people around the world. Proactive measures to promote healthier lifestyles, improve access to appropriate treatment and raise awareness about the long-term consequences of obesity are essential. Of course, while these medicines may provide valuable support for eligible patients, their use should always be guided by qualified healthcare professionals, with due attention to safety and individual health needs. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India

title: US lifting sanctions on 'dark fleet' not expected to solve tanker crisis
body: Lifting sanctions on “dark fleet” or shadow fleet vessels is not expected to solve the tanker crisis engulfing oil markets while the Iran war continues and owners remain wary of sailing through the Strait of Hormuz and risking crews' safety. The US move “could provide some relief, particularly around the Arabian Gulf where tanker availability has been strained, but I wouldn't expect it to solve the current tanker crisis”, said Salih Yilmaz, senior industry analyst of energy at Bloomberg Intelligence. The administration of US President Donald Trump this week authorised the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in a move to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude and ease pressure on oil prices that have surged since the outbreak of Iran war in February. “A large share of sanctioned vessels appears to be already operating in Russian, Iranian or other restricted trades rather than sitting idle, so sanctions relief would mainly redistribute existing capacity into mainstream markets,” Mr Yilmaz added. Another big constraint is ship owner’s reluctance to operate in the Arabian Gulf as attacks on tankers continue, killing and injuring crew members. There have been 120 confirmed attacks on ships as of October 22, with 22 seafarer fatalities since the war began in February, according to the latest update from the International Maritime Organisation . Tanker owners are paying as much as $100,000 per month to ship's captains, along with a bonus of $50,000 for each trip, because of risks involved in sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a recent Financial Times report. “The bigger constraint today is the risk of operating around Hormuz. Owners are demanding very high compensation for exposing vessels and crews to attacks,” Mr Yilmaz said. The US government is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport non-sanctioned oil, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said at an event in New York this week. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet'," Mr Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more.” Wanying Zhang, a freight analyst at Vortexa, was also not optimistic about the US move increasing tanker availability in the markets. “Our analysis suggests that any easing of Ofac [Office of Foreign Assets Control] sanctions is unlikely to trigger a significant return of sanctioned tankers to mainstream trades,” she said. “A substantial share of Ofac sanctioned tankers remain subject to UK or EU sanctions, which could continue to restrict their access to European trades even if US restrictions are lifted.” Ofac is a financial intelligence and enforcement agency of the US Treasury Department that administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on US foreign policy and national security goals. It has been imposing sanctions on vessels linked to Iran and Russia for carrying crude to global markets. The relatively old age of these vessels could also delay their return to mainstream trade, given potential maintenance, inspection, insurance and commercial requirements. About 70 per cent of Ofac-listed tankers are at least 20 years old which limits the number likely to be accepted by mainstream charterers, analysts added. Ship broker Braemar said 170 very large crude carriers (VLCCs) were currently under US sanctions. It added that only 44 vessels are under 20 years old and acceptable to charterers, with 33 at least 25 years old and 92 between 20 and 24 years old. “Given the advanced age of most the ships sanctioned by the US, and the fact that a lot of the ships sanctioned by the US are also sanctioned by the EU or UK, we do not expect this move to lead to too many extra additions to the available tanker fleet,” said Mary Melton, senior tanker analyst at Braemar.

title: The UN's next leader must be given room to deliver
body: The UN was founded in 1945 on the belief that countries emerging from an apocalyptic global conflict could rebuild and find common ground. Eight decades later, that principle remains important, but as wars multiply and alliances shift, there are growing questions about the organisation’s ability to meet the demands of a fragile world. With its leadership model and institutional structure designed for another era, can the UN to renew itself? As the race to succeed Antonio Guterres as secretary general heats up, the answer to this question becomes even more demanding. A new era with a new leader can give the UN new impetus, even if many of the challenges remain. The candidacy of Lana Nusseibeh , UAE Minister of State and former permanent representative to the UN, brings even more interest to this issue for the UAE and the wider region. Her credentials as a candidate are impressive. Ms Nusseibeh’s diplomatic experience and familiarity with multilateral negotiations make her a serious contender for the secretary general’s office. She represented the UAE during its two-year term as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council in 2022-2023. Her bid deserves real consideration, even as other candidates bring their own considerable strengths. The prospect of an Arab woman from the Middle East leading the world’s foremost multilateral institution is also significant. When long-standing security relationships become less certain, and threats to shipping and regional stability intensify, the international community needs effective diplomacy and co-operation. The UN too often struggles to translate its convening power into action. Its deliberations can be paralysed by divisions among major powers, while its agencies face overlapping responsibilities and limited resources. Such apparent inertia erodes public confidence in multilateralism itself. The next secretary general, whoever it may be, must do more than mediate disputes and issue statements. The office should become a catalyst for institutional reform, with a stronger emphasis on early intervention, effective mediation and better co-ordination between UN agencies. Clear priorities and measurable accountability would help ensure that commitments translate into tangible improvements that people can see. The prospect of an Arab woman from the Middle East leading the world’s foremost multilateral institution is significant Ms Nusseibeh has spoken of bringing countries together and achieving concrete results. These are welcome ambitions that build on the UAE’s experience of working with states that hold divergent interests. For the UN, which increasingly needs to restore trust across geopolitical divides, such an approach could be rejuvenating. However, even an accomplished secretary general cannot overcome every obstacle alone. Meaningful reform will require member states, particularly the permanent members of the Security Council, to accept that a lack of direction and consensus carries its own costs. The UN remains too important to be allowed to drift into irrelevance. Its next leader must have the vision to renew its purpose, and its member states must give that leader room to deliver. The measure of success is not in promises but results.

title: This I Believe (1952)
body:
I am not going to talk about religious beliefs but about matters so obvious that it has gone out of style to mention them. I believe in my neighbors. I know their faults, and I know that their virtues far outweigh their faults. Take Father Michael down our road a piece. I'm not of his creed, but I know that goodness and charity and loving kindness shine in his daily actions. I believe in Father Mike. If I'm in trouble, I'll go to him. My next-door neighbor is a veterinary doctor. Doc will get out of bed after a hard day to help a stray cat. No fee -- no prospect of a fee -- I believe in Doc. I believe in my townspeople. You can knock on any door in our town saying, "I'm hungry," and you will be fed. Our town is no exception. I've found the same ready charity everywhere. But for the one who says, "To heck with you -- I got mine," there are a hundred, a thousand who will say, "Sure, pal, sit down." I know that despite all warnings against hitchhikers I can step up to the highway, thumb for a ride and in a few minutes a car or a truck will stop and someone will say, "Climb in Mac -- how far you going?" I believe in my fellow citizens. Our headlines are splashed with crime yet for every criminal there are 10,000 honest, decent, kindly men. If it were not so, no child would live to grow up. Business could not go on from day to day. Decency is not news. It is buried in the obituaries, but is a force stronger than crime. I believe in the patient gallantry of nurses and the tedious sacrifices of teachers. I believe in the unseen and unending fight against desperate odds that goes on quietly in almost every home in the land. I believe in the honest craft of workmen. Take a look around you. There never were enough bosses to check up on all that work. From Independence Hall to the Grand Coulee Dam, these things were built level and square by craftsmen who were honest in their bones. I believe that almost all politicians are honest ... there are hundreds of politicians, low paid or not paid at all, doing their level best without thanks or glory to make our system work. If this were not true we would never have gotten past the 13 colonies. And finally, I believe in my whole race. Yellow, white, black, red, brown. In the honesty, courage, intelligence, durability, and goodness of the overwhelming majority of my brothers and sisters everywhere on this planet. I am proud to be a human being. I believe that we have come this far by the skin of our teeth. That we always make it just by the skin of our teeth, but that we will always make it. Survive. Endure. I believe that this hairless embryo with the aching, oversize brain case and the opposable thumb, this animal barely up from the apes will endure. Will endure longer than his home planet -- will spread out to the stars and beyond, carrying with him his honesty and his insatiable curiosity, his unlimited courage and his noble essential decency. This I believe. --Robert A. Heinlein

I believe in my townspeople. You can knock on any door in our town saying, "I'm hungry," and you will be fed. Our town is no exception. I've found the same ready charity everywhere. But for the one who says, "To heck with you -- I got mine," there are a hundred, a thousand who will say, "Sure, pal, sit down." I know that despite all warnings against hitchhikers I can step up to the highway, thumb for a ride and in a few minutes a car or a truck will stop and someone will say, "Climb in Mac -- how far you going?" I believe in my fellow citizens. Our headlines are splashed with crime yet for every criminal there are 10,000 honest, decent, kindly men. If it were not so, no child would live to grow up. Business could not go on from day to day. Decency is not news. It is buried in the obituaries, but is a force stronger than crime. I believe in the patient gallantry of nurses and the tedious sacrifices of teachers. I believe in the unseen and unending fight against desperate odds that goes on quietly in almost every home in the land. I believe in the honest craft of workmen. Take a look around you. There never were enough bosses to check up on all that work. From Independence Hall to the Grand Coulee Dam, these things were built level and square by craftsmen who were honest in their bones. I believe that almost all politicians are honest ... there are hundreds of politicians, low paid or not paid at all, doing their level best without thanks or glory to make our system work. If this were not true we would never have gotten past the 13 colonies. And finally, I believe in my whole race. Yellow, white, black, red, brown. In the honesty, courage, intelligence, durability, and goodness of the overwhelming majority of my brothers and sisters everywhere on this planet. I am proud to be a human being. I believe that we have come this far by the skin of our teeth. That we always make it just by the skin of our teeth, but that we will always make it. Survive. Endure. I believe that this hairless embryo with the aching, oversize brain case and the opposable thumb, this animal barely up from the apes will endure. Will endure longer than his home planet -- will spread out to the stars and beyond, carrying with him his honesty and his insatiable curiosity, his unlimited courage and his noble essential decency. This I believe. --Robert A. Heinlein

Thank you for posting this, but... This first aired in 1952, and Heinlein died in 1988. Please, please correct the date. That sort of accuracy... would have been important to Robert.
Discussion notes from Wednesday ... What do I believe? Accumulation of wealth is accumulation of sin. Inconvenient Truth This author hasn't lived in my neighbhorhood; it's hard to trust! The problem of our times is values. A felon is disallowed to vote for the rest of your life; assumes that once you make a mistake, you're not a good person. What I am is more important than what I believe in. I stayed with my friend for two days; another friend stayed in the same place and saw God . It's all about perspective. You have earn your beliefs; you can't just believe. By being who you are, you allow others a chance to be who they are. If everyone gave, there wouldn't be homeless. I wonder if this is true elsewhere? "southern hospitality"? Was try to help three women who didn't speak much English. Cops pulls us over and asks, "Why I want to do good?" Maybe it's my youth, but I believe in the optimism of the passage. Person behind me paid for me at the grocery store when I forgot my wallet. Time and time again, good has always prevailed in my life. Whatever I end up believeing will become true; but you have to truly believe it, can't fake it. Can't project your belief to your kids; they have to find it themselves. Lost our license during a family trip to Hawaii; the receptionist called her boyfriend at midnight to help. Bonanza of goodness. My world is a projection of my own self; I gotta take full responsibility. 'Inconvenient Truth' movie made me get a hybrid. Life has made me a believer. Got a flat tire on 280 freeway and dear old man helped me out. We are products of multiple circumstances and multiple realities; Heinlen starts with his neighbors, goes to towns people and goes to the whole race. We have to start with our corner of the world. There has to be critical mass of people who believe in a particular for mass adoption of that practice. People really need to know that others care about what they care about. Of all the beliefs, you must believe in yourself first. Best thing you can do for someone is to make them self-sustaining. Goodness is an experience, not words. Accumulation: there's needs and then wants; when you stick with your needs, you wants get taken care of. I tend to be tragically optimistic; and I have been hurt by it. Can't have good without bad. X-men III: power of belief can carry you against all odds. Played a game called "Would you rather?" Trust everyone or no one? Made us realize that without trust, our world would be horrible place to live. I feel like I live like this guy's world; but you need critical mass. I believe in openness; open heart opens doors. 50 facts to change world -- give your phone number to five neighbors you don't know. Why not go a little farther and make 'em a meal? At the end of the day, just do 10 pay-it-forward acts for every goodness you receive and humanity will be fine. Hide full comment

title: ‘Starshield Still Limited’ – Zelensky Says Restrictions Continue to Hamper Ukraine’s Drone Defenses
body:
Ukraine’s military satellite communications remain restricted, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour published Thursday, Oct. 22, warning that the limitations continue to undermine Ukraine’s ability to intercept fast-moving Russian attack drones.
Separately, US President Donald Trump said Thursday that Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s satellite service, but declined to confirm whether he personally intervened to have the restrictions lifted.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that he had called Musk and requested the restoration of the service.
It was not immediately clear whether the reported restoration had significantly improved Ukraine’s satellite communications capabilities.
In the CNN interview, Zelensky described continuing restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, SpaceX’s satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces.
“Now it’s still limited,” Zelensky said.
CNN reported that while some Ukrainian military units experienced higher connection speeds following the reported restoration of Starshield, the improvements were uneven and speed restrictions remained in place.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN that the available speeds were “clearly not enough to intercept jet-powered drones.”
Zelensky explained that Ukraine had developed high-speed interceptor drones capable of destroying Russian jet-powered Shaheds, but the restrictions had severely reduced their operational capabilities.
“When an Iranian drone goes with a speed of 450 or 500 kilometers per hour, and you limit [the speed] one night to 70 or even 100, you cannot intercept anything,” Zelensky said. “And this is terrible.”
Zelensky clarified that Ukraine does not use Starlink to strike Russian military or energy facilities on Russian territory.
“We don’t attack Russian military targets or energy targets using Starlink. Never,” he said. “That’s why it was strange they limited us in Ukraine. It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves.”
Asked who was responsible for limiting Ukraine’s satellite communications, Zelensky said he did not know whether the decision originated with SpaceX or government institutions.
“Technically, I think SpaceX can do it. But whether the decision comes from them or from some institutions, I don’t know.”
The question of responsibility has become increasingly contentious in Washington.
Musk has said Starshield, the military-grade satellite service, is controlled by the US government, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Starlink is a commercial product whose operating decisions are made by SpaceX.
Rubio has also said that Ukraine’s request for broader access to Starshield remains under discussion.
The Pentagon has denied issuing instructions to slow the system.
The conflicting accounts have left the cause of the restrictions unresolved, even as Ukrainian forces continue to report reduced capabilities.
Zelensky also confirmed that Ukraine’s access to critical early-warning intelligence about Russian ballistic missile launches had been restored following discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
He said Ukraine had experienced serious problems receiving warnings, leaving civilians without crucial information needed to reach shelters before incoming missiles struck.
“We had real problems with intelligence,” Zelensky said.
He explained that the missing information concerned Russian ballistic missile launches and was essential to protecting the civilian population.
“We didn’t get this message. That’s why it was so dangerous for us.”
Zelensky said he raised the matter directly with Rubio and requested the restoration of intelligence sharing.
“Now intelligence works,” he confirmed. “Thanks to the secretary, thanks to Congress, thanks to the president. I don’t know who did it, but thanks. It came back.”
Rubio has denied that the US ordered any interruption in intelligence sharing, saying American policy had not changed.
Zelensky also strongly opposed easing sanctions against Russia, warning that additional revenues would allow Moscow to finance its continuing invasion.
His remarks followed disagreements over recent US decisions affecting Russian energy exports.
The Ukrainian president emphasized that his concerns were not personal disagreements with Trump but reflected Ukraine’s security interests.
“I think that if you lift sanctions, you make him stronger,” Zelensky said.
He warned that concessions would not satisfy the Kremlin.
“If you give something to Putin, he will need everything. He will want everything, and will not calm down before he has it all.”
Zelensky argued that increasing Russian revenues would provide additional resources for Moscow’s military campaign.
“And it will only give much more money for Putin for this war. And that’s why I’m against it.”
He stressed that Ukraine’s position was not simply about the amount of land under Russian control.
“For us, our land is very important. Because it’s about people. It’s not about kilometers,” he said.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainians had sacrificed their lives defending the country’s sovereignty and independence.
“Nobody will recognize these territories which are temporarily occupied as Russian territories,” he said.
He said Ukraine was prepared to pursue negotiations aimed at stopping the killing, regardless of the terminology used.
“We can call it ceasefire. We can call it stop the killings. We can call it freeze the conflict,” he said.
“The only one thing what is important – not the name, the result.”
Zelensky insisted that any discussion concerning Ukrainian territory must involve Ukraine directly and take place at the level of national leaders.
“Putin is playing, you know. He’s a player,” Zelensky said. “It’s a pity because he plays with the lives of other people.”
Despite the continuing Russian attacks, Zelensky described his recent meeting with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Oslo as productive.
He expressed hope that further negotiations could produce progress toward ending the war.
He warned that Moscow’s objective remained to destroy Ukraine’s infrastructure, undermine civilian morale and weaken the country’s ability to defend itself.
Zelensky closed the interview with an appeal for additional Patriot interceptor missiles and the restoration of satellite communications needed to defend Ukrainian cities.
Acknowledging Washington’s focus on the Middle East, he stressed that Ukraine was not asking the US to abandon its other commitments.
“We don’t want to compare. We’re just asking not to forget about us,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine was prepared to pay for additional interceptors, he emphasized, but European-funded supplies remained insufficient to protect the country from Russian attacks.
Despite the shortages and continuing restrictions, Zelensky vowed that Ukraine would keep fighting, regardless of whether its partners could immediately meet its requests.
“We will do everything to bring peace closer, but we will not let Putin win this war.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
body: Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with its growing demand for what comes next. On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the Alem.AI program. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy. Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models. Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said. He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.” The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems. Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture. Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people. “If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.” Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally. Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity. For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI. “I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.” The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace. Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships. Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials. “What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.” Kazakhtelecom , the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale. AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them. Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow. More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute. Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications. Today’s announcements represent different layers of that stack — infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale. title: Woman diagnosed with arthritis after 10 years of pain dismissed as stress
body: When Afna Shanavas first complained of pain at 16, doctors suspected stress. It would take another 10 years for her to discover she had arthritis. Writing during school exams became increasingly painful, and she was constantly exhausted. But despite visits to specialists, her symptoms were repeatedly treated with painkillers and she was asked to rest. “I knew I was in pain, but people did not believe me,” Ms Shanavas, now 26, said. “My mother took me to orthopaedic and neurological specialists, and the answer was always painkillers. “Because I was doing well in academics and sports, one doctor suggested I was under too much pressure and that my parents were expecting too much from me.” “I was even referred to a psychologist because doctors thought the pain was psychosomatic.” Ms Shanavas, a psychologist, has now finally been diagnosed with inflammatory polyarthropathy and ankylosing spondylitis, two conditions that can cause chronic pain and inflammation. Cycle of pain At 17, while in Grade 12, she had experienced a severe episode in which her neck seized up. She was admitted to hospital for emergency treatment amid concerns that she might be having a stroke. Doctors later ruled out a stroke. While recovering in intensive care, Ms Shanavas decided to pursue a career in psychology, hoping to better understand the relationship between the brain and physical health. The cause of her symptoms remained elusive despite consultations with doctors in the UAE and India. However, a minor cut to a finger that refused to heal led to rheumatology tests in Sharjah. “I had never even heard of a rheumatologist , who did an antinuclear antibody test, which helps guide investigations to understand why my finger cut was not healing,” said Ms Shanavas. The ANA test was positive, although several other markers were negative. Ms Shanavas subsequently became pregnant and postponed further investigations. After her pregnancy, her symptoms worsened. It was only then that she underwent further investigations and was diagnosed with inflammatory polyarthropathy and ankylosing spondylitis Inflammatory polyarthropathy, or polyarthritis, is an autoimmune condition that causes inflammation in five or more joints. As a type of arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis usually affects the spine and pelvis, reducing flexibility and leading to a stiff, hunched-over posture. “It was a huge surprise as I thought this was a disease for the elderly,” she said. The conditions are usually only diagnosed in people under 45 following three months of chronic pain and an in-depth evaluation of medical history, a physical examination, internal imaging and blood tests. Ms Shanavas is now urging people to recognise that arthritis can affect young people , too. Invisible condition Ms Shanavas, now head of inclusion and well-being at The Oxford School in Dubai, takes several medications to manage her symptoms. Her treatment schedule includes a biological injection every two weeks that slows down her overactive immune system, as well as multiple probiotics, supplements and corticosteroid creams to manage her flare-ups. She has kept a journal documenting her experiences over the past decade, which she hopes to publish. One of the most difficult aspects of living with the condition, she said, is that its effects are not always visible to others. “The hardest part is that I can look completely fine on the outside,” she said. “People don’t always understand why I need a day off. They cannot see the pain or fatigue. “I have often felt misunderstood because of this.” Rare in young people Arthritis in young people remains relatively rare. It is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions affecting the joints and surrounding tissues. Symptoms and causes vary, and some forms can begin in childhood or early adulthood. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory condition that commonly develops in adulthood, while osteoarthritis is associated with changes in the joint's structure and becomes more common with age. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis refers to a group of inflammatory conditions that begin before the age of 16. Dr Humeira Badsha, a rheumatologist in Dubai, said arthritis care was moving away from general pain relief towards precision medicine and individualised therapy. “Treatment is increasingly targeted at the specific inflammatory pathways driving each patient's disease,” she said. “Anyone on chronic, long-term medication needs a thorough baseline medication review before a new drug is started, and regular monitoring afterwards. “Arthritis can appear at any age, depending entirely on the underlying classification.” GLP-1 weight-loss therapies can help arthritis by reducing wear and tear on overstressed joints. Dr Usama Hassan Saleh, a consultant in orthopaedic surgery at the Medcare Orthopaedics and Spine Hospital in Dubai, said genetics can also play a role. “Some forms of arthritis, including osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, have a hereditary component, meaning that having a close relative with the condition may increase a person's risk,” he said. “However, family history does not mean that someone will inevitably develop arthritis, as other lifestyle and environmental factors can also contribute.” Early symptoms include joint pain, stiffness, swelling and difficulty moving the affected area. “Seeking medical advice early can help establish the type of arthritis and ensure that appropriate treatment begins promptly,” said Dr Saleh. “With the right combination of medical care and lifestyle measures, many people can manage their symptoms, remain active and maintain a good quality of life.”

title: Israel's elections: What would a new government change?
body: Israelis will vote on Tuesday in the first national election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and subsequent war on Gaza . Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s Likud party could win, but polls are showing that opposition candidates also have a good chance. No single party is likely to secure a majority. Whoever wins will almost certainly have to form a coalition. Israelis will be casting their ballots with security and the economy among their main concerns. Palestinians, who cannot vote, are also waiting to see whether a new, potentially less right-wing government will be elected. Under Mr Netanyahu, the West Bank has experienced increasing settler violence and land grabs. In Gaza, a post-ceasefire plan has mostly stalled as Israel refuses to withdraw and Hamas has yet to disarm. In this episode of Beyond the Headlines , host Nada AlTaher asks whether there is any meaningful alternative to Mr Netanyahu and his party and what it could mean for Israelis and Palestinians if he does win. She speaks to non-profit Rand's distinguished chair for Israel policy, Shira Efron, and Palestinian political scientist Xavier Abu Eid.

title: What You Eat, How You Sleep and the Air You Breathe May Affect Your Risk of Dementia
body: Scientists are uncovering stronger links between everyday habits and neurological disease, with new research examining why diet, exercise, sleep and environmental pollution matter to the ageing brain. The food on your plate, the quality of your sleep and the air you breathe could all influence your chances of developing dementia later in life. A scientific review published in February 2026 has examined how these everyday factors affect the brain, adding to growing evidence that neurological health is not determined by genetics alone. Published in Frontiers in Pharmacology, the research, conducted by scientists at the University of Bern in Switzerland, brings together findings on nutrition, environmental pollution and lifestyle habits, and their relationship with conditions including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and cognitive decline. The findings offer a more detailed understanding of how the brain changes over time and why some people may be more vulnerable to neurological disease than others. Although ageing and inherited risk remain important, researchers increasingly recognise that diet, cardiovascular health, physical activity and environmental exposure can influence the biological processes involved in brain deterioration. One of the most interesting findings concerns the Mediterranean diet, long associated with cardiovascular health but now attracting considerable attention in neuroscience. A traditional Mediterranean eating pattern, built around vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil, nuts and fish, has been linked to slower cognitive decline and a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers believe the combination of healthy fats, antioxidants and fibre may help regulate inflammation and protect blood vessels supplying the brain. Omega-3 fatty acids, found in oily fish such as sardines and salmon, are particularly important for maintaining the structure of nerve cells. Meanwhile, plant compounds found in berries, olive oil, vegetables and other foods are being investigated for their potential to protect cells from damage associated with ageing. There is also growing evidence that nutritional deficiencies can affect memory and concentration. Vitamin B12, for instance, is essential for normal nerve function, and a deficiency can cause neurological symptoms, including cognitive difficulties. Folate, vitamin D and magnesium also play important roles in brain function, although the evidence does not establish that taking additional supplements prevents dementia in people without a deficiency. The distinction is important. Researchers are not advocating a particular superfood or vitamin regimen. Rather, the evidence increasingly favours the nutritional benefits of a balanced diet maintained over many years. What happens outside the kitchen may be just as significant. The review highlights research linking prolonged exposure to air pollution with an increased risk of cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Fine particulate matter, commonly produced by vehicle exhausts, industrial activity and other combustion sources, is of particular concern because it can contribute to inflammation and damage to the body’s vascular system. Some studies have associated long-term exposure to these particles with a higher incidence of Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Researchers are also examining how certain pesticides and heavy metals, including lead and mercury, can interfere with normal neurological function. These findings raise questions about the environments in which people live and work. Unlike decisions about exercise or food, exposure to polluted air and industrial chemicals is not always within an individual’s control. The review therefore emphasises the importance of environmental regulation and public health policies alongside personal prevention strategies. Sleep is another area attracting increasing scientific attention. During sleep, the brain performs essential functions involved in memory, learning and cellular maintenance. Persistent sleep disturbance has been associated with poorer cognitive performance and a higher risk of dementia, although the relationship is complicated. Changes associated with developing neurological disease can themselves interfere with sleep, making cause and effect difficult to separate. Physical activity offers more encouraging evidence. Regular movement improves circulation, helps regulate blood pressure and blood sugar, and supports the brain’s ability to maintain and adapt its neural connections. Studies have associated consistent physical activity with better cognitive function and a lower risk of several neurological conditions. The benefits do not appear to depend on extreme exercise. Walking, swimming, cycling and strength training can all contribute to better cardiovascular health, which is closely connected to the health of the brain. The broader findings are consistent with a major 2024 report from The Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, which identified 14 potentially modifiable risk factors, including physical inactivity, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking, hearing loss, social isolation and air pollution. The commission estimated that addressing these factors could potentially prevent or delay approximately 45 per cent of dementia cases worldwide. This is a population-level estimate rather than a prediction of any one person’s risk, but it illustrates how significant prevention could become. There are important limits to what the latest research can tell us. The University of Bern publication is a review of existing scientific evidence, not a new clinical trial, and many of the studies it examines establish associations rather than proving direct causes. The findings also vary between conditions. What helps reduce the risk of dementia may not necessarily prevent Parkinson’s disease or alter the progression of an existing neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the practical implications are becoming clearer. Maintaining a healthy blood pressure, eating a varied diet, exercising regularly, getting sufficient sleep and avoiding tobacco are not simply recommendations for protecting the heart or maintaining a healthy weight. They may also contribute to preserving cognitive function as we age. For people already living with neurological disease, these measures may support general health and wellbeing, but they are not substitutes for established medical treatments. Perhaps the most significant message is that the foundations of brain health are laid long before problems with memory or concentration become apparent. Research increasingly points towards the cumulative influence of habits and environmental conditions across decades, rather than a single decision made later in life. The prospect of preventing every neurological disorder remains beyond the reach of current science. What is becoming clearer, however, is that looking after the brain involves many of the same ordinary decisions that shape our health throughout life. Source: Chakif, D. and Furrer, J. (2026). The Impact of Nutritional, Environmental, and Lifestyle Factors on Neurological Disorders: Therapeutic Implications and Mechanistic Insights. Frontiers in Pharmacology.
