title: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does
body:
This post is part of a collection on UUIDs .
Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:
But none of these properties are strictly held. Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees. The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance. I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable , so this post explores the other properties.
Addendum: this post isn’t intended as an intro to UUIDv7 and does not cover popular use cases. It aims to dispell common misunderstandings, especially seen in casual blog posts and implementations they inform.
Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations. If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.
Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time. The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.
RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock. This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy. In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.
Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1
This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1
… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2
Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem. If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future. Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits. A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems. This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.
One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7. The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows. Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.
We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp. But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound. At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.
The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”. I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations. Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior. There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.
Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.
It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters. One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.
This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments. Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it. If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata.
This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough. Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements.
When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered. This was proven impossible back in the 1970s , and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision. Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is. Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering.
Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is.
For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted. It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them. At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect.
But even on a single node, using a single implementation, UUIDv7 IDs are not strictly monotonic. The easiest way to get out-of-order UUIDv7 IDs is to use an implementation that uses a millisecond timestamp without a counter. This approach trivially generates out-of-order IDs inside a small for loop .
So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing. Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable.
In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful. So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet. Just be wary of what assumptions you have.
The RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards. Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed.
We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used. To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart.
I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage. So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards.
Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates . When this happens, the backwards jump would align the timestamp to the actual time, but a last-used-timestamp guard would force timestamps to use keep using that incorrect timestamp until the system clock catches up. If the system clock takes a long time to catch up, you may start experiencing counter rollovers.
My mental model for UUIDv7 is that it’s a mash-up of a bunch of different ideas which implementations are free to choose as they see fit. There’s a wide variance of properties that UUIDv7 implementations can provide, with varying degrees of certainty they can successfully provide those properties. If you’re building your own implementation you can likely build something that has the properties you need. But most of us want to reach for an off-the-shelf version, especially when standard libraries provide an implementation, so we’re generally at the mercy of someone else’s implementation decisions. Implementations can change over time, making broad changes to their behavior while still being RFC compliant. Distributed systems may have multiple implementations across their subsystems, each with distinct properties. The only thing you can really expect is strong collision avoidance and ID uniqueness.
Be sure to ask these questions when picking a UUIDv7 implementation:
Unfortunately, this sort of analysis is much more difficult than building an RFC compliant generator. Authors of UUIDv7 generators may not know the answers to these questions and may themselves be surprised that the RFC does handle this for them.

title: Cyprus High Commissioner Begins Diplomatic Role in Australia
body: Cyprus’ new High Commissioner to Australia, Haralambos Kafkarides, has formally presented his credentials to Governor-General Sam Mostyn, with both sides highlighting the close ties between the two countries and the contribution of the Cypriot Australian community. Cyprus High Commissioner Haralambos Kafkarides presents his credentials to Australian Governor-General Sam Mostyn at Government House in Canberra. The ceremony took place at Government House in Canberra on October 20, 2026, where Kafkarides presented his Letters of Credence to Mostyn, formally assuming his diplomatic role. Mostyn welcomed the High Commissioner and praised the Cypriot diaspora’s contribution to Australia’s development as a multicultural nation, highlighting its longstanding economic and social impact. She noted that the Cypriot community had played an important role in shaping Australian society over several decades. Australia’s longstanding role in Cyprus The Governor-General also highlighted Australia’s contribution to the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), particularly through Australian police personnel. She described the mission as Australia’s longest-running United Nations peacekeeping deployment, noting its contribution to peace and stability on the island. Australia has supported UNFICYP for more than five decades, a commitment acknowledged by Kafkarides during the ceremony. The High Commissioner thanked Australia for its continued support for a just, viable and comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus problem that would lead to the island’s reunification. Cyprus and Australia look to strengthen ties Kafkarides highlighted the strong relationship between Cyprus and Australia, as well as their cooperation in international organisations, particularly the Commonwealth of Nations. Mostyn also congratulated the Cypriot government on its recent Presidency of the Council of the European Union, describing Cyprus as an important link in strengthening relations between Australia and the EU. The discussions underscored the potential for further cooperation between the two countries across diplomatic and international forums. Cypriot community numbers more than 80,000 Kafkarides highlighted the estimated 80,000-strong Cypriot community across Australia, describing its contribution to Australian society as significant. He also emphasised that preserving and promoting Cypriot traditions, heritage and culture would be a priority during his tenure. The High Commissioner said initiatives supporting the community’s cultural identity would help ensure Cypriot heritage continues to thrive within Australia’s multicultural society. The ceremony was attended by Dr Fiona Webster, Deputy Secretary responsible for International Security, Legal and Consular Affairs, Chief of Protocol Jonathan Muir and other Australian officials. Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Cyprus and the High Commission of Cyprus in Canberra. title: Huckabee questions Board of Peace’s ability to carry out Trump's Gaza peace plan - report
body: US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee questioned whether the Board of Peace would be able to carry out US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza without additional planning and resources from the US government, according to a cable obtained by Politico.The cable, reportedly sent to State Department leadership on Thursday, detailed Huckabee's concerns about whether the Board of Peace and the US Embassy in Jerusalem had enough personnel to oversee plans to disarm Hamas and begin reconstruction of the Gaza Strip.Jerusalem embassy unprepared to take over IGSC responsibilitiesHuckabee's concerns focused on the International Gaza Support Center, the main hub for coordinating between the US, Israel, and international partners, according to Politico. The cable questioned whether the center could maintain operations as the Pentagon planned to reduce its personnel presence over the next year, with civilian staff expected to take over their responsibilities.“Embassy Jerusalem is not currently staffed to assume these roles, but can be if it has an idea of the human, financial and logistical resources that will be needed,” Huckabee wrote. “The BoP is working to increase staff, but its ability to cover all functions at the IGSC remains unclear.”The cable, marked “sensitive but unclassified,” also warned that replacing military personnel with civilians at the coordination center could complicate cooperation with the Israeli military, particularly regarding intelligence sharing, Politico reported.“How will roles and responsibilities shift to State and the BoP as DoW reduces its presence?” Huckabee asked State Department leadership. “How will we keep critical IGSC workstreams running and what conditions should be met before this transition begins?”Huckabee told Fox News that the Board of Peace “could be moving forward progressively, but the only reason that there's any slowdown is because of Hamas.”Huckabee specifically cited Hamas's failure to follow through on its commitment to disarm as an obstacle to progress on the cable.The Jerusalem Post reported in August that the high representative for the Board of Peace, Nikolay Mladenov, criticized Israel for continued strikes on Gaza after a cease-fire was reached in October 2025, and Israel's refusal to allow the NCAG into Gaza."There is a ceasefire, and it holds, but it is not perfect. It is far from perfect. There are violations every day, some of which are very serious and significant. And let's be honest about these violations and what they actually mean: the meaning is that civilians are still being killed. Families are living in fear. Delays and restrictions continue to affect humanitarian access and the daily lives of many Palestinians," Mladenov said after meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May.“The National Committee is ready to enter, govern, and protect wherever coercion is removed, and the conditions are right,” he added.Mladenov also condemned Israel's decision to cut off commercial goods from entering Gaza at the time.“As I have warned repeatedly, such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately. The intimidation of merchants and interference in the supply chain only deepen the suffering of Gaza's civilians,” Mladenov posted.“These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) supported by the International Stabilization Force (ISF) is urgently needed,” he wrote.Board of Peace not familiar with Huckabee's cableThe Board of Peace said it was not familiar with the cable but expressed confidence in its preparations for Gaza.“We are confident in the highly detailed plans that have been developed for improved humanitarian assistance, security, governance, the rule of law, infrastructure development, and reconstruction in Gaza,” the organization said in a statement. “Our capacities and systems in place are strong and ready for implementation.”The cable also raised concerns that delays in reconstruction could weaken the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the Palestinian technocratic body established to govern the Strip.Huckabee argued that humanitarian assistance should be coordinated with the committee's priorities and longer-term reconstruction plans to prevent setbacks and strengthen its credibility.“Humanitarian assistance should surge in line with NCAG and administration priorities,” he wrote, adding that aid should complement longer-term reconstruction efforts “to prevent backsliding and demonstrate the NCAG's credibility.”The cable also said the US would press foreign donors to “do their fair share to address humanitarian needs.”Sarah Moskowitz contributed to this report.

title: Trump Says Musk Restored Ukraine’s Starshield
body:
US President Donald Trump said Thursday, Oct. 22, that Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield satellite communications service following restrictions that disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, but declined to confirm whether he personally called the billionaire to demand the changes be reversed.
“I don’t want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called – doesn’t make any difference,” Trump told reporters when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that he had intervened.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk, whose SpaceX company operates the satellite network.
Trump’s comments followed a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) investigation reporting that the president contacted Musk on Wednesday and asked him to remove restrictions that had sharply reduced Ukraine’s ability to operate certain military drones.
According to the newspaper, citing US officials, Trump expressed frustration that the service remained capped at approximately 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour), a restriction that interfered with communications aboard fast-moving Ukrainian drones.
US and Ukrainian officials cited by the WSJ said network performance improved after the reported conversation. However, some Ukrainian officials cautioned that the service had not returned to full functionality.
The latest developments leave a central question unresolved: whether Ukraine has regained the satellite communications capabilities it needs to conduct strikes against Russian military targets and intercept incoming drones.
The controversy began on Oct. 14, when Ukrainian military units reported unexpected limitations on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network.
Unlike ordinary Starlink terminals, Starshield supports specialized military communications and can be used aboard high-speed unmanned aircraft.
Ukraine relies on the system for battlefield coordination, strikes against Russian military positions in occupied territory, reconnaissance and interceptor drones designed to destroy incoming Russian attack drones.
The sudden speed restrictions caused terminals to lose connectivity aboard moving platforms, disrupting missions and limiting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian aerial attacks.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: The foolishness of "natural language programming" (1978)
body:
On the foolishness of "natural language programming" .
Since the early days of automatic computing we have had people that have felt it as a shortcoming that programming required the care and accuracy that is characteristic for the use of any formal symbolism. They blamed the mechanical slave for its strict obedience with which it carried out its given instructions, even if a moment's thought would have revealed that those instructions contained an obvious mistake. "But a moment is a long time, and thought is a painful process." (A.E.Housman). They eagerly hoped and waited for more sensible machinery that would refuse to embark on such nonsensical activities as a trivial clerical error evoked at the time.
Machine code, with its absence of almost any form of redundancy, was soon identified as a needlessly risky interface between man and machine. Partly in response to this recognition so-called "high-level programming languages" were developed, and, as time went by, we learned to a certain extent how to enhance the protection against silly mistakes. It was a significant improvement that now many a silly mistake did result in an error message instead of in an erroneous answer. (And even this improvement wasn't universally appreciated: some people found error messages they couldn't ignore more annoying than wrong results, and, when judging the relative merits of programming languages, some still seem to equate "the ease of programming" with the ease of making undetected mistakes.) The (abstract) machine corresponding to a programming language remained, however, a faithful slave, i.e. the nonsensible automaton perfectly capable of carrying out nonsensical instructions. Programming remained the use of a formal symbolism and, as such, continued to require the care and accuracy required before.
In order to make machines significantly easier to use, it has been proposed (to try) to design machines that we could instruct in our native tongues. this would, admittedly, make the machines much more complicated, but, it was argued, by letting the machine carry a larger share of the burden, life would become easier for us. It sounds sensible provided you blame the obligation to use a formal symbolism as the source of your difficulties. But is the argument valid? I doubt.
We know in the meantime that the choice of an interface is not just a division of (a fixed amount of) labour, because the work involved in co-operating and communicating across the interface has to be added. We know in the meantime —from sobering experience, I may add— that a change of interface can easily increase at both sides of the fence the amount of work to be done (even drastically so). Hence the increased preference for what are now called "narrow interfaces". Therefore, although changing to communication between machine and man conducted in the latter's native tongue would greatly increase the machine's burden, we have to challenge the assumption that this would simplify man's life.
A short look at the history of mathematics shows how justified this challenge is. Greek mathematics got stuck because it remained a verbal, pictorial activity, Moslem "algebra", after a timid attempt at symbolism, died when it returned to the rhetoric style, and the modern civilized world could only emerge —for better or for worse— when Western Europe could free itself from the fetters of medieval scholasticism —a vain attempt at verbal precision!— thanks to the carefully, or at least consciously designed formal symbolisms that we owe to people like Vieta, Descartes, Leibniz, and (later) Boole.
The virtue of formal texts is that their manipulations, in order to be legitimate, need to satisfy only a few simple rules; they are, when you come to think of it, an amazingly effective tool for ruling out all sorts of nonsense that, when we use our native tongues, are almost impossible to avoid.
Instead of regarding the obligation to use formal symbols as a burden, we should regard the convenience of using them as a privilege: thanks to them, school children can learn to do what in earlier days only genius could achieve. (This was evidently not understood by the author that wrote —in 1977— in the preface of a technical report that "even the standard symbols used for logical connectives have been avoided for the sake of clarity". The occurrence of that sentence suggests that the author's misunderstanding is not confined to him alone.) When all is said and told, the "naturalness" with which we use our native tongues boils down to the ease with which we can use them for making statements the nonsense of which is not obvious.
It may be illuminating to try to imagine what would have happened if, right from the start our native tongue would have been the only vehicle for the input into and the output from our information processing equipment. My considered guess is that history would, in a sense, have repeated itself, and that computer science would consist mainly of the indeed black art how to bootstrap from there to a sufficiently well-defined formal system. We would need all the intellect in the world to get the interface narrow enough to be usable, and, in view of the history of mankind, it may not be overly pessimistic to guess that to do the job well enough would require again a few thousand years.
Remark . As a result of the educational trend away from intellectual discipline, the last decades have shown in the Western world a sharp decline of people's mastery of their own language: many people that by the standards of a previous generation should know better, are no longer able to use their native tongue effectively, even for purposes for which it is pretty adequate. (You have only to look at the indeed alarming amount of on close reading meaningless verbiage in scientific articles, technical reports, government publications etc.) This phenomenon —known as "The New Illiteracy"— should discourage those believers in natural language programming that lack the technical insight needed to predict its failure. (End of remark.)
From one gut feeling I derive much consolation: I suspect that machines to be programmed in our native tongues —be it Dutch, English, American, French, German, or Swahili— are as damned difficult to make as they would be to use.

title: Veterans ask federal judge to block Trump's arch unless Congress approves it
body:
The Justice Department said Wednesday construction will begin on Nov. 5.
With the Trump administration signaling that work on the triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery could begin two weeks from Thursday, opponents of the project urged a federal judge to issue an order blocking the construction unless it is authorized by lawmakers.
The request for a preliminary injunction comes a day after the Justice Department filed notice with a federal judge indicating that construction on the arch could begin on Nov. 5, immediately after the National Capital Planning Commission is set to grant its final approval of the project.
Judge Tanya Chutkan had previously ordered that the government must give at least 14 days' notice before starting work on the arch. Wednesday's notice would keep with that timeframe.
The Vietnam-era veterans who have brought a lawsuit against the arch asked Chutkan to step in so that the administration can't "render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has made a final determination whether Defendants' project is unlawful."
The veterans' filing accuses the administration of having "barreled ahead, doing site testing, drawing architectural plans, and seeking approvals from commissions populated by friends of the administration."
All the while, the filing says, the Trump administration has "failed to obtain (or even to seek) approval from the one body that, by law, must authorize the project: Congress."
The administration argues that the bill signed by President Calvin Coolidge in 1925 providing for the construction of Memorial Bridge also authorizes the arch, because the initial plan called for columns at the end of the bridge.
Opponents describe the administration's argument as "entirely untethered" from the text of that 1925 law.
Trump's proposal would put the 250-foot arch in a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial at the foot of the national cemetery. It currently faces legal challenges by the veterans and preservationists.
The administration acknowledged in September that the arch would cause "adverse effects" on the setting and views along the rive, but those impacts "cannot be fully avoided" because the arch's location is "central to the undertaking."

title: Please don't mess with links
body:
A link is just a button that takes you somewhere when you click it right?
Except that's a pale, shallow imitation of a link. A real link can be:
Opened in a new tab. (ctrl) ... or a fresh window. (shift) ... or saved as a file (alt). Copied as a URL (right click) Used with the keyboard (tab + enter) Seen by tools like search engines and screen readers. Hovered over to see the URL.
Another common offense is to use a real link, but hook the click event to open a popup. However, with a real <a target="_blank"> link, I can:
See the loading progress... ... or/and cancel it. ... see descriptive error pages and retry if needed. Open multiple at once. Read the original page while it loads. Use my browser's tabs or/and window manager to organize them. Bookmark the page. Copy the URL and send it to a friend.
I've long lost count of how many times I've accidentally closed the whole site while trying to close a popup that was a little too convincing.
It's also extremely common to click a link with a slow connection, only to be greeted with perpetual spinner. I have no idea if anything is actually happening or how long it will take. Worse, it usually covers up the original page so I can't even read that!
Browsers are good at links and loading pages: It's the whole point.
Don't use javascript buttons as links. Don't build your own loading animations. Link previews should open and close on hover, not on click. Don't open links in javascript popups: Use target="_blank" instead.
Infinite scrolling breaks ctrl-f, bookmarks, the home/end keys and often the back button.
You can have a 100k of text on a page: Browsers will render partially downloaded HTML and the user won't even notice. Using a 5 MB javascript framework just do a worse job of downloading text is dumb.
To optimize speed, it's best to minimize the total number of round trips. Just putting everything in a single TCP connection will always be better than breaking it up because of TCP's slow start algorithm.
Don't reimplement <details> which will break search tools and screen readers.
... but using fancy CSS to make it look nice is fine.
Don't roll your own date picker (or any other built-in form inputs)
This will always used the user's preferred date format, covert it to the standard yyyy-mm-dd, and works with the keyboard... also, it's one line of code that works with dark mode by default.

title: Meghan Markle Father Investigated Over Alleged Child Abuse Material
body: Thomas Markle Senior, the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is reportedly under investigation after his son allegedly discovered a large collection of child sexual abuse material at his home in the Philippines. The Sun reports that Thomas Markle Jr, Meghan’s half-brother, found hundreds or potentially thousands of images and videos while sorting through family belongings and alerted police in Cebu. According to the newspaper, investigators are preparing to seize the alleged material, while the FBI is also expected to investigate after Markle Jr reportedly contacted the agency. However, Meghan’s half-sister, Samantha Markle, has rejected the allegations and accused her brother of fabricating them to damage their father. “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him,” Samantha told the Daily Mail. She alleged that her brother made the accusations after their father stopped providing him with money, claiming he had relied on their father financially for years. The Sun reports that Markle Jr initially alerted the FBI and authorities in Pennsylvania in July, when his father was living there, but became concerned after receiving no follow-up information. He allegedly examined four additional boxes and discovered further material, including books and a hard drive containing images. Speaking to The Sun, Markle Jr said he felt “horrified” by what he had found and believed he had no choice but to report it to authorities. “I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” he told the newspaper. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” The allegations emerge after Thomas Markle experienced serious health problems this year, including a stroke in May and a blood clot that led to the amputation of his left leg. He subsequently returned to the United States to receive ongoing medical care. Meghan and her father have been estranged since her 2018 wedding to Prince Harry. The Duchess, who lived with her father from the age of 11 to 18, reportedly became furious after he arranged paparazzi photographs in the lead-up to the wedding. Thomas subsequently withdrew from attending the ceremony and walking his daughter down the aisle, saying he had suffered a heart attack and was in hospital. He later described feeling hurt by a phone conversation with Meghan and Harry. Last December, reports emerged that Meghan had sent her father a handwritten letter while he was recovering from lifesaving surgery in the Philippines. A spokesman for the Duchess confirmed at the time that she had reached out after learning of his hospitalisation. Thomas subsequently disputed reports that she had contacted him or the hospital, prompting a source close to Meghan to tell The Times that she had made attempts to communicate with him, including by email. In a statement to the Daily Mail, Thomas appealed for a reconciliation with his daughter, saying he hoped to see Meghan, Prince Harry and his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, before his death. “I have never stopped loving her. I don’t want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too,” he said. The allegations against Thomas Markle remain allegations, and the reports cited do not establish his guilt. title: Khartoum denies role in Abyei attack as RSF allies seek probe
body: Sudan’s army-aligned government has denied that its armed forces carried out a deadly drone strike on Amiet Common Market in the disputed Abyei region, while the RSF-aligned Government of Peace has called for an international investigation into the attack. Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Thursday that the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had no involvement in the October 19 attack on the market, a major trading centre serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities. “The Sudanese Armed Forces have absolutely no connection to this unfortunate incident,” the ministry said in a statement, expressing condolences to the victims’ families and wishing the wounded a speedy recovery. South Sudanese officials have blamed Sudan’s military for the attack. Abyei officials initially reported that at least 73 people had been killed and 19 wounded, before raising the death toll to 153 . The victims included Sudanese, South Sudanese and foreign nationals, according to the officials, who said the dead were buried in two mass graves. The attack has heightened tensions between Sudan and South Sudan. Following the incident, South Sudan summoned Sudan’s ambassador to Juba to protest the deadly drone strike. The Sudanese ministry did not provide evidence to support its denial or detail the circumstances of the attack. It also accused the RSF of carrying out other attacks, including a December 2025 assault on a United Nations peacekeeping camp in Kadugli, South Kordofan, which it said killed several members of the Bangladeshi contingent. The RSF and the Sudanese army have been at war since April 2023 in a conflict that has killed thousands of people, displaced millions and triggered a major humanitarian crisis. UN probe sought The RSF-aligned Government of Peace has filed a complaint with the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan, seeking an investigation into the attack and the identification of those responsible, its foreign minister told Radio Tamazuj on Thursday. Ammar Amoun Deldoum, the group’s minister of foreign affairs and international cooperation, said the complaint was submitted on October 19 through the group’s permanent representative to the United Nations. It was addressed to the mission’s chair and members through its secretariat at the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, he said. Amoun accused the Sudanese Armed Forces of striking the market in Abyei with drones. He said the complaint called on investigators to establish the circumstances of the attack, determine criminal responsibility, preserve evidence and protect witnesses. “We asked specifically to investigate the incident, collect evidence, analyse it, preserve it and determine the responsible parties as soon as possible,” Amoun said. He said the Government of Peace had established a local committee to gather information from traders, survivors and market workers. Amoun said the market is a civilian trading centre and a source of livelihood for local communities. He added that there had been no military presence in the demilitarised area of Abyei. “The market is the source of livelihood for many citizens. They depend on the market in their lives,” he said. Amoun said the committee had also found documents belonging to foreign traders, including Pakistanis and Somalis, but did not provide details of foreign nationals believed to have been killed. “We hope that the Human Rights Council will gather all the evidence and use it to authenticate the number of foreigners killed in the incident,” he said. Amoun said the complaint sought an independent investigation, with findings submitted to relevant United Nations bodies. He acknowledged that the fact-finding process would not itself constitute a final judicial ruling. He also urged the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) to document evidence relating to the attack. UN condemnation The United Nations has condemned the October 19 drone attacks in the Abyei area, saying civilians, including women and children, were killed and others wounded. The UN said the casualty toll was expected to rise as peacekeepers continued to verify the number of victims. Abyei, an oil-rich region claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, remains disputed, with its final status unresolved. The conflict between Sudan’s army and the RSF has devastated large parts of the country since it erupted in April 2023, forcing millions from their homes and disrupting access to food, healthcare and other essential services. The post Khartoum denies role in Abyei attack as RSF allies seek probe appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

Etsy is announcing stricter rules about how AI can be used in listings to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform. In a post, the company says that “many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content” and that sellers are “concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways,” spurring the new policies and restrictions.
Under the new policies, every listing must include “at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background,” and all photos must “accurately represent the item a buyer will receive.” The photos that aren’t the first one can be edited with software or AI-powered tools, as long as “the final result remains an accurate representation of the physical product.” The company shared a few examples to demonstrate the type of misleading images that are prohibited, including the cat stuffed animal at the top of this post.
While uploading images for a listing, if Etsy detects that any may be AI-generated, the platform will show a pop-up where you can note if an image was made with AI or not, as shown in a video . If a buyer reports that what they receive is “materially different” from a listing, a seller may be responsible for a refund.
For sellers who offer “functional guides,” which include patterns, recipes, or instructions,” Etsy says that the information in those products “must be your own work, not generated by AI.” Sellers will have to show an “actual result” made from a guide. The company also says that listings made by bots are no longer allowed.
Selling AI-generated art is still allowed on the platform, but a seller must disclose that it was made with AI, Etsy says.

title: ‘Putin Has Killed Thousands’ – Downing Street Rebukes Witkoff for Calling Russian Leader ‘Humanitarian’
body:
The British government on Thursday, Oct. 22, firmly rejected US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff’s description of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian,” pointing to the thousands killed in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and Moscow’s systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Downing Street issued the unusually direct rebuke after Witkoff praised Putin during their meeting in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, hours before Russian forces launched another massive missile and drone assault on Kyiv.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We certainly do not recognize that characterization,” a Downing Street spokesperson told reporters.
The spokesperson said Putin had killed thousands of people, including innocent Ukrainians and Russian soldiers sent to die on the battlefield.
“He is starving children and the elderly of the heat and warmth, and systematically targeting critical national infrastructure,” the spokesperson said.
Downing Street also quoted Ukraine’s foreign minister, who said Russia’s overnight attack on Kyiv showed what Putin’s so-called “humanitarianism” really meant.
“This night, the residents of Kyiv heard what Russian humanitarianism really sounds like,” the Ukrainian minister said, according to Downing Street.
The controversy began Wednesday when Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss the possible resumption of trilateral peace talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
At the beginning of the meeting, Putin announced the release of 74-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had been held in Russia since 2022.
Witkoff thanked the Russian leader, describing him as a humanitarian in remarks captured on video by Russian state media.
“You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin.
The comment immediately triggered criticism from US lawmakers, including members of Trump’s Republican Party.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called Witkoff’s remarks embarrassing and outrageous, urging the envoy to consider the suffering of Ukrainian families whose children have been killed or forcibly taken to Russia.
Senator John Cornyn also rejected the characterization, describing Putin as a killer.

title: NORTHCOM Wraps Radar Test to Boost Arctic Early Warning
body: U.S. Northern Command and multiple research organizations just wrapped up a joint, three-year experiment to test new radar technology that could enable the Northern Warning System to detect incoming threats at longer ranges across Alaska and northern Canada. The Sept. 7-14 test event marked the conclusion of live-fly testing in the experiment series, which explored how existing radar infrastructure and emerging technology could complement current surveillance capabilities, according to an Oct. 19 release from Alaskan Command, a subordinate command under NORTHCOM. The Arctic air domain awareness experiment series focused on closing surveillance gaps across a region where vast distances, harsh weather and limited infrastructure present challenges for air surveillance. The Air Force Research Laboratory and Defense Research and Development Canada also participated in the exercise alongside scientific organizations in the region. The Air Force and NORAD have relied on the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77 radar systems to detect and track incoming threats out to 250 miles throughout the region. The experiment paired an existing high-frequency transmitter, paired with a newly developed, low-cost receiver array, according to the release. Initial results show the system was “successfully able to achieve full skywave (beyond line of sight) detections” of an E-3 Sentry from the 962nd Airborne Air Control Squadron, HC-130J Combat King IIs from the 211th Rescue Squadron, and KC-135 Stratotankers from the 168th Air Refueling Wing—aircraft that served as cooperative targets, providing known positions against which researchers could compare the experimental data, the release states. Researchers used the University of Alaska Fairbanks’ High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program, or HAARP, facility and a receiver array in Cold Bay developed by MITRE to collect data on participating aircraft over the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea. The effort supported a broader focus of Alaskan Command to improve how units detect and track aircraft across Alaska and its approaches and help commanders assess potential threats for homeland defense, the release states. “Understanding what this technology can do in the Arctic starts with collecting data under real operating conditions,” Dr. Carolyn Stwertka, chief scientist for Alaskan Command, said in the release. “Working with operational units allows us to compare the experimental observations with known aircraft positions and assess where this approach could help address gaps in air surveillance.” The experiment occurred as NORAD is building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network. The Homeland Defense OTHR , which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion , respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031. Meanwhile, the Air Force is looking to replace its Air Route Surveillance Radar-4 , a three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations. The ARSR-4 system, which was built in the 1990s, was designed to help operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. The system has been very effective, but Air Force officials maintain that newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly, according to a recent Air Force Life Cycle Management Center sources sought notice . title: Supreme Court allows New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting in midterms
body:
The Supreme Court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting during the midterm elections
WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court cleared the way Thursday for New Hampshire to fully ban the use of student IDs for voting during the midterm elections.
The justices granted a Republican-backed emergency appeal and blocked the use of student IDs as a backup method of identification. The Supreme Court cited a longstanding legal principle that judges shouldn’t change voting rules too close to Election Day.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent.
New Hampshire passed a law this year that said student IDs would no longer be an expressly accepted form of identification for obtaining a ballot. The secretary of state then issued guidance barring them as a backup way to prove a voter's identity.
A judge left the law in place but blocked the guidance in early October, prompting the appeal to the Supreme Court. The Republican National Committee weighed in to support the state.
The decision comes less than two weeks before New Hampshire voters cast ballots in a closely contested U.S. Senate race.

title: Docker is weird
body:
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though Iâm still early on, Iâve learned that Docker is weird . Hereâs some weird things I learned about Docker.
Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.
Thereâs not really a linux feature thatâs just âcontainersâ either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.
Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and thereâs a whole bunch of networking magic I donât understand that lets you isolate a containerâs network.
Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container processâs new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to:
Dockerâs container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Goâs runtime is natively multi-threaded. Thatâs a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc .
Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Goâs runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.
Go also doesnât have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so itâs kind of a footgun in a runtime like Goâs. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.
This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.
This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If youâre running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!
Iâve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like Iâve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!

title: UAE confirms oil spill off coast and temporarily closes Umm Al Quwain beaches
body: UAE authorities are working to contain an oil spill from a supertanker in the Arabian Gulf, with Umm Al Quwain Municipality intensifying efforts to limit pollution and protect marine habitats. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the incident early on Friday morning. It said the spill is causing a strong smell that residents of Dubai and the northern emirates have reported in recent days. The ministry did not name the vessel, but international maritime agencies say the Gem No.2 was struck in a suspected Iranian drone attack on October 9 to 10. Twenty-two Indian sailors were rescued from the 330-metre vessel at the time. The extent of the oil slick is unclear, but the incident was confirmed amid growing concerns about the environmental impact of the Iran war on the Gulf and the Arabian Sea. Umm Al Quwain Municipality said it was carrying out field operations to contain the effects of the spill and minimise damage to marine and coastal environments. The municipality will monitor conditions, identify affected areas and support clean-up and treatment work as part of those efforts. Specialists will also help to assess the impact of the spill and determine appropriate measures. Acrid and strong fuel smell People in the UAE have in recent days reported an acrid and strong fuel smell in the air. The ministry said there was no health risk from the odour, but advised the public to stay away from any oil that washes ashore. "The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirms the UAE’s technical monitoring and environmental assessment system detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches," it said in a statement. "Odours noticed in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain pose no health risks to residents. "Teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation with local and federal authorities to limit environmental impacts. Precautionary coastal surveys, monitoring and assessments continue to gauge impacts and protect the marine environment. "With relevant authorities, the ministry has temporarily closed all Umm Al Quwain beaches and coastal areas until technical teams complete assessments and identify safety and marine protection measures. Fishermen and sea users are urged to follow authorities’ instructions and avoid fishing in affected areas." Lingering effect Dr Diana Francis, an associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences Lab at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said oil spills caused by the regional conflict could create odours. A VLCC-size tanker is leaking oil 25 km off Umm Al Quwain. Currents are setting it southwest toward the coast, and Windward’s drift model shows it reaching Sharjah’s and Ajman’s desalination intakes and ports by 22–23 Oct if the leak isn’t stopped. More maritime intelligence… pic.twitter.com/OY8Vq9W2aB — Windward (@WindwardAI) October 20, 2026 “When an oil spill happens, it continues to move with the currents unless it is removed and cleaned completely,” she told The National before the ministry confirmed the oil slick incident. “Several spills can also move with the currents and accumulate in favourable gyre [rotating ocean current] areas. Then with time, heat and winds, they evaporate into the air and give off fuel-like odours. “Oil doesn't mix with water. It continues to float until it is removed or evaporate with time.” Prashant Kumar, professor of air quality and health at the University of Surrey in the UK, said air pollution – and the smells that it brings with it – can travel over long distances. “The smell can travel tens of kilometres,” he said, in comments also made before the ministry's statement on Friday. “It depends on the meteorological conditions, it depends on the wind speed and the wind direction. You can easily have the longer-range transport of pollutants from one place to another.” Dealing with oil spills When it comes to reducing the effects of oil spills, containment is key because “prevention is better than cure”, Prof John Burt, director of NYU Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said after it was confirmed that the smell was caused by an oil spill. “If floating booms can be put out to contain the spill and collect it before it reaches a coastline, this would be the ideal scenario,” he added. “Remediation is timely, cost intensive, and full return to normal can take years in the event that a spill reaches a coastline.” He said that the Gulf War of 1990-91 offered lessons on the potential impacts of oil spills in the region. Then, millions of barrels of oil were released in the northern Arabian Gulf. “Because oil is buoyant and floats, there were minimal impacts on subtidal habitats such as coral reefs and seagrass beds at that time,” he said. “And as it was volatising to the atmosphere as it drifted down the Gulf, the oil slick back then only made it as far south as Qatar before dispersing fully. “That said, where it reached coastlines in the northern Gulf, particularly around Kuwait and northern Saudi Arabia, it caused considerable impacts in the intertidal zones.” In these areas, Prof Burt said, tar mats formed in the sands of beaches that persisted for years, and there were significant impacts in mangrove areas and on mudflats where many birds feed.

title: ‘More Money Means More Dead Ukrainians’ – Kasparov Warns Against Deals With Moscow
body:
Russian opposition leader and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov has condemned proposals to ease sanctions against Moscow in exchange for the release of Russian political prisoners, warning that any such deal would strengthen Vladimir Putin’s military machine and lead directly to more Ukrainian deaths.
In a heated interview with independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain (Dozhd) , Kasparov rejected arguments that the humanitarian goal of freeing Kremlin critics could justify concessions that might help Russia continue its invasion of Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Exchanging political prisoners for sanctions relief means Russia will have greater capacity to kill Ukrainians,” Kasparov said. “It does this every day.”
He argued that sanctions are not merely diplomatic pressure but a direct constraint on Russia’s ability to finance and manufacture weapons.
“Lifting sanctions means increasing military power,” he said. “Lower prices mean more drones and more missiles. These missiles fly toward Kyiv and every Ukrainian city, killing people every day.”
Kasparov’s remarks come amid renewed US-Russian diplomatic contacts and reports that the Trump administration has considered easing some sanctions in return for the release of Russian prisoners.
The proposal was reported by The Atlantic in September , which said US envoy John Coale had discussed the idea with Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov before presenting it to President Donald Trump. According to the report, Trump agreed to explore the approach.
Kasparov argued that the sanctions regime makes it more expensive for Russia to obtain Western-made components used in missiles and drones, even when those components reach Moscow through intermediaries.
Reducing restrictions, he said, would lower procurement costs and enable Russian manufacturers to increase weapons production.
“The fewer sanctions there are, the more of these components will reach Russia,” he said.
“Oil sanctions, gas sanctions – more money means one thing: Putin’s war machine will kill more people in Ukraine,” he said.
Despite his criticism of the peace process, Kasparov defended Zelensky’s participation in the talks, saying Ukraine could not afford to alienate Washington while it remained dependent on American military and intelligence capabilities.
“Zelensky can only be sympathized with, because he has to participate in these meaningless negotiations,” Kasparov said.
Following the Oslo discussions, Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia and met Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, where Moscow signaled its willingness to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US.
Kasparov argued that the negotiations would continue as long as Washington retained significant influence over Kyiv through its military and intelligence support.

title: Opinion| A transition buried without accounting: a response to Juol Nhomngek
body: Juol Nhomngek Daniel’s response to my article raises an important constitutional argument: dissolving South Sudan’s transitional government cannot substitute for implementing the peace agreement. I agree. Our disagreement concerns his interpretation of my position. Explaining why an administration has been dismantled does not mean endorsing its dissolution. My concern is that the transitional institutions have been displaced while their unfinished responsibilities remain unresolved. My original article explicitly distinguished ending an institution from completing its mandate. It questioned the continuation of presidential authority, warned against indefinite executive discretion, and demanded accountability for outstanding commitments. It also described the fourth explanation as the reorganization and concentration of executive authority amid financial uncertainty, not an end to that concentration. These distinctions matter because Mr. Nhomngek’s response attributes support for dissolution to an argument that was principally scrutinizing it. The central question therefore remains: has South Sudan completed its transition, or has the transition been bypassed through a new administrative arrangement? Three developments explain my position: the limited practical resistance to institutional displacement, the ambiguity of international responses, and the growing separation of election preparations from unfinished transitional obligations. First, the response of those displaced must be assessed through its institutional consequences. The September order removed the vice-presidents and dissolved national and state legislatures while retaining the president and establishing caretaker authorities. Whatever objections individuals or parties may express, the replacement administration has become the machinery through which government operates. That is a substantial political change, regardless of whether its constitutional justification is accepted. It would be too sweeping to claim that every removed official has remained silent. Nor should silence automatically be interpreted as consent: political restraint may reflect insecurity, restricted opportunities, negotiation or uncertainty. The stronger question is whether those entrusted with the transitional settlement have presented an effective, collective and publicly accountable response to its displacement. Former officeholders owe citizens more than statements about their removal. They should explain which obligations remained unfinished, what they did to implement them, and how those responsibilities will now be protected. Without that accounting, the departure of leaders can overshadow the disappearance of the institutions through which citizens were promised reform. Second, international conduct deserves scrutiny, but careful scrutiny. The suggestion that a caretaker arrangement may satisfy external frustration with repeated extensions is a plausible political interpretation. It is not proof that international partners collectively requested, endorsed or welcomed this particular arrangement. Diplomatic engagement with an administration also does not, by itself, establish approval of every measure that created it. Indeed, the African Union’s Peace and Security Council called in August for credible December elections while also demanding inclusive dialogue, implementation of the peace agreement, security-sector reform and transitional justice. Its position combined electoral urgency with substantive conditions. It cannot fairly be reduced to a demand for polling at any cost. My concern is the gap between such commitments and their enforcement. International partners should explain publicly how their engagement with the caretaker authorities protects the obligations they previously supported. If they prioritize an election date while accepting the erosion of safeguards, their practical conduct may weaken their stated principles. That possibility requires examination rather than assumptions about hidden agreements. Third, the unfinished transitional agenda risks being pushed aside by the concentration on December elections. The clearest evidence is the reported amendment of electoral legislation separating the vote from completion of a permanent constitution and a national census. This changed the sequencing of the process. It did not demonstrate that the underlying questions of representation, constitutional legitimacy and public confidence had been resolved. Here, Mr. Nhomngek’s argument strengthens my warning. If the agreement’s obligations remain necessary, removing the institutions established to pursue them creates an immediate accountability problem. Who now owns those obligations? Which deadlines apply? Who scrutinizes implementation? An appeal to fulfil the agreement must answer these questions within the political circumstances that now exist. This is what I mean when I say that the transition appears to have been buried without funeral arrangements. The metaphor describes institutional closure without an adequate public reckoning. It does not declare the peace agreement legally extinguished. A government may lose its offices while its obligations remain binding, contested and politically indispensable. Mr. Nhomngek also identifies motives involving control over security institutions, public finances and political competition. These are serious interpretations deserving investigation. However, claims about what particular leaders fear or secretly intend require evidence. Criticism is strongest when it distinguishes documented actions, observable consequences, and conclusions about motive. The same discipline applies to Tumaini. An additional peace initiative should be judged by whether it broadens participation and strengthens enforceable commitments. Its existence does not establish that it caused the dissolution, nor does invoking its principles authorize the abandonment of earlier obligations. A practical roadmap should now connect constitutional responsibility with the reality of caretaker rule. First, the authorities should publish the complete legal record underlying the dissolution, including the enacted amendments and relevant orders. They should explain how these measures relate to the constitutional framework and the peace agreement, and provide an effective avenue for independent legal scrutiny. Second, an inclusive political dialogue should agree on the caretaker administration’s mandate, limits and duration. Signatories, other political actors, women, young people, displaced communities and civil society should participate meaningfully. Administrative control should not be treated as sufficient evidence of national agreement. Third, every unfinished transitional commitment should enter a public implementation schedule identifying the responsible institution, financing, deadline, and reporting mechanism. Security arrangements, constitutional reform, justice, and financial accountability must retain identifiable institutional owners. Dissolution should not become a mechanism for dissolving responsibility. Fourth, electoral readiness should undergo an independent, publicly explained assessment. Authorities must demonstrate accessible registration, adequate resources, impartial administration, political freedoms, security and workable dispute resolution. Any decision about the timetable should follow transparent evidence and lawful procedures rather than political convenience. Finally, caretaker spending and official conduct require scrutiny throughout this period. Public resources must not become campaign resources, and temporary authority must have enforceable limits. Regional and international partners should report against these safeguards consistently. Mr. Nhomngek and I share the essential objective of a peaceful, accountable constitutional state. My position is that recognizing an unfinished transition also requires recognizing how its institutions have been displaced. South Sudan cannot recover the transition’s purpose through labels alone. Its leaders must account for what was abandoned, protect what remains obligatory, and demonstrate how citizens will finally gain a meaningful voice in government. The writer is a researcher and writer specializing in humanitarian and development issues in South Sudan. He holds a degree in Sociology and Political Science from the Catholic University of Eastern Africa and a Master’s in Peace and Development Studies from the University of Juba.
