title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
body:
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross
Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit . The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem , however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs . As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.
Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.
Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.
However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it . Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code .
But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V 1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.
We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics . Theorem , our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects , and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.
Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.
The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs— especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.
In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.
To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083 ) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.
To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.
For this project, we started with fuzz tests . In these tests, developers write an entry point 2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.
To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB. 3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.
We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer 4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities ). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.
Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.
While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:
This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof . Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.
We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.
Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.
Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec. 6
Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB , and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.
The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.
Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.
This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.
Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.
We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950 , the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA. 7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.
In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We then measured the adherence to CPython’s behavior empirically, running over 1.7 million randomly generated Python programs, finding identical behavior with CPython in 99.95% of tests, with remaining test differences as unsurprising known corner cases.
We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year.
See the Appendix for more details on some of these efforts.
One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.
We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code . Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.
When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.
We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).
This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib , a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).
As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.
This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.
In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.
“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.
The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.
The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller . To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.
We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.
The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.
In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.
01 RISC-V is a processor design, like x86 or ARM, that defines the assembly instructions (the basic commands a chip carries out) that software is compiled into.
02 An entry point is a front door into the code, provided by its authors for testing. Any input to the entry point that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about.
03 Increasing this requires trivial human effort to change the parameter and regenerate the spec, then have Claude reprove the statement.
04 AddressSanitizer is a compiler tool that adds checks to a program so that memory errors, such as buffer overflows and use-after-free, are detected and reported the moment they occur at runtime.
05 This technically also means we have to trust the hardware, OS, OCaml compiler that the Rocq proof checker relies on.
06 Note this leaves open the door to reward hacking. Reward hacking is when an AI model finds a shortcut that technically meets the goal it was given without doing what was actually intended, like a student who passes an exam by memorizing the answer key instead of learning the material. In this context, Claude could make any theorem provable by rewriting the program into one that trivially never crashes. To discourage this, we penalized any patch and offered extra credit for proving which inputs it changes and how few they are. We also logged and audited the patches for these failure modes.
07 We think that the ability of Claude to—entirely autonomously—generate the formal semantics of an ISA is a separate interesting lesson. While we can not be sure our semantics themselves are perfect, empirically we have found that single-stepping through our semantics can boot an Ubuntu userspace on top of a Linux kernel. Generating these semantics also identified hundreds of mistakes in the official reference documentation, along with a smaller number of bugs in the hardware itself.

title: US and Israel drawing up plans to resume attacks on Iran post-election, sources say
body:
The White House said Thursday the U.S. will not strike Iran before the midterms.
The Israeli Defense Forces and the United States military have drawn up plans to renew joint strikes on Iran in the coming weeks, according to two Israeli sources familiar with the plans.
The Israeli sources said the strikes would almost certainly take place after the U.S. midterm elections, citing President Donald Trump’s reluctance to further destabilize oil markets in the final days of the campaign.
The White House said Thursday that the U.S. will not resume attacks on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement to ABC News.
"Hunting season is open as soon as the elections end and it's obvious that they're not going to wait long," one Israeli source said.
The New York Times was first to report on the planning.
Asked about the Times' reporting, a White House official said the administration does not comment on "sensitive military plans that may or may not exist."
The official added that Trump "keeps all options on the table" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is firmly in favor of renewed action against Iran, but both sources said the decision for joint strikes to resume is "only for Trump to decide."
One Israeli source did not rule out Israel striking unilaterally should the U.S. choose not to participate, but added Israel would still require U.S. consent.
Trump has repeatedly said that he would restart the war after the midterm elections and has threatened to "end" it after the midterms.
He gave a somewhat conflicting answer on the status of negotiations with Iran when asked Wednesday night, initially saying talks are ongoing "a little bit," but moments later saying "I think we're not negotiating."
"A little bit, but we'll see what happens," Trump said, when asked for an update on negotiations.
Asked if he is "over" negotiating with Iran, Trump responded, "No, I think we're not negotiating with -- We are going to have something one way or the other that'll happen fairly soon."
"Most people seem to think it's after the election, and we're going to see what happens," he added.
The plans to renew joint strikes were discussed during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's unannounced visit to Israel earlier this week, according to one Israeli source, who added that new intelligence was shared between both sides.
New strikes would aim to further erode Iran's economy and build on the ongoing U.S. blockade, with targets to include petrochemical facilities crucial to Iran's oil industry, one of the sources said.
The source added that striking Iranian nuclear facilities, such as those at Pickaxe Mountain, is also part of the new plans, but added there are no plans to strike civilian infrastructure like power plants.
The source emphasized that regime change in Iran, and not a negotiated deal, is the Israeli government's top goal.
"The only question is the timing," they said.
The U.S. military has been repositioning personnel at U.S. military bases in the Middle East, a source familiar with the matter told ABC News.
The repositioning of forces is similar to what occurred quietly prior to the start of the war with Iran in February, according to the source.
Asked for comment on an NBC report about the reduction of military and diplomatic personnel in the region, CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said in a statement: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
Earlier Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of non-essential personnel and family members in Saudi Arabia -- a decision officials say is a direct response to the risk posed by Iranian-backed Houthi militants, who have attacked Saudi oil infrastructure and airports on Saudi Arabia from Yemen.
There have been much smaller posture adjustments at several other embassies in the Middle East -- changes officials say are also linked to the Houthi threat and other matters not connected to any plan to resume combat against Iran.
ABC News' Nick Kerr and Emily Chang contributed to this report.

title: Three Maritime Strike Groups Spearhead NATO’s Neptune Strike 26-4
body: ITS Cavour, TCG Anadolu, and HMS Prince of Wales are leading the fourth and final element of NATO’s Neptune Strike enhanced vigilance activity for 2026, featuring more than 20 warships and 40 aircraft. Running from Oct. 16 to Nov. 5, Neptune Strike 26-4 involves participation from 17 nations across the breadth of the NATO alliance. Those participating are Albania, Croatia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and the United States. Rather than a traditional exercise, Neptune Strike forms part of what NATO terms enhanced vigilance activity (eVA) . While often including large scale training exercises under its umbrella, the primary aim of these activities is to demonstrate NATO’s presence and capability as a deterrent, mainly, to increasingly aggressive Russian activity against NATO nations and allies following the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. For Neptune Strike 26-4, individual maritime strike groups will operate across a wide range of NATO’s geographic area, running drills up in the High North as well as over the warmer waters of the Mediterranean. HMS Prince of Wales , accompanied by an air wing of F-35B Lightning IIs, Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and Royal Norwegian Navy frigate HNoMS Fridtjof Nansen , will hold down the fort in the Northern Atlantic and Arctic regions. That confidence is built through rigorous planning, close coordination with Allied nations and the daily work of turning national capabilities into an integrated NATO force,” said Rear Admiral Eduardo Guitian Crespo, STRIKFORNATO’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations. “Neptune Strike is particularly relevant in today’s security environment. For our Allies, Neptune Strike provides reassurance backed by credible military capability. It demonstrates that NATO is ready to defend Allied territory and deny a potential adversary its objectives. Our purpose is to preserve peace—and we have the capability, cohesion and resolve to defend it,” said Admiral George Wikoff, Commander of Allied Joint Force Command (JFC) Naples. 3 @NATO Maritime Strike Groups: @RoyalNavy @COMUKCSG, with @HMSPWLS, @HMSDauntless & HNOMS Fridtjof Nansen @ItalianNavy Carrier Strike Group, with ITS Cavour, ITS Andrea Doria & ITS Carlo Margottini Turkish Expeditionary Strike Group, with TCG Anadolu, TCG Gaziantep, & TCG Gur — Dr Phil Weir (@navalhistorian) October 19, 2026 While Neptune Strike is lacking the presence of a U.S. Navy carrier strike group (CSG), with the impact to availability of these potent task groups by the U.S.-Iran war now well noted, the ability of Europe to generate three of its own, independent, maritime strike groups led by ships capable of operating fixed wing aircraft is to be particularly noted. Although, individually, none of these task groups can match the sheer capability or endurance of a U.S. carrier group, it is never certain – particularly in the modern political landscape – how many, if any, of these groups would be allocated to NATO’s home turf in Europe when the time came.

title: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC has raised $354M this cycle
body: Democrats’ top Senate-focused super PAC will report raising $354 million since the start of the start of the cycle through Oct. 14 — including roughly $29 million in the first two weeks of the month— as Democrats race to seize control of the upper chamber in the election’s closing weeks. Senate Majority PAC shared their fundraising totals, which are higher than any previous cycle, with POLITICO ahead of a Federal Election Commission deadline later Thursday. The super PAC affiliated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer had $32.7 million in the bank as of Oct. 14. “This is already the strongest cycle in Senate Majority PAC’s history, and it’s arriving exactly when it counts,” SMP spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement. “We’re on the air across the battleground through Election Day, and every dollar is going toward beating price-gouging Republicans and winning back the Senate.” That’s more than the $306 million SMP raised in the 2024 campaign cycle, according to FEC filings , its previous high. SMP is still being outraised by the Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s top Senate super PAC, in large part thanks to billionaire Elon Musk and other Republican megadonors. Musk gave $158 million to SLF in the third quarter , according to its most recent FEC report, and the super PAC in turn sent that money to Texas’ Senate race in order to boost the scandal-plagued GOP nominee Ken Paxton. SLF has raised more than $545 million for the cycle, according to its latest filing . Democrats have been able to offset much of Republicans’ super PAC cash advantage on the airwaves because of stronger candidate fundraising. But Republicans still have the advantage of a favorable map — and more outside money — as they hope to maintain control of at least one chamber of Congress next month. CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misstated the timeframe SMP raised $354 million. It also misstated how much the super PAC raised over the last two weeks.

title: We have Traits at Home
body:
I have had more time recently to write code in Zig [1] , and it has been good for my soul. I wanted to share some insights I have arrived at regarding abstractions in Zig, including some techniques that I have found useful but not seen employed more broadly.
Considerable [2] ink [3] has [4] been [5] spilled [6] on Zig Interfaces, and justifiably so. While not a language feature, interfaces are the de-facto way of implementing runtime polymorphism in Zig. Yet [7] more [8] has been said about zig's comptime, and how it may be leveraged to avoid the performance woes of dynamic dispatch and write slick, data-oriented code.
To put it briefly, polymorphism in Zig is conventionally obtained in one of two ways:
This state of affairs has proven to be quite effective so far, but it is not without its tradeoffs.
Interfaces offer the sort of type contracts that we are used to from other languages. A function that accepts an interface has a guarantee of its method signatures, but not its implementation. However because interfaces are, by design, modular at runtime, they also introduce a hard barrier for the compiler and thus a performance overhead. There is enough indirection that it often cannot effectively apply the optimizations that it would to monomorphic code.
For cases of performance critical code, Zig code typically relies on comptime duck typing. A function argument is either anytype or parameterized by a type argument T , and the function implementation will either perform compile-time reflection or make assumptions about the type's methods that can be checked at compile-time. Implementations can then be monomorphised, similar to C++ templating or C macros. This is slightly more safe than runtime duck typing, because any interface violations will be caught at compile time rather than runtime, but the caller and callee must still be careful to document and follow the contract of what types may be passed.
If you are coming from another strongly typed language, you would be forgiven for finding this arrangement rather simplistic. This is perhaps by design -- Zig aims to be simple. However if you have grown accustomed to Rust's traits or Haskell typeclasses, there appears to be no ready equivalent in Zig.
I will argue that, with a little adaptation, it is perfectly possible to express similar abstractions over types in Zig userland. I would propose a new convention for defining compile-time type contracts as Traits in Zig. It doesn't require any libraries or machinery - in fact if fits remarkably well into vanilla Zig. It is inspired by the functional programming world in general, and OCaml in particular.
Definition: a Trait is a compile-time struct which contains related functions over a given type. [9]
So as not to bury the lead, let me begin with a brief example of how we might define a trait for folding (reducing) on a type.
Ugh. Isn't that just buttery smooth? [10] The contract is clear, LSP autocompletion picks it up, the compiler even knows to inline it and unroll the loop.
Traits are just bags of functions and types that tell the receiving function how to execute subtasks that it's not responsible for defining. They behave a lot like vtables, except that they are evaluated at comptime rather than runtime.
To justify traits, let's take a tour through Zig polymorphism with a common motivating example: arithmetic operations. I've seen a few complaints over the years about how awkward is it to do math in Zig over user-defined types. In its pursuit of explicit control flow, Zig has eschewed operator overloading, and this can be jarring if you're coming from other typed languages.
Let's imagine we have some user-defined types like Rational and Complex , and we want to define their basic arithmentic operations. We would probably end up with something like the following.
For the sake of having something to do with them, let's say that we want to compute the Möbius transformation : (a * x + b) / (c * x + d) , which is useful for complex numbers as well as rationals. To keep things simple, we'll assume that all arguments to the function are of the same type.
If we were to implement the Mobius transformation naively, we could just use built-in operators.
This would work fine, as long as the inputs were all floats of the same type. Division would break for integers, and of course it wouldn't work with our user-defined types, but it's a starting point.
We could of course notice that both of our user-defined types have arithmetic functions with matching names and similar signatures, which would lend themselves to duck typing as well.
This will work for our user-defined types, but obviously not with Zig's primitive types. We would have to wrap those in our own user-defined types with their own functions. More troublingly, this sort of ties us to a sort of object-oriented pattern: the de-facto way to obey this abstraction contract is to define methods on the struct.
The good news is that it's all monomorphised at compile time, allowing the compiler to simplify and inline these function calls.
If we wanted this to work dynamically at runtime, we could perhaps declare a Num interface that uses a VTable and opaque pointer to dynamically dispatch these math operations.
We would then need to wire up Complex and Rational to expose fn num(self: *Self) Num (or some such) that wraps our arithmentic functions, which is a little too tedious to reproduce here, but it would work fine on the happy path. You would of course need to be a bit careful: there's nothing stopping you from mixing complex and rational numbers in your function calls, and this would lead to undefined behavior. You could probably add some saftey checks with a bit of overengineering, but we won't get into that here.
Not only is this clunkier than comptime duck typing, it will also be slower. We are effectively demanding dynamic dispatch whenever we want to do a math operation, which will trip up the compiler and have a significant performance impact if we're doing a lot of math.
When we define the mobius function, we really want to say "I don't know what type I'm dealing with, but it needs to have arithmetic operations." In this sort of case, I think it makes the most sense to just pass the functions it needs to use at compile-time. This would remove any ambiguity, at the cost of being rather explicit.
This is effectively compile-time dependency injection at a really fine-grained level. The signature is rather verbose, but there's actually a lot less boilerplate to write for Complex or Rational compared to runtime interfaces.
From here, it's not a huge leap to traits. We're effectively just cleaning up the function signature by gathering together the arithmetic functions into one struct. [11]
From here, I usually just declare the trait implementation as part of my type.
What I really like about this approach is how flexible it is, while remaining very clear about the contract between the function and type. For example, imagine that we wanted to extend our definition of Num to the primitive types like i32 and f32 . There are a bunch of ways we could do this, but I would probably just define a function that produces something appropriate for integer and float types.
Traits are also transparent to the compiler, which will happily monomorphize and inline these functions. I prefer this over runtime polymorphism most of the time, especially in hot loops or for library functions that are unopinionated on data layout.
You'll notice that traits have to be explicitly conditioned on a known type. Unlike interfaces, there's no way to say "give me a number, I don't care what kind." For some applications, it would be nice if we could have an associated type.
Unfortunately, the above isn't valid Zig, and it's unclear how that would even work at a language level. Instead, traits insist that the types they are operating on are known in advance.
I have not yet found an ergonomic way around this. Traits do not play very well with type erasure.
Before proceeding, I want to introduce some small helper functions that have streamlined how I work with traits.
If you adopt traits as a programming pattern and convention, you'll quickly end up defining functions and passing them around. You will have already noticed above that I define a lot of throwaway inner struct types, just so that I can pull functions out of them. This has led to the following convenience function for declaring trait implementations, which removes some of the boilerplate.
I use this all over the place to derive trait implementations from anonymous structs. For example, we could use it to rewrite builtinNum to be a little more concise and functional. Note that the declarations need to be public for the type reflection to work.
Most of the time, I don't mind passing trait implementations around explicitly. I've gotten into the habit, and just don't find it to be that big of a deal. Trait functors make it pretty easy to reduce the boilerplate, and I like having explicit control over how things are implemented.
However when I'm dealing with my own structs, 99% of the time the trait implementation I'm looking for is going to be declared as a const on the struct itself. I use the function below to to easily retrieve or construct the most common cases.
This is basically equivalent to saying "eh, it's duck typed. figure it out". Just because we are explicit, doesn't mean that we can't be lazy. If we want to take this full circle back to duck typing, we can even define trait functors that rely on getTrait to extract traits from the types they pass.
With some helpers defined, let's return to the Num example.
Traits in Zig resemble traits in Rust, typeclasses in Haskell, or modules in Ocaml. In Rust or Haskell, they would be resolved from a global registry managed by the compiler. This can feel very convenient, but it violates Zig's principle of explicit control flow. Rust and Haskell can require a fair bit of hunting for where a trait is defined, especially when something's wrong and the LSP isn't resolving it properly. It can also be a contributor to long compile times. Resolving a generic trait in these languages is often equivalent to evaluating a proof, and that can take time.
Ocaml modules, however, work quite a bit like Zig traits: modules are first-class objects, and they are passed as arguments to the functions that consume them. There is no inference of what modules apply to a type - you locate them and pass them explicitly. If we were to define Num as a module, it might look something like the following.
Because modules in Ocaml are first-class values, they can actually take it a step further. Rather than defining mobius as written above, it is common in Ocaml to make use of "module functors", which are simply functions that take modules as arguments and return new modules. If we wanted to define mobius in terms of a given numeric type, we might instead write it:
This is effectively currying: we are applying the module arguments now, and the value arguments later. However it derives a mobius function that doesn't need to be taking a bunch of type arguments all the time, and that module can in turn be used in later constructions. This translates straightforwardly to Zig. If we wanted to adhere strictly to the traits pattern, it might look like the following.
This works fine, but I think it's even simpler to move the functor into Mobius(T) :
However for single functions like this, unless I knew it would need to be consumed by another function as a trait, I would probably be tempted to just implement it as a type-curried function rather than a full-blown trait:
The versatility of Zig's comptime makes all of these more or less equivalent to the compiler. It's just a stylistic choice, depending on what the situation calls for.
Also, notice that technically we have already used trait functors when we defined builtinNum . It's not a deep, technical concept. It's just a function that constructs a trait implementation for you.
Having thoroughly introduced traits, let's talk about what we can do with them.
In this section are a few traits that I find myself reaching for with enough regularity that I keep a file around containing them. All of these are fairly humdrum (but wildly applicable) abstractions that I lifted wholecloth from other languages.
I need to convert one type into another all the freaking time. Often there are multiple ways to do this, depending on how you want to interpret the upstream type. I use Into and From to canonicalize methods for converting one type into another.
Sometimes, rather than iterating, we need keyed access to a value. The container could be a slice or a hash table - we don't care. For this, I use Index .
Another common case: we have a function that iterates over a type, but we don't care what sort of iterable data structure we're going to be working with. We usually need two traits: one for the Iterable collection, and another for the Iterator , which keeps track of our progress through the collection.
You'll notice that this is a little awkward, because we don't usually care what the iterator implementation is. It's probably just a usize index over an array or something. It would be nice if we could just define Iterable(T: type, Elem: type) . I've chosen to just let it be awkward. It's usually not a big deal.
I really don't want you to walk away from this article thinking "I need to convert all my code to use traits". Traits should not be thought of as a totalizing pattern. The last thing I want is for Zig code to start looking like Rust or Haskell.
Traits are a sometimes treat. They are useful for functions that need abstractions inside of hot loops, where you know that you want monomorphization and static dispatch. They can become legible building blocks for some neat metaprogramming tricks. However most of the time I only reach for them in a pull-based manner: I have a function where it would be useful to consume a trait, because it's undecided on some implementation detail.
Used improperly, traits can explode the size of your binary and actually make it slower. Each function parameterized on comptime parameters gets its own templated assembly, and if you nest these a few layers deep, it's easy to end up with a combinatorial explosion. This can thrash your CPU cache, and depending on the situation, easily be outperformed by dynamic dispatch and vtables.
Traits are ultimately handy and very powerful. I wish I saw more codebases that made use of them, especially for abstraction inside of hot loops. I like that they are a design pattern more than a language feature, and this gives you a lot of explicit control over when and how you use them. I was looking for a solution like this for a long time, and I'm glad I found it.
I'm sure that other Zig users have stumbled onto this trick, but I have yet to see it in the wild. I think that part of the reason is that it doesn't really lend itself to a library. It's more of a convention that you can choose to use or ignore.
My hope is that for someone reading, traits are the right tool for the job.
Zig Interface Revisited by William Wong ↩
A Practical Guide to Applying Data-Oriented Design by Andrew Kelley ↩
Zig Comptime is Bonkers Good by Scott Redig ↩
"Traits" are directly inspired from OCaml modules, but the term "module" already refers to something else in Zig. ↩
This is a pretty simplistic definition of a numeric trait. In practice, you would probably want to look into std::ops from Rust or Num from Haskell. ↩

title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
body:
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/canva-craft-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/canva-craft-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/canva-craft-4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/canvacraft-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/canvacraft-5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.
Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

title: a hacky fucked up way to portably access errno from outside of c
body:
here's something really cursed i made a while back. the goal here is to create a portable way to obtain the value of errno from outside of c, without using a wrapper function written in c. for those unaware, errno is defined as a macro, and its expansion is non-portable and usually comes with no stability guarantees. so if you're calling libc functions from some other language (such as hare, which i'll be using in this post), it's not possible to retrieve error values from them without relying on an implementation detail or writing a wrapper function in c which returns errno. ...unless you're willing to resort to some fucked up hacks, that is. preamble use io; use sys; use types::c; @symbol("close") fn c_close(fd: int) int; @symbol("dup") fn c_dup(oldfd: int) int; @symbol("dup2") fn c_dup2(oldfd: int, newfd: int) int; @symbol("lseek") fn c_lseek(fd: int, offs: io::off, whence: int) io::off; @symbol("mkstemp") fn c_mkstemp(template: *c::char) int; @symbol("perror") fn c_perror(s: nullable *c::char) void; @symbol("read") fn c_read(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; @symbol("strerror") fn c_strerror(errnum: int) *c::char; @symbol("unlink") fn c_unlink(path: *c::char) int; @symbol("write") fn c_write(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; def SEEK_SET = 0; def STDERR_FILENO = 2i; there aren't any libc functions which return the value of errno. there are, however, functions which return a string that describes errno. so let's start there. export type error = !str; standard c defines two promising functions: strerror and perror. posix defines two more functions: strerror_r and strerror_l . unfortunately, the strerror functions all take in the error number as an argument. only perror reads from errno directly. perror prints an error string to stderr, so our goal now to is to somehow capture the error string from perror , without actually writing anything to stderr. alright, so let's do it. during program initialization, i dup STDERR_FILENO (2), open a temporary file, and change STDERR_FILENO to refer to the temporary file: let stderr = -1; let tmpfd = -1; let tmpname: [_]u8 = ['/', 't', 'm', 'p', '/', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', '\0']; @init fn stderr_tmp() void = { stderr = c_dup(STDERR_FILENO); assert(stderr != -1); tmpfd = c_mkstemp(&tmpname: *c::char); assert(tmpfd != -1); const n = c_dup2(tmpfd, STDERR_FILENO); assert(n != -1); }; @fini fn stderr_tmp() void = { if (tmpfd != -1) { c_close(tmpfd); c_unlink(&tmpname: *c::char); }; }; all low-level functions (libc wrappers or syscall wrappers) which may interact with stderr will silently adjust the fd from STDERR_FILENO to the dup'd stderr file descriptor if necessary. (i'll give an example later on, if you're confused by that.) when an error occurs, the below function is called to obtain the error string: fn get_errno() error = { c_perror(null); if (c_write(STDERR_FILENO, &0u8, 1) == -1) { return "Unknown error"; }; c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); defer c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); static let buf: [256]u8 = [0...]; const n = c_read(STDERR_FILENO, &buf, len(buf)); if (n == -1) { return "Unknown error"; }; const n = c::strnlen(&buf: *c::char, n: size); return *(&buf[..n]: *str); }; when perror is called, it writes to the temporary file. ( STDERR_FILENO needs to refer to the temp file from the beginning because dup2 may overwrite errno , so it can't be used right before calling perror ). the message is then read back and returned. so cool, we have an error message string. now let's use that to obtain the actual errno value. export type error = !str; export type errno = !int; to do that, i'll write another initialization function to construct a table of error messages: let strerror_table: [256][256]u8 = [[0...]...]; @init fn strerror_table() void = { for (let i = 0; i < len(strerror_table): int; i += 1) { const msg = c_strerror(i); const n = c::strlen(msg); strerror_table[i][..n] = (msg: *[*]u8)[..n]; }; }; the above function copies the strings returned by strerror into strerror_table . if you're familiar with posix libc, you may be confused why i'm not using strerror_r here, since that function directly writes error messages into a user-supplied buffer. the reason is really annoying: there's two versions of strerror_r ! there's a non-standard GNU version which returns an error message directly but may use its own immutable static storage, and there's a POSIX version which always writes to the user-supplied buffer and returns int . i want the POSIX version of course, but on glibc, the symbol " strerror_r " refers to the GNU version. the POSIX version uses the symbol " __xpg_strerror_r ". but other posix-compliant libcs (such as musl and all the BSD libcs) only provide the POSIX version, under the symbol " strerror_r ". fitting with the theme of this blog post, glibc makes it impossible to portably call the function i want without relying on an internal symbol name, which i really don't want to do (since that makes the code libc-dependent). but anyways, now that the strerror_table is constructed, let's update the errno() function to use it: fn get_errno() error errno = { c_perror(null); if (c_write(STDERR_FILENO, &0u8, 1) == -1) { return "Unknown error" -1 ; }; c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); defer c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); static let buf: [256]u8 = [0...]; const n = c_read(STDERR_FILENO, &buf, len(buf)); if (n == -1) { return "Unknown error" -1 ; }; const n = c::strnlen(&buf: *c::char, n: size); return *(&buf[..n]: *str); if (n != 0) { buf[n - 1] = '\0'; // strip trailing newline }; for (let i = 0z; i < len(strerror_table); i += 1) { if (c::strcmp(&buf: *c::char, &strerror_table[i]: *c::char) == 0) { return i: errno; }; }; return -1; }; btw, here's an example of what a libc wrapper of write looks like: export fn write(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) (size | errno) = { const fd = if (fd == STDERR_FILENO) stderr else fd; const n = c_write(fd, buf, count); if (n == -1) { return get_errno(); }; return n: size; }; another fucked up hack to make it actually portable the original thing that actually caused me to make this was that i wanted to see if i could make a generic "posix" target for hare. like, if you have a posix system which hare doesn't natively support, you could compile for the "posix" target and link to the system libc and things would just Work. the errno stuff was just a fun detour from that (the generic posix version would just return an error string, since the actual error numbers aren't portable). but in this context, there's one problem with the errno stuff. you can see it in this snippet from get_errno() : c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); defer c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); i define SEEK_SET as a constant earlier on: def SEEK_SET = 0; this is usually true, but posix doesn't guarantee that SEEK_SET is 0! its value is completely implementation-defined. this is yet another place where it's not really possible to do stuff outside of c without relying on an "implementation detail". (in practice i can't imagine any reason SEEK_SET wouldn't be 0, but unnecessary fucked up hacks are fun so for now let's just pretend that any of this actually matters) it's actually possible to work around this! lseek returns the new offset after seeking. so we can call lseek with an arbitrary whence value, and use the return value to determine whether it did what we wanted. if not, just repeat with different whence values until it works! let i = 0; for (i <= 2; i += 1) { if (c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, i) == 0) { break; }; }; assert(i <= 2); defer c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, i); i just loop from 0 to 2, because i figure that it'll probably always be one of those values. but there's no reason higher values couldn't also be checked. conclusion export fn main() void = { // demonstration: pass in -1 as the fd to cause EBADF match (write(-1, &0u8, 1)) { case size => abort("expected error"); case let err: errno => assert(err: int == sys::EBADF); }; }; i just think it's kinda cool that this is possible

@symbol("mkstemp") fn c_mkstemp(template: *c::char) int; @symbol("perror") fn c_perror(s: nullable *c::char) void; @symbol("read") fn c_read(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; @symbol("strerror") fn c_strerror(errnum: int) *c::char; @symbol("unlink") fn c_unlink(path: *c::char) int; @symbol("write") fn c_write(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; def SEEK_SET = 0; def STDERR_FILENO = 2i; there aren't any libc functions which return the value of errno. there are, however, functions which return a string that describes errno. so let's start there. export type error = !str; let tmpfd = -1; let tmpname: [_]u8 = ['/', 't', 'm', 'p', '/', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', '\0']; @init fn stderr_tmp() void = { stderr = c_dup(STDERR_FILENO); assert(stderr != -1); tmpfd = c_mkstemp(&tmpname: *c::char); assert(tmpfd != -1); const n = c_dup2(tmpfd, STDERR_FILENO); assert(n != -1); }; @fini fn stderr_tmp() void = { if (tmpfd != -1) { c_close(tmpfd); c_unlink(&tmpname: *c::char); }; }; all low-level functions (libc wrappers or syscall wrappers) which may interact with stderr will silently adjust the fd from STDERR_FILENO to the dup'd stderr file descriptor if necessary. title: USAF Confirms Bombers Could Have A Major Air-To-Air Combat Role
body: The U.S. Air Force is exploring options for adding air-to-air combat capabilities to its bombers as part of efforts adjacent to its latest fighter force structure plans . The service has raised the possibility of the B-21 Raider, specifically , taking on an air-to-air role, and potentially doing so in cooperation with Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drones, in the past. As TWZ has explored for years , the B-21’s inherent attributes – size, extreme range, high operating ceiling, broadband low-observability (stealthiness), and advanced sensors – could actually make it especially well suited to taking part in air-to-air combat missions. The Air Force’s other bombers could also be part of these future plans. Aviation Week was first to report on the potential for bombers to help bolster the Air Force’s air-to-air combat capacity after obtaining a copy of a new long-term fighter force structure report submitted to Congress last week. Media coverage of this report first began to appear earlier this week following a roundtable on Tuesday with Lt. Gen. David Tabor, the service’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Plans and Programs. The full report, which is unclassified, was not disseminated to reporters at that time. Pre-production B-21 Raider bombers at Edwards Air Force Base in California. USAF The Air Force’s central goal now is having 1,509 combat-coded fighters in inventory by 2035, which is hundreds more than it has in service today. This will come from the acquisition of new F-35As , F-15EXs , and F-47s . There are already questions about how realistic this plan might be, and the service has acknowledged several hurdles it will need to overcome. You can read more about this in our initial reporting here . The F-47, a rendering of which is seen here, is a critical component of the Air Force’s current future fighter force structure plans. USAF “Accordingly, the USAF is also evaluating additional recapitalization options, including a new capacity fighter, increased reliance on CCAs [Collaborative Combat Aircraft], and developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers,” the latest fighter force structure report says, per Aviation Week . “A new capacity fighter” may refer to the possible acquisition of new-production F-16 Vipers, which Lt. Gen. Tabor said at the roundtable could be an option in the future, according to an earlier story from Air & Space Forces Magazine . He also said making any such decision was not an “urgent” priority. This is just one possibility here. The Air Force has floated ideas for other new fighter concepts beyond the F-47 in recent years. Lockheed Martin has talked about the potential for expanding on the F-35 design . The possibility of the Air Force buying a version of the current-generation Block 70 F-16, an example of which is seen here, has been raised. USAF A Bahraini Block 70 F-16D flown by members of the 416th Flight Test Squadron pulls away after receiving fuel from a KC-135 tanker with a crew from the 370th Flight Test Squadron during a sortie out of Edwards Air Force Base in California on March 7, 2024. USAF At the roundtable on Tuesday, Tabor also made clear that the introduction of CCAs would influence future fighter force structure plans, but the expected scale and scope of those impacts remain unclear. He does not appear to have addressed the role bombers could play in this equation at that time. The new fighter report itself does not elaborate further on the potential use of bombers, based on Aviation Week ’s story. TWZ is seeking more information. When it comes to the possibility of Air Force bombers, and the B-21 more specifically, taking on an air-to-air role, this is not the first time the possibility has been raised, as mentioned earlier. “As the NGAD [Next Generation Air Dominance] review goes forward, like, is it possible that what that ends up with could be the B-21 taking a larger role?” reporter Stephen Losey, working at the time for Defense News , asked then-Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin at the Military Reporters & Editors (MRE) Conference in 2024. “We have not taken that off the table,” the Air Force’s top officer said in response to Losey’s question, but did not elaborate. At that time, the Air Force’s NGAD program was undergoing a deep review, and the future of the sixth-generation fighter component of the effort had come into question. The decision was ultimately made to continue pursuing plans for what has now become the F-47 . For years now, TWZ has been highlighting how the B-21 could serve in multiple roles beyond just that of a traditional bomber, including in an air-to-air capacity . Air Force officials have themselves described the Raider as having multi-mission capabilities, which could extend into the realm of air-to-air combat. “If we were to characterize it [NGAD] as a fighter, we would be… thinking too narrowly about what kind of airplane we need in a highly contested environment,” then-Air Force Maj. Gen. Scott Pleus told what was then just Air Force Magazine back in 2019. This could be “a B-21 that also has air-to-air capabilities” and can “work with the family of systems to defend itself, utilizing stealth – maybe that’s where the sixth-generation airplane comes from.” Pleus’ comments had tied in with adjacent discussions at the time and thereafter about how the B-21 might operate together with future CCA drones . Pleus, who was subsequently promoted to lieutenant general and whose lasting posting was as Director of Staff at the Air Force’s top headquarters at the Pentagon, retired in August of this year. A composite image showing the two drones – General Atomics FQ-42 Vengence and Anduril’s FQ-44 Fury – that the Air Force is acquiring now under the first phase of its CCA program. USAF It remains unclear how the Air Force might be considering employing the B-21, or any of its other existing bombers, in air-to-air combat. This could entail loading out bombers for direct air-to-air engagements, or the integration of new capabilities to help them find targets or to otherwise enable new supporting roles, or a mix of all of the above. The process of achieving air superiority is not limited to neutralizing aerial threats, either. As TWZ has written in the past in the context of an air-to-air role for the Raider in particular: “The Raider has the potential to serve as a launch platform for air-to-air missiles, especially outsized very long-range types . Its payload capacity would give it the ability to carry a large volume of smaller air-to-air missiles, as well. B-21s could also employ air-to-ground munitions in support of the suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses mission (SEAD/DEAD), which is also part of the air superiority equation.” “Maybe most significantly, the B-21s could also act as airborne nerve centers in support of counter-air missions, especially for controlling drones like the Air Force’s planned fleets of Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), and have the ability to do so even in the most heavily contested of airspaces. Uncrewed aircraft, in turn, could feed targeting data back to Raiders with air-to-air loadouts. B-21s might even be able to launch some of those drones themselves.” A head-on view of the first pre-production B-21 Raider. USAF Deeply networked ‘kill webs’ that bring together distributed arrays of sensors and other supporting elements across vast distances and multiple domains, coupled with very-long-range air-to-air missiles , open up new operational possibilities more generally. This applies to Air Force bombers beyond the B-21. When it comes to longer-range air-to-air missiles, the Navy has notably already fielded the AIM-174B air-launched version of the Standard Missile-6 (SM-6). The service more recently disclosed another such missile in flight testing now, the AIM-424 Malice . A US Navy Super Hornet fighter seen carrying a load of AIM-424 missiles during a flight test. USN The Air Force has pursued similar missile developments in the past and put out a call for a new anti-air missile with a maximum range of at least 1,000 nautical miles just in June. The service has been exploring multi-stage types with modular designs that could be configured for longer- and shorter-range engagements, as well. These are all just programs we know about, and do not speak to the developments the Air Force and others could have underway in the classified realm. There is also the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) LongShot program , which the Air Force, as well as the U.S. Army and Navy, have been involved with over the years. The aim of that effort is to demonstrate the concept of an air-to-air missile-carrying drone to help extend the reach and reduce the vulnerability of tactical fighters and bombers . A rendering depicting LongShot drones being launched from a B-52 bomber, as well as F-15 fighters. General Atomics On top of all this, tactical fighters are generally ill-suited to, and in some cases outright incapable of, carrying the kinds of outsized payloads being discussed here. This underscores the potential value of incorporating bombers into this equation as a means to engage targets at extreme ranges. Even in a closer proximity support role of fighter aircraft, B-21s, as well as B-52s , could contribute to air-to-air fight as arsenal ships for longer-range weapons, firing on demand from the rear in coordination with crewed and uncrewed platforms operating at the tip of the tactical edge. B-21s could also use their penetrating capabilities to command drones of their own that provide penetrating fighter-like capabilities. New air-to-air capabilities on Air Force bombers could include self-protection systems, too. Years ago now, the B-21’s prime contractor, Northrop Grumman, patented an anti-missile defense system for stealthy aircraft designed to fire hard-kill interceptors. The Air Force, as well as the Navy, have openly expressed interest in similar defensive capabilities for aerial refueling tankers and other larger planes . Just being able to provide localized close-in defensive ‘bubbles’ around individual bombers could impact the calculus when it comes to future air-to-air combat requirements. Drawings from Northrop Grumman’s aircraft anti-missile defense system patent. USPTO To reiterate, these are all concepts we have discussed in depth for roughly a decade . Speaking more broadly about Air Force future fighter force structure demands, as we wrote previously : “In recent years, sustainment costs, broadly, have only become an increasingly serious concern for the Air Force, as well as the other branches of the U.S. military, especially when it comes to complex manned platforms, such as the F-22 Raptor and the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter . Fleet size and the readiness of those fleets are also highly pressing issues. So, at least in the near term, it’s not surprising that NGAD may end up focusing more on exploring available lower-cost options with distributed capabilities as alternatives to traditional air combat assets with highly centralized capabilities, such as manned fighter jets packed with ‘exquisite’ technologies.” Despite the decision in the end to proceed with the more exquisite F-47, these points have only become more pronounced as time has gone on. How many F-47s the Air Force ultimately intends to buy is another question that looks to remain unanswered by the latest fighter force structure report. At the same time, there are clear signs that the Air Force is planning to significantly increase its planned B-21 fleet size. The official acquisition target has long been at least 100 Raiders, but the Air Force and Northrop Grumman have said a new topline figure is expected to come in the Fiscal Year 2028 budget proposal next year. The service is now explicitly aiming to have at least 500 CCA drones in service by 2032 , too. All of this will compete for funding and other resources, at least to a degree. A pre-production B-21 seen during a test flight. USAF In the meantime, there has been a “persistent decline in AA [aircraft availability] rates across the USAF tactical fighter fleet,” which “is the direct mathematical consequence of operating an inventory with an average age exceeding 31 years,” the Air Force’s latest fighter force structure report says, according to Aviation Week . “As legacy platforms – such as the F-16C/D, F-15E, and A-10C – operate well beyond their original engineering service lives, they experience compounding structural fatigue, widespread corrosion, and subsystem degradation.” “Achieving the mandated AA rates required for a peer-conflict scenario necessitates aggressive divestment of the oldest airframes to fund the procurement of highly available, modernized platforms like the F-35A and F-15EX,” the report adds, per that outlet. Furthermore, “to counter the [Chinese] industrial capacity and numerical advantage in fielding fighters like the J-20 and J-16 , the USAF must embrace a hybrid force of manned and unmanned systems.” A Chinese J-20 fighter. PLAAF With all this in mind, active consideration of new air-to-air roles for bombers, as well as the possibility of “increased reliance on CCAs” and the potential to acquire new current-generation F-16s, at least seems to reflect a hedge strategy on the part of the Air Force. If nothing else, the door clearly remains open to bombers being a key part of the Air Force’s ‘fighter’ vision in the future. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post USAF Confirms Bombers Could Have A Major Air-To-Air Combat Role appeared first on TWZ .
