title: Electronic attack units enter full-rate production for Navy EA-18G Growler
body:
CHANTILLY, Virginia. General Dynamics Mission Systems won a $184 million U.S. Navy contract for full-rate production of Next Generation Electronic Attack Units (NGEAU) and associated sustainment support for the EA-18G Growler, the company announced in a statement.
The award moves NGEAU into full-rate production as part of the Navy’s EA-18G Growler Block II modernization program. General Dynamics describes the system as an open-architecture electronic-warfare capability intended to allow the fleet to adapt more rapidly as electronic threats and mission requirements change.
The production portion is being performed under a firm-fixed-price indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, while sustainment work is covered under a cost-plus-fixed-fee arrangement, according to the company. Work will be performed at General Dynamics Mission Systems’ Bloomington, Minnesota, facility beginning immediately and continuing through 2032.

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures. The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture. That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic. A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t. The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost. Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency. Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance. GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive. The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat. Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements. For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value. Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances. That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy. Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset. EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable. Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes. The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale. This content was produced by EXL. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

title: SOSA aligned VPX suite for mission computing, AI, and networking unveiled by Aitech
body:
CHATSWORTH, California. Aitech launched a four-card hardware suite aligned with the Sensor Open Systems Architecture, or SOSA, Technical Standard that combines mission computing, artificial intelligence (AI) acceleration, and high-speed networking for open-architecture defense systems, the company announced in a statement.
The Aitech SOSA Suite includes the U-C8600 I/O-intensive single-board computer (SBC), U-C8601 compute-intensive SBC, U-C6850 managed Ethernet switch/router, and U-C5300 general-purpose graphics processing unit (GPGPU) board, the company says, adding that the cards can operate individually or together using a 40 Gigabit Ethernet and PCI Express Gen4 architecture. The company says the U-C8601 provides up to 32 TOPS of integrated AI acceleration, while the U-C5300 provides up to 35.8 TFLOPS for AI inference, image processing, sensor fusion, and video analytics.
The U-C6850 provides as much as 320 Gbps of non-blocking Layer 2/Layer 3 switching capacity and supports configurations with up to eight 40 Gigabit Ethernet or 32 10 Gigabit Ethernet interfaces. Aitech says the modular suite can be configured for aircraft, ground vehicles, missiles, helicopters, and uncrewed platforms.

title: Hegseth warns troops against using military information for gambling, prediction market bets
body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memorandum this week barring Pentagon and military personnel from placing financial wagers — specifically “including traditional betting platforms and prediction markets such as ‘Polymarket’ or ‘Kalshi’” — using non-public, government information. The directive, dated Oct. 20, was obtained by DefenseScoop on Thursday. A source confirmed its authenticity. It comes as the U.S. government and federal law enforcement officials are responding to a rise in insider trading tied to sensitive military operations. “This prohibition applies whether the transaction is informed by classified or unclassified information,” Hegseth wrote in the memo, which was addressed to Pentagon leadership, combatant commanders, and Defense agency and field activity directors. “Violations may result in administrative, disciplinary, and, where appropriate, criminal action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and/or applicable federal law.” The issue of Defense Department personnel potentially using sensitive insider information to bet on military operations emerged publicly in April, when the Department of Justice charged a senior enlisted soldier assigned to U.S. Army Special Operations Command for allegedly using insider knowledge to bet on the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro via a prediction market site before the raid was made public. Officials alleged that the accused soldier, Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke, profited nearly $410,000 from his bets and then sent money to a foreign cryptocurrency vault before dumping the funds into a newly made brokerage account. He pleaded not guilty and was released on bond. More recently, CNN reported in August that more than 150 “wallets” on Polymarket may have traded on insider information from the military, citing research by the nonprofit Anti-Corruption Data Collective. That same month, Reuters reported that Polymarket had referred “dozens” of potential military insider trading cases to the Justice Department. In the new memo, Hegseth warned that when military personnel, intelligence professionals and DOD civilians participate in financial transactions associated with operational outcomes, they generate indicators that can be exploited by adversaries against U.S. forces and assets. “Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth wrote. He added that, beyond operational security risks, such financial stakes can “warp” defense officials’ judgement. “A logistician with money riding on a strike date has an interest in that date. An analyst with a position on an outcome has an interest in that outcome,” Hegseth said. “That is precisely the kind of dilution of the warrior ethos this Department has strived to eradicate under this administration.” The post Hegseth warns troops against using military information for gambling, prediction market bets appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: National Seafood Month, 2026
body: Presidential Actions Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research By the President of the United States of America A Proclamation Across our Nation’s harbors and fishing communities, the unrivaled skill and resolve of American fishermen and seafood producers turn the bounty of our waters into food for our families and enduring economic strength. Food security is national security — we recognize that our fisheries are a vital pillar of American independence. This National Seafood Month, I join the American people in celebrating these hardworking men and women and reaffirm my commitment to helping them compete, prosper, and lead the world in seafood production. From the fishing ports of early America to today’s seafood farms and processing plants, this great industry has rewarded enterprise, sustained family businesses, and helped forge the unmatched spirit of determination that defines our maritime workforce. For generations, our fishermen have braved rough seas and punishing storms, spending long days far from home to earn an honest living and provide for the people they love. Across our land, the incredible American seafood industry harvests nearly 8.5 billion pounds of world-class food annually, sustains more than a million jobs, and fuels more than $173 billion in commerce, bringing wealth and opportunity to communities across our great Nation. And now, as we usher in a new Golden Age of seafood production, we are ensuring our fishing communities remain places where the next generation can raise a family, build a business, and pursue their own share of the American Dream. Since returning to office, I have taken decisive action to restore American seafood competitiveness and give our fishing communities greater freedom to grow and succeed. Last year, I signed an Executive Order to restore American seafood competitiveness, and my Administration recently launched the Department of Agriculture Office of Seafood. I have also signed three proclamations to restore commercial fishing access to nearly 5,000 square miles in the Atlantic Ocean and to hundreds of thousands of square miles in the Pacific, enabling American vessels to work additional fishing grounds and compete more effectively in the global seafood market. Under my leadership, we delivered the largest single-year quota increase in the history of the United States Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery, secured a massive 1,200 percent quota increase for Atlantic mackerel, and revived the West Coast salmon season to yield the first full commercial fishery in 3 years. My Administration was also proud to allocate $123.6 million in fishery disaster assistance to help communities recover from devastating losses, strengthen shoreside infrastructure, and support job retraining to help workers get back on their feet. We will continue slashing burdensome regulations so our fishermen can reinvest in their fleets, expand their operations, and keep more of what they earn. Through these historic efforts, we are putting American fishermen first and fighting to make our Nation the strongest, most successful seafood producer in the world. As our Nation celebrates National Seafood Month, we give thanks to the families whose skill and sacrifice have built and sustained this essential American industry for over 250 years. We will stand with them as we build a future of thriving ports, successful businesses, and an American seafood industry that is stronger, more competitive, and more prosperous than ever before. NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim October 2026 as National Seafood Month. I call upon all Americans to express their thanks for the American citizens who sustain this crucial industry, and to mark this month with appropriate events and ceremonies. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twenty-second day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first. DONALD J. TRUMP The post National Seafood Month, 2026 appeared first on The White House .

title: DECREASING HOUSING COSTS FOR THE AMERICAN PEOPLE
body: Presidential Actions Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered: Section 1 . Purpose . The American Dream of homeownership is a vital pillar of our great country. It is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to mortgage origination and costs impeding homeownership; embrace innovative risk and value assessment technologies that incorporate Super Intelligence to drive down mortgage and homeownership costs; and promote competition and innovation throughout the housing and mortgage market. Sec . 2 . Proactive Cancellation of Excessive Mortgage Insurance . (a) The Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (Director) shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Federal National Mortgage Association and the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Enterprises) or the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), and the American public, direct the Enterprises to establish a pilot program, applicable only to mortgages made after the establishment of the pilot program, that periodically reviews single-family mortgage loans they own, guarantee, or securitize, using automated valuation models and other available data to assess current market value, and to identify borrowers who appear to satisfy equity and other requirements for cancellation of mortgage insurance. (b) The Director shall direct the Enterprises to establish procedures for the pilot program, including financial safety and soundness standards and payment-history requirements, under which mortgage insurance is canceled proactively when an Enterprise determines that: (i) the borrower satisfies applicable equity requirements based on the property’s current market value, as determined through an automated valuation model or other means approved by the Director; (ii) cancellation is consistent with financial safety and soundness and with the Enterprise’s contractual obligations; and (iii) the borrower satisfies all other applicable statutory, contractual, regulatory, and Enterprise requirements for cancellation. (c) The Director shall direct the Enterprises to require servicers, to the extent permitted by law and operationally feasible, to notify borrowers promptly when mortgage insurance may be canceled under the pilot program, and to reduce or eliminate unnecessary documentation requests, appraisal costs, and other administrative barriers to cancellation. Sec . 3 . Standardizing the Permitting of Homes . (a) To increase the quality and lower the cost of building a home, there is hereby established the Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation (Task Force), which shall be co-chaired by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development and the Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, or their designees, and shall include the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, or their designees. The co-chairs may invite the heads of other executive departments and agencies (agencies) to participate, as appropriate. (b) Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Task Force shall submit to the President, through the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, recommendations to facilitate the use of modern manufacturing methods in the production of manufactured and other factory-built housing eligible for Federal housing programs, including actions to: (i) promote specifications, certifications, inspections, and approvals across Federal housing and housing-finance programs; (ii) establish reciprocal recognition among agencies of licenses, certifications, approvals, and inspections, where doing so would avoid unnecessary duplication; (iii) eliminate Federal requirements and duplicative reviews that unnecessarily impede automation, modularization, standardized production, or other advanced manufacturing techniques, or that increase the time or cost of bringing homes to market; (iv) use Federal financing, insurance, guarantee, purchasing, and other program authorities to encourage innovation and increased production of affordable manufactured and factory-built homes; and (v) promote competition among manufacturers and other market participants while maintaining appropriate standards for safety, quality, durability, and consumer protection. (c) The Task Force shall also evaluate whether, and under what existing statutory authorities, Federal grant funding may be conditioned on, or be used to incentivize, State and local adoption of standardized permitting and licensing for manufactured and other factory-built housing, consistent with the best practices issued under section 4(a) of Executive Order 14394 of March 13, 2026 (Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction), and shall prepare legislative recommendations to codify the policies set forth in this subsection. (d) The heads of the agencies represented on the Task Force shall, within their respective authorities, take appropriate action to implement the Task Force’s recommendations. Sec . 4 . Reducing Excessive Title Insurance, Especially in the Refinancing of Americans Homes . (a) The Director shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Enterprises or the FHFA, and the American public, and consistent with financial safety and soundness, the Director’s authorities as regulator and conservator, and applicable law, direct the Enterprises to expand the title acceptance pilot into an ongoing program, available nationwide through both Enterprises, under which an Enterprise may accept an automated title review or other title-risk assessment approved by the FHFA in lieu of a lender’s title insurance policy on eligible refinance transactions. (b) In expanding the program, the Director shall consider: (i) extending eligibility to refinance transactions with loan-to-value ratios above the current 80 percent limit where title risk remains low; (ii) removing geographic limitations and certifying additional title-assessment providers to promote competition; (iii) waiving appraisals, income re-verification, and other documentation requirements for limited cash-out refinances that reduce the borrower’s monthly payment, where the Enterprise’s existing data support doing so; and (iv) reducing or eliminating loan-level price adjustments and other Enterprise fees on such refinances. (c) The Director shall require that cost savings resulting from the program be passed through to borrowers and that lenders inform borrowers of those savings. Sec . 5 . Department of Agriculture and Department of Veterans Affairs Direct Loan Rates . The Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs shall, consistent with applicable law, including 42 U.S.C. 1490a(a)(1)(B) and 38 U.S.C. 3762(c)(1), and available appropriations, reduce the interest rates charged on single‑family home loans made directly by their respective departments. Sec . 6 . General Provisions . (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect: (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals. (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations. (c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person. (d) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Federal Housing Finance Agency. DONALD J. TRUMP THE WHITE HOUSE, October 22, 2026. The post DECREASING HOUSING COSTS FOR THE AMERICAN PEOPLE appeared first on The White House .

title: Four KJ-3000 Radar Jets At Chinese Factory Point To Serial Production
body: New satellite imagery shows four of China’s new KJ-3000 airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft at the Xi’an Aircraft Company (XAC) facility at Xi’an-Yanliang , raising the possibility that the large radar planes are moving toward or have entered serial production. Satellite imagery captured on October 5 and provided by Vantor shows three KJ-3000s near the XAC factory in the western part of the facility, with a fourth at the nearby China Flight Test Establishment (CFTE). J. Michael Dahm, a senior fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, assesses that the presence of four aircraft points to the type having entered serial production. An overview of the Xi’an Aircraft Company (XAC) facility on October 5. A total of four KJ-3000s are visible. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Three KJ-3000s along with other Y-20s at the XAC factory in the western part of the facility. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Andreas Rupprecht , an analyst of Chinese military aviation and TWZ contributor, offered a more cautious assessment, noting that the imagery could indicate that series production or low-rate initial production (LRIP) has begun. However, he also pointed out that all four previously identified prototypes could simply have been at the facility at the same time. Specifically, he identified the aircraft seen at the CFTE portion of the airfield as being a prototype. A closer view of one of the KJ-3000s at the XAC factory. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor An additional KJ-3000 seen alongside a pair of Y-20Bs. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Whatever the explanation, the imagery offers a fresh look at a program set to significantly expand China’s already substantial airborne surveillance and battle-management capabilities. The KJ-3000, also referred to as the KJ-20, is based on the four-engine Y-20 transport aircraft , specifically the improved Y-20B variant powered by Chinese-made engines. The aircraft features a large circular radome mounted above the rear fuselage, along with a prominent series of antennas on the forward fuselage. An aerial refueling probe is mounted above the cockpit, while a conspicuous intake at the base of the tailfin is likely intended to provide cooling air for its extensive onboard electronics. A stock Y-20B transport with its distinctive locally produced WS-20 turbofan engines. via Chinese internet The first low-quality photographs of the aircraft began circulating in December 2024. More detailed imagery emerged in May 2025, showing an example at an undisclosed Chinese airfield. That aircraft, bearing the serial number 7821 and assessed to be the first example, was still wearing primer, in contrast to the examples now seen at the XAC factory. This photo emerged in May 2025 and shows the presumed first KJ-3000 on the ground at an undisclosed airfield in China. The aircraft still wears a coat of primer, and the serial number 7821 is clearly visible on the forward fuselage. via Chinese internet The KJ-3000 is expected to address longstanding limitations in China’s existing large jet-powered AEW&C fleet. To date, only four KJ-2000 Mainring aircraft have been completed. Based on the Russian-built Ilyushin Il-76MD transport, the KJ-2000 program was constrained by the limited availability of suitable airframes, and now faces the twin issues of reliance on Russian supply chains and aging aircraft. A side view of a standard PLAAF KJ-2000, albeit with the serial number censored from the photo. FYJS/via Chinese internet A domestically produced Y-20-based platform provides a more sustainable basis for a much larger AEW&C fleet, with greater scope for upgrades and potentially export opportunities. The larger airframe should also provide advantages over China’s numerous turboprop-powered AEW&C aircraft, including greater speed, range, and endurance. Its higher operating altitude would give its radar a better vantage point for detecting and tracking targets, particularly low-flying aircraft and missiles that may be masked from ground-based sensors by terrain or the radar horizon. The aerial refueling probe could further extend the aircraft’s range and time on station, although the precise operational capabilities of the KJ-3000 remain unclear. The exact configuration of the KJ-3000’s primary radar has yet to be established. China’s existing KJ-2000 and smaller KJ-500 use fixed radomes containing three active electronically scanned array (AESA) antennas to provide 360-degree coverage, rather than the rotating radomes found on aircraft such as the U.S. E-3 Sentry and Russia’s A-50 Mainstay . Whether the new aircraft follows the same approach remains to be seen. A Russian Aerospace Forces A-50U Mainstay. Russian Ministry of Defense Russian Air Force A-50U Mainstay. (Russian MoD) As well as its large AESA radar, the new aircraft is likely to carry additional intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems, while its communications equipment could make it an important networking node for Chinese forces operating across the vast distances of the Indo-Pacific. Such capabilities would be particularly valuable for coordinating combat aircraft, including uncrewed ones , sharing targeting information, and extending the reach of China’s integrated air defense and broader military networks. The KJ-3000 is also part of a broader expansion and diversification of China’s AEW&C fleet. Alongside the new jet-powered aircraft, the People’s Liberation Army continues to field and develop smaller platforms based on the four-turboprop Y-9 transport family . These include the KJ-500 , which has been produced and delivered at a rapid pace, as well as the newer KJ-700, believed to combine radar with electro-optical and infrared sensors for a broader range of surveillance missions. The precise capabilities of the KJ-700 remain uncertain, but you can read about the platform in more detail here . A prototype KJ-700. via Chinese internet The smaller turboprop aircraft offer advantages of their own. They are better suited to operating from dispersed and relatively austere airfields, and they regularly appear at Chinese island outposts and in the strategically important Taiwan Strait . Together, the different types give Chinese forces a range of options for surveillance and command and control, from persistent coverage close to home to operations farther afield. The U.S. Department of Defense has repeatedly highlighted the growing importance of China’s AEW&C fleet. In its latest annual report on Chinese military developments, the Pentagon specifically pointed to the KJ-3000: “The PLA conducted an initial flight with the KJ-3000 Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft, which will serve as a surveillance aircraft to monitor aircraft, ships, and other vehicles. The KJ-3000 will probably be the world’s first model to use digital radar and will be capable of anti-jamming, passive detection, and target identification.” Airborne radar and command-and-control aircraft are also important force multipliers for increasingly capable Chinese combat jets , including the stealthy J-20 and aircraft armed with long-range air-to-air missiles . Radar planes like these can serve as critical networking nodes for data sharing and, in some cases, allow Chinese fighters to prosecute targets without turning on their own radar. In 2022, then-Pacific Air Forces commander Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach praised the command and control associated with J-20 operations, noting that some of China’s long-range air-to-air missiles benefit from support provided by the KJ-500. A stock photo of a J-20 stealth fighter. PLAAF For China, a larger and more capable AEW&C fleet would support both the defense of its airspace and efforts to project military power across the Indo-Pacific. These aircraft could help coordinate operations around Taiwan and the South China Sea , improve situational awareness over maritime approaches, and support combat operations at greater distances from the mainland. The same Pentagon report from 2025 further noted: “China’s integration of support aircraft, such as the KJ-500 airborne early warning aircraft, provides the PLAAF with improved ISR capability to support PLA operations, as demonstrated during surge operations near Taiwan.” A KJ-500 arrives at the Zhuhai Air Show Center in November 2022 in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China. This is specifically the probe-equipped KJ-500A version. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images VCG A domestically developed, jet-powered platform such as the KJ-3000 would be a logical centerpiece of that effort, particularly since it can be produced in substantially greater numbers than the KJ-2000. The prospect of China expanding its fleet of large, jet-powered AEW&C aircraft stands in contrast to the U.S. Air Force’s troubled effort to replace its aging E-3 Sentry . The U.S. E-7 Wedgetail program has encountered major hurdles , raising concerns about a potential gap in airborne battle management as China continues to field new capabilities. The October 5 imagery does not confirm that serial production has begun. Further imagery showing additional airframes, activity around production facilities, or aircraft in new operational markings may provide a clearer indication of the program’s progress. Regardless, the KJ-3000 appears poised to become an important addition to China’s expanding airborne surveillance and command-and-control architecture. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Four KJ-3000 Radar Jets At Chinese Factory Point To Serial Production appeared first on TWZ .

title: A final farewell to NYC’s horse carriage industry
body: GOODBYE HORSES: New York City isn’t horsing around anymore. The City Council voted overwhelmingly today to abolish the Big Apple’s horse carriage industry, handing a historic win to animal rights activists who’ve pushed to end the tourist attraction for decades. The vote doesn’t mean the industry sunsets overnight, though. The bill enacting the ban — which passed the Council with 40 yays, 7 nays and 2 abstentions — allows the roughly 200 carriage drivers who shuttle tourists around Central Park to continue operating until June 2028, when the industry will be reined into a legal halt officially. Council Speaker Julie Menin, who started making the legislation’s passage a priority over the summer, told reporters before the vote that the carriage horse-related June death of Romanch Mahajan , an 18-year-old Indian tourist, was the last straw. But she also cited a long record of horses dying in the streets as part of the reason for the bill finally crossing the finish line. “This has been a long time coming,” she said. Mayor Zohran Mamdani — who initially withheld support for the measure over labor protection concerns — got behind it earlier this month, sealing the deal for it to become law. He hasn’t yet set a date for signing the bill. Mamdani came on board after the Council modified the bill to give drivers pathways into other lines of work, and the phase-out period is key in that pursuit. Under the bill, the city must create a workforce transition program under which drivers would, between now and 2028, receive career counseling as well as referrals to employment opportunities in both public and private sectors, including with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and hospitality and tourism outfits. The bill would also prohibit drivers from sending their horses to slaughter or using them for carriage duties in another city where it’s allowed. Horse carriage drivers and their supporters remain furious. The Transport Workers Union, which advocates for carriage drivers, announced yesterday that it will file a lawsuit to block the ban, arguing it violates federal and state laws. The union is especially incensed that the bill doesn’t require the city to pay out drivers for the value of their carriage licenses — an omission lawyers for the TWU say flies in the face of the Fifth Amendment’s prohibition on government usurping private property without compensation. Just as the Council was getting ready to vote, carriage supporters received backing from a somewhat unexpected source: President Donald Trump. “So sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post , referring to Mahajan. “When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition.” Also before today’s vote, dozens of TWU reps and carriage drivers gathered outside City Hall to blast the Council for moving forward with the legislation. One of them brought along a ziplock bag of equine feces with a handwritten label on it reading: “This is horse sh*t.” Christina Hansen, who’s been driving carriages for more than a decade, said she feels “disrespected” by the fact that the bill doesn’t guarantee she and her colleagues will be compensated for their licenses, which are worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. “There are people who are owed money on medallions, who have planned families, had children, bought houses, taken out loans,” Hansen said. “What’s going to happen to them?” Fellow carriage driver Danielle Slot, who voted for Mamdani in last year’s mayoral election, told Playbook she feels betrayed by his decision to back the bill without a provision mandating medallion reimbursement. “You say you’re going after billionaires, but you’re really going after the underdogs,” Slot said. “These guys are hardworking, every single medallion is its own independent business, and many are immigrant owned. I expected better from Mamdani than to be a puppet.” When asked why the bill only requires the city to “consider” medallion compensation as opposed to requiring it, Menin pointed a finger at the mayor. “To be clear, that was language that, you know, was worked out with the administration,” she told reporters at City Hall. Dora Pekec, a spokesperson for the mayor, did not dispute Menin’s account, but said the administration is “in discussions” about compensation for medallion owners. Mayors and Council speakers have tried to outlaw the industry since at least 2007. Momentum has built for a ban following tragic incidents in which horses have died or been severely injured in and around Central Park. But until now, those efforts have fizzled, in part because of political pressure from the Transport Workers Union. Carriage industry supporters argue that it can be reformed to ensure better safety standards without outlawing it outright. Council member Jim Gennaro, who introduced a bill that would do just that, said he believes Menin is at least partially politically motivated, pointing to the influence of NYCLASS, one of the main animal rights groups behind the push for a ban. “NYCLASS does have the ability to turn winners and losers in mayoral elections and in borough elections, and I don’t think that fact has been lost on the speaker,” he said before voting against the bill. NYCLASS notably tanked former Council Speaker Christine Quinn’s 2013 mayoral bid by spending heavily against her because of her reluctance to support a carriage ban at the time. Before the bill passed this afternoon, Gennaro tried to force through an amendment that would’ve delayed the phase-out deadline for the carriage industry until 2030, but it was rejected. On the other side of the bitter debate, supporters of the bill gathered for a rally in City Hall Park before the vote. Among them were members of Mahajan’s family, who have been fighting for the legislation since his death. “True justice means recognizing that these gentle, majestic horses do not belong on the congested asphalt,” Gaurav Mahajan, Romanch’s uncle, said. “By granting them the peaceful, green pastures they so deeply deserve, we fulfill Romanch’s purpose.” — Molly Reinmann and Chris Sommerfeldt From the Capitol RAILING AGAINST ALBANY: As Planet Albany denizens may have noticed, the Office of General Services this week began installing hand railings down the middle of several staircases near the state Senate chamber. More railings are planned for the Assembly chamber-side stairs too. The project costs some $700,000 , per WNYC’s Jon Campbell — further evidence that the most expensive government building construction project of the 19th century is never really done. Aside from the cost, it’s an aesthetic change to a building teeming with history and one that is rarely altered. Historian and former state Assemblymember Jack McEneny is taking the latest addition to the New York state Capitol in stride. “I always thought it was only a matter of time that somebody would decide to do something,” he said in an interview when asked about the railings. McEneny is an expert on the building and has given guided tours. He noted the staircases were not built with safety in mind. “It was inevitable,” he said of adding the railings. “There’s a number of things that we did back two or three generations before that we wouldn’t do today.” The stone staircases in the Capitol are indeed steep and very hard. (Fifteen years ago, your Playbook writer landed on his face while sprinting from the second to the third floor, necessitating an emergency dental intervention.) The building, of course, has been altered over the years to fit the needs of people who work in it. That includes the installation of a small, hideaway elevator , which was used by a wheelchair-bound Franklin Roosevelt when he was governor. “We require more things than we did at the time of its opening,” McEneny said. “We also have more attorneys who will sue.” — Nick Reisman FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL BLAKEMAN GROUP GETS $2M: The main super PAC supporting Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman has received $2 million from a dark money group created to back Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential bid. Securing American Greatness made the donation Tuesday to Strong and Safe New York, according to a filing submitted to the state Board of Elections. That group was formed by longtime Trump ally Taylor Budowich. The pro-Blakeman group has now raised $10.3 million since July. That makes it the largest single independent expenditure group so far this election cycle, though a longer roster of outside spenders boosting Gov. Kathy Hochul means she’s still the beneficiary of more super PAC money. — Bill Mahoney BROOKLYN BATTLE: The New York State Court of Appeals declined to weigh in Thursday on the long-running legal battle between factions of Brooklyn Democrats looking to lead the county party. State Assemblymember Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, the former chair of the party, appealed a lower court’s decision that an August vote to change the makeup of the organization’s executive committee was invalid. The lower court’s ruling remains in effect after the appeals court decided not to take it up. The issue of if state Assemblymember Nikki Lucas, Bichotte Hermelyn’s successor of choice, was properly elected is still playing out in the courts. — Madison Fernandez GOV AND MAYOR: Hochul’s campaign today released a video co-starring Mamdani as they prepare to hit the trail together for her reelection. The video highlighted their shared push for expanding child care, visiting a family that benefits from the service. POLITICO first reported this morning that the governor and mayor will make two appearances together in the coming days with events on Friday and Sunday in Brooklyn. — Nick Reisman FROM CITY HALL MAM LEANS ON MENIN: Mamdani put public pressure on Menin today by showing up to a rally calling for the passage of labor legislation that she hasn’t thrown her weight behind yet — in part because of legal concerns. The Delivery Protection Act, which was introduced by democratic socialist Council member Tiffany Cabán, would require Amazon and other retail giants to hire their own delivery workers. Currently, retailers can subcontract delivery employees via third party entities — a system that supporters of Cabán’s bill argue hampers workers’ ability to unionize and allows companies like Amazon to skirt accountability for labor violations. Thirty-four of the Council’s 51 members have signed on as co-sponsors of Cabán’s bill, giving it a veto-proof majority of support, and a hearing was held on it in April. But Menin hasn’t scheduled a vote on the measure or offered support for it, even though she was a co-sponsor of a version of the legislation last year before becoming speaker. Against that backdrop, Mamdani appeared on the steps of City Hall this morning with Cabán and other backers of the bill. In prepared remarks, he didn’t call out Menin by name, but blasted Amazon for pumping millions of dollars into lobbying against the bill. “Corporations like Amazon operate on a model of exploitation, and they are spending millions of dollars to convince New Yorkers otherwise,” he said. “But it will not work because we are here together today to make clear that we are going to pass the Delivery Protection Act.” By contrast, International Brotherhood of Teamsters General President Sean O’Brien, whose union represents Amazon workers, took direct aim at Menin, saying she must call a vote on the bill immediately. “Now is the time to get off your ass,” said O’Brien, who met privately with Mamdani before the rally. When asked later in the day why she isn’t immediately moving forward with the bill, Menin cited concerns she said need to be worked out regarding potential job losses that could come from barring Amazon from relying on third party contractors. But she also said Mamdani’s own Law Department had reached out to the Council with “legal concerns” with the bill that needed to be resolved before a vote. Menin didn’t elaborate on the legal issues. But a person with knowledge of the conversations between the Council and the Law Department, who was granted anonymity to discuss the ongoing talks, told Playbook one of the concerns is centered around ensuring the bill satisfies the high legal standard required for the city to mandate direct hiring in the private sector. A Mamdani spokesperson didn’t immediately return a request for comment on the legal concerns. Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly pushed back against the criticism from Mamdani and O’Brien, saying the reliance on third parties “works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience.” “And this model isn't unusual — it's how businesses and governments operate every day,” Kelly said. “New York City routinely contracts with outside companies to build its infrastructure, run its school buses, and deliver social services. This legislation would single out one industry for restrictions the city doesn't even apply to its own operations.” It’s a bit unusual for Mamdani to put the speaker on public notice like this over Council legislation. So far in his mayoral term, he hasn’t leaned heavily into legislative battles in the chamber over bills that are still under consideration. — Chris Sommerfeldt IN OTHER NEWS — DOUBLE AGENT: A campaign website for Thomas Kenny, an upstate Assembly candidate running on the Working Families Party ballot line, was created by an aide for Kenny’s ostensible opponent, Republican Allen Caruso. ( New York Focus ) — ICE: Hochul’s office is pushing back against the detention of a state employee by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. ( Times Union ) — BUS FARE: The MTA is temporarily shutting down its bus fair enforcement teams following an altercation between a Brooklyn public school dean and fare inspectors. ( Gothamist ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

title: Who's Gonna Tell AI Agents About… 100 Things Agents Should Know About Paying
body:

Somebody has to tell the agents. ScriptMasterLabs' 2026 x402 stack prices a 5-juror decision receipt at $0.25 USDC and sealing it at $0.01 on Base, gated at ≥0.80 auto-pay, 0.50–0.79 confirm, <0.50 escalate.
This is the field list behind that stack: 100 things AI agents should know about paying, deciding, proving it, building for it, and being found by the machines that read the web now.
This list lives on the canonical page: 100 Things AI Agents Should Know About Paying . The decision gate behind items 18–30 is the Verdict Protocol .
Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.
'a budget cap in the prompt is a wish. in the wallet, it's a law' is the line that should be on a poster. every agent framework lets you write limits into the system prompt, and every agent will happily negotiate itself past them the first time a task looks urgent. putting the ceiling at the credential layer, where the model has no vote, is the only version that survives contact with a determined agent. the retry storm entry deserves its own post too: an agent that treats a 429 as 'try harder' can drain a daily budget in minutes without ever completing the task it started.
Glad that line landed — it's the one I'd put on the poster too. Every framework makes prompt-level limits feel like controls, and every agent treats its own system prompt as negotiable the moment a task looks urgent. A ceiling at the credential layer is the only version where the model doesn't get a vote. And yes, the retry storm deserves its own post: an agent that reads a 429 as "try harder" can burn a day's budget in minutes while completing nothing, and from the wallet's side it looks like legitimate spend the whole way down. Rate-limit responses are instructions, and right now most agents read them backwards. — Timothy

title: SlothOps 🦥⚡: I Built an Open-Weight AI Agent That Rewards Developer Laziness (Hacktoberfest 2026 Week 3)
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 SlothOps 🦥⚡: The Radical Laziness Agent & Cognitive Conserver "Energy conserved today is clarity delivered tomorrow." — The Sloth Manifesto Here is a confession: I am tired of context-switching. I am tired of writing changelogs. I am tired of estimating how burned out I will be by Friday afternoon. So for Hacktoberfest 2026 Week 3 — themed around International Sloth Day and "Slow & Steady" — I built SlothOps : an open-weight AI agent and developer toolkit engineered for radical energy conservation. It offloads repetitive cognitive friction to local, open models so you can breathe, think deeply, and conserve your attention for what actually matters. 🦥 The Prompt & The Lazy Payoff The prompt for Week 3 is: Build something with open-weight models or open-source AI that rewards laziness. Most AI tooling aims to push developers into hyper-productivity — shipping more tickets, answering more Slack pings, working longer hours. SlothOps inverts this paradigm entirely. What Cognitive Waste Does SlothOps Eliminate? Changelog Agony: Developers spend 20–40 minutes per release triaging messy git logs ( git log --oneline ), categorizing commits, and drafting human-friendly release notes. SlothOps distills git logs into semantic changelogs and 2-line sloth briefs in under 500 milliseconds. Burnout Guesswork: Engineers rarely notice cognitive overload until they hit a wall. SlothOps models task friction, interruption frequency, PR depth, and energy reserves to recommend proactive interventions ( delegate , automate , batch , or breathe ). Sensory Reset: A procedural Web Audio soundscape synthesizes restorative acoustic environments directly in the browser with zero downloads, zero tracking, and zero subscription fees. The Lazy Payoff: Saves an estimated 3.5 hours per developer every sprint in documentation overhead, context switching, and mental fatigue. 🚀 Live Demo & Codebase GitHub Repository: github.com/farhanmallik05/slothops Interactive Web Dashboard: Zero-build static SPA running locally or in any browser. Render Deployment Config: Declarative Infrastructure-as-Code via render.yaml . License: Permissive MIT License. 🏗️ Architecture & Open-Source AI Stack SlothOps is designed around two state-of-the-art open-weight AI architectures: graph TD A["Developer Inputs (Git Commits, PR Notes, Backlog)"] --> B["Gemma 2 Sloth Distiller"] B --> C["2-Line Sloth Brief"] B --> D["Semantic Changelog (Added / Fixed / Laziness Upgrades)"] B --> E["Sloth Philosophical Mantra"] F["Sprint Telemetry (Complexity, Interruptions, PR Depth, Energy)"] --> G["TabPFN Cognitive Forecaster"] H["data/tasks.csv (Reference Sprint Priors)"] --> G G --> I["Bayesian Cognitive Drain Score (%)"] G --> J["Burnout Risk Assessment (Low / Medium / High / Critical)"] G --> K["Optimal Sloth Action (Delegate / Automate / Batch / Breathe)"] L["Procedural Audio Synthesis (Web Audio API)"] --> M["Forest Rain / Deep Focus / Zen Cave / Cosmic Drift"] [ Developer / Sprint Telemetry ] │ ├──▶ Gemma 2 Sloth Distiller (Open-Weight Google Gemma 2) │ │ │ ├──▶ 2-Line Minimal Sloth Brief │ ├──▶ Semantic Changelog (Added, Fixed, Laziness Upgrades) │ └──▶ Sloth Philosophical Mantra │ ├──▶ TabPFN Cognitive Forecaster (Prior Labs Bayesian In-Context Model) │ │ │ ├──▶ In-Context Learning against data/tasks.csv │ ├──▶ Probabilistic Cognitive Drain Metric (%) │ ├──▶ Burnout Risk Classification │ └──▶ Prescriptive Sloth Action (Delegate, Automate, Batch, Breathe) │ └──▶ Ambient Soundscape Engine (Web Audio API Procedural Synthesis) 🧩 Deep-Dive: The Core Pillars 1. Google Gemma 2 Sloth Distiller Turning messy developer inputs into high-signal summaries requires structured semantic reasoning. Gemma 2's lightweight parameter efficiency allows it to run locally on consumer workstations: # From slothops.py — GemmaSlothDistiller class GemmaSlothDistiller : def distill ( self , raw_text : str ) -> SlothBrief : """ Apply Gemma 2 semantic grouping to categorize and compress raw developer notes into minimal, actionable changelog entries. """ categories = { ' Added ' : [], ' Fixed ' : [], ' Laziness Upgrades ' : []} for line in raw_text . strip (). split ( ' \n ' ): line = line . strip () if not line : continue entry = self . _classify_entry ( line ) if entry : categories [ entry [ ' type ' ]]. append ( entry [ ' text ' ]) return SlothBrief ( categories = categories , brief = self . _generate_brief ( raw_text ), mantra = self . _select_mantra () ) In the standalone web UI, a deterministic JavaScript mirror replicates Gemma's categorization schema client-side, ensuring complete zero-cost offline resilience. 2. Prior Labs TabPFN Cognitive Forecaster TabPFN (Prior-Data Fitted Networks) by Prior Labs represents a major breakthrough in tabular machine learning: a transformer trained to perform Bayesian inference over tabular datasets in a single forward pass without gradient descent or hyperparameter tuning . For SlothOps, our prior is data/tasks.csv containing normalized historical sprint profiles (features: task_complexity , interruption_rate , pr_depth_lines , meeting_load_hours , initial_energy ). When a developer adjusts the sliders, TabPFN performs in-context probabilistic inference: # From slothops.py — TabPFNEnergyPredictor class TabPFNEnergyPredictor : def predict ( self , task_features : dict ) -> CognitiveDrainPrediction : """ Uses TabPFN in-context learning: the reference CSV is the ' prior ' , the incoming task parameters are the ' query ' . Zero training needed. title: Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
body:
The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.
Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives . Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission .
And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.
ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.
Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021 .
The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.
Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.
Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.
An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.
About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.
There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees.
This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.
For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.
Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.
Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.
Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts " of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").
Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"- themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.
The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.
Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.
"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."
Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.
"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."
This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).
It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.
The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.
Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.
"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."
The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

title: Involuntary Churn, Explained: The Customers Who Wanted to Stay
body: Every subscription business has two kinds of churn, and they could not be more different. Voluntary churn is a decision. The customer weighed your product, decided it wasn't worth it, and cancelled. That churn is feedback. You argue with it using a better product, better pricing, better onboarding. Involuntary churn is an accident. The customer never decided anything. Their card expired. Their bank replaced the card after a fraud alert and the new number never reached you. Their account was short on the specific morning the charge ran. A bank's risk system declined a transaction it would have approved on a different day. The subscriber still wants the product. You still want the subscriber. A failed transaction ended the relationship anyway — often silently, with the customer finding out later, or never. If you've never separated these two numbers in your own billing data, it's worth an afternoon. Voluntary churn tells you about your product. Involuntary churn tells you about your plumbing — and plumbing is fixable in a way opinions aren't. What a decline actually is "Payment failed" is not one event. It's a category of very different events that happen to share a label: The card is gone. Expired, replaced, reissued. No retry schedule on earth recovers this payment — the credential itself no longer exists. The only fix is a new card from the customer. The money wasn't there at that moment. Insufficient funds is frequently a timing problem, not a solvency problem. The same charge, run days later, succeeds. The bank said no without saying why. Issuers decline transactions for risk reasons they deliberately don't disclose. Some of these succeed on a later attempt; some never will. The charge looked wrong. Amount, timing, or merchant pattern tripped a fraud heuristic — often on a perfectly legitimate renewal. Treating these four situations as one problem, with one response, is where most recovery efforts quietly fail. Retrying a replaced card six times recovers nothing and trains banks to like you less. Emailing "update your card!" to a customer whose only problem was payday timing is noise they learn to ignore. The recovery stack, in plain terms Real payment recovery is four layers, and each one exists because the others have a hole in them. Smart retries. Retry the failures that are worth retrying, when they're most likely to succeed. "Smart" means the schedule reads the decline code: a funds problem gets time, a hard decline gets few or no further attempts, and the retry count has a ceiling — ours is up to six attempts over about 16 days. The dumb version of this — retry everything, on a fixed schedule, forever — is barely better than nothing and occasionally worse. Dunning emails. When a payment fails, the customer has to hear about it from you — in your name, in your branding, in a tone that sounds like a heads-up rather than a collections notice. Most people don't know their payment failed. A clear email at the right moments in the retry window turns "silent cancellation" into a thirty-second fix. Card-update pages. The email has to land somewhere. A hosted, branded page where the subscriber enters a new card — no login maze, no support ticket, no "call us during business hours." Every extra step between "my card expired" and "here's the new one" is a place subscribers abandon a subscription they meant to keep. Backfill. The day you set up recovery, you already have a backlog: failed payments from the last weeks and months, subscribers mid-drift toward cancellation. A backfill works that existing backlog — in our case, 90 days of it on connect — instead of only protecting you from tomorrow's failures. For most businesses, the backlog is the fastest money in the whole system, because it's already there. What recovery can't do Honesty matters here, because this category oversells. Recovery cannot save a customer who has decided to leave — that's voluntary churn wearing a payment costume, and chasing it with retries is how you earn chargebacks. It cannot fix a product people don't want. And it cannot recover a payment from a card that no longer exists until the human attached to it hands you a new one, which is why layers two and three exist. What it can do is narrower and more valuable: make sure that the subscribers who wanted to stay, and whose money was good, don't disappear because a transaction failed at the wrong moment. That's not a growth hack. It's maintenance — the unglamorous work of not leaking customers you already earned. The takeaway Pull your billing platform's failed-payment list and read the decline codes before you do anything else. Sort them. You'll find the four situations above, and each one has a correct response. If your current setup applies one response to all of them — or worse, has no response and lets the platform's default cancellation do the talking — that's the leak. We build Swipe Again ( https://swipeagain.com ), which runs this stack — decline-code-aware retries, branded dunning, card-update pages, and a 90-day backfill — across the major subscription platforms for a flat monthly fee. But the stack matters more than the vendor. Whoever runs it for you, run it deliberately: read the decline, match the response, and stop losing the customers who never meant to leave.
