title: When the WAF is the entry point: SiteGuard CVE-2026-106931 and patching before forensics
body: When the WAF is the entry point: SiteGuard CVE-2026-106931 and the order of patching versus forensics A web application firewall sits in front of the applications it protects. That position makes its own administrative interface a high-value target, and SiteGuard Server Edition's statistics module turned out to be exactly that. CVE-2026-106931 is an OS command injection, CWE-78, in SiteGuard Server Edition from EG Secure Solutions. NVD scores it 8.5 under CVSS v4.0, and describes the impact plainly: an attacker can execute arbitrary OS commands with root privileges on Unix or SYSTEM privileges on Windows. Exploitation in the wild has been confirmed. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 20 October 2026 with a remediation deadline of 3 November 2026, and Japan's national CERT issued an urgent advisory. The mechanism, in the terms vendors use The injection point is the product's statistical reporting function. That function ingests data and executes commands to produce output, and the input it accepts is not adequately separated from the command interpreter. The details that would matter most for writing a precise detection rule, namely the exact parameter and the encoding required, are in the vendor advisory and in the exploit analysis rather than in the CVE description. For defenders, the operational conclusion is simpler and does not depend on those specifics: an unauthenticated or low-privilege request to the statistics functionality can yield system-level execution. The problem with a compromised WAF Everything a web application firewall does depends on the WAF being trustworthy. It terminates or inspects TLS, so it sees cleartext for traffic that is otherwise encrypted. It logs requests and the decisions it made about them, so it produces the audit trail that an investigation would otherwise rely on. It holds the rules that implement blocking, so it can silently stop blocking. And it sits at the network position from which the protected applications appear as clients. A WAF compromised with root privileges is therefore a ready foothold for the exact analysis an incident responder would want to perform. The logs may be altered, the blocking rules may be relaxed, and the traffic already observed may include credentials for the applications behind it. Forensics before patching, and why the vendor said so The vendor guidance, echoed by national CERT reporting, states that applying the patch may destroy evidence of intrusion. That is an unusual instruction and it deserves to be followed literally rather than paraphrased. The operational sequence that satisfies both obligations: capture a disk image or a snapshot of the appliance, forward current logs off the device to a collector it does not control, record the running configuration and rule set, and only then patch. On virtual appliances the snapshot is cheap. On hardware, the configuration export and the forwarded logs are the minimum. Users whose platforms cannot be isolated for that procedure face a decision. The vendor's own framing helps: the question is whether the device shows signs of compromise or not, and if that cannot be established, treating the device as untrusted until it can be is the conservative choice. What to look for On the appliance: commands executed under the statistics function that are not part of the product's normal operation, unexpected files, and scheduled jobs or startup entries that do not match a known baseline. The vendor advisory carries the specific indicators. Outside the appliance: authentication attempts against the administrative interface, including from networks that should never reach it, and outbound connections from the WAF's address that are not to the protected applications or to update services. Downstream: since a compromised WAF sees decrypted traffic, session tokens and credentials for the protected applications should be treated as potentially exposed for the period of suspected compromise. That reaches past the WAF itself into the applications it fronts, and it is the consequence teams most often miss when scoping an appliance incident. Placement and access decisions that limit the damage next time The administrative interface of a WAF should not be reachable from the internet. This is the control that most reduces exposure, and it is the one most often compromised for convenience, because administrators want to reach the console from wherever they happen to be. Where remote administration is genuinely required, put it behind a separate access path or a management VPN rather than exposing it on the same interface as the protected traffic. Log forwarding to an external collector belongs in the standard build. If the WAF is compromised, its own log store is not evidence. A collector the appliance can write to but not modify is. The category point SiteGuard is one entry in a longer list of security appliances that have been compromised through their own management surfaces in 2026, alongside remote-access gateways, email gateways and backup servers. The common property is not a shared codebase. It is that these products are reachable, privileged, and often outside the patch process that covers servers. A security control that runs on a device nobody patches is not a control. It is a target that happens to block some traffic while it remains intact. References EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition advisory for CVE-2026-106931 NVD entry for CVE-2026-106931, CWE-78, CVSS v4.0 8.5 CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue entry added 20 October 2026 Japan CERT / JPCERT coordination notice BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek coverage, October 2026

title: Percentage-of-Recovered Pricing Is a Tax on Your Worst Month
body: Disclosure: we're the Swipe Again team. We sell the flat-fee option in this comparison, so don't take our word for any of it — the math below is the whole argument, and you can run it with your own numbers in about two minutes. Percentage-of-recovered pricing has the best pitch in SaaS: "You only pay when we recover money for you." It sounds perfectly aligned. If the software recovers nothing, you pay nothing. If it recovers a lot, well, you're happy to share. And this pricing model is real, not hypothetical — established recovery providers publicly price their service at 10–20% of whatever revenue they recover for you. Here's the thing nobody puts in the pitch: the percentage is charged on your worst month, at the worst rate, precisely because it's your worst month. Run the math Say your subscription business has a bad month — a bank changes its risk rules, a card network has an issue, a batch of annual renewals hits expired cards. Failed payments pile up, and your recovery software does its job and recovers $10,000 of it. At 10% of recovered revenue, that month costs you $1,000. At 20%, it costs you $2,000. Now a genuinely terrible month — the kind where recovery matters most. $25,000 recovered: At 10%: $2,500. At 20%: $5,000. A flat fee of $179 costs $179 in both months. And in the good months. And in the catastrophic ones. The bill never reads your Stripe dashboard and decides to grow. The alignment runs backwards The pitch says the vendor only wins when you win. But look at what the meter is actually attached to. A percentage-of-recovered vendor earns more when more of your payments fail and get recovered. Their best month is your worst month, monetized twice: once by whatever caused the failures, and once by the recovery fee on top. It also quietly penalizes the merchants with the biggest problem. A store with sloppy card hygiene and a high failure rate pays a fortune in recovery fees. A store with the same revenue and a low failure rate pays almost nothing — for the same software, running the same retries. The price isn't attached to the product. It's attached to the size of your leak. And there's a subtler cost: you can't budget it. Nobody can tell you in January what recovery will cost in October, because it depends on how badly October goes. Flat infrastructure — your billing platform, your email tool — doesn't work this way. You know the number before the month starts. The honest case for the percentage We're not going to pretend the percentage model has no place, because it does: Zero fixed cost is real. If you're pre-revenue or tiny, paying something only when money comes back is genuinely easier than a monthly bill. It's a low-commitment trial. Percentage pricing lets a skeptic test recovery without a subscription decision. For very small recovery volumes, it's cheaper. If a service recovers $300 for you in a month, 20% is $60 — less than our $179. That last point is the honest break-even, and it's worth doing on your own numbers. At 10% of recovered, the percentage model costs more than $179 the moment a service recovers more than $1,790 in a month. At 20%, the line is $895 a month of recovered revenue. If your failed payments are anywhere near those figures — and for a subscription business doing even modest volume, a bad week can get there — the "aligned" pricing is the expensive option wearing the friendly costume. What we'd actually check before buying either model Your monthly failed-payment volume. Not your revenue — the dollar value of payments that fail and are realistically recoverable. That's the base both models charge against. What the recovery includes. Retries alone aren't recovery. Are dunning emails, card-update pages, and a backfill of your existing failures in the price, or add-ons? What happens in the worst month, in writing. Multiply your worst plausible recovery month by the percentage. That's your real price ceiling — or rather, it has no ceiling, which is the point. We built Swipe Again ( https://swipeagain.com ) to be the boring option here: failed-payment recovery across Stripe, Recharge, Chargebee, Recurly, and the other major subscription platforms for $179 a month flat — no percentage, no tiers — because we think recovery is infrastructure, and infrastructure should have a price you can say out loud in January. But run your own numbers first. If your recoverable volume is small, the percentage might honestly be cheaper for now. Just know exactly where your break-even sits — because your worst month will find it.

title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
body:
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering .
The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.
OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.

title: RL 8: Q-Learning, Model-Free Breakthroughs, and the Off-Policy Meta (1988–1994)
body: In Blog 7 we watched Sutton teach machines to predict : chase a moving target of better and better value estimates, and the estimates settle down on the truth. That was a big deal. But there was a catch. Prediction without action is a weather forecast you can't do anything about. Knowing "this situation is worth 8 points" is nice. Knowing "so I should turn left" is what actually wins games. This post is about the five years (1988–1994) when RL went from predicting to deciding , and did it without ever being handed a map of the world. By the end of this post you'll be able to explain, in plain words: why "knowing how good a state is" isn't enough to act what Q-Learning does and why it was a breakthrough what on-policy and off-policy mean (the most important vocabulary split in RL) why the fastest route along a cliff edge can be the wrong thing to learn Quick refresher (and four new words) Blog 7 already covered state, action, reward, policy, return, value, the discount γ , bootstrapping and the TD error δ , so I won't re-explain them here. If any feel fuzzy, a quick skim of Blog 7 will set you up. Four words show up in this post that are new: Word Plain meaning Model A map of the world: "if I do X here, I end up there" Model-free Learning what to do without that map Q-value The score of a specific action in a specific state (not just the state) On-policy / off-policy Whether you learn about the way you actually behave, or about some ideal way of behaving (the big idea of this post) The gap: knowing the score vs knowing the move Blog 7's value function V(s) answers "how good is it to be here ?" That's the exact gap: it scores places , not moves . Now suppose you're standing at a crossroads and you know: the road left leads to a town worth 7 the road right leads to a town worth 9 Easy, go right. But notice what you needed: you had to know where each road leads. That's the model, the map: P(s' | s, a) , the probability of landing in s' after doing a in s . In a board game with clean rules, you can write that map by hand. In a robot's kitchen, a stock market, or a video game you've never seen? Nobody hands you the map. And building one is often harder than the original problem. The fix, in one sentence: stop scoring places and start scoring choices . If you know "taking road right from this junction is worth 9," you don't need to know where it goes. You just pick the best-scoring choice. Algorithms that work this way, without a map of the world, are called model-free . Three ideas, arriving between 1988 and 1994, made that practical. We'll take them in order. Idea 1: TD(λ), a dial between "impatient" and "patient" (Sutton, 1988) Technically this one is still about prediction, so why is it here? Because it upgrades the credit-assignment machinery from Blog 7, and Watkins is about to reuse that machinery for choosing actions. Blog 7 left you with two separate tools: TD(0) (update from the very next state) and Monte Carlo (wait for the whole episode, then update). Sutton's 1988 paper, Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences , showed they're not two tools at all. They're the two ends of one dial . The dial is λ (lambda), a number from 0 to 1. At λ = 0 you get TD(0). At λ = 1 you get (roughly) Monte Carlo. Everything in between is a blend. How the dial works: eligibility traces. Think of breadcrumbs. Every state you visit gets a breadcrumb, and the crumbs fade as time passes: e t ​ ( s ) = γλ e t − 1 ​ ( s ) + 1 [ S t ​ = s ] In words: "a state's crumb fades by a factor of γλ each step, and gets topped up whenever you visit it." When a surprise arrives (the TD error δ from Blog 7), it gets spread backward along the breadcrumb trail. Fresh crumbs get a big share of the credit. Faded ones get a little. V ( s ) ← V ( s ) + α ⋅ δ t ​ ⋅ e t ​ ( s ) The eligibility trace idea has roots in Klopf's biological thinking from Blog 6. Sutton turned it into a precise, tunable tool. Why it matters for what comes next: TD(λ) gives RL its credit-assignment machinery . Watkins would soon bolt the same trick onto action-learning (his version is called Q(λ)). But first he needed to solve the bigger problem: learning actions at all. Idea 2: Q-Learning, scoring choices instead of places (Watkins, 1989) Chris Watkins introduced Q-Learning in his 1989 Cambridge PhD thesis, Learning from Delayed Rewards . The idea sounds almost too simple to be a breakthrough. Instead of V(s) (how good is this state ?), learn Q(s, a) (how good is this action in this state ?). The "Q" stands for "quality." Formally, Q*(s, a) is the total future reward you'd expect if you take action a in state s and play perfectly from then on: Q ( s , a ) = E [ R t + 1 ​ + γ a ′ max ​ Q ( S t + 1 ​ , a ′ ) ∣ ∣ ​ S t ​ = s , A t ​ = a ] That's Bellman's optimality idea from Blog 3, rewritten for actions. And here's the payoff: once you have Q* , the best policy is trivial. In every state, pick the action with the highest Q. No map required. The table Picture a spreadsheet. One row per state, one column per action. Each cell holds the agent's current guess for "how good is this action here?" At the start, every cell is 0 (or random). The agent knows nothing. The update rule Every time the agent takes a step, it fixes one cell of the table: Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ← Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) + α [ r t + 1 ​ + γ a ′ max ​ Q ( s t + 1 ​ , a ′ ) − Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ] Let's unpack it piece by piece: Q(s_t, a_t) is the old guess for this action. r_{t+1} is the reward the agent actually got. γ max Q(s_{t+1}, a') is the best the next state can offer , discounted. (Bootstrapping again, just as in Blog 7.) r + γ max Q(...) together form the target : "what this action looks like now that I've seen what happened." The bracket is the TD error : target minus old guess. How wrong was I? α is the learning rate: how much of the error to correct per step. A worked example (with actual numbers) Say the agent stands in state A and takes action "right," landing in state B. Old guess: Q(A, right) = 0 Reward for the step: r = 0 Best option in B: max Q(B, ·) = 10 (it already learned that B is next to the goal) γ = 0.9 , α = 0.5 The target is 0 + 0.9 × 10 = 9 . The error is 9 − 0 = 9 . The update is 0 + 0.5 × 9 = 4.5 . So Q(A, right) jumps from 0 to 4.5, even though the agent got zero reward on that step. It earned that credit because it led somewhere good . Now repeat this for thousands of steps. The goal's reward leaks into the square next to it, then into the square next to that , then the next, the same backward-spreading "rumor" from Blog 7's 3-step robot, only now it travels through action scores. Eventually every cell holds a sensible number and the best move from anywhere is "follow the biggest number." The guarantee Here's the part that made people sit up. Q-Learning isn't just "usually works." It has a proof. Watkins outlined it in his thesis, and Watkins and Dayan published the full proof in 1992 ( Machine Learning journal, "Technical Note: Q-Learning"). The result: with a table of values, and every action tried repeatedly in every state , Q-Learning converges to the optimal action-values with probability 1. Later, Tsitsiklis (1994) and Jaakkola et al. (1994) re-proved it with a more general toolkit. The fine print matters, and it'll matter later in this post: Every (state, action) pair must keep getting visited (so you must explore ) The learning rate α must shrink at the right pace over time The values are stored in a table , not squeezed into a function approximator Exploring: how does the agent visit everything? Condition #1 above hides a puzzle. If the agent always picks its current best-looking action, it'll never discover that the road it dismissed early on was actually great. That's the explore vs exploit tension, one we've met before: Samuel wrestled with it in checkers (Blog 4) and Tsetlin built it into his learning automata (Blog 5). The simplest practical recipe is ε-greedy : a t ​ = { random action ​ with probability ε ar g max a ​ Q ( s t ​ , a ) ​ with probability 1 − ε ​ Roll a die. Most of the time (say 90%), do what the table says is best. The rest of the time (10%), do something random, just to see. Early in training, ε is large; as the table gets trustworthy, ε shrinks. Hold on to this one detail, because it sets up the whole second half of the post: while exploring, the agent sometimes does dumb things on purpose. The quiet superpower: off-policy learning Look back at the Q-Learning update. The target uses max Q(s_{t+1}, a') : the value of the best next action. But what did the agent actually do next? Maybe it explored and did something random. The update doesn't care. It always learns as if the agent will play perfectly from the next step on. This means two different "policies" are in play: Behavior policy: what the agent actually does while collecting experience (messy, exploratory) Target policy: what the agent is learning about (the greedy, best-possible policy) When these two are different, the algorithm is called off-policy . Q-Learning is the classic example. An analogy: imagine learning to drive by studying dashcam footage of other people, including clumsy drivers. You can still extract "what's the ideal move at this intersection?" from footage of someone who wasn't playing ideally. That's off-policy. On-policy would be learning to drive only from your own hands-on driving and judging yourself on exactly how you drive. Why this matters in practice: Reuse old data. Experience collected yesterday under a worse policy is still valid for updating Q today. Explore wildly without poisoning what you're learning. Learn from other people. A human demo, a different bot's game logs: all usable. This one property is the reason the deep RL systems of the 2010s could store millions of past game frames and keep learning from them. Remember it when we reach DQN. The table's fatal flaw Q-Learning worked beautifully on small worlds: grid mazes, toy problems, dozens or hundreds of states. Then people tried it on something real. Take an Atari game. The "state" is the screen: 210×160 pixels, each with one of 128 possible colors. The number of possible screens is beyond astronomical. You can't build a table with a row for each. You couldn't even store it. This is the curse of dimensionality from Bellman's era (Blog 3), coming back for revenge. And the fine print from earlier bites: Watkins & Dayan's guarantee covers tables . Swap in a function approximator and the proof no longer applies (and, as people found, training can get unstable). The natural fix: don't store a row per state. Learn a function that takes any state and estimates its Q-values, generalizing from states it has seen to ones it hasn't. A neural network is exactly that kind of function. Replace the table with a network that outputs one Q-value per action, keep Watkins's update rule almost unchanged, and you get the Deep Q-Network (DQN) . That's DeepMind's 2013 breakthrough, and the star of Blog 11. The table was never the destination. It was the prototype. Before we get there: Blog 9 takes a detour to 1992, when Gerald Tesauro mixed TD learning with a neural network on a board game. It worked remarkably well, and it happened two decades before DQN. Idea 3: SARSA, when being realistic beats being optimistic (Rummery & Niranjan, 1994) By the early 90s, Q-Learning looked great. Then researchers noticed something uncomfortable: it's an optimist . Its update assumes that after this step, the agent will always make the best possible move. But during training, the agent explores. It stumbles on purpose, on a schedule (remember ε). Q-Learning learns as if those stumbles will never happen. Most of the time that's harmless. Sometimes it's a disaster. Enter the cliff. The cliff-walking problem This is a classic from Sutton & Barto's textbook. A grid, a start square, a goal square, and between them a row of cliff squares. Every step costs -1. Stepping on the cliff costs -100 and sends you back to the start. The shortest path hugs the cliff edge. If you never slip, it's the best route. Q-Learning correctly figures this out: the edge path is the optimal path for a perfect agent. So it learns to walk along the edge. But the agent is still doing ε-greedy exploration while it learns. Occasionally it takes a random step... off the cliff. Ouch, -100. Q-Learning logs the penalty, but its update rule still says "the best move from here is great," so it keeps hugging the edge and keeps falling during training. The SARSA fix Gavin Rummery and Mahesan Niranjan (Cambridge, 1994) proposed a small change with a big consequence: learn from what the agent actually does next, not from what it could ideally do. Compare the two updates. Only one term changes: Q-Learning: Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ← Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) + α ⎣ ⎡ ​ r t + 1 ​ + γ best possible next action a ′ max ​ Q ( s t + 1 ​ , a ′ ) ​ ​ − Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ⎦ ⎤ ​ SARSA: Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ← Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) + α ⎣ ⎡ ​ r t + 1 ​ + γ action actually taken Q ( s t + 1 ​ , a t + 1 ​ ) ​ ​ − Q ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) ⎦ ⎤ ​ Because each update needs the five things S tate, A ction, R eward, next S tate, next A ction, the algorithm is called SARSA. What SARSA does on the cliff: when it wobbles near the edge and falls, the next-action value it bootstraps from is the real, wobbly one, so the penalty drags down the value of walking near the edge. Over time it prefers a longer, safer path with a buffer from the cliff. Not because that path is theoretically shortest, but because it's the best path for an agent that sometimes makes random moves . This makes SARSA on-policy : the policy being learned and the policy generating experience are the same thing. So which one is "better"? Open Google Colab Notebook : QLearning vs SARSA Cliff Problem Neither. They answer different questions: Q-Learning SARSA Type Off-policy On-policy Learns the value of... the ideal greedy policy the policy it's actually following (with exploration) Attitude Optimist Realist Cliff behavior Learns the risky edge path, falls more while training Learns the safer detour, fewer falls while training Great for Reusing data, learning from demos, squeezing out the true optimum Settings where mistakes during learning are costly Two honest footnotes so nobody gets the wrong idea: Q-Learning's final greedy policy really is the optimal one. The edge path is shortest. Its problem is the cost it pays during training , not the policy it ends up with. SARSA isn't permanently stuck being cautious. If you shrink ε toward zero as training goes on, SARSA's behavior and Q-Learning's converge on the same optimal policy. SARSA is cautious because of exploration , not by nature. The divide that never went away Q-Learning vs SARSA looks like a niche algorithm detail. It turned out to be one of the big forks in the road of all of RL : Off-policy (Q-Learning, DQN, SAC): learn about the best policy regardless of how you collected the data . Superpower: you can recycle old experience, which makes learning sample-efficient . Cost: learning can be less stable, especially once neural networks get involved. On-policy (SARSA, PPO, most policy-gradient methods): learn only from data produced by your current behavior. Superpower: updates are consistent with what the agent really does, which tends to be more stable . Cost: you have to throw data away after you use it, so it's less sample-efficient . You'll see both camps again. PPO, an on-policy method, became the workhorse for fine-tuning large language models with human feedback (RLHF). DQN-style and SAC-style methods, off-policy, dominate where interaction with the world is expensive. Many of today's design debates in RL are really the same question Watkins and Rummery put on the table: do I learn about what I could do, or about what I actually do? What 1988–1994 actually established Three things that weren't true in 1987 but were by 1994: 1. A machine can learn good behavior without a map of its world. Given a small enough problem (one a table can hold), Q-Learning learns the optimal policy purely from trial and error, with no transition model, and Watkins and Dayan proved it. 2. How you explore is a design choice, not a side effect. Learn about the ideal (Q-Learning, off-policy) or learn about reality (SARSA, on-policy). Both are useful, and the choice shapes everything downstream. 3. The Q-table is just a function approximator in its simplest form. Swap the table for something that generalizes, and the same update rule keeps working. The theory was already pointing at DQN, twenty years early. What was missing was the generalizing part. Tables collapse at scale, and neural networks were the obvious replacement, but training them with TD updates turned out to be surprisingly unstable. That problem stayed open for a long time. Next up: a neural network teaches itself backgammon While theory was getting tidy, one researcher quietly tried the "obviously unstable" thing anyway. In 1992, Gerald Tesauro paired a neural network with TD learning and had it play backgammon against itself, millions of times, with no hand-written strategy. It reached a level that rivaled the world's best human players. TD-Gammon was the first big proof that neural networks and RL could work together at scale. It also made self-play a training paradigm, the same idea that eventually leads to AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and beyond. That's Blog 9. Quick recap (if you only read this) Model-free = learn what to do without learning how the world works. TD(λ) = a dial between impatient and patient learning; breadcrumbs (eligibility traces) spread credit backward. Q-Learning = score choices , not places; guaranteed to converge for tables; off-policy . SARSA = learn from what you actually do; on-policy ; safer when exploring is risky. The table breaks at scale , which sets up neural networks.

title: Presidential Determination Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as Amended, on Domestic Petroleum Production, Refining, and Logistics Capacity
body: Presidential Actions Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research MEMORANDUM FOR THE SECRETARY OF WAR SUBJECT: Presidential Determination Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as Amended, on Domestic Petroleum Production, Refining, and Logistics Capacity On January 20, 2025, I issued Executive Order 14156 (Declaring a National Energy Emergency), under the National Emergencies Act. That order found that America’s inadequate energy production, transportation, refining, and generation capacity constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the Nation’s economy, national security, and foreign policy. It emphasized that our Nation’s current inadequate and intermittent energy supply leaves us vulnerable to hostile foreign actors and poses an imminent and growing threat to the prosperity and national security of the United States. Consistent with that declaration, I find that ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness. Petroleum fuels the Nation’s Armed Forces, industrial base, and crucial infrastructure. Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption. Therefore, by the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, including section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (the “Act”) (50 U.S.C. 4533), I hereby determine, pursuant to section 303(a)(5) of the Act, that: (1) domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity, including exploration and production, gathering and transmission pipelines, storage, and marine terminals, are industrial resources, materials, or critical technology items essential to the national defense; (2) without Presidential action under section 303 of the Act, United States industry cannot reasonably be expected to provide these capabilities for the needed industrial resource, material, or critical technology item in a timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations; and (3) purchases, purchase commitments, financial support for the development of production capabilities, or other action pursuant to section 303 of the Act are the most cost-effective, expedient, and practical alternative methods for meeting this need. I have declared a national emergency under Executive Order 14156, and I further determine that action to expand the domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is necessary to avert an industrial resource or critical technology item shortfall that would severely impair national defense capability. Therefore, pursuant to section 303(a)(7) of the Act, I waive the requirements of section 303(a)(1)-(a)(6) of the Act for the purpose of expanding such capability. You are authorized and directed to implement this determination, including making necessary purchases, commitments, and financial instruments to enable these projects, and to publish this determination in the Federal Register . Any provision of previous memoranda, proclamations, and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this determination is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency. DONALD J. TRUMP The post Presidential Determination Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as Amended, on Domestic Petroleum Production, Refining, and Logistics Capacity appeared first on The White House .

title: Building inspectable systems: my portfolio, Sentra–Hermes, and five public projects
body: I build systems where authority, execution, and evidence stay connected. A task can finish and still leave an operating problem. Was it authorized against the right state? Does the evidence support advancing? What happens if the next run inherits something it should not? Those are the problems behind my portfolio . Sentra–Hermes is the flagship case study . Five public repositories give you tools to inspect and try. Sentra–Hermes: authority before advancement Sentra–Hermes explores a bounded lifecycle for governed agent execution: Readiness → Authorization → Execution → Verification → Advancement → Completion The Hermes name refers to Nous Research’s Hermes Agent . My contribution is the surrounding operating infrastructure: Sentra’s decision layer, authorization boundaries, readiness checks, verification, and preserved evidence for workflows involving Hermes agents. The case study examines this operating infrastructure and its bounded validation. The checkpoint evidence does not establish that Hermes Agent executed those tasks. Two failures make the operating problem concrete. One involved candidate selection treating a consumed authorization as live authority, blocking successor intake. Another involved successor state still referencing the predecessor’s execution. The corrections separated historical evidence from live authority and isolated successor activation within a rollback boundary. At the documented July 24, 2026 checkpoint: 13 of 13 repository-integrity checks passed. Three of three governed tasks completed. Four single-transition authorizations were consumed. Predecessor and successor evidence was preserved. A later read-only replay of that historical snapshot found zero recovery issues. That result is separate from the original checkpoint results. This is evidence for a bounded prototype checkpoint. It does not establish general agent safety, production readiness, or current runtime health. The public evidence guide includes extracts and provenance. You can inspect the cited records, but the extracts are not the full implementation and are not sufficient to reproduce the entire system. Five public projects 1. Pick Up Here Pick Up Here helps you resume work in a Git repository using saved evidence, change comparisons, and optional local AI guidance. Prototype release candidate. Facts and comparisons work without AI. They help establish what changed; they do not establish runtime correctness. 2. Commonfeed Commonfeed is a local RSS and Atom reader with finite reading sessions, explained selections, and private feedback. Published local reader; focused product probe. The README includes a fictional sample session. Long-term reliability and improved reading outcomes remain unproven. 3. Backsolve Backsolve records decisions, evidence, tests, and outcomes behind AI-assisted work in Whyfiles and portable archives. Local v0.1 CLI prototype. Records are assembled deterministically from explicit captures. The confidence score is a heuristic, not independent verification. 4. LineForge LineForge turns chess games into annotations, mistake cards, review sessions, and portable study artifacts. Local v0.1 application prototype. Coach lenses are deterministic; optional Stockfish analysis is separate. Learning gains and broader usability have not been established. 5. Hermes Observability Hermes Observability provides observability standards, structured trace contracts, and local readiness reports for governed workflows. v0.1 standards and validation tooling. A fixture PASS supports the behavior that fixture exercises. It does not establish live ingestion, another repository’s compliance, or production readiness. Each README has first-run steps, an example output or development screenshot, and the current limits. What I want feedback on The common thread is making the next action easier to judge: what can run, what changed, what evidence survives, and where a person needs to make the call. The public tools also need to earn their place in someone’s workflow. Passing checks cannot answer that on their own. If you try one, I’d like to know: Could you follow the first-run instructions? Did the example make the intended behavior clear? Were the evidence and limits specific enough to judge the claims? Start with the portfolio , read the Sentra–Hermes case study , or pick a repository from my GitHub profile .

title: Provisioning Resilient Azure Infrastructure with Terraform, DevPod, and mise: A Hands-On Guide
body:
When transitioning from the manual, error-prone world of "ClickOps" in cloud portals to production-grade engineering, mastering Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is non-negotiable. In this walkthrough, we will explore a real-world project that provisions foundational Azure cloud networking using Terraform and the latest AzureRM 4.x provider , all orchestrated within an isolated DevPod containerized development environment powered by mise . Whether you're studying for cloud certifications or standardizing your team's cloud infrastructure footprint, this guide breaks down the architecture, codebase, security hygiene, and lessons learned along the way. 🎯 Project Objectives Before writing a single block of HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), we outlined clear requirements: Deterministic & Repeatable Provisioning : Zero reliance on manual Azure Portal configurations. Predictable Developer Workspace : Avoid version discrepancies across developer machines by leveraging DevPod, Docker, and mise . Sound Networking Foundations : Establish an isolated Virtual Network (VNet), dedicated application subnet, and Network Security Group (NSG). Strict Security Hygiene : Isolate credentials using Microsoft Entra ID service principals with zero secrets leaking into version control. 🏗️ Architecture Overview The infrastructure deployed by this project represents the foundational landing zone for any cloud-hosted application: +-------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Azure Subscription | | | | Resource Group: rg-terraform-lab (Central India) | | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | Virtual Network: vnet-terraform-lab (10.10.0.0/16) | | | | | | | | +-------------------------------------------------------+ | | | | | Subnet: snet-app (10.10.1.0/24) | | | | | | | | | | | | [ Protected by NSG: nsg-terraform-lab ] | | | | | +-------------------------------------------------------+ | | | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | +-------------------------------------------------------------------+ Component Breakdown Resource Terraform Resource Type Configuration / Purpose Resource Group azurerm_resource_group Logical container ( rg-terraform-lab ) hosted in Central India with common tagging. Virtual Network azurerm_virtual_network Isolated address space ( 10.10.0.0/16 ) defining the private cloud boundary. Subnet azurerm_subnet Application tier subnet ( 10.10.1.0/24 ) allocated for compute or workloads. NSG azurerm_network_security_group Firewall filter governing ingress and egress rules. Subnet Association azurerm_subnet_network_security_group_association Decoupled link binding the NSG to the application subnet. 🧰 The Modern Developer Toolchain One common headache in cloud engineering is tool mismatch: "It works on my machine because I'm on Terraform 1.5, but CI failed because it's running 1.9." To eliminate this friction, this project couples DevPod / Dev Containers with mise : 1. Unified Tooling with mise Instead of cluttering the host machine with multiple version managers (tfenv, nvm, pyenv), mise.toml pins exact binaries: [tools] terraform = "1.16.6" uv = "0.13.1" 2. Isolated Workspace via Dev Containers Our .devcontainer/Dockerfile layers mise directly on an official Ubuntu 24.04 base: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-24.04 COPY --from=jdxcode/mise /usr/local/bin/mise /usr/local/bin/ RUN echo 'eval "$(mise activate bash)"' >> /home/vscode/.bashrc && \ echo 'eval "$(mise activate zsh)"' >> /home/vscode/.zshrc RUN usermod -aG root vscode Whenever a developer spins up this workspace via DevPod, VS Code Dev Containers, or GitHub Codespaces, they immediately enter an identical, battle-tested environment. 🔐 Authentication & Credential Hygiene For automated Terraform deployments against Azure, authenticating as a Microsoft Entra ID Service Principal is the industry standard. Exporting AzureRM Credentials We configure authentication using the four core environment variables consumed natively by the HashiCorp AzureRM provider: ARM_CLIENT_ID ARM_CLIENT_SECRET ARM_TENANT_ID ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID These are stored locally in .env.azure (which is strictly added to .gitignore ): export ARM_CLIENT_ID = "
" export ARM_CLIENT_SECRET = "
" export ARM_TENANT_ID = "
" export ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID = "
" To load them cleanly in your active shell: set -a source .env.azure set +a ⚠️ Security Tip : Always verify that your credentials file is ignored by Git prior to making commits: git check-ignore -v .env.azure 💻 Terraform Code Structure A clean, modular folder layout ensures that code remains readable and easy to maintain as infrastructure grows: azure-terraform/ ├── .devcontainer/ │ ├── devcontainer.json │ └── Dockerfile ├── .gitignore ├── .env.azure # Keep local & secret! ├── mise.toml ├── README.md └── terraform/ ├── versions.tf # Terraform & provider constraints ├── providers.tf # Provider configurations ├── variables.tf # Configurable input parameters ├── main.tf # Resource definitions └── outputs.tf # Exported attributes Let's inspect the key configuration files: 1. terraform/versions.tf & providers.tf Pinning modern versions avoids surprise breaking changes: # versions.tf terraform { required_version = ">= 1.6.0" required_providers { azurerm = { source = "hashicorp/azurerm" version = "~> 4.0" } } } # providers.tf provider "azurerm" { features {} } Note: In azurerm v4.0+, the features {} block remains mandatory. 2. terraform/variables.tf Parameterizing region, names, and CIDR blocks keeps our configuration DRY: variable "resource_group_name" { description = "Name of the Azure resource group" type = string default = "rg-terraform-lab" } variable "location" { description = "Azure region for the infrastructure" type = string default = "Central India" } variable "vnet_address_space" { description = "Address space for the virtual network" type = list ( string ) default = [ "10.10.0.0/16" ] } variable "subnet_address_prefixes" { description = "Address range for the application subnet" type = list ( string ) default = [ "10.10.1.0/24" ] } 3. terraform/main.tf Here we provision the resource group, virtual network, subnet, NSG, and their association: resource "azurerm_resource_group" "lab" { name = var . resource_group_name location = var . location tags = { environment = "lab" managed_by = "terraform" project = "azure-infrastructure" } } resource "azurerm_virtual_network" "lab" { name = "vnet-terraform-lab" location = azurerm_resource_group . lab . location resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group . lab . name address_space = var . vnet_address_space tags = { environment = "lab" managed_by = "terraform" } } resource "azurerm_subnet" "app" { name = "snet-app" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group . lab . name virtual_network_name = azurerm_virtual_network . lab . name address_prefixes = var . subnet_address_prefixes } resource "azurerm_network_security_group" "lab" { name = "nsg-terraform-lab" location = azurerm_resource_group . lab . location resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group . lab . name tags = { environment = "lab" managed_by = "terraform" } } # Explicit decoupling: association resource rather than an inline subnet block resource "azurerm_subnet_network_security_group_association" "app" { subnet_id = azurerm_subnet . app . id network_security_group_id = azurerm_network_security_group . lab . id } 💡 Best Practice Note : Avoid declaring subnets inline within the azurerm_virtual_network resource. Managing azurerm_subnet and azurerm_subnet_network_security_group_association as dedicated resources avoids configuration drift, circular dependencies, and unexpected resource replacements. 4. terraform/outputs.tf Outputs expose resource attributes that downstream modules or CLI scripts can consume: output "resource_group_name" { description = "Azure resource group name" value = azurerm_resource_group . lab . name } output "virtual_network_name" { description = "Azure virtual network name" value = azurerm_virtual_network . lab . name } output "virtual_network_id" { description = "Azure virtual network resource ID" value = azurerm_virtual_network . lab . id } output "subnet_id" { description = "Application subnet resource ID" value = azurerm_subnet . app . id } output "network_security_group_id" { description = "Network security group resource ID" value = azurerm_network_security_group . lab . id } 🚀 Execution & Verification Flow Navigating to the terraform/ directory, the deployment follows the canonical Terraform workflow: 1. Initialization & Linting # Initialize working directory & download AzureRM provider terraform init # Canonical format checking terraform fmt -recursive # Syntax and structural validation terraform validate 2. Planning terraform plan Terraform determines the execution graph and confirms the exact 5 resources to be created: Plan: 5 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. 3. Application terraform apply Type yes when prompted. In less than 30 seconds, Azure confirms all resources are created. 4. Verification Inspect the live state directly from your terminal: terraform state list Expected output: azurerm_network_security_group . lab azurerm_resource_group . lab azurerm_subnet . app azurerm_subnet_network_security_group_association . app azurerm_virtual_network . lab You can view the exported IDs at any time: terraform output Or verify them using the Azure CLI: az network vnet show \ --resource-group rg-terraform-lab \ --name vnet-terraform-lab \ --output table 🛡️ Critical Lessons Learned & Production Considerations 1. Local State vs. Remote Backend In this learning lab, local state ( terraform.tfstate ) is used. However, in a team or production setup, never rely on local state. Local state cannot prevent concurrent writes and risks leaking secrets. Production path: Migrate to an Azure Blob Storage backend with state locking via Azure Blob Leases: terraform { backend "azurerm" { resource_group_name = "rg-tfstate" storage_account_name = "sttfstatelab123" container_name = "tfstate" key = "networking.terraform.tfstate" } } 2. Avoid Static Client Secrets in CI/CD While .env.azure is great for fast local iteration, CI/CD pipelines (like GitHub Actions or GitLab CI) should utilize Azure Workload Identity Federation (OIDC) . OIDC uses short-lived tokens without storing long-lived passwords or client secrets in your repository settings. 3. Tagging Strategy Tagging resources early ( environment = "lab" , managed_by = "terraform" ) makes cost attribution and lifecycle tracking drastically easier as the infrastructure expands. 🧹 Tearing Down (Zero Cost Surprise) When your lab session concludes, cleanup is just as important as creation to prevent runaway cloud charges: # Review what will be destroyed terraform plan -destroy # Tear down all resources cleanly terraform destroy -auto-approve 🗺️ What's Next? From here, this foundation is primed for expansion: [ ] Add Compute: Provision an Azure Virtual Machine or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) inside snet-app . [ ] Implement GitHub Actions with OIDC for automated pull-request validation ( fmt , validate , tflint , and plan ). [ ] Modularize the networking configuration into a reusable Terraform Module. 💬 Let's Connect How do you manage your local vs. remote Terraform environments? Are you using DevPod or containers for cloud tooling? Let me know in the comments below! If you found this helpful, feel free to ❤️ or 🦄 this post!

title: Find Event Photos by Selfie with a Face Search API (Python)
body: After a wedding, a conference or a race, the photographer delivers 2,000 photos and every guest asks: which ones am I in? A face search fixes it. The guest takes one selfie, and the gallery shows only the photos that contain them. Below is the full flow in Python, with real results from a live 18-photo birthday gallery. Want to try it on your own gallery? Get a key for the Face Analyzer API and point the script at a folder of event photos. How it works Index the gallery once. Each event photo goes to a face repository. Every face in it is stored, labeled with the photo's file name. Search with a selfie. Each match carries the label of the photo it came from, a similarity score and the face's position. A group photo with five people produces five stored faces with the same label. The label turns a face match into a photo match. Step 1: one repository per event import os import requests from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor BASE = " https://faceanalyzer-ai.p.rapidapi.com " HEADERS = { " x-rapidapi-host " : " faceanalyzer-ai.p.rapidapi.com " , " x-rapidapi-key " : " YOUR_API_KEY " , } EVENT = " birthday-2026-10-17 " requests . post ( f " { BASE } /create-facial-repository " , headers = HEADERS , data = { " repository_id " : EVENT }, ) Step 2: index every event photo def index_photo ( path ): """ Save every face in one event photo, labeled with the photo ' s file name. """ with open ( path , " rb " ) as f : r = requests . post ( f " { BASE } /save-face-in-repository " , headers = HEADERS , files = { " image " : f }, data = { " repository_id " : EVENT , " external_id " : os . path . basename ( path ), " max_faces " : " 20 " , }, ) return os . path . basename ( path ), len ( r . json ()[ " body " ]. get ( " FacesId " , [])) photos = sorted ( os . path . join ( " event_photos " , n ) for n in os . listdir ( " event_photos " )) with ThreadPoolExecutor ( max_workers = 4 ) as pool : for name , faces in pool . map ( index_photo , photos ): print ( name , faces , " faces indexed " ) 18 photos, 76 faces, one call per photo. Step 3: find a guest's photos MIN_SIMILARITY = 95 def find_my_photos ( selfie_path ): """ Return the event photos that contain the person in the selfie. """ with open ( selfie_path , " rb " ) as f : r = requests . post ( f " { BASE } /search-face-in-repository " , headers = HEADERS , files = { " image " : f }, data = { " repository_id " : EVENT }, ) body = r . json ()[ " body " ] if " error " in body : return None # no face found in the selfie: ask for a new one best = {} for m in body [ " FaceMatches " ]: photo = m [ " ExternalImageId " ] if m [ " Similarity " ] >= MIN_SIMILARITY and ( photo not in best or m [ " Similarity " ] > best [ photo ][ " Similarity " ] ): best [ photo ] = m return sorted ( best . values (), key = lambda m : m [ " Similarity " ], reverse = True ) matches = find_my_photos ( " selfie.jpg " ) print ( len ( matches ), " photos found " ) 14 photos found IMG_7336946.jpg 100.0 IMG_7337110.jpg 99.99 ... IMG_7336992.jpg 98.89 She appears in exactly those 14 photos, and the 4 left out are the ones she is not in. Five-person group shots, a side view and a face cut by the frame edge all matched. The search took about half a second. Edge cases: a selfie with no face returns an error in the body (handled above), and a person who was not at the event gets an empty FaceMatches list. Step 4: highlight the guest from PIL import Image , ImageDraw def highlight ( photo_path , match , out_path ): """ Draw a box around the guest ' s face in one matched photo. """ im = Image . open ( photo_path ). convert ( " RGB " ) w , h = im . size box = match [ " BoundingBox " ] rect = [ box [ " topLeft " ][ " x " ] * w , box [ " topLeft " ][ " y " ] * h , box [ " bottomRight " ][ " x " ] * w , box [ " bottomRight " ][ " y " ] * h , ] ImageDraw . Draw ( im ). rectangle ( rect , outline = ( 52 , 211 , 153 ), width = 6 ) im . save ( out_path ) The whole script (create, index 18 photos, search, highlight 14) ran in under 8 seconds. Production tips Ask for a clear, front-facing selfie Show guests only their own matches Get consent before the selfie, do not store it, and call /delete-facial-repository when the gallery closes Index new uploads as the photographer delivers them Genuine matches scored 98.89 and above, so a 95 cutoff keeps a wide margin More on the full guide at ai-engine.net , including where selfie search fits (photographers, races, weddings, conferences, schools). Sources: GDPR Article 9 (biometric data), test photos by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels . 👉 Grab a key from the Face Analyzer API page and run a search with your own selfie.

title: I stopped losing background jobs to sleep mode: a patient queue with leases
body: I don't lose work to sleep mode anymore. Not because I built a smarter agent — because I finally wrote down what happens when a background job is interrupted. Every "personal AI helper" demo has the same hole in it. The agent starts some long job (organising a folder, summarising a thread, checking a feed), you close the lid to go make coffee, and when you come back the thing is either still spinning, silently dead, or has run the same step four times. Nothing in the pipeline knows the difference between slow and gone . slothqueue is my fix for that, and it is deliberately boring: one SQLite file, one process, no network calls, no broker, no cloud. Two ideas do all the work. Idea 1: a running job is a lease, not a flag The naive version sets status = 'running' and clears it at the end. Kill the process and the row stays running forever — the classic zombie job. The other naive version has no status at all, so a crash means the work is simply lost. A lease fixes both: job = q . claim ( " laptop:8123 " ) # attempts += 1, lease_until = now + 60s q . heartbeat ( job . id , " laptop:8123 " ) # extend while the work is genuinely going q . complete ( job . id , " moved 4 files " ) If the process dies between claim and complete , nothing needs to notice. The lease simply expires, and the next claim() re-issues the job with attempts == 2 and a reclaimed event in its history. No reaper daemon, no cron job whose only purpose is to guess whether something is dead. There's a second, subtler property here: ownership is part of the where-clause . A worker that lost its lease cannot complete the job it no longer holds: UPDATE jobs SET lease_until = ? WHERE id = ? AND state = 'running' AND lease_owner = ? If that updates zero rows, the worker knows it was replaced. That single check is what stops the "two workers, one job, doubled side effects" bug that shows up the moment a job runs longer than expected. Idea 2: waiting should cost nothing The lazy version of retries is a loop. while True: try; sleep(1) . On a laptop that is a fan spinning at 3 a.m., and it burns battery to accomplish nothing. Here failure reschedules into the future instead of retrying now: fail -> not_before = now + 2**attempts (capped) and claim() only ever looks at jobs whose not_before has passed. When nothing is due, claim() returns None , the worker exits, and the machine actually goes idle. That is the whole "sloth" idea: correctness by not doing things , not by doing them faster. The honest failure mode matters too. When attempts reaches max_attempts , the job goes to failed with the last error attached. It does not retry forever, and it does not pretend to be pending. You can read the story: $ python -m slothqueue.cli --db demo/demo.db status {'pending': 1, 'running': 0, 'done': 1, 'failed': 0, 'due_now': 0} $ python -m slothqueue.cli --db demo/demo.db work --dir demo/jobs --once ok tidy_downloads (403e48fb481d) tidy: moved 4 files fail disk_check (d6a6528950ad) -> pending: disk check: 82% full One job done, one failed and backed off with a real delay — not a spin. What I refused to add The temptation with anything "AI-powered" is to bolt a model onto it. I didn't, and I think that's the more useful position: the model isn't the unreliable part of a personal agent. The unreliable part is the waiting — the crash, the sleep, the second run of a step that already happened. Fix that and the model becomes a normal component you can reason about. So the scope stays small on purpose: no distributed workers (a laptop doesn't need them — run two queues in two folders if you want two lanes); no parallelism (concurrency is what makes local background work noisy); no dependencies at all — sqlite3 and subprocess from the standard library. Proof instead of promises The part I'd want to see in someone else's post is whether the recovery story is actually tested rather than asserted. There are nine behavioural tests with an injected clock, so lease expiry and backoff are verified without sleeping: a delayed job is not claimed early; a dead worker's lease is recovered with attempts == 2 and the event trail pushed, claimed, reclaimed, claimed ; failure schedules 2, 4, 8 seconds, capped, then lands in failed ; a heartbeat from a non-owner returns False and cannot steal the lease; a lease that expires after max_attempts goes to failed , not back to pending. python -m unittest discover -s tests -v # 9 tests, ~0.3s Code: https://github.com/ciperx/slothqueue (MIT) If you take one thing from this: the thing worth engineering in a personal agent is not the intelligence, it's the bookkeeping around interruption. Slow is fine. Gone is not.

title: IDF sources: Detention of US lawmaker nominee, 90 West Bank volunteers was complex - exclusive
body: The incident on Wednesday in which the IDF detained a US congressional nominee and around 90 foreign volunteers, including senior members of Rabbis for Human Rights (RHR), as they attempted to assist Palestinians in harvesting olives in the West Bank, was a highly complex situation, IDF sources told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.Given extensive recent reports of Jewish extremists harassing Palestinians and preventing them from completing their harvests, the activists sought to assist in the olive harvest.Claims from both sides involved were subjected to careful examination. One issue that remains unclear is the status of communications between the sides before the incident.RHR initially said that they had sent letters requesting to coordinate their visit with the IDF Chief's office and with the IDF Central Commander, to the IDF head of COGAT, to the Samaria Brigade Commander, and to the Etzion Brigade Commander, but had received no response.Letter requesting to coordinate visit seen by 'Post'The IDF and the Foreign Ministry initially said that RHR had failed to coordinate its visit to the West Bank area and that the area was a prohibited zone.However, on Thursday evening, the Post received a copy of the letter sent by Rabbis for Human Rights to the IDF. The letter is undated, but the organization said that it was sent to the IDF on August 25, nearly two months in advance of the visit.At press time, the military had not clarified whether or not it had received the letter.Earlier on Thursday, IDF sources had expressed that they were unaware of such a letter.Further, they indicated that the IDF receives many letters and sometimes may not see or respond to all of them on time.If the RHR had indeed sent such a letter to the IDF, and the military simply had not read it in time due to being overwhelmed with paperwork, this would neutralize one of the main justifications for its detention of the activists seeking to assist the Palestinian olive harvesters.Yet there is another complex series of arguments regarding the incident.RHR said that the village they visited was in a Palestinian area and, as such, did not require coordination with the IDF.Faced with this claim, the IDF sources explained to the Post that 90% of the area where the olives were harvested was open and did not require coordination with the military, but 10% did require such coordination.Regarding the visit, IDF sources argued that a large part of the problem – which had prevented a slower and more careful assessment of the situation – was the very large number of foreign visitors and the fact that they had come within some 50 meters of a Jewish village known to have provocative and aggressive members.In other words, when the IDF arrived in the area, some two hours after the olive harvesting had begun, they were seriously concerned that even if the RHR group was peaceful, the extremists from the nearby Jewish village would attack them, given the size of their group.Of course, RHR and the Palestinian harvesters could respond that it was the IDF's job to protect them and allow them to do their harvesting; not to forcefully evacuate them – let alone detain them – to avoid provoking extremists into breaking the law.IDF sources did not have a satisfactory answer to that question, saying that the soldiers on the ground had not known that US Congressional candidate Brad Lander (D-NY) was present or understood much about the group when they arrived.Rather, IDF sources said that since a series of provocative incidents involving Palestinians, Jews, and foreign visitors have taken place and since there was no registered coordination, the military assumed that the visitors were provocateurs who had to be detained and removed from their proximity to potential Jewish extremists, in the interests of avoiding a potentially large-scale and deadly incident – in light of recent occurrences.  Later, when the IDF officials realized who Lander was, they immediately released him. Further, they said, they released almost all the detainees within a matter of hours.While the military's narrative of the incident was not particularly favorable, IDF sources said that the broader olive harvesting situation was very favorable.They said that a huge area of Palestinian West Bank olive harvesting had been properly coordinated with the IDF in the last week and a half.The IDF said that over 100 olive harvest trips had been coordinated with the IDF without any problems. The military added that 22,500 tons of olives were harvested, and 5,600 tons of olive oil were packaged, worth around NIS 225 million.The Foreign Ministry said that one quarter of the entire area had already been harvested.However, the letter from RHR to the IDF noted data indicating that there had been a 63% increase in Jewish crimes against Palestinians during the first half of the year. The military had not allowed harvesting in the specific area in question.Lander was specifically released with a warning, he recalled in a statement.“I've been released from IDF custody with a 'warning,' apparently because of my public profile (I told them I wasn't even a congress member yet, just a nominee),” he wrote. “But several dozen rabbis and participants harvesting olives with me are still in detention. For harvesting olives. They should all be released immediately,” he said, adding that “Palestinians face far worse consequences every day.”Rabbis for Human Rights activists detained in West BankRHR said that the volunteers had worked in the village of Nahalin near Bethlehem, accompanying Palestinian farmers to groves during the olive harvest.RHR leadership said that their work in the West Bank was peaceful, and that it was the organization's policy to comply with IDF orders.“We came to accompany farmers to land they had been unable to access for three years, and after two hours of peaceful olive harvesting, large numbers of troops arrived and closed off the area. No one could have known about this order in advance.“Instead of protecting people working their land, the army is keeping them away from it and detaining those who came to accompany them for identification,” acting HRH Executive Director Anton Goodman said.“The fact that Israeli and American rabbis are compelled to stand alongside Palestinian farmers to help them harvest their olives and protect them from settler violence is a damning indictment of the Israeli government. The fact that these same rabbis are detained by security forces, rather than the authorities protecting the farmers and taking action against those perpetrating the violence, is nothing short of a disgrace,” Yizhar Hess, vice chairman of the World Zionist Organization, said.Meanwhile, the IDF and the Foreign Ministry view the entire incident as planned and designed to be more of a public relations incident than focused on helping with the olive harvest, which they say is generally proceeding well, despite some increased Jewish extremist violence.Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

title: ChatGPT Teaches Messi Chess—On a Board It Set Up Wrong, With an Opening That Loses in Four Moves
body:
Lionel Messi posted an ad on Instagram on Wednesday in which ChatGPT teaches him chess. The trillion-dollar chatbot flubbed the lesson so hard, Chess-knowing commentators online are losing it.
The digital board on screen in the ad has each side’s king and queen swapped, and OpenAI's chatbot recommends Messi open it up with a move that is almost guaranteed to lose in four turns.
The post, from the second most-followed person on the platform with more than 517 million followers, collected roughly 1.9 million likes and 19,600 comments in about a day.
OpenAI says more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT every week, and its latest pitch to them is one of the most famous athletes alive getting a chess lesson from a tutor that cannot set up the board.
If the thing sold as your all-knowing teacher fumbles move zero, it’s fair to wonder what else it delivers with a straight face.
In the post, Messi says he asked ChatGPT “to teach me a chess opening that matched my style,” and the chatbot suggested the “GOAT Horns,” a pun on the nickname Messi has carried for years. (GOAT stands for greatest of all time, for those who don’t follow sports lingo.)
Messi, of course, is known for winning games—not losing them in record time.
An opening is just the first few moves of a game. Magnus Carlsen, the world’s top-ranked player and arguably the best player in the history of the game, has played this opening , but he is also the man who played the Bongcloud—a joke opening that drags the king out on move two—against Hikaru Nakamura in 2021, so copying what Carlsen does for fun is not exactly a beginner’s syllabus.
In real chess each queen starts on a square of her own color with the king beside her, and in the ad both armies have those two pieces trading places.
The swap is not just cosmetic, because the Goat Horns moves played from that setup hand White’s queen a clear diagonal that ends up on a check mate on move four against Black—as fast as the Scholar’s mate, the fastest way to lose in Chess.
On a correct board the same moves produce no forced mate.
Reddit noticed. “How did no one like, oh I don't know, look at this for less than 5 seconds before sending it to the whole world?” pseudonymous user Cannonheim asked .
Another wrote: “Two options, either they are idiots or they are too clever, which is exactly why people are talking about it,” another one mused . A third user argued that maybe this whole thing was the fault of some random intern.
Messi asked ChatGPT to teach him a chess opening that matched his style. It suggested Goat Horns 🤘 pic.twitter.com/7w25w8LEZP
Users on r/chess said an earlier OpenAI ad had already made the same mistake , putting Black’s queen on e8 instead of d8, and one commenter wrote: “Nearly a trillion dollar evaluation and they can’t put the queen on the right square lol.”
The ad landed exactly two weeks after OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 with Intelligent UI, a feature that lets ChatGPT answer with interactive charts, buttons, and forms instead of plain text. Messi’s marketing deal with OpenAI started in June, when he posted an image made with ChatGPT Images ahead of the World Cup.
ChatGPT isn’t exactly Stockfish. Back in 2025 , ChatGPT lost the final of a chatbot chess tournament, hosted by International Master Levy Rozman, after making illegal moves such as promoting pawns that did not exist but spawned out of thin air.
Thankfully, OpenAI fixed it in post and changed the pieces in a separate ad for X. The pieces are OK, the opening is still horrible to play, especially for a beginner like Messi.
The original video is still live on Messi’s Instagram.
