title: PicoCTF Crackme-py Writeup — Reverse a Python Password Check
body: The Python script compares user input, after applying a transformation to it (base64 encoding, character shift, etc.), to a hardcoded string. Instead of guessing via brute force, we read the code to identify the transformation, then reverse it mathematically to directly recover the correct password. Platform: picoGym Category: Rev Eng Points: 250 pts Difficulty: Intermediate Tools: python3source reading Challenge description The challenge provides a script, crackme.py , which asks for a password and prints a success or failure message based on the result of a comparison: $ python3 crackme.py Enter the password: test123 Wrong! Try again. Unlike a binary crackme that would require a disassembler, here the source code is directly readable — the goal isn't to deobfuscate assembly, but to understand the transformation logic and turn it against itself. Step 1 — Read the code and locate the comparison We open crackme.py and look directly for the line that decides success or failure — usually an if comparing a function's result to a constant: $ cat crackme . py import base64 EXPECTED = " cGljb0NURntmNGs " # truncated, for example def transform ( pw ): encoded = base64 . b64encode ( pw . encode ()) return encoded . decode () user_input = input ( " Enter the password: " ) if transform ( user_input ) == EXPECTED : print ( " Correct! Here ' s your flag. " ) else : print ( " Wrong! Try again. " ) The logic is clear: the user's input goes through transform() , and the result is compared to the constant EXPECTED , hardcoded in the file. Step 2 — Identify the transformation We look at the body of transform() : here it's a simple base64 encoding applied to the input. Other variants of this challenge may use a Caesar-style character shift, an XOR with a fixed key, or a string reversal — the principle stays the same: precisely identify the operation being performed. def transform ( pw ): encoded = base64 . b64encode ( pw . encode ()) return encoded . decode () # possible variant seen on other versions of the challenge: # def transform(pw): # return ''.join(chr(ord(c) + 3) for c in pw) The key point: base64.b64encode is a perfectly reversible operation — there's an exact inverse function, base64.b64decode , that loses no information. It's not a one-way hash like MD5 or SHA-256, so there's no need for brute force whatsoever. Step 3 — Reverse the transformation Since EXPECTED is known (hardcoded in the file) and the transformation is reversible, we just need to apply the inverse operation directly to EXPECTED to recover the expected password, without ever having to guess or test anything: import base64 EXPECTED = " cGljb0NURntmNGs... " # full value copied from crackme.py password = base64 . b64decode ( EXPECTED ). decode () print ( password ) # -> picoCTF{***} (recovered password, masked here) # If the transformation had been a +3 shift on each character, # the inverse would simply be a -3 shift: # password = ''.join(chr(ord(c) - 3) for c in EXPECTED) In a handful of lines, the expected password falls out directly — no attempts, no iteration, just the exact mathematical inverse of the operation applied by the script. Step 4 — Verify and grab the flag We rerun the original script and enter the recovered password: $ python3 crackme.py Enter the password: picoCTF{***} Correct! Here's your flag. picoCTF{***} The success message appears, confirming the transformation was correctly reversed, and the flag is revealed. 🚩 picoCTF{ flag intentionally hidden } The flag is deliberately hidden — follow the method, you've earned it. 💪 Key takeaways This challenge illustrates a fundamental distinction in reverse engineering and applied cryptography: As soon as a transformation is reversible (encoding, simple arithmetic shift), mathematically inverting the check is always faster and more reliable than brute force The real lesson of this challenge is to spot when an operation is invertible before choosing an attack strategy — encoding ≠ one-way hash Carefully reading the source code before acting often saves hours of unnecessary brute forcing Originally published on CTFdojo — join the CTFdojo Discord to discuss writeups and get notified about new ones.

title: Will the Iran war resume before the US and Israeli elections?
body: Two US aircraft carrier strike groups are in the region, and another is on the way. Families of US government personnel have been ordered to leave Saudi Arabia. And Israel has reportedly conducted a military sortie near the Iranian border. Recent developments have left the Gulf on edge and have increased concerns that the US and Israeli could resume strikes against Iran, perhaps even before Israel's general election on October 27 and the US midterms on November 3. US President Donald Trump said on October 8 that he would not renew attacks against Iran before the midterms. But reports that Washington and Israel are preparing for renewed military operations have raised questions about whether the conflict could escalate before then. On Wednesday, the US State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. Some interpreted this to mean an attack against Iran was coming, especially amid reports that personnel could be withdrawn from other countries. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia and was prompted by the threat from Yemen's Houthis, who have attacked Saudi airports and other critical sites. But another State Department representative said that "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area”. Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran programme at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said Iranian officials appeared to view a renewed conflict as a real possibility and he warned that the political thinking around both elections could influence decisions about whether to escalate. “It’s not so much the logic of the war that might be in the driver’s seat; it’s the logic of the politics, particularly in Israel, that might be in the driver’s seat,” Mr Vatanka said. Quoting senior Iranian officials and a US official, Drop Site News reported that Washington and Israel believe large-scale bombing could begin before Israel's election. An unidentified senior Iranian official told the outlet that Tehran's intelligence assessment indicated a high likelihood of an attack before October 27, with Israel potentially striking Iranian air defences first to clear the way for US bombers. Iran's national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei , has repeatedly said that Iran can continue missile and drone attacks against US assets across the region if fighting resumes. He has also warned that Tehran could widen its targets to include data centres, artificial intelligence sites and undersea cables, he warned. Mr Vatanka said he did not think the strike would come before the US and Israeli elections. "If I had to gamble, I'll say it's unlikely to happen," he said. "Any new round [of fighting] is just going to be that much more devastating for the region. And when the region is devastated, US interests are also going to suffer massively. I do suspect that's going to be one of those areas where Trump might be sensitive to pressure." Quoting US officials and other sources, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that the US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms. The proposed campaign could attack Iranian energy and nuclear sites, and missile and drone arsenals, with the aim of forcing Tehran to make diplomatic concessions. The report said a strike before the midterms had not been entirely ruled out, however, and that Mr Trump could ultimately decide against further military action. Still, he has hinted at renewed strikes after the midterms. At last month's UN General Assembly, he said he was deciding whether to annihilate Iran. And in a Newsmax interview on October 15, he spoke about the Mother of All Bombs, the largest non-nuclear device in the Pentagon's arsenal, but he did not say if he would use it against Iran. Mr Trump and Mr Netanyahu launched the Iran conflict on February 28. The Trump administration initially projected the war would only last a few weeks but it has been unable to topple the regime in Tehran, strike a durable deal or completely defeat Iran militarily. If Mr Trump and Mr Netanyahu do resume the war, the consequences could be devastating for the region, Mr Vatanka said, with Iran threatening to retaliate against Israel and Gulf states, as well as US interests. Axios on Wednesday reported that dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a "power projection" sortie this week, close to the Iranian border.

title: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
body:
In case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.
Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3.
The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's mega-cap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home.
Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion.
"If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."
Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."
The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said.
"There were many driving factors that led the board and special committee to approve the Class C shares, and it would be misleading to attribute it to any single reason," Meta told CNBC in a statement.
The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure.
In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.
Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.
Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said, "I don't want California to end up in the same place."
Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking , with a net worth of $185 billion.
Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure , recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared with 43% who oppose it.
Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs , which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang .
"The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.
Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."
Instead, the new stock incentive will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.

title: I Wanted a Guardian. I Kept Building Things I Had to Babysit.
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built I have been building agents for months. Different jobs, different conversations, bots I could reach through Telegram. Somewhere in all that work, I started noticing something uncomfortable. I was still the one holding everything together. I had to remember what mattered. Bring one agent what another had said. Notice when the work had drifted. Ask whether a task was actually finished. Then ask again, with the right question this time. I wanted a companion that could carry some of that responsibility. Something that understood what we were trying to accomplish, investigated what we were missing, and came back with a reason to care. Something I could talk with, challenge, and build alongside. We kept turning that into smaller assignments. One agent checked my DEV articles every morning. It could tell me a reaction count had changed. The job worked, but I had to ask how that moved us toward the agent I had wanted in the first place. The answer was that it barely did. For this challenge, I started a new integration on Hermes Agent : the SCS Guardian. The public package contains a companion template, a procedural skill drawn from our corrections, and a GitHub watcher that gives it something concrete to investigate. The watcher is one tool. It is not the whole Guardian, and its list of observations is not a list of everything the agent is allowed to think or say. The person who is supposed to get a little lazier is me. I want to spend less time being the reminder system for my own reminder systems. Demo This is the full 16-minute, 37-second recording. No narration, no cuts. The repository, offline demo, and scheduled-job record come first. Then I ask the Guardian: What did your 7am run find, and what can't you see yet? It investigates rather than immediately answering. During that work, it changes its own monitor, checks the result, and records a lesson. The answer finishes before the recording ends. When we discussed cutting the wait, I wanted to keep the whole run. The work between my question and its answer is what I wanted people to see. That includes how long it took. The repository includes an offline demonstration anyone can run without a key. It walks through a baseline, unchanged data, a new pull request, and a failed lookup. It is labelled synthetic throughout. It demonstrates the observation code, not the model's judgment. The Guardian's conversational work is separate. I gave it this assignment: Understand what we are trying to accomplish. Examine the approved work, choose something consequential we may be missing, investigate it, and bring me your reasoning. Ask me when information or authority is missing. It investigated our files and GitHub changes. The reviews of its answers are part of the story too. It initially treated stale drafts as current and later overstated what reading a patch established. Its third report separated what it inspected, what it tested, and what remained uncertain, but its closing verdict still exceeded its evidence. The reviewer did not pass it. I want readers to see that result, not just the best-looking response. Code The code is public: SCS Guardian . The initial CI run passed at commit 2610698 . The portable collector uses Python's standard library. It records repository revisions, pull request identities, forks, workflow files, collaborators, and Actions runs. It emits a stable snapshot for Hermes to compare and keeps a timestamped receipt separately. The separation matters. Putting a fresh timestamp in the snapshot would make every check look like a change. The package has eight offline development tests. They include a second pull request from the same author, a failing workflow alongside a successful one, and an API permission failure. The last case must not become “no collaborators.” Failure to observe is different from observing nothing. This portable version is a candidate, separate from the first watcher installed on my Mac. When the repository says no scheduled run of the candidate is claimed, that's about this package. The 7am run below was the installed watcher. The package's tests are not evidence that the installed version has the same behavior. How I Built It The biggest implementation decision was to stop writing the entire agent runtime ourselves. Hermes supplies the agent framework. We are building the Guardian's purpose, working practices, and observation tools around it. In my setup, inference comes from a hosted model through Nous Portal. The application running on my Mac does not mean all of its reasoning happens locally. The soul file describes the relationship and purpose: understand the work, speak plainly, challenge weak reasoning, notice missing work, and preserve my agency. The public version removes my personal archive and the team's private letters. The procedural skill deals with how the work gets checked. Read the current source. Distinguish a new finding from something already recorded. Say what was actually tested. Don't end a careful report with a conclusion the report doesn't support. Then the Guardian hit a practical limit: its memory was nearly full. I asked it to solve that problem. It moved the longer procedural lessons into a skill and left a short reminder in always-on memory. The files changed, and the lessons remained available. That gave us a more useful question than whether it had “learned.” Would it retrieve and apply those lessons in a fresh situation, especially one that did not look like Guardian work? We have not established that yet. Moving text is measurable. Keeping a correction across different tasks needs another kind of evidence. For scheduled work, a deterministic collector supplies observations. Hermes can skip the model when later output is unchanged and invoke it when the output changes. I checked the installed scheduler source: the first monitor tick also invokes the agent with baseline context . There is no previous observation to call a discovery. The first morning On October 22, the scheduler dispatched the job at 7:00:01 AM Eastern. The collector logged 12 public repositories at 7:00:39. The job finished at 7:01:28 with status ok and the response [SILENT] . That establishes a scheduled run. It does not establish that the Guardian found something useful. The starting snapshot had a problem: two collaborator fields showed - . The installed collector used that same symbol for both an empty list and a failed lookup. A reviewer raised the gap; I took it back to the Guardian. It changed the failure path to emit unavailable and updated its procedural lesson. The follow-up run it reported showed that label on both repositories. The repair makes the missing information visible. We still have to see whether the scheduled agent treats it appropriately. And changing the monitor changes its output too: a new label is not proof something changed on GitHub. What happened during the recording My question was about the morning run. I did not tell it to repair a noisy comparison. While investigating, the Guardian identified a problem with hashing the generated work summary. That file includes a timestamp which changes when it is regenerated. The watcher could therefore wake the model even when the underlying work had not changed. It removed that hash, kept the file-age check, and compared two consecutive monitor outputs. The Guardian's own tool result reports that they were identical. That shows two quiet runs matched; it doesn't prove the timestamp was the cause. The proof the hash is gone is the script itself. It also reset the stored baseline and added the lesson to its skill. There is a tradeoff: removing the whole hash also removes detection of changes to that file's content. Two matching runs do not prove every future wake will be useful, and resetting a baseline can absorb genuine changes alongside a repair. This one already did: the new baseline includes my own commit to scs-guardian, so tomorrow's run won't wake for it. This needs further review, not a victory stamp. Still, this was more than a promise to improve. I asked about its work, and it found a specific mechanism to change, changed it, and checked the result. That is the part I wanted from a companion. Whether the repair holds up is the next question. This is where the project actually stands. It can wake up without me. I am still checking whether it brings me the right thing. The GitHub collector uses a dedicated read-only token. That limits that credential. It does not magically sandbox every tool available to a model running under my user account. The public setup explains that distinction rather than calling a prompt a lock. The same distinction applies to my instructions. What I said, what the agent thinks I meant, and what I authorized are separate things. “Review this pull request” does not mean “merge it,” even if a credential could. Preserving that boundary is part of the Guardian's job. This entry does not demonstrate a mechanism that enforces it across other agents' tools. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? I can inspect the runtime that carries this relationship. When the agent and another assistant disagreed with what the scheduler actually did, the source was there to read. I can keep the purpose, skills, and observation code as files I control. I can adapt the runtime and change the model configuration without starting the companion's working practices over from a blank chat. That freedom is useful even while paying for hosted inference. This project is not an offline claim or a claim that reasoning is free. Hermes is Nous Research's work. Our earlier Agent One and SCS research informed this project, but those months of work are not being passed off as a new build this week. The new work is the Guardian integration and the package around it. Claude Code, Codex, and the Guardian assisted with development; their role names are not additional human teammates. I still want more from it: useful investigations it chooses, opportunities supported by outside evidence, and eventually a conversation that reaches me on my phone. Those are directions, not features I can honestly demonstrate today. The change I am looking for is simple to describe and harder to build: I should not have to supply every next thought. That is why a scheduled job is only the beginning. The work has to become something I can hand over, check, and trust enough to stop carrying all of it myself.

title: Dune launches real-time data feeds covering 200 onchain trading venues
body:
The new service aims to bring onchain trading data into institutional financial systems as tokenized stock markets expand and face growing scrutiny.
Blockchain analytics platform Dune has launched real-time market data feeds covering more than 200 onchain trading venues, aiming to bring decentralized market activity into the trading systems used by traditional financial institutions.
The new service provides trade data from 12 blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana, Base and XLayer, roughly one second after execution, according to a Thursday announcement.
The feeds cover spot trading across decentralized exchanges, as well as perpetual futures trading on Hyperliquid and Lighter, with standardized data on prices, trade sizes and transaction details across markets.
According to Dune co-founder and CEO Fredrik Haga, quant funds, market makers, asset managers and bank trading desks are among the first clients using the service, although he declined to identify them, citing nondisclosure agreements. Dune said the firms use the data to assess liquidity, compare prices across venues and evaluate trading strategies before committing capital.
“Most institutions are watching onchain markets first, because they can’t price these assets properly without them anymore,” Haga said. He expects direct onchain trading to follow as liquidity improves and regulatory rules catch up, adding:
Related: Ondo lets institutions convert stocks directly into tokenized shares
The market for tokenized stocks has grown sharply over the past year, but fragmented liquidity and disputes over whether companies should have a say in how their shares are traded onchain have raised questions about the market’s development.
Recently, tensions surfaced around OKXICE, a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange. The venture announced plans for a tokenized stock trading platform on Oct. 4, but has since faced objections from several publicly traded companies.
So far, 16 companies, including Microsoft, Alphabet and Goldman Sachs, have filed objections to having their shares traded on the proposed platform, although they did not specify their reasons.
Beyond issuer objections, market fragmentation poses another concern. In May, Tiger Research director Ryan Yoon warned that trading the same tokenized stocks across multiple blockchain platforms could create price discrepancies , increase slippage and reduce market efficiency.
According to RWA.xyz data , the distributed value of tokenized stocks has reached $3.58 billion, up from about $627 million a year earlier, a roughly 470% increase.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab .
Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.
Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
body:
President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton , his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar.
Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur , was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.
In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life."
"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad . "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."
Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.
Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."
"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.
"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.
Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."
"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.
Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.
Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.
But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."
Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.
Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.
Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."
Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.
"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."
Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.
"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."
— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

title: U.S. Air Force Uses Virtual Reality to Improve B-52 Air Refueling Training
body: The U.S. Air Force is using virtual reality to help B-52 student pilots master aerial refueling before their first live flight, reducing the time, sorties and costs needed to reach proficiency. The U.S. Air Force is incorporating a virtual reality (VR) training device into the training of B-52 Stratofortress student pilots, helping them prepare for aerial refueling, one of the bomber’s most demanding flying tasks, before they take to the air. The system provides an accessible way to practice aerial refueling without requiring a tanker, a flying aircraft or the associated operating costs. Known as the Experiential Air Refueling Lightweight Simulator (EARL), the device is being used at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, where the B-52 Formal Training Unit prepares new pilots. According to the Air Force, students who trained with the device after it was integrated in the syllabus have been able to secure contact with the tanker “on their very first live flight.” B-52 student pilots are mastering aerial refueling in virtual reality before their first live flight—cutting training sorties & saving critical flight hours. See how we use advanced tech to prepare our heavy bombers for the fight: https://t.co/d5ZY39jOyH https://t.co/iMN6WXyV1o — U.S. Air Force (@usairforce) October 20, 2026 Bringing Aerial Refueling Practice to the Ground Aerial refueling is a particularly challenging skill for B-52 pilots . Similarly to other aircraft, the B-52 must maintain a precise position relative to a tanker, and small control inputs and anticipatory corrections are essential to maintaining the correct position for contact with the refueling boom. However, the bomber’s inertia complicates the maneuver, and the response to the pilot’s inputs is anything but instantaneous. Students thus need to learn how to anticipate the bomber’s behavior, instead of reacting to it. For years, during the first refueling training mission, student pilots would get the aircraft into position roughly 50 feet behind a tanker’s boom and hold that position from 20 to 30 minutes, without attempting contact. That also comes with a cost, as the B-52 burns approximately 3,000 gallons of fuel per hour, according to the press release. U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Kiel Spencer, 307th Operations Group, observes as a teammate practices B-52H Stratofortress air refueling on the EARL (Experiential Air Refueling Lightweight Simulator) trainer at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, Oct. 6, 2026. | Source: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Master Sgt. Theodore Daigle Lt. Col. Brandon Wolf, a B-52 instructor pilot with the 93rd Bomb Squadron, described the challenge, saying: “I’m trying to park a half-million-pound aircraft into a twelve-foot box in the sky.” The training would also be subject to a tanker’s availability , unpredictable weather, maintenance delays, and compounding fuel costs. These constraints would create a challenge themselves. “Air refueling was the long pole in the tent for our training pipeline,” Wolf said. “It was very difficult for students to master in the allotted flights we had. We had to go to heroic efforts to get everyone graduated on time.” EARL provides an additional opportunity to practice the task before students encounter it in the aircraft. The setup combines a VR headset with a custom set of throttles and a control yoke mounted to a chair, allowing trainees to experience a simulated aerial-refueling approach on the ground. The system was developed by Specular Theory, a small technology company, in collaboration with Wolf. EARL is not intended to replace actual flight training, but instead helps students to prepare students for it, allowing them to become familiar with the required control inputs and visual cues before attempting the maneuver with a live tanker. Why the Training Method Matters EARL is not being used as a standalone system, but was integrated in a specific syllabus. The instructional approach, called Integrated B-52 Unit Flight Familiarization (I-BUFF), was developed with support from researchers at Louisiana Tech University. It integrates VR practice into the training process , with instructor guidance helping students develop the skills required for aerial refueling. The team also collected data to evaluate EARL’s effectiveness. A U.S. Air Force B-52 Stratofortress aircraft refuels from a KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft over the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, during Operation Epic Fury, March 26, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo) | Source: U.S. Air Force The results were examined in a study involving 233 B-52 student pilots. According to the Air Force, trainees who followed the structured VR curriculum required an average of 1.7 fewer sorties and 39 fewer minutes of flight time to achieve aerial-refueling proficiency than those trained using traditional methods. “Cutting nearly two sorties saves real money, but more importantly, we’re reinvesting that time in other parts of training,” Wolf said. “More time in the range simulating weapons employment, and doing landings, because we’re not as constrained by how much air refueling, we still need to check off.” These results suggest that VR can help reduce the amount of live flying required to master a specific training task. Additionally, with students developing familiarity with the task before their first live attempt, instructors can concentrate on refining their performance in flight rather than introducing every aspect of the maneuver for the first time. Cognitive workload and safety of flight Col. Aaron Bohl, commander of the 307th Operations Group, explained that the introduction of the VR training helps increase the safety of air refueling. “Really for me, especially as a commander, it’s the safety element,” Bohl said. “Students are now working on the fine-tuning of air refueling before their first time behind a live aircraft.” U.S. Air Force Maj. Ben, left, and Capt. Justin, right, 96th Expeditionary Bomber Squadron pilots, takeoff to execute air operations in support of Operation Inherent Resolve Feb. 13, 2017. | Source: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Jordan Castelan One of the most important factors is the cognitive overload. “Wrestling 20 to 30 pounds of physical force through the yoke while strapped into a parachute and breathing through an oxygen mask is exhausting enough,” explained the service. “Doing so while reading a tanker’s position and calculating split-second corrections creates immense cognitive overload.” Air Force Global Strike Command Striker STEEL program Chief Scientist Dr. Tucker Readdy further explained how the cognitive skills could influence safety of flight. During aerial refueling, students must constantly track three separate points of visual reference. “The real difficult cognitive skill is change detection,” Readdy said. “If those three points are aligned, then you should stay connected to the boom, and fuel is good.” This also needed training on its own. In fact, the release says that initially the VR device was provided without a formal curriculum, resulting in low student engagement. Readdy’s team introduced cognitive training on top of the physical task, intentionally dialing up the mental workload as students improved, simulating high-stress scenarios that would be too dangerous to deliberately test in a live jet. The addition led to a breakthrough, with statistically significant performance difference as data indicates that pilots who trained with EARL excelled in comparison to their counterparts. “You can absolutely pull the classes that had training on the trainer versus those that did not,” Readdy said.

title: NATO’s weapons-buying agency opens dedicated door for Ukraine, non-member, letting it buy arms through its contracts and its firms bid for tenders
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has just become the first country with which NATO’s weapons-buying agency has ever established a dedicated partnership. Under a new agreement, Kyiv has gained the right to purchase weapons through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), and Ukrainian firms can bid on its tenders, the Defense Ministry reports . The deal, approved by the Ukrainian government in August and signed last week, is called the Security Cooperation Support Partnership. Through it, Ukraine can tap the agency’s 45 procurement partnerships, which cover the purchase, maintenance, and lifecycle support of weapons systems. A single window into NATO’s arms market For Ukraine’s military, the partnership is meant to make buying faster and cheaper. Orders can run through existing NSPA contracts or through new tenders, including an emergency-procurement track, and pooling Ukraine’s needs with those of other countries is designed to sharpen prices. The purchases can be paid for from Ukraine’s state budget, by international partners, or through joint financing. “Ukraine is the first and only country, and a non-member of NATO at that, for which a separate partnership was created as a single entry point to the agency’s work, and Ukrainian industry was given broad access to the agency’s tenders,” said Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik. And a way in for Ukraine’s arms makers The agreement cuts both ways, too. Ukrainian defense companies can now register in the agency’s supplier database, submit proposals, compete in tenders on equal footing with foreign firms, and sign contracts with NSPA under a mechanism that runs for five years from April 2025. “We want our partners to gain access to this experience and these technologies, and Ukrainian producers to gain new opportunities for cooperation,” said Deputy Defense Minister Hanna Hvozdiar. This is a partnership that benefits both sides, the Ukrainian official added. The signing was announced on 14 October at an NSPA industry event in Kyiv that drew about 150 Ukrainian defense manufacturers. Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company’s internal revenue review and a small business owner’s loan application.
Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation’s title and written into public DNS. Ars Technica said Tuesday that Meta paused the sharing feature after it reached out about what was going on.
In a post today on X, Meta’s David Singleton says that “The underlying issue is now fixed, and sharing is back on.” According to Singleton, the issue was with URLs for shared Muse artifacts, which Meta says are things like documents and images inside Muse, and wasn’t a flaw with chat sharing.
“If you shared an artifact before the fix: it now has a new URL,” Singleton says. “Anyone visiting the old link will see a note asking them to get the new one from you. We know that’s a pain, and we’re sorry for the disruption — but protecting user data has to come first.”

On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security . Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims .
The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC , a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress.
The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk .
Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets , and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters.
As with the router ban and the Roomba ban , he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement ? We’ve asked the agency many times to chat about its efforts, but it won’t engage.

title: Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo continue to return to wild – video
body: Nine red deer born at Tbilisi Zoo have returned to the wild — or, more precisely, to a semi-wild environment. They have moved to Algeti National Park, near Tbilisi. Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: video Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo were first moved to Algeti National Park in the summer of 2025. It was the first attempt to reintroduce the species into the wild in Georgia. The process will continue in the coming years until the park has enough deer to restore the population. Tbilisi Zoo releases deer born in captivity into wild for first time in Georgia. Video Deer from Tbilisi Zoo have been released into the wild, marking Georgia’s first reintroduction attempt. The idea of restoring Georgia’s deer population emerged in the 1990s, when their numbers in the country fell sharply. Poaching and uncontrolled hunting contributed to the decline. Today, the red deer features on Georgia’s Red List of threatened species. In 2023, at the initiative of the Ministry of Environmental Protection and with funding from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency, authorities drew up a national plan to restore endangered species. Zurab Gurielidze , a professor at Ilia State University and director of Tbilisi Zoo, led the development of the plan. As part of the project, authorities established an enclosed area of around 60 hectares in Algeti National Park, providing the deer with a suitable habitat and the conditions they need. The process will take time and require continuous monitoring, adequate protection and cooperation between various agencies. Once the deer population in the park reaches a sufficient level, authorities will release the animals fully into the wild, where they will be able to live independently. Tbilisi Zoo ‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series , we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
body: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business. V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers. Don't let the door hit you on the butt “However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” Read full article Comments

title: Lawsuit accuses Trump of illegally profiting off foreign crypto deals
body:
A lawsuit filed Thursday accuses President Donald Trump and his family's crypto company of "corruptly profiting" off more than $2 billion in digital currency -related deals, violating constitutional restrictions on accepting foreign money.
"No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly," alleges the federal civil complaint from a shareholder of Circle Internet Group , a publicly traded U.S. crypto company and competitor of the Trump family business, World Liberty Financial .
The suit filed in U.S. District Court in Washington by shareholder and former Circle employee J. Benjamin Greenberg centers on two allegedly "illegal foreign emoluments" involving World Liberty and Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security advisor to the United Arab Emirates.
Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million.
The company told The Wall Street Journal , which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures.
The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1.
The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress.
"This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, counsel for World Liberty Financial, said in a statement. "All we know about it is from media reports. Anyone can file a lawsuit in America, even a frivolous one."
"This is yet another frivolous lawsuit that echoes the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest."
In a statement to CNBC, Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt. He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people.
"We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said.
The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle. The company said in a statement to CNBC it was not behind the lawsuit and does not comment on pending litigation. "Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson.
The suit names Trump, World Liberty and U.S. Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies.
"World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC. "No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government. These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court."
The White House and a spokesperson for Witkoff did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the lawsuit.
In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal.
Trump and his family have rapidly expanded their crypto business since he returned to the White House. World Liberty Financial, launched with members of the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024, operates the USD1 stablecoin, and an entity affiliated with Trump and his family owns about 38% of the company. The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as investors in the so-called governance token WLFI suffered steep losses . Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 annual financial disclosure , including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty. WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026. The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE. Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expanded UAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips , including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon. U.S. lawmakers have sought information about those dealings and signaled that Trump family business transactions could face further investigation if Democrats gain subpoena power in Congress in the 2026 midterm election.

title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
body:
CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors.
With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis."
CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 36% this month after plunging 10% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.
The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 179% in the past year and 39% in October. It last stood at 1,145 basis points, or 11.45%.
The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 33% this month, while IREN's stock is down 38%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions.
U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month.
A representative from Nscale declined to comment.
CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft .
That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.
Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing.
"Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options.
"Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."
CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet.
One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027.
"Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."
Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?
Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors.
"Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

title: Ground-Launched Rusty Dagger Low-Cost Cruise Missile Seen For The First Time
body: Zone 5 Technologies has shared with TWZ the first photos of its latest Block 40 Rusty Dagger low-cost cruise missile in a surface-launched configuration. The images offer a new look at a weapon developed first with air-launched applications in mind , and for export to Ukraine . It is now being adapted for use from land and sea, including by U.S. and other allied forces . Zone 5 has not disclosed where or when the pictures were taken, or which programs, specifically, the ground-based launches were conducted under. The images do not offer a clear view of the trailer-mounted launcher, either. A spokesperson for the company did stress to TWZ that versions of Rusty Dagger have now been selected for separate U.S. Army and Navy programs , in addition to its initial development through the U.S. Air Force . One of the first images showing the surface-launched version of the Rusty Dagger in action. Zone 5 Technologies In May, Zone 5, as well as Anduril, CoAspire, and Leidos, received framework agreements from the Pentagon under the Low-Cost Containerized Missile (LCCM) program. The U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive Fires (PAE Fires) is running LCCM in cooperation with the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering (OUSW R&E). The aim of this program is to procure more than 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles , in total, over three years, beginning in 2027. Then there is also the Consolidated Affordable Ordnance System (CHAOS) effort from the U.S. Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions (PAE Munitions). CHAOS is focused on low-cost anti-ship cruise missiles, particularly for U.S. allies and partners. CoAspire is also on contract for CHAOS with a version of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range (RAACM-ER) design. “We designed a surface-launch Rusty Dagger to be the foundation of U.S. and allied mass-produced affordable precision deep strike weapons,” Tom Kanewske, chief strategy officer at Zone 5, told TWZ in a statement. “Our team went from design to demonstration in less than three months, bringing Rusty Dagger from pylons and pallets to ground launcher and shipping containers,” added Kyle Maxhimer, Zone 5’s president. Another picture of a Block 40 Rusty Dagger being fired from a launcher on the ground. Zone 5 Technologies Zone 5 says the Block 40 version of Rusty Dagger can accommodate warheads in the 100-to-250-pound classes. It can still be configured for air-launch, either from pylons under the wings of aircraft or via palletized munitions systems . In order to be fired from launchers on the ground or at sea, the new version of the missile is fitted with a solid-fuel booster rocket at the tail end. More specific details about the Block 40’s capabilities compared to the preceding air-launch-only version, also referred to as the Block 20, remain limited. From what we can see now, the two variations appear outwardly similar in many respects, at least broadly speaking. Earlier variations had a distinctive tail configuration with four squared-off fins, two facing upward and two more angled to either side. The shaping of the fins on the Block 40 does look to be more rounded. It’s also possible the missile may have a new cruciform tail fin arrangement, but this could also be a trick of the angle from which the missile is being viewed, coupled with the low resolution of the available images. A side-by-side comparison of the Block 40 Rusty Dagger configured for surface launch, at top, and an earlier air-launched version, at bottom. Zone 5 Technologies/USAF Previous reports have said that Rusty Dagger has a range of 300 nautical miles when delivered at low altitude, which is increased to 500 nautical miles when launched by aircraft at medium altitudes and flying at higher speeds . In general, surface-launched versions of missiles typically have shorter maximum ranges compared to their air-launched counterparts. Zone 5 Rusty Dagger. #AffordableMass pic.twitter.com/Pzj1KnceHC — Air-Power | NatSec Ledger (@NatSecLedger) June 7, 2025 Regardless, the Block 40 version is an important further evolution of the Rusty Dagger design. The initial air-launched version of the missile, now designated the AGM-188A, has already been in development for several years, in part now under the U.S. Air Force’s Extended Range Attack Munition (ERAM) program. This has included live-fire tests conducted at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida in January 2025. We now know that Rusty Dagger has been cleared for use on four different types of fighters, including the F-16 . Development of CoAspire’s Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile (RAACM) was also conducted as part of the ERAM effort. Three views of a Rusty Dagger live-fire test on January 22, 2025, at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida. The service did not identify the weapon by name at the time. via U.S. Air Force Like the Navy’s CHAOS effort, ERAM has been focused primarily on supporting allies and partners, starting first with Ukraine . A Zone 5 spokesperson told TWZ that, as things stand, Rusty Dagger remains the only publicly reported operational missile in its class fielded by the Ukrainian military. It appears that the AGM-188A “Rusty Dagger” cruise missile has undergone field testing in Ukraine. Russian sources are publishing photos of an unknown 8-element CRPA antenna. On the back side of the unit there is a circuit board with a large heatsink, which carries the CAGE code… pic.twitter.com/phZeOJfHJ0 — 𝔗𝔥𝔢 𝕯𝔢𝔞𝔡 𝕯𝔦𝔰𝔱𝔯𝔦𝔠𝔱 (@TheDeadDistrict) June 7, 2026 ERAM has also been feeding into the Air Force’s own Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) plans. The service wants to acquire 28,000 FAMM munitions in pylon-launched and palletized configurations over the next five years. A U.S. Air Force F-16 carrying a pair of Rusty Dagger missiles, as well as other stores, under its wings. U.S. Air Force photo by Staff Sgt. Blake Wiles As we reported earlier this year , Rusty Dagger is now part of a broader portfolio under Norwegian defense company Kongsberg, which acquired a 90 percent stake in Zone 5. Kongsberg has positioned the missile alongside its stealthy Joint Strike Missile (JSM) , with the two weapons serving different, complementary roles. KONGSBERG announced today that it has closed the acquisition of US missile company Zone 5 Technologies LLC, following approval by US regulatory authorities. https://t.co/meRxfmYHH6 pic.twitter.com/EXVbYhDers — KONGSBERG (@kongsbergasa) June 10, 2026 Rusty Dagger is designed around affordability and volume, while JSM offers a sophisticated, low-observable strike capability. The concept gives customers a mix of weapons suited to different targets and mission requirements, rather than relying exclusively on expensive, high-end missiles. Zone 5 says it is now expanding manufacturing in the United States. Production is established in San Luis Obispo, California, with production beginning in the Dallas-Fort Worth area of Texas. A franchised facility is also being developed in Miamisburg, Ohio, with Hawthorn Aero, a company that describes itself as specializing “in high-rate airframe manufacturing, offering scalable solutions from design to full vehicle integration for aerospace industries.” The company says each site is designed to reach a capacity of more than 2,500 missiles annually by the end of 2027. If all three reach that level, combined annual capacity would exceed 7,500 missiles. The expansion reflects the growing emphasis on affordable weapons that can be manufactured in large quantities and replenished quickly, something that is considered especially critical if the United States is to face China in a future high-end conflict in the Indo-Pacific region. The ground-launched Rusty Dagger shown in the photos underscores how far the missile family is moving beyond its original air-launched role. With production expanding and multiple U.S. military programs in the picture, the surface-launched variant adds another potential route to getting the weapon into service. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Ground-Launched Rusty Dagger Low-Cost Cruise Missile Seen For The First Time appeared first on TWZ .

title: ‘Another attempt is being prepared to deprive Armenia of its independence’ — Pashinyan
body: Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence “For the first time in our history, the ‘metropolis’ is not drawing us towards it. Instead, it seems to be saying, ‘We will push you away’,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said, commenting on a report on the possibility of suspending Armenia’s participation in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Speaking at his weekly briefing, he stressed that the documents governing the EAEU do not give member states the authority to expel another member. The report makes the same point. However, he drew a parallel with another organisation operating under Russia’s auspices: the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO). “The CSTO allows for such a possibility. Since the EAEU and CSTO have essentially the same member states, the question arises: why don’t they expel Armenia from the CSTO?” Pashinyan asked. According to the prime minister, the restrictions Russia has imposed on Armenia in recent months have failed to achieve the results that certain circles, both inside and outside the country, had hoped for. The measures include a ban on exporting most Armenian food products and other goods to Russia. Pashinyan said the move had failed to achieve either its economic or political objectives. The prime minister sees Russia’s economic pressure as an attempt to trigger domestic political instability and deprive Armenia of its independence. Journalists asked him to clarify whether Russia itself was destabilising Armenia. “I said very specifically: certain circles in the Russian Federation — yes. Is that news to you?” he replied. Nevertheless, Pashinyan said he was confident that Armenia was “resilient enough and would overcome this situation too”. Russia seeks to retain Armenian railway concession as Yerevan avoids confrontation Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev’s statement about ‘Ukrainisation’ of Armenia How Armenia is reacting to export restrictions on Russia: farmers’ views and official statistics “Time will tell”: on the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council’s report Armenian journalists asked Pashinyan what he thought about the risk of a catastrophic economic downturn if Armenia left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), as experts from the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council have forecast. “Time will tell. Our main priority is Armenia’s continued development and the protection of our independence and sovereignty, as well as diversifying our relations. We will follow this path,” the prime minister replied. In his view, forces both inside and outside Armenia are trying to exploit the current situation and problems in Armenia-Russia relations. Their aim, he said, is not only to trigger political instability in the country but also to effectively abolish Armenia’s independence. The prime minister did not specify which forces he meant. However, he noted that several such attempts had taken place over the past three years. First, he recalled the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, particularly the exodus of the entire Armenian population from their homeland while Russian peacekeepers were present. “The aim was to channel the flow of people into Armenia, while calls for a change of political power were coming from well-known quarters,” he said. Pashinyan considers the situation surrounding the 2026 parliamentary elections to be a second attempt. He appears to be referring to hybrid attacks on Armenia and an alleged attempt to bring Armenians living in Russia to the polls to vote for pro-Russian forces. “A third attempt is now being prepared. It is part of a certain ‘secret plan’ that is currently the subject of widespread discussion,” he concluded. Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition party Strong Armenia, has recently spoken openly about a “secret plan” to change the government. He has invoked the plan when asked what steps the opposition intends to take to overthrow the authorities after losing the election. The prime minister believes the struggle is political rather than economic: “The aim is to provoke domestic political instability in Armenia. As a consequence, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to deprive Armenia of its independence — first de facto, and then de jure.” He added that events over the past several decades had also been directed towards achieving this goal. Russian-led EAEU bloc warns Armenia of possible ‘serious blows’ to its economy A report by the EAEU’s intergovernmental council discusses the possible suspension of Armenia’s membership and the consequences, even though the bloc’s founding treaty makes no provision for such a move. “There will be no apocalypse”: on a possible rise in Russian gas prices Pashinyan stressed that there was no guarantee that gas prices would remain unchanged. He also said that prices had risen at least twice over the past eight years. “Gas prices have gone up before. You simply didn’t know about it. They rose in 2019 and then — I can’t remember exactly whether it was in 2022 or 2023. The point is that, thanks to citizens who work in Armenia, create added value and pay the taxes required by law, the Armenian government managed to ensure that the public did not notice these increases.” The prime minister is convinced that even if gas prices rise by 69%, as the EAEU has warned, the Armenian economy will not face an “apocalypse”. “Those who talk about an apocalypse simply don’t understand economics. I say that quite plainly.” As the prime minister noted, people also predicted an “apocalypse” in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Yet Armenia’s economy grew throughout those years, Pashinyan said. “You cannot erase history”: on relations with Russia Speaking about his communications with Putin and Armenian-Russian relations, Pashinyan stressed that the relationship had always been positive and would remain so. However, he said this did not mean Armenia could simply erase the events of 2020, 2021 and 2023 from its history. “That does not mean our history will no longer record the weapons we paid for but never received. Nor will it erase September 2022. That month, when Azerbaijani forces invaded Armenia’s sovereign territory, the CSTO failed to fulfil its treaty obligations to Armenia. This had extremely serious consequences.” The prime minister’s conclusion was clear: dependence on a single country for weapons, gas and even apricots poses a threat to the state. “We must address this threat. We are increasing Armenia’s level of independence. Are we doing so deliberately? Let’s put it this way — yes. We are consciously, you could even say relentlessly, strengthening the independence and sovereignty of the Republic of Armenia.” Pashinyan concluded the discussion by saying that “the current situation is much more serious than many people think”. He said Armenia’s independence and statehood were at stake. “We must learn the lessons of history,” he added. Pashinyan: 'Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing' The Armenian prime minister said Russia’s approach is that relations between the two countries should either be exclusive or not exist at all. He stressed that Yerevan does not share that view Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence

title: Meta stock sinks nearly 7% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
body:
Meta shares slumped nearly 7% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.
The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans.
Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion.
Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.
The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."
Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.
Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.
Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable with the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for.
— CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.
