title: The Library of Things Toolkit: A comprehensive resource to help create thriving community sharing hubs
body: It was just a couple of years ago when a small group of friends had the idea to start a tool library (also known as a Library of Things) in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, U.S. The idea was exciting, but creating a thriving sharing hub felt daunting. So they began looking for available resources to help them get started and found the Tool Library Alliance (TLA) , which unites tool libraries across the U.S. to foster community resilience, increase sustainability, and build a culture of generosity through the sharing of tools, skills, and knowledge. It was during a TLA workshop that they learned about Shareable’s comprehensive Library of Things Toolkit , a step-by-step guide for anyone to start a sharing project, regardless of a person’s background. Libraries of Things (LoTs) are community-based systems that make it easier for people to borrow, share, and collectively steward physical resources. LoTs follow the traditional mechanics of a public library while pushing the boundaries of what can be borrowed: tools, sewing machines, emergency supplies, and much more! LoTs are more than tool-sharing; they often become critical community resilience hubs and “third spaces.” The organizers in Harrisburg started with the goal of raising an initial $15,000 in lifetime tool library memberships to secure a space for their tool library. Veronica Adams, one of the Harrisburg Tool Library ’s co-founders and its current vice president, said the toolkit’s templates and examples made this task much easier: “I’ve never done a membership model before. Being able to just copy from the toolkit was so helpful.” Fellow co-founder and President Kate Lally echoed how helpful the toolkit was, “It was like a best friend holding my hand through the opening of our tool library.” And the team in Harrisburg isn’t alone; another group of local organizers used the Library of Things Toolkit to start the Northeastern Tool Library (NeTL) in Keeseville, New York. “Instead of feeling like we were starting from scratch in an isolated silo, we felt connected to a whole network of people who had already been there who could help us along the way. A physical copy of the toolkit lives in the tool library, and the NeTL team continues to refer to it often!” said Morgan Ingraham and Lindsay Eberhart, from the Institute for Sustainability Engagement and who helped create and manage the NeTL. Morgan and Lindsay printed out their own copy of the original Library of Things Toolkit. When the Shareable team heard this, we knew we wanted to offer a printed book version of the expanded second edition of the toolkit (in addition to the free interactive web and PDF formats!). And now, the second edition of the Library of Things Toolkit is available as a printed book for purchase ! The possibilities of Libraries of Things There are roughly 2,000 formal LoTs worldwide, along with countless informal ones. Modern LoTs have been in operation since the 1970’s (the longest-running, since 1979, is a tool library that’s part of the Berkeley Public Library system in California, U.S.), but communal resource sharing has always been an essential part of the human experience. Households are expected to purchase and maintain tools, equipment, and other expensive, rarely used items. The result is financial strain, wasted resources, and neighborhoods that are less resilient, less connected, and unprepared for disruption. Shared resource infrastructure builds systems for accessing physical items, turning underused goods into community assets. By shifting from isolated ownership to shared infrastructure, LoTs help communities become more affordable, economically vibrant, sustainable, connected, and resilient—often with lower start-up costs than many traditional community development practices. LoTs and other shared resource infrastructure can help address: Household financial fragility and equitable access: Affordable shared access reduces the need for large, infrequent purchases and high-interest debt. For the cost of buying or even renting a single tool at a big-box store, a member of an LoT can access hundreds or thousands of tools for an entire year. In affordable housing communities like Connect Highstar in Houston, Texas, U.S., integrated LoTs expand access to essential equipment without increasing household debt. Economic opportunity and small business development: Shared tools lower barriers to entry for tradespeople, landscapers, and entrepreneurs. The Minneapolis Tool Library , in Minnesota, U.S., was launched with Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds to support homeowners maintaining properties in blighted neighborhoods and has operated a robust trades program . In the City of Oakland, the public tool library stocks dozens of professional-grade string trimmers and other equipment, often borrowed by people starting a new yard care or construction business, allowing them to save money on upstart costs like equipment purchases without relying on costly credit. Sustainability and waste reduction: Reporting has estimated that the average power drill is used for only about 15 minutes over its lifetime. Sharing dramatically increases utilization rates, reducing material consumption and waste. LoTs like the Buffalo Tool Library have paired access with environmental initiatives such as Lead Safe mitigation programs, showing how shared tools can support both public health and climate goals. Emergency preparedness and climate resilience: Communities with an LoT can mobilize resources more quickly during crises because tools are collectively stewarded and relationships already exist. The Asheville Tool Library in North Carolina, U.S., played a critical role alongside the WNC Repair Café in response to Hurricane Helene , while the Central Florida Mutual Aid Tool Library was established as a central tool hub for post-Hurricane Ian repairs. Community cohesion and social infrastructure: LoTs function as trusted “third places” (neither home nor work) where neighbors meet, volunteer, share skills, and practice collective governance. They counter isolation, strengthen networks of mutual aid and care, and build habits of cooperation that extend beyond borrowing items. By shifting from isolated ownership to shared infrastructure, LoTs help communities become more affordable, economically vibrant, sustainable, connected, and resilient—often with lower start-up costs than many traditional community development practices. Shareable’s dedication to Libraries of Things In addition to Shareable’s regular reporting over the past 17 years (including the publication of a free e-book, “ Library of Things: A Cornerstone of the Real Sharing Economy,” in 2020), we have directly supported the development of LoTs across several sectors. Projects have included an official advisory role to the former mayor of Seoul, South Korea, as they developed a pilot program with 32 lending libraries in apartment buildings ; an inspiration and advisory role on the creation of La BOM , a three-story community center and sharing hub in Montreuil, France; and our program director, Tom Llewellyn, was a co-founder of the Asheville Tool Library in North Carolina, U.S. We began our current multi-year focus on Libraries of Things by first surveying 82 LoTs in 11 countries to produce the State of Libraries of Things 2024 Report . Key findings include: Many LoTs are making a difference in their communities with just a handful of volunteers and a small space like a storage unit or garage. The vast majority of LoTs are fully volunteer-run with annual budgets of less than $10,000 per year, limited inventory, and average memberships of less than 200 people. Larger independent LoTs typically include a storefront, a significant annual budget, and at least one paid staff person (often a volunteer coordinator). For financial sustainability, LoTs rely most heavily on a combination of membership fees, grants, and donations. Most LoTs have been operating for less than five years and are open one to three days per week when they have capacity (with limited hours). A key takeaway from our research is that most LoTs are very small and don’t require much space, inventory, or cost to begin operating. The most important thing is to just get started and then consider growth later. We believe that shared resource infrastructure, such as LoTs, should be a core, scalable solution for affordability, resilience, and sustainability. Later in 2024, we hosted the Library of Things Co-Lab to train organizers to start (or grow) an LoT in their communities. Over the course of three months, 200 people from around the world participated in the training, proving a universal need for LoTs (and the support to launch them). Following the conclusion of the Co-Lab: The initial 12 live presentations were adapted into the first edition of The Library of Things Toolkit, which has now been downloaded in over 60 countries. Shareable became a fiscal sponsor and incubator for the Tool Library Alliance (TLA), a newly formed network of established LoTs in the U.S., which is playing a pivotal role in the continued development of the field. We supported 10 local organizers from communities across the U.S. who were working on six LoTs, including a campus LoT at the University of North Florida in Jacksonville, Florida, and the Connect Highstar LoT at an affordable housing development in Houston, Texas. Replicating these models across university campuses and housing developments is now a key component of our strategy to rapidly scale LoTs worldwide. We believe that shared resource infrastructure, such as LoTs, should be a core, scalable solution for affordability, resilience, and sustainability. We envision a world where every community has access to some form of shared resource infrastructure—whether that is a lending kiosk, a decentralized library app, a public library with a collection of things, or a full-scale, independent LoT. These aren’t one-off programs or charity giveaways. LoTs are rooted in Solidarity Economy and mutual aid practices. Crucially, though, they are mutual aid in the form of durable, everyday infrastructure, just like public libraries, parks, or transit, created to meet both daily needs and moments of crisis. When thoughtfully designed and rooted in trusted local institutions, LoTs can help reduce household financial shock, increase access to new opportunities and skills, improve disaster resilience, and help support circular and solidarity economies. Rather than launching isolated projects, Shareable focuses on building the connective tissue that allows LoTs to thrive across different settings. That means: Identifying what successful sharing systems have in common Supporting real-world pilots embedded in housing developments, public libraries, campuses, and community organizations Translating on-the-ground learning into clear models, tools, and evidence Making shared resources legible and investable for institutions, funders, and public systems Our goal is not just to launch more LoTs, but rather to build a recognized field of community sharing infrastructure that communities can adopt, adapt, and sustain. We hope the expanded second edition of the Library of Things Toolkit will provide organizers (like you!) with best practices, inspiration, and tools for making your LoT a reality. The printed version of The Library of Things Toolkit is currently on sale for 25% off when you buy it directly from Shareable . title: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia
body:
The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI.
“Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote.
“Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”
The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser.
On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store.
While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed , with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open source.
But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK) — a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property.
“While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.”
For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.”
Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional.
The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company — which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025 — conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “ novelty tax ” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.

title: The secret to fast startup growth isn’t early sales, top names in tech say
body:
The AI era has changed how fast startups can grow. Startups can grow so fast that they hit high annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers, only to crash and burn a few months later. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , Lovable go-to-market lead Luke Arno, Ben Broca of the AI platform Polsia, and Theory Ventures’ Tomasz Tunguz gave founders some tips on how to set their companies up for success in those first 90 days.
Broca, whose company Polsia uses AI agents to build and run businesses with almost no human staff (Broca says he is its only employee), said that product-market fit is one of the hardest things to find right now, especially in an era when so many products can easily be copied by competitors. In response, Arno said that durable go-to-market strategies are those that can be reliably repeated.
“The most critical thing for founders or earlier-stage companies to do is develop learning density or pattern recognition for where your customers are,” Arno said. “Don’t rush to build out a top-down go-to-market motion if you’re not there yet.”
That’s why, in those first 90 days after launching a commercial product that’s ready to sell, founders should not mistake early, fast revenue for a sign that the startup is ready to scale, Arno said.
Once a startup finds use cases that work, it will only be ready to build out a sales team and go for growth after it can attract new customers by repeating what has worked. If every sale requires new tactics, the startup hasn’t truly hit product-market fit.
“If I bring on 10 new customers in 10 different ways to solve 10 different problems, sure, I brought revenue in, but I don’t have a way to go scale a go-to-market,” Arno said. “If I bring three customers in with a similar motion to solve a similar problem, now I have high confidence that I can go scale.”
Lovable, the AI app-building startup, set a lot of those early benchmarks with how fast it grew, and now founders everywhere are feeling the pressure to do the same. Lovable is valued at more than $13 billion by its investors, says its ARR has passed $600 million, and has raised more than $700 million in funding to date.
“The expectations for overall execution speed are absolutely tremendous,” Tunguz said.
But Tunguz said growth like Lovable’s is still the exception, though founders should still move fast. The pressure they feel is real, he said, because far more money flows through the startup ecosystem at every stage than when he began investing in 2008. Today, a seed deal brought in by one of his partners could just as easily be a $5 million raise, a $50 million raise, or a $500 million raise.
The winners all focus on one thing: understanding their customers well enough to know what will keep them around even after any hype subsides.
“Community building is very important and being close to customers is very important,” Broca said. He said founders can send emails and throw events, and he personally likes to talk to a lot of his customers: “The general rule is always to be talking to customers.”

title: Asia Needs $1 Trillion a Year to Secure Energy Supplies
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Asia will need as much as $1 trillion annually in energy investment over the next 15 years to meet rising demand and reduce its exposure to supply disruptions, according to a McKinsey report released Thursday.
That amounts to $15 trillion through 2040, with the Iran war exposing just how vulnerable the region remains to disruptions in oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
McKinsey now expects Asian energy demand to reach 370 million terajoules by 2040, a 15% increase over its forecast from just a year ago. The region is expected to account for roughly 70% of global net energy demand growth through 2040.
Data centers, industrial expansion, and rising demand for cooling are driving much of that growth.
Coal, meanwhile, isn't going anywhere particularly fast.
McKinsey expects Asian coal consumption to remain broadly flat over the next decade, with declining demand in China offset by increased consumption in India and Southeast Asia.
Natural gas demand growth is expected to slow over the next five to ten years as countries prioritize coal and renewables for power generation. Industrial demand could drive a longer-term recovery.
Solar and wind investment is projected to reach approximately $300 billion annually through 2040, particularly in India and Southeast Asia, but that comes with additional challenges.
A Bain and Standard Chartered report found that 50% to 60% of renewable projects in Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia were canceled or stalled between 2021 and 2025, with inadequate infrastructure and policy support among the obstacles.
McKinsey also sees opportunities for governments to support higher-cost domestic oil and gas development in China, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, and Turkmenistan as countries look to reduce reliance on imports.
Biofuels could displace another $90 billion to $100 billion in fuel imports by 2040.
The investment requirements extend well beyond renewable generation, with domestic oil and gas production, transmission infrastructure, and alternative fuels all competing for capital as Asia attempts to secure enough energy to support its growing industrial and electricity demand.

title: Why Fossil Fuel Demand Can Rise Even as Clean Energy Wins Terrain
body: French historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz has offered energy-transition skeptics an appealing historical argument.  In More and More and More, he argues that humanity has never really moved from one energy source to another. Wood was joined by coal, coal by oil, oil by gas and all of them by renewables. Energy sources accumulate rather than replace one another.  Global primary-energy charts make the argument look convincing. Fossil use remains near record levels after trillions in clean-energy investment. Biomass did not disappear when coal arrived, nor coal when the oil age began.  But the chart uses the wrong scale and watches the wrong indicator. Technologies compete in particular services and markets, not one global bucket labelled "energy." Replacement appears first in sales, then installed equipment, fuel demand and finally the global aggregate.  By the time the last chart turns downward, the transition may already be irreversible.  Global Growth Can Hide Local Destruction  Michael Liebreich's recent rebuttal of Fressoz makes the scale problem clear.  Many once-important energy systems did not merely lose market share; they disappeared from the services they formerly supplied. Whale oil stopped lighting homes. Town gas was replaced. Pit ponies, canal horses, district hydraulic power and wind-powered grinding mills largely vanished from their original markets.  Humanity still uses animals, biomass and manual labor. That does not make horses competitive with cars for urban transportation or whale oil with LEDs for lighting.  Aggregation hides substitution because different populations move at different times. Traditional biomass could collapse in wealthy countries while growing in poorer ones as population expanded and modern fuels remained inaccessible. Adding the two trends together creates apparent continuity between changes that have little causal connection.  Related Higher Oil Availability Pressures Middle East Crude Benchmarks  The same happens geographically with coal. Coal generation can decline in Europe and North America while rising in India or Southeast Asia. The global number may remain flat, but individual electricity markets are clearly replacing it.  In the European Union, wind and solar produced 30.1% of electricity in 2025, compared with 29% from all fossil sources combined. A decade earlier, fossil generation was almost three times wind and solar output. That is not addition. It is a crossover.  Sales Turn Before Fleetsand Fleets Turn Before Fuel  Transport demonstrates why transitions are so easily underestimated. The first mobile phone was demonstrated in 1973, yet global landlines rose until 2006. Nobody concludes mobile telephony failed because the incumbent grew for another 33 years.  The US horse population similarly peaked in 1920, more than three decades after the first practical combustion-engine cars appeared. New technology captured sales long before the old installed base disappeared.  Cars are repeating the pattern. Global sales of combustion-engine cars peaked in 2017. By 2024, they had fallen by nearly one-third, according to IEA data, while electric-car sales exceeded 17 million and continued growing. Yet most vehicles on the road still burn petrol or diesel because a car fleet turns over slowly.  This produces three different stories depending on the chosen metric. New sales show rapid substitution. The installed fleet shows gradual change. Global oil demand shows only the first signs of pressure.  All three can be true simultaneously.  Liebreich estimates that roughly 58 million EVs represented just under 4% of the global vehicle fleet by the end of 2025, but were already displacing slightly more than 2 million barrels of oil per day. The IEA expects displacement to reach around 5 million barrels per day by 2030 under current policies and about 9 million by 2035.  Oil will not disappear. Aviation, shipping, petrochemicals and the existing vehicle fleet will preserve substantial demand. But road transportthe largest source of oil consumptionis no longer simply adding electric vehicles on top. New combustion-car sales are being squeezed. The stock takes time to follow the flow.  Efficiency Makes Primary-Energy Charts Misleading  Fressoz's aggregate also treats units of energy as though they deliver equal services. They do not.  An internal-combustion engine discards most of its fuel energy as heat. An electric motor converts a much larger share into motion. A heat pump can deliver three or four units of heat for each unit of electricity because it moves ambient heat rather than creating all of it through combustion.  Replacing a petrol car with an EV can therefore reduce primary-energy consumption even if both travel the same distance. Replacing a gas boiler with a heat pump can do the same while maintaining a warm home.  If the transition is measured mainly through primary energy, eliminating waste can look like lost energy rather than increased productivity.  The economy needs mobility, light, heat and industrial work. It does not need barrels, tonnes or cubic metres for their own sake.  This is why electrification is the transition's central multiplier. Liebreich estimates that electricity supplied roughly 10% of useful-energy demand in 1970 and around 30% today. As transport, heating and parts of industry electrify, fewer units of primary energy are needed to provide the same or better service.  The global economy has grown by roughly 50% over the past 15 years while emissions increased only 9%. That is not sufficient absolute decarbonization, but it is substantial evidence that economic growth and fossil-energy growth are separating.  Additive Today Does Not Mean Additive Forever  Fressoz retains one important point a rising clean-energy share does not guarantee fossil fuels decline quickly enough for climate goals.  Electricity is easier to decarbonize than aviation, cement, steel, shipping and food production. Renewables can dominate power additions while fossil fuels persist elsewhere. EV production still consumes energy and materials. Substitution is not environmental purity.  The transition can therefore be real and still be too slow.  That distinction matters. Declaring the transition fictional encourages governments and companies to preserve incumbent assets on the assumption that clean technologies will remain permanently additive. Declaring it inevitable encourages complacency about grids, permitting, finance and hard-to-abate sectors.  Neither conclusion follows from the evidence.  What matters is simple arithmetic. If clean energy grows faster than demand for energy services, it first meets all incremental demand. Once it grows faster still, fossil supply must contract. BloombergNEF estimates that wind and solar already provided 20% of global electricity by 2025, after annual installations rose from 300 GW in 2021 to 815 GW four years later.  The threshold between addition and replacement is not ideological. It is the moment clean-energy growth exceeds total demand growth.  The Transition Is Visible Where Competition Happens  Energy systems have enormous inertia. Power stations last for decades. Cars remain on roads long after manufacturers stop selling similar models. Buildings outlive their heating systems, while fuel infrastructure survives through sunk costs and political protection.  That is why incumbents can keep growing after their eventual replacement becomes apparent.  The useful question is not whether every fossil-fuel total has already declined. It is whether clean technologies are capturing new investment, sales and energy-service demand faster than incumbents can replace their aging assets.  In power and passenger vehicles, the answer is increasingly yes. In aviation, shipping and heavy industry, it is not yet.  The energy transition is neither instant nor imaginary. It is a long sequence of competitive defeats that appears additiveright until it does not.  By Leon Stille for Oilprice.com

title: Blockchain Association Presses Congress on Crypto Taxes as Clarity Act Stalls
body: Bitcoin Magazine Blockchain Association Presses Congress on Crypto Taxes as Clarity Act Stalls The Blockchain Association sent a letter to Senate and House leadership on Thursday asking Congress to pass bipartisan digital asset tax legislation, the group’s first broad push on taxes since the Clarity Act failed in the Senate last month. The letter, signed by Chief Policy Officer Lindsay Fraser and addressed to Majority Leader John Thune, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, argues that the rules governing the 67 million Americans who hold digital assets “were written for a different era.” The group paired it with a new site, TaxClarityforAmerica.com , built for constituents to contact their representatives. The asks will sound familiar to anyone who has followed the tax fight: a de minimis exemption for small transactions, cash treatment for stablecoins, tax on mining and staking rewards at sale instead of receipt, broker reporting limited to firms that hold customer assets, and wash sale rules that close loss harvesting without catching everyday transactions. The letter adds a safe harbor for foreign traders on U.S. exchanges, a mark-to-market election, and R&D credit eligibility for blockchain development. What the letter leaves out is an endorsement. Two bills are somewhat in play, and the association named neither. Where the tax bills stand The House moved first. One day after the Clarity Act failed in the Senate, the Ways and Means Committee approved the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, H.R. 10357, a 114-page package from Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO). It exempts network fees under $10 from capital gains reporting, with a carve-out for taxpayers who made more than 5,000 transfers in the prior year, and extends wash sale and constructive sale rules to digital assets. Qualified dollar stablecoins are exempt from the wash sale rule. The package left out the provision the industry wanted most. Rep. Mike Carey’s Tax Clarity for Mining and Staking Act, H.R. 9175, which would have let miners and stakers defer tax until they sell, was in an early discussion draft and gone from the text the committee released on September 14. Instead the bill classifies validation rewards as ordinary income, taxable on receipt. Rep. Steven Horsford (D-NV), who had proposed capping the deferral at five years, voted for the package and said it leaves the question open for further work. The Blockchain Association, Crypto Council for Innovation and Digital Chamber had asked the committee in June to pass that bill without changes. The committee did the opposite. The Senate has its own version. Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT) introduced the ADAPT Act on September 30 with Sens. Cynthia Lummis, Bernie Moreno and Tim Scott as cosponsors. It exempts purchases made with GENIUS Act stablecoins from gain or loss, sets the same $10 fee threshold, and applies wash sale rules with grandfathering for existing holdings and exemptions for mining and staking rewards. It sits in committee. Lummis’s earlier bill , S. 2207, with a $300 per-transaction de minimis exemption capped at $5,000 a year, has been in the Finance Committee since June 2025. Neither chamber’s bill contains the exemption for small bitcoin purchases that the industry made a centerpiece at Bitcoin 2026 . The House bill’s $10 threshold covers fees, not purchases. The Senate bill’s spending exemption covers stablecoins, not bitcoin. The Bitcoin Policy Institute and others have argued that any de minimis rule should cover bitcoin, and Thursday’s letter asks for a “meaningful” exemption without naming a figure. Awkward timing Congress is in recess until after the November 3 midterms. When members return, they will have a lame-duck session measured in weeks, and crypto taxes compete with government funding and whatever else leadership decides to clear before the 119th Congress ends. Lummis, the Senate’s loudest voice on digital asset taxes, retires in January 2027. The Clarity Act’s collapse shapes all of this. The market structure bill passed the House 294-134 in July 2025, then stalled in the Senate for more than a year while the banking lobby fought the crypto industry over stablecoin yield and Democrats pressed for ethics language aimed at the Trump family’s crypto ventures. The cloture vote on September 15 failed 49-50. No Democrat crossed over, and Republicans Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Jerry Moran voted no. Sen. Thom Tillis switched his vote so he could file a motion to reconsider, which keeps the bill alive on paper and little more. With market structure off the table, the industry has shifted its lobbying to what might move. Tax is the obvious candidate: the House package cleared committee with bipartisan votes, and the wash sale provisions raise revenue, which gives tax writers a reason to attach them to a larger vehicle. Punchbowl News reported Thursday that the association’s refusal to back either bill signals the industry wants more than what Congress has produced. Regulators keep filling the gap in the meantime. The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rule on Wednesday, and the SEC and CFTC have been setting market structure policy through rulemaking and enforcement in the absence of a statute. This post Blockchain Association Presses Congress on Crypto Taxes as Clarity Act Stalls first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman .

title: Errors in disability cases for ‘painful scars’ resulted in overpayment: VA watchdog
body: The error of Veterans Benefits Administration staff has resulted in approximately $5.6 million in overpayments to veterans, a VA watchdog found. During a review period from June 1, 2024, through May 31, 2025, the VA made at least one error in 17,900 cases, roughly 38%, regarding disability decisions for painful scars, according to a recent VA Office of Inspector General report . 920 of those decisions, per the report, led to millions in overpayment and will continue to accrue without “corrective action.” For service-connected painful scars, as a result of burns, surgeries, shrapnel and gunshot wounds, among other sources, the VA requires a physical examination to support a veteran’s claim. However, the OIG found that the Disability Benefits Questionnaire “does not clearly define objective versus subjective evidence. Therefore, claims processors sometimes provided evaluations for painful scars without objective evidence to support the evaluations, which led to overpayments in disability compensation.” In addition, the report found that physical manifestations of the disability were often evaluated under two separate diagnostic codes, often resulting in “pyramiding” and overpayment. The report notes that more than a half-million veterans currently receive VA disability benefits for painful scarring caused or worsened by military service, but it took a random sample of 70 decisions from a review population of 47,300. title: Errors in disability cases for ‘painful scars’ resulted in overpayment: VA watchdog
body: The error of Veterans Benefits Administration staff has resulted in approximately $5.6 million in overpayments to veterans, a VA watchdog found. During a review period from June 1, 2024, through May 31, 2025, the VA made at least one error in 17,900 cases, roughly 38%, regarding disability decisions for painful scars, according to a recent VA Office of Inspector General report . 920 of those decisions, per the report, led to millions in overpayment and will continue to accrue without “corrective action.” For service-connected painful scars, as a result of burns, surgeries, shrapnel and gunshot wounds, among other sources, the VA requires a physical examination to support a veteran’s claim. title: African Union condemns deadly drone strikes in Sudan, Abyei
body: The African Union (AU) has added its voice to a chorus of international condemnation after reported drone attacks kill scores of civilians in West Kordofan, South Darfur, Khartoum, and Abyei. AU Commission chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf calls for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire. The African Union has condemned a series of deadly drone attacks in Sudan and the disputed Abyei area, amid reports that more than 250 people have been killed in strikes over several days. As reported by Radio Dabanga yesterday, the UN secretary-general has strongly condemned drone attacks in Abyei on Monday that reportedly killed dozens of civilians, including women and children, near Amiet and Todach markets, and injured many others. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, chairperson of the African Union Commission (Photo: AU) Today, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf , chairperson of the African Union Commission, expressed deep concern over the civilian toll of the attacks, which have caused deaths, displacement, destruction of livelihoods, and disrupted access to food, healthcare, and other essential services. Media reports citing local and medical sources say about 80 people were killed in El Dibb, West Kordofan, on 18 October, while 23 people died in Nyala, South Darfur, on 16 October. At least three children were reportedly killed in Khartoum on 19 October. Separately, reports citing local authorities say the death toll from a drone attack on Ameet market in Abyei on 19 October has exceeded 150. Call to protect civilians Youssouf called on all parties to stop attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, protect humanitarian and medical personnel, and ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access in accordance with international law, including international humanitarian law. Aftermath of a drone attack on El Obeid, on April 25 (Photo: Social media) He also stressed the need to respect Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, urging all parties to refrain from actions that could intensify the conflict, threaten the country’s unity, or endanger neighbouring states. The AU Commission chairperson reaffirmed his support for ongoing regional and international mediation efforts, calling for coordinated action to secure an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and launch an inclusive, Sudanese-led political process. Debris from a drone attack in Sudan (File phtoto: Anthony Headley / UNHCR) Share article The post African Union condemns deadly drone strikes in Sudan, Abyei appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

title: Quad9 DNS Resolver to exit France
body:
Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.
The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France.Â
The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from â¬580,000 to â¬1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.
We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.
This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.
beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.
Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users.Â
We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.
For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map usersâ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way to force users to identify themselves before they can connect to the internet. Our core goals â privacy of user data and honesty of responses - are directly opposed to the methods necessary to implement the blocking this court ruling would require us to perform. There is no way we can determine which users this ruling applies to â we have no list of French users, because we do not keep dossiers of our users at all.
If we do not comply, we will face a daily penalty of 1.000 euros until the blocking concludes on November 14 (i.e., 24.000 euros) not including our legal defense. Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN. Inaction is, therefore, not an option to challenge this decision.
We could add these names to our global malicious domain blocking database, which is what we use to provide internet users with malware and phishing protection. This is a single, monolithic set of names applied to all users of our protective services (9.9.9.9 & secondaries) globally but not to our nonprotective services (9.9.9.10 & secondaries). Blocking these names for all users globally would satisfy the requirements of the court.Â
However, this would have the âextraterritorialâ effect of applying French legal decisions to every internet user worldwide, when they are meant to solely apply to France, for the commercial benefit of a single private, foreign-owned company. We suspect if other nations wished to impose their national legislation within France, there would be a strong reaction from French users and authorities. The converse is equally true: the findings of a French court are not applicable to the rest of the world. Such a system would set a precedent that any nation could impose their laws, morals, economic demands, or social constructs upon any other nation by the means of blocking DNS names, and thus blocking communication and content.Â
Therefore, this global blocking method is entirely unworkable for us as a solution to be compliant with the court order.
There are more important reasons geoIP blocking will not work. We already prevailed in a similar legal case in Germany in 2021-2023 in which we learned an important lesson: we tried to use geoIP blocking as a âhackâ in a similar circumstance at the start of the legal proceedings, allowing us to continue services in Germany until the case concluded. The plaintiff (Sony Music Entertainment GmbH) then used a VPN to access the blocked content from Germany in circumvention of the geoIP blocking. The court agreed with Sony in their assertions of noncompliance, and we were fined for contempt of court.Â
From this experience, we know that the geoIP-based model is not only unfit from a technical perspective, but we have proven, historical evidence that using geoIP methods results in fines being levied against us by courts. To any technology-aware person, this seems absurd and outrageous â but this is what we face in these lawsuits where there is a disconnect between the courtsâ understanding and how (and why) the technical protocols of the internet actually operate. We cannot risk this negative outcome in this or any other future instance, as absurd decisions apparently are de rigueur in these cases.
We eventually won that case against Sony , but it took several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time â all of which set us back in our ability to deliver services and is a resource debt we are still paying for today. This case is just more of the same â the opposition has more lawyers than we have money and time.
Given these conditions and as a result of our unwavering mission, our historical experience, our desire to remain within the law, and the outcome of the court decision, we are left with an uncomfortable choice.
The demands lead us to an impossible requirement: we must adhere to the courtâs decision, or we face growing risks to our existence. However, in implementing the blocking, we must either extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally) or create a vulnerability condition whereby we continue to be at risk because the available technical methods are imprecise,Â impossible to validate, and do not meet any user privacy and security requirements.
This leads us to the only conclusion we can understand to eliminate our legal risk and keep us true to our mission: we must make our cybersecurity protection and general services unavailable to French users. Our departure is scheduled for November 24, 2026.
In any event, for Quad9, this is a matter of principle regarding the potential misuse of these types of blocking measures. Allowing private corporations to have the ability to block what is seen on the internet seems to us to be a dangerous and infinitely deep problem. Actions that seem reasonable and infrequent today will tomorrow become an avalanche of petty demands used to suppress political, religious, economic, or social outcomes. We will not be even a small part of that degradation of the freedom of knowledge. Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly.
This case with beIN is not the only litigation we face in France. There are approximately 20 different lawsuits pending against Quad9 (and other recursive resolver operators) that demand we comply with blocking hundreds of different names. We expect many of them to escalate to the same conditions as we have seen with beIN, which puts Quad9 at risk regardless of the outcome of this case.Â
Based on the generalized, high-level traffic statistics we keep, we know we have many users in France. With our departure, those users will be put at risk from the threats we have protected them from for nearly 9 years. We deeply regret that result, but we have no other choice. Below is a partial list of the networks from which we see traffic in France. You will see many infrastructure, national security, finance, education, and other networks of critical importance in addition to ISP users and mobile users. All these users will lose service on November 24 because of the legal risks facing Quad9 in France.
The most troubling part of this decision is that it is ineffective in practice. Forcing Quad9 to block domain names does not take the content out of circulation and has no effect on the servers that house the data.Â
We offer a free service, and there are thousands of other open DNS systems that do what Quad9 does but with lower trust, safety, and reliability. Users seeking blocked content will simply shift their DNS to use one of those other free services, possibly using systems in other nations that have less-than-honorable intentions from a privacy and security perspective. This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert. It is an unsolvable problem via recursive DNS, and the effect of legal rulings like this is not measurable outside of the amounts paid to lawyers and the number of words in press releases declaring hollow victory.Â
Even beIN will not see any changes. Perhaps that is understood and the cruelty may be the point - we cannot say with certainty why such expenditures have been made against a small nonprofit like Quad9, which tries only to bring safer, trusted service to users. But of this we are certain: these actions are a tragic waste of time and resources and create a real, negative outcome for the internet community of France, whether or not they are our users.
Quad9 will not block the domains in question - we wish to remain committed to our integrity of providing a complete view of the DNS for users who wish that service. However, starting on November 24, we will no longer serve French users, thus keeping Quad9 out of danger from similar, perhaps even larger risks in the future. Our hope is that 30 days will be sufficient time for conversion, though we regret that this message will undoubtedly not reach some users in time.
An appeal is pending, and we will continue to legally defend our position in court in this case and as many other cases as we are able. We will continue to oppose court-ordered DNS blocking of this nature everywhere. Our resources are limited, but we are determined to keep the internet open and free. You can donate here to help us continue to deliver on our mission and assist us in the legal costs we incur in this and other fights.
We think this problem is reversible. French citizens: tell your legislators that looking up names is not a criminal offense. The internet needs to remain open and freely available to anyone, and neutral intermediaries like Quad9 (or any DNS resolver) should not be implicated in legal proceedings because we map names to IP addresses. Further, we know there are potential plans in consideration in France (and other European nations) to give private corporations and others automated and unvalidated abilities to filter DNS content that they alone determine to be unwanted, making it possible for a wide range of badly-managed or anti-democratic activities to be implemented. We believe you disagree with this as much as we do. Make yourself heard, or you will lose your rights silently.
ARCOM is your regulatory authority, and you should tell them this precedent places France at risk both from a practical and strategic perspective.Â
Let them know that under their mandate, they have to balance your digital rights as citizens as well as the audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts of rights holders. Balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.
Fighting piracy via DNS resolvers blocking is ineffective. It is disproportionate and misguided, ill-fitted and futile to fight piracy, as the source content remains completely available to resurge under another name. Forcing Quad9 to depart harms French digital strategy and sovereignty in the long run relating to security, privacy, and integrity - contradicting Franceâs supreme national interests in exchange for a short-term, imaginary commercial victory.
We deeply regret that we must leave our French users without cybersecurity protection, but we hope the future will see a more reasonable interpretation of the law which allows us to return.
* This post was authored and translated into French by humans on the Quad9 TeamÂ
This list is extracted from network metrics of an hour or so of typical usage. Quad9 tracks network autonomous systems number origins as per our privacy policy , but we do not identify individual IP addresses or users within those networks. There are hundreds of additional French networks using Quad9; we picked only these at random to show the breadth of usage. Autonomous systems are not exclusively geographically-mapped and cannot be used as a jurisdictional identifier; though it is safe to say that most of these networks have a significant portion of their user base in France.

title: a16z Drops Crypto From Its Name, Widens Bets to AI and Frontier Tech
body:
Andreessen Horowitz, the venture capital firm better known as a16z, is renaming its crypto fund “a16z Frontier” and widening its mandate to AI and other emerging technologies, according to an email shared with its newsletter subscribers on Thursday.
a16z is among the biggest backers of the crypto industry, and when a firm that size drops “crypto” from its name, it shows where it may expect the next wave of cash to go. Chris Dixon, a general partner who runs the crypto team, says the firm’s bets include Coinbase, the blockchain network Solana, and Uniswap, a platform where people swap tokens without a middleman.
a16z calls the move “an expansion” and says crypto stays: “we will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation,” the firm wrote.
The argument is that blockchains—shared digital ledgers that record who owns what without a bank in the middle—have faded into the background of products people already use.
“Wall Street and fintech companies now regularly launch products built on blockchains. Does that make them crypto companies? The label matters less now,” Dixon wrote, adding that it makes more sense to define companies “by what they do rather than by the technologies they use.”
In January, a16z said it had raised more than $15 billion across its funds, and co-founder Ben Horowitz wrote in a firm post that the mission “starts with winning the key architectures of the future—AI and crypto.”
Dixon expects more “native use cases,” which he defines as “brand-new activities you couldn’t do before,” since AI so far has mostly made existing work like coding “faster, better, and cheaper.” Early versions, he says, “will look strange and unserious, like toys and hobbies,” before some grow into mainstream products.
The new label covers startups “building new technologies and creating markets that may take years to develop,” a bet Dixon says goes back more than a decade.
“When I joined a16z in 2013, I made these kinds of long-horizon investments a focus,” Dixon wrote. “The growth of smartphones made cameras, sensors, and chips better and cheaper, enabling new devices like drones, AR/VR headsets, and wearables. That theme led to investments in Oculus and drone startups like Skydio and Zipline.”
The next wave, he says, includes “autonomous machines that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world” as well as advances in biology and medicine.
He also envisions a post-AGI society referring to artificial general intelligence, a still-theoretical AI that can match or beat humans at nearly all thinking tasks.
Crypto stays in the picture because Dixon sees it giving AI agents, meaning programs that act on their own, a way to pay each other. “Crypto can give new networks native economic capabilities, enable machine-to-machine transactions, and create new ways to bootstrap them,” he wrote.
Dixon made a similar argument in 2022, when crypto’s total market value had fallen about two-thirds from its 2021 peak. “What I look at is not prices,” he said then , pointing to developer and entrepreneur activity as the core metric.
Dixon will lead the new fund alongside a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz and general partners Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. His post gives no size for the renamed fund, so the latest figure on record is the $2.2 billion announced in May.

title: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
body:
Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Macrohard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
> It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Shares and shares alike
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.
Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.
What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.
What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.
Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.
So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

Teenage Engineering is branching out into instrument amps with the previously leaked EP-35 , a multi-input, multi-instrument, battery-powered amp with built-in effects. The back of the unit has a line-in port, as well as a 1/4-inch guitar input and an XLR input for mics, including mics that require phantom power. You can also stream audio to it via Bluetooth and connect multiple EP-35s together over Bluetooth using Auracast . If you have them paired in stereo, tilting a unit to the left or right sets it to the appropriate stereo channel, which is pretty neat.
There are separate effects processors for guitar and vocals, though you have limited control over them. Instead of adding, say, a delay and dialing in the delay time, you pick a style-based preset like “blues,” “indie,” or “twang,” which applies a specific selection of effects, and you control the “amount” with a single knob. The vocal channel works the same way, but with different effects like “radio” and the all-essential “robo choir.”
TE is also offering a number of accessories to pair with EP-35. The most interesting are the “ amptenna ,” which turns the unit into an FM radio, and the EP–127 KO Pedal . The pedal is a wireless MIDI controller that gives you additional control over the built-in effects, unlocks a simple looper and metronome, and includes an expression pedal jack which can be used to control the volume of a selected channel on the amp. And since the EP-127 also has a 3.5mm MIDI output and works as an HID controller, it can also be used with your other synths, pedals, or even to control video playback from your computer.
The EP-35 amp is available now for $399 .

title: Aipac ends US candidate endorsements as backlash over Israel grows
body: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, said it would no longer endorse candidates or make direct campaign contributions, as debate intensifies over American aid to Israel, the Gaza war and the influence of outside money in elections. Instead, the group will continue operating through its United Democracy Project committee, known as a super Pac, which is allowed to raise unlimited amounts for campaign advertising but is not allowed to co-ordinate with candidates, Jewish Insider first reported. The development comes amid growing criticism of Aipac , particularly within the Democratic Party, and declining support for Israel among Americans after the war in Gaza. Aipac began contributing directly to politicians in 2022. Polls show a substantial shift in American public opinion on Israel and US policy towards the country, particularly among Democrats and independents. Jim Manley, a Democratic strategist, said Aipac had become “radioactive” for many candidates. “I was surprised that Aipac did that,” Mr Manley said. “Aipac typically signifies a very aggressive posture towards politics. They're not in the habit of backing away from a fight.” He said the move could become a “major headache” for Democratic leaders, including House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer, who have received contributions from Aipac's political network. Aipac did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It told NPR that its strategy remained unchanged despite the decision to end direct campaign contributions and candidate endorsements. "Our goal is to build support for the US-Israel relationship,” spokeswoman Deryn Sousa told NPR, adding that Aipac members had given more than $90 million directly to candidates during the current election cycle and that such giving would “continue and increase”. But Trita Parsi, a political analyst in Washington, said it was "hard to overstate" the significance of the development. "Historically, Aipac sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover. If you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn't even bother to fight you," Mr Parsi said on X. "Rather than invincibility, Aipac's name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn't want its own name on its political donations." The decision, observers say, changes how Aipac channels political money, rather than its political involvement. Ending formal endorsements and direct contributions could help candidates avoid the political fallout of receiving the group's explicit backing. The move is likely to have an almost immediate impact in Michigan , a battleground state where the Senate race is being closely watched and Aipac spending and US policy towards Israel have become major campaign issues. Aipac's involvement in the race has been particularly contentious. Its super Pac spent more than $30 million seeking to defeat Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and backing Representative Haley Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel. It was the organisation’s largest single investment in a single contest. Mr El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American physician and a progressive candidate, won the nomination in August, in a major setback for the pro-Israel lobby. The group later continued its involvement in the race with advertising opposing Mr El-Sayed as he faces Republican Mike Rogers, an ally of President Donald Trump, in the November 3 midterm elections. Mr Rogers was initially wary of Aipac's involvement, concerned that the group's unpopularity could hurt his campaign amid declining support for Israel among some Republicans. He later publicly welcomed support from the group. Mr El-Sayed, who is endorsed by Senator Bernie Sanders, has called for an end to US military aid to Israel and described Israel's war in Gaza as a genocide. If he wins he would become the first Muslim US senator. "Aipac is now spending as much as $9 million against Abdul El-Sayed," Mr Sanders wrote on X. "Aipac is why we’re at war in Iran. Aipac is why the US has supported genocide in Gaza. We must say no to Aipac." AIPAC is now spending as much as $9 million against Abdul El-Sayed. AIPAC is why we’re at war in Iran. AIPAC is why the U.S. has supported genocide in Gaza. We must say NO to AIPAC. YES to electing Abdul as Michigan’s next U.S. Senator. — Bernie Sanders (@BernieSanders) October 22, 2026 This week, Aipac directed about $9 million to a group supporting Mr Rogers, according to The Washington Post . The money was reported as independent political spending, rather than a direct contribution to his campaign.
