title: Are You Sure Your USDC Rewards Are Safe?
body: Under the GENIUS Act, the stablecoin law Congress passed in July 2025, companies that issue stablecoins can’t pay interest to the people who hold them. Some exchanges pay holders anyway. Coinbase (COIN) pays 3.75% a year to customers who hold USDC, the dollar-pegged stablecoin issued by Circle, as long as they belong to Coinbase One, its paid membership tier. Coinbase pays those rewards itself, and under a revenue-sharing agreement it receives a share of the interest Circle earns on USDC’s reserves. Whether rewards programs like these violate the GENIUS Act’s ban on interest remains a gray area. Banks say they amount to the same interest paid another way, and have urged the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to tighten its rules on money passed to holders through partners. (Rewards were also a major sticking point in talks over the CLARITY Act, the broader crypto market-structure bill, which failed in September .) On Oct. 21, the OCC, the federal regulator for nonbank stablecoin issuers, finalized its rule , effective Jan. 18, 2027, and dropped its proposed presumption that such payouts break the ban, choosing to judge each arrangement case by case. In other words, the OCC went the opposite way from the stricter test the banks wanted. For Coinbase, that means, at least for now, its USDC rewards can continue unabated. The rule gives them no safe harbor, so they remain open to challenge. For USDC holders, the 3.75% is not guaranteed. If the OCC decides Coinbase’s program is just a loophole to bypass the GENIUS Act’s ban on stablecoin interest, the payouts could be shut down. For Coinbase shareholders, the question is how much of the company rides on those rewards. Coinbase fought to keep them: in January, CEO Brian Armstrong pulled the company’s support for a Senate draft of the CLARITY Act, objecting to “draft amendments that would kill rewards on stablecoins, allowing banks to ban their competition” and other provisions. Stablecoins brought in $292.1 million in Coinbase’s second quarter, its 10-Q shows , about a quarter of its net revenue. Whether losing the rewards would hurt depends on two things: how much the rewards already cost Coinbase, and how much of its stablecoin revenue comes from USDC that earns no rewards at all. What the Rule Says The agency has kept the ban on issuers paying holders “any form of interest or yield” “solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention” of a stablecoin. However, the rule also says a payment that reaches stablecoin holders through an intermediary “might be made, at least in part, for other reasons,” which could put it outside the ban. Coinbase describes its rewards as “a loyalty program funded by Coinbase.” Whether that is enough is now the OCC’s call. The agency wrote that it “declines to presume that rewards programs that predated the GENIUS Act comply with the GENIUS Act,” so Coinbase’s program gets no grandfathering. On payments more generally, the rule says “payments for bona fide services generally would not be prohibited” when no other facts point the other way, without naming any particular arrangement. The agency added that as the payment stablecoin market evolves, it expects to gain enough real-world “experience with identifying prohibited transactions” to eventually propose a clearer rule defining its “yield prohibition.” Rob Nichols, president and CEO of the American Bankers Association, said the result “will preserve the status quo for crypto platforms despite Congress’s clear intent to protect local lending.” Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer, posted that in the rule “there’s a lot to like.” How the Money Moves Circle (CRCL) earns interest on USDC’s reserves. Under its agreement with Coinbase, described in Circle’s IPO filing , Coinbase receives the reserve income on USDC held in Coinbase products, after a slice Circle keeps, plus half of what remains on most USDC held elsewhere. Circle said it paid about $819 million, or 59 cents of every revenue dollar, to distribution partners and transaction costs in the first half of 2026. In the rest of the issue, subscribers get: How much of what Coinbase earns on its customers’ USDC the rewards already eat , and how that changed What happens to Coinbase’s stablecoin revenue if the rewards end , and how much customer USDC would have to leave for it to hurt The one scenario that puts all $292 million of Coinbase’s quarterly stablecoin revenue in play, and who holds the leverage Why Circle’s planned move to a New York trust company leaves open which rulebook judges USDC’s rewards Bull, base and bear ranges for Coinbase’s stablecoin revenue after rewards, and the dates that decide them Already a subscriber? title: Reported fraud losses among older Americans hit $3 billion in 2025 as big losses surge: FTC report
body:
Fraud losses reported by older Americans jumped in 2025, driven largely by an increase in victims losing sums of at least six figures, according to a new report from the Federal Trade Commission.
Americans ages 60 and older reported losing about $3 billion to fraud last year, a 25% increase from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to the FTC's annual report to Congress , released Monday, on fraud among older adults. That figure is up 400% from the $600 million reported lost in 2020.
Just 6% of older fraud victims reported losing $100,000 or more last year, but those losses accounted for 70% of the age group's total reported losses. The number reporting losses of that magnitude rose nearly sixfold to 6,769 in 2025 from 1,136 in 2020.
Additionally, because many scams go unreported, the FTC estimates actual losses in 2025 could have been anywhere from $13.3 billion to $119.5 billion. In 2024, the estimated range was from $10.1 billion to $81.5 billion.
"The numbers and the increases are staggering," said Bob Blancato, national coordinator for the Elder Justice Coalition, an advocacy group for ending elder abuse. "Part of it is that the perpetrators are always ahead. They seem to be one step ahead of everybody."
The rising losses come as scammers increasingly target Americans' life savings by impersonating banks, businesses and government agencies, according to an August 2025 analysis by the FTC. The schemes often involve fabricated emergencies that convince victims to transfer money to supposedly protect their accounts from being compromised.
The volume of scams has increased with the use of artificial intelligence. AI-generated scams are also increasingly difficult to detect and easier to produce, according to the FBI .
In many impersonation schemes, criminals pose as representatives of banks or government agencies and falsely warn that a consumer's money is in danger of being stolen. Victims are then instructed to transfer funds, mail cash or deposit money into cryptocurrency ATMs, supposedly to protect their assets.
However, investment scams were the costliest fraud type reported by older Americans last year, with losses exceeding $1 billion, a 42% jump from 2024, the FTC's new report shows. These scams often begin with social media ads promoting investment opportunities or messages from people posing as financial advisors, according to the FTC. Victims may then be directed to fraudulent trading platforms.
Government impersonation scams ranked second in total reported losses among older consumers, with $448 million in reported losses, followed by business impersonation scams, which resulted in $422 million in reported losses.
Congress is considering legislation intended to provide additional protections and relief for people who lose money to scams.
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 temporarily restricted victims' ability to claim their fraud losses as a deduction on their tax return in certain cases. Prior to that legislation, fraud losses were generally deductible. The provision was scheduled to expire in 2025, but President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" law enacted last year made that change permanent.
While investment fraud losses may be deductible , according to an IRS memorandum issued in March 2025, money lost to other scams — such as some impersonator or romance scams — is not, experts said.
In addition, if the victim tapped a tax-deferred retirement account such as a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account as part of the fraud, income taxes may be due on the distribution. And if the victim is younger than age 59½, an early withdrawal penalty of 10% may be imposed.
"You get scammed out of $100,000 and then you're paying taxes on that $100,000," Blancato said. "That's crazy."
The bipartisan Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act , which was passed by the House in September in a 408-17 vote, would eliminate the deductibility restrictions and waive the 10% penalty if it applies, among other provisions. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee. It's uncertain whether it will gain traction in the upper chamber before this session of Congress is over.
Separately, the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act , which cleared the House in June by a vote of 414-2, would allow certain financial institutions such as mutual fund companies to temporarily delay transactions when they reasonably believe a customer is being financially exploited. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee; whether it will get a floor vote is unknown.
Already, many banks and other financial institutions ask account holders for a "trusted contact," which is someone who can be contacted in certain circumstances, including when financial exploitation is suspected. That person may be able to intervene to prevent the fraud by reaching out to the account holder. The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, requires brokerages to make a reasonable effort to add a trusted contact to accounts, although investors are not required to provide one.
If you suspect an older adult in your life is being victimized, it's important to approach the situation with care, experts say.
"It's usually best to start with an open, nonjudgmental, compassionate approach," said Marti DeLiema, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota and associate director of education for the school's Center for Healthy Aging and Innovation.
"You never say 'you're being scammed,' because they'll throw their guard up," DeLiema said. "Scammers will try to intentionally isolate the target from potential interveners. They'll say, 'Don't tell anyone about our relationship' or 'Don't tell anyone that you won the lottery.'"
If the money is already gone, it's important not to blame the victim, DeLiema said. "We do that to scam victims all the time. We say, 'What were you thinking? How could you be so foolish?'" she said.
"We really need to move away from the shame, because I guarantee you, they're already doing that to themselves," DeLiema said. "They're already pointing the finger inward."

title: Elon Musk invests about $1 billion in Skydance
body:
Elon Musk has made an investment in Skydance of roughly $1 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The financial injection comes as the company looks to cut costs. Paramount closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, naming the combined entity Skydance . Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with merging two major film studios in Paramount and Warner Bros., two popular streaming platforms — Paramount+ and HBO Max — and a host of corporate functions to support a portfolio of TV networks and two news divisions.
Skydance has said it expects to see $6 billion in cost savings over three years, though it faces a debt burden of nearly $80 billion.
Musk's commitment is part of a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments, according to Semafor, which first reported the news Thursday . Representatives for Musk and Skydance did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
Shares of Skydance were down about 1% Thursday.
Ellison's father, Larry Ellison, has a history with Musk. The Oracle co-founder invested $1 billion in Musk's 2022 deal to purchase Twitter, now called X. Larry Ellison also invested in Tesla in 2018 and served on the company's board of directors.
The elder Ellison also personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of equity financing in Paramount's offer to take over WBD.

title: Adjusting Imports of Wind Turbines and Their Parts and Components into the United States
body: Presidential Actions Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA A PROCLAMATION 1. Within the past 90 days, the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his investigation into the effects of imports of wind turbines and their parts and components on the national security of the United States under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232). Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States and provided me recommendations for action under section 232 to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States. 2. Among other things, the Secretary found that wind energy is an unreliable and intermittent energy source and that the use of wind energy diverts the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources. The Secretary also found that products used to generate and use wind energy pose serious national security concerns, including by relying on foreign parts that contain cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could lead to remote control access to wind turbines and cause power disruption; undermining the United States’ electrical grid, and potentially causing disruptions to critical infrastructure; interfering with national airspace and air safety; and causing radar interference that can affect air traffic control, weather forecasting, homeland security, and national defense missions. And the Secretary found that imports of wind turbine components and subcomponents have increased over the last decade, and that United States wind energy is reliant on imports of foreign produced wind turbine components and subcomponents. 3. The Secretary found that wind energy is intermittent and burdensome on the United States electrical grid. Wind energy is inherently intermittent, and this unpredictability undermines wind’s suitability as a standalone energy source compared to the steady output of fossil fuel or nuclear energy, particularly if used for critical infrastructure. And even though wind energy comprises only a small portion of total utility scale power generated in the United States, grid operators must frequently rely upon fast-ramping fossil fuel backup generators to compensate for wind energy’s high net load variability and maintain grid stability. This results in higher operational costs and increased maintenance burdens. 4. The Secretary found that the unpredictability of wind energy makes it less reliable than other energy sources that conversely provide steady output as standalone energy sources. Given wind energy’s intermittent reliability, use of wind energy diverts the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources. And resources that are used to support wind energy and wind energy projects could instead have been used to strengthen more reliable energy sources that are essential to the national and economic security of the United States. 5. The Secretary found that the use of wind energy poses unique national security risks compared to other energy sources. Among other things, wind energy products have serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can cause power disruption; interfere with radar, thus significantly affecting air traffic control, weather forecasting, homeland security, and national defense missions; and burden the United States electrical grid, including by diverting the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources. 6. More specifically, the Secretary found that wind energy products — particularly foreign imported products — present unique cybersecurity risks that could lead to remote control access to wind turbines and cause power disruption. Inverters are a crucial piece of electrical equipment for using wind energy, as inverters convert the electrical energy generated by wind turbines into a form of energy that can be used by the power grid or local systems. The vast majority of these inverters are produced outside the United States and imported into the United States. But modern networked inverters used in wind farms — particularly those produced and imported from outside the United States — are an exploitable vulnerability that can allow remote access and interference with United States power systems. Attackers could gain remote control over power generation, which presents risks of power disruption or sabotage of installation facilities. 7. The Secretary found that wind turbines can affect ground and air-based radars by creating “clutter,” reducing detection sensitivity, obscuring potential targets, and scattering radio wave returns. For example, clutter from wind projects obscures legitimate moving targets and generates false targets in the vicinity of the wind projects, and some mitigation techniques can lead to missing actual targets. These circumstances thus pose grave national security risks to the United States, particularly in response to threats (e.g., unauthorized aircraft) targeting sensitive United States critical infrastructure. And degraded radar performance from wind turbines can also have negative implications on weather forecasting, air traffic management, and military radar systems. 8. The Secretary found that the United States is reliant on imports of foreign produced wind turbine components and subcomponents and that imports of wind turbine components and subcomponents have increased over the last decade, while domestic manufacturing capacity for certain products, such as blades, has not meaningfully increased. 9. In light of these findings and the other findings in the Secretary’s report, the Secretary recommended a range of actions to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security. 10. Moreover, in Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting Imports of Steel Into the United States), and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Copper Into the United States), I found that aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States and took action under section 232 to address the national security threats found in those proclamations. Certain wind turbine components and subcomponents are made of significant amounts of aluminum, steel, or copper and contribute to the national security threat found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. Accordingly, certain wind turbine components and subcomponents are subject to the tariffs imposed in Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; or Proclamation 10962, as amended, to address the national security threats found in those proclamations. 11. After considering the Secretary’s report, the factors in section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), and other relevant factors and information, I concur with the Secretary’s finding that wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States. 12. In my judgment, and in light of the Secretary’s report, the factors in section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), and other relevant factors and information, I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to enter into negotiations with foreign trading partners to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents to address the national security threat found in this proclamation. 13. I therefore direct the Secretary and the United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) to jointly pursue negotiation of agreements or continue any current negotiations of agreements to address the threatened impairment of the national security with respect to imported wind turbines and their components and subcomponents, with any foreign trading partner the Secretary and the Trade Representative deem appropriate, and to update me on the progress of such negotiations within 180 days of the date of this proclamation. Under current circumstances, this plan of action is necessary and appropriate to address the threatened impairment of the national security found in this proclamation. Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future. 14. Section 232 authorizes the President to take action to adjust the imports of an article and its derivatives that are being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States. Section 232 includes the authority to adopt and carry out a plan of action, with adjustments over time, to address the national security threat. That initial plan of action may include negotiations of agreements along with other actions to adjust imports to address the national security threat, including tariffs. Moreover, if action under section 232 includes the negotiation of an agreement, such as one contemplated in section 232(c)(3)(A)(i) (19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A)(i)), the President may also take other actions he deems necessary to adjust imports so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States, including if such an agreement is not entered into within 180 days of the date of this proclamation or is not being carried out or is ineffective. See 19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A). 15. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of duty or other import restriction. NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, including section 232; section 604; and section 301 of title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as follows: (1) The Secretary and the Trade Representative, and any senior executive branch official they deem appropriate, shall jointly pursue or continue pursuing negotiations of agreements to address the national security threat found in this proclamation. (2) The Secretary and the Trade Representative, in consultation with any other senior executive branch officials they deem appropriate, shall, from time to time, update me on the status or outcome of the negotiations described in this proclamation. The Secretary and the Trade Representative shall provide at least one of these updates within 180 days of the date of this proclamation. (3) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents. The Secretary also shall, from time to time, in consultation with any senior executive branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, review the status of such imports with respect to the national security. The Secretary shall inform me of any circumstances that, in the Secretary’s opinion, might indicate the need for further action by the President under section 232. (4) Nothing in this proclamation modifies the tariffs imposed pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and Proclamation 10962, as amended, or any other tariffs imposed pursuant to section 232. (5) Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency. If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any provision of this proclamation to any individual or circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its provisions to any other individual or circumstance shall not be affected. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twenty-second day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first. DONALD J. TRUMP The post Adjusting Imports of Wind Turbines and Their Parts and Components into the United States appeared first on The White House .

title: Winklevoss PAC moves into Texas Senate race with $81K ad buy
body:
While crypto-aligned PACs have stepped up spending in Ohio, a committee launched by the co-founders of crypto exchange Gemini made one of its first forays into the Lone Star State.
Digital Freedom Fund, the Super political action committee (PAC) launched by Gemini co-founders Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss in 2025, announced additional expenditures for US Senate races in the 2026 midterm elections, attempting to influence voters in Texas, Iowa and Ohio.
In a Tuesday filing with the US Federal Election Commission (FEC), the Digital Freedom Fund reported its first spending on ads to support Republican candidate Ken Paxton for one of Texas’ Senate seats. According to the PAC, it had spent more than $81,000 on direct mail media to support Paxton and oppose Democratic candidate James Talarico, with early voting having already begun in the state.
The Winklevoss-backed Super PAC, which reported raising about $34 million as of Sept. 30, did not limit its spending to Texas, reporting involvement in other key midterm election races using ads. Digital Freedom Fund disclosed additional expenditures in Ohio’s Senate race between Republican Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown, bringing the PAC’s total support for Husted to about $7 million.
The expenditures into candidates that could support crypto policies and laws come as event contracts on prediction market platforms Kalshi and Polymarket heavily favored Democrats retaking majority control of the House of Representatives and Senate in 2027. Whichever party holds a majority in each chamber would have a significant impact on passing legislation like the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, a market structure bill that failed to pass a procedural vote in the Senate last month.
Related: PACs laud Texas primary wins, look to back more pro-crypto candidates
Paxton already benefitted from $500,000 in supportive ads ahead of the May Republican primary, in which he defeated incumbent Senator John Cornyn. The ads, funded by the Anchorage Digital- and Cantor Fitzgerald-backed Fellowship PAC, went through the Nxum Group, a marketing company co-founded by Bo Hines, a former crypto adviser to US President Donald Trump who became CEO of Tether US after leaving the White House.
According to an October Wall Street Journal report, Nxum profited from Hines’ role in government, as he helped push a stablecoin bill while keeping a stake in the company. Nxum reportedly received $6.3 million as part of a deal with stablecoin issuer Tether, the first payment of which went through while Hines was still at the White House.
Early voting began in Texas on Oct. 19, with Election Day coming up on Nov. 3. Cointelegraph reached out to the Talarico and Paxton campaign teams for comment but did not receive an immediate response.
Fairshake, a separate PAC aligned with the interests of the crypto industry and largely funded by Ripple Labs, Coinbase and Andreessen Horowitz, reported more than $13 million combined in spending on a direct mail campaign to support what it considered to be “pro-crypto” candidates this week. The PAC’s latest FEC filing showed more than $4 million to oppose Independent candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska’s Senate race and an additional $9 million to support Husted over Brown.
While the battle for Ohio’s Senate between Brown and Husted has seen significant spending by PACs — Fairshake had invested about $56 million as of Wednesday and Digital Freedom Fund reported $7 million in total media purchases — Texas races have also spawned interest from Republican donors looking to prevent the state potentially losing Senate and gubernatorial seats to Democrats for the first time in more than 30 years.
FEC filings showed that Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and founder of SpaceX, had poured more than $150 million into the Senate Leadership Fund. The PAC, supporting Republican Senate candidates, sent the same amount Musk donated to the Texas PAC, which has supported Paxton through ads.

title: Zelenskyy names three postwar security guarantees for Ukraine. Even Russia needs one of them, he says
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); The hardest part of ending Russia's war is making sure it cannot start it again. As the peace talks have escalated ahead of the US elections, Ukraine is weighing three options for its postwar security. Among them are NATO membership, direct US guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5, and a European “Coalition of the Willing” backed by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says , according to UNIAN. But none of them have been agreed to yet. Zelenskyy describes the guarantees as a single package, with each layer still under discussion with partners. All of it, he says, rests on a strong Ukrainian army, in both numbers and quality. Three guarantees, none of them signed Everyone counts on NATO, Zelenskyy says, but Kyiv is also negotiating direct guarantees from the US, including an Article 5-style collective-defense clause, alongside the European Coalition of the Willing that would act together with Washington. The arithmetic, he said, is already done. “Our colleagues in Europe and America know this. We have already calculated everything: both the financing and the corresponding number of our soldiers, so that our state can be at peace,” he states. Why Zelenskyy says even Russia should want Ukraine in NATO He went further, arguing that NATO membership would serve not only Ukraine and the Alliance but also Russia. “I think, honestly, the Russians need our accession to NATO too, because for them that is more security than Ukraine outside NATO,” he claims. The talks come as Washington pushes toward negotiations. Zelenskyy says he expects signals from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio within a day or two, as well as a call with envoy Steve Witkoff. He adds that Jared Kushner, on his way to Kyiv in November, told him Russia supports a trilateral meeting of the US, Ukraine, and Russia, at the level of technical teams. title: US Army seeks manufacturers for 155mm howitzer barrels amid boost in demand
body: The U.S. Army is looking for new manufacturers to build barrels for 155mm howitzers amid concerns at the Pentagon that the government’s only plant for manufacturing them can’t keep up with the increased demand for artillery. The Army wants contractors that can manufacture up to 10 barrels per month within three years, according to the Sources Sought notice . The deadline is Nov. 23. Companies were asked to provide details of their ability — or their subcontractor’s capacity — to make barrels, including whether they could add “chrome bore coatings on a steel tube up to 30 [feet] long and up to 7,500 pounds in weight,” the notice said. They should also provide the maximum length and weight of tube that they could coat. Also desired are details on a company’s boring, milling and rifling capabilities, as well as details on raw materials, such as “steel preform production, forging, guide bore, and heat treatment.” The notice asks contractors to estimate their capacity to manufacture 155mm barrels within 18 months, and up to 10 barrels per month within 36 months. Companies should also offer a cost estimate for an “initial production quantity of 40 cannon tubes (broken down by caliber or indicating pricing for a combined/flexible mix),” the Army said. Currently, the Army makes large-caliber barrels for howitzers and tanks only at the aging Watervliet Arsenal in New York. While America and Europe have been focused on expanding production of howitzer ammunition to meet demand in the Ukraine war and replenish domestic stockpiles, another problem is a lack of manufacturing capacity to replace worn-out cannon barrels. A 2024 Pentagon budget document stated that Ukraine’s heavy use of M777 howitzers created a demand for more than 30 M776 tubes per month, according to The War Zone . The document admitted that Watervliet could not keep up with demand, and asked for emergency funding to be transferred to enable a second manufacturer of barrels. The new notice doesn’t mention how many additional barrel manufacturers are needed. However, the Army is exploring whether to replace the M777 with a weapon based on Korea’s popular K9 howitzer.

title: Moderna shares plunge after leak of cancer vaccine data despite positive results
body:
Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck .
Shares of both drugmakers fell even though the data, released in full later Thursday following the leak, appeared meaningful for patients and positive relative to Wall Street expectations.
The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.
The data also showed that the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy.
The companies said about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years after receiving the shot, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is a huge development for our patients," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, about the results.
He said that the added benefit of the vaccine also comes with much milder toxicity, or side effects like injection-site pain, compared to other cancer treatments.
The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend.
"Whenever you put a therapy on top of something that works really well, like Keytruda, sometimes it's harder to show additional benefit. We have no problems of showing additional benefit here," Dr. Dean Li, Merck Research Laboratories president, said in an interview ahead of the results.
The benefit appeared even larger after the six-month vaccine regimen, with a separate analysis showing a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death. The companies say it is still too early to determine whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall.
Several analysts acknowledged investors' elevated expectations ahead of the release, but noted that the data is overall positive.
"We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Thursday following the leak. "Such a [stock] reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."
Oncologists and investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used to treat other forms of cancer in the future. Merck and Moderna are studying the vaccine in several trials across other tumors, such as non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
But Li acknowledged the companies have more work to show the product can be effective across tumor types.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Li said. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
For now, the vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators to get the drug fully approved next year.
"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.
The shot is designed to target the specific mutations in each patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Keytruda, which helps the body attack the cancer more effectively.
It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.
In a research note Thursday, UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data.
Against the backdrop of those high expectations, Moderna shares have spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon.
Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.
Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

title: Brent crude tops $113, highest level since May, after Trump hints at action on Iran
body:
Oil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.
The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, unnamed U.S. officials told The New York Times . Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, the officials said.
President Donald Trump subsequently said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran when asked by a reporter late Wednesday. Trump said "something one way or the other" will "happen fairly soon" on Iran without elaborating.
"Most people seem to think it's after the election," Trump said. "We're going to see what happens."
The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, dismissing reports that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.
Pigott pointed to escalating attacks by Iran-allied Houthis on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as the reason for the order. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saudi Arabia's east coast Wednesday, according to Saudi state media .
Meanwhile, oil giant Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely, people familiar with the matter told Reuters Thursday. Aramco facilities have repeatedly come under attack by the Houthis.
The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.
He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.
"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

title: Trump says US gave Russia nothing to free American, but reality is more complicated
body:
In a push to close deals, Trump has pivoted toward Putin.
President Donald Trump claims that the U.S. "gave nothing in exchange" for Moscow's release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard , but his administration has made several moves seen as highly advantageous to Russia in recent weeks -- drawing backlash from members of his own party and fueling a dynamic some hostage advocates and officials fear could set a dangerous precedent.
The State Department determined in January 2025 that Hubbard, a retired teacher who was captured by Russian forces in Ukraine and accused of acting as a mercenary for the country, was wrongfully detained, declaring that the allegations against him were fabricated.
Still, when Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced he would release Hubbard at the top of a meeting on Wednesday with Trump’s Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, Witkoff responded by publicly praising him for freeing the American the U.S. government says he jailed on false charges -- calling Putin a “humanitarian."
After Hubbard was freed, Trump indicated he had taken a softer approach toward the Kremlin in order to secure the release -- saying his controversial decision to waive some new Russia-related sanctions that were set to take effect this week was made in part because he thought imposing them would derail the negotiations.
After Hubbard was freed, Trump indicated his surprise and controversial decision to waive some new Russia-related sanctions that were set to take effect this week was made in part because he thought imposing them would derail the negotiations.
"I was in the midst of getting Stephen out of Russia. And if we did what these foolish people wanted me to do, he wouldn't be coming out right now. He'd be in there for another 20 years,” Trump said during a roundtable event at the White House on Wednesday. "So, the last thing I was going to do is break up that."
The president extolled the agreement, asserting Hubbard's return hadn't come at a price.
"The past administration gave massive amounts of money and other things. You can't do that. And when you do that, the problem is, is greatly exacerbated,” he said.
In September 2023, the Biden administration facilitated the release of $6 billion in frozen Iranian assets in exchange for the release of five Americans detained by Tehran.
The money was moved into a restricted account in Qatar intended to ensure that Iran could only spend the funds on humanitarian goods. But the U.S. froze the assets again after the Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel before any of the money was spent.
Kurt Volker, former U.S. ambassador to NATO and U.S. special representative for Ukraine negotiations during Trump’s first term, said the circumstances surrounding Hubbard's release on Wednesday perpetuates a pattern -- encouraging Moscow to take more Americans captive in order to gain political leverage over Washington.
"Russia has been playing this game for years, and of course they will take more hostages. Sanctions relief is just another sort of payoff, like getting intelligence officers or Viktor Bout released," Volker said, referring to the convicted arms dealer the Biden administration exchanged for WNBA player Brittney Griner in 2022.
Some critics of the president’s decision to waive the majority of sanctions and tariffs included in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , which was passed by Congress with broad bipartisan support and signed into law by Trump last month, said the decision provided Moscow with a significant financial lifeline. Analysts project that the sanctions outlined by the law could cost Russia billions in energy revenue if fully implemented.
The provisions included in the legislation named for the late senator aimed to weaken Russia's ability to fund its war against Ukraine by cutting billions from its export revenue.
Following Hubbard’s released, Trump claimed that some opponents of his decision to push off the penalties for at least 60 days had called him to apologize.
But even some Republicans appear to still be harboring misgivings about the administration’s approach to Putin.
"Vladimir Putin is not our friend," Republican Sen. Jodi Ernst posted to X on Wednesday. "His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life. Appeasement won't end this war. Pressure will."
Earlier this month, the Trump administration also eased some preexisting sanctions to facilitate a deal to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets, issuing a license authorizing transactions related to its sale and delivery through April 2027.
A bipartisan group of senators protested the agreement, writing in a letter to the president that the revenue the Kremlin receives will "undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition" against Ukraine.
Volker said Trump could be using Hubbard's release to help strengthen his case for granting sanctions relief to Russia, something the president insists will bring down costs for Americans.
"Trump wanted to do all that anyway -- to claim he is doing something about high diesel prices in the U.S.,” he said. "The release of Hubbard now gives him the opportunity to say this was for a higher cause."
Trump's wavering support for Kyiv has also been described by many as a gift to Putin. The president has significantly ramped up pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian energy targets and reach a broader truce with Moscow, declaring Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should have made a deal "a long time ago."
As Trump has grown more vocal in his dissatisfaction with Kyiv, Ukrainian officials say the country's military has been grappling with speed restrictions on Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite network.
According to the Institute for the Study of War, these restrictions have "significantly degraded Ukraine's intermediate-range strike campaign targeting primarily Russian logistics across the frontline."
SpaceX founder Elon Musk has suggested that Trump is the only one who could have authorized the slowdown, while the president and members of the administration have denied issuing directives related to Starshield and maintain the company has the authority to enforce its own terms of service.
"I don’t believe that Elon Musk would do this without at least the acquiescence of the White House," Republican Sen. John Cornyn said. "I think it's frankly shameful. I think we should be supporting the victim, not the aggressor."

title: Kyiv denies reports that Trump, Musk have restored Starlink speeds in Ukraine
body:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional comments from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine's military Starlink service is still operating at a speed cap of 161 kilometers per hour, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 22.
The official's statement contradicts claims quoted by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), which reported on Oct. 22 that Starlink functionality was back to normal in Ukraine following a phone call between SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump called Musk on Oct. 21 to request he lift restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield service, the military application of the Starlink program, according to the WSJ. Following the call, sources reportedly told the outlet that Starlink was functioning more normally — though some Ukrainian officials said it wasn't fully restored.
But when asked about these claims, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent they were "all false."
"Overall, nothing has changed anywhere," the official said. The 161 kph speed cap remains in place, severely limiting key military operations, including mid-range strikes and high-speed drone interceptions.
Trump was evasive about whether or not he called Musk, but also claimed that Starlink was back up and running as usual in Ukraine in comments to reporters.
"Yeah, I don't want to comment on it, whether I called, or whether somebody else called, it doesn't make a difference," Trump told a journalist when questioned about the WSJ story.
Ukraine has been trying to sort out the reasons behind the restriction — and restore service to its previous speed level — ever since Starlink was disrupted without warning on Oct. 14. While fingers have been pointed at SpaceX, the White House , and a Trump-Musk alliance, no one has claimed responsibility for the move.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Trump had a hand in the change, saying on Oct. 18 that "no one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed."
Zelensky spoke with Rubio again on Oct. 20, as Starlink disruptions persisted. Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 22 that he was waiting for a response from Rubio as to whether Starlink communications could be restored to speeds of up to 400 kph.
Rubio promised to get back with him within 48 hours, Zelensky said, but definitive answers may take longer.
"Maybe something will become clear by morning," the official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said.
"For now, the main interesting aspect of this is that there are absolutely no explanations for what's happening. Even though this is a top-priority system."
CORRECTION: A previous version of this story said it was reported that Musk called Trump to discuss Starlink. The WSJ reported that Trump phoned Musk. The error has been corrected.

title: Pentagon Launches 120-Day “Sprint” to Field Counter-UAS Armed USVs
body: The Pentagon and DIU launched a 120-day sprint to acquire and field new counter-UAS armed USVs to defend surface fleets against low-cost drone threats. The Pentagon and Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) is searching for new uncrewed vessels capable of engaging a broad number of low-cost adversary aerial and maritime weapon systems that the unit says should be ready for operational fielding in the next four months, according to a new search announced Oct. 19. The search, launched in partnership with the Pentagon’s Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS), opens the door for rapid acquisition and fielding of new counter-air and counter-surface unmanned surface vessels (USVs) in the next 120 days for further forward deployment to combat theaters. “The cost-exchange ratio for detecting and neutralizing asymmetric maritime and airborne threats in contested environments is heavily skewed in favor of the adversary,” the DIU says in its solicitation. “Low-cost, low-signature threats—including explosive Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs), Group 1–3 Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), attack helicopters, go-fast vessels, and low-flying aerial vectors—directly threaten surface-fleet operations.” The solicitation seeks production-ready USVs capable of integrating existing counter-air weapons, including the AGM-114L Longbow Hellfire, AGM-179 Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM), Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) and Stinger missiles, to interdict those threats. The vessels would be tasked with detecting, tracking and engaging low-flying aerial threats, including Group 1-3 drones and helicopters, at ranges exceeding three nautical miles. The Pentagon is also interested in systems capable of engaging larger Group 5 aircraft, considering that capability as highly valuable for potential submissions. Naval News previously covered the wide array of options for Hellfire, JAGM, and APKWS counter-drone initiatives at Sea Air Space 2026. Several USVs on display at the show featured Hellfire, APKWS, and JAGM launchers for counter-UAS and anti-ship operations. Under the solicitation, proposed vessels must have a minimum operational range of 200 nautical miles and sustain a cruising speed of at least 10 knots. The systems must also support autonomous navigation, station-keeping and collision avoidance, while integrating onboard sensors capable of providing 360-degree detection and tracking of aerial and surface threats. Weapons employment would remain under human supervision, with the vessels expected to operate in environments where communications and satellite navigation are degraded or denied. Overall, the new drones are expected to add another layer of loss-tolerant uncrewed ships capable of interdicting hostile airborne systems traveling toward their targets. During potential operations, the vessels could be rearmed and redeployed with minimal logistical support, with the solicitation stating that “rapid field rearming executable by a two-person crew with minimal support equipment in pier-side, austere, or shipboard environments is highly desired.” The effort is part of a broader, three-phase, 12-month prize challenge offering up to $100 million in awards, including up to $40 million for the second phase focused on counter-air capabilities. A number of U.S. firms have tested solutions to the DIU’s solicitation, including Saildrone which recently conducted a missile test using JAGM anti-air and anti-surface missiles at the U.S.-led Rim of the Pacific 2026 exercise off the coast of Hawaii. Saildrones have previously deployed to the Pacific and Middle East supporting intelligence collection. BlackSea Technologies has also demonstrated a number of capabilities that can fulfill the solicitation’s request using its Comet USV. L3Harris has also proven a number of integration opportunities with its VAMPIRE counter-UAS system that can be rapidly fitted to USVs to engage airborne and surface targets. Beyond U.S. manufacturers, Naval News recently reported that French firm Exail will supply a DriX H-9 USV to the Office of Naval Research (ONR) to serve as a testbed for an unspecified counter-drone system. An L3Harris VAMPIRE system showing the WESCAM MX-10 RSTA electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensor ball (left) alongside the 4-cell launcher loaded with laser-guided rockets (right). L3Harris photo. Companies will be required to demonstrate their integrated systems within 30 days of selection, with subsequent operational testing planned at Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek in Virginia in early 2027. The Pentagon has also budgeted an additional $200 million for potential follow-on prototyping and production agreements. Iran’s Shahed drone family has been proven extremely difficult to counter with existing counter-UAS capabilities aboard U.S. Navy guided missile destroyers. The USS Carl M. Levin (DDG 120), attached to the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group currently underway for a Middle East deployment to relieve the USS George Washington, has already been upgraded with counter-UAS capabilities, including a new Coyote missile launcher identified by Naval News in April . DDG 120 is currently operating in the Arabian Sea supporting the Pentagon’s blockade of Iran, and the Roosevelt is expected to transit to the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of operations to reinforce the destroyer after Exercise Keen Sword, underway in Japan, concludes in late October. The post Pentagon Launches 120-Day “Sprint” to Field Counter-UAS Armed USVs appeared first on Naval News .

title: Republican politicians have embraced anti-Indian racism — and it’s costing them votes
body:
Two years ago, University of Houston student Vasant Bhatt was doing everything he could to help Republicans regain power. He knocked doors for Sen. Ted Cruz’s reelection campaign and helped organize his community for Donald Trump, two victories he, like many other Republicans, celebrated in 2024. But this week, Bhatt did something unexpected: He voted for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, and he publicly urged others to do the same.
Bhatt, whose father is a small-business owner, tells The Verge he was initially drawn to the Republican Party due to its economic principles. “The strong belief in individual liberty and limited government,” he says, led him to identify as a conservative. More recently, however, another aspect of his family’s experience has driven him away from the party. As an Indian American, Bhatt feels increasingly unwelcome in a party where racist rhetoric is becoming far too common.
[Media: https://twitter.com/vasantbhatt14/status/2112227425761300827]
“There’s isolated individuals, but I think there’s an ecosystem as well,” Bhatt says. He has gotten used to people telling him to go back to India, but recently, he’s noticed anti-Indian racism increasing in both frequency and intensity. He wasn’t surprised when prominent conservative commentators replied to his post implying he’s not a real American. The X account for the Waco Young Republicans accused him of voting “entirely based on his loyalty to a foreign people over Americans.”
Indian Americans are reliable voters, with about 70 percent of the voting-eligible population showing up to the polls in presidential election years. And there were signs that the electorate was moving to the right, albeit only slightly: The percentage of Indian American voters who lean Democrat dropped from 59 percent in 2020 to 55 percent four years later. About one-third of Indian Americans supported Trump in 2024 — by no means a majority, but still a sign their votes were up for grabs. Since then, however, they’ve become a favored target for racist self-proclaimed “heritage Americans.” Both fringe and mainstream conservatives have portrayed Indian Americans as stealing high-paying tech jobs from white workers and undermining American unity. Conservative commentator Chris Rufo — who rose to prominence by agitating against diversity efforts in public schools — even posted a video dissecting the so-called “Indian Question” in which he concluded that it’s “natural” for people to want to stick to their own kind. The right’s embrace of anti-Indian racism is now threatening to reverse Republicans’ recent gains with Indian American voters while promoting immigration restrictions that could shape the country for years to come.
Bhatt began to notice the shift shortly after Trump’s 2024 victory but says it has become especially intense in the run-up to the midterm elections. In September, Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, posted a picture of hundreds of University of Texas fans celebrating a football victory. “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” French wrote, referring to the fact that many students in the foreground appeared to be of South Asian descent. Some Texas Republicans condemned French’s racism, but French stood by his comments, and others have defended him.
“Watching people like Jack Posobiec rationalize, excuse, minimize, and even prop up this rhetoric by defending folks like Bo French, I’m not really surprised,” says Bhatt.
[Media: https://twitter.com/bofrench/status/2099118916282810552]
A few weeks after French’s comments, Vice President JD Vance used his announcement that the Trump administration would be reducing some tech companies’ ability to hire foreign employees as an opportunity to call workers on H-1B visas “foreign indentured servants.” India’s Ministry of External Affairs called Vance’s comments “deeply offensive.”
Anti-Indian rhetoric has also translated into policy change. The Washington Post notes that Republican politicians became more willing to engage in attacks on legal immigrants — including Indian Americans — after Trump’s immigration crackdown led to a drastic decrease in unauthorized border crossings. Now that Trump appears to have “solved” the problem of illegal immigration by shutting down asylum at the border, and has unleashed ICE on immigrants living in the country, nativists have found a new target in H-1B workers, many of whom are Indian immigrants.
Since returning to office, Trump has raised the price of H-1B visas to upwards of $100,000 and waged a silent war on legal immigration, not only slashing the number of people who could legally come to the US but also sending naturalization rates plummeting. Spokespeople for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security now promote the idea of “remigration,” or forcibly returning immigrants to their countries of origin regardless of their legal status. The White House has even celebrated the fact that legal immigration has fallen since Trump’s return to office. These policies are animated by a belief, prevalent among a faction of Republicans led by White House adviser Stephen Miller, that the problem with immigration isn’t whether people come to America legally, but what types of people come here. A growing chorus of “heritage Americans” see all non-white immigrants as incapable of assimilating to American culture, and they’ve selected Indians as their primary target.
“I spent years within conservative politics, and I realized that my convictions don’t mean anything if I’m not going to be regarded as an American, or if I’m going to be regarded as a second-class citizen,” says Bhatt.
Signs of the Republican Party’s anti-Indian turn have been percolating for years. Shortly after Trump selected Vance as his running mate, far-right streamer Nick Fuentes declared a “groyper war” on the Trump-Vance campaign. Fuentes, who is Mexican American, claimed that Vance’s marriage to an Indian American woman meant he “doesn’t value his racial identity.” In response, Vance denounced Fuentes, calling him a “white supremacist” — but that was all before the election.
Trump’s 2024 inroads among voters of color, including Indian Americans, shocked pundits who expected that his nativist rhetoric and policies would drive Black, Latino, and Asian voters toward the Democratic Party. Former White House adviser Steve Bannon even claimed MAGA had become a multiracial, working-class coalition — and he wasn’t entirely wrong. But in late 2024, as the GOP should have been taking a victory lap, two factions of the MAGA movement clashed over H-1B visas.
The debate scrambled political alliances, with Elon Musk — a promoter of the racist “great replacement” conspiracy theory — arguing that foreign-born workers are essential to American innovation. Though Musk is an immigrant himself, his comments received far less vitriol than those made by former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who said H-1Bs are needed in part because American culture “has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long.” Critics pointed to Ramaswamy’s comments as proof that Indian Americans — even those who, like him, were born in the United States — are incapable of assimilating. On X, Ramaswamy’s opponents said that his comments were indicative of “thinly veiled ethnic resentment” and doubled down on their claims that the primary function of H-1B visas is to replace American workers.
Despite Musk’s position on visas, it should come as no surprise that X has helped push anti-Indian rhetoric from the fringes to the forefront of conservative politics. Conversations that wouldn’t seem out of place on 4chan or The Daily Stormer are now happening on a mainstream social media site with millions of users.
“It really started after Elon’s takeover of Twitter, and it went into full overdrive mode after the ’24 election, in November, when Vivek joined DOGE,” says Anang Mittal, a longtime conservative strategist who previously worked for Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY). “That was the beginning of, ‘Okay, it’s open season on out-and-out racism.’”
Mittal suspects that Republican politicians feel like they can entertain anti-Indian racism without losing much support among voters, in part because Indian Americans are such a small slice of the population. An estimated 5.2 million Indian Americans live in the United States, constituting just over 1.5 percent of the total US population. “They decided there’s no price to be paid when it comes to engaging in language that treats Indian immigrants as outsiders and not compatible with American culture,” says Mittal.
Republicans’ increasingly explicit anti-Indian sentiment may help cost them in the midterms. A February survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that seven in 10 Indian Americans disapprove of Trump’s second-term performance — but it also shows that Democrats have lost support among Indian Americans since 2020, and just 46 percent identify as Democrats today.
These remarks have had real-world consequences far beyond the realm of electoral politics: Last week, authorities arrested a 19-year-old man who allegedly attempted a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. Law enforcement reportedly seized weapons, ammunition, Nazi paraphernalia, and a gas canister with an anti-South Asian slur written on it, as well as a manifesto in which the alleged shooter fantasized about killing non-white people.
The alleged shooter’s manifesto echoed “a lot of the narratives that you see online,” says Bhatt.
“When you spend months watching people make generalizations about your community, and question your loyalties, and somehow make the presumption that our presence in America is undesirable, you are painting a target on people’s back.”

title: Russia Strikes Crowded Market in Lozova, Killing 2, Wounding 36
body:
Russian forces struck the Central Market in Lozova, in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, with a Shahed drone and a Banderol missile on Thursday, Oct. 22, killing two women and wounding 36 other people.
Head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov earlier identified the two women killed as aged 50 and 60.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
In his latest update , he said the number of people affected by the strike had risen to 36, with two of those treated only for acute stress reactions. The injuries of the other 34 people range in severity, although all received necessary medical care. Some were hospitalized in serious condition and understood to be fighting for their lives, Lozova Mayor Serhii Zelenskyi said .
“This was a deliberate, targeted strike on civilians” Zelensky said, noting that the market had been struck during the middle of the , around lunch time, while it was crowded.
“The occupiers aimed specifically at civilians to cause as many casualties as possible. At an ordinary market, where everything is in plain sight, there never were and never could be any military targets,” he continued.
The strike caused extensive damage to market pavilions, private houses, apartment buildings, nearby shopping centers, a church and private vehicles.
Local authorities are still assessing the full damage, they said.
Emergency and municipal services switched to mass-casualty response mode, Zelenskyi previously said, warning that the threat of repeated strikes remained and urged residents to head to shelters immediately whenever an air raid alert sounded.
The number of casualties climbed steadily after the attack. Syniehubov initially reported 17 injured shortly after the strike, a figure Zelenskyi also gave in his preliminary update.
Around the same time on Thursday, Russian forces struck a private house in the Zhytomyr community with a jet-powered Shahed drone, leaving eight people wounded, including two children.
In Sloviansk, regional authorities have extended mandatory evacuation of families with children to the entire community after Russian forces struck the settlements of the Donetsk region 42 times on Wednesday, Oct. 21, injuring two boys aged seven and 12.
The attack on the community came around the same time Russian forces used an FPV drone to strike an armored evacuation vehicle of the Proliska Humanitarian Mission near Kramatorsk, also located in the Donetsk region.
Although strikes on civilians, civilian sites and organizations are strictly prohibited under international humanitarian law, Russian forces completely destroyed the vehicle in what marked the 120th time that the humanitarian organization has been attacked since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
During the same week, on Monday, Oct. 19, Russia struck a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv region with a drone, killing six people, including two children.
The youngest victim , a little girl just over a year old, was killed while sitting in her stroller.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

As the US gets closer to permanently adopting daylight saving time following the House advancing the Sunshine Protection Act in July , there could be some unforeseen consequences to getting an extra hour of sun in the evening all year long. Following the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Manitoba permanently switching to daylight saving this year, Google has shared some suggested fixes if Android devices are showing the incorrect time when clocks aren’t turned back an hour there on November 1st.
In an announcement shared to the Android community help forums , Google suggests a simple fix for Canadians experiencing issues as a result of recent time zone changes. “If you are in Canada and your device is showing an incorrect time due to the new time zone laws beginning Nov 1, please apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device.”
If your device is still displaying an incorrect time or time zone, Google suggests enabling location-based time zone detection by searching the “Date and Time” in Android’s settings and enabling both the “Automatic time zone” and “Use location for time zone” options. If all else fails, Google also suggests disabling “Automatic time zone” detection in the Android settings and manually selecting a time zone that matches the correct time offset for your region.
While daylight saving time rules vary from province to province in Canada (and even within smaller regions) making it occasionally difficult for devices to stay on top of changes in a timely manner, it will potentially be less of an issue in the US if the entire country decides to adopt permanent daylight saving time all at once.
