title: SpaceX and Tesla have high election stakes as Elon Musk pours $366 million into campaigns
body:
Elon Musk's business empire is tying itself ever closer to the federal government just as he spends record sums to help decide who controls it in the 2026 midterm election .
SpaceX has racked up at least $6.78 billion in federal work so far through Oct. 1 this year, according to FedScout, a research firm that tracks government spending and contracts, nearly twice its total for all of 2024. Tesla , SpaceX, including Musk's artificial intelligence business, also face high-stakes government decisions over defense spending, launch licenses, spectrum, autonomous vehicles, electricity and data centers.
At the same time, Musk has committed roughly $366 million to the 2026 election cycle across at least 40 races, making the world's richest person the midterms' biggest individual donor so far.
At least $276 million of that money has flowed to Republican groups and Musk's own political operation, America PAC, since July, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings, as Republican candidates have faced attacks on the cost of living and the war in Iran .
For Musk, Republican victories could help preserve his influence and a favorable political environment for his companies. Democratic control of either chamber could instead bring subpoenas and investigations into his businesses, federal contracts and his work leading President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency .
Democrats are favored to win control of the House, while the battle for the Senate remains a toss-up.
"With all that spending, [Musk] wants favors in Congress and from the administration and influence on regulatory contracts as well as being shielded from oversight," said Bruce Freed , president and co-founder of the nonpartisan Center for Political Accountability and a former chief investigator for the Senate banking committee.
Musk did not respond to CNBC's request for a comment on this story. However, he lashed out at the possibility of Democrat-led investigations in a Wednesday post on X, which he owns, saying: "Live by the sword, die by the sword."
"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets," he wrote.
Nowhere is the overlap between Musk's business interests and political spending clearer than in his home state of Texas .
Tesla is headquartered in Austin, where it operates its largest U.S. vehicle factory. SpaceX operates a launch facility at its company town, Starbase, in South Texas. Musk's tunneling venture, The Boring Co., is based in Pflugerville.
That gives Texas officials sway over taxes, electricity, permitting, infrastructure and economic-development incentives that can carry enormous consequences for Musk's companies.
At least $189.6 million of his political money is targeted to help elect Republican Ken Paxton through various avenues, prompting his Democratic opponent, James Talarico , to accuse Musk of trying to "buy this Senate seat in Texas."
Musk went after Talarico on Wednesday, saying on X that "There is something deeply wrong" with the Democrat.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator," Talarico responded .
Musk is spending at the state level, too. According to the nonpartisan Transparency USA, which tracks money in state politics, Musk and his trust have given at least $6 million this cycle to state candidates and political groups, including Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows.
The Musk-Abbott connection also extends to personnel: Tesla policy chief Karen Steakley previously served as Abbott's deputy director for legislative affairs.
Tesla and SpaceX are also planning to build a sprawling AI chip factory with Intel outside of Austin in Grimes County, Texas, where longtime Musk lawyer and America PAC attorney Chris Gober is running for Congress.
For SpaceX, the federal government is one of its most important customers .
Since 2008, the company has received more than $30.7 billion in federal work, according to FedScout. The figure excludes classified contracts and some state-funded spending on services such as Starlink terminals and satellite internet service, which states have used during disaster recovery.
That federal business has accelerated during Trump's second administration, FedScout found. SpaceX has racked up $6.78 billion in 2026 so far, compared with $3.97 billion in 2025 and $3.8 billion for all of 2024.
In late May alone, the Space Force awarded SpaceX $2.29 billion for a military communications network tied to the "Golden Dome" missile shield and, three days later, another $4.16 billion for threat-detection satellites.
Congress does not award those contracts, but it funds and oversees the agencies that do, including the Defense Department and NASA, each a major SpaceX customer.
"Keeping allies in committee powers in Washington helps [Musk] wield power in the halls of Congress better," said Hilary Braseth , executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan research group that tracks money in politics.
Musk's America PAC is backing Sen. Susan Collins , R-Maine, who is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which helps write funding bills for NASA and the Pentagon.
Collins' Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson , has accused Musk of trying to "buy a government that serves his interests."
Musk has already learned how quickly that kind of political influence can evaporate.
After spending nearly $300 million to help elect Trump and congressional Republicans in 2024, Musk gained extraordinary access to the administration. He led DOGE's push to slash the federal workforce and pressed for deregulation on several fronts.
Then the relationship blew up. A June 2025 feud over Trump's tax-and-spending bill escalated into threats from the president to cut government support and contracts for Musk's companies.
Now Musk is back in Trump's orbit. In recent weeks, he has attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping , sat beside the president at his AI summit and received the National Medal of Science . On Sept. 30, the DOD appointed Musk to co-lead Project Meridian , advising the Pentagon on future warfare.
Musk’s political spending extends well beyond the states where his business empire is concentrated.
Across six other battleground states, America PAC had spent about $22.7 million on general election expenditures through Oct. 20, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings, including roughly $8.9 million in Ohio, $7.2 million in Michigan and $2 million in Maine.
In Michigan, America PAC is paying for digital ads, mailers, printing and postage, and text and phone outreach supporting Republican Mike Rogers and attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed , according to FEC filings.
Rogers backs a one-year moratorium on new data centers; El-Sayed wants to pause advanced AI development and new data centers until tougher federal safeguards are in place.
In Ohio, America PAC is funding ads, text and phone outreach among other measures helping Republican Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown , according to FEC filings. Husted wants large data centers to shoulder more grid costs; Brown has attacked industry tax breaks and pledged to make data centers pay their full electricity costs.
Those debates matter more as Musk pushes deeper into AI.
SpaceX's AI division, formerly known as xAI, was awarded a Pentagon contract last July with a $200 million ceiling, while a General Services Administration agreement makes the company's Grok chatbot available across federal agencies through March 2027.
Musk's companies also depend on a web of federal regulators whose decisions can directly affect their ability to expand.
The Federal Aviation Administration licenses SpaceX launches, while the Federal Communications Commission controls satellite licenses and spectrum used by Starlink. Congress funds and oversees both agencies, and the Senate confirms FCC commissioners.
Tesla has its own stakes in Washington, where Congress and federal agencies can reshape electric-vehicle tax breaks, battery subsidies, autonomous-vehicle rules and trade policy affecting Chinese competitors.
Musk's companies are spending directly on those fights, too.
Since January 2025, SpaceX has spent about $5.3 million lobbying on issues including NASA funding, defense spending, military launches, missile defense and procurement, while Tesla has spent about $3.6 million lobbying Washington, according to disclosure reports.
"Elon's spending is virtually unprecedented in recent elections for its scale in such a short period for one individual donor," Freed told CNBC. "He seems to be spending with basically no budget, and he got the money to do so."

title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
body:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.
Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.
The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.
1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.
“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”
Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.
This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.
Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

title: Meta Creates Non-Voting Stock to Fund AI Buildout, Keeping Zuckerberg in Control
body:
Meta's board has approved a new class of non-voting stock, and every holder of Class A and Class B shares will receive one new share for each share they own. The company disclosed the plan on Wednesday with its third-quarter results , and the Class C shares come into existence on Jan. 19, 2027.
The one-for-one dividend works as a two-for-one stock split, and Meta says it will not change anyone's voting power. Because Class C shares generally carry no vote, Meta can sell them for cash, or use them as pay and acquisition currency, without shrinking Mark Zuckerberg's control.
Zuckerberg held about 60.6% of the voting power on Oct. 1 against a 13.4% economic interest, according to the information statement Meta filed with the SEC. The gap comes from the dual-class setup, where Class A shares carry one vote each and Class B shares carry 10, and he beneficially owns about 341 million Class B shares.
According to the SEC filing, advisers at Moelis told the board's special committee that Meta could raise about $700 billion in equity over several years before Zuckerberg's voting power fell below 50%, according to the filing. Management also told those advisers that its long-term forecasts showed a need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years, starting as early as fall 2026.
CFO Susan Li framed the filing's "hundreds of billions" language differently on a follow-up call with analysts, calling it "a theoretical maximum" computed to determine what level of equity financing would trigger a loss of founder control. It is "not actually a description of our present equity financing needs or plans," she said, and Meta does not have "anything to announce on that front." The structure is approved, while the size and timing of any equity sale are not disclosed.
Under a Founder Alignment Agreement signed Oct. 20, only 20% of the Class C shares Zuckerberg receives can be sold freely. Selling any of the other 80% generally requires him to sell or convert a matching Class A or Class B share within two business days, which trims his voting power.
The agreement also commits Zuckerberg to remain a California resident, or live wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. The filing says California's Proposition 40, a wealth tax on the Nov. 3 ballot, could make him liable for a multi-billion dollar payment, and that Zuckerberg stated selling Class B shares to cover it could cut his voting interest to about 53%.
The board has also agreed to pay another one-for-one Class C dividend each time the 30-day volume-weighted average price of Class C reaches a successive doubling of the $580.60 Class A price from Sept. 10, adjusted for splits, as long as shareholder returns compound at 10% or more a year.
Class C shares are identical to Class A and Class B except for voting rights, but the filing warns they will likely trade at some discount to Class A, and Meta may need to issue more of them for any equity sale. Class C also will not count as "voting stock" under Section 368(a) of the tax code, so sellers who want to defer taxes on a deal may push for a different structure.
Meta's board had not set the record or payment dates for the dividend as of its filing, and the payment must come within five business days after the charter takes effect on Jan. 19, 2027.

title: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports
body:
President Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX 's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials.
The Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk by phone, U.S. and Ukrainian officials told the Journal.
Trump said later Thursday he did not "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk.
"Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump told reporters outside the White House as he departed for a campaign rally in Iowa.
"The bottom line, he put it back," Trump said of Musk.
The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX and a critic of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had ordered the Starlink slowdown.
Two unnamed sources in that report said Trump and Musk had discussed the decision to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, while one source said Musk had spoken to Trump prior to imposing the speed cap.
Trump has repeatedly denied involvement in the decision and said he does not know if Musk was behind it.
"I don't know who did it, but I was not involved," Trump said Wednesday.
The Starlink controversy, which drew bipartisan concern and criticism from lawmakers, emerged as Trump has ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy for continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure. At the same time, Trump has pursued a deal to ease sanctions on Russia so it can supply some diesel on the global market.
Sen. John Cornyn , R-Texas, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Wednesday that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."
Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the ranking member of the Senate homeland security committee's investigations subcommittee, on Thursday launched an inquiry into how SpaceX's satellite tech was "degraded for Ukraine without notice."
"This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally not only put Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril, but raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," Blumenthal said in letters to Musk and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth .
The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Thursday's report that Trump had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

title: Denmark to buy Kongsberg, Covenant missiles for new long-range strike option
body: COLOGNE, Germany — The Danish government plans to buy two types of “long-range,” precision-strike missiles, one air-launched and one ground-launched, to retaliate against adversaries after an attack on the country, officials announced on Thursday. The shopping list includes the Kongsberg-made Joint Strike Missile, which F-35 fighter aircraft can carry, and the Anthem missile by U.S.-based company Covenant as a ground-launched option, Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said. Officials released few details, leaving open the question of when the armed forces would receive the missiles, how many of them and at what cost, broadcaster TV2 reported in a live blog of a defense ministry press conference about the planned acquisitions. Long-range missiles are very much en vogue in Europe at the moment, as countries are equipping themselves as a deterrent against Russian aggression. Governments here consider the capability to strike back on their own all the more urgent because U.S. assistance with such weaponry in case of a conflict is considered uncertain under the presidency of Donald Trump. The ranges of strike missiles labeled as long-range are a bit of a guessing game, as manufacturers and governments keep performance information close to their chests so as to avoid tipping off adversaries. Typically, they fall in the range of 500 kilometers to 1,500 kilometers, depending on engine and warhead configurations. Danish officials cite a NATO contribution target as a key motivator for the envisioned weapons class, which would constitute a qualitatively new capability for the small country, according to TV2. Copenhagen is on the hook to offer the alliance a long-range strike capability by 2030, according to the defense ministry. “These acquisitions represent a significant step toward improving Denmark’s self-defense capabilities, strengthening NATO, and enhancing our capacity to strike back,” Defense Minister Bruus was quoted as saying in an agency statement. According to TV2, the envisioned Anthem missiles for Denmark, which have never seen combat, are to be produced in Germany. Manufacturer Covenant announced a new production site in Leipzig, Germany, last month, claiming it could churn out missiles there beginning in early 2027. The German defense ministry has so far said only that there are talks with Covenant about buying the weapons to plug Germany’s long-range strike gap. The manufacturer’s pitch is that Anthem missiles will be cheaper than products available on the market now. Reuters has previously reported a mid-six-figure target price per unit set by company executives during serial production.

title: Empire State VII to Return to New York After Months-Long Navy Mission Plans Scrapped
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment supporting the U.S. Navy.
The reversal comes just weeks after the vessel departed New York for Norfolk, Virginia, where it was scheduled to undergo maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of a classified national security mission.
In an October 21 message to the college community, SUNY Maritime President Rear Admiral John A. Okon confirmed the change.
“I am pleased to share an important update on Empire State VII. The federal activation plan has changed, and the ship is now expected to return to Fort Schuyler for academic use, ship work, and with watches resuming no later than the middle of November,” Okon wrote.
The announcement marks a significant shift from the original plans outlined by the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), which ordered the vessel’s activation in August for an anticipated 170-day federal mission.
An August 28 decision memorandum reviewed by gCaptain said the ship was needed to meet an urgent Military Sealift Command requirement and that no other suitable vessel was available within the required timeframe. Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel described the activation as a “compelling strategic necessity.”
The ship subsequently departed New York for Norfolk on September 30, with plans to remain there through October 30 for maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of follow-on operations supporting the Navy.
The nature and destination of those operations were never publicly disclosed.
It remains unclear what prompted the change in plans, whether the original military requirement has been withdrawn or reassigned, or how much of the planned work in Norfolk has been completed.
For SUNY Maritime, however, the early return is welcome news. The vessel’s absence had threatened to disrupt academic programs, shipboard training and the sea time cadets need to qualify for U.S. Coast Guard licenses.
“Empire State is more than a training ship. It is a classroom, a laboratory, and an essential part of the Maritime experience,” Okon said.
Okon previously warned that losing the ship for much of the academic year would create significant challenges, and he pressed MARAD to return the vessel by February to keep the college’s 2027 Summer Sea Term on schedule.
The revised timeline would bring the ship home roughly three months earlier than that requested deadline.
Empire State VII , delivered in 2023, is the first of five purpose-built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) developed by MARAD. The ships are designed primarily to train future merchant marine officers while also providing the federal government with additional sealift and emergency response capabilities.
The vessel’s activation was expected to provide an early test of the NSMV program’s dual-use concept, demonstrating how a federally owned training ship could be called into service for national security missions. Instead, the shortened deployment raises questions about the circumstances behind the original urgent military requirement and the subsequent decision to release the vessel.
“We will continue working with MARAD to confirm the exact details of the ship’s return and ensure we are ready to resume normal operations,” Okon said.

title: Book Reading Is on the Rise in America
body: “In America, the reading of books is up. Sales of print books have increased nearly twenty-five per cent from a decade ago. The number of independent bookstores in the United States has climbed steeply since 2009, with a seventy-per-cent increase since 2020. A survey by the Pew Research Center found that thirty-eight per cent of American adults read one to five books in 2025, and fourteen per cent read at least twenty. The global book market is expected to grow five per cent annually for the next several years; for the generation now entering college, book sales are at a lifetime high. In its lament for fading literacy, the Atlantic mentioned current data from the National Assessment of Educational Progress, whose reading survey of thousands of students began in 1971. ‘Just 35 percent of high-school seniors were ‘proficient’ at skills such as analyzing complex fictional themes and evaluating the effectiveness of an author’s argument,’ the magazine’s staff writer Rose Horowitch observed. That sounds bad, but the same figure a decade ago was thirty-seven per cent—just two points higher—and in the gloriously unwired age of 1992 it was forty. And the survey’s broad news was good. American nine-year-olds performed much better on reading assessments in 2025 than in 1971, and thirteen-year-olds’ performance held steady. The reading skills of English learners have risen in the past two decades, and, unlike in 1971, the top quarter of Black and Hispanic students today out-read the average white child.” From The New Yorker . The post Book Reading Is on the Rise in America appeared first on Human Progress .

title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
body:
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company .
TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.
Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.
“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”
Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.
Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.
The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.
Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

title: Canva releases its first image generation model
body:
Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.
The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.
Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image.
The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.
That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Magic Layers, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers .
Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.
Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.
In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.
Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon.
The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts.

title: Strathcona Pitches 250,000-Bpd Oil Export Route to Asia
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Canadian oil producer Strathcona Resources wants to export up to 250,000 barrels per day of crude from British Columbia’s northern coast using rail shipments and a new marine terminal to reach Asian markets. But first, it needs Ottawa to make an exception to its oil tanker ban.
Strathcona Chairman Adam Waterous told Bloomberg that the company plans to approach Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government as early as next week with a proposal to move crude by rail to a new export terminal in Prince Rupert.
Waterous believes exports could begin within two years, considerably sooner than Canada’s proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific coast, which isn't expected to operate until the early to mid-2030s.
Canada currently sends roughly 90% of its oil exports to the United States, a dependency Carney has been looking to reduce amid trade tensions with Washington.
There is, however, the matter of a federal law.
Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's 2019 Oil Tanker Moratorium Act prohibits tankers carrying more than 12,500 metric tons of crude or persistent oil from loading or unloading along British Columbia's northern coast.
Carney reaffirmed his commitment to that ban in July, complicating Alberta's efforts to develop a 1-million-bpd pipeline to the coast.
Strathcona's proposal would avoid the need for a new cross-province pipeline, but not the tanker restrictions.
Waterous argues Prince Rupert already has much of the necessary infrastructure because the port handles propane shipments arriving by rail. Strathcona also has experience moving crude by train, shipping up to 80,000 bpd to the U.S. Gulf Coast through terminals in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The political obstacles remain substantial. B.C. Premier David Eby, environmental groups, and numerous coastal Indigenous communities oppose lifting the ban. Waterous hopes partnerships with Indigenous communities could help advance the project.
If approved, the proposed 250,000-bpd terminal would increase Canada's existing crude export volumes from British Columbia's coast by nearly 50%.
For now, the proposal offers a faster route to Asian markets, provided Ottawa is willing to reopen a tanker debate it appeared to have settled just three months ago.

title: WATCH: Fueled by a life's mission, Netanyahu asks Israelis for time to 'finish the job' in Iran
body: It was 2:14 a.m., and Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to know whether we were tired.He had just turned 77. Members of his staff were dozing on couches and chairs. Netanyahu was alert, focused, and apparently in no hurry to end the night. We admitted that we were probably more tired than he was.“You're not the first to say that.”A little earlier, his staff had surprised him with a birthday celebration: krembos, the chocolate-covered marshmallow treats; along with chocolates and gummies; and an individual tiramisu for the prime minister. He ate it with evident enjoyment. Outside, aides had been searching for “the chair,” the one he preferred sitting in. Even at this hour, the small machinery of looking after a prime minister kept turning.Some of those around him had spent years at his side. They brought drinks, attended to him, and spoke with the conviction that he would win again. They believed Israel needed him. Netanyahu himself would give us a less comfortable assessment of the race.How did it feel to be 77? “Feels fine. If you know what you're about, and you have good health and a lot of energy, and a purpose.”That word, “purpose,” came up repeatedly during the next half-hour. So did Iran, US President Donald Trump, and the danger Netanyahu saw in handing the country to someone else. With the October 27 election approaching, he was asking voters to let him finish work that he regards as the reason for his political life. His partnership with Trump was central to that request. We wanted to know how his case would hold up when the American president was someone else.Netanyahu: Iran does not want me electedCould Iran attack before the election? Could Israel strike first?Netanyahu said military intelligence and the Mossad had delivered “clear warnings” that Iran and its proxies were considering ways to influence the vote.“They don't want me elected.”He suggested rockets or drones could be used to puncture Israelis' confidence in the military campaign's achievements. “If they do, it'll be a big mistake because we'll respond with force and might they cannot even imagine.”People on his team, speaking on background, separately told us that current senior defense officials had contacted Netanyahu to say he needed to win because Israel's enemies would see his defeat as their success. They also described serious security threats in the near future. That account of private conversations has not been independently verified.Netanyahu moved quickly through the destruction of enemy capabilities and the killing of their leaders. October 7 was the starting point of his account of Israel's recovery; the failures that permitted the attack under his government received little attention.Iran still had capabilities, we pointed out. He acknowledged that it did. For as long as its present leadership survived, he argued, it would try to rebuild its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.“My purpose is to break Iran's murderous regime, remove the threat from our heads, and have multiple peace treaties.”Finishing the job, by that definition, would require an outcome extending far beyond another successful strike.Netanyahu says he can withstand a post-Trump US, expand Arab tiesTrump's recent endorsement was quite an item for Netanyahu's campaign literature: the American president wanted him reelected.Netanyahu said the decision had surprised him. The motivation had not. He described a president who saw Iran as a danger to American cities and believed he had one reliable partner in confronting it.We raised Vice President JD Vance's refusal to offer an endorsement of his own. Vance had also made clear he was not opposing Netanyahu. Still, the question reached beyond this election. What would happen to the relationship when Trump left office?Netanyahu's answer began with the remaining opportunity under Trump, then moved to the possibility of a less friendly administration. He disliked that formulation.“That's really laundering words,” he said.“What happens if you have a hostile administration? Who will withstand the pressures? Who will stand up to them? And I think the answer in both cases is the same.”He meant himself. Experience with Washington, he argued, qualified him to make the most of Trump's friendship and to resist a successor's demands. Palestinian statehood was the example he returned to, describing it as the prospect of an Iranian terror base overlooking Israel's population centers.“You're not going to withstand the pressure by succumbing to it, because then you're finished.”An Israeli government elected now will have to prepare for an America whose politics are already changing. Netanyahu placed considerable weight on the character of the man sitting across from the American president. He spent more time explaining how he would withstand American pressure than how he would broaden American support.He did identify three tasks: strengthen the existing American base of support, fight the information war, and widen Israel's international partnerships. India was one example. In the Middle East, he said, more Arab governments were interested in relations with Israel after seeing it act against Iran.We tried to get the names. “Since it's just the three of us, so who are we talking about? Which countries?”“Well, we're definitely talking about more than two.”He gave us a number. Later, it grew to “many more than two.”He traced the beginnings of the Abraham Accords to his confrontation with former president Barack Obama over the Iran nuclear agreement, recalling calls from Arab officials impressed by his willingness to challenge Washington. Trump's presidency had helped turn those contacts into agreements. Further military action against Iran, he argued, had made Israel still more attractive as a partner.We challenged his suggestion that Arab leaders were untroubled by his coalition partners. Their reservations, we said, were expressed privately too.“Most of them couldn't care less.”He went further: “And they couldn't care less about the Palestinian issue, and they said, 'We have to say it, but we don't mean it.'”That is his account of their private words. Their public position remains quite different: Saudi Arabia and other Arab governments reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood in a joint statement on October 16.Qatar, Qatargate, and Netanyahu's defense against allegations of influenceQatar brought the discussion of Israel's standing abroad uncomfortably close to home.We asked whether it should again mediate on matters involving Israel. Netanyahu had accused Doha of spreading hatred of the Jewish state; Israel had nevertheless relied on its role in hostage negotiations.He maintained that Israel used Qatar because the United States did. He then accused it of driving antisemitism and anti-Zionism in American universities and on social media. “Qatar was one of the engines of our vilification, only one.”This led him to cite his late father, Benzion Netanyahu, the historian of the Inquisition and modern Zionism. He recalled asking him whether America offered Jews an exception to the recurring dangers of European history.“There are no exceptions if certain things happen,” he remembered his father replying.Netanyahu described social upheaval and resentment exposing a visible minority to danger. “The Jews are prominent and weak,” he said, “and that's a very dangerous place to be in a society.”His father's warning still shaped his explanation of America. Israel's strength, he argued, gave Jews the means to prevent the physical destruction that had so often followed their vilification. He saw the current hostility as a historical danger that better public diplomacy alone could not resolve.Then he returned to Qatar, offering a military action as his answer to suspicions about his own position.“They accused me of being pro-Qatar; I attacked Qatar.”Israel's September 2025 strike in Doha targeted Hamas leaders. It did not answer the question we put to him next: What about the allegations concerning people in his own circle and their connections to Qatar?“Except that the judge said there was nothing there.”He continued: “The judge said it's a witch hunt. Basically that's what he said.”He did not identify the judge or ruling. 'Qatargate' remains under investigation. The affair concerns allegations that aides, including Yonatan Urich, promoted Qatari interests while working for Netanyahu. They deny wrongdoing. Netanyahu has given evidence to police but has not been named a suspect.Netanyahu argued that others who had worked with Qatar were now attacking him over it. “This is one hoax,” he said, before describing a campaign video mocking successive television controversies as manufactured storms.“The idea is to divert attention and to mask the real issue in this election.”He did not say whether Israel would use Qatar as a mediator again.Who gets to join Netanyahu's next government - and on what terms?Netanyahu wants to build his next government with his present partners. On one possible appointment, however, he was explicit. Asked about Itamar Ben-Gvir's ambition to become defense minister, he said: “I think the next defense minister should be from Likud.”“But it's going to be our government. We decide what the policy is.”The conduct of the present government raised a different test of control. We pressed him on extremist settler violence against Palestinians, pointing to criticism from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, hardly an unfamiliar face among Israel's friends.Netanyahu argued that international coverage distorted the scale of the violence compared with terrorism against Israelis. We persisted: “Huckabee knows that, but not everyone does, right?”“No, I understand that, believe me.”“We know you do,” we replied.“You don't have to explain it to me. I don't want vigilantism.”He rejected extremist Jews who have been taking the law into their own hands. The acts were wrong, he said, did “enormous damage to Israel abroad,” and harmed the reputation of the wider settlement community. He spoke about families killed by terrorists and the sons that those communities had lost in military service.“That's why I put the Shin Bet onto this and continue to do that.”When we asked about bringing opponents into a broader government, the conversation turned to the courtroom.“Why not have a unity government? Would you agree to sit with him?” we asked, referring to Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff.Netanyahu said his opponents had ruled him out because of his corruption trial. “The trial's collapsed.”He spoke about what he and his family had endured, the conduct of investigators, and former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit's testimony. We returned to the political question.“You would offer them a hand?”“No, first of all, let me finish this because this is important.”His objection was to proposals barring an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Such a law, he argued, would hand prosecutors the power to decide who could govern, removing that choice from voters. He termed it “Iranian Bolshevism.”Then came a demand concerning the trial itself: “It should be ended right now, and we should start an immediate criminal investigation against those who led it.“You cannot do this to any citizen, and I'm a citizen, but also you cannot try to destroy democracy with the abuse of state power.”The trial continues. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in three cases, and bribery in Case 4000. He denies wrongdoing. The allegations concern gifts from businessmen, discussions with newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in return for steps against rival Israel Hayom, and regulatory favors for Bezeq in exchange for intervention in Walla's coverage.Mandelblit, testifying for the defense, has acknowledged investigative steps beyond his approvals while defending his authorization of the investigations and the basis for the bribery charge.Eventually, he answered the coalition question. If he secured a majority of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, he would form a government and establish its principles. Others could then accept them and join.“First principle, no Palestinian state, period.”He added Israel's identity as the Jewish nation-state, with minority rights respected; an active security doctrine; a free-market economy; and expanded peace agreements. A broader coalition could follow victory, on terms that he would set.Explaining his security doctrine, he searched for an English rendering of tachbulot, or stratagems. “My English isn't that good.” He invoked King James's translators and the 70 wise men of Alexandria. Biblical translation was one difficulty he was willing to concede.Victory itself was less certain. We pointed out that polls also showed him struggling to assemble a majority.“I think right now it's an even tie. That's what I see in the big numbers.”Netanyahu says he wants 'five more terms' as Israel's prime minister We returned to the birthday. If he won, would this be his last term?“Oh no, I'm gonna have five more terms.”He had a proposal for those who described him as worn out or physically inactive. “I invite them to come to the gym with me.” There was a condition: “But they'll have to do the same thing.”He recalled a commentator predicting, after his defeat in 1999, that he would not merit a footnote. The commentator was still around, he said; we pointed out that Netanyahu was too. He has had considerable practice reading his political obituaries.“I don't need the job. I don't need the job,” he said. “I'm fueled by a mission.”He described preventing Iran from acquiring the means to destroy Israel as the work of his adult life. Again came the question he wanted voters to ask: “Who will finish the job?”It was 2:45 a.m. Netanyahu thanked us for our tenacity. His staff had celebrated another birthday and were expecting another victory; his own assessment still left the election in the balance. After we left, he continued working.He had turned 77 in the middle of a working night. How much longer he would serve was now a question for the voters.■

Discord’s latest update released today has a big improvement for Markdown previews: they should now render correctly instead of with “a bunch of symbols,” according to the company. LLMs and AI agents often rely on Markdown files for instructions and context, so these improved previews could be helpful for people sharing information about AI projects on the platform.
“When you upload a Markdown (.md) file, you’ll now see the file rendered all nice and neat and pretty instead of with a bunch of symbols,” Discord says . “This includes tables, formatting, all that good stuff. Google has also improved its Markdown support, as it recently started letting users edit Markdown files directly in Docs without having to convert the files to the Docs format.
Discord says its new update also lets you organize servers and channels by right-clicking the icon on the sidebar and using a new “Move to…” feature. Discord Nitro members are also now able to upload files as large as 1GB.

title: Nvidia is pitching AI factories, but 81% of companies say their GPUs run at half capacity or less
body:
In VentureBeat Intelligence’s September VB Pulse survey , most companies running AI in production reported using half their GPU capacity or less — and most of those companies still plan to adopt new AI infrastructure.
Of the 102 qualified respondents, 68 were running AI in production and provided a GPU utilization figure. Fifty-five of those (81%) reported average utilization of 50% or less, and 71% of that group planned to adopt a new, additional or replacement AI infrastructure platform within 12 months.
Those findings raise a useful question about what buyers expect their next platform to solve. A replacement could improve scheduling, integration, or the economics of an existing workload. A new platform could support work the current environment handles poorly.
That question comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is urging companies to build their own AI factories. At his October 21 GTC Berlin keynote , he said, "To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI; you want to be producing the AI."
The AI factory pitch is expanding beyond compute. HPE is emphasizing governed APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, while VAST has announced an Agent Sandbox Foundation Stack with Nvidia designed to preserve agent state, data access and audit trails as the underlying compute scales up and down. In my conversation with Nebius ahead of the event , its security team highlighted GPU confidential computing as a way to protect data and model weights during processing and let customers verify the environment before releasing encryption keys.
My view is that integration and security are becoming more important in infrastructure decisions. Obtaining compute is one decision. Building an architecture that turns model capability into useful work requires several more.
As agents take on longer assignments, those decisions include how they access enterprise knowledge, preserve task progress, use different models, and recover when something goes wrong. Memory is an important part of that architecture. Cost per successfully completed task is one way to judge whether the pieces work together.
Across all 102 September qualified respondents, 63% planned a new, additional or replacement platform within a year. Only 10% reported an infrastructure ROI figure reviewed and signed off by finance. Among planned adopters, 91% had no such figure. Among respondents with no plans to change platforms, 89% also lacked a finance-reviewed ROI figure, a statistically insignificant difference.
Companies are making their next platform decisions before finance has validated the returns on their existing AI infrastructure.
Among respondents whose primary platform was in production, overall satisfaction averaged 4.0 out of 5.0, ease of implementation averaged 3.9, and value for money averaged 3.6.
A platform can work well enough to earn a favorable operational assessment while leaving a harder question unanswered: Is the work it enables worth its total cost?
For agentic applications, I would make cost per successfully completed task a central operating measure. That calculation should include inference, retrieval, storage, repeated attempts, and human review. Finance should then compare those costs with the value delivered against an agreed baseline.
A completed task needs a quality standard. A support case closed incorrectly should not count as a success, and the cost of repairing a code change should count toward the cost of completing it.
September’s respondents identified several infrastructure-buying considerations. Integration with the existing cloud and data stack received selections from 48%, performance from 42%, and GPU availability from 35%. The difference between integration and performance was not statistically significant.
The architectural question is where a particular workflow loses time, repeats work, or consumes resources without improving the outcome. A more capable model may help. So might a better information path or context layer, a different serving configuration, or a clearer division of work between models and tools.
“Memory” can refer to different things, and treating them as one problem makes infrastructure decisions harder.
Institutional memory is the organization’s durable knowledge: policies, records, operating procedures, and past decisions. Agent task memory is the state needed to continue an assignment: what has happened, what remains, and what earlier actions produced. Inference memory refers to the resources and cached computation used during model serving.
Institutional knowledge must be current, relevant, and available under the task’s permissions. Task memory must preserve useful progress without allowing a temporary conclusion to become an authoritative enterprise fact by accident. Inference-memory techniques must be evaluated against the workload they are intended to improve.
Anthropic’s context-engineering guidance describes structured notes stored outside the context window as one way to preserve information during extended work. vLLM’s automatic prefix caching addresses a different layer: reusing cached computation when requests share a prompt prefix. Its documentation notes that this reduces prompt-processing work rather than the time spent generating new tokens.
September’s survey measures the inference-memory layer. Nvidia and Dell were the most frequently selected options for use or evaluation, at 41% and 39%, respectively, a statistically insignificant difference. Open-source KV-cache tooling and model-level efficiency techniques were each selected by 21% of respondents for use or evaluation. Another 16% had not addressed inference-memory limits or were unaware of them.
I expect the relationship between these forms of memory to become a more important architectural decision. Teams will need to determine what an agent retains, what it retrieves again, what it can share, and when a result becomes part of the organization’s durable record.
I have argued that small language models will form the long tail of enterprise AI. Their value will depend on where they run, which tasks they perform, and how they work with enterprise context, other models, and people.
The practical test is whether a smaller model, placed appropriately within the workflow, meets the required quality at a lower total cost.
For a bounded task, a smaller model may be sufficient. A more demanding step may require another model or human judgment. The system needs criteria for choosing that path and evidence that the resulting configuration meets the required quality and cost.
That evaluation belongs in the software development lifecycle. Teams should test model choice, information retrieval, task-state handling, and escalation together against representative work. They should repeat those evaluations when a component changes.
Token price is one input. September’s report found that 23% selected cost per million tokens as a buying factor, up from 11% in August , a statistically significant difference between the two monthly samples.
The final cost of a task also depends on token consumption, retries, tool use, and human intervention. Model selection should therefore be evaluated at the workflow level, with successful completion as the denominator.
The seniority results suggest that infrastructure discussions begin from different priorities.
Among vice presidents and directors, 52% selected total cost of ownership as a buying factor, compared with 4% of individual contributors. That difference is statistically significant under the report’s test for small independent groups. Individual contributors selected integration most frequently, at 58%.
Leaders and builders need to connect economic goals with the technical decisions that determine cost. Leaders need to understand the economic consequences of architecture. Builders need a cost metric tied to the technical decisions they can influence, so they can weigh performance against cost.
Cost per successfully completed task can provide that connection. It lets teams examine whether changes to retrieval, model selection, caching, or task-state management improve the outcome enough to justify the cost.
The next infrastructure decision should begin with a specific agent workflow and a clear understanding of what's limiting its performance.
Enterprise AI leaders should treat memory, integration and measurement as infrastructure design decisions. The place to start is:
Have the application or product owner define successful completion and acceptable human intervention.
Have the data team identify authoritative information and its access rules.
Treat observability as you would for any other application, with the platform engineering team measuring latency, utilization, caching behavior and total operating cost.
Involve finance, agree on the baseline and validate the resulting benefit.
Then change one part of the architecture at a time and measure the change in cost per successfully completed task.
Smarter models expand what agents can attempt. Smarter infrastructure, measured by the task, makes that work dependable and economically defensible.
We will take on inference economics, including how teams do more with less memory and fewer tokens, at VentureBeat's Agentic Infrastructure Stack Summit on October 28 in San Francisco. Applications to attend are open.
Research note: Survey figures come from the September VB Pulse AI Infrastructure and Compute report , published by VentureBeat Intelligence, with 102 qualified respondents at organizations with 100 or more employees, including consultants answering for their main client. Results are self-reported by a self-selected group. The utilization finding covers 68 production respondents who supplied a figure; 55 reported average GPU utilization of 50% or less. Companies reporting higher utilization number 13. The seniority comparison rests on 23 vice presidents and directors and 26 individual contributors.
The August and September token-price figures come from different groups of respondents; the difference between them is statistically significant. The inference-memory question combined use and evaluation. The institutional-memory, agent-task-memory, and small-model arguments are analyst interpretations rather than findings directly tested by the survey.

title: No money for Camp Lejeune toxic water victims unless GOP wins midterms, Trump says
body: President Donald Trump suggested that monetary compensation for victims of contaminated water at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, hinges on Republicans winning control of Congress, telling a crowd at a Tuesday political rally that outstanding claims would be settled if his party wins the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Addressing a crowd in Greenville, North Carolina, Trump claimed his administration had already distributed $1 billion in cash settlements to victims of the pollutants. He also pledged to direct the Justice Department to resolve unsettled claims; however, he tied the possibility of future payments to partisan politics. “If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible and get it off the books and get it finished,” Trump said amid a slew of attacks on Democrats. He later added, “If we don’t win, there’s no money. If we do win, you’re getting it.” Trump also said, “We don’t want to give any [money] to the trial lawyers.” From the early 1950s to the late 1980s, service members and families drank and used water contaminated with trichloroethylene, a chemical that leaked into the water supplies from a local dry cleaning firm, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Underground storage tanks and industrial pollution also contributed, the National Research Council reported. Military authorities were unaware of the pollution until 1982, nearly three decades after it started. The toxic compound has been linked to a slew of devastating health consequences — including deaths — and led to dozens of lawsuits. A study released in 2023 found that veterans and family members stationed at the base are 70% more likely to develop Parkinson’s disease than other veterans, and those who spent time at the base have linked cancer diagnoses to the exposure. In 2022, President Joe Biden’s administration passed the Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxins (PACT) Act, which expanded care for veterans exposed to different toxins and enabled affected individuals to pursue compensation. In March, the Justice Department pledged to expedite settlements under the Camp Lejeune Justice Act, part of the PACT Act. The U.S. Navy and Department of Justice opened a settlement option for faster payout in 2022, with applicants agreeing to waive litigation. The Justice Department announced in March that it approved 649 settlement offers totaling $175 million over three weeks for those affected by the contaminated drinking water. Since the program began, the department said it has approved more than 2,500 offers worth around $706 million. Individual payments range from $100,000 to $550,000.

If we do win, you’re getting it.” Trump also said, “We don’t want to give any [money] to the trial lawyers.” From the early 1950s to the late 1980s, service members and families drank and used water contaminated with trichloroethylene, a chemical that leaked into the water supplies from a local dry cleaning firm, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Underground storage tanks and industrial pollution also contributed, the National Research Council reported. Military authorities were unaware of the pollution until 1982, nearly three decades after it started. The toxic compound has been linked to a slew of devastating health consequences — including deaths — and led to dozens of lawsuits. A study released in 2023 found that veterans and family members stationed at the base are 70% more likely to develop Parkinson’s disease than other veterans, and those who spent time at the base have linked cancer diagnoses to the exposure. In 2022, President Joe Biden’s administration passed the Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxins (PACT) Act, which expanded care for veterans exposed to different toxins and enabled affected individuals to pursue compensation. In March, the Justice Department pledged to expedite settlements under the Camp Lejeune Justice Act, part of the PACT Act. The U.S. Navy and Department of Justice opened a settlement option for faster payout in 2022, with applicants agreeing to waive litigation. The Justice Department announced in March that it approved 649 settlement offers totaling $175 million over three weeks for those affected by the contaminated drinking water. Since the program began, the department said it has approved more than 2,500 offers worth around $706 million. Individual payments range from $100,000 to $550,000.

title: Musk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. Few exist
body:
Elon Musk 's latest clash with Ukraine underscores the critical role that his company's Starlink satellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022.
It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering.
On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself.
SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits on Starshield . SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology."
The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 mph that Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander told The New York Times the Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by three days.
Musk and President Donald Trump , both critics of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation.
On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place. Trump insisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved."
Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger " that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication."
"People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power."
The disruptions have prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath.
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful."
"There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a " Squawk on the Street " interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake."
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in a social media post Wednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine."
On SpaceX's earnings call this week, executives didn't address the issue and weren't asked about it by analysts.
CNBC has reached out to Musk, SpaceX SVP of Global Business and Government Affairs Tim Hughes and a spokesperson for the company concerning Starlink restrictions in Ukraine and did not receive a comment before publication.
Governments or companies looking for an alternative to Musk, SpaceX and its satellite internet services have few options.
Amazon 's Leo , which also delivers internet connectivity via a low Earth orbit satellite constellation, is seven years in the making and has yet to fully come online, with only 390 satellites in orbit.
SpaceX, by comparison, boasts a Starlink constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan C. McDowell . Starlink connectivity is live in 174 countries, SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on Tuesday's earnings call.
Blue Origin , Jeff Bezos' space company, in January unveiled a service called TeraWave for enterprise and government customers. It's targeting deployment of the first batch of satellites in the fourth quarter of 2027.
France's Eutelsat , also a competitor to Starlink, has more than 600 satellites in orbit. The stock surged 23% on Oct. 14 as reports emerged that Musk had restricted Starlink in Ukraine.
Several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The European Union is building IRIS² , which is expected to span hundreds of satellites, but the first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Most of these planned systems are unlikely to "come anywhere close" in terms of capacity, coverage, resilience or cost compared with Starlink, said Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant. The cost, size, weight and power draw of Eutelsat's terminals make them particularly unsuitable on the battlefield, he added.
While SpaceX's Connectivity business has raced ahead of rivals, the company also has the advantage of overseeing a hugely successful rocket launch business, which has carried satellites to orbit for many of its competitors.
SpaceX is now phasing out commercial rides on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, while it tests and develops its massive Starship rocket.
Many new constellations "could therefore face substantial delays and materially higher launch costs," von der Ropp said.
This week, Ukraine and European lawmakers moved to explore alternatives to Starlink, framing the issue as a matter of national security.
Their concern is that access to a critical communications service could potentially be disrupted "as a consequence of Musk's political agenda," said von der Ropp.
"The degree of soft power SpaceX has accumulated over companies, governments and militaries is substantial, and that has now become very visible," von der Ropp said. "Inevitably, this is creating mistrust and accelerating demand for alternatives."
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
Musk enjoyed accolades for providing Starlink terminals and satellite internet service during the early days of the war, but relations have soured between the world's richest person and Ukrainian officials over the years.
Musk previously ordered SpaceX engineers to shut off Starlink's satellite network over Crimea to thwart a Ukrainian attack on Russian warships, according to a chapter in the 2023 Musk biography written by Walter Isaacson. Musk disputed the report. The revelation drew a rebuke from Ukrainian officials, including a top Zelenskyy aide, who said it led to Ukrainian civilians being killed.
"This is the price of a cocktail of ignorance and big ego," Mykhailo Podolyak, a top Zelenskyy advisor, wrote in a post on X, then known as Twitter.
Musk has also repeatedly contended that Ukraine should strike a "truce" with Russia and cede ownership of Crimea, a strategically important territory, to Putin.
Musk's treatment of Ukraine played a part in Canada 's decision to cut ties with Starlink. Officials in India and Taiwan have also expressed wariness of Starlink, citing national security concerns and preferring to adopt a mass communications service that's not controlled by SpaceX.
Musk lashed out at Indian "oligarchs" for stalling the Starlink rollout in the country.
He's also targeted some of Starlink's prospective enterprise customers.
Starlink has become the dominant provider for airlines' in-flight satellite Wi-Fi service, signing on dozens of carriers, including United Airlines , Alaska Airlines , American Airlines and Southwest Airlines .
But Delta Air Lines is one of the few carriers to choose Amazon's Leo service.
Earlier this month, Musk posted on X that Delta CEO Ed Bastian would "lose his job" over not choosing Starlink, following unconfirmed comments posted on X that Bastian told employees, "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me."
Bastian denied making the comment, and told CNBC on Oct. 9 that he's a "big fan" of Starlink and even drives a Tesla.
"All this nonsense about it being personal is not true at all," he said.
-- CNBC's Elsa Ohlen and Leslie Josephs contributed reporting to this story.

title: Space Force Picks Six Companies for Commercial Reserve Fleet
body: The Space Force has selected six commercial space domain awareness companies to support military operations with both steady-state and surge capacity, as part of the service’s new Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve. Officials have been working since 2022 to establish a fleet of commercial satellites and other assets to provide capabilities like satellite imagery, space domain awareness, and communications during peacetime that can be surged on demand. The concept is not unlike the Air Force’s Civil Reserve Air Fleet, which leases aircraft capacity from commercial airliners for use during a conflict. Last year, the Space Force announced it would pilot the CASR program with four unnamed companies who specialize in identifying and tracking objects in space—also called space domain awareness. The service awarded them 90-day contracts worth a combined $1.1 million , and in the ensuing months conducted a series of wargames and training events to better understand how to integrate their capabilities and services into its operations. These new contracts announced Oct. 22 are meant to operationalize that capability and create a pool of CASR companies specifically focused on SDA. Those firms include: Anduril Intrack Slingshot LeoLabs EOS, an Australian firm Northstar, a Canadian firm Space Force officials explained to reporters Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days conference that the six companies initially tapped for CASR are firms that operators already trust today and would turn to should something happen on orbit that requires more visibility or object tracking capabilities. According to Lt. Col. Brandon Galindo, all of the companies in this initial cohort currently work with the Joint Commercial Operations Cell, a Space Force hub that integrates commercial space data and services and shares it with joint international partners. “What we heard from the operational community is that … if something were to happen on orbit, debris or some breakup scenario, these are the companies on the commercial side that we would really depend upon,” Galindo said. That said, the initial cohort of space domain awareness companies isn’t meant to be static. Col. Tim Trimailo, director of the Commercial Space Office said other companies will have a chance to onboard in the future. “This is not a chalk line that we’ve snapped that says you can never get into CASR for the space domain awareness mission,” he said during. “It’s a living program. So, we’re always looking for new entrants, new opportunities, new companies that have proven themselves and that are trusted partners to be part of CASR.” While these are operational contracts, Trimailo said the initial dollar values—which he didn’t disclose—are fairly low. As the Space Force gets a handle on how much demand there is for the capabilities from operators within combatant commands, it will look at options to adjust funding. Galindo echoed that sentiment, describing the program’s work to establish the reserve as an iterative process that will include regular updates within each mission area as well as opportunities to add new mission areas under the CASR umbrella. He also noted that contract terms and strategies will vary by company and by mission. “It’s not cookie cutter,” he said. “Each mission area is so unique, the companies within a mission area are unique. And we love that, because then we can assemble the best companies that offer something unique and we can put them together.” The Commercial Space Office has started to look at what its next CASR mission will be and is considering commercial satellite communications, launch, and telemetry, tracking, and command—which would leverage the Space Force’s existing Joint Antenna Marketplace —as potential options. The post Space Force Picks Six Companies for Commercial Reserve Fleet appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Trump Says Musk Restored Ukraine's Starlink Access, Declines to Say if They Spoke
body:
Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access but the U.S. president declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Thursday that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
"I don't want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference, I guess. The bottom line — he put it back," Trump told reporters when asked if he spoke to Musk. Trump did not elaborate further.
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.
The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, the WSJ reported earlier, citing U.S. and Ukrainian officials.
Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper the system had not been restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier on Thursday that speed on Starlink systems had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days.
Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped, according to the newspaper.
Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House.
Zelensky's relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskiy.
Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest U.S. push to end the conflict. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Trump had promised to end the war when he took office but the goal has remained elusive.
