title: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
body:
PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said Thursday.
The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to change drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements.
Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.
Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC.
Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.
The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

title: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case
body:
Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas has been charged in a federal indictment with leading an alleged marijuana racketeering conspiracy that included family members of the powerful Democrat , according to court documents made public on Thursday.
The indictment and the FBI said the five-year scheme, which was worth an estimated $4.5 million, obtained and illegally distributed "large quantities of illegal marijuana," and aimed to procure "generational wealth" for members of the enterprise.
Lucas, 82, is a critic of President Donald Trump , and was an architect of ultimately failed efforts in Virginia to redraw the state's congressional map for November to boost chances for Democrats to win certain districts. She also has been a proponent of legalizing marijuana in the state.
The criminal case, which also charges members of Lucas' family, was made public by the Department of Justice less than two weeks before the midterm election . Those contests will determine what political party controls both chambers of Congress.
Lucas, the state Senate's president pro tempore and chairman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, is not on the ballot this year. The indictment alleges that Lucas, who was first elected to the Senate in 1991, leveraged her position as chairman of the powerful committee to protect her marijuana enterprise.
The indictment says Lucas "was the leader of the enterprise," that she "arranged for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana, supervises the laundering of marijuana proceeds," and "used her political influence to attempt to influence Virginia legislation for the benefit of herself and her family and maintained a premise for the distribution of marijuana." The alleged scheme used two stores, CBD Shopped and The Cannabis Outlet, for its operation.
"On May 6, the FBI executed federal search warrants at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe," the Department of Justice said in a statement. "Agents recovered marijuana and firearms at both locations."
Six other defendants are charged in the alleged scheme, among them Lucas' two daughters and her grandson, Ryan Eichelbeger. One of the daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke, is running for mayor of Portsmouth.
Lucas is in custody with the other defendants, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced at a press conference Thursday. She is scheduled to appear before a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Virginia, at 2:30 p.m. ET Thursday.
In addition to racketeering conspiracy, Lucas is charged with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana; conspiracy to launder money; conspiracy to commit honest services fraud; and maintaining a drug involved premises.
"Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," Lucas said in a statement posted on X.
"I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now," she said. "I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."
Blanche, when asked at the press conference about criticism from Lucas's attorney that the case is politically motivated, said, "We don't do political paybacks."
The attorney general noted the investigation of Lucas began before the current Trump administration, and that a federal grand jury had determined there was enough evidence to indict her.
"There's decision and processes in place at the department when we're bringing a case against a political official, and the ... first question is: is this investigation proper?" Blanche said. "And the conclusion of that is yes. Is the timing proper? And the conclusion of that is yes."
The indictment was issued by a grand jury on Oct. 14, but was only unsealed Thursday.
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in a statement, said,"In our American system of justice, people are presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that is true for Senator L. Louise Lucas."
"She and her family deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented," Spanberger said.
The governor also said, "The timing of this indictment undermines the U.S. Department of Justice's previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions — to include indictments or significant investigative steps — close to an election and sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice."
The indictment says that after he was hired in 2022, a senior law enforcement officer "warned Louise Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and was going to get her in trouble one day."
Lucas since 2021 has been a partner in The Cannabis Outlet, a shop that sells selling hemp and CBD, or cannabidiol products.
After a 2024 burglary at the store, two of Lucas' co-defendants claimed to Portsmouth Police that about $3,000 of marijuana products were missing.
One of the overt acts listed in the indictment was an April 2022 meeting between Lucas, her two daughters and an indicted co-conspirator at Lucas' office. At that meeting, the indictment alleges, Lucas asked the unidentified co-conspirator "if they were a member of law enforcement before purchasing between three and five pounds of marijuana" from the co-conspirator with a check for $6,600 from Lisa Lucas-Burke. The check was made out to "Freedom is Dope."
On Feb. 5, 2026, the indictment says, Lucas called an unindicted co-conspirator and discussed the language surrounding the recreational marijuana legislation pending in the Virginia General Assembly, and the possibility of [the co-conspirator] receiving a license and sharing the proceeds with her because 'this is our last chance at generational wealth . . .. I've got too old to not be greedy.'"
The charges come five months after FBI agents executed a search warrant at Lucas' Portsmouth office.
At the time of that May 6 raid, Lucas noted in a statement that it came two weeks after Virginia voters approved the redistricting plan, adding, "Virginians sent a powerful message when they voted to stop Trump's scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections."
"I was proud to help lead that effort and I have never been afraid to stand up to Donald Trump."

title: One year of Ukrainian arms exports, and industry has questions: how much army gained, where Berlin office is, who joins joint ventures
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine now builds far more weapons than it can afford to buy. A year ago, it promised to sell the surplus abroad and turn the proceeds back into its own army. However, 12 months later, that promise has barely materialized : a state fee of up to 30% is pricing Ukrainian arms out of foreign markets, and no one can say how much the army has actually gained, said Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Council of Armorers. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the resumption of controlled weapons exports in October 2025, resting it on four promises: 1) sell what Ukraine makes beyond its own needs, 2) channel part of the proceeds into a special fund for the army, 3) open export offices in Europe and the US, and 4) establish joint ventures abroad. The surplus is real: Ukraine's defense output is projected to reach $55 billion in 2026, far beyond what the state can finance. A year on, Fedirko checked each promise in turn. 1) Export of surpluses: rules that strangle businesses On 1 July 2026, the government approved rules for controlled arms exports. They shortened the maximum application review period from 90 to 30 days, but also introduced an export fee: 20% for finished products and technologies, and 30% for components. For finished products exported under the special procedure, the contract value must be at least $334,000. In September, the Ukrainian Council of Armorers, together with other associations, proposed a zero rate, no advance collection of the fee, refunds for deals that fall through, and simplified test shipments. The industry was promised that its amendments would be taken into account and that the resolution would be rewritten. Even in early October, however, the rules still needed work. According to Fedirko, the new mechanism has effectively not started working. Whether it can bring in additional funds for defense depends on how acceptable the export terms are to manufacturers. Fedirko says, though, that judging by current decisions, the state intends to keep the export fee. “The industry is ready to discuss its contribution to defense financing. But the rate must be economically justified,” he says. 2) Procurement for the Ukrainian military: balance is only being established He adds that the Ukrainian Council of Armorers intends to push for a rate significantly lower than 20%, one that would let companies fulfill contracts and invest in production. With such high rates, Fedirko says, the competitiveness of Ukrainian weapons on foreign markets is in question, as is the ability to send even small test batches to potential buyers. “The fundamental requirement is post-payment: after the contract has actually been fulfilled and the manufacturer has been paid. A company should not pay the state in advance a share of income it has not yet received,” h e says. He added that, given all this, the real export figures remain unclear, as does how much exports have actually brought the military. “The military and manufacturers must feel the benefit of exports. I sincerely hope that next year will bring much better results,” he says. In addition, on 12 October, the Ukrainian Parliament passed bill No. 15400 in the first reading. It provides for crediting the export fee to a special fund directed to the Ministry of Defense: 50% for the procurement, modernization, and repair of weapons and equipment, and 50% for the pay of Armed Forces personnel. The bill has not yet been adopted, but Fedirko says he expects “final adoption and launch of the mechanism.” 3) Export offices: offices in Germany and Denmark On 3 November, the Ukrainian government named the first cities for export offices: Berlin and Copenhagen. On 15 December, it again spoke of preparing an office in Berlin. In reality, Fedirko says he does not know the office’s status, and it likewise remains unclear how companies can apply to it and how many contracts it has helped close. 4) Joint ventures abroad: There are concrete results in this area According to Fedirko, eight joint ventures have been created, five of which are already supplying products to Ukraine. He stresses that this is the result of work by Ukrainian companies, foreign partners and the state, and that it deserves recognition. As early as February 2026, the authorities spoke of plans to create ten joint ventures in Europe within a year. At the same time, they announced Quantum Frontline Industries in Germany, with a planned annual capacity of 10,000 drones for Kyiv. Beyond the number of ventures and deliveries, however, it is important to understand how other manufacturers can join the Build with Ukraine program. “Who accepts applications, by what criteria are decisions made, and what support does a company receive?” Fedirko asks. In other words, joint ventures are already delivering results, but the rules of participation and the state support mechanism must be clear to companies that want to develop production abroad. title: The Foundations of Scalable AI
body: A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. This session from MIT Technology Review’s EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic systems, into lasting value for investors. About the speaker Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard Jing Wang leads Vanguard’s Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm’s AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities. Her team drives enterprise-wide innovation, research, and delivery, enabling Vanguard to translate emerging technologies into trusted solutions that enhance client experiences, improve investor outcomes, and create measurable business value. Before her current position, Jing served in a range of leadership roles across Vanguard’s Financial Services, Workplace Solutions, International, and Corporate Services divisions. Throughout her tenure, she has led teams and enterprise initiatives that advanced strategic priorities, strengthened client outcomes, and drove business performance across the firm. She joined Vanguard in 2009 after several years as a Principal at the Boston Consulting Group. Jing earned a B.S. in Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China, a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an M.B.A. in Finance and Marketing from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania. Jing holds Series 7, 24, and 65 licenses.

title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
body:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”
The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.
In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.
“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”
In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.
The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.
Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.
Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.
With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.
DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.
Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.
Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.
“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”
Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.
“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.
He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”
“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”
Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.
“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.
He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”
Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes.
“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs.
Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.
“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

title: Former OpenAI science lead launches Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots
body:
Former OpenAI science lead Kevin Weil has launched Warp Sciences, a new AI startup focused on automating lab work for drug discovery. The company, which trains robots to make and test promising compounds identified by researchers, has raised $215 million at an $865 million valuation, according to Weil, who announced the startup and funding on X.
The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from IVP, Mayfield, Lux Capital, Premji Invest, and Menlo Ventures.
For years, biotech companies have outsourced the most labor-intensive work of synthesizing thousands of variations of molecules to contractors in China, such as WuXi AppTec. With Warp Sciences, Weil hopes to reshore that work and insulate the entire drug development process from geopolitical supply-chain risks.
Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks. By automating wet-lab work, Warp Sciences aims to accelerate drug discovery using robots that can operate around the clock.

title: Enzymes Speed Compostable Polymer Breakdown
body: “We demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation.” From Nature . The post Enzymes Speed Compostable Polymer Breakdown appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Microbes May Help One Mine Recover More Copper
body: “To extend the lifespan of one mine past its prime, Arizona’s Carlota Mine, its owner, KGHM Polska Miedz S.A., has recently recruited a group of unconventional miners. They arrived by the millions, transported in barrel-sized containers from a laboratory in Colorado. These miners are specialized microbes, acid-loving microorganisms that liberate copper from ore by digesting surrounding iron and sulfur compounds. Endolith, a Denver-based startup that supplies the microbes to KGHM, will continue to grow them in bioreactors onsite. From there, the microbes are channeled into a sprinkler system to mix with sulfuric acid. That liquid then drips into vast heaps of crushed rocks — some as large as 10 sports stadiums — setting off a series of biochemical reactions in a process known as bioleaching to release copper. If all goes as planned, Endolith’s microbial miners will help squeeze more copper out of the heaps and reduce the use of sulfuric acid at a time when the war in Iran has sent the feedstock’s price sky-high.” From Bloomberg . The post Microbes May Help One Mine Recover More Copper appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Healthy Coral Helps Bleached Coral Recover Faster in Lab Tests
body: “When coral bleaches during a heat wave and ejects its symbiotic algae, it usually means either a death sentence or a slow recovery over months or years. But scientists working separately at two labs an ocean apart have found a faster acting shortcut, one that has scientists hoping it could eventually help coral recover from bleaching and endure future heat waves. The approach, reported in a 2 October paper in Environmental Microbiology Reports and one published today in Science Advances, is deceptively simple. By touching a piece of bleached coral to a healthy piece, a kind of algal transfusion can occur. Symbionts flow through a bridge of tissue and then rapidly reproduce, repopulating the bleached piece in as little as 4 weeks.” From Science . title: Coinbase Fined Again in Ireland, This Time $3.6M Over Fund Safeguarding
body:
Coinbase’s Irish arm has been fined roughly $3.6 million by the Central Bank of Ireland for failing to properly protect customer funds, the regulator’s second enforcement action against the exchange’s European operations in less than a year.
The regulator said Thursday it penalized Coinbase Ireland €3,252,618 for breaching safeguarding and outsourcing rules under the country’s Electronic Money Regulations between November 2020 and August 2025.
The figure reflects a 30% discount off a €4,646,597 penalty for settling, which Coinbase Ireland reached with the regulator on Oct. 21. The sanction still requires confirmation by Ireland’s High Court before taking effect.
Coinbase Ireland is an e-money institution within the broader Coinbase Group, issuing the digital money customers use to buy crypto on the platform. The Central Bank found three main failures: the company leaned too heavily on its U.S.-based parent to handle safeguarding processes required under Irish and EU rules, lacked enough local expertise to oversee the protection of customer funds, and allowed its designated safeguarding account to be underfunded for lengthy periods. It also faulted the firm’s internal controls and its failure to flag material safeguarding changes to the regulator.
Coinbase Ireland admitted the breaches. Karen O’Leary, the Central Bank’s director of enforcement, said payment and e-money firms have a “fundamental obligation to fully safeguard customers’ funds” and that the regulator has “no tolerance for weaknesses in safeguarding arrangements.”
O’Leary added that failing to honor assurances made during authorization, or to report material changes, was “completely unacceptable.”
The penalty is the second Irish hit to Coinbase’s European business this year. The Central Bank fined a separate Coinbase entity, Coinbase Europe, €21.5 million in May over anti-money-laundering failures.
Coinbase has leaned on Ireland as its EU hub, securing an e-money license there ahead of Brexit and later obtaining a MiCA license to passport its services across the bloc.
The action lands even as Coinbase expands its European footprint , having recently rolled out crypto futures for traders in the region. It also underscores how the exchange’s reliance on a single jurisdiction for EU access carries regulatory risk, with Irish authorities signaling they intend to hold firms to the commitments they made to win market entry.

title: Storage Growth Surges but May Miss Global Pledge
body: “Deployment of storage capacity is outpacing existing policy targets. Storage additions hit a record 118 GW in 2025, including 108 GW of battery storage. If that pace were sustained through 2030 with no acceleration, energy storage would reach 1,020 GW, more than the sum of current national targets. Additions have been growing at almost 80% a year since 2020, which is much faster than the modest growth needed to hit the full 1,500 GW storage pledge. Storage additions are at least in part being driven by the dramatic declines in battery costs.” From Ember . title: Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close.
body: AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can use it to do better work next time. Letta’s new FrontierMemory benchmark, released Wednesday, tests that gap by measuring whether agents can learn from experience rather than by just retrieving stored information. Early results show a widespread in performance across agent harnesses, the the infrastructure that manages how an agent operates. Letta Dream came out on top with a 73.3% score, followed by Prime Agent at 60%. OpenAI Agents SDK scored 40%, while Claude Managed Agents and Hermes Agent trailed at 33.3% and 26.7%, respectively. Recall isn’t learning “Modern ‘memory’ benchmarks are saturated since they measure recall of facts,” Letta co-founder and CEO Charles Packer writes on X , saying that in the coding harness and bash loop era, recall is solved, while continual learning in token space, meaning learning through the context an agent keeps rather than through weight updates, remains unsolved. Sarah Wooders , also a Letta co-founder, points to another problem on X . Most coding and knowledge-work benchmarks evaluate unrelated tasks with all the necessary context provided upfront. But that’s not how people actually work. Wooders compares it to starting a new job: A new hire needs plenty of direction, while someone who’s been there for years can often get the job done with little explanation. Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.” FrontierMemory takes a different approach. Agents receive transcripts of earlier work, including successful and failed attempts, and then generate their own memories to help complete later tasks. Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.” Developers have already embraced the underlying idea, building continually learning agents by pairing a language model with memory systems and feedback loops. Letta reworked existing coding and knowledge-work tests so agents had to use what they learned from previous tasks instead of having everything spelled out for them. After reviewing and fixing problems with the original tests, Letta narrowed FrontierMemory 1.0 to just 15 tasks. Harness beats model The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it. Letta tested five agent systems to see how well they could learn from previous work and use those lessons on new tasks. The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it. Letta Dream beat OpenAI Agents SDK 60% to 40% when both used GPT-6.1 Sol to create memories and GPT-6 Sol to complete tasks. The results were even further apart with Claude Opus 5.5. Dream scored 73.3%, Prime Agent hit 60%, and Claude Managed Agents came in at 33.3%. Packer says the the way agents handle AI “dreaming” makes a big difference. Dreaming is when an agent reviews past work and turns what it learned into instructions or memories it can use later. He also points to Prime Agent outperforming Hermes Agent as another example of how much these systems can vary. But there’s a downside: without checks on what gets saved, agents risk learning and repeating bad habits . FrontierMemory also compared seven frontier models on how well they generate useful memories. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 tied for first at 73.3%, Kimi K3 followed at 66.7%, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon both scored 60%. Muse Wonder reached 46.7%, and Grok 4.7 finished at 33.3%. Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol. Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol. Cheaper memory, lower scores But OpenAI had a big price advantage. GPT-6.1 Sol cost an estimated $0.77 per task, compared with $2.80 for Opus 5.5 and $3.58 for GLM-5.3. So while OpenAI scored lower, it was much cheaper to run. Letta used its Dream harness to create memories with each model, then tested how well those memories worked on tasks run in Letta Code. The results show a tradeoff between better memory, stronger performance and lower costs. Memory that travels Letta also looked at why some memories worked better than others. In one test involving company pricing data, Opus 5.5 created a skill telling the agent when to use certain information. GPT-6.1 Sol created four separate skills, but the agent never found the one it needed. Gemini 4 Argon made a different mistake. It remembered specific file sizes, which wasn’t much help when the next task involved different files. Opus 5.5 instead told the agent to check both the usual file and email for information. That worked even when the task changed. Memories created by Opus 5.5 helped GPT-6 Sol complete tasks, suggesting developers could use a more expensive model to build memories and a cheaper one to do the work. Other developers have taken notice. After Letta’s Sarah Wooders posted about the benchmark on X , the OpenClaw account responded that it would like to see a plugin for its platform. The account says its multiplayer environment would be an interesting place to test the benchmark, raising questions about how memory works when several agents share the same harness. “Yes definitely – would love to add OpenClaw to the harness comparison!” Wooders writes. “Extending to multiplayer memory is also a very interesting future direction.” What the benchmark misses FrontierMemory is still early. With just 15 tasks and one attempt per task, a single result can shift the scores by roughly 6.7 percentage points. The benchmark currently focuses on agents learning from past work rather than updating memories as they go. Packer says the next release will add longer-running tasks and online memory updates. The post Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close. appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon Falls to a Record Low
body: “Deorestation in Brazil's Amazon rainforest declined to the lowest ‌level on record in the 12 months through July, according to data released by Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday. Some 3,335 square kilometers (1,287.65 square miles) of Amazon jungle were destroyed in the 12 months through ​July, an all-time low in the historical series that goes back to 1988. It was ​a fall of about 42% from the preceding period. The previous lowest ⁠level for Brazil's Amazon deforestation was reached in 2011-2012, when 4,571 square kilometers were ​destroyed. In the mid-90s, the figure had reached a record high of nearly 30,000 ​square kilometers destroyed a year.” From Reuters . The post Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon Falls to a Record Low appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Poland’s Incomes Are Rapidly Catching Up With Western Europe
body: “Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year… For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote. Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived. Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.” From The Guardian . The post Poland’s Incomes Are Rapidly Catching Up With Western Europe appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Hybrid American Chestnut Trees Return to Bronx Zoo
body: “The Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo today welcomed 20 hybrid American chestnut trees, donated by New York Restoration Project (NYRP) in partnership with The American Chestnut Foundation (TACF), marking the first time American chestnut trees have been planted at the zoo since the devastating chestnut blight eliminated billions of American chestnut trees across North America and rendered the species functionally extinct… The return of the American chestnut to the zoo represents a meaningful connection between the zoo’s history and the tree’s ongoing conservation efforts. In 1904, the zoo’s Chief Forester, Hermann Merkel, was the first to document the devastating chestnut blight, which would go on to decimate nearly 4 billion American chestnut trees across North America… The planting is part of NYRP's ongoing effort to help return the American chestnut to its native range.” From Wildlife Conservation Society . title: China Moves to Confiscate $5 Billion in Bitcoin From Fraudster Who Fled to UK: Report
body: Bitcoin Magazine China Moves to Confiscate $5 Billion in Bitcoin From Fraudster Who Fled to UK: Report Chinese authorities are working to seize nearly 62,000 bitcoins — worth around $5 billion at today’s prices — linked to one of the country’s largest-ever fraud cases. Prosecutors allege that Qian Zhimin, the alleged controller of Tianjin Lantian Gerui Electronic Technology, recruited associates to sell fake wealth management products nationwide from 2014 to 2017 without financial regulatory approval, promising guaranteed returns to investors, according to a report last week from Shanghai’s The Paper. The scheme raised some RMB 40.3 billion ($2.8 billion). Qian allegedly used investors’ cash to pay off earlier participants — Ponzi-style — while channeling funds into the bitcoin holdings, property, cars, and jewelry. Little of the money went toward legitimate business operations. In July 2017, as the scheme unraveled, Qian fled to the UK carrying computers holding the bitcoin wallets. British authorities later seized the crypto assets and other property, including roughly 61,900 BTC along with cash, jewelry, and other cryptocurrencies. The case took a significant turn recently when the UK High Court ruled that Chinese law — not UK law — applies to ownership disputes over the seized bitcoin. The coins have appreciated enormously since 2017, and the applicable law determines whether victims share in those gains. The UK’s Crown Prosecution Service says victims may recover losses through China’s compensation mechanism, but representatives from Fieldfisher law firm, acting for some victims, are considering an appeal. Further hearings will determine whether victims can prove their entitlement to the assets. Meanwhile, the Second Intermediate People’s Court of Tianjin announced it accepted the prosecution’s application on September 28 to confiscate Qian’s illicit assets. Victims can register to participate in asset recovery proceedings through a WeChat platform, with a six-month notice period before the formal trial begins. China has some of the world’s strictest rules in regulating crypto. Its government banned digital asset trading and bitcoin mining back in 2021. This post China Moves to Confiscate $5 Billion in Bitcoin From Fraudster Who Fled to UK: Report first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: New AI Model Answers Questions About DNA Effects
body: “The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open-source model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop. Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return. Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.” From Wired . title: A-4 ‘Super’ Skyhawks Playing The Bad Guys In European Skies
body: Northern Germany probably isn’t the first place you’d think of to look for a U.S. Navy and Marine Corps classic attack jet. However, contract aggressor company Top Aces flies a squadron of deeply upgraded Douglas A-4N Skyhawks to support European air arms for their “red air” training needs. Nearly 3,000 A-4s were built between 1956 and 1979, and TWZ’s Jamie Hunter traveled to the Germany Navy base at Nordholz for the latest episode of our “Special Access” to witness some of the last, and by far the most modern, Skyhawks operating up close. There he learned what it was like operating the iconic but nearly antique jets against some of the world’s most capable fighters. He also discovered that significant developments are on the horizon for Top Aces in Europe, principally the arrival of F-16s that will further enhance the company’s aggressor services for its growing list of European customers. title: Sudan lifts ban on 46 imports as inflation rises and Dollar hits SDG 10,300
body: Sudan has lifted import restrictions on 46 goods as the Dollar climbs to SDG 10,300 and annual inflation reaches 28.29%, deepening pressure on consumers already struggling with soaring food prices. Sudan’s Sovereignty Council chairman Abdelfattah El Burhan has cancelled a cabinet decision banning imports of 46 goods, as Sudan’s currency and consumers remain under pressure from rising prices. Finance minister Jibril Ibrahim says the decision takes account of consumers’ needs while providing measures to protect domestic producers. Traders and consumers have reported an immediate fall in some prices following the announcement. Vegetables at Khartoum Central Market (File photo: Supplied) The National Importers’ Chamber welcomed the move but called for Prime Minister Kamil Idris to issue a clear, enforceable decision cancelling Resolution No. 74, which introduced the restrictions. The chamber’s chairman, El Sadiq Jalal El Din Saleh, said the import ban had disrupted markets and caused substantial losses to importers. However, foreign-exchange dealers reported that the Dollar rose on Thursday to SDG 10,200 for buying and SDG 10,300 for selling, an increase of SDG 100 from Wednesday. Experts expect further increases, particularly following the lifting of the import restrictions. Inflation and food prices rise Sudan’s annual inflation rate rose to 28.29% in September, up from 26.14% in August, while monthly inflation reached 7.5%, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics. Food and drink prices rose by 17.26% during the month, with annual inflation in the category reaching 36.81%. Annual inflation was significantly higher in urban areas, at 40.35%, than in rural areas, at 21.18%. War compounds economic crisis Economists attribute rising inflation to the destruction of Sudan’s productive base during the war, growing dependence on imports, the depreciation of the pound, and the use of the customs Dollar to calculate duties. Taxes, customs charges, and transport costs have added to the burden. The conflict has also prevented many people from returning to agricultural and other productive areas, restricting domestic supplies. Markets remain fragmented between areas controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, while production and supply chains have yet to recover. The latest figures point to a difficult economic balance: easing import restrictions may improve the availability of goods, but the continuing rise in the Dollar and the cost of food threaten to erode any relief for consumers. title: SOCOM seeks common PaaS environment to support testing and fielding of new tech
body: U.S. Special Operations Command is conducting market research as it looks to fulfill a requirement for a common platform-as-a-service environment near its headquarters. The command is eyeing an “integrated contracting vehicle” for the initiative, according to a draft performance work statement published Wednesday night on a government contracting website . A common PaaS environment is needed near MacDill Air Force Base, Florida, to enable collaboration among traditional and non-traditional vendors, users, and government program teams, per the draft PWS. The SOF Acquisition, Technology and Logistics directorate “requires an integrated contracting vehicle to rapidly discover, assess, prototype, integrate, test, and field mission‑relevant technologies and software-intensive capabilities across multiple Program Executive Offices and operational contexts,” officials wrote in the document, adding that the vehicle would boost Joint Acquisition Task Force research and experimentation, “digital applications platform services” for PEO SOF Digital Applications, and “system-of-systems” integration for PEO Tactical Information Systems. Officials also seek assurance of cybersecurity Risk Management Framework compliance as well as “market analytics” to monitor, evaluate and incorporate commercial capabilities. The contract vehicle would encompass mission support platform services, integration facility operations, engineering support services, cybersecurity RMF, network connectivity, hardware/software support, data access coordination, documentation, and delivery of technical findings, according to the draft PWS. The engineering support services would require software engineers, among other labor categories, focused on cloud‑native solutions and design, coding and testing, among other tasks. An objective is to operate a “cutting‑edge integration test platform (open and operationally representative environments) to verify communication, data exchange, security/privacy, performance/scalability, resilience/redundancy, emergent behaviors, and change/configuration management” across PEO Tactical Information Systems programs, according to the draft PWS. Another objective is to deliver “end‑to‑end RMF support” to achieve and maintain authority to operate (ATO) in line with Defense Department, SOCOM and National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guidance, including “system categorization, control selection/implementation/assessment, RMF documentation, body‑of‑evidence artifacts, A&A coordination, continuous monitoring, risk analysis, and lifecycle integration of requirements.” Responses to the RFI are due Nov. 5. title: Award-Winning AI Literature
body:

ð¯ðµ Short story Are You There? by Kamome Ashizawa â 9th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2022 Ashizawa made 101 stories in three weeks with AI. The story that won was mostly written by Ashizawa with a little AI; the other hundred experiments were mostly machine-generated. This was the first AI-assisted story to win a Hoshi prize.
ð¯ðµ Short story The Last Painter by Toh Katagiri â 12th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2025 The organizers classified it as AI-assisted, but never said exactly how. A fellow finalist says Katagiri told the group that every sentence was written personally.
ð¯ðµ Short story Genome Tower by Shamizui â 13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Grand Prix, 2026 The disclosed AI use was apparently limited to inventing the name of a fictional disease. The organizers still counted it among the yearâs AI-assisted winners.
ð¯ðµ Short story Parallel Self-Mediation Co., Ltd. by En Shijima â 13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2026 Shijima described working with AI as feeling more like âchoosingâ than âwriting.â This sounds like a much more generative collaboration than Genome Tower . The prize stood.
ð¯ðµ Short story Erinnerung by Rino Takinouchi â 13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2026 ChatGPT produced initial material. Takinouchi corrected confused pronouns, dated phrases, and broken logic, then changed the title and ending and added the CRISPR-Cas9 material. Of the 2026 Hoshi winners, this has the clearest public account of AI-generated prose being extensively rewritten.
The 13th Hoshi award received 2,107 entries. Organizers counted 491 as partly AI-created and said three of the four general-division winners had used AI somewhere in the process.
ðºð¸ Artist books The Library of Nonhuman Books by Karen Ann Donnachie and Andy Simionato â Robert Coover Award, First Place, 2020 An AI reading machine uses computer vision, OCR, and language processing to find short poetic combinations in physical books, erase the surrounding words, pair them with images, and publish new volumes. One of those volumes, Perception , also won Australiaâs Cornish Family Prize.
ð¸ð° Poetry collection VÃ½sledky vzniku by Liza Gennart â ZlatÃ¡ vlna, 2021 Zuzana HusÃ¡rovÃ¡ and Ä½ubomÃ­r PanÃ¡k trained GPT-2 on 2,108 Slovak works, then curated and lightly edited its poems. The collection won Slovakiaâs annual prize for the best original Slovak poetry book.
ðºð¸ Poetry series ReRites by David Jhave Johnston â Electronic Literature Organization Robert Coover Award, 2022 Twelve books of poetry built from neural-network output selected and edited by Johnston. The project openly calls itself âHuman + A.I. poetry,â which is exactly the kind of thing an electronic-literature award exists to recognize.
ðºð¸ Chapbook A Black Story May Contain Sensitive Content by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram â DIAGRAM/New Michigan Press Chapbook Contest, Winner, 2023 Bertram used GPT-3 and Warpland, a model trained on Gwendolyn Brooks. Three sections contain machine responses to her prompts. The press knew how the book was made and published it openly.
ðºð¸ Short story Stargazers by Ruei-Jie Chang â UCSB Mind & Machine Intelligence Writing Contest, First Prize, 2024 Chang used ChatGPT for the seed of the story and Claude to organize and translate a Mandarin-English draft, then revised it. The contest explicitly welcomed human-only, machine-only, and hybrid entries, and required everyone to document the process.
ð·ðº Short story 30â70 by Yana Vagner â Valentin Kataev Literary Prize, Winner, 2025 Vagner wrote the story with Alice, Yandexâs AI assistant. It begins by showing her prompt and the AIâs response, then uses the system for recurring climate reports. The collaboration was visible when the story won.
ð¬ð§ Generative poem WORDS BEYOND WORDS by Sasha Stiles â Lumen Prize Literature & Poetry Award, 2025 A fine-tuned language model uses Stilesâs prompts, source texts, and code to make a new poem whenever the work is refreshed. The system itself, rather than a single fixed output, received the award.
ð¬ð§ Interactive fiction Flesh & Blood by Chris Joseph â Electronic Literature Organization Robert Coover Award, 2026 An interactive story where readers solve puzzles in a disturbing world of bodies and machinery. Joseph openly lists it among his AI-assisted works .
ð«ð· Novel CâÃ©tait Ã§a ou mourir by ThÃ©lyson OrÃ©lien â Prix du Roman Fnac, 2026 The novel won Fnacâs prize, then was removed from the Goncourt longlist after AI allegations. On October 21, BorÃ©al dropped OrÃ©lien after an external review reportedly found AI markers in working-document metadata. The publisher said it still did not know how much AI had been used. OrÃ©lien had denied that any sentence was machine-generated.
ð¸ð¬ Poems Migrant Writers of Singapore poetry competition â Migrant Literature Festival, 2024 Eight winners were announced, then the entire list was recalled after organizers said three winning entries were AI-generated. Their review relied partly on Scribbr and QuillBot.
ðºð¸ Poems Poetry.com November and December contests â Two Monthly First Prizes, 2024 Poetry.com said both original winners were created âwith assistanceâ from AI, changed the results, and redistributed the prizes. The removed poems and writers are no longer reliably identifiable. The names on the current result pages are the replacements, not the accused entrants.
ð¯ðµ Novel Sympathy Tower Tokyo by Rie Kudan â 170th Akutagawa Prize, 2024 Kudan first guessed that about 5% of the novel involved ChatGPT, then gave a much smaller figure: about one page out of 143. She consulted its output for the replies written by the AI inside the novel. The prize stood.
ð¨ð³ Short story The Land of Machine Memories by Shen Yang, writing as âQuartZenâ â 5th Youth Popular Science and Science Fiction Competition, Second Prize, 2023 AI generated the title, prose, illustrations, and pen name over 66 rounds of prompting. The organizer invited Shen and hid the experiment from the judges. This is often called a national literary prize, but it was a broad Jiangsu association contest: 18 stories shared second prize and 90 of roughly 200 entries received awards.
ð¯ðµ Web novel Modest Skill âTidying Upâ Is the Strongest! â 18th AlphaPolis Fantasy Novel Awards, Grand Prize and Readerâs Choice, 2025 The author said a large majority of the web novel was made with generative AI. AlphaPolis later canceled the print edition and manga adaptation and changed its rules. Reporting confirms those cancellations, but not that the two award labels were formally revoked.
ðºð¸ Memoir How to Win One Million Dollars and $#!T Glitter! by Luke Stoffel â IBPA Book Award, Benjamin Franklin Silver Medal for Neurodivergent Communities, 2026 Stoffel says he used ChatGPT for grammar and structural scaffolding and disclosed it in the book and award submission. IBPAâs guidelines did not prohibit AI-assisted work , and the book received Silver. IBPA has not publicly commented on his AI use.
ð¿ð¼ Short story The Blue Fighter by Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza â Caine Prize for African Writing, Winner, 2026 Pangram flagged almost the entire story as AI-generated, according to The Atlantic . Kundizeza denied using AI and said the story drew on his familyâs experiences. The prize opened a review. No final finding or revocation had been announced as of October 21.
ð¬ð§ Short story The Serpent in the Grove by Jamir Nazir â Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Overall Winner, 2026 Pangram called it 100% AI-generated. Nazir denied it and described six or seven drafts made with Android speech-to-text because of a chronic condition. The Commonwealth Foundation reviewed drafts, timestamps, notes, and testimony, accepted his account, and kept the award. The allegation is disputed, not proven.
ð¬ð§ Short story The Bastionâs Shadow by John Edward DeMicoli â Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Canada and Europe Winner, 2026 Pangram also returned 100% here. DeMicoli produced handwritten drafts, notes, and years of research and denied using AI. The Foundation accepted the evidence and the prize stood.
ð¬ð§ Short story Mehendi Nights by Sharon Aruparayil â Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Asia Winner, 2026 Aruparayil denied using AI at any stage and kept a paper trail. She also found that adding three Marathi words and removing one word made a flagged section register as 100% human. The Foundation kept the award.
ð¬ð§ Short story Descend by Chanel Sutherland â Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Overall Winner, 2025 Pangram scanned the story a year later and labeled it 88% AI-generated. Sutherland denied using AI and said its repetition and rhythm come from Vincentian oral storytelling. Her publisher and agent backed her. No public provenance review of the 2025 story has been released.
ð¬ð§ Short story Back and Forth by Kavyta Kay â Harperâs Bazaar UK Short Story Competition, Winner, 2026 A screenshot of a 100% Pangram result spread online. No author response, organizer investigation, admission, or revocation has surfaced.
ð¬ð§ Poem + unknown Peter Doolan and an unnamed winner â Plaza Prizes, 2025 The Plaza disqualified both after detector flags while admitting it could not know how much AI had been used, âif any.â Both denied it. Doolan said his poem had already been published in 2018. This looks less like an AI scandal than a detector-driven procedural failure.
ðºð¸ Comics anthology Stardust the Super Wizard Anthology â Eisner Award for Best Anthology, Nominee, 2026 One page was an AI-generated comic credited to the invented âAlex Irons.â The editor and other contributors reportedly did not know. After Comic-Con said the judges would not have nominated it had they known, the editor withdrew the anthology from the ballot.
ð§ð· Illustrated edition Frankenstein, Clube de Literatura ClÃ¡ssica edition â PrÃªmio Jabuti Illustration Category, Finalist, 2023 The book openly credited designer Vicente PessÃ´a and Midjourney and was marketed as fully AI-illustrated. Two judges said they did not realize Midjourney was AI. The edition was disqualified under rules that had never anticipated generative art.
ð¬ð§ Illustrated book Unnamed illustrated title â Ink Book Prize, Shortlisted, 2026 The prize removed one title after complaints about AI in its illustrations. A different shortlistee withdrew in protest. Comparing the old and new lists suggests possible titles, but neither the organizers nor the reporting named the accused book, so I wonât either.
ð³ð¿ Novellas + stories Angel Train and Obligate Carnivore by Elizabeth Smither and Stephanie Johnson â Ockham New Zealand Book Awards, 2026 Both books were initially barred because their publisher used AI-generated covers, then reinstated after the awards trust decided the rule had arrived too late. Neither reached the longlist.
ð¯ðµ Short story Cage of Algorithms by Keiji Aono â 12th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Finalist, 2025 Aono says roughly 80% was AI-generated and 20% human-revised. It reached the final ten out of 1,250 entries but did not win.
ð¯ðµ Short story The Day a Computer Writes a Novel â 3rd Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, First Round, 2016 Humans supplied the plot, characters, and language components; software assembled the prose. It passed the first screening but did not win. The rules explicitly allowed nonhuman entrants, making this a pre-LLM precursor rather than a deception.
