title: Show HN: Buildnotes – Turn pull requests into "how it's made" posts
body:
A skill for coding agents. It reads a feature's issues, PRs and reviews, and finds the few decisions that shaped it.
/buildnotes before and after screenshots, side by side How we built room walkthrough videos
A frame from chapter 2. Point at a note.
Reads the issues, PRs, commits and reviews.
Picks the few decisions worth a chapter.
Draws the figures, writes it up, and checks it.
Ask in plain words, inside the repo. The first word picks the output; the post is the default. Ask for a technical deep dive or a release story to write for engineers or for users.
Chapters, drawn figures and real code, as a page you can publish as is or move to your own site.
The post as a short video that plays itself.
The video as slides you click through, and a PDF.
Any figure on its own, as an image, GIF, video or SVG.
Figures come from the real product. This one started as a screenshot of the weekly digest card in Release Notes Index, redrawn straight on so each part can be named.
Before and after screenshots: tag two, and the pull request comment shows them side by side.
Weekly digests: a card, a replay of the week, and one email a week per reader.
Turn pull requests into posts and videos worth sharing. A skill for coding agents.

title: Major US banks are locking out AI agents that log in with customer credentials
body:
AI agents are using customer-provided credentials to access bank accounts without bank approval. Several major US banks, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, are restricting external AI agent access, Axios reports . That violates bank policies requiring account holders to log in personally. Some AI agents appear to act on their own , without direct instructions from users. Morgan Stanley already blocks AI agents entirely, and JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are doing the same. Morgan Stanley stressed that it has not seen any " rogue AI agents " on its platforms.
Most banks want to limit agents to read-only access, letting them view account data but not carry out any actions. The banks say customers want to use AI agents, but the security risks are too high for now. Many banks also can't tell whether an agent is acting on a user's behalf or accessing an account on its own.
Users can give their agents access to accounts through a browser, using tools like Computer Use or open-source agent software such as OpenClaw . Blocking that on the provider side will be hard. OpenAI has even launched a dedicated ChatGPT service for financial tasks in the US with read-only access to financial data. Ad Ad

title: Ukraine Expands Satellite Cooperation With Finland as Starlink Doubts Linger
body:
Ukraine signed seven agreements with Finland, including deals to expand Kyiv’s use of Finnish satellite capabilities through Nokia and ICEYE after recent Starlink disruptions exposed how much of the country’s defense hinges on a single private provider that can restrict service with no prior warning.
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the agreements in a statement on Thursday, Oct. 22, after holding discussions with the government of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo. The documents, signed at the Ukrainian-Finnish Business Forum, outlines possible cooperation in defense production, rail transport, energy and housing construction, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We agreed that we will make greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities,” Zelensky said. “This is important for our defense and for Ukraine’s resilience.”
The total estimated value of today’s agreements is nearly €300 million (roughly $337 million).
Among the agreements, Finland committed to hand over 10 Dv12 diesel locomotives and spare parts to Ukraine’s state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, free of charge.
Rail transport has become one of Ukraine’s most vital lifelines, with the country’s airspace closed to civilian flights from February 2022. Ukrainian citizens heavily rely on trains for travel, and the railway also carries critical cargo, including food shipments, across the country, making it a frequent target for Russian forces.
According to Koretskyi, Finland has become the first country to donate locomotives to Ukraine free of charge.
Earlier this week, Estonia has confirmed it will send a substantial number of locomotives to Ukraine. Although Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha did not provide additional information on the shipment, he said on Tuesday, Oct. 20, that during talks with Estonia, he had “outlined our urgent needs to strengthen Ukraine’s defense and resilience ahead of winter, with a particular focus on Russian strikes against our railways”
The appeal for railway help initially came mid-September, when Sybiha urged allies to provide Ukraine with replacement locomotives after a Russian strike hit a railway infrastructure just kilometers from the Polish border in Volyn region , in what may have been a deliberate attack on a train carrying diplomats .
Western allies were asked in particular to assist in finding locomotives compatible with the 1,520-milimeter railway gauge Ukraine uses, as well as provide funding to accelerate the procurement of new ones.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 locomotives, with over half of those losses recorded this year alone, according to Sybiha’s estimates.
Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine’s Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport said on Aug. 23 that Russia has attacked Ukraine’s railway infrastructure at least 1,534 times so far in 2026.
Ukrainian drone manufacturers are also exploring expanding joint production with Finnish companies on Finnish soil, Koretskyi said.
Separately, employers’ associations from the two countries plan to establish a Ukrainian-Finnish Industrial Council, while another project focuses on industrial housing construction.
The two governments also agreed to share experience in protecting critical infrastructure and discussed Ukraine’s need for mobile shelters.
Meanwhile, Kyiv invited Finland to join its War Risk Insurance Fund.
“We expect Finnish companies to become key investors and long-term partners of Ukraine,” Koretskyi said. “Together, we can create products, technologies and businesses that will be competitive in Ukraine and across Europe.”
Ukraine’s large unused gas storage capacity and developed gas transmission system were on the agenda as well, with the two sides discussing how they could help Europe build strategic non-commercial gas reserves.
The discussions come as the EU works to cut off Russian gas entirely.
According to the European Commission , the EU’s dependency on gas imported from Russia has fallen from 45% of total imports to 12% in 2025, while all imports of Russian coal have been banned under EU sanctions.
“The remaining 35 billion cubic meters of Russian gas still imported to the EU annually will be out of our markets in less than two years,” the EC said on its official website.
In January 2026, EU member states gave final approval to a law banning Russian gas imports by late 2027, despite opposition from Hungary and Slovakia, both of which remain heavily reliant on Russian energy.
Under the law, imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) will end by the end of 2026, and pipeline gas by Sept. 30, 2027. According to The Baltic Times , Brussels built the ban on trade and energy legislation rather than sanctions, which require unanimity, so that it could not be blocked by Budapest and Bratislava.
The agreements with Finland come as Ukraine and its European partners search for alternatives to Starlink, the satellite service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, speed restrictions were imposed on Starlink terminals without prior warning, crippling Ukraine’s drone operations. The limits disrupted several types of drones Ukraine uses to defend itself against Russian attacks, including interceptor drones deployed against jet-powered Shaheds.
The connectivity was lost on terminals moving at roughly 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) or faster, while Ukraine needed the operating speeds to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour).
The restrictions coincided with a reported week-long suspension of US intelligence sharing, which left Kyiv without allied warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks , saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and, by doing so, endangered civilians.
After meeting senior US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday, Oct. 20, Zelensky confirmed the intelligence sharing had resumed . He added that progress on Starlink restrictions and Patriot interceptors could come within 48 hours.
Separately on Thursday, US Vice President JD Vance said Musk should not be at the center of the dispute over restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite service, framing the issue instead as a matter of US policy toward Russia’s war.
“Well, I think that fundamentally Elon Musk runs a private corporation, and I think it’s completely understandable that he doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the US government effectively directing him on what to do,” he said, leaving unanswered who ordered the restrictions.
Both Musk and the White House denied responsibility for the restrictions, while pinning the blame to the other.
Meanwhile, the European Union is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program that could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027.
Currently, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones and political pressure to develop alternatives is growing.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Human rights group petitions Germany to investigate Iranian crimes against ethnic minorities
body: The human rights organization Hiwa has petitioned Germany's Federal Public Prosecutor General to initiate a structural investigation into possible crimes against humanity in Iran and the systematic use of violence against protesters of ethnic minority backgrounds, the human rights organization's president told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.Human rights organizations have reported that tens of thousands of protesters were killed by the Islamic regime during its attempts to suppress the January protests. Hiwa has urged the prosecutor general to examine specifically whether members of the Kurdish and Baloch minorities were targeted because of their ethnic identity.The petition is also based on documented human rights violations committed in connection with the suppression of the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protest movement in 2022 and 2023, as well as the most recent mass killings and subsequent wave of repression.Hiwa President Sardar Pashaei told the Post that the petition was intended to send a message to Iran, ensuring that every member of the regime understood that even if they “escape justice today, they cannot count on escaping accountability forever.”“Under the Islamic Republic's judicial system, victims of state violence have virtually no path to justice. Where can people turn when they have been imprisoned, tortured, or sexually assaulted? Where can parents seek justice when their children have been shot and killed for protesting? When judges and prosecutors are part of the machinery of repression, who will hold the perpetrators accountable? These families are often denied even the right to mourn,” Pashaei said. “But if justice is denied inside Iran, we cannot allow it to be denied outside Iran as well. Impunity must not follow the perpetrators beyond Iran's borders.”Human rights orgs. document unlawful killing, torture, sexual violenceInternational human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, have repeatedly documented the regime's use of unlawful killings, torture, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, and the denial of medical care against demonstrators. According to Amnesty International's findings, 62% of the recorded deaths associated with the Women, Life, Freedom protest movement were among Kurds and Baloch, even though these groups together make up a comparatively small proportion of Iran's population.Citing Amnesty International's conclusion that the disproportionate impact on Kurds and Baloch indicated that killings and torture were also committed with discriminatory intent on ethnic grounds, Hiwa called for an investigation into the crackdown on protesters. It urged Berlin to independently examine whether the selection of victims, the severity of the violence, and the state's treatment of the affected communities indicated systematic persecution on ethnic grounds.As part of the evidence submitted with the petition, Pashaei said Hiwa had presented the prosecutor general with the testimony of Farideh Salavati, a Kurdish woman now living in Germany who lost much of her vision after Iranian security forces fired at her eyes during the Women, Life, Freedom protests. Salavati has undergone surgery in Germany that restored some of her vision, but she continues to suffer from pellets lodged in her body.Hiwa argued that the regime's documented actions in 2022, 2023, and 2026 should not be examined in isolation, but as part of a recurring pattern of state repression. It said a structural investigation could help establish broader patterns of criminal conduct, institutional links, and possible chains of command and responsibility, while preserving evidence for potential future criminal proceedings.Hiwa calls on Berlin to investigate links between rights violators and GermanyHiwa also called on Berlin to investigate potential links between those responsible for the human rights violations and Germany, so that relevant sanctions, asset seizures, and arrest warrants could be pursued.Dr. Dunja Hodaie, legal counsel for Hiwa, told the Post, “Preserving evidence and witness testimony now is critical. We do not know when those responsible may face justice, but evidence collected today could make future prosecutions possible.“The message is clear: time and distance should not guarantee impunity. Those responsible for international crimes may still face prosecution years from now, including when they travel beyond Iran's borders.

title: Department of War and Lockheed Martin Finalize Landmark 10-Year F-35 Deal
body: Today, the Department of War and Lockheed Martin finalized a landmark 10-year framework agreement to strengthen the F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter fleet. The agreement creates a stable, long-term procurement signal to modernize and expand America’s 5th generation tactical aircraft. Execution of the agreement remains subject to Congressional authorization and appropriations. “We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” said Under Secretary of War Michael P. Duffey. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.” This framework marks a major operational milestone for the Department’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy, which drives industrial base resilience through long-term procurement visibility and rapid private capital investment. In exchange for this decade-long commitment, Lockheed Martin will self-fund at least $7 billion in initiatives that support the F-35 Program. Furthermore, it guarantees a minimum floor of 850 U.S. aircraft over the ten-year period and includes procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, plus sustainment of the global F-35 Fleet. By integrating hardware requirements across the supply chain, this deal maximizes purchasing power and delivers true economies of scale. From Pentagon News, Oct. 22, 2026 The post Department of War and Lockheed Martin Finalize Landmark 10-Year F-35 Deal appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: SMWDC Hosts Directed Energy Working Group
body: SAN DIEGO — Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center (SMWDC) hosts a directed energy working group Oct. 19, bringing together stakeholders to advance the integration of directed energy capabilities into surface force operations. The working group focused on the Surface Navy’s evolving directed energy tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), doctrine and capability development priorities. SMWDC enhances the surface force’s lethality and readiness. Photo credit: U.S. Navy The Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center (SMWDC) hosted a directed energy working group Oct. 19, bringing together stakeholders to advance the integration of directed energy capabilities into surface force operations. The working group focused on the Surface Navy’s evolving directed energy tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), doctrine and capability development priorities. “Directed energy gives our warfighters another means to fight, defend and sustain combat power in a contested environment,” said Cmdr. Rob Toohig, SMWDC experimentation lead. “Our focus is ensuring Sailors have the tactics, training and technical understanding needed to employ these capabilities effectively.” The event concluded with a capability gap discussion in which SMWDC Warfare Tactics Instructors examined concepts for employing directed energy systems across the surface fleet. Warfare Tactics Instructors from the Integrated Air and Missile Defense warfare area and the Directed Energy Community of Focus discussed current capabilities and limitations and identified potential paths forward. Participants from the Surface Requirements Group (SURFRG) also provided insight on surface force tactical gaps and how today’s working group could help address those gaps through technology. SMWDC’s SURFRG executes a process to provide the single voice for Commander, Naval Surface Forces, to cover the surface fleet’s most pressing tactical gaps and identify prioritized solutions to close them rapidly. SURFRG, as the type commander’s executive agent to the Department of the Navy Rapid Capabilities Office (DONRCO) and lead for the DONRCO Surface Adoption Team, aims to increase surface force lethality at the speed of relevance. Directed energy is an increasingly important element of naval warfare, providing the fleet additional means to defend itself, preserve combat power and sustain operations during prolonged conflict. “Warfighting advantage comes from putting capability in the hands of Sailors, learning through operational employment and rapidly applying those lessons across the fleet,” said Col. Joseph Rosal, director of directed energy for the Office of the Secretary of War for Research and Engineering. “This effort helps ensure directed energy is developed and integrated to meet the demands of future maritime combat.” Fleet Sailors will play a central role in advancing these capabilities. Operational employment, at-sea experimentation and fleet feedback will help inform future TTPs, training, doctrine and capability development. SMWDC’s efforts are intended to place emerging capabilities in the hands of Sailors early, learn through operations and rapidly incorporate lessons into the surface force. About the Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center: SMWDC is the Navy’s warfighting development center for surface warfare and mine warfare. Its mission is to increase the lethality and tactical proficiency of the surface fleet across all domains by providing tactical expertise and solutions through the development and assessment of warfighting doctrine, concepts, tactics, techniques and procedures. From Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center, Oct. 19, 2026 The post SMWDC Hosts Directed Energy Working Group appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse
body:
Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?”
Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.”
The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said during the call, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which, as of today, bring in pretty much all the money Meta makes.
This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.”
Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years.
All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned in to Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one.
To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by more than 10 million users in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce: A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending, on average, more than $200 per purchase.
Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time.
Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a YouTuber said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been reports of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told Bloomberg earlier this week that it would consider blocking Muse from accessing its customers’ financial data.
Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending, Supermarket Sweep episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New research from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up.
If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care.
“Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s CFO Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees.
Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday, it owes New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it.
Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency.
It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already research on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy-use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it.
Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself.
“One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base.
Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said, adding, “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.”
Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.”
Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens.

title: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over
body:
From AI companies financing data center projects to France's heavily indebted government, credit markets are flashing warnings as investors grow warier of borrowing risks.
Five-year credit default swap spreads have widened for CoreWeave , Oracle and SoftBank Group , as well as France and Italy, according to CNBC's analysis of FactSet data.
AI-related bonds have been selling off as markets raise the cost of capital amid concerns of a financing crunch. Neocloud demand is "off the charts," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday, but he warned of a "scarcity of capital." "The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," he said, adding, "that's going to get solved."
Countries like France face a similar crunch. Pressure is building in bond markets as investors demand more compensation to finance public debt. Recent mass protests and rioting in France have heightened the market's concerns.
"Markets may no longer want to underwrite massive capex, heavy leverage, and uncertain future cash flows, and that same shift is widening French sovereign spreads as investors demand more compensation to hold long‑duration, debt‑financed obligations from a strained state," FedWatch Advisors CIO and founder Ben Emons wrote on his "French Neoclouds " Substack post.
CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are at the heart of the AI infrastructure buildout, spanning data centers, cloud services and financing.
Their five-year CDS spreads offer a window into investors' anxiety about the cost of it all and eventual payoff. Higher spreads mean more expensive default protection and can signal greater concern about a borrower's creditworthiness.
CoreWeave has experienced some of the sharpest increases in default-protection costs. Its five-year CDS spread reached 1,065.84 basis points on Oct. 21, according to FactSet, reflecting heightened concerns about the debt-heavy company's ability to finance its expansion.
At the same time Oracle's spread rose to 308.25 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 141 on Jan. 2. S&P Credit Ratings downgraded Oracle's debt to the lowest level of investment grade in July, citing the expanding infrastructure business raised the overall credit risk.
Softbank is a major AI investor with a large stake in OpenAI and investments in data centers and power infrastructure, including an $87 billion commitment for data centers in France. Its five-year CDS spread stood near a four-year high of 432 basis points on Oct. 20, up from 284 basis points on Jan. 5.
France isn't in a full-fledged debt crisis, but markets are signaling unease with the cost of protecting against a sovereign default rising above that of Italy's, which has also increased.
France's five-year credit default swap spread reached 89.8 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 29.74 basis points on Jan. 2, according to CNBC's analysis. Italy's spread increased to 67.1 basis points on Oct. 22 from 28.33 on Jan 2. France's budget uncertainty and debt burden have become a focus, raising concerns that the risk could spill over to other countries in Europe.
Germany's spread also rose but remained much lower at 12.15 basis points on Oct. 22, compared with 7.47 at the start of the period.
Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, pointed to France's mounting debt burden and persistent fiscal deficits as key drivers of rising default-protection costs.
"The key drivers are the large amount of French sovereign debt (120% of GDP) and the inability to reduce the deficit," Wizman told CNBC. In comparison to France, German government debt is 65% of the country's GDP.
Investors are also watching the spread between French and German bonds, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, which has also surged to 1.6 percentage points. France's 10-year bond yield also topped 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread between the 10-year yield on French OATs and German Bunds is the extra payment investors demand to hold French bonds instead of German.
While the Franco-German spread is relatively wide, the Eurozone saw far larger gaps in borrowing costs during the Eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s.
France faces another test on Oct. 23 when Moody's is scheduled to review its Aa3 sovereign rating , which carries a negative outlook. The review comes as political divisions complicate efforts to repair the country's public finances.
While stresses are popping up in some pockets of AI financing, debt markets are also pricing in higher costs. S&P Global warned on Oct. 19 that major cloud providers may have more AI-linked debt exposure than publicly recognized.
CDS indexes offer a broader picture of credit-market pressure by tracking default-protection costs across baskets of companies.
North America's CDX High Yield index captures credit risk across speculative-grade companies. Its five-year midpoint spread reached 355.35 basis points on Oct. 20, up about 39 basis points from the end of 2025, according to data from LSEG.
The widening suggests investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk beyond AI-linked borrowers.

title: Israeli intelligence helps Saudi Arabia target Houthis as IDF prepares for potential escalation
body: IDF intelligence continues to provide Saudi Arabia with exceptional capabilities to assist its military operations against the Houthis through US mediation, a defense official confirmed on Thursday.The assistance is being provided in accordance with Israel's national interests and directives from the political leadership, the official said, emphasizing that the Shi'ite-Sunni confrontation reflects developments taking place beneath the surface across the Middle East.According to the official, Sunni countries are watching the escalation led by the Houthis against neighboring Saudi Arabia, with encouragement and support from Iran, and understand that they could be next.Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is concentrating its efforts on launching powerful attacks against an extensive range of targets in Houthi-controlled areas, seeking to degrade critical military capabilities, including infrastructure."Two main points need to be made about this. First, it serves Israel's interests quite well because it wears down the military strength of an Israeli enemy that is preparing and planning to harm us in the future. In addition, we are monitoring and observing methods of operation and tactics, and learning a great deal from what is happening there, including about weapons that are not necessarily manufactured by the Houthis," the official said.IDF helps Saudi Arabia combat HouthisThe defense official added that the relentless attacks against the Houthis are eroding their capabilities and forcing them to expend considerable effort. "The Houthis are accustomed to building up their forces, not employing them on this scale. They are a serious enemy, well structured for the long term, but this presents them with a significant challenge. It is no coincidence that they operate sequentially rather than simultaneously against their enemies."The official further said that the pressure on Saudi Arabia is reshaping alliances and relationships across the Middle East, creating new opportunities."The question here is who will intervene on Saudi Arabia's behalf. There is apprehension among countries, but we assess that there will be intervention. Everything remains open, and it is not too late for that to happen."Meanwhile, the IDF is completing preparations across the sea, air, land, and electromagnetic spectrum domains for a potential Houthi attack as part of a multi-front scenario involving Iran, Hezbollah, and Shi'ite militias operating from Iraq.The preparations include not only the integration of new technologies and sensors, along with improved connectivity within the IDF and between organizations, but also coordination with the US military. The US military has a clear interest in protecting Israel's home front because thousands of American troops, aircraft, and US military systems, including air defense systems, are stationed in Israel.

title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation

title: SMWDC Hosts Directed Energy Working Group at Naval Base San Diego
body: SAN DIEGO — Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center (SMWDC) hosts a directed energy working group Oct. 19, bringing together stakeholders to advance the integration of directed energy capabilities into surface force operations. The working group focused on the Surface Navy’s evolving directed energy tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), doctrine and capability development priorities. SMWDC enhances the surface force’s lethality and readiness. Photo credit: U.S. Navy The Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center (SMWDC) hosted a directed energy working group Oct. 19, bringing together stakeholders to advance the integration of directed energy capabilities into surface force operations. The working group focused on the Surface Navy’s evolving directed energy tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), doctrine and capability development priorities. “Directed energy gives our warfighters another means to fight, defend and sustain combat power in a contested environment,” said Cmdr. Rob Toohig, SMWDC experimentation lead. “Our focus is ensuring Sailors have the tactics, training and technical understanding needed to employ these capabilities effectively.” The event concluded with a capability gap discussion in which SMWDC Warfare Tactics Instructors examined concepts for employing directed energy systems across the surface fleet. Warfare Tactics Instructors from the Integrated Air and Missile Defense warfare area and the Directed Energy Community of Focus discussed current capabilities and limitations and identified potential paths forward. Participants from the Surface Requirements Group (SURFRG) also provided insight on surface force tactical gaps and how today’s working group could help address those gaps through technology. SMWDC’s SURFRG executes a process to provide the single voice for Commander, Naval Surface Forces, to cover the surface fleet’s most pressing tactical gaps and identify prioritized solutions to close them rapidly. SURFRG, as the type commander’s executive agent to the Department of the Navy Rapid Capabilities Office (DONRCO) and lead for the DONRCO Surface Adoption Team, aims to increase surface force lethality at the speed of relevance. Directed energy is an increasingly important element of naval warfare, providing the fleet additional means to defend itself, preserve combat power and sustain operations during prolonged conflict. “Warfighting advantage comes from putting capability in the hands of Sailors, learning through operational employment and rapidly applying those lessons across the fleet,” said Col. Joseph Rosal, director of directed energy for the Office of the Secretary of War for Research and Engineering. “This effort helps ensure directed energy is developed and integrated to meet the demands of future maritime combat.” Fleet Sailors will play a central role in advancing these capabilities. Operational employment, at-sea experimentation and fleet feedback will help inform future TTPs, training, doctrine and capability development. SMWDC’s efforts are intended to place emerging capabilities in the hands of Sailors early, learn through operations and rapidly incorporate lessons into the surface force. About the Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center: SMWDC is the Navy’s warfighting development center for surface warfare and mine warfare. Its mission is to increase the lethality and tactical proficiency of the surface fleet across all domains by providing tactical expertise and solutions through the development and assessment of warfighting doctrine, concepts, tactics, techniques and procedures. From Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center, Oct. 19, 2026 The post SMWDC Hosts Directed Energy Working Group at Naval Base San Diego appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: AI-enabled logistics to aid Pentagon in asset tracking, management
body:
RESTON, Va. Leidos announced that it signed a new $95 million, five-year contract with the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) to use artificial intelligence (AI) automation to streamline and accelerate the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) asset-management system that more than 50 federal agencies use to manage more 80 million items of government property, collectively valued at more than $140 billion.
Under the terms of the new accord, Leidos will extend its 20-plus of support for the Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS), a tool that helps the DoD manage and account for assets throughout their life cycle, supporting the logistics enterprise that keeps warfighters equipped and ready.
Leidos officials say the company will will apply AI-driven automation, cloud, and modern software-development practices to accelerate software delivery, streamline processes, and support reliable ELMS operations.
Under the auspices of this contract , Leidos is advancing its "NorthStar 2030" strategy by bringing mission-ready defense technology to a critical logistics system.

title: Mammoet, Port of Argentia and Argentia Capital Partner to Advance Floating Dry Dock
body: Mammoet, Port of Argentia and Argentia Capital Partner to Advance Floating Dry Dock and Marine Repair Facility Mammoet Canada Eastern Ltd., Port of Argentia Inc., and Argentia Capital Inc. (ACI) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance the development of a floating dry dock and marine repair facility at Port of Argentia. The initiative brings innovative marine technology and new industrial capacity to Newfoundland and Labrador. Partnership builds on Mammoet’s established presence at Port of Argentia and shared confidence in the growing market for ship repair and marine industrial services. The partnership integrates Mammoet’s global expertise in engineered heavy lifting, transport, and marine operations, specialized technology from its subsidiary Tugdock Submersible Platforms Ltd., and Port of Argentia’s strategic marine infrastructure and development capabilities. At the centre of the initiative is Tugdock’s Submersible Platform (TSP), a modular floating dry dock system designed to accommodate a wide range of vessels and industrial applications. Its scalable design provides a flexible alternative to conventional dry-docking infrastructure and can adapt to evolving market requirements. “This partnership represents an exciting opportunity to build on Mammoet’s established presence at Argentia and introduce advanced, scalable marine technology to the Canadian market,” said Jeremy Asher , Managing Director. “By combining our technical expertise and Tugdock’s adaptable platform with the Port’s strategic infrastructure, we see significant potential to develop a competitive marine repair and servicing operation.” The proposed facility would leverage Port of Argentia’s world-class graving dock infrastructure, deep-water and ice-free harbour, extensive industrial land base, and separation from residential areas, conditions that support year-round, around-the-clock marine industrial operations. The project would also benefit from access to a skilled regional workforce with extensive experience in marine, industrial, and heavy construction sectors. “We have developed a strong working relationship with Mammoet through its operations at the Port, including its presence at the Cenovus Graving Dock site and its role in the Port’s offshore wind marshalling projects,” said Scott Penney , CEO, Port of Argentia. “Our advanced marine infrastructure, combined with Mammoet’s global expertise and innovative technology, presents an exciting opportunity to expand marine industrial capabilities at Argentia. This partnership aligns perfectly with the opportunities we see emerging across Canada’s marine industry.” The facility is intended to serve a diverse marine market, including commercial vessel operators, the Canadian Coast Guard, the Royal Canadian Navy, offshore oil and gas operators, and the emerging offshore wind industry. “Port of Argentia should be viewed not just as a location for individual projects, but as a strategic national industrial and marine hub capable of supporting Canada’s long-term trade, economic security, critical minerals, defence, and industrial development objectives,” said Carl Sheppard , CEO, Argentia Capital Inc. “The former Cenovus Graving Dock site is a valuable marine industrial asset. This MOU provides an opportunity to work collaboratively with partners who bring proven technology and expertise to explore new marine industrial opportunities at Port of Argentia.” Through the MOU, the partners will advance plans for a scalable, multi-client facility that strengthens Newfoundland and Labrador’s marine supply chain, creates opportunities for local businesses and skilled trades, and expands the province’s marine industrial capabilities. In the coming months, the partners intend to initiate a formal Expression of Interest (EOI) process to identify a globally recognized marine industrial operator with the expertise and capacity to operate the proposed facility and support the development of marine services at Port of Argentia. The post Mammoet, Port of Argentia and Argentia Capital Partner to Advance Floating Dry Dock appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine
body: Amazon Polly Generative engine now offers more natural and accurate speech output. We’re introducing an upgrade to the Amazon Polly Generative engine that delivers more expressive, more accurate speech output with low latency. The upgrade adds 14 new voices across 9 locales, including general availability of Generative voices in Hindi and Finnish for the first time. The upgrade is now generally available in production. Importantly, this is a drop-in upgrade for existing generative voices. Voice names and API calls are unchanged, so your existing applications continue to work as they do today. Amazon Polly is a fully managed AWS service that converts text into natural-sounding speech for contact centers, large language model (LLM)-based agentic applications, media and entertainment, e-learning, accessibility, and other applications that require reliable voice output at scale. Hear the difference You can use sample audio to evaluate the improvements directly. The more natural, authentic, and expressive voices. Hear how Tiffany welcomes you in a delightful tone. “Hi there! I’m Tiffany, one of Polly’s generative voices. I was built to sound natural, expressive, and a little bit delightful. What should we talk about?” Accurate speech generation for numbers, currency, addresses, and so on. Kenneth reads back an order confirmation, including the tracking number, date and time, currency and address accurately. “Thanks for calling. Your order, number 4471 9902 ships today to 85 Harbor View Drive, Apartment 4B, Portland, Oregon 97209. It should arrive on Thursday, October 22nd, between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your total was $1,284.50 and your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.” Net new languages. Arjun and Kiara for Hindi, and Suvi for Finnish. Hindi and Finnish are generally available for the first time on the Amazon Polly Generative engine. Arjun : नमस्कार, आप सुन रहे हैं आज की मुख्य ख़बरें। देश के कई हिस्सों में मानसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम सुहाना हो गया है। (Hello, you’re listening to today’s top stories. As the monsoon retreats across much of the country, the weather has turned pleasant.) Kiara : नमस्ते! मेरा नाम कियारा है। आइए, आज मैं आपको एक छोटी सी कहानी सुनाती हूँ।(Hello! My name is Kiara. Come, let me tell you a little story today.) Suvi : Majakanvartija ei ollut nähnyt laivaa yhteentoista päivään. Sitten, vähän puolenyön jälkeen, horisontissa välähti yksi ainoa valo. Kerran. Kahdesti. Ja sitten, uskomatonta kyllä, se vilkutti takaisin hänen nimensä. (The lighthouse keeper hadn’t seen a ship in eleven days. Then, just after midnight, a single light blinked on the horizon. Once. Twice. And then, impossibly, it blinked back his name.) Different styles of speech delivery based on textual context. Powered by the new Amazon Polly Generative engine, the voices can reflect emotion and prosody even better based on the text input, without manual setup. Neutral : “Your package arrived early.” Uncertainty : “So, um… your package arrived early. I think?” Surprised : “Wait, what? Your package arrived early?” New voices, languages, and Region availability A larger catalog overall for Amazon Polly Generative engine – Totaling 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales. 14 new voices across 9 locales – US English (Kenneth, Nate), Australian English (Russell, Curtis), Indian English (Kiara, Arjun), German (Tina), US Spanish (Carlos), Brazilian Portuguese (Leo, Carolina), Korean (Hyunduk), Hindi (Kiara, Arjun) and Finnish (Suvi). Net new languages generally available in Generative engine – Hindi and Finnish. Region expansion to AWS GovCloud (US-West) – Totaling 11 AWS Regions. Built for production-ready speech workflows for enterprise The upgraded Amazon Polly Generative engine uses a standard Amazon Polly API call to build your speech applications. With Amazon Polly, you can continue to build with familiar AWS patterns: call the same Amazon Polly API, manage access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), use the output in your existing applications and contact-center flows, and monitor the workloads that synthesize speech for your customers. This launch is designed to elevate the speech output quality that you can hear with your existing Amazon Polly implementation. No changes to your code are required to get the upgraded voices. For applications that already use Amazon Polly Generative voices, the upgrade happens in place. For new applications, the same SynthesizeSpeech API gives you access to a larger set of generative voice catalogs. With the Bi-Di Streaming API StartSpeechSynthesisStream , you can stream text to Amazon Polly and receive synthesized audio back simultaneously. This is well-suited for real-time applications like voice agents and bespoke characters in games. Competitive price-performance The Amazon Polly Generative engine offers competitive pricing on a pay-as-you-go basis. With this model upgrade, you get improved voice quality and accuracy at the same price. There’s no cost increase, no new SKU, and no changes to your existing integration. You can cache and replay synthesized static prompts with no additional cost. Refer to Amazon Polly pricing for complete cost information. The Amazon Polly Generative engine now delivers more natural, expressive speech alongside low-latency streaming for real-time applications, Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) support for fine-grained control, and the operational reliability of a fully managed AWS service. This combination of quality, performance, and cost efficiency supports a wide range of production use cases. What you can build Contact centers. Accuracy matters most in customer service conversations. When a caller checks an order, a voice that reads back the tracking number, address, and confirmation code correctly helps resolve the call in self-service rather than escalating to a human agent. Amazon Polly Generative voice’s accurate entity pronunciation and low-latency generation make automated interactive voice response (IVR) interactions sound more conversational. Cascaded voice agents. Using Amazon Polly in a voice agent framework, you can convert LLM response text into clear, natural-sounding speech and stream it back to users in near real time over WebSockets or telephony channels. This makes live conversational voice possible. The primary benefits are low-latency playback, high scalability, and cost efficiency. Media, localization, and dubbing. Convert scripts into finished audio for video, advertising, podcasts, product overviews, and audiobooks. You can use one voice or many, without a studio session. More natural intonation reduces post-production. The expanded locale coverage, including first-time generative Hindi and Finnish, means you can localize a single piece of content into more markets from the same pipeline. E-learning and training. Narrate courseware, onboarding, and knowledge-based articles at scale, and update them as soon as the source text changes. No re-recording is required. More expressive delivery supports engagement through long-form material. Accessibility. Provide a clear, natural spoken version of articles, documents, and applications so more people can consume your content by listening: read aloud, on the go, or with a screen reader. Interactive and transactional experiences. Voice-enable games, kiosks, IVR menus, and IoT devices with responses generated on demand. Use Amazon Polly when the voice needs to sound natural and read names, numbers, product details, addresses, and confirmations reliably. “At Sanoma Media Finland, we use Amazon Polly to turn our real-time news articles into audio, giving the listener the choice to listen whenever it suits them better. Today we publish over 10,000 articles per month using Polly’s Finnish neural voice. Based on our testing, Suvi’s new generative voice is a clear improvement over the previous neural voice – it sounds noticeably more natural and makes for a more enjoyable experience for the listener.” — Justus Reinikainen, Product Manager, Sanoma Media Finland Getting started You can access the new voices using the AWS Management Console , AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , or the AWS SDKs. Prerequisites: Active AWS account with Amazon Polly access. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured. Python 3.10+. Boto3 installed: pip install boto3 . AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: polly:SynthesizeSpeech . Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with the SynthesizeSpeech API and a generative voice: import boto3 polly = boto3.client("polly", region_name="us-east-1") response = polly.synthesize_speech( Text="Hello! This is Amazon Polly's next-generation generative voice.", VoiceId="Kenneth", # any generative voice in the catalogue Engine="generative", OutputFormat="mp3", ) with open("speech.mp3", "wb") as f: f.write(response["AudioStream"].read()) You can also make the same request with the AWS CLI: aws polly synthesize-speech \ --region us-east-1 \ --voice-id Kenneth \ --engine generative \ --output-format mp3 \ --text "Hello! This is Amazon Polly's next-generation generative voice." \ speech.mp3 To retrieve the full, current voice list programmatically, call DescribeVoices . You can use this in deployment checks to confirm that a selected generative voice is available in the Region where your application runs. Availability The next-generation Generative engine and the new voices are now generally available. The 14 new Generative voices are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). Getting started, by audience: Developers – Call synthesize_speech with Engine="generative" in your existing application. No other changes are required. Contact-center teams – The improvements reach Amazon Connect and Genesys flows automatically. Everyone – Access any voice in the Amazon Polly console . A few things to know: Standard and neural voices are unaffected. Speech marks are not available on generative voices (unchanged from today). If your application requires them, standard and neural voices continue to support them. Generative engine continues to support SSML tags. See supported SSML tags for more details. Use current voice availability at runtime. Call DescribeVoices or check the console when deploying across Regions. Conclusion The next-generation Generative engine of Amazon Polly is available today, delivering more natural and more accurate voices, adding 14 new voices, including generative voices generally available in Hindi and Finnish for the first time, and requires no change to your code. See Amazon Polly pricing page for pricing information. To get started, open the Amazon Polly console to try the voices, and see the Amazon Polly documentation to build with them. About the authors Suyin Wang Suyin is a Senior Generative AI Solutions Architect at AWS. She has years of experience building data-driven and machine learning applications that solve real-world problems. She enjoys helping customers identify the right problems to solve and build generative AI solutions that drive business value. In her spare time, she loves singing, or trying out new recipes in the kitchen. Gosia Brylowska Gosia is a Program Manager at Amazon IMAX Polly. With almost 20 years of experience in journalism, marketing and AV production & over 10 in program & product management (last 7 being in Amazon TTS), Gosia strives for excellency translating engineering goals into customer delights on a daily basis. Outside of work you can find her dog walking or watching Star Trek TNG for 100 th time… or catching waves &sightseeing with friends somewhere in Sri Lanka – you just never know with this one. Nikie Xiong Nikie is a Senior Technical Product Manager at Amazon Polly. She has 10+ years of experience in AI, voice technology, and bringing innovative products from ideas to launch across consumer and enterprise sectors. With a background in product design and media entertainment production, she thrives at building products that delight customers. Outside of work, she creates interactive art and enjoys techno.

title: Tesla's Profit Drops 43% as Musk Starts Building Robots and Plans to Sell Driverless Cabs
body:
Tesla’s profit fell 43% last quarter to $787 million, down from $1.37 billion a year earlier, per its quarterly filing . The carmaker poured money into humanoid robots and driverless taxis while delivering about 2% fewer cars.
Revenue stayed flat at $28.05 billion, but operating profit, which is what’s left after the costs of running the business, fell 56% to $718 million. Research spending rose 69% to $2.76 billion, and capital expenditures, the money spent on factories and equipment, more than doubled to $4.73 billion.
That spending targets two products headed for factory floors and city streets. Optimus is a humanoid robot meant to take over dangerous and repetitive jobs, and the Cybercab is a two-seat robotaxi (a self-driving taxi you summon from an app) with no steering wheel or pedals.
Tesla said Wednesday that Optimus has entered production, and an executive said on the earnings call that the company is trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of the year.
Optimus is now coming off a production line at Tesla’s Fremont, California, factory. “The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its shareholder letter.
Musk wants to reach 20,000 Optimus units a week, but said getting there will take at least a year because the design is still changing. He put deliveries to outside customers around the end of 2027 and called the robot’s hand the hardest hardware problem, along with whether it holds up beyond a month of use.
Tesla has missed Optimus targets before, including a goal of about 10,000 robots in 2025, and rivals are already in the race. Figure AI, a startup backed by Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, unveiled its Figure 02 humanoid in 2024.
On the Cybercab, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice president of vehicle engineering, said on the earnings call that they may be available this year: “We’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026.” Every Cybercab built so far is headed to Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet, and Musk said most will stay Tesla-owned and offered as “transport as a service.”
Tesla has not said who will buy Cybercabs first, though it posted a form last month for people interested in buying robotaxis, and it has not announced a price. The target price Tesla has cited is under $30,000 .
Musk said the robotaxi business should become noticeable in Tesla’s overall financials in the second quarter of 2027 and will “probably” be “a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.” Tesla has not disclosed how much money the service brings in.
Musk also said Tuesday, on SpaceX’s earnings call, that the Tesla and SpaceX boards have each formed special committees of independent directors to study a combination, and no terms have been agreed.
A deal needs support from holders of 50% of all outstanding Tesla shares, a hurdle Musk called “quite a high hurdle,” and Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting is December 3, though no merger vote is on the agenda.

title: AI analysis of CT scans finds 42.9% of patients have coronary inflammation
body:
The study evaluated whether AI analysis of coronary inflammation in cardiac CT scans can help identify early cardiovascular risk before symptoms or obstructive plaque appear
The study evaluated whether AI analysis of coronary inflammation in cardiac CT scans can help identify early cardiovascular risk before symptoms or obstructive plaque appear
The study, available to clinically eligible Biograph Black tier members, combined Biographâs advanced diagnostics â including high-resolution coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) imaging and cardiometabolic profiling â with Caristoâs CaRi-Heart and CaRi-Plaque Â® technologies*. This collaborative methodology enabled researchers to assess the prevalence of coronary inflammation using the AI-enabled CaRi-Heart technology to determine cardiovascular risk in individuals who may otherwise appear low risk through traditional screening.
The study found that coronary inflammation is common (42.9%) in asymptomatic, low-risk adults and frequently occurs without any plaque buildup or blockage. Specifically, 42.9% of participants exhibited elevated inflammation with 17.9% of participants exhibiting very high inflammation in at least one major heart artery. The results also suggest a potential limitation in standard assessment: About 47% of participants with no detectable coronary plaque exhibited elevated coronary perivascular inflammation. By evaluating coronary inflammation alongside traditional imaging assessment of plaque burden and stenosis, we get a more complete picture of cardiovascular risk..
Importantly, routine bloodwork and clinical tools â including cholesterol markers (ApoB, non-HDL-C), blood sugar (HbA1c), systemic inflammation (hs-CRP), and a widely used cardiovascular risk calculator (AHA PREVENT-ASCVD) â showed no correlation with the presence of coronary inflammation and failed to identify which patients had inflamed arteries. These results reinforce Biographâs core philosophy: standalone bloodwork and isolated metrics do not tell the full story. By directly analyzing the biology of the tissue surrounding the coronary arteries, this non-invasive AI technology uncovers potential cardiovascular risk years before the onset of irreversible heart disease.
For Biograph, the completion of this study reflects its broader mission to advance proactive, personalized healthcare through comprehensive diagnostics, clinical interpretation, and earlier insight into long-term health risks. To review the clinical study manuscript, readers can access the published preprint here.
