title: Deploy AI in a HIPAA-eligible environment with Amazon Quick
body: Healthcare organizations want the same thing from AI that every other business wants: faster answers, less manual work, and insights that reach decision-makers in time to act on them. However, what makes the healthcare industry different is that the data is uniquely complex, deeply contextual, and strictly regulated. So this post starts with a few definitions to set the foundation for everything that follows. Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited. Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records. Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf. Connectors are pre-built integrations that let Amazon Quick securely read from and take action in your external systems, such as Slack , Microsoft Outlook , Salesforce , Atlassian Jira , and Microsoft SharePoint . You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible. When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop. To support that governance, Amazon Quick exposes ACL-aware retrieval, chat and feedback logging, and controls over what each chat agent is allowed to do. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA -eligible service. This eligibility applies across the Amazon Quick web, desktop, and mobile clients, subject to the shared responsibility model and your configuration. This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser. In this post, we start with the foundations: who HIPAA applies to and the difference between HIPAA-eligible and HIPAA-compliant. We then introduce Amazon Quick as a platform and the two data flows for PHI (unstructured and structured). From there, we cover what Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments and what it doesn’t, walk through a fictional health plan (AnyCompany) deployment, and distill the best practices and irreversible decisions you should make up front. We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading. Who does HIPAA apply to? HIPAA reaches further than hospitals and clinics. Under the law, two categories of organizations carry obligations, and most AI projects touch both. Covered entities (CEs) Health plans – Health insurance companies, HMOs, employer-sponsored plans, Medicare, and Medicaid. Healthcare clearinghouses – Organizations that process nonstandard health information into standard electronic formats. Healthcare providers – Doctors, clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, nursing homes, and any provider that transmits health information electronically. Business associates (BAs) A business associate is any person or entity, outside the covered entity’s workforce, that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information (PHI) on the covered entity’s behalf. Common examples include cloud service providers, IT vendors, billing companies, data analytics firms, claims processors, law firms, and consulting firms. Subcontractors who handle PHI on behalf of another business associate are themselves business associates. Covered entities and business associates must both sign a business associate addendum (BAA) before PHI changes hands. After you accept the AWS BAA through AWS Artifact, AWS acts as your business associate for that specific AWS account, and only when you use HIPAA-eligible services like Amazon Quick to process PHI within it. The addendum doesn’t extend to your other accounts, to PHI placed in services that are not HIPAA-eligible, or to how you configure the service. Those remain your responsibility. Always review and confirm the current AWS BAA terms and your obligations with your own legal and compliance teams. HIPAA eligible is not the same as HIPAA compliant While HIPAA eligible is an AWS designation, HIPAA compliant is a property of your entire environment. HIPAA eligible means AWS has assessed the service and permits you to use it to process, store, and transmit PHI under a signed AWS BAA. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA-eligible service, and third-party auditors assess it under AWS compliance programs including HIPAA, FedRAMP, PCI DSS, SOC, and ISO. No official HIPAA certification exists for AWS as a cloud service, and AWS itself is not “HIPAA eligible.” Amazon Quick eligibility serves only as a building block. That alone doesn’t make your application and environment HIPAA compliant. You still need to sign the BAA, classify your data, configure the controls correctly, and own the administrative and physical safeguards HIPAA requires, including workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures that AWS doesn’t perform for you. An eligible service such as Amazon Quick, a signed BAA, correct configuration, governance, and your own safeguards is what produces a HIPAA-compliant deployment. Amazon Quick being eligible means you can build a compliant workflow on it. It doesn’t mean that turning it on makes you automatically compliant. What is Amazon Quick Amazon Quick is often introduced through its chat agents, but HIPAA eligibility applies to the entire workspace, not to a single feature, so a platform-level view matters for compliance. All capabilities in Amazon Quick are assembled from the following building blocks: Chat is the primary interface. A user can pose a question or provide an instruction in natural language, and Amazon Quick decides how to respond. Chat agents process every request. This is what you see on the console, under the Chat agents menu. Each chat agent can be configured with instructions, grounded by knowledge sources, and given tools to take action. Amazon Quick ships a default chat agent (My Assistant), and you can create custom chat agents for specific domains. Spaces organize the resources a chat agent needs, such as documents, dashboards, datasets, knowledge bases, and action connectors. A space can be shared with a team. Integrations connect Amazon Quick to your environment: knowledge bases for unstructured content such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , Microsoft SharePoint , and Atlassian Confluence ; structured data connections that link Amazon Quick Sight to your structured databases, data warehouses, and data lakes; action connectors (built from OpenAPI specifications or Model Context Protocol servers); and extensions (Chrome, Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft 365). On top of those building blocks sit the features. The What it draws on column matters for compliance, because it shows which building blocks, and therefore which data paths, each feature draws on. Feature What it does What it draws on Amazon Quick Sight Interactive dashboards and analytics (BI) Structured data connections, SPICE, datasets Amazon Quick Flows Task automation Action connectors, spaces, agent logic Amazon Quick Automate End-to-end process automation with human-in-the-loop Action connectors, agents, human review Amazon Quick Research In-depth, cited research reports Spaces, knowledge bases, web Apps in Quick Interactive web applications Structured data, connectors, Amazon Quick Sight visuals Note: SPICE is the in-memory query engine of Amazon Quick Sight. A SPICE dataset uses the account default customer managed key at creation, and to import an existing dataset onto a new default key you must perform a full refresh . If your data includes PHI, include SPICE in your encryption strategy (protect it with your customer managed AWS Key Management Service (KMS) key if you use one) and in your data-minimization decisions about what to import, such as querying live or loading a de-identified extract instead. The same eligibility, BAA, encryption, access control, and audit posture extend across every feature. But as noted at the start, PHI reaches Amazon Quick through two paths, and each is secured differently. The unstructured path runs through knowledge bases, where the documents are controlled by document-level ACLs and evaluated at query time. The structured path runs through Amazon Quick Sight reading your databases and data lakes, where row and column access is controlled by row-level and column-level security. These two data flows carry PHI differently and, as the following section shows, controls are enforced differently in each path. What Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments Amazon Quick is HIPAA eligible, and we outline what that means in practice. Managed infrastructure Amazon Quick is a fully managed service. AWS operates the underlying infrastructure and is responsible for security of the cloud, verified by third-party auditors as laid out in the AWS Shared Responsibility Model . Encryption Amazon Quick encrypts data at rest by default and supports encryption for data in transit. Encryption at rest is on by default using AWS owned or AWS managed keys. Registering a customer managed key is optional and is not a HIPAA requirement. If you require direct control over the encryption keys, you can register a customer managed AWS KMS key (requires an Enterprise subscription) for participating resource types, including SPICE datasets, data source credentials, OAuth tokens, and report artifacts. Where no customer managed key applies, AWS encrypts the data with an AWS owned or AWS managed key. One nuance to note: User feedback on chat responses, including optional free-text comments, isn’t encrypted with your customer managed key or the key that protects Amazon Quick’s AI-indexed data. User feedback should be treated as a potential PHI surface and governed accordingly. For data in transit, Amazon Quick secures encrypted transfers with Transport Layer Security (TLS). For some database connections, you can choose whether the transfer is encrypted, so you should explicitly enable TLS/SSL on those data-source connections rather than assuming it is always on. Your data does not train the models Amazon Quick doesn’t use your customer data to train or improve the underlying large language models (LLMs). Access control and identity federation Amazon Quick supports role-based access control (RBAC) and single sign-on (SSO) through AWS IAM Identity Center, Microsoft Active Directory, and SAML 2.0 identity providers. For business intelligence (BI) workloads, you can supplement this with row-level and column-level security and run-as roles to limit data access at query time. With these capabilities, you can enforce unique user identification and least privilege. Audit and monitoring signals Amazon Quick emits several distinct signals. They aren’t interchangeable, and confusing them is a common audit gap. AWS CloudTrail records supported API operations and a documented set of non-API events, such as dashboard views and user-management actions. It captures who did what and when, but not chat message bodies or response content. Amazon CloudWatch vended logs deliver the AI-specific records to a destination you control (CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Firehose). There are five log types: chat conversations (CHAT_LOGS), user feedback (FEEDBACK_LOGS), agent and research hours (AGENT_HOURS_LOGS), index storage usage (INDEX_USAGE_LOGS), and knowledge base file sync (KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS). This is where “what a user asked and what Amazon Quick answered” lives, not in CloudTrail. CloudWatch metrics and alarms provide near-real-time operational monitoring as well. The analytics dashboard surfaces usage and adoption for administrators. Note that it can expose detailed query text and full conversation context in the scope of negative-feedback review, so grant access only to authorized administrators. Because chat logs and feedback can contain PHI, apply CloudWatch Logs data-protection masking, and confirm that a given signal actually covers the event you intend to track before you rely on it for compliance. Translating features into HIPAA controls That Amazon Quick is an eligible service is useful because it maps each feature to a specific HIPAA safeguard, as shown in the following table: Amazon Quick capability How you use it HIPAA control it supports Federated SSO + RBAC IAM Identity Center / AD, least-privilege roles 164.312(a)(1) access control. Unique user ID Document-level ACLs on knowledge bases ACL-aware KBs. Fail-closed at query time 164.312(a)(1) access control. Minimum necessary Encryption at rest and in transit On by default with AWS managed keys. Optionally a customer managed key for key ownership 164.312(a)(2)(iv) / (e)(2)(ii) encryption CloudTrail + CloudWatch vended logs Capture API events and chat/feedback records 164.312(b) audit controls Log retention + masking Retention policy, S3 Object Lock, PII masking 164.316(b) documentation retention AI guardrails + built-in screening Blocked words/phrases, content safety checks Supports minimum-necessary and integrity goals What Amazon Quick doesn’t do While Amazon Quick offers the preceding controls, this section addresses what Amazon Quick doesn’t offer and how to bridge this gap. Amazon Quick governs access, retrieval, and interaction. It isn’t a data-engineering or data-lake governance platform. In a HIPAA context, several needs fall outside Amazon Quick and are met by other AWS services upstream of it. De-identification and transformation. Amazon Quick doesn’t de-identify PHI or reshape source data. When your use case calls for a limited data set or a de-identified extract, prepare it before it reaches Amazon Quick using appropriate AWS services, for example, with AWS Glue DataBrew , a capability of AWS Glue, for visual data preparation and redaction, or AWS Glue for extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines. Data lake governance and fine-grained table permissions. For structured data that Amazon Quick Sight queries through a data lake, column- and row-level governance on the lake itself is the role of AWS Lake Formation , not Amazon Quick. Amazon Quick Sight enforces its own row-level and column-level security at the analytics layer, but the authoritative lake-level grants live in Lake Formation and the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The administrative and physical safeguards. Workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures remain yours regardless of tooling. A general best practice is to delineate responsibilities and allow the upstream services to decide what data exists and who can query it at the source. Let Amazon Quick decide who can ask questions of it and what the agent may do with the data. AnyCompany Health Plan: A sample use case AnyCompany Health Plan, a fictional health plan, illustrates a use case and pattern. AnyCompany Health Plan is a covered entity that wants two things: let its care-management team ask questions of policy and member-appeals documents in natural language, and give operations leaders self-service dashboards over claims data. Both touch PHI, so AnyCompany needs to confirm the solution is HIPAA compliant. AnyCompany’s environment has two data paths, and each is architected and governed by distinct solutions before Amazon Quick can access the data. Unstructured path (policy and medical records documents) → Amazon S3 bucket (ACL-aware KB source) → Amazon Quick Knowledge Base (document-level ACLs, fail-closed at query time) Structured path (claims) All claims data currently resides in a lake (Amazon S3). → Glue ETL (curate) → Glue DataBrew (de-identify) → Lake Formation (row/column grants and AWS Glue Data Catalog ) → Amazon Quick Sight dataset ( Amazon Athena ) (row-level and column-level security, run-as role) Both of the preceding data flows for structured and unstructured data converge into an Amazon Quick chat agent with federated SSO, least-privilege space, guardrails, and CloudWatch vended logs. Here is how AnyCompany’s administrator implements the solution: Sign the BAA and provision through the AWS Management Console . The admin accepts the AWS BAA in AWS Artifact against the AWS account, then provisions Amazon Quick from the AWS Management Console with IAM Identity Center. AnyCompany records the agreement ID, timestamp, and account in its compliance register. Only the web version of Amazon Quick, provisioned through the AWS Management Console, can be brought under a signed BAA through AWS Artifact, which is a necessary component for customers building HIPAA-compliant workflows that touch PHI, subject to proper configuration and the customer’s own compliance responsibilities. Set the irreversible controls on day zero. Because AnyCompany’s security policy calls for control of its own encryption keys, the admin chooses to register a customer managed key as the account default before any Amazon Quick AI data is created. The data key is set once and can’t be changed later. (Default AWS managed encryption is also HIPAA-eligible. Using customer managed keys is not a prerequisite for the service to be HIPAA eligible.) The admin also settles the identity model on IAM Identity Center so that inactive-user detection applies. The Amazon Quick data key is set once on first data creation and can never be changed. If the key is deleted, the only recovery is to unsubscribe and resubscribe, which permanently removes all Amazon Quick data. Prepare the structured path outside Amazon Quick. Before Amazon Quick Sight touches claims, AnyCompany’s data team uses AWS Glue to build the curated claims tables and Glue DataBrew to produce a de-identified extract for the operations dashboards. AWS Lake Formation grants row- and column-level access on those tables through the AWS Glue Data Catalog. As a result, Amazon Quick never sees raw PHI that it does not need. Create an ACL-aware knowledge base for the documents. The admin connects the policy-and-appeals S3 bucket as a knowledge base with document-level ACLs enabled at creation. Because ACLs can’t be turned on later, this needs to be configured when you create the S3 bucket. Amazon Quick evaluates each user’s identity at query time and returns no documents when it can’t confirm access. Build a dedicated space and a custom chat agent. AnyCompany creates a PHI space with restricted membership, separate from general-productivity spaces. The care-management chat agent is scoped to only the ACL-aware knowledge base, with open web search disabled and guardrails configured. Read-only connectors are implemented for anything PHI-adjacent. Connect the dashboards with query-time security. The operations dashboards read the de-identified Amazon Quick Sight dataset over Athena, with Amazon Quick Sight row-level and column-level security and a run-as role layered on top of the Lake Formation grants. Turn on the audit signals before onboarding users. The admin creates a CloudTrail trail and configures CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS, and the rest) to a retained, masked destination. Feedback is treated as a PHI surface. Validate, then scale from non-PHI to PHI. AnyCompany starts with non-PHI workflows, such as policy Q&A and document search, to confirm governance, tests with adversarial prompts to verify fail-closed ACL behavior, reviews the logs to confirm the events are captured, and only then expands the care-management team into PHI-adjacent work. Amazon Quick enforces identity, retrieval, guardrails, and the audit trail. But the de-identification, the ETL, and the lake-level grants happen upstream in Glue, Glue DataBrew, and Lake Formation. This division is the recommended pattern, and is the practical answer to augmenting Amazon Quick in a federated environment. How to make it compliant: Best practices Eligibility gives you a platform that can handle PHI. You still must configure it so that it does. This section helps you understand the shared-responsibility decisions involved. Because a few of these decisions are irreversible, make them before you create resources or onboard users. Start with the security model for agentic AI Amazon Quick agents don’t wait for instructions at every step. They invoke tools, modify data, and interact with external systems on their own. That changes how you approach securing your environment. AWS published four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026, and they apply directly here. Principle 1 — Layer agent safeguards onto your existing security framework. Don’t stand up a parallel security posture for Amazon Quick. Add agent-specific measures (guardrails, topic blocking, and PII redaction) on top of the IAM, network, and encryption policies you already enforce. Principle 2 — Trust deterministic controls over prompt-based ones. A well-crafted adversarial input can circumvent a prompt instruction. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, document-level ACLs, network boundaries, and admin-configured guardrails can’t be talked around. Use those as your primary enforcement. Agent instructions are your second layer, not your only one. Principle 3 — Apply defense in depth across perceive, reason, and act. Map every agent capability to one of three layers: Perceive: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, connector inputs, MCP tool outputs. Reason: the LLM processing context, controlled by guardrails and topic controls. Act: Connectors, Quick Flows, Quick Automate, scheduled tasks, MCP tool calls. Apply controls at each layer independently. A gap in one shouldn’t cascade into the others. Note that HIPAA BAA obligations extend to supporting services and solutions like MCP tools. Principle 4 — Expand autonomy progressively. Start agents in read-only mode against non-PHI data. Add capabilities one at a time. Test for data leakage, prompt-injection resilience, and permission-boundary adherence at each step before moving to the next. Decide before you deploy Because these three choices are permanent, make these decisions before implementation. Register your KMS key first. If your organization requires control of its own encryption keys, register a customer managed key as the account default before creating any Amazon Quick AI resources. The data key is set the first time Quick AI data is created in the account. After that, it can’t be changed. Customer managed key support requires an Enterprise subscription. Note that a customer managed key disables chat memory. Accounts configured with a customer managed key do not support this feature. Choose your identity model deliberately. You have four options: IAM Identity Center, Active Directory, IAM federation, and Quick local users. They differ in provisioning, offboarding, and governance behavior. Inactive-user detection, for instance, works only with IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Switching identity providers after deployment means reprovisioning every user’s permissions and space memberships. Pick once. Make PHI knowledge bases ACL-aware at creation. For supported sources (Amazon S3, Google Drive, SharePoint, Confluence Cloud, and OneDrive), you decide at creation whether a knowledge base enforces document-level ACLs. That setting is permanent. You can’t enable ACLs on a knowledge base that was created without them. For anything PHI-adjacent, create it ACL-aware from the start. Warning: Misconfigured user-store mappings can silently expose restricted documents to the wrong users, without errors or alerts. It’s critical to validate your identity-to-ACL mapping before you ingest PHI content. AWS Region, network, and account boundaries Plan your deployment Region based on the following factors: Data residency: Amazon Quick processes and stores data in the Region where you provision it, and you need to confirm that Region satisfies your organization’s data-localization requirements. Note that Amazon Quick is a single-Region service: it benefits from multi-AZ resilience within a Region, but it doesn’t fail over across Regions. If you support business-critical workflows that require cross-Region resilience, provision a separate Amazon Quick deployment in a second Region, along with its supporting data, for example, replicating S3-based knowledge base sources across Regions. Service availability. Features are at times launched in different Regions at different times. Verify that everything your agents need, such as knowledge bases, connectors, and Amazon Quick Sight capabilities, is available where you plan to deploy. Multi-account strategy. Place Amazon Quick in a dedicated workload account in AWS Organizations. Use Service Control Policies (SCPs) to enforce Region restrictions and block accidental provisioning in out-of-scope Regions. For network boundaries: Amazon Quick is a managed service accessed over HTTPS. You don’t deploy it into a virtual private cloud (VPC). But your data sources (S3 buckets, databases, on-premises systems) might sit behind VPC boundaries. Use VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink where available. Make sure DNS resolution and firewall rules let Amazon Quick’s connectors reach your authorized data sources without opening the network wider than necessary. Minimize the agent’s attack surface Amazon Quick’s own documentation frames adversarial risk as a two-condition problem: risk exists when (1) an agent can read content from outside your trust boundary, and (2) it can take a consequential action. Narrow either condition and you reduce exposure. Constrain what agents can read (Perceive layer). Know every source that feeds an agent’s context: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, third-party research providers, connector responses, MCP tool outputs, and retained conversation memory. For PHI workflows: Scope agents to trusted, ACL-aware knowledge bases. Turn off open web search where it isn’t needed. Turn off file upload if the agent doesn’t require it. Limit conversation-history retention to the minimum useful window. Constrain what agents can do (Act layer). Inventory every outbound path: connectors, MCP tools, web queries, Quick Flows, Quick Automate workflows, scheduled agent runs. For PHI-adjacent agents: Prefer read-only connector access. Be cautious with automated and scheduled workflows, because they run without anyone watching. Block write actions unless explicitly justified and approved by your security team. Use connector-level permission scoping to restrict which operations an agent can invoke. Know the identity an action runs as. On-demand actions authenticate as the invoking user, bounded by that user’s connector permissions. Automated workflows run without an interactive session. Match the autonomy level to the sensitivity of the action, and document which agents operate in which identity mode. Enforce least privilege and data segregation Separate PHI-containing knowledge bases and spaces from general-productivity ones. Restrict membership. Grant space and agent access on a need-to-know basis. Review both sharing permissions (who can use a knowledge base) and source-document ACLs (which indexed documents an authorized user can actually retrieve). The default knowledge-base refresh cycle is 24 hours. Shorten it when your access-change requirements demand faster propagation. Refresh ACLs before reassigning or recycling email addresses. A PHI agent shouldn’t share a space with general-purpose productivity tools. This means you need to isolate use cases at the space level. Review connector permissions regularly. Rotate credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager on a schedule that matches your credential-management policy. Practice data minimization AWS recommends against entering confidential data into resource names or tags, to avoid accidental mention in billing or diagnostic logs. Prefer de-identified data wherever the use case allows it. When ingesting structured data from databases or APIs, filter columns and rows at the source before indexing. Configure agent guardrails to redact PII in responses, hiding Social Security numbers (SSNs), medical record numbers (MRNs), and dates of birth, using the built-in PII detection filters. Configure audit logging and retention Amazon Quick provides several distinct audit signals. None of them flow by default and you might need to turn them on. Signal Source What it captures API operations CloudTrail Admin actions, configuration changes Chat interactions CloudWatch CHAT_LOGS — full conversation records User feedback CloudWatch FEEDBACK_LOGS — thumbs up/down with context KB sync events CloudWatch KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS — ingestion status Operational metrics CloudWatch Latency, error rates, invocation counts Usage analytics Quick console Adoption, top queries, user activity Here is how to set them up: Create a CloudTrail trail for the accounts and Regions in scope. Configure CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS) shortly after you turn on Amazon Quick’s AI features. Apply CloudWatch Logs data-protection masking to chat logs so PHI isn’t stored in cleartext. Set a retention period of at least six years. Consider S3 Object Lock on the log archive. Add CloudWatch alarms for anomalous activity. Enable AWS Security Hub for continuous compliance checks. Route critical alerts to your security information and event management (SIEM) or incident-response platform. Validate before you scale Before expanding scope, check the following: BAA acceptance is recorded in your compliance register. Data classification is documented: Which knowledge bases and spaces contain PHI, which agents can reach them. Adversarial queries and prompt-injection scenarios have been tested. Logs are being captured and masking works correctly. A tabletop breach exercise has been completed. InfoSec has signed off. Known limitations Here are some known limitations of Amazon Quick. No BAA on the Free or Plus path. You must use the path provisioned through the AWS Management Console to get BAA coverage. No cross-Region replication. Disaster recovery (DR) is constrained to a single Region. Guardrails are probabilistic, not deterministic. They reduce risk. They don’t eliminate it. Supplement with the infrastructure-level controls described earlier. Third-party connectors extend your BAA obligations. When a connector sends data to an external system, your compliance responsibility follows the data. Conversation memory might contain echoed PHI. Set retention policies and apply masking. Implementation guide The AnyCompany Health Plan example showed how to roll out Amazon Quick. This section turns that pattern into a step-by-step project plan you can hand to your platform team. Step 1: Execute the BAA (Day 1) Sign in with AWS Artifact permissions and accept the BAA. Record the agreement ID, timestamp, principal ARN, and account ID. Notify your legal and compliance team. Step 2: Set foundational, irreversible controls (Days 1–2) Register a customer managed key as the account default. Verify the key policy grants the required permissions: Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, DescribeKey. Configure your identity model (IAM Identity Center is recommended). Confirm the account sits in a dedicated workload organizational unit (OU) with Region-restricting SCPs. Step 3: Create ACL-aware knowledge bases (Days 3–7) Classify your data sources: PHI, PHI-adjacent, and non-PHI. Create knowledge bases with ACL awareness turned on for PHI and PHI-adjacent sources. Map the identity store to source permissions and validate with multiple test users. Verify sync logs confirm successful ingestion. Keep PHI knowledge bases separated from general content. Step 4: Create spaces (Days 5–8) Separate PHI-adjacent spaces from general-productivity spaces. Attach knowledge bases, dashboards, and action connectors. Restrict membership. Confirm that unauthorized users are blocked. Step 5: Create custom agents with guardrails (Days 7–12) Define each agent’s purpose narrowly. Attach only the knowledge sources it needs. Configure PII redaction, blocked topics, content filters, and grounding controls. Test with normal queries, boundary queries, and adversarial prompts. Document results and remediation steps. Step 6: Configure action connectors (Days 10–14) Start with read-only mode for PHI-adjacent data. Scope each connector to specific resources. Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation turned on. Document the justification for any write access. Get security sign-off before turning it on. Test scope limits to confirm connectors can’t reach resources beyond their intended scope. Step 7: Configure audit, retention, and monitoring (Days 12–16) Enable CloudTrail and CloudWatch vended logs. Apply data-protection masking. Set retention to at least six years. Enable S3 Object Lock. Configure alarms, enable Security Hub, and integrate with your SIEM. Step 8: Validate with InfoSec (Days 14–21) Compile the evidence package: BAA confirmation, KMS configuration, identity setup, data classification, test results, and log samples. Run a tabletop breach exercise. Present to your InfoSec team. Remediate findings. Obtain sign-off. Expansion phase (Weeks 4–8) Start with non-PHI workflows: policy Q&A, document search, meeting prep, workflow automation. These let your team build confidence with the platform before PHI enters the picture. Then expand to PHI-adjacent workflows: clinical documentation assistance, claims processing, prior authorization, regulatory Q&A, patient communication drafting with human review in the loop. Monitor closely: review chat logs weekly, track guardrail trigger rates, and watch access patterns for 30 days after each new workflow goes live. Conclusion Amazon Quick gives regulated healthcare organizations, and the business associates who serve them, a managed AI workspace that is HIPAA-eligible across its full range of capabilities: agentic AI, knowledge retrieval, business intelligence, automation, and research. The path to a compliant deployment follows a clear sequence: Understand the difference between eligible and compliant, and own your side of shared responsibility. Execute the BAA on an account provisioned through the AWS Management Console. Set the irreversible controls first: KMS keys, identity model, ACL-aware knowledge bases. Minimize the agent’s read and action surfaces, enforce least privilege, and mask PHI in logs. Validate with your InfoSec team, then scale from non-PHI to PHI-adjacent workflows. The compliance expectations are moving as fast as the technology. AWS published its four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026 and the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens in June 2026. Organizations that build on deterministic, infrastructure-level controls today will likely be well positioned as regulatory expectations catch up to what agentic AI can do. What to do next If you’re evaluating Amazon Quick: Request a compliance-focused briefing from your AWS account team. Ask about BAA scope, shared responsibility for agentic AI, and the latest HIPAA-eligible service additions. If you’re ready to deploy: Use the implementation guide as your project plan. The irreversible decisions in Step 2 deserve a dedicated architecture review before you start creating resources. If you’re already running Amazon Quick: Audit your deployment against the best practices in this post, especially the agentic security principles and the known limitations list. For architecture guidance, reach out to your AWS Solutions Architect or the AWS Healthcare and Life Sciences team. title: Another mining-linked pollution incident raises alarm over Zambia’s Kafue River
body: The Zambian government has ordered a copper miner to assess its infrastructure for weaknesses and clean up areas affected by pollution of the Kafue River, after residents downstream of the plant that processes the mine’s waste reported changes in the river’s color, taste, and smell on Sept. 28. The order also requires Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) to cover laboratory testing and related costs. The pollution was traced to a leaking pipe at KCM’s tailings leach plant and an overflow from a pollution control dam on the Mushishima Stream, a tributary of the Kafue. The company disputes allegations that it caused the pollution, saying it detected the river’s discoloration and reported the incident to local authorities. The incident has renewed concerns about recurring pollution in the Kafue, which Misozi Ngulube, director-general of Zambia’s Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA), has described as the country’s most polluted water body. In February 2025, the breach of a tailings dam operated by Sino-Metals Leach Zambia, also on the Kafue, released more than 50 million liters (13 million gallons) of toxic sludge into a tributary. The spill killed fish more than 100 kilometers (60 miles) downstream, damaged crops, and disrupted local water supplies. The government reported three cases of minor illness, but the event raised broader concerns for communities and wildlife. Ngulube told Mongabay that pollution in the Kafue comes largely from agriculture, industry, and mining. She said WARMA has acquired a water-quality monitoring system and is working toward real-time pollution detection. However, monitoring alone can’t…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Ethereum Scraps Glamsterdam’s Hoodi Fork After ChainSecurity Flags Gas Risks
body: Ethereum developers have called off Glamsterdam’s activation on the Hoodi testnet , four days before the upgrade was due to go live there. The decision leaves the network’s next hard fork without its final public test date, and with it the trigger for picking a mainnet date. Christine D. Kim, founder of research and advisory firm Protocol Watch, said in a post on X on Oct. 22 that the cancellation was “due to security issues found in” Glamsterdam by the security firm ChainSecurity . Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Gas Accounting Concerns ChainSecurity’s Oct. 13 analysis focused on EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 , two Glamsterdam proposals that change how Ethereum charges gas for creating and accessing state. The firm warned that code handling a failed call could behave differently after the upgrade even if no one edits it. “Even with unchanged contract code, a failure path that previously reverted can now complete,” it wrote, adding that continuing in that situation “can turn a retryable operation into a permanent failure.” A day before the Oct. 22 All Core Devs Execution call, security researcher pcaversaccio asked developers on GitHub to discuss the findings, writing that “these findings call for a reassessment of this hard fork” while noting the decision was not his to make. What Node Operators Need to Do Kim’s message to operators , posted on X minutes before her post on the cause, gave them two choices: “revert to an older release without the Hoodi upgrade scheduled,” or hold off until their execution-layer client publishes an update that drops it. Besu developers merged a pull request titled “Unschedule Amsterdam on Hoodi” on Oct. 22, but merging code does not update nodes already running the old build. The PR states that Hoodi nodes on Besu 26.10.0 “still activate Amsterdam at that timestamp until they run a release with this change.” On the network’s side, Barnabas Busa, who works on DevOps at the Ethereum Foundation, unscheduled the fork in Hoodi’s shared configuration files. That took out the Amsterdam start time set for Oct. 26 , the Gloas fork at epoch 132,352 and a scheduled jump in Hoodi’s gas limit to 200 million at that epoch, returning the files to how they looked before the fork was scheduled. December Candidates Hinged on Hoodi The agenda for the Oct. 22 call listed Dec. 1, Dec. 8 and Dec. 9 as candidate mainnet dates, with a plan to pick one on the following week’s consensus-layer call “if Hoodi goes smoothly.” Glamsterdam, which would move proposer-builder separation into the protocol (EIP-7732) and add block-level access lists (EIP-7928), went live on the Sepolia testnet on Oct. 6 . The Ethereum Foundation announced the Hoodi schedule on Oct. 16. Neither Busa’s rollback nor Kim’s posts named a new date for the Hoodi test. title: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
body:
A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts. This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice. Solution overview This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic. Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations , which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream , which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions. The following diagram shows the request path from client to model: Figure 1: Request path from the client to the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint over a bidirectional stream Prerequisites Before you begin, you need: An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI endpoints; AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles; and an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository, including at minimum the sagemaker:CreateEndpoint , sagemaker:CreateEndpointConfig , sagemaker:CreateModel , sagemaker:InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream , and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream actions. The sample container pins an older PyTorch with a known advisory ( PYSEC-2026-2286 , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 , installed and bootstrapped in your target account and AWS Region. A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint deployed from a container that declares the com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true Docker label. Python 3.12 or later, uv , and Docker to build the container image (the underlying HTTP/2 client only ships pre-built wheels for Python 3.12 and newer). The AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with support for invoke_endpoint_with_bidirectional_stream . Familiarity with WebSockets and Starlette or a comparable ASGI framework. The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post. Walkthrough The walkthrough first deploys the endpoint and agent, then works through the client-side changes that make incremental streaming work end to end. Deploy the endpoint and agent The Kokoro-82M endpoint and the agent runtime deploy through two CLI tools, each wrapping its own AWS CDK stacks: uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m uv run agent-infra deploy --bedrock-model-id
speech-infra deploy provisions the Kokoro-82M endpoint. This includes the foundation and model-cache stacks that create the underlying IAM roles and sync the model’s weights into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). The endpoint stack then builds the container image and creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. agent-infra deploy provisions the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosting the Strands agent, which calls the endpoint you just deployed, so deploy the endpoint first. Step 1: Handle the WebSocket frame type SageMaker AI actually sends The bidirectional transport SageMaker AI uses delivers every piece of a client’s message to your container as a binary WebSocket frame. A common way to write a Starlette WebSocket handler is calling receive_text() , which reads message["text"] and raises KeyError if that key isn’t present. Because every message this client sends arrives as binary, that handler fails on every request. The failure is commonly misdiagnosed. A generic exception handler that forwards str(e) to the client turns KeyError('text') into an error frame reading 'text' , which looks like a missing field, not a framing issue. The endpoint itself reports InService throughout, since it accepts connections and responds to every message, with an error each time. Accept either frame type explicitly instead of assuming one will show up: from starlette.websockets import WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect async def _receive_message(websocket: WebSocket) -> str: message = await websocket.receive() if message["type"] == "websocket.disconnect": raise WebSocketDisconnect(message.get("code", 1000)) payload = message.get("text") if payload is None: payload = message.get("bytes", b"").decode("utf-8") return payload This decodes bytes as UTF-8 when no text field is present, rather than assuming one frame type. Test it by sending a binary frame, because this failure mode produces a well-formed error frame and a healthy endpoint status, not an obvious crash. Step 2: Keep the session open between messages After your container finishes synthesizing one message’s audio, the instinct is to close the session, the way an HTTP cycle ends. That’s wrong here. After sending a message’s audio and a synthesis_complete control frame, the container loop should go back to waiting on receive() for the next message on the same, still-open session. Close the connection only when the client sends an explicit {"type": "close"} message. The following diagram shows one session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end: Figure 2: One bidirectional session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end This way, you can send several sentences, one after another, on one persistent session, with no reconnection cost between them. Closing eagerly after one response would force a new connection per sentence, undoing most of the latency benefit. Step 3: Stream sentences as the agent produces them With the session behavior in place, the client-side fix for the latency problem is a class that normalizes text arriving in two shapes: a complete string known up front, or a live token stream. It produces the same output either way: complete sentences, ready to send as soon as each one is complete. import re _SENTENCE_RE = re.compile(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+") class IncrementalSentenceChunker: def __init__(self) -> None: self._buffer = "" def feed(self, fragment: str) -> list[str]: self._buffer += fragment parts = _SENTENCE_RE.split(self._buffer) if len(parts) == 1: return [] self._buffer = parts[-1] return [s.strip() for s in parts[:-1] if s.strip()] def flush(self) -> str | None: remainder = self._buffer.strip() self._buffer = "" return remainder or None Call feed() once per fragment of text as it arrives. It returns any newly completed sentences, holding back trailing text. Call flush() once, at the end of input, to release whatever partial text remains even without trailing punctuation. This keeps a stream that ends before a period arrives from dropping a final sentence. This isn’t concurrent synthesis. Every bidirectional handler is a strictly sequential loop: receive a message, synthesize its audio, send that audio, send synthesis_complete , then receive the next message. Sentence two’s audio isn’t generated while sentence one’s still transmits. What incremental sending buys is narrower: synthesis on sentence one begins the instant it exists, rather than waiting for the full response. For a multi-sentence response with real generation time between its first and last sentence, that’s the entire latency win. We verified this against a live endpoint sending a three-sentence input over one session. All three chunks arrived with audio matching the text sent for each: Chunk Text Audio bytes Duration (s) 1 “Hello there.” 73,200 1.525 2 “This is a post deployment check.” 108,000 2.250 3 “It has three sentences.” 98,400 2.050 Step 4: Choose a transport for getting audio back to the client Streaming text into the model incrementally solves half the problem. The other half is getting the resulting audio out to whatever renders it, commonly a browser. Most agent and chat frontends already stream text over Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-directional, and supported natively by most browsers. SSE is a text protocol, not built to carry a raw binary payload. A team adding voice to an existing SSE pipeline naturally reaches for the pattern it already has: base64-encode the audio and wrap it in a JSON event. We measured the cost of that approach across 24 clips, confirmed with Amazon Transcribe that quality didn’t differ across encodings, and compared MP3 against AAC: Candidate Raw bytes Base64 bytes Bitrate Raw PCM 2,396,400 3,195,200 384 kbps MP3 48k 308,304 411,072 49.5 kbps AAC 32k fMP4 258,039 344,084 41.6 kbps Base64 inflates every payload by close to the expected 33%. The subtler cost is frame alignment. SSE events are delimited by a blank line, but the audio inside is delimited into MP3 frames. The two schemes don’t necessarily align with how the transport chunks the data. In one measured response, four logical MP3 frames arrived as six delivery chunks, two ending mid-frame. A consumer that treats each delivery chunk as one complete unit fails on ordinary, healthy traffic. The fix buffers incoming bytes and acts only once a delimiter is found: buffer = b"" for event in resp["Body"]: if "PayloadPart" not in event: continue buffer += event["PayloadPart"]["Bytes"] while b"

" in buffer: frame, buffer = buffer.split(b"

", 1) handle(frame) The alternative used today for the model-facing leg skips base64 and SSE framing entirely. It multiplexes raw binary audio and JSON control frames over the same bidirectional session already carrying incremental text input, and tells them apart with one rule. import json def _decode_control_frame(chunk: bytes) -> dict | None: try: decoded = json.loads(chunk.decode("utf-8")) except (UnicodeDecodeError, json.JSONDecodeError): return None return decoded if isinstance(decoded, dict) else None A chunk that fails to decode as a JSON object is audio, forwarded as received, with no encoding step anywhere in the path. One edge case matters: raw PCM audio can legitimately begin with byte 0x7b , the ASCII character { , the same character that opens a JSON object. This rule avoids misclassifying that audio because it requires the entire chunk to parse as valid JSON, not its first byte alone, something a PCM frame will essentially never do. Note: If your frontend already has a working SSE pipeline for text, base64-encoded audio inside an SSE event is the pragmatic choice. It costs roughly 33 percent extra payload and a buffer-and-reassemble step, but reuses infrastructure you already operate. If you’re building the voice path fresh, or latency is the priority, the unified binary and JSON approach avoids both costs and reuses the connection already carrying text. Step 5: Put it together in a real agent The fuller, end-to-end case is a live, generative agent composing its response one token at a time, with no way to know sentence four until sentence one exists. This example runs as a Strands agent, backed by Amazon Bedrock, deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, calling the Kokoro endpoint with the pattern from Step 4. Three communication legs connect in this design: the browser-facing leg carrying Server-Sent Events back to the caller, the agent’s streaming call to Amazon Bedrock for text generation, and the agent’s bidirectional session with the Kokoro endpoint for synthesis. The following diagram shows those three communication legs, and where the overlap between generation and synthesis happens: Figure 3: The three communication legs connecting the caller, Amazon Bedrock, and the Kokoro endpoint The request payload carries a mode field, either "bidi" or "batch" , dispatched to two code paths inside the same entrypoint function. A benchmark between them changes exactly one variable: when synthesis starts. In run_bidi , two tasks run concurrently. One drains the Bedrock text stream and feeds completed sentences into the chunker. The other drains the Kokoro session and emits audio chunks as they arrive. Both push into one shared queue, so a consumer yields events in true arrival order: audio for an early sentence can reach the caller while Bedrock still generates a later one. run_batch is the deliberate opposite: it waits for the full response before one synthesis call, kept as a fair baseline. Going the other direction, the leg from the agent container back to the caller does use base64, for a different reason than Step 4 describes. BedrockAgentCoreApp ’s entrypoint must yield plain, JSON-serializable dictionaries, which its SDK turns into data: {json}

 frames automatically. There’s no way to hand it a raw binary frame. That’s a consequence of the JSON-native managed runtime, not the choice Step 4 measured and moved away from. Both run_bidi and run_batch pay that identical cost on this leg, so the measured difference between them is purely timing: when the first audio chunk is emitted. Testing and validation We isolated the TTS transport’s own contribution to time to first audio by sending the same 267-character, four-sentence block of text two ways: as one message (batch), and as only its first sentence (incremental). We ran five trials each against the live endpoint. As measured earlier, sending only the first sentence cut mean time to first audio byte from 329.3 ms to 156.7 ms, a 52.4 percent relative improvement, isolated to the TTS transport itself. We then measured the fuller, end-to-end case with a real language model producing the text, running the identical prompt through run_bidi and run_batch against the same live Bedrock model and endpoint, so the only variable is when synthesis starts. Using that same methodology, bidi mode’s time to first audio measured 2.4 times faster than batch mode against a local container, and 3.5 times faster against the deployed AgentCore runtime. The following chart shows that gap across both environments: Figure 4: Relative time to first audio for batch and bidi modes, locally and on the deployed runtime The gap widens, rather than narrows, for the deployed case once a real network hop is added. run_bidi absorbs that hop inside the overlap it’s already exploiting between generation and synthesis. run_batch has no equivalent overlap to hide that cost in, since it does one thing at a time, so every added millisecond of network overhead lands directly on its serial wait. To reproduce this comparison against your own deployment, run the same bidi-vs-batch test the agent container exposes: uv run agent-infra demo --endpoint-url
--prompt "
" This sends the prompt through both modes and reports the timestamp of the first audio_chunk event against agent_start for each. If you see errors instead, check for the KeyError: 'text' symptom from Step 1. An endpoint reporting InService while every request fails signals that bug, not a deployment issue. Clean up To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources this walkthrough creates in reverse deployment order, agent first, then endpoint: uv run agent-infra destroy --bedrock-model-id
uv run speech-infra destroy kokoro-82m agent-infra destroy removes the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime resource. speech-infra destroy removes the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. Neither empties the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or deletes the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed. Conclusion We showed how to remove one source of avoidable latency from a voice agent, waiting for an agent’s full response before starting speech synthesis, and how to quantify a second, quieter cost: base64-encoded audio inside SSE inflates payload by about a third and can misalign with MP3 frame boundaries if you don’t buffer for it. Streaming each sentence into a SageMaker AI bidirectional endpoint as soon as an agent produces it cut time to first audio by more than half in isolation, and by 2.4 to 3.5 times in a deployed agent. Multiplexing binary audio and JSON control frames over that session, instead of encoding audio as text, removes the size inflation and frame-realignment work a naive SSE relay requires. If you’re adding voice to an agent that already streams text over SSE, start with the base64 approach in Step 4 and revisit the unified transport once latency becomes the priority. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference documentation and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . If you’d like help applying this pattern to your own architecture, contact your AWS account team. About the author Joseph Cottingham Joseph is a Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he designs and delivers AI systems that move organizations from idea to production. His technical background spans firmware, software, and machine learning, with deep expertise in high-throughput, event-driven architectures that keep AI workloads performant at scale. Joseph focuses on the intersection of state-of-the-art research and operational reality, delivering solutions that materially transform organizations and the systems they operate.

title: ‘Wrong and Unacceptable’: Zelensky Accuses Trump of Shifting Iran Blame to Kyiv
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused US President Donald Trump of shifting responsibility for Russia’s aggression onto Ukraine and diverting attention from problems surrounding Iran, in an interview published Thursday, Oct. 22.
Speaking to Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO podcast , Zelensky rejected Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were responsible for rising diesel prices in the US.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I think it’s wrong and unacceptable that he pins Russia’s aggression and Russia’s killings on me,” Zelensky said.
He argued that disruptions in the Middle East, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz, were at the heart of the energy problem. Zelensky accused Trump of redirecting the discussion toward Ukraine and making him personally the target of criticism.
Zelensky said he had repeatedly proposed a reciprocal halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. Such an arrangement would protect Ukrainian electricity supplies while allowing Russia to sell its energy exports.
But Putin had refused to agree to an energy ceasefire, Zelensky said, arguing that Trump was blaming Kyiv rather than confronting Moscow over that refusal.
He maintained that he had a good relationship with Trump but described the US president’s accusations as unfair.
Zelensky said that if Washington could not secure an energy truce, it should provide Ukraine with the air defense missiles needed to protect its infrastructure.
He stressed that Kyiv was seeking deliveries financed by European partners, rather than asking for the weapons free of charge. He also complained that supplies had been directed toward the Middle East while Ukraine’s needs remained unmet.
The president argued that Trump could bring Putin to the negotiating table by directing the same forceful rhetoric toward the Russian leader that he used against Ukraine.
He pointed to sanctions approved by Congress as another instrument available to Washington. Asked why Trump had not applied greater pressure, Zelensky said he did not know, offering possible explanations without claiming to know the US president’s motives.
The interview follows Trump’s criticism of Ukraine’s renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries , which he called a “disgrace” in an Oct. 15 interview with Newsmax.
Trump blamed Kyiv for higher energy prices and portrayed Zelensky as more difficult to negotiate with than Putin.
Ukraine had temporarily suspended refinery attacks at Washington’s request, but Zelensky said the pause could not continue while Russia kept striking Ukrainian energy facilities.
His position has been that any restriction on Ukrainian attacks must be matched by an end to Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s electricity grid.
The dispute intensified after Trump agreed with Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports. Zelensky has criticized that arrangement as economic relief for Moscow while its invasion continues.
Energy analysts have also questioned whether additional Russian diesel supplies would significantly reduce fuel prices, pointing instead to the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war with Iran.
The interview’s publication also came after another major Russian missile attack on Kyiv , following Putin’s meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Zelensky said Russia launched 21 ballistic missiles toward the capital in three waves overnight. Residential buildings, energy facilities, railway and metro infrastructure, shopping centers, and industrial sites were among the damaged locations.
Across Ukraine, he reported two deaths and 34 people wounded, including five children, in attacks affecting 12 regions.
The strikes followed a meeting at which the Kremlin signaled willingness to resume negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia, and the US. Witkoff also praised Putin as a humanitarian after Russia released an American detainee.
Responding to the attacks, Zelensky argued that negotiations must be accompanied by real pressure on Moscow. He called for stronger air defenses, faster missile deliveries, sanctions, and the capability to destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: China Tightens Grip on Global Shipbuilding as Order Book Hits Near-Record High
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
The 24,188 TEU capacity OOCL Spain pictured at the Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering (NACKS) shipyard in Nantong, China. Photo courtesy OOCL
China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new analysis from BIMCO.
The global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2 million compensated gross tonnage (CGT) as of September 1, 2026, up 13% from 180 million CGT a year earlier. While slightly below the all-time high of 210.4 million CGT reached in May, the backlog remains above the previous record of 195.4 million CGT set in 2008.
Chinese shipyards have been the biggest beneficiaries of the ordering boom, securing 74% of all CGT contracted over the past 12 months. China now controls 64% of the global order book, well ahead of South Korea at 19% and Japan at just 6%.
China’s lead is even more pronounced across the major commercial shipping sectors. Its yards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main vessel categories, including containerships, tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, other dry cargo ships and RoRo vessels. Together, those segments account for 88% of the global order book.
Containerships are driving much of the growth.
“Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” said Niels Rasmussen, BIMCO’s Chief Shipping Analyst.
Chinese yards hold an especially commanding 81% share of the global containership order book.
But the massive backlog also presents a growing challenge for shipbuilders, particularly in China, where scheduled deliveries are set to far exceed recent production levels.
Based on each country’s highest annual output between 2021 and 2025, Chinese shipyards have enough orders to keep them busy for an average of 4.2 years. That compares with just 1.9 years for South Korean yards and 1.7 years for Japanese yards.
The challenge is the sheer volume of ships scheduled for delivery.
Combined output from China, South Korea and Japan reached 40.1 million CGT in 2025, but scheduled deliveries climb to 55.9 million CGT in 2027 and 60 million CGT in 2028.
China faces the steepest increase, with its shipyards scheduled to deliver a record 44 million CGT in 2028, nearly double the 22.7 million CGT delivered in 2025.
Meeting those commitments will require a significant increase in production capacity.
BIMCO estimates that if capacity is instead measured against the highest annual output delivered or scheduled between 2021 and 2030, China’s order book coverage falls to 2.1 years, compared with 1.6 years for both South Korea and Japan.
The figures highlight a potential downside to China’s rapid shipbuilding expansion. While its yards currently enjoy an enormous backlog, the investments needed to meet delivery commitments could leave the industry with excess capacity if demand for new ships slows.
“China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver,” Rasmussen said.
“The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future.”

title: Show HN: Light captured – An interractive workshop on photography
body:
From a hole in a wall to the four cameras in your pocket.
Light travels in straight lines. Light from the top of the tree can only pass the hole downward, so the image lands upside down.
Big hole: bright but blurry. Tiny hole: sharp but dark, and then blurry again from diffraction. A lens solves both.
Film: silver halide crystals of random size and position. A hit crystal turns to black silver in the developer, so you get a negative.
Sensor: a regular grid of light buckets under red, green and blue filters. Software guesses the two missing colours per pixel.
Bayer filter. Each pixel only sees red, green or blue. Half are green, because our eyes are most sensitive to green. The camera fills in the rest.
Big vs small. A full-frame camera sensor next to a tiny one. A bigger sensor collects far more light in the same exposure. That's why a system camera beats a phone in the dark.
The film leaves the camera with an invisible image. Chemistry makes it visible; a second exposure turns the negative into a print.
1827 · ~8 hours or more Niépce coats a pewter plate with bitumen, which hardens where light hits it. The view from his window.
1838 · several minutes Daguerre's silver plate. The busy street looks empty because traffic moved too fast to register. Bottom left: a man stood still long enough to get his boots shined.
1888 · Kodak No. 1. $25 with film for 100 shots. When the roll was full you mailed the whole camera back, and Kodak sent prints and a reloaded camera.
Inside: a roll of film, one lens, one fixed shutter speed. No focusing at all.
1975 · Kodak again. Steven Sasson's prototype: 100 × 100 pixels, 3.6 kg, 23 seconds to save one photo to a cassette tape. Kodak didn't sell it.
Focusing means moving the lens until that point lands exactly on the film or sensor.
Close the aperture and the blur circle shrinks. That is why a small aperture gives more of the scene in focus.
Shutter speed. The same scene, shutter open for longer and longer. Short freezes the motion. Long smears it, but lets in more light.
ISO. Same shells, darker light each time: 1 s at ISO 200, 1/30 s at ISO 5000, then 1/140 s at max. Faster shutter, more noise.
Aperture. Wide open, only the chestnut is sharp. The background melts into bokeh.
Take as many as you like in each category, whenever you have the chance. The link keeps working, so you can keep adding photos.
