title: Putin’s War On Ukraine Puts Oil Giant Rosneft Under Mounting Pressure
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Valentin Pikul at Vostok Oil Project in the Russian Arctic. (Source: Rosneft)
(Bloomberg) — Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life.
Hundreds of miles of pipeline now connected oil fields to storage tanks and a new port for Vostok Oil, part of an almost $50 billion investment. With Putin watching by video link, Sechin, the powerful head of state-run Rosneft PJSC, asked to begin loading the first tanker with crude. “Permission granted,” Putin said.
The ceremony carried particular weight for Russia’s increasingly battered oil industry. Years of war and sanctions are making it harder for oil producers — including Rosneft, the nation’s largest — to maintain volumes today while developing reserves for tomorrow. Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project was supposed to show Russia could still do both. Sechin said it would add as much as 10% to the country’s current output by 2030 and supply millions of barrels to world markets for a century or more.
But the milestone obscured a more complicated reality: Years behind schedule, Vostok Oil is still far from becoming Russia’s new oil province.
The vast majority of crude flowing through the costly new Arctic network has been diverted from fields that have been producing for years. Just before the terminal opened in September, new oilfields in the Payakha cluster, expected to become key assets of Vostok Oil, accounted for less than 5% of its flows, according to a person familiar with the data, who asked not to be identified to discuss sensitive matters that aren’t public. Satellite imagery shows development continuing, but bringing those fields up to scale will require years more work and investment, according to Bloomberg analysis of the imagery and conversations with analysts.
“The development of the company’s fields is carried out in a planned manner, which allows maximum efficiency to be extracted both from existing fields and from new projects,” Rosneft said in a statement, adding that production ramp-ups at Vostok Oil depend on market needs and general economic conditions.
Viktor Kurilov, a senior analyst on the oil markets team at Rystad Energy, said building out Vostok Oil “is just one of the challenges Rosneft — and the Russian oil industry — is facing.” Among them is Ukraine’s dramatically expanded campaign of drone strikes against the country’s oil sector, which is inching closer to Vostok Oil facilities and repeatedly damaging refineries run by Rosneft and others in the European part of Russia. One of its biggest, Ryazan, which supplies fuel to Moscow and surrounding regions, has been shut for more than half the time since it was first attacked in May and has run well below full capacity when operating, according to damage assessments seen by Bloomberg.
In turn, Rosneft’s finances are suffering. The company’s profits are falling and debt is rising despite what should have been a windfall from the Iran war. Rosneft officials have expressed concern that even a few more months of the war in Ukraine could leave lasting damage across the business, according to people familiar with the matter.
The mounting toll to Rosneft and Russia’s wider oil industry helps explain why stopping Ukraine’s strikes on refineries has become such a priority for Moscow. This month, Putin and US President Donald Trump struck a deal opening the door to American purchases of Russian diesel, providing a potential boost as Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks, an important contributor to the squeeze on global diesel supplies. But an attempted energy truce quickly unraveled, narrowing Rosneft’s avenues for relief — and raising the stakes for a government that gets roughly a fifth of federal revenues from oil and gas.
This story is based on conversations with people familiar with the situation at Rosneft, expert analysis and a series of documents reviewed by Bloomberg over the last six months, including damage assessments and company plans for protecting and repairing refineries.
Vostok Oil was conceived in a different era, when Russia’s oil refineries were not under constant threat of Ukrainian attacks and production was expected only to grow. Laying out his plans to Putin at a Kremlin meeting in February 2020, Sechin described a vast new Arctic oil province that would create jobs and industry in a remote part of the country. One goal, he said, was to turn the Northern Sea Route into a major global energy corridor.
The project was also intended to address a longer-term challenge: Many of Russia’s biggest oilfields had been producing since Soviet times, making new reserves increasingly important to offset their decline. The ambition attracted foreign investors, including commodity trading giant Trafigura, which acquired a 10% stake in 2020, and a Vitol-led consortium, which bought another 5% the following year.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 upended those plans. Both Trafigura and the consortium exited, while Western sanctions restricted access to the technology and equipment needed to develop Vostok Oil and build specialized tankers capable of navigating icy waters.
As the war dragged on, Ukraine intensified its campaign against Russia’s infrastructure, increasingly targeting the refineries that turn crude oil into fuel. So far this year, Ukrainian drones have carried out at least 114 strikes on Russian refineries, more than double the number over the same period last year, according to a Bloomberg tally, based on public statements from both countries.
The attacks have pushed Russian refinery runs to multi-year lows, triggered fuel shortages and forced Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Rosneft has borne a significant share of the damage. The company operates 12 refineries accounting for about a third of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity. Of 15 confirmed drone strikes on the country’s oil-processing plants in September, five targeted major Rosneft facilities supplying fuel to European Russia, the largest consuming region, according to Bloomberg’s tally.
Rosneft is “taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants,” and will continue to make sure they are protected, the company said in its statement. “Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices,” it said.
In March, while reflecting on Rosneft’s 2025 results, Sechin, a longtime Putin ally, said Russia’s oil producers had faced a “perfect storm” of low oil prices, Western sanctions and soaring borrowing costs. Since then, repeated attacks have forced some of Rosneft’s biggest refineries to operate at reduced capacity or shut altogether.
Ryazan has been among the hardest hit, repeatedly coming under attack as Rosneft has sought to restore operations. Another refinery, Syzran, has spent much of the past six months either completely shut or operating at less than a third of capacity, according to data reviewed by Bloomberg, and the company’s Tuapse refinery on the Black Sea coast has been offline since April.
Rosneft has managed to restart some refineries within weeks of an attack, only to see them struck again as repairs are completed or nearing completion. The need to repeatedly repair damaged equipment is straining operations and causing costs to pile up to levels that Rosneft officials have privately warned cannot be sustained long-term, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. Some plants have deliberately slowed repairs as a result, stretching work that should take days into weeks, the people said.
Efforts to protect the facilities with shipping containers, nets and steel cables have proved ineffective against swarms of drones, according to company plans reviewed by Bloomberg. The damage is particularly difficult to repair when strikes hit complex secondary units such as catalytic crackers, reformers and hydrocrackers, whose parts would previously have been sourced from the West.
Sanctions are compounding the problems by restricting access to replacement equipment, forcing Rosneft to rely on Russian-made copies and Chinese imports that can take months to obtain and are not always compatible with existing machinery, people familiar with the matter said.
More broadly, the International Energy Agency said drone strikes on Russian refineries are having a “cumulative negative effect.” In September, the agency cut its outlook for Russian oil processing over the next 18 months to around 4 million barrels a day, roughly 30% below prewar levels.
The financial toll is mounting. Rosneft’s first-half net income fell by almost a fifth to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion). Its ratio of net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose to 1.8 times at the end of June, the highest in more than five years, according to quarterly statements dating back to 2020, though three reports over the period don’t disclose the ratio, making estimations of the exact size and scope more challenging.
To be sure, conditions have improved since then. Middle East disruptions have pushed the price of Russia’s Urals crude used for tax calculations above $90 a barrel, more than double its level at the start of the year, while Moscow is providing billions of rubles in subsidies to domestic fuel producers, including Rosneft, in recent months. Russia’s central bank has also cut its key rate from a record 21% to 14% over the past two years, though Rosneft has complained that the pace of reductions is “clearly insufficient.”
The company’s financial picture and the extent of damage to its infrastructure are being closely monitored by the Qatar Investment Authority, which owns 18.46% of Rosneft and has seen its dividend payments fall sharply during the Ukraine war, according to three Qatari officials familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. QIA hopes for a swift end to the conflict so its investment is protected longer-term, one of the people said.
Rosneft’s problems have coincided with signs of distress at Credit Bank of Moscow PJSC, which market participants and officials view as being in the orbit of Sechin and his oil giant. MKB, as it is known, is dealing with $8 billion in problem loans, Bloomberg reported last month. That development highlights how both Russia’s energy and banking sectors are coming under strain at the same time, a dynamic that Russian finance officials have expressed concern about, people familiar with the matter said.
Rosneft said in its statement that its “relations with MKB, as with other Russian banks, are standard,” adding that “neither Rosneft nor its Chief Executive Officer are or have ever been beneficiaries of MKB.”
Rosneft faces another financial challenge: the enormous spending still required at Vostok Oil. The project remains heavily dependent on production from Vankor, a group of established fields that began pumping crude in 2009. Its new Arctic terminal gives Rosneft another route to market for that oil, but does little on its own to increase Russia’s output.
Rystad Energy, which has analyzed satellite imagery of construction at the project, expects Vostok Oil to produce about 310,000 barrels a day in 2027, with around 90% coming from the Vankor cluster, where fields have been producing for years. Output could rise to 440,000 barrels a day by 2030 — well short of the roughly 1 million Sechin has promised — with the new Payakha fields contributing only about 80,000 barrels a day, according to the consultancy.
Getting the oil to market is another obstacle. Rosneft needs specialized tankers to navigate frigid Arctic waters, but Western sanctions have complicated efforts to build them. At least 30 would be needed by 2030 to transport Vostok Oil’s planned output, according to Sergey Vakulenko, an industry veteran and scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
“They simply don’t exist today,” he said.
With Russia’s war in Ukraine well into its fifth year, Putin has secured a potential reprieve from Washington. In an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, the Russian president said Russia would partially relax its diesel export ban, releasing thousands of barrels a day into the global market. It’s unclear what, if anything, Russia will receive in return. But in the days since, Ukraine has faced temporary restrictions on its military access to SpaceX satellite technology and US intelligence.
For Trump, the immediate concern was closer to home. Diesel prices had surged to near-record levels ahead of November’s congressional elections, squeezed by the war in Iran and disruptions to global fuel supplies. The agreement was intended to help bring prices down, though US officials have acknowledged it is unlikely to have much effect on the international diesel market. Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt refinery strikes that had constrained Russian exports.
“Unless President Putin agrees to stop attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure, or President Trump agrees to give Ukraine additional offensive and defensive capabilities, Kyiv is unlikely to abide by a unilateral ceasefire,” said Fernando Ferreira, director of geopolitical risk at Rapidan Energy Group.
The limits of the arrangement soon became apparent. Neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed the energy ceasefire Trump subsequently announced, and Kyiv resumed refinery attacks last week after accusing Moscow of continuing strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Even if the diplomacy eventually produces a more durable pause, Ukraine is already changing the battlefield. In 2022, its attacks reached targets some 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the border. By July this year, drones had struck the Omsk refinery deep in western Siberia, roughly 2,500 kilometers away.
Vostok Oil’s Arctic terminal lies another 800 kilometers beyond that, still outside Ukraine’s demonstrated reach. But the vast distances that have long sheltered Russia’s most remote energy assets offer less reassurance than they once did: If the range of Ukrainian drone strikes continues expanding at its recent pace, Vostok Oil could plausibly come within reach within months.
At last month’s opening ceremony, Sechin was still looking ahead. Bundled against the cold beside the Valentin Pikul , he told Putin that Vostok Oil would ship 30 million tons of crude as early as the second half of 2027.
It was another sign of how much the project has suffered: The terminal was meant to be ready for that volume two years ago.

title: Third-party evaluators found vulnerabilities in OpenAI monitoring system during test pilot
body:
Nonprofit evaluators METR and Redwood Research on Thursday said they conducted a pilot review of an internal monitoring system at OpenAI , the artificial intelligence company's latest effort to determine how it will deepen its work with third-party safety organizations .
METR and Redwood said the exercise was designed for OpenAI to test what it would look like to give external researchers "a deep level of access" to its internal infrastructure.
From July 21 to Aug. 11, an employee from each organization had access to OpenAI's internal codebase, documentation and some technical staffers. The employees were chaperoned while on-site and used OpenAI-issued devices that "never left the premises," according to a release.
The evaluators discovered several "novel vulnerabilities," including an exploit that would allow agents to prevent "hundreds" of recent actions from being monitored. OpenAI told METR and Redwood that it has patched the identified vulnerabilities that impact its production safeguards, according to the release.
METR and Redwood said they agreed to only publish a high-level public post about their findings since the pilot was not designed to "provide robust public transparency about OpenAI's monitoring system." They shared a 61-page internal report with OpenAI, and said they expect to publicly share more details about future exercises.
"This collaboration builds on our longstanding commitment to pioneering new approaches to third-party testing, and we're using what we learned to strengthen our safeguards and shape future collaborations with independent evaluators," an OpenAI spokesperson told CNBC in a statement.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators " employee-like access " to the company in September, after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed the idea as part of his plan to slow the pace of AI development . Anthropic has since announced agreements with organizations like Accenture , METR and SecureBio. OpenAI said earlier this month that it's "actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors."
President Donald Trump , who has taken a light-touch approach to AI regulation, has also shown support for third-party assessment. He encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented at the White House. Anthropic's Amodei signed the accord, as did top executives at Google , Meta , OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia .
Independent evaluators have historically occupied a relatively quiet corner of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry, so experts told CNBC that questions remain about how these groups will be funded and what their reporting structures will ultimately look like.
METR and Redwood said Thursday that they stress-tested OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system during its three-week pilot. In AI, alignment is how researchers describe whether a model behaves in line with human interests and values.
The evaluators assessed the monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21, and noted that OpenAI was expanding the system during the exercise.

title: Elon Musk made a $1 billion investment in Skydance, report says
body:
Elon Musk has invested approximately $1 billion in the newly formed media company Skydance, according to a new report from Semafor . News of the investment comes a few weeks after Paramount completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to create the combined company.
Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with bringing together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with a portfolio of networks, including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network, under a single corporate umbrella.
Semafor reports that Musk’s investment was made around the same time as equity contributions from other Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs. The investment will provide a much needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price, the report notes.
Skydance has already committed to reducing costs by $6 billion over the next three years.
Musk has publicly praised the Ellisons in the past and has close ties with Larry Ellison, whom he appointed to Tesla’s board of directors in 2018. The Oracle founder invested $1 billion to help Musk purchase Twitter in 2022 and also invested in Tesla in 2018.
Skydance did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: Objects, attributes, maps, oh my
body:
In many dynamically typed programming languages, objects look like a big ol’ mapping of names to values. The languages encourage this flexibility. Consider for example Python:
This might encourage the VM implementor to model object attributes using a hash table. Hash tables, after all, are very good at mapping names to values.
Here is, by way of example, a Python sketch of what this object model looks like. Because it is a sketch, it uses write_attr and read_attr instead of the much more common syntax that your programming language comes with.
This means that literally every operation a.b is doing hundreds or thousands of CPU instructions, including multiple dependent memory loads. This is not good for performance.
So runtime implementors tend to implement this thing called maps, or layouts, or shapes, or hidden classes, or structures, or probably a secret sixth name I don’t know about, which optimizes reading, writing, and storage of attributes.
But what does this shape code look like? How does it actually help performance? A lot of big production runtimes have pretty hairy code with domain-specific edge cases so they may not help get a handle on the basics. And a lot of blog posts, while excellent high-level overviews, are lacking in implementation. So here we go once more, blogging where everyone else has already blogged before. With any luck, you should be able to write a page of code and hold the whole thing in your head at once.
I decided to once more give CF Bolz-Tereick’s A Simple Object Model the thorough read it deserves. In the past, I tried a couple times and bounced off of it because it models Python with reasonable fidelity and the Python object model is really hairy .
But did I read it thoroughly this time? Well, no. This time I allowed myself to skim the class- and method-related parts and instead focus on the instance attribute and map parts. Inside CF’s post is the core of a very clean map system and I wanted to experiment with that, so I extracted it out.
CF’s post starts off very similar to our own sketch, modeling objects as unordered maps of attributes. It also fills in some of the TODO stuff I left out earlier around classes. I’ll copy my reduced implementation of it here so you can take a gander:
Which you can use like this (test code also taken from CF’s post):
There’s a bit of delegation going on in the Base class because the post already anticipates what we’re about to do: swap out the Instance implementation for _read_dict and _write_dict for better performance.
OK, let’s add on this “map” data structure. The purpose of the map is to do three things:
For the former , we can think of an object’s map field as an (database) index or a write-through cache. It is responsible for reflecting on the layout of a given object:
You can ask the map questions like “what attributes does this object have?” and “where is attribute a relative to the start of the object?”
Just looking at the diagram, it may seem silly: after all, we have exchanged one hash table for another. There’s one big difference, though, which is that in the shape model, we don’t have to always use the hash table. If we remember the offset since the last time we looked it up in the shape, we can re-use the offset. This mostly appears in an interpreter feature called an inline cache.
This brings us to the second bit : if we have the offset into the object, we can read right off of it. No need to go do a second load from another region of memory. We have the object in hand and hopefully already in the cache.
…At least, until the map changes . Then we can’t re-use the offset. Remember, these languages encourage this flexibility. An object could gain or lose an attribute at any time. What then? Ideally we have a very fast check that can tell us if the object’s in-memory layout changed.
This brings us to the third bit . We need to be able to rely on the map to be immutable, up-to-date, and a stable identifier for a given in-memory layout. This way we can do a very quick check (“is the map the same as last read?”) before a load.
This means that when we add a new attribute to an object, we need to give it a new map. Maps are actually trees (tries?) and are allocated like a persistent data structure. Every new object starts with an empty map. As the program adds attributes, it follows the edges in the tree to find or create its new map.
I recommend reading the section on maps because it goes into a little more detail.
Keeping all of that in mind, let’s take a look at CF’s Python implementation of objects-with-maps and also of maps themselves:
You may notice that the storage is not in-line, as I had originally promised. This is because we don’t have that kind of object layout control in Python. Attribute storage, when implemented in a language such as C++ or Rust, is typically in-line with the object header.
Ignoring that, though, we can see that the common case still seems to read and write attributes using string names. What gives? Well, let’s use the index storage as intended in an inline cache .
Let’s start by looking at the string attribute API. We’ll make a point class and read the x attribute. We’ll keep the attribute name constant since this is generally fixed in the program: obj.x normally looks like some bytecode LOAD_ATTRIBUTE, "x" where the name x is embedded in the bytecode somehow.
This is important for the inline cache: varying the receiver is one thing but varying the name being looked up adds a lot more complexity. It’s doable but irritating.
Then we will make a memory/speed trade-off. We will allocate space for the aforementioned expected map and the cached index mentioned earlier. This lets us do a really fast check followed by an indexed load in the (hopefully) common case.
If the attribute is missing, we don’t (for now?) cache the negative lookup. Hopefully this case is rare.
You may note that I used is (pointer equality) instead of == (user-defined/deep equality). This is intentional! Because we are guaranteeing the maps are immutable, we don’t need to check equality on the fields of the map; just its pointer/numeric ID.
This InlineCache class is mostly just a “sketch” of what an inline cache does. It is an “interpreted IC”. This shape, if you make sure the fast path is inlined and the slow path is outlined, can help your interpreter a lot. It does definitely improve performance—I recommend benchmarking a silly little attribute lookup function—but most runtimes with inline caches also come with JIT compilers. These compilers try to remove the “interpreted”-ness of the inline cache implementation. See for example:
Another thing to notice is that order matters . Adding attributes in different orders (e.g. a then b vs b then a ) will result in different shapes. Another frequent cause of this is conditionally storing attributes in initialization (e.g. if cond: self.a = 1 ).
This shape and cache behavior is not really visible to the application programmer except in performance regressions 2 , where either your inline caches will frequently miss or you will not have optimal (monomorphic) caches. This might not sound scary but the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss in a hot path could be 2x performance or more and is worth investigating in your application.
Also, quantity matters . VM implementors measured and determined that most objects are small (<20 ish fields). You may find that putting too many fields on an object leads to it getting penalized and put back in “hash table mode”. Ruby, for example, has some fixed number of in-object instance variables (attributes) before its shape becomes “complex”.
Last, notice that this cache is not specific to this object; any number of Point instances can get a cache hit. Actually, looking at it, an object need not even be a Point …
What does it mean that two objects with different classes can have the same shape?
For one, it means that the inline cache may have a higher hit rate. Instances of subclasses that share code, for example, may still count as monomorphic in the IC.
It also means that you can’t use the shape as a proxy for knowing about the class. If you have something like attr_reader in Ruby, where the VM generates a synthetic method just for looking up an instance variable, you need to do two things:
This two-stage lookup adds both complexity and run-time overhead. If we specialized maps so that having a different class implied having a different map, we would be able to specialize that two-stage dispatch with just one field load.
This is kind of an interesting idea: what else can we specialize the map on?
Perhaps unsurprisingly, CF Bolz-Tereick reappears with Lukas Diekmann and Laurence Tratt in Storage Strategies for Collections in Dynamically Typed Languages (PDF, 2013).
The main idea is that some facts about objects (properties, attributes, har har) are both:
Their treatment is for collections (for example, optimizing the common cases of an empty list, or a list of small integers, …). In addition to giving more information to the optimizer, it helps both reduce memory and reduce pointer chasing.
This kind of thinking extends beyond collections: do you ever have objects where an attribute is always a certain type? Maybe your Point class always has floats in it? Consider, then, what I think of as CF’s follow-up paper, type freezing: Type Freezing: Exploiting Attribute Type Monomorphism in Tracing JIT Compilers (PDF, 2020)
This paper changes object maps from {name: offset} to {name: (offset, type)} to reduce guards. Then it goes further by even addressing nested attributes and their types. This nesting extension is mostly motivated by the meta-circularity of the implementation and would have less impact for a “normal” runtime.
You can make even stronger bets about classes. See for example the PyPy blog class versioning section .
I felt like this blog post would not be complete without a manual memory layout rehashing of CF’s article. It’s all well and good to write the Python but what do “real” runtimes look like?
Well, they have compact object headers that contain the shape/map and some other flag bits. They allocate their attributes inline with an object. And they probably also have an “overflow” slot for when their initial object sizing estimates were too small.
So I made a very very small runtime in C++ that allocates objects and adds attributes and has a shape system. It is probably riddled with bugs. But it sketches the kind of memory layouts that underpin Skybison, V8, JSC, and so on.
It doesn’t have the overflow slot but it’s a decent sketch of the underlying model.
I fear I am running out of steam on this blog post but there is more to talk about. I originally wanted to go add object shapes to someone’s Lox interpreter and then add inline caches to the interpreter.
Perhaps I will come back and update this post. Or perhaps you will write a sequel.
Thank you to CF Bolz-Tereick, Nery Campusano, and Jacob Denbeaux for thoughtful feedback on this post.
See this Rails PR by Hartley to make shapes more monomorphic. It was initially filed because ZJIT was not capable of handling shape polymorphic reads, but it helps other JITs stay monomorphic too. Also in this vein is my PR to optcarrot .
ZJIT now does much better with polymorphic shapes but this kind of stuff is generally important across languages and runtimes. Enough for people to do large bodies (PDF) of research (PDF) about intelligibly surfacing this kind of information to the application programmer. ↩

title: Oil Climbs Above $111 as AI Stocks Slide, Dragging the S&P 500 and Global Markets With Them
body:
Brent crude, the global benchmark price for oil, jumped 2.6% to $111.66 a barrel on Thursday, its highest level in five months, as AI-linked stocks slid and dragged markets lower from Asia to Wall Street.
By mid-morning in New York, the Nasdaq, an index heavy with tech companies, was down 1.5% and the S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the largest US companies, had lost 0.8%.
Nvidia, the largest US company by market value, fell 2.3% and weighs so heavily on the S&P 500 that its slides reach the index funds inside many retirement accounts. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September alone, which means the same oil shock rattling the stock market is already showing up at the pump.
South Korea's Kospi, the country's benchmark stock index, fell 3.52% to 5,533.77 after a recovery yesterday, while Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.65% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 3.03%. China's CSI 300, which tracks 300 large companies listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, entered a bear market, the term for a fall of 20% or more from a recent peak.
The selloff followed the Kospi plunging 7.57% in a single session on Oct. 15 that local coverage dubbed “Black Thursday,” triggering a circuit breaker, an automatic trading pause meant to calm panic selling. The index is still more than 40% below its June peak.
CoreWeave, which borrowed to buy Nvidia chips that it rents out to other companies through the cloud, fell 3.8% on worries about its debt. Meta dropped 5.8% after its profit missed forecasts, and Lam Research, a chip equipment maker, slid 7.7% after guiding profit slightly below analyst estimates.
Citadel founder Ken Griffin said Tuesday that investors are “almost certainly” in an AI bubble, comparing AI chips to airline seats that cost little to run once bought, so prices can collapse when supply outruns demand. He did not tell investors to sell, but his message still feels contrarian in the middle of a market that has been permabullish since the advent of ChatGPT back in 2023.
The Federal Reserve’s next decision comes Oct. 28, with markets pricing roughly a 15% chance of another hike and a December increase still widely expected. This may be at least partially priced in, but a hike would be bad news for the markets as it makes investments more expensive.
Core PCE inflation data, a price measure that strips out food and energy, follows Oct. 29, and October payrolls arrive Nov. 6.

title: Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs
body: Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL , short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget. TL;DR Engine : Serves LFM2.5 models from 230M to 2.6B parameters Runs on: Enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Benchmarks used a single B200. Performance: 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM, per Liquid’s own tests. Best: LFM2.5-1.2B hit 155.8 ms p95 vs 4,431 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B, a 28.4x gap (256 in, 128 out). Worst: LFM2.5-2.6B gained only 5.6x (449.1 ms vs 2,499 ms). Sub-50 ms fails on longer requests. What problem does Liquid RIPL solve? Most serving stacks target large batches and long agentic jobs. A few seconds per request is acceptable there. Search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues teams default to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow. RIPL is built to remove that trade-off. How does RIPL work? Liquid AI describes RIPL as optimizing the full path, from request arrival to completed response. In several workloads, Liquid AI plots the same model, LFM2.5-350M, on vLLM and on RIPL. RIPL’s p95 line sits well below the vLLM line in each case. That isolates part of the gain to the engine, not just the model architecture. The LFM2.5 models themselves are hybrids. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct has 16 layers: 10 double-gated convolution blocks and 6 GQA blocks. LFM2.5-2.6B has 30 layers: 22 convolution blocks and 8 GQA blocks. RIPL benchmarks: how fast is it vs vLLM? Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM. Sealf-reported. Liquid AI also mapped 6 real-time workloads against fixed budgets: Adtech query rewriting: 32 in, 32 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-350M. Search intent classification: 128 in, 1 out, 20 ms budget. Search reranking: 1k in, 1 out, 30 ms budget. Payments risk scoring: 512 in, 16 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-1.2B. Credit decisioning: 8k in, 64 out, 150 ms budget. Yes, according to Liquid AI. Shopify is deploying LFMs across latency-sensitive commerce workloads. In search enhancement, LFMs run with sub-20 ms inference on production traffic. According to Liquid AI’s blog, they use about 50% fewer parameters than alternatives and deliver 2 to 10x faster inference. Key Takeaways RIPL is Liquid AI’s engine for LLMs inside live request paths. Liquid claims 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM. Same-model tests (LFM2.5-350M) show RIPL itself beats vLLM. Shopify runs LFMs at sub-20 ms in production search. Enterprise-only, closed, and all figures are self-reported. title: Citi’s $60 Oil Call Meets $112 Brent
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Citi sees more upside risk for oil prices despite recovering Middle Eastern crude exports, a considerably less bearish assessment from the bank that predicted $60-to-$65 Brent by year-end just three months ago.
Brent December futures traded at $111.70 on Thursday, up $2.88, or 2.65%, after touching $112.68 earlier in the session.
The problem, Citi says, is that getting crude out of the Gulf and getting it to buyers at a reasonable cost are two different things.
More than 1 million barrels per day of Gulf crude was transferred between vessels in September, representing about 7.5% of regional exports. Before the U.S.-Iran war, these transfers were virtually nonexistent.
Freight rates for very large crude carriers traveling from the Gulf to China recently approached $250 per metric ton, or roughly $35 per barrel, Citi estimates. That's more than 20 times the previous decade's average.
Excluding Iran, Gulf crude exports recovered to more than 81% of prewar levels in September, aided by increased Saudi shipments. Iran's own exports have fallen to zero under a U.S. blockade.
Before the war began in February, the Strait of Hormuz handled about one-fifth of the world's oil and LNG supplies.
Citi has had to rethink its oil market outlook repeatedly. In July, it urged investors to sell summer rallies and predicted Brent would fall to $60-$65 by year-end as Hormuz shipping normalized.
In August, Citi raised its third-quarter Brent forecast from $75 to $80 but left its fourth-quarter call at $70 and its 2027 forecast at $65. Brent was trading at $83.11 when Citi issued that revision.
The bank offered no new price target in Thursday's assessment. Instead, it warned that the recovery in Gulf exports has been a recovery in volumes, not shipping efficiency.
Buyers are receiving more crude, but the added transfers and soaring freight costs are keeping delivered supplies expensive.

title: USS Abraham Lincoln crew prepares for base move weeks after extended deployment
body: After a 10-month deployment that was extended twice, including 40 days of combat operations against Iran that kept sailors at sea for 265 days without a port call , the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln and their families are preparing to move to a new base just weeks after arriving home. By the end of this year, the aircraft carrier will shift its home port from San Diego, California, to Bremerton, Washington, for long-planned maintenance, a Navy spokesperson told Task & Purpose. The Navy has set Dec. 31, 2026, as the administrative date for the change. As of Oct. 22, the Navy’s Dec. 31 administrative benchmark is just 10 weeks away, as sailors and their families navigate post-deployment leave and preparations for relocation. Top Stories This Week News Airman dies in rappelling demonstration at Navy football game By Nicholas Slayton News Hegseth’s plan to restore Confederate memorial at Arlington expected to cost taxpayers $9 million By Austin Campbell News Hundreds of 10th Mountain Division soldiers deploying to Latin America By Nicholas Slayton The 5,000 sailors aboard the Lincoln spent 321 days away from home, including 40 days in combat, and were awarded a Presidential Unit Citation for valor upon their return to San Diego. “This will be a deliberate pause from high-tempo operational tasking to focus on restoring material readiness, upgrading warfighting capabilities, and preparing the carrier and its crew for future tasks,” a Navy spokesperson told Task & Purpose. The carrier’s extended deployment drew national scrutiny earlier this year after military families raised concerns about deteriorating living conditions and sailors’ mental health. Navy and Pentagon officials initially disputed reports of a crisis , though within days the service began sending additional mental health support personnel to the carrier . The following month, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirmed that eight sailors across the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment. The long-planned home port change from San Diego to Naval Base Kitsap in Washington now presents another challenge for sailors and their families. At an August town hall in San Diego, family members expressed frustration to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and other senior officials about uncertainty surrounding the carrier’s impending move to Washington, according to Military Times. Sailors with the USS Abraham Lincoln return to home port in San Diego, California, on Oct. 8, 2026. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Maliq J. Martin. Permanent change of station moves have long presented challenges for military families, who must navigate housing, employment, school enrollment and the logistics of transporting their belongings between duty stations. In 2017, Task & Purpose reported that Navy families were receiving less than eight weeks ’ notice to relocate, leaving some scrambling to arrange moves and manage the financial burdens of uprooting their households. More recently, the war with Iran has complicated military relocations. In March, Task & Purpose reported that disruptions to international shipping , heightened security at military installations and rising transportation costs were creating additional challenges for families moving between duty stations, including within the United States. For some families, the relocation comes as sailors are getting to know children born during their deployment. According to Navy Times, 122 sailors from the Lincoln and its embarked air wing became fathers while deployed , meeting their children for the first time when the carrier returned to San Diego on Oct. 8. It remains unclear how many of those families will relocate to Washington with infants less than a year old. “Abraham Lincoln sailors and their families are moving to Bremerton individually, with full support from the chain of command and permanent change of station resources,” a Navy spokesperson told Task & Purpose. That support, according to the Navy, includes standard PCS benefits such as the shipment and storage of household goods and travel allowances. Eligible sailors relocating dependents may receive up to four proceed days, while commanders may authorize up to 10 days of house-hunting time, subject to operational requirements. The Navy also said Naval Base Kitsap and regional partners have established transition programs for incoming families, including childcare support, housing assistance and a “Welcome to Kitsap” resource fair. title: US permitting: Environmental review overhaul could speed mine approvals, but hurdles remain
body: A bipartisan permitting reform proposal introduced in the US Senate on September 30 could deliver some of the most consequential changes to federal environmental approvals in decades, potentially shortening project development timelines and reducing legal uncertainty for mining companies. Sweeping bipartisan legislation targeting environmental reviews, litigation deadlines and water permits could reshape how mining projects are developed in the United States, but significant political negotiations are imminent. Its sponsors anticipate consideration after the November midterm elections, but the bill’s path through Congress remains uncertain, according to an October report authored by Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman attorneys. The proposed reforms would affect major federal environmental statutes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act, with implications extending beyond mining to renewable energy, transmission infrastructure and other major industrial developments, co-author of the report, and Houston office managing partner Amanda Halter told MINING.COM in an interview. Halter, an environmental lawyer who advises mining companies on project development, permitting, environmental liabilities, and cross-border regulatory matters, said the legislation represents a rare opportunity for meaningful reform. “It’s a really big deal that we have a real, large-scale, bipartisan permitting reform bill on the table,” Halter said. The proposal addresses longstanding concerns among mining companies about lengthy federal approval processes and the potential for litigation to delay projects even after permits have been granted. However, Halter cautioned that the legislation remains at an early stage. The Senate has not voted on the proposal, and it has yet to reach the House of Representatives. Supporters are pushing for passage before the current Congress ends on January 3, while others favour waiting until after the November mid-term elections, potentially reopening negotiations under a new Congress. Faster environmental reviews Among the most significant proposed changes for mining companies is an expansion of categorical exclusions under NEPA, which allow certain activities to proceed without preparing an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement . Halter said the changes could substantially shorten NEPA review timelines for qualifying components of larger mining developments. The bill would let lead agencies combine different categorical exclusions and allow agencies to adopt another agency’s exclusion. When the lead agency for the project determines that no NEPA document is required, it would bar other agencies from preparing one. While the bill stops short of proposing project-level exemptions from NEPA, it would nevertheless be beneficial for streamlining necessary approvals overall. “Most mining projects won’t, but aspects of the project may,” she said, referring to eligibility for categorical exclusions. The bill also addresses a practical issue for hard rock mines on federal land. Subject to a federally approved plan of operations, it would allow claim holders to also locate multiple mill sites for waste rock, tailings, and related operations on eligible federal land. The legislation would also seek to strengthen existing environmental review deadlines and sharply reduce the time available to challenge certain federal approvals in court. Under the bill, certain NEPA challenges would have to be brought within 150 days, a significant reduction from the potentially six-year period available for some challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act. “How good is your approval if someone can sue on it for six years?” Halter said, describing the current litigation window as a major source of uncertainty for mining project investment decisions. The proposal would also generally require challengers to have raised substantive concerns during the administrative review process and to demonstrate actual or imminent injury. Halter said the intention is to encourage objections to be addressed while federal agencies are reviewing projects, rather than allowing disputes to emerge years after decisions have been made. The broader objective, she said, is to get relevant information before regulators more quickly and make permitting decisions more durable. Changes to the Clean Water Act could also have significant financial implications for mine operators by potentially doubling the maximum term of discharge permits. The proposal would extend the statutory maximum duration for National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits from five to 10 years. These permits regulate pollutant discharges into US waters and can require mining companies to make substantial investments in water treatment and discharge management systems. Halter said extending the durations of permit terms could improve the economics of those investments by providing greater regulatory certainty, though a 10-year term would be a maximum and not a guarantee. “If the permit for your major investment is only good for five years, that’s a harder business case than, hey, ‘I’m going to make a major investment that’s going to be good for 10 years,’” she said. However, Halter expects the provision to become a significant negotiating point. Environmental advocates could argue that longer permit terms reduce opportunities to revisit discharge requirements as environmental conditions, scientific understanding and treatment technologies evolve. “I think what the environmentalists would say is that the world is changing far too rapidly to have 10-year time horizons on discharge permits,” Halter said. Endangered species protections Proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act could prove equally contentious. The legislation seeks to refine the scientific and commercial information agencies must consider in endangered species determinations and shorten some consultation timelines, with the aim of making regulatory decisions more focused and timely. For mining companies, endangered species requirements can become a major obstacle when projects overlap with sensitive habitats or protected species. Halter expects this section of the legislation to undergo substantial negotiations between conservation groups and project proponents. The proposed changes reflect an effort to balance species protections with greater predictability in project approvals, she said. Bipartisan opportunity, uncertain outcome Despite potential opposition to individual provisions, Halter said the proposal has an unusual advantage: both conventional energy and renewable energy developers have an interest in faster permitting. Transmission infrastructure in particular has become a bottleneck for renewable energy expansion, creating common ground among constituencies that otherwise disagree on environmental and energy policy. “There’s something in here for everyone,” Halter said. That shared interest could give the legislation a realistic chance of advancing, even if its final provisions differ substantially from those currently proposed. For mining companies evaluating US projects, the reforms could eventually provide greater certainty over permitting schedules, environmental obligations and litigation exposure. But Halter warned against assuming the proposed changes will become law in their current form. “This is a really big potential deal, but it isn’t a done deal,” she said. “So pay attention. There’s a lot that’s going to happen in the sausage making.”

title: Underdog taps zerohash to bring crypto deposits to prediction markets
body:
The new funding option, expected to launch later this year, will allow eligible Underdog users to deposit digital assets around the clock.
Prediction market operator Underdog has partnered with crypto infrastructure provider zerohash to introduce cryptocurrency and stablecoin deposits, with the new funding option expected to launch later this year.
Eligible users will be able to fund their accounts directly through the Underdog app using supported digital assets, with the service designed to enable near-instant transfers around the clock, according to a Thursday announcement.
Underdog did not specify which cryptocurrencies or stablecoins would be supported and did not respond to Cointelegraph’s request for clarification before publication.
The new funding option will supplement existing methods, including debit and credit cards, Apple Pay and bank transfers. Users will not need to manage wallet addresses or select blockchain networks when making deposits.
Founded in 2020, Underdog has more than 11 million registered accounts, according to IG Group, which agreed in July to acquire the company in a deal worth up to $1.3 billion. The transaction is expected to close in late 2026 or early 2027.
According to DeFiRate data , the company recorded $1.4 billion in trading volume over the 30 days ending Oct. 21, a 133% increase from the previous period, though it remained well behind Kalshi’s $81.5 billion and the combined $17.2 billion recorded by Polymarket’s US and international platforms.

The Nintendo Switch 2 has apparently been jailbroken, and a modder has already shown the console running a custom version of Mario Kart World featuring new playable characters like Cinnamoroll, the red Angry Bird, Peter Griffin, and Steve from Minecraft .
OpenAI’s Codex helped make this “ ns2jb ” jailbreak, according to Sammy Hajhamid , aka “pepsipu.” It’s a software-only, tethered jailbreak, which, in this case, means that you’ll have to run it from a game every time you turn the console on for it to work. This exploit requires the game SmileBASIC 4 , which lets users program and play games (though another modder claims that the title is “not strictly needed”).
This jailbreak still seems extremely complex for most people, and its full impact isn’t clear yet; users on the Switch 2 hacks subreddit are debating how big of a deal it actually is. Still, this could mark the beginning of a string of exploits for the Switch 2, especially if modders use AI to help .

title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
body: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site . As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n , a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly. How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program? I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on. What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why? I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity. How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends? It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize. What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend? I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool. Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating. Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding? I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application. Think of a request parameter, uploaded file, API input, or data coming from another service. A sink can be a security-sensitive operation that consumes this data, for example, a network request, file access, process execution, database query, or authorization decision. The interesting part is tracing the path between the two. I look at how the data is transformed, validated, or passed across trust boundaries, and whether those controls are sufficient before it reaches the sink. I like this approach because it lets me reason about attack paths without forcing my investigation into a predefined bug class. Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation. I consider a finding confirmed once I understand the attack path, can produce a working PoC, and can explain the impact. Do you use AI in your research? Where does it genuinely help and where does it fall short? Yes. Quite a lot, actually, but mostly as an accelerator. I use it for navigating unfamiliar code, finding call sites, tracing data through the codebase, and understanding how a system is structured and how its components interact. I also find it helpful for writing PoC scripts once I’ve identified the vulnerability. Where it works best is when the question is specific. “Is this application vulnerable?” usually isn’t a very useful prompt. Give it the right context, explain what you already know, and ask a narrow question, and the quality goes up dramatically. There’s a bit of a paradox there. AI becomes more useful as you understand the problem better yourself. And I never treat its conclusions as facts. Hallucinations, false positives, bad assumptions, and confidently wrong answers are all common. Everything should still be manually verified. AI makes my work faster. However, it doesn’t replace understanding the application, developing intuition, or proving that something actually works. What’s your guidance on using AI responsibly in bug bounty? Use it to improve your research, not to outsource responsibility for it. If AI tells you it found a vulnerability, that doesn’t mean you found a real vulnerability. You still need to reproduce it yourself. You should understand exactly what’s happening, which security boundary or control is being violated, and what the real impact is. Ideally, you should understand the issue well enough that you could write the report without AI at all. Build a clear PoC. Make sure the security team can follow it. Know why every step matters. AI has lowered the barrier to doing security research, which is great in a lot of ways. But you can also see the downside in the number of unverified reports teams now have to deal with. AI should make research better. Not just make more reports. As the industry ships more AI-powered features, does testing them require a different mindset than traditional web bugs? Yes. Conventional vulnerabilities still matter, but attackers may also be able to influence a probabilistic decision-making component through the data, instructions, or context it receives. But getting a model to say or do something unexpected isn’t necessarily the interesting part. The more important question is what that influence allows an attacker to achieve. Can they access something they should not or cause the system to act with privileges the attacker does not have? That’s why I don’t think model-level guardrails should ever be treated as the only or primary security boundary. You still need deterministic controls around the model. This includes proper authorization, least-privilege access, isolation, and validation. The surrounding systems matter just as much as the model itself. And traditional application security doesn’t disappear just because AI is involved. Model output should still be treated as untrusted input. If that output ends up in a browser, database query, shell command, web request, or another downstream system without the right controls, you can still end up with very familiar vulnerabilities: XSS, SQL injection, command injection, SSRF, and so on. I think the model is new. A lot of the dangerous sinks aren’t. What’s one thing you wish you’d known when you first started? Learn systems, not checklists. When I started, I was tempted to collect huge lists of techniques, payloads, tools, and bypasses and then work through them one by one. Those lists can be useful. I still use them. But understanding how a system works has been far more valuable. Its internal logic. The data flows. Trust relationships. Assumptions. Why one component is allowed to talk to another. Why a particular restriction exists in the first place. I also learned not to assume something is secure because it looks secure, or because plenty of researchers have already tested it. A lot of interesting research begins with: “Why does this work this way?” rather than “Which payload should I try next?” There’s some luck involved too. Sometimes you spend days following something that goes absolutely nowhere. Then you notice one tiny detail almost by accident and it turns into a high-impact finding. You can’t control that part. You can control whether you keep questioning things long enough to notice it. What advice or resources would you recommend to researchers trying to land their first valid report? Get comfortable with the fundamentals, then pick one program and one target and stick with them for a while. Constantly jumping between targets makes it difficult to build a real mental model of any of them. Use the application. Explore weird flows. Test different roles and permission levels. Read the documentation. Watch the requests and responses. Look at the APIs. Labs, courses, public write-ups, disclosed bug bounty reports, and intentionally vulnerable applications are all useful too. They teach you where bugs tend to hide and, over time, help build the intuition to recognize similar situations elsewhere. One mistake I see a lot is relying on tools too early. Another is giving up because the obvious tests didn’t find anything. Tools help. They don’t build the mental model for you. And when you finally do find something, spend the extra time validating it properly. Create a working PoC. Make reproduction easy for the security team. Understanding one target deeply will usually get you further than trying to find a bug as quickly as possible. What do you enjoy doing when you aren’t hacking? Endurance sports, mainly road cycling, especially in the mountains. I enjoy the physical challenge of a long climb and pushing myself over longer distances. It’s also a great way to get away from screens for a while and spend some time outside. There’s actually something about climbing that feels pretty similar to vulnerability research. You can put in a lot of effort without seeing much progress. Sometimes you have no idea whether what you’re doing is going to lead anywhere. You just keep going. And every now and then, it pays off. Any social media profiles you’d like to share with our readers? You can find me on HackerOne . Thank you, @r31n , for participating in GitHub’s bug bounty researcher spotlight! Each submission to our bug bounty program is a chance to make GitHub, our products, and our customers more secure, and we continue to welcome and appreciate collaboration with the security research community. So, if this inspired you to go hunting for bugs, feel free to report your findings through HackerOne . title: Dual-Fuel Ship Fleet Tops 500 as Industry Investment Passes $200 Billion
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Jane McAllister works a ZIM containership at the Port of Virginia. Photo courtesy McAllister Towing
The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC).
The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 vessels.
The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook.
“The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.”
Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. However, their ability to reduce emissions depends heavily on the availability and cost of cleaner fuels.
According to WSC, alternative-fuel-capable vessels now account for 65% of containerships and 97% of vehicle carriers on order, measured by deadweight tonnage. That compares with just 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet.
Despite that shift, orders for conventionally fueled ships have also increased over the past year as the overall orderbook continues to expand.
The mixed picture comes amid continued uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Adoption of the framework was postponed in October 2025, with negotiations set to resume later this year.
WSC argues that a global regulatory framework is needed to close the cost gap between conventional fuels and renewable and near-zero-emission alternatives while giving shipowners and fuel producers the certainty needed to invest.
Without an international agreement, the industry also faces the prospect of an increasingly fragmented system of regional emissions rules, adding costs and complexity to global shipping.
“Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said.
The IMO is scheduled to hold its next Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3, with a possible resumed session on the Net-Zero Framework on December 4.
“We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework,” Kramek said. “Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.”

title: Vance: Starlink Use Depends on US Policy Toward Kyiv, Moscow – Not Musk
body:
US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday, Oct. 22, that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk should not be at the center of the dispute over restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite service, framing the issue instead as a matter of US policy toward the war in Ukraine.
Vance spoke to reporters before departing for a rally in North Platte, Nebraska, a day after senior US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Well, I think that fundamentally Elon Musk runs a private corporation, and I think it’s completely understandable that he doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the US government effectively directing him on what to do,” Vance said.
“So I don’t think this is about Elon,” he continued, leaving unanswered who ordered the restrictions – a decision for which both Musk and the White House denied responsibility while pointing to the other.
Asked by a reporter whether he supported Republican calls for an investigation, Vance turned to European governments instead of answering directly.
He said it was ironic that countries with nothing comparable to SpaceX’s technology had spent years targeting the company with regulation and licensing restrictions, now relying on the company.
Currently, the EU is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program that could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027.
“Now they’re all running to SpaceX saying, ‘Please do what we need you to do,’” he said, arguing that the situation proved a point that US President Donald Trump has long made; that European countries rely on American technology, businesses and military power.
At the same time, Vance claimed that “European political leaders love to bash the US allies that they depend upon so much.”
The remark comes amid European criticism of Trump’s abrupt Oct. 9 diesel deal with Putin, which eased US sanctions on Russian fuel and effectively cleared the war for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel to reach the global market.
While Europe has sanctions imposed on Moscow since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Trump has waived new sanctions on Russia which he signed into law just three weeks before striking a deal with the Kremlin leader.
On Monday, Oct. 19, a member of Trump’s Republican party, US Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, warned that anyone who tries to restrict Ukraine’s use of Starshield will face accountability , including a full investigation, public hearings and steep budget cuts.
Fitzpatrick also pledged to introduce bipartisan legislation , the “Roland Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” blocking all purchases of Russian oil.
One of the reporters pointed out that Ukraine has repeatedly agreed to negotiations, while Russia has not, and asked what gives Vance confidence that the current peace negotiations, led by Witkoff, will be different.
Vance claimed that both countries have agreed to join the negotiating table, adding that “the reason why we haven’t struck a peace deal is because they’ve [Kyiv and Moscow] just been too far apart on some of the details of that negotiation.”
According to him, Witkoff re-engaged the process.
“I mean, the nature of these things is you take a swing at it, you see how much progress it can make, and you’re back at it. And sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t,” he said, praising Witkoff and Trump’s administration for taking on difficult work, knowing that they “have a tall mountain to climb.”
So far, the Kremlin rebuked every proposition for a direct meeting with Ukraine, as well as proposals for a ceasefire.
In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, 51 countries issued a joint statement supporting Ukraine and urging Russia to accept an immediate ceasefire.
During the same summit, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who represented Putin, said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations . He also blamed Europe for “engaging in their shenanigans,” saying Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if they hadn’t.
At Witkoff’s request during their three-hour meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, Putin said he would be willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in November.
During the same visit, Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for releasing an American prisoner held in Russia, drawing sharp criticism from both Republicans and Democrats.
The Starlink (Starshield) controversy is just one of the latest strains in diplomatic relations between Ukraine and the US.
Tensions began when Trump announced the controversial diesel deal while the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami with US officials, hoping for a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
Kyiv later said it had been warned that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine kept striking Russian oil refineries. Around the same time, Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president, claiming Putin was easier to negotiate with.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukrainian military units lost connectivity on terminals moving at roughly 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) or faster, without prior warning. The disruption crippled several types of drones Ukraine uses, including interceptor drones used against Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds.
On Oct. 14, Musk claimed that limits on the military Starshield service were set by the US military, and ultimately the president himself, while Trump denied involvement.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said.
Since then, reports have pointed in both directions. While Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that the order originated inside the White House, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, Oct. 20 that Musk ordered the restrictions himself.
On Oct. 21, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Musk determines Ukraine’s access to Starlink under a private commercial contract.
The episode has even drawn criticism from within Trump’s own party. Besides Fitzpatrick, Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen led nine senators in asking the Pentagon’s inspector general on Oct. 15 to investigate the disruptions.
Following a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine for early warnings of Russian attack is working again , adding that Ukraine could see results within the next 48 hours on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Water, carbon & the ‘tree of life’: Interview with Venezuela’s guardian of morichales
body: While global climate conversations tend to center on the Amazon and temperate forests, a vital, quiet freshwater oasis across the Venezuelan savannas and floodplains is disappearing under the radar. Standing tall in these landscapes is a palm intrinsically linked to the culture of Latin America’s Indigenous peoples, a palm whose unique physiology regulates freshwater bodies and conceals a massive, overlooked potential for climate change mitigation: the moriche palm (Mauritia flexuosa). This species forms dense ecosystems known as morichales, dominating the landscapes of the Eastern Llanos and the Orinoco Delta in Venezuela, with its presence stretching across the Neotropics. Studies conducted in the Colombian Altillanura show that morichales are capable of capturing 590.8 tons of carbon per hectare, positioning them among the ecosystems best adapted to capture carbon in soil and biomass. Yet, the moriche palm faces mounting pressures. Standing on the frontline of its defense and conservation is Miguel Ángel Sánchez-Mercado, a Venezuelan biologist, professor and researcher at the Universidad Bolivariana in Maturín, Monagas state. For him, conservation should strive to build a profound collective awareness of the ecosystem. His ultimate hope, after countless sunrises in the morichales, is the continued fight to preserve these ecosystems by fully integrating human beings as an active part of the solution rather than merely treating them as a threat to these invaluable guardians of the climate. Miguel Ángel Sánchez-Mercado, a Venezuelan biologist, professor and researcher is on the frontline of the moriche palm’s defense and conservation. Image courtesy of Miguel Angel Sánchez-Mercado.
