title: Trump, Putin negotiate release of US Air Force veteran from Russian prison
body: Stephen Hubbard, a retired U.S. teacher and Air Force veteran, was released from Russian custody on Wednesday after spending over four years in prison. Hubbard was serving a roughly seven-year sentence after being accused by Russia in 2022 of working with Ukraine as a mercenary. American President Donald Trump announced his release from prison on social media, saying it was out of respect for the president and nothing was asked of the U.S. in return. “This release was not part of an exchange — and we extend our thanks to President Putin for releasing him on President Trump’s request,” Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on social media after he retrieved Hubbard in St. Petersburg. Hubbard, 74, was an active-duty airman beginning in March 1974, an Air Force spokesperson told Military Times. He was an Airman 1st Class as an apprentice administration specialist, with his last duty station at Mather Air Force Base, California. He separated from the service in March 1978. Mather closed as a military base in 1993 and is now operational as the Sacramento Mather Airport. After active duty, Hubbard served in the Air National Guard, but due to the age of the records, information regarding his role as a guardsman in the force’s system is sparse, the spokesperson said. The National Guard did not return a request for comment. U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, middle, and Russian Presidential Envoy Kirill Dmitriev, left, attend a meeting with Stephen Hubbard, right, in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026. (Video screenshot/Reuters) Although Trump said “no swap” was necessary for Hubbard’s release, he told reporters outside the White House and in a subsequent social media post that if he placed sanctions on Russia, Hubbard’s release would not have occurred. He said that people who “don’t know how life works” questioned his decision to waive sanctions on Russia during the negotiations to release Hubbard. “If I would’ve done that, you would not have Mr. Hubbard coming back,” he told reporters. “If you would’ve put those sanctions on, or whatever you want to call them, you could forget about him, you’d never see him again,” he continued. “He’d be back in jail for 25 years.” Hubbard’s release comes less than a week after Trump prevented new sanctions on Russia, which were intended to target the country’s largest buyers of oil and gas, drawing criticism from members of Congress who support the legislation and Ukraine. Alongside Hubbard, the administration has negotiated the release of other Americans from Russian custody since returning to office last year, including Robert Gilman, Ksenia Karelina and Marc Fogel, Witkoff said.

title: Sudan hunger crisis deepens as aid cuts collide with crop failure in Darfur
body: Cuts to food aid and a near-total crop failure are leaving displaced families and vulnerable communities struggling to find food as prices soar and malnutrition worsens. Cuts to World Food Programme (WFP) assistance threaten displaced families across Sudan, while a near-total crop failure in East Darfur has left households short of food and income. Residents of Sheairia report soaring prices, worsening malnutrition, and shortages of medicines and therapeutic food for children. In a statement to reporters following an eight-day visit to Sudan last month, the WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, says the agency has the capacity to reach millions of people caught between war, displacement and worsening drought – but is running out of money. The General Coordination for Displaced People and Refugees now warns that reduced food assistance could force families to skip meals and sell their remaining possessions to survive. Adam Rijal, the coordination body’s spokesperson, told Radio Dabanga that funding shortages and cuts to WFP assistance could deprive displaced families of essential meals and force them to adopt increasingly desperate coping strategies, including withdrawing children from school, selling their remaining possessions, and reducing the number and size of meals. Children, women, older people, and people with disabilities face particular risks of malnutrition and disease, he said, calling on donors and international institutions to close the funding gap and ensure food assistance reaches those most in need. Distribution of seeds to small farmers in the Um Shujaira area of ​​Sha’iriya locality, East Darfur – July 2026 (Photo: Supplied) Failed harvests deepen food insecurity The warning comes as residents of Sheairia locality in East Darfur report a near-total failure of the agricultural season, sharply higher food prices, and shortages of medicines for people and livestock. Resident Babiker Ishaq told Radio Dabanga that farmers had harvested almost nothing of their main crops, including groundnuts, millet, sorghum, and okra. The losses have deprived households of a crucial source of food and income, leaving some unable to find enough to eat amid the absence of humanitarian assistance. A sack of millet costs about SDG 350,000 when paid for through bank transfers, while a sack of sorghum costs a similar amount, Ishaq said. A pound of onions costs around SDG 4,500, a bottle of cooking oil between SDG 13,000 and SDG 14,000, and a pound of sugar about SDG 4,000 when paid for through bank transfers. He said deductions on transfers through the Bankak app, which he estimated at 40% in some cases and 50% in others, further reduce the money available to families for essential purchases. Malnutrition and medicine shortages The food crisis is also affecting children and pregnant women. Ishaq said pregnant women were unable to obtain adequate diets and children were suffering from malnutrition, while supplies of therapeutic food were limited. He called for increased supplies to treat malnourished children and urgent deliveries of medicines and medical supplies. Livestock are also at risk because of shortages of veterinary medicines. Ishaq reported illnesses among cattle, horses, and donkeys, adding that about six or seven children had reportedly been bitten by dogs suspected of having rabies. A rabies treatment injection costs about SDG 300,000, he said, putting it beyond the reach of many families. Calls for urgent humanitarian assistance Rijal called on donors and international institutions to maintain food assistance, strengthen nutrition and food security programmes, and prioritise the worst-affected areas. He also urged the authorities to ensure safe, unhindered access for aid deliveries and called for an end to the war and a humanitarian truce to allow relief to reach civilians. Ishaq appealed to humanitarian and health organisations to provide food, medicines, therapeutic nutrition supplies, and veterinary care to protect both residents and the livestock on which many families depend. title: Fireblocks Calls $2.5 Billion Visa Takeover Rumor ‘Not True’
body: Fireblocks , the crypto custody and stablecoin infrastructure company, pushed back on Thursday against a report that Visa is close to acquiring it for about $2.5 billion . Axios Pro, citing several unnamed sources, said on Oct. 22 that the card network was in late-stage talks to buy Fireblocks. “We are aware of the rumors about a possible acquisition of Fireblocks by Visa. This is news to us, and not true at present time,” Fireblocks told The Block . Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Coinbase Also Named Visa was not the only company tied to a possible deal. Anonymous sources told CoinDesk that Coinbase had also been considered as a buyer, as talk of a Fireblocks sale circulated over the past three to four weeks. Coinbase reportedly denied any involvement after CoinDesk’s story ran. Coinbase has explored a large stablecoin infrastructure purchase before. It and BVNK called off talks on a roughly $2 billion acquisition in November 2025. Card Networks and Stablecoins Visa has been growing its stablecoin business. In August, it began working with Zerohash so that Visa Direct could support stablecoin funding and payouts, and it later said stablecoin settlement was running at an annualized pace above $20 billion , up more than 15-fold in a year. Mastercard in August closed its purchase of BVNK , the stablecoin infrastructure provider Coinbase had been interested in. It had agreed in March to pay up to $1.8 billion for the company, including $300 million in contingent payments. Below the 2022 Valuation Founded in 2018, Fireblocks serves institutions holding digital assets and secures keys with multi-party computation (MPC). In September 2025 it launched a stablecoin payments network with more than 40 participants, among them Circle, Bridge, Zerohash and Yellow Card. A sale at the reported price would value Fireblocks at less than a third of its last public valuation. The company raised $550 million in a Series E round in January 2022 at an $8 billion valuation . title: Facing pushback on data centers, tech giants are promising hosts more money and fewer secrets
body: With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses. The promises come as anti-data center sentiment has become a potent issue in the midterm election with control of Congress and 36 governors’ offices on the line. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build. title: Pentagon, Lockheed agree to 10-year deal for 850 F-35 jets
body: The Defense Department and Lockheed Martin agreed to a 10-year framework that the Pentagon says guarantees at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighters for the U.S. military, pending congressional approval and funding. The framework, announced Thursday , includes initial spare parts plus 10 years of modification kits and sustainment. It also covers orders from foreign customers, with production continuing at 156 aircraft per year, according to Lockheed. In exchange for the decade-long commitment, Lockheed will self-fund at least $7 billion in initiatives supporting the F-35 program, the Pentagon said . “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain,” Lockheed CEO Jim Taiclet said in a statement. “That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.” Neither announcement gave a total value or per-jet price. Lockheed said the F-35 Joint Program Office and the company will work out terms, pricing and schedules in a formal contract if Congress approves a multiyear buy and provides the money in the coming months. A multiyear buy lets the Pentagon purchase a weapon across several years under one contract instead of negotiating annually, which generally lowers unit cost. Lockheed said the framework is expected to save taxpayers billions of dollars through “long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” “We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” said Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.” Neither the Pentagon nor Lockheed described those performance-based incentives. At 850 jets over 10 years, the framework averages 85 U.S. aircraft per year. That matches the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 request for 85 F-35s across the services. In fiscal 2026, Congress funded just 47 F-35s . The framework comes days after the Air Force told Congress it needs 1,509 combat-coded fighters, or jets assigned to combat units, by 2035. The request came in a force structure report sent Oct. 16. F-35As would make up about 40% of that fleet. A U.S. Air Force F-35 Lightning II receives fuel from a KC-135 Stratotanker in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility on May 11, 2026. (Senior Airman Adriana Jordan-Alcaniz/U.S. Air Force) The House and Senate versions of the annual defense policy bill would both let the Pentagon sign multiyear F-35 contracts. The House passed its bill in July. Senate Democrats blocked theirs from reaching the floor that month, and leaders have put it off until after the November midterm elections. The framework can’t become a contract until both bills pass and are merged into a single law. The framework also faces a funding hurdle. Congress has not yet approved a full-year defense budget. A stopgap funding law keeping the government open through Dec. 11 holds spending at last year’s levels and generally bars the Pentagon from starting new programs or multiyear buys. Lockheed pitched the framework as a readiness fix, saying steady orders will improve the F-35’s mission-capable rate, the percentage of time jets can fly at least one assigned mission. “Predictable demand from long-term contracts with suppliers will enable bulk procurement of raw materials and critical parts, slashing turnaround times and reducing logistics bottlenecks,” Lockheed said. “This will result in better mission-capable rates by eliminating the annual contracting cycle that has historically strained the industrial base.” A Government Accountability Office report in June found that the rate fell from 67% in fiscal 2021 to 44% in fiscal 2025, while the share of time jets could fly all assigned missions dropped from 38% to 25%. Later that month, F-35 program chief Lt. Gen. Gregory Masiello told senators the fleet had outgrown its support system. The F-35 deal follows a string of Pentagon framework agreements aimed at speeding up weapons production. In January, Lockheed reached an agreement to speed PAC-3 MSE output, then signed another weeks later to quadruple THAAD interceptor production. The THAAD deal led to a contract worth more than $35 billion in June. Last year’s defense bills had already approved multiyear buys for both interceptors. On Oct. 19, the Pentagon announced a framework with BAE Systems covering up to seven years of buys of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System laser-guidance kits. Lockheed said the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and roughly $79 billion in yearly economic activity over the decade.

Lockheed said the framework is expected to save taxpayers billions of dollars through “long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” “We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” said Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.” Neither the Pentagon nor Lockheed described those performance-based incentives. At 850 jets over 10 years, the framework averages 85 U.S. aircraft per year. That matches the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 request for 85 F-35s across the services. In fiscal 2026, Congress funded just 47 F-35s . The framework comes days after the Air Force told Congress it needs 1,509 combat-coded fighters, or jets assigned to combat units, by 2035. The request came in a force structure report sent Oct. 16. F-35As would make up about 40% of that fleet. A U.S. Air Force F-35 Lightning II receives fuel from a KC-135 Stratotanker in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility on May 11, 2026. (Senior Airman Adriana Jordan-Alcaniz/U.S. Air Force) The House and Senate versions of the annual defense policy bill would both let the Pentagon sign multiyear F-35 contracts. The House passed its bill in July. Senate Democrats blocked theirs from reaching the floor that month, and leaders have put it off until after the November midterm elections. The framework can’t become a contract until both bills pass and are merged into a single law. The framework also faces a funding hurdle. Congress has not yet approved a full-year defense budget. A stopgap funding law keeping the government open through Dec. 11 holds spending at last year’s levels and generally bars the Pentagon from starting new programs or multiyear buys. Lockheed pitched the framework as a readiness fix, saying steady orders will improve the F-35’s mission-capable rate, the percentage of time jets can fly at least one assigned mission. “Predictable demand from long-term contracts with suppliers will enable bulk procurement of raw materials and critical parts, slashing turnaround times and reducing logistics bottlenecks,” Lockheed said. “This will result in better mission-capable rates by eliminating the annual contracting cycle that has historically strained the industrial base.” A Government Accountability Office report in June found that the rate fell from 67% in fiscal 2021 to 44% in fiscal 2025, while the share of time jets could fly all assigned missions dropped from 38% to 25%. Later that month, F-35 program chief Lt. Gen. Gregory Masiello told senators the fleet had outgrown its support system. The F-35 deal follows a string of Pentagon framework agreements aimed at speeding up weapons production. In January, Lockheed reached an agreement to speed PAC-3 MSE output, then signed another weeks later to quadruple THAAD interceptor production. The THAAD deal led to a contract worth more than $35 billion in June. Last year’s defense bills had already approved multiyear buys for both interceptors. On Oct. 19, the Pentagon announced a framework with BAE Systems covering up to seven years of buys of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System laser-guidance kits. Lockheed said the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and roughly $79 billion in yearly economic activity over the decade.

title: Greece Says It is Implementing Sanctions Linked to Iran
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Russia's shadow fleet vessels wait in the unofficial anchorage area in the Gulf of Finland near Vaindloo, Estonia April 10, 2026. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins
ATHENS, Oct 22 (Reuters) – The Greek finance ministry said on Thursday it was implementing sanctions in place linked to Iran and that it backed efforts to effectively combat money laundering and the financing of terrorism.
The statement comes after the US Treasury Department said on Wednesday it imposed sanctions on Karnakis & Karnakis , a law firm based in Greece and Panama, saying it had for years provided legal assistance to Iranian shipping networks.
The Treasury also said that the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued an administrative subpoena to advance an investigation into a Greek bank, which it did not name.
The Greek finance ministry said it had taken note of the US Treasury statement, adding that “all available information is being evaluated, and appropriate measures are being taken in accordance with established procedures and applicable national, EU, and international law.”
(Reporting by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

title: Ottawa finally matches C$1B Ring of Fire funds
body: Ottawa has pledged up to C$1 billion ($712 million) to help build roads into Ontario’s Ring of Fire, backing a long-delayed route to undeveloped critical mineral deposits. The three-year commitment, announced Wednesday by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, matches the province’s long standing billion-dollar pledge. The road network would connect remote First Nations and mineral deposits in the James Bay Lowlands, about 500 km northeast of Thunder Bay, to Ontario’s highway system. “Working in partnership to protect Canadian workers, Ontario and Canada are fortifying our industrial base and securing the good-paying jobs of the future,” Ford said in a joint statement. The federal contribution addresses a barrier that has kept the region’s nickel, copper and chromite deposits beyond the reach of year-round road transport. Developers such as privately held Wyloo, which is advancing the Eagle’s Nest nickel-copper-platinum group metals project , need that access to turn exploration sites into operating mines. Funding alone won’t resolve the region’s remaining permit approvals and Indigenous consent disputes. Long wait Ontario first committed up to C$1 billion for Ring of Fire infrastructure in its 2014 budget under then-premier Kathleen Wynne. The federal match comes more than 12 years later, pairing a new Ottawa commitment with the province’s existing pledge. Ford was still pressing Ottawa to match the provincial investment in June, Northern Ontario Business reported. Wednesday’s announcement answers that demand, although the joint release didn’t specify how the federal contribution would be divided among individual road projects or when payments would begin. Federal decision on remote road could unlock Ring of Fire access The road funding forms part of an $8.7-billion federal-provincial package for Ontario’s steel, automotive and critical minerals industries as authorities seek to counter US tariffs and strengthen domestic supply chains. Canada and Ontario also pledged closer coordination of federal and provincial permitting and said they would identify priority Ring of Fire projects eligible for other funding, tax credits and cost-sharing arrangements. Efforts to combine reviews predate this week’s announcement. The two governments signed an agreement in December to reduce duplication through a single assessment process. Road access Construction has already begun on parts of the corridor. Upgrades to the Anaconda and Painter Lake roads near Aroland First Nation started June 30, according to an August provincial announcement. The work would turn 97 km of existing forest roads into a route suitable for heavy industrial traffic. Canada’s 20-year mine timeline hits multibillion-dollar wall Ottawa issued its environmental assessment decision for the 107-km Webequie Supply Road in June. The road is to connect Webequie’s airport with the McFaulds Lake area, where mineral development is proposed. The federal decision imposed legally binding environmental conditions and required the proponent to obtain remaining permits and authorizations. Remaining disputes First Nations hold differing positions on development. Webequie and Marten Falls are proponents of road projects, while Neskantaga has opposed the wider industrial corridor and said it hasn’t consented to the proposed Northern Road Link across its homelands. Wednesday’s package includes a new federal-provincial working group on First Nations engagement, economic opportunities and possible conservation or Indigenous protected areas. Neskantaga warned investors about the unresolved dispute in a statement distributed last month by Mining Watch Canada , before Chief Gary Quisess attended a rally against the Canadian Investment Summit on the same day and ahead of the new funding announcement. Canada courts C$1 trillion with mining at centre of pitch “The same governments that can mobilize billions of dollars, ministries and regulatory machinery for mining roads have failed to provide Neskantaga with dependable drinking water, adequate housing and safe health infrastructure,” the First Nation said in its statement. “There is no certainty for Ring of Fire investments as long as our people are alive. We will defend our home and waters.”

title: eMudhra To Exit Certificate Business As Security Flaw Triggers Distrust
body: Bengaluru-based cybersecurity company eMudhra, which recently found itself at the centre of a security key issue, has announced plans to voluntarily wind down its global secure sockets layer and transport layer security (SSL/TLS) certificate business. In a filing, the company said that the decision followed a security incident in which a researcher discovered that the private keys of eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates were weak enough to be recovered. The discovery prompted browser root programmes, including Google and Mozilla, to distrust eMudhra’s certificates, affecting its global TLS business. eMudhra said it revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovering the incident and disclosed it promptly. It added that no end-entity certificates had been issued by the affected CAs, its infrastructure remained uncompromised and no data was breached. “The impact has been quite severe over the last 24-48 hours. Given the risk to the rest of the business and our obligations as a publicly listed company, the board felt it was prudent to withdraw from this business,” Kaushik Srinivasan, cofounder, told Inc42. The company also cited rising compliance costs, declining returns and limited revenue contribution as the reason behind the move. The segment accounts for around 1% of its global revenue. The company reported revenues of ₹701.6 Cr in FY26. The segment’s future commercial prospects also triggered the closure. With Let’s Encrypt offering free TLS certificates and Cloudflare planning to do the same, Srinivasan said the commercial return from the business looks limited, particularly as browser guidelines move towards 90-day certificates. “The board evaluated the social media reaction, but also took cognisance of the ROI, future potential and competitive landscape,” he said, adding that eMudhra would focus on more complex customer problems in areas such as AI and quantum computing. What Does This Mean For eMudhra’s Customers eMudhra said existing customers would be transitioned to alternative certificate providers free of charge over the next three to four weeks, with the company working with other certificate partners to avoid service disruptions. Srinivasan said the distrust of its G3 ECC root had already affected around 30,000 certificates in the US, which were transitioned to its G1 RSA root. To be sure, G1 and G3 are eMudhra’s root certificate hierarchies: G1 uses RSA cryptography, while G3 uses elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). Google and Mozilla distrusted G3 as a precaution following the security incident, while G1 continues to operate and issue certificates. All certificates in India and various adjoining markets were issued from the G1 root. However, the G3 root distrust impacted an undisclosed US client . “It resulted in around 30,000 certificates in the US market being affected because they were under ECC. We had to transition them to RSA. Following our announcement, we have to transition them to another provider. We are actively working on that,” Srinivasan said. The Incident That Shook The World On October 17, researcher Wayne notified browser root programmes and eMudhra that he had recovered the private keys corresponding to eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates. The keys had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them vulnerable to reconstruction. Such keys could potentially be used to issue fraudulent certificates for websites or software, although eMudhra said none of the eight intermediates had issued end-entity certificates. Six were intended for TLS and two for software signing. Browser root programmes from companies like Mozilla and Google moved to block the affected TLS intermediates. eMudhra, at the time, said the certificates were created on April 30, 2025, and had undergone independent audits, though it did not name the auditors or disclose the audit scope. The company said only one affected intermediate was deployed in production, none had issued end-entity certificates, and all eight had been revoked. The incident prompted a worldwide reaction, casting aspersions on eMudhra’s security controls and the reliability of its certificate issuance processes. Security experts were also unsatisfied with eMudhra’s clarification on the matter. Responding to this, Srinivasan said that it was a script error and a human oversight problem; no hardware problem was found. “We will share the facts in due course, and this will also be verified through independent research. It was a one-off, a bad day. That’s exactly what happened.” Notably, the flaw went undetected for around 18 months, spanning two independent audit cycles. Srinivasan said eMudhra will now appoint an auditor to prepare the final report on the incident, which would take 2-3 weeks. Further, the company would strengthen internal accountability, maker-checker controls and independent reviews for critical processes such as key generation. The company is also exploring AI-based checks to detect weaknesses and flag potential errors. [Edited by Akshit Pushkarna] The post eMudhra To Exit Certificate Business As Security Flaw Triggers Distrust appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: FIFA launches tender of 2030 men's World Cup U.S. media rights, plans to choose winner by end of year
body:
The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.
The FIFA men's World Cup U.S. television rights are formally up for auction.
FIFA is launching its tender offer Thursday for the 2030 U.S. media rights with an option for potential partners to also buy rights for the 2034 World Cup. FIFA wants bids in by Nov. 19.
YouTube, Netflix, Amazon and Disney are all interested, CNBC reported in July. Rights could sell for between $1.5 billion and $2 billion, some media executives predicted at the time. FIFA hasn't sold U.S. men's World Cup TV rights since 2011.
Fox paid $425 million for the 2026 World Cup, which broke U.S. ratings records. Matches averaged 13.5 million viewers — up 166% from 2022.
The 2030 World Cup will take place in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.
FIFA would prefer to sell the English and the Spanish-language rights packaged together to one media partner – a departure from previous deals. For this past World Cup, NBCUniversal's Telemundo owned the Spanish rights while Fox owned the English rights. That led to some tension between the broadcasters and FIFA, as Peacock carried the Spanish-language rights for a less expensive price than Fox One, which streamed the games with English announcers.
FIFA Chief Business Officer Romy Gai said it's too early to gauge what price is realistic for the 2030 World Cup. FIFA is willing to listen to offers where just one media company buys the entire package or a joint offering – potentially between a streamer and a traditional broadcaster.
"We want to be flexible," said Gai in an interview. "We expect a big number of participants, both from the linear side and from the streamer side, but we want to listen to what is relevant for them, and then we can build up the best case together."
While the 2026 World Cup took place in the U.S., Canada and Mexico — allowing matches to be played during U.S. afternoons and nights — the 2030 World Cup will have a significant time difference. The 2034 World Cup will be played in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is seven hours ahead of New York.
The time zones may make it difficult for games to be played during U.S. primetime hours. That will play a role in how much media companies are willing to spend on both tournaments, but Gai doesn't expect the time zone challenges to play too much of a role in the bidding.
"I'm sure that we will have every day matches that will be available in the right time zone for the U.S.," Gai said. "We expect it to have an impact [on the bidding], but not as big as you think."
If a streaming service wins the rights, FIFA will ensure that a certain number of matches are available for free, either by forcing the streamer to sublicense certain rights or by putting some games on a free version of the service, if such a thing exists.
Netflix has already acquired the 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. That deal allows a free-to-air broadcaster to show at least one game each day.
After Nov. 19, when bids are due, a contingent from FIFA will come to the U.S. around Thanksgiving and begin speaking with media companies in person, Gai said. At that point, FIFA could narrow down the field and ask for one more final bid – or it could just choose a winner.
FIFA intends to select its next media partner before the end of the year, said Gai.

title: Tehran Turns to Central Asia for Trade as Conflict With U.S. Simmers
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Eurasianet is an independent news organization that covers news from and about the South Caucasus and Central Asia, providing on-the-ground reporting and critical perspectives on…
Iran is making a push to expand connectivity with Central Asian states, with high-level Iranian officials engaging their counterparts from four of the five regional states over the past week alone.
On the sidelines of the October 19 Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Dushanbe, Tajik leader Emomali Rahmon talked trade with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref. Without providing specific numbers, Aref claimed that bilateral volume had increased 50 percent since the start Tehran’s low-boil conflict with the United States. Tajik figures show trade volume experienced a roughly 15 percent increase during the first half of 2026, reaching $254 million.
Rahmon stated that the two countries will look to “broaden the range of goods and products for bilateral trade and develop joint production ventures.”
Earlier in October, Iranian Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh met with trade officials from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, touting the benefits of a north-south trade route centered on the Iranian port of Chabahar, which is designed to widen access to India and beyond. Sadegh also promoted a soon-to-launch Chabahar-Zahedan railway as an avenue for expanding trade with Afghanistan.
The Iranian transport minister secured a commitment from Kazakh officials to work on a comprehensive transport and logistics cooperation agreement, according to Iranian media reports. Sadegh also announced that Iran and Uzbekistan would form working groups to troubleshoot overland transit issues, including border procedures.
Meanwhile, Iranian and Turkmen officials agreed to implement procedures to increase overland cargo volume at the Sarakhs border crossing, the Iranian customs service reported .
Both countries are interested in "increasing the volume of road and rail freight transport between Iran and Turkmenistan, simplifying customs procedures, and developing trade cooperation," according to the Iranian statement.

title: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11: Reports
body:
A federal judge in Miami on Thursday ordered that President Donald Trump sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11, according to multiple news outlets.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, at a court hearing Thursday, also warned Trump's attorneys that if the president does not comply with court orders to give lawyers for the British media outlet records that are relevant to the lawsuit, his complaint could be dismissed, Politico reported.
Trump's lawyers had requested that his deposition be conducted between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22.
Charles Tobin, the attorney for the BBC , told Lett at the hearing that although Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on Oct. 16, the president canceled it for a "matter of national importance," The Associated Press reported.
But in fact, Tobin said, Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day, the AP reported.
"He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition," Tobin told judge.
When contacted by CNBC for comment, the BBC said: "We have nothing to add."
Lawyers for the BBC in a recent court filing had accused Trump's legal team of foot-dragging in complying with requests for documents and records relevant to the case, a process known as discovery.
"With just two months of discovery remaining, Plaintiff has not even tried to comply with his discovery obligations," the filing said. "Neither production included documents that were even plausibly in Plaintiff's possession. Instead, Plaintiff has repeatedly sent back documents that the BBC already produced to him during discovery, and his counsel trawled the internet in the days before production to find publicly available webpages."
Trump sued the BBC on Dec. 15, alleging that the outlet produced a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump" in a Panorama documentary aired one week before the 2024 presidential election .
The suit alleges that the documentary was produced as part of a "brazen attempt" to interfere with and to influence the outcome of the election "to President Trump's detriment."
The complaint claims that the documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance," was edited to make it falsely appear that during his Jan. 6, 2021, speech outside the White House, Trump explicitly urged his supporters to attack the U.S. Capitol.
The BBC's chair apologized for the edit shortly before the suit was filed.
The BBC also promised not to air the documentary again or show it on any of its platforms.
"While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim," the broadcaster said in a statement on Nov. 13 , 2025.
— CNBC's Ryan Ruggiero contributed to this article.

title: Swiggy To Begin Instamart Inventory Model Transition, Eyes Pivot Within Three Quarters
body: Over two months after attaining the IOCC (Indian-Owned and Controlled Company) tag, Swiggy announced that it will shortly commence transitioning its quick commerce business, Instamart, to an inventory-led model. In its Q2 shareholders letter, the company announced that it will pivot Instamart to the inventory model by mid-Q3 FY27. The transition is expected to take 2-3 quarters to complete. Swiggy expects the transition to improve Instamart’s working capital cycle by 8-10 days. “As we have mentioned in our previous communications, this has the potential to add 80 bps to Instamart’s contribution margin when fully rolled-out while giving us greater flexibility and control over assortment, pricing, availability and day-to-day operations,” the company said. The inventory model will give Instamart greater control over product assortment, pricing, availability and day-to-day operations in comparison to its current model where Instamart operates as a marketplace hosting seller entities. Eternal’s quick commerce arm Blinkit was the first to complete the inventory-led model pivot. The company has seen a significant improvement in its bottom line performance since then. Blinkit has emerged as the largest revenue contributor for Eternal , contributing ₹19,152 Cr to the company’s total ₹24,138 Cr operating revenue for Q2 FY27. Swiggy has been bidding to undertake a similar transition for some time now. Its initial May 2026 special resolution to become an IOCC failed after receiving 72.36% of shareholder votes in favor, narrowly missing the required 75% threshold It managed to get shareholder approval to enable the transition earlier in August . Today, the company said its domestic ownership has increased to over 58%. Instamart Margins Under Pressure Swiggy’s quick commerce margins further weakened in the September quarter (Q2 FY27). The quick commerce business reported a contribution margin of -1% of gross order value (GOV), compared with -0.2% in Q1 FY27 on the back of higher spending on pricing and customer retention. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹778 Cr in the preceding quarter. Its net order value rose 34.8% year-on-year to ₹6,594 Cr, while Swiggy added 69 net dark stores during the quarter, taking the network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities. “Contribution margin was -1.0% of GOV within the range guided earlier, as we added 69 net stores, taking the network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities, and invested in differentiated assortment, availability and service quality,” the management added. While Instamart NOV grew 13.4% sequentially to reach ₹6,594 Cr and orders were up 29.3% YoY to 130 Mn, the adjusted EBITDA loss rose to ₹895 Cr in the quarter. At the consolidated level , Swiggy’s revenue from operations increased 36.1% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr in Q2 FY27. Its net loss narrowed 15.6% year-on-year to ₹922 Cr, but widened from ₹791 Cr in Q1 FY27. Shares of Swiggy ended today’s trading session 5.01% lower at ₹211.30 apiece on the BSE. title: Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0
body:
Gradium has open-sourced Phonon , a family of small text-to-speech models built to run on the device. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Developers get natural speech with no cloud call, no GPU and no per-character bill. TL;DR Size: 31M parameters (excluding the audio tokenizer), 64.5 MB q8 GGUF, 24 kHz mono output. Phonon 40m: 40M, 74.6 MB. Runs on: CPUs, phones, Raspberry Pi 5, browsers (WASM, WebGPU) and NVIDIA GPUs. No GPU required. Performance: top English Elo among open models Gradium tested; about 7 ms to first audio on CPU. Best: 1.70% WER on a 500-sentence hard set, versus 3.50% for Kokoro (Gradium’s eval). Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%). What is Gradium Phonon? Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. The family has three models : Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0. Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0. Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0. How does Phonon work? Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. Phonon 40m uses 9 layers at the same width. Both are distilled from a larger Phonon teacher. Training ran on an NVIDIA H100 cluster with NCCL and CUDA Graphs. The work builds on Kyutai’s Continuous Audio Language Models research and Pocket TTS.

Gradium ran blind pairwise listening tests with 1,189 raters and 17,270 votes. In US English, Phonon 40m scored 2117 Elo and Phonon 31m scored 2098. Kokoro scored 2043, NeuTTS 2034 and Magpie 1939. Accuracy was tested on a public hard-sentence set . It holds 500 sentences per language, full of phone numbers, emails and postal codes. Phonon 31m scored 1.70% WER against 3.50% for Kokoro and 8.71% for NeuTTS Nano. Built-in text normalization drives much of that gap. On the easier Seed-TTS set, the gap closes. Phonon 31m scored 0.51% LLM WER, while Kokoro scored 0.45%. How fast is Phonon on a CPU? On a MacBook Air M5 CPU with 4 threads, Phonon 31m reaches first audio in 6.9 ms. It runs 29.9x faster than real time. Kokoro takes 517 ms, because it does not stream. With Arm KleidiAI and Apple Accelerate, Phonon 31m reaches 46.7x real time. On a Raspberry Pi 5, Phonon 31m starts in 38 ms and runs 3.7x faster than real time. Gradium says Kokoro needs 7 seconds to start there. On Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, Phonon starts in 7.5 ms at 24x real time. On an NVIDIA L40S, CUDA reaches first speech in 5 ms. An AMD EPYC 7413 CPU takes 43 ms, per the press release . Size, language and license rows come from each model’s own card. How can developers deploy Phonon? The runtime is MIT or Apache-2.0 licensed. It covers Rust, Python ( pip install ptts ), Swift, C, C++ and the browser via phonon-tts . It also ships an OpenAI-compatible server and a WebSocket server. Phonon loads in Transformers, MLX-Audio, Ollama and LM Studio. Voice cloning and voice design run in Gradium Studio, then the voice runs locally. Key Takeaways Phonon 31m is a 31M, 64.5 MB English TTS model under Apache 2.0. It reports 1.70% WER on hard text, against 3.50% for Kokoro. First audio arrives in 6.9 ms on a MacBook Air M5 CPU. It runs 3.7x faster than real time on a Raspberry Pi 5. Multilingual 40m models exist, but under a non-commercial license. title: Bitcoin hashrate hits seven-month high as AI shift fails to ease mining competition
body:
According to BlocksBridge, Bitcoin’s mining difficulty is rising despite the industry’s AI transition, with smaller operators potentially absorbing equipment abandoned by larger competitors.
Bitcoin’s network hashrate has climbed to a seven-month high despite major publicly traded miners shifting capacity toward artificial intelligence, suggesting other operators are replacing lost computing power and intensifying competition among remaining network miners.
According to BlocksBridge Consulting’s latest Miner Weekly newsletter , Bitcoin’s seven-day average hashrate has recovered above 1 zettahash per second (ZH/s), equivalent to 1,000 exahashes per second (EH/s), its highest level since March 3.
Hashrate measures the computing power securing the Bitcoin network. The recovery suggests that miners still operating on the network are seeing little relief from competition, despite the industry’s ongoing transition to AI workloads .
Bitcoin’s mining difficulty increased 5.92% on Oct. 16, with BlocksBridge projecting another 5.16% increase at the next adjustment. If the estimate holds, difficulty will have risen roughly 11.4% across two consecutive adjustments.
“That’s hardly the breathing room remaining miners might have expected from the AI migration,” BlocksBridge wrote, referring to the growing competition facing operators that have continued mining Bitcoin.
The shift toward AI has already taken substantial mining capacity offline. BlocksBridge previously reported a 23% decline in publicly traded miners’ realized hashrate, alongside a 52% quarterly increase in their reported AI and high-performance computing revenue. It estimated that the displaced capacity represented roughly $1.5 billion in mining hardware.
Related: Crypto Biz: AI took a back seat when Bitcoin started climbing
Some of the lost capacity may be returning to the network through smaller and mid-sized miners buying equipment from larger operators. BlocksBridge pointed to Sazmining, which advertises secondhand Antminer S21 XP machines that buyers can deploy through hosting facilities in Paraguay and Texas.
For miners with access to cheaper electricity, buying used machines could be more economical than investing in new equipment. It also means hardware displaced by AI conversions could continue mining Bitcoin elsewhere.
However, it’s unclear how much of the equipment being sold actually comes from publicly traded miners, or how much has returned to the network.
The hashrate recovery comes as some industry observers view rising computing power as an “indirect bullish signal” for Bitcoin , reflecting continued institutional investment in publicly traded mining companies.
CryptoQuant founder and CEO Ki Young Ju recently made that argument on X, writing that “higher hashrate means stronger security and better fundamentals as a store of value.

title: Irish cenbank fines Coinbase arm $3.6M for oversight, safeguard failures
body:
According to the Central Bank of Ireland, Coinbase Ireland had agreed with the facts around the enforcement action and will be subject to fines and sanctions upon approval by a high court.
The Central Bank of Ireland announced an enforcement action against Coinbase Ireland for failures to safeguard user funds and provide oversight between 2020 and 2025.
In a Thursday notice, the regulator said that the Coinbase arm had “admitted the prescribed contraventions and has agreed to the undisputed facts,” settling for $3.6 million in fines. The notice said that Coinbase Ireland had violated regulations related to oversight and safeguarding of customer funds and improperly relied on the exchange’s US company to outsource certain services.
The company’s user agreement currently states: “We use a variety of service providers (some belonging to the Coinbase Group and some not) in the context of outsourcing arrangements to help us provide the Coinbase Services in an efficient and qualitative manner.”
In Thursday’s notice, the central bank’s enforcement director, Karen O’Leary, said firms operating in Ireland “must have the appropriate culture and expertise to comply with the rules, respond to risks and to protect customer interests,” adding:
The sanctions against the Coinbase arm require approval from Ireland’s high court before taking effect. The crypto exchange launched its operations in Ireland in 2018, receiving an e-money license from the central bank in 2019 and securing registration as a virtual asset service provider in 2022.

title: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
body:
The bad week for cybersecurity just got worse for thousands more companies, who were spied on by Chinese hackers following the breach of IT management and remote access giant ConnectWise.
Security researchers at Microsoft say the China state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials that are used to establish data links between ConnectWise and its corporate customers, who rely on the cloud service to back up their company’s data.
By stealing the credentials, the hackers could log in to the customer’s Microsoft-hosted environment as if they were an authorized user and access their emails and other files.
According to Microsoft, the hackers used AI agents to rapidly hack into around 2,250 organizations at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders “little time to detect and respond.”
The speed of the mass-hacks was attributed to the use of AI agents, specifically ARTEX, an open source AI framework that works with AI models to stress-test cyber defenses. The same AI software was used in a recent compromise of South Korea’s financial systems, many of which had weak security and lacked multi-factor authentication.
ConnectWise said it’s paused access to its cloud backup system and is investigating the breach. As of Thursday, the company said it was working on restoring the service.

title: Starknet Opens Layer 1 Research After 93.5% Poll Vote, Targets Quantum Safety by 2027
body: Starknet has started researching whether to stop operating as an Ethereum layer 2 and run as its own blockchain, after a community poll backed the study. The network says it wants full post-quantum security by 2027 , though the vote does not commit it to the switch. The non-binding Snapshot poll closed on Thursday, Oct. 22, after running for seven days. The option “Yes, this should be researched” took 93.52% of the roughly 489 million STRK in voting power cast across 3,236 votes . About 4.6% of voting power chose “No,” and about 1.9% picked the neutral option asking for more information. In a results post on its governance forum, the Starknet Foundation maintained that the vote “does not approve Starknet’s transition to an L1,” and that formal approval would be sought once research and design work is finished. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . What Happens Next According to the Foundation, StarkWare and the Foundation will now run a joint working group and post its findings to the forum. If the work supports moving ahead, detailed proposals would then go back to the community for further votes . The Foundation asked node operators, app builders and STRK holders to reply with the questions they want the research to address. StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson wrote on X that “any path to transition to an L1 will be brought to a community vote” and that STRK will stay the network’s token. He called the result “a huge shift and a milestone,” adding that “the AI and quantum challenges ahead require it.” The poll discussion thread also said no new token would be issued and that bridges from Ethereum to Starknet would stay open whatever the outcome. Why Starknet Is Looking at an L1 The Foundation said Starknet “has an architectural head start on post-quantum security,” pointing to proof systems built on hash functions and user accounts that can switch to new signature schemes without a protocol upgrade. In a separate post , Ben-Sasson wrote that ZK-STARKs “were designed with post-quantum security in mind” and that the team “will do the needed work to ensure all of Starknet is post-quantum secure.” The constraint, according to Starknet, is its reliance on Ethereum. Its official account said on X it is “targeting full post-quantum security by 2027,” while Ethereum’s target is 2029 , and that as an L2 it “cannot complete that transition while its bridge and data availability remain tied to Ethereum’s timeline.” Starknet first set the 2027 goal on Oct. 8, when it said it was considering becoming an L1. Ben-Sasson raised the idea the same day in a post on X , writing that “chains need to become future-proofed. And fast.” Two days later, StarkWare said in its own post on X that “Starknet becoming an independent L1 is our clearest path forward.” StarkWare’s three-phase post-quantum roadmap from June 30 had left the bridge and blob data availability tied to Ethereum’s own upgrade, and did not mention an L1. title: Cruise lines chase luxury travelers with suites for up to $25,000 a night
body:
The latest push into high-end travel is taking place on the high seas, as cruise lines increasingly lean on luxury offerings.
On Regent's Seven Seas Splendor, an all-luxury ship, cabins cost anywhere from $1,800 to $15,000 per night for its top-of-the-line booking, the Regent Suite.
The difference is not just the roughly 5,100 square feet of space. The top-tier suite has a Steinway piano, a private dining room and a wraparound deck with a hot tub and a view comparable to the one from the ship's bridge.
Multiple passengers wanted the suite for the Splendor’s 151-night global cruise that embarks in January, Regent told CNBC, and it is almost always occupied.
Regent is setting its sights even higher, as the cruise line plans to debut the Seven Seas Prestige in December, its first new ship class in a decade. Its top suite will cost $25,000 per night.
While megaships with surfing and waterslides can carry more than 7,500 passengers, the smaller, elite ships — some carrying fewer than a thousand passengers — are powering profits for companies like Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings . The company owns luxury lines Regent and Oceania.
Norwegian CEO John Chidsey has said he's focused on sharpening the luxury brands' positioning, improving the products and guest experience, and strengthening their commercial performance.
Regent and Oceania, he said, are in good shape for 2027, though Chidsey did not break out metrics between the companies.
Cruise competitors are also betting big on luxury offerings, investing in new ships and more specialized experiences.
Regent competes with established luxury cruise lines including Royal Caribbean's Silversea and Carnival's Seabourn, as well as newer entrants carrying hotel names into the market. Four Seasons, Aman and Orient Express are among the brands bringing luxury hospitality to yacht-style vessels.
The cruise industry projects the luxury cruise fleet will grow from 104 ships in 2026 to at least 130 by 2036.
And while global cruise passengers are forecast to increase about 11% between 2025 and 2028, according to the Cruise Lines International Association, or CLIA, the industry's investment dollars are increasingly flowing to luxury and expedition brands, with orders rising for smaller ships and fewer berths through the next decade.
From 2020 through 2025, there has been a 71% increase in the number of luxury ships and an 84% increase in berths, according to CLIA. The orders indicate another 26% jump in the number of ships through the end of 2029 and a 32% increase in capacity.
Other hospitality companies are investing and expanding their uber-upscale offerings, too. Hotels, casinos, airlines, restaurants, spas and other travel and leisure companies see the trend: Affluent customers remain willing to pay for more space , personal service and distinctive experiences.
United Airlines this year launched its larger Polaris Studio suites with privacy doors and caviar service. American Airlines increased its lie-flat capacity and reported on Thursday that its premium passenger unit revenue rose 18.5% in the third quarter, compared with 14.4% in its main cabin.
Marriott’s second-quarter results showed luxury revenue per available room growing faster than the broader hotel business in the U.S. and Canada, rising 9.1% year over year, compared with 5% for all Marriott hotels in the region. In June, CEO Anthony Capuano told CNBC there's an “almost insatiable appetite” for luxury travel.
Wynn Resorts, which caters almost exclusively to high-end customers, has opted to maintain its high room rates in Las Vegas even as visitation has slowed over the past year, rather than filling every room with travelers looking for a bargain.
Asked onstage at the Global Gaming Expo in September whether Wynn is extracting more profit from fewer customers, CEO Craig Billings said, "We will always focus on what's the most comfortable experience for the customer and where can we drive the highest possible EBITDA."
But offering luxury vacations doesn't guarantee a company's fortunes.
The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, for instance, has struggled with occupancy despite major marketing campaigns and has accumulated nearly $700 million in losses since 2017, according to the Financial Times.
More competition in the space could undercut the perception of scarcity. As more companies add luxury products, they have to convince travelers that the experience is worth the price.
Las Vegas Sands reported earnings Wednesday that missed expectations for revenue and profit, hurt by the high-end segments in both Macao and Singapore.
"When the customers don't show up, it's a little problematic," CEO Patrick Dumont said on the company's earnings call.
Dumont said he couldn't point to any single cause for the softness, adding, "perhaps people are not feeling as good about the market," but he said he believes this quarter is an aberration.
CNBC asked Dumont during the NBA China Games in Macao on Oct. 9 whether luxury travel could become overcrowded.
In response, he pointed to the long-term wealth creation in Asia and said the challenge was making experiences customers want to return to.
“It’s not about, are there enough customers,” he said. “It’s, can we create enough of an interesting set of experiences where people find us indispensable in their lives.”

title: Iran Claims More Ships Struck Near Hormuz as Trump Accuses Tehran of ‘Faking Hits’
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Thursday that seven commercial vessels were struck overnight in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including four ships conducting oil transfers, prompting President Donald Trump to accuse Tehran of fabricating attacks to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said four vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were struck simultaneously on Wednesday and caught fire. The vessels were allegedly transferring oil for an American company using routes Iran considers illegal.
In a separate claim, the IRGC said three additional vessels struck naval mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires that left them disabled, according to Reuters .
None of the seven incidents has been independently confirmed. Iran did not identify the ships, their owners or the American company allegedly involved. There were also no immediate details about casualties or potential oil spills.
UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which tracks attacks on commercial shipping in the region, has not issued new incident reports corresponding to the claims.
President Trump responded Thursday by accusing Iran of inventing attacks as part of an effort to influence oil prices ahead of the November 3 elections.
“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict.”
The president’s accusation follows weeks of increasingly aggressive Iranian statements claiming that merchant vessels using routes outside Tehran’s control have been struck by mines or other weapons.
But the absence of UKMTO reports does not necessarily mean the attacks did not occur. In its October 16 weekly assessment , UKMTO acknowledged that it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were not reporting incidents directly to the organization.
UKMTO said it was aware of additional attacks through other sources but could not publish warnings without sufficient verification. That reporting gap has become increasingly important as the United States and Iran offer competing accounts of what is happening in the waterway.
The most significant element of Iran’s latest announcement is its claim to have targeted four vessels actively engaged in ship-to-ship oil transfers. If confirmed, the attacks would appear to mark the first reported direct targeting of an active ship-to-ship oil transfer operation during the conflict.
Such transfers have become a critical part of the improvised shipping network that has allowed Persian Gulf producers to restore much of their oil exports despite repeated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
Under a system operating with U.S. military assistance, tankers make short voyages through the strait, frequently with their AIS transponders switched off, before transferring cargoes to other vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The receiving tankers then carry the oil to international markets.
The system has allowed producers to move substantial volumes of crude without relying on routes controlled by Iran, although at extraordinary cost.
The International Energy Agency reported Wednesday that tanker freight costs from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed above $37 per barrel, more than five times prewar levels. For a fully loaded 2-million-barrel VLCC, that translates to more than $74 million in freight costs alone.
The location of Iran’s latest alleged attacks, in the northern Persian Gulf, is distinct from the Gulf of Oman transfer operations used by the U.S.-facilitated shuttle system. There is currently no independent evidence connecting the four vessels to that network.
Nevertheless, a confirmed attack on vessels during cargo transfers would represent a potentially significant expansion of the threat to regional oil shipping.
Iran’s latest claims also follow a series of announcements alleging that tankers have struck naval mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorization.
Those claims have repeatedly been challenged by maritime security authorities.
In its October 18 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) addressed Iranian statements that two supertankers had struck mines the previous day, saying there was “no substantiation to these claims.”
U.S. Central Command has also rejected previous Iranian mine-strike announcements as false, accusing the IRGC of attempting to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation.
However, JMIC continues to warn of a credible threat of renewed mining in and around the strait’s traffic separation scheme. Its latest assessment maintains the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, with further deliberate attacks considered highly likely.
Trump’s assertion that more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the conflict also comes amid conflicting assessments of the recovery in Gulf exports.
Overall Middle East oil shipments have approached or exceeded prewar levels in recent weeks, aided by an expanded network of pipelines, short-haul tanker voyages and offshore transfers.
But the recovery in total exports does not necessarily mean that more oil is moving through the strait itself.
According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal cited by gCaptain , flows through Hormuz, including offshore transfers, remained at approximately 82% of prewar levels, even as overall regional exports recovered.
UKMTO’s latest weekly overview also recorded just 254 vessel transits during the seven days ending October 14, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Those figures include U.S.-reported facilitated transits that UKMTO says it cannot independently verify.
The figures measure different things—vessel movements, oil flows through Hormuz and overall regional exports—but illustrate the difficulty of determining how much shipping has actually recovered.
Meanwhile, the security situation continues to deteriorate.
UKMTO documented 12 attacks during the reporting period ending October 16, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz. One vessel was lost, two were disabled or left not under command, and the outcomes of three others remained uncertain.
The escalation has included the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride following an October 13 attack, as well as strikes on tankers operating inside the Persian Gulf.
Iran’s latest announcement adds another seven potential incidents to an already incomplete picture.
For now, neither Tehran’s claim that seven vessels were attacked nor Trump’s assertion that the incidents were fabricated has been independently established. What is clear is that merchant ships continue to face serious threats, even as oil producers find increasingly costly ways to keep cargoes moving.

title: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
body:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.
Correction: The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6. An earlier version misstated the month and date.

title: Air Force special ops trainees are graduating months faster in revised pipeline
body: Airmen training to join the Air Force’s special operations roles are moving through the service’s training courses months faster and with less downtime, officials said. Over the last year, the Air Force has changed its training pipeline for airmen who want to join pararescue, combat control, Tactical Air Control Party (TACP), or special reconnaissance fields, which the Air Force refers to as its special warfare roles. Jennifer Gangemi, a spokesperson for the Air Force Special Warfare Training Wing, said that a revamped Special Warfare Assessment and Selection program, a new intro course, and new start dates for existing training have reduced the time that airmen spend in training for those jobs. The skills and standards required of the training, she said, have not changed. “This reduced the average time to beret by nearly 70 days,” Gangemi told Task & Purpose, referencing the distinctively colored headgear airmen earn when they graduate the training pipeline for each job. The changes to Air Force special operations training are part of the service’s Pipeline Optimization effort, which aims to eliminate bottlenecks and match the number of students to an available number of slots at each schoolhouse. “The wing spent the past year optimizing its pipeline to reduce delays and maximize throughput within current constraints,” Gangemi said. “Optimization reduced unnecessary training pauses, Students Not in Training (SNIT), and multiple training redundancies. This cut man-years of time-out-of-training, [and] reduced SNIT by over 50%.” To join one of the four Air Force special operations career fields, students first attend the challenging four-week assessment & selection Course. Then they move on to the Air Force’s new 16-week “Zulu” course at Lackland Air Force Base, Texas. The Zulu course teaches airmen headed to any of the four special warfare jobs the basic skills of how to shoot, move, and communicate as a team, surface warfare skills, infiltration/exfiltration techniques, and the seven Air Force special warfare missions. In all, the course covers 100 training tasks that students previously had to be taught later in their training pipeline. “This meant apprentice courses would reinforce the common skills learned in Zulu, rather than having to teach those initial skill sets late in their training, reducing apprentice course days,” Gangemi said. About 1,200 airmen on average will go through the new course each year, according to the Air Force. Once an airman headed into any of the Air Force’s four special operations specialties graduates from the selection and Zulu course, they enter a pipeline of as many as five training schools at bases around the country. The pipelines vary for each job. Airmen training in pararescue, for instance, attend pre-dive, combat dive, and military free fall schools, while airmen headed to TACP do not. The final step in the training pipeline for all four special warfare jobs is a final apprentice school for each role. Officials told Task & Purpose last year that the training pipelines for each of the distinct career fields will not change. Gangemi said the new pipeline has “drastically” decreased the amount of time that airmen wait around between courses, or continuing on in their training journey after rehabbing from an injury. Previously, students had more downtime between courses because they were treated as a “first-come, first-served process,” but now trainees have set start dates for each course. Under the old way of doing things, students could have gaps between courses that could add up to two months or more of downtime during a training pipeline. With the new structure, Gangemi said, the course dates are scheduled to keep that downtime closer to two weeks. Gangemi said airmen can finish their special operator training between six and 18 months “faster” with the same necessary requirements that they need to graduate. The six- to 18-month range, she said, depends on the career field because each has different graduation requirements.
