title: Salaries, food and sumo wrestling suits: What I learned paying the bills for war
body: Editor’s note: This article first appeared on The War Horse , an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter . The midsummer heat reflected off the flightline at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in North Carolina. It was the summer of 1990 and the beginning of Operation Desert Shield . The entire base was in full deployment mode, with planes forming a long line for departure, sequenced by priority. I climbed the ladder into the second airplane and handed a briefcase full of cash and checks to the noncommissioned officer. It was reminiscent of an old gangster movie payoff scene, with the cash neatly stacked and bound by rubber bands. I also showed the young airmen a small metal safe, crammed in with the deployment gear, where they could store the money. As I exited the plane, I understood for the first time the significance of my wartime mission as the base chief financial officer. Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel is greeted by the Vice Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Larry Spencer and the commander of the Air Force District of Washington, Maj. Gen. Darryl W. Burke at Joint Base Andrews in 2015. (DoD photo by Casper Manlangit) My job included assembling a small cadre of financial troops. Once our team landed in Saudi Arabia, their tasks ranged from tracking and funding the daily costs of the war to paying the troops. They worked 12-hour days, cashing personal checks, purchasing local goods and services, and balancing the books. They also worked with the contracting team to buy fresh food, portable showers, and construction support. In the days before online banking, cashing personal checks was a daunting challenge for deployed airmen and their families. As troops cashed checks, their spouses drew from the same accounts back home, making an accurate cash balance nearly impossible to maintain. This led to confusion and, more critically, overdrawn accounts. At the time, my first officer was a young female lieutenant who was legally responsible for our base’s financial account. But local restrictions on women conducting business with men meant a male junior noncommissioned officer discussed contract terms with local vendors over cups of tea while the female lieutenant could only observe and occasionally nod in agreement. To complete a transaction, she counted out the cash payment to her male assistant, who in turn recounted the money before handing it to a local merchant. The Saudi men simply wouldn’t accept payments from a woman. Our systems were somewhat antiquated back then, and tracking operational expenditures against our installation budget was dicey at best. The deployed finance team boxed dozens of vouchers each week and mailed them back to the states, where we sorted through pay stubs and invoices, oftentimes months after the money was spent. I often felt as though I was juggling a dozen balls in the air, trying desperately not to violate any appropriation laws and guidelines while ensuring our base checkbook remained solvent. Fortunately, the war was relatively short; however, the intensity of financial support continued after the war ended. As troops began returning home, our finance teams met each arriving aircraft. If we were lucky, we snagged our base members to ensure their overseas pay entitlements were discontinued and avoid overpayments before they left with their families. Even as the base began settling back into normal training operations, the war-related financial demands rolled on. We replaced used equipment and repaired damaged gear. We restocked aircraft munitions and parts and replenished supply inventories. My experience echoed that of Syracusan general Hermocrates circa 400 B.C.: “[Carthaginians] have abundance of gold and silver, and these make war, like other things, go smoothly.” Operation Desert Shield/Storm was an overwhelming success and marked the first major U.S. war since Vietnam. Matching airpower with resources and financial support was an intense yet rewarding experience. I had assumed it was a once-in-a-career opportunity to defend our country during war — I was mistaken. Ten years later, I was a senior colonel at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia, serving as the chief financial leader for Air Combat Command. I was in the base gym playing basketball when my assistant said I needed to come to the office immediately. I had been summoned to the commander’s conference room, where we were briefed on the beginning of Operation Iraqi Freedom . The colonel commander I served with at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base during Operation Desert Storm was now the commander of ACC as a four-star general. Once again, we would support a major war together, albeit on a much larger scale. This time, I would be responsible for ensuring financial support for the war by directing operations from 14 major bases. Like my previous war experience at a single base, quickly scrambling finance teams to myriad overseas locations was an around-the-clock operation. And the challenge of ensuring the tight linkage between war and money was multiplied exponentially. Dozens of deployed finance offices were established in the Middle East and at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean. Tracking purchases at these deployed locations became an enormous challenge as financial documents were boxed and mailed to a single command location at Shaw Air Force Base, South Carolina, for processing. I once visited and was shocked to see boxed financial documents stacked to the ceiling. Pogs were used during the Global War on Terrorism to address the lack of coins and have since become a collector’s item. (Photo courtesy of Army & Air Force Exchange Service HQ) Deployed finance offices also supplied currency to the base exchange service, but there were weight restrictions, and we had to reserve the allotment for high-priority cargo. Consequently, we could not provide coins. To solve this problem, we worked with the Army & Air Force Exchange Service to use “ pogs ,” which were thin cardstock cutouts of coins in 5¢, 10¢, and 25¢ denominations to use as change. Technically, pogs were considered gift certificates that were redeemable at any base exchange. They featured pictures of fighter jets, tanks, historical figures, and military insignia. Pogs were used during Operation Iraqi Freedom and have now become collector’s items. In addition to maintaining supplies and salaries, money could help bolster spirits. As any commander or first sergeant can attest, maintaining high morale is integral to a ready fighting force. Seemingly routine actions like troop pay became especially important as financial teams updated pay accounts for promotions and hostile pay entitlements, allowing troops to see the financial rewards of their hard work. Our mantra was, “Troops take care of fighting the war; we take care of their pay.” But our work wasn’t limited to pay stubs. We once bought sumo wrestling suits! During the initial troop buildup, our forces were on hold, waiting for the order to attack. So when the troops were not training, local commanders sought opportunities for them to blow off steam and have fun. Sumo wrestling, a troop favorite, featured large, bulky costumes that resembled the “ Michelin Man ” commercial. The objective was to put two opponents in a ring and have them bounce off each other until one tumbled. Sumo wrestling became a popular morale boost within the military community. Here, airmen participate in the Comprehensive Airman Fitness week mental health day at Travis Air Force Base, California, in 2024. (Photo by Kenneth Abbate 60th Air Mobility Wing) But benefits could also stir interbranch sensitivities. A bomber commander asked me about the fiscal legalities of providing free haircuts and free Stars and Stripes newspapers for his deployed airmen at Diego Garcia. The Air Force shared the remote location with the Navy, whose sailors were afforded these benefits free of charge. The commander said the perceived double standard had become a real morale issue. I elevated the issue to the lawyers at the Pentagon, but we couldn’t change it. At the time, Navy regulations allowed sailors to receive those services gratis while they were at sea; the Air Force did not offer similar benefits. Today, as U.S. forces are once again engaged in hostilities abroad, defense financial officials are juggling accounts to fund a war while supporting the troops. Once again, military lethality is proving to be closely tied with strong financial support. During my 40-year career, I served in the Air Force from the Vietnam War through Operation Iraqi Freedom. I had a bird’s- eye view on how money and war are inextricably linked. As Milanese commander Gian Giacomo Trivulzio told King Louis XII: “To carry on war, three things are necessary: money, money, and yet more money.” This Reflection from The War Horse was edited by Kim Vo, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mollie Turnbull.

Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel is greeted by the Vice Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Larry Spencer and the commander of the Air Force District of Washington, Maj. Gen. Darryl W. Burke at Joint Base Andrews in 2015. (DoD photo by Casper Manlangit) My job included assembling a small cadre of financial troops. Once our team landed in Saudi Arabia, their tasks ranged from tracking and funding the daily costs of the war to paying the troops. They worked 12-hour days, cashing personal checks, purchasing local goods and services, and balancing the books. They also worked with the contracting team to buy fresh food, portable showers, and construction support. In the days before online banking, cashing personal checks was a daunting challenge for deployed airmen and their families. As troops cashed checks, their spouses drew from the same accounts back home, making an accurate cash balance nearly impossible to maintain. This led to confusion and, more critically, overdrawn accounts. At the time, my first officer was a young female lieutenant who was legally responsible for our base’s financial account. But local restrictions on women conducting business with men meant a male junior noncommissioned officer discussed contract terms with local vendors over cups of tea while the female lieutenant could only observe and occasionally nod in agreement. To complete a transaction, she counted out the cash payment to her male assistant, who in turn recounted the money before handing it to a local merchant. The Saudi men simply wouldn’t accept payments from a woman. Our systems were somewhat antiquated back then, and tracking operational expenditures against our installation budget was dicey at best. The deployed finance team boxed dozens of vouchers each week and mailed them back to the states, where we sorted through pay stubs and invoices, oftentimes months after the money was spent. I often felt as though I was juggling a dozen balls in the air, trying desperately not to violate any appropriation laws and guidelines while ensuring our base checkbook remained solvent. Fortunately, the war was relatively short; however, the intensity of financial support continued after the war ended. As troops began returning home, our finance teams met each arriving aircraft. If we were lucky, we snagged our base members to ensure their overseas pay entitlements were discontinued and avoid overpayments before they left with their families. Even as the base began settling back into normal training operations, the war-related financial demands rolled on. We replaced used equipment and repaired damaged gear. We restocked aircraft munitions and parts and replenished supply inventories. My experience echoed that of Syracusan general Hermocrates circa 400 B.C.: “[Carthaginians] have abundance of gold and silver, and these make war, like other things, go smoothly.” Operation Desert Shield/Storm was an overwhelming success and marked the first major U.S. war since Vietnam. Matching airpower with resources and financial support was an intense yet rewarding experience. I had assumed it was a once-in-a-career opportunity to defend our country during war — I was mistaken. Ten years later, I was a senior colonel at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia, serving as the chief financial leader for Air Combat Command. I was in the base gym playing basketball when my assistant said I needed to come to the office immediately. I had been summoned to the commander’s conference room, where we were briefed on the beginning of Operation Iraqi Freedom . The colonel commander I served with at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base during Operation Desert Storm was now the commander of ACC as a four-star general. Once again, we would support a major war together, albeit on a much larger scale. This time, I would be responsible for ensuring financial support for the war by directing operations from 14 major bases. Like my previous war experience at a single base, quickly scrambling finance teams to myriad overseas locations was an around-the-clock operation. And the challenge of ensuring the tight linkage between war and money was multiplied exponentially. Dozens of deployed finance offices were established in the Middle East and at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean. Tracking purchases at these deployed locations became an enormous challenge as financial documents were boxed and mailed to a single command location at Shaw Air Force Base, South Carolina, for processing. I once visited and was shocked to see boxed financial documents stacked to the ceiling. Pogs were used during the Global War on Terrorism to address the lack of coins and have since become a collector’s item. (Photo courtesy of Army & Air Force Exchange Service HQ) Deployed finance offices also supplied currency to the base exchange service, but there were weight restrictions, and we had to reserve the allotment for high-priority cargo. Consequently, we could not provide coins. To solve this problem, we worked with the Army & Air Force Exchange Service to use “ pogs ,” which were thin cardstock cutouts of coins in 5¢, 10¢, and 25¢ denominations to use as change. Technically, pogs were considered gift certificates that were redeemable at any base exchange. They featured pictures of fighter jets, tanks, historical figures, and military insignia. Pogs were used during Operation Iraqi Freedom and have now become collector’s items. In addition to maintaining supplies and salaries, money could help bolster spirits. As any commander or first sergeant can attest, maintaining high morale is integral to a ready fighting force. Seemingly routine actions like troop pay became especially important as financial teams updated pay accounts for promotions and hostile pay entitlements, allowing troops to see the financial rewards of their hard work. Our mantra was, “Troops take care of fighting the war; we take care of their pay.” But our work wasn’t limited to pay stubs. We once bought sumo wrestling suits! During the initial troop buildup, our forces were on hold, waiting for the order to attack. So when the troops were not training, local commanders sought opportunities for them to blow off steam and have fun. Sumo wrestling, a troop favorite, featured large, bulky costumes that resembled the “ Michelin Man ” commercial. The objective was to put two opponents in a ring and have them bounce off each other until one tumbled. Sumo wrestling became a popular morale boost within the military community. Here, airmen participate in the Comprehensive Airman Fitness week mental health day at Travis Air Force Base, California, in 2024. (Photo by Kenneth Abbate 60th Air Mobility Wing) But benefits could also stir interbranch sensitivities. A bomber commander asked me about the fiscal legalities of providing free haircuts and free Stars and Stripes newspapers for his deployed airmen at Diego Garcia. The Air Force shared the remote location with the Navy, whose sailors were afforded these benefits free of charge. The commander said the perceived double standard had become a real morale issue. I elevated the issue to the lawyers at the Pentagon, but we couldn’t change it. At the time, Navy regulations allowed sailors to receive those services gratis while they were at sea; the Air Force did not offer similar benefits. Today, as U.S. forces are once again engaged in hostilities abroad, defense financial officials are juggling accounts to fund a war while supporting the troops. Once again, military lethality is proving to be closely tied with strong financial support. During my 40-year career, I served in the Air Force from the Vietnam War through Operation Iraqi Freedom. I had a bird’s- eye view on how money and war are inextricably linked. As Milanese commander Gian Giacomo Trivulzio told King Louis XII: “To carry on war, three things are necessary: money, money, and yet more money.” This Reflection from The War Horse was edited by Kim Vo, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mollie Turnbull.

title: Cohere Releases Rerank 5 With Passage-Level Context Focus and Calibrated Scores
body: Cohere AI has released Rerank 5 , a new reranker family in Pro and Fast tiers. Cohere Rerank 5 is a retrieval model that reorders search results before they reach an LLM. It adds 2 developer features: Context Focus, which returns relevant passages inside each document, and calibrated relevance scores. For RAG and agent builders, the message is simple. Send fewer, better tokens to the LLM. TL;DR Size: Parameter count not disclosed. 32K token context window. Two tiers: rerank-v5.0-pro and rerank-v5.0-fast . Runs on: Hosted API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, or private VPC and on-prem. Cohere benchmarks speed on a single NVIDIA A100. No open weights or quantized builds. Performance: Pro ranks first on 39 of 46 composite datasets in Cohere’s own evaluation. Best: Pro scores 82.2 on BRIGHT (RCP-nDCG@10), 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3. Worst: Pro median latency is 11.7 s per 96-document request, versus 4.1 s for Fast. What is new in Cohere Rerank 5? Rerank 5 ships as two models. Pro targets ranking quality on reasoning-heavy queries and long, domain-specific documents. Fast targets low latency and high throughput for agents running many searches. Both models support over 100 languages and a 32K context window. They also rerank semi-structured data such as JSON, tables and YAML records. Upgrading needs no re-indexing. Developers change the model parameter and keep their existing keyword, vector or hybrid search. How does Context Focus work? Context Focus is an optional feature, off by default. A single Rerank call returns document scores plus scored character spans. Each span carries start and end offsets into the original text. Developers set it through the relevant_spans field, with a threshold and max_spans value. Cohere tested it on 30 QA datasets . Removing half the retrieved text kept 96% of answer quality. Removing three quarters kept 87%. Cohere says teams can push to 10x less context at some quality cost. In a search-agent test across 17 datasets, BM25 alone scored 46% accuracy. Adding Rerank 5 Pro raised it to 49%. Context Focus at the default 0.1 threshold cut tokens per task by 19% and reached 57%. At 0.4, tokens fell 34% and accuracy hit 58%. Versus BM25 alone, the full stack used 35% fewer tokens. On 6 deep-search benchmarks, tokens fell 41% and accuracy rose from 39% to 52%. What do calibrated relevance scores change? Rerank 5 scores read as probabilities. A score of 0.7 means a 70% chance the document is useful. Cohere team measured expected calibration error (ECE) against blind human graders and NIST TREC-DL assessors. Rerank 5 scores about 0.06 on both. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 0.234 and 0.307. Rerank 4 Pro scores 0.384 and 0.309. In practice, dev teams can filter by threshold instead of a fixed top-k. An agent can also detect when nothing relevant came back. How does Rerank 5 perform on benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Cohere using RCP-nDCG@10 , a Cohere-developed variant of nDCG. Cohere ran the competitor models itself. Pro leads all four main benchmarks. It scores 92.2 on ViDoRe V3 , 90.4 on BEIR , 82.2 on BRIGHT and 87.3 on nanoMTEB. BRIGHT shows the largest jump: 12.4 points over Rerank 4 Pro. Fast beats Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Rerank 4 Pro on all 4. It ties Voyage AI Rerank 3 on ViDoRe V3 at 90.6. It trails it on BEIR, 88.1 versus 88.6. On parsed PDFs, averaged over 47 datasets, Pro scores 89.9 and Fast 88.5. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 88.4. Pro ranks first on 14 of 19 non-English languages in Cohere’s internal suite. It also runs on Microsoft Foundry ( Pro , Fast ) and Amazon SageMaker ( Pro , Fast ). It is also available to all North users. API pricing is $0.05 per 1M tokens for Pro and $0.02 for Fast. Model Vault lists $4.00 per instance-hour for both tiers on its Medium tier. Integrations include LangChain, Haystack, Elasticsearch and Weaviate, per Cohere’s integration docs . Key Takeaways Rerank 5 ships in Pro ($0.05) and Fast ($0.02) per 1M tokens, both with 32K context. Pro scores 82.2 on BRIGHT, 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3. Context Focus returns scored passages in 1 call, cutting agent tokens 35% to 41%. Calibrated scores reach about 0.06 ECE, so 1 threshold works across domains. All benchmarks are self-reported on Cohere’s RCP-nDCG@10 metric. Check out the official announcement , the Rerank 5 changelog and the full results sheet . title: Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift
body: Ramp spent months testing managed agent APIs, open-source frameworks, and third-party platforms before concluding it would be better off building its own. The result is Laminar, an internal agent harness that took six weeks to reach a first version and now powers every agentic product at the fintech company. “We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house.” “We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house,” Sam Kronick , the Ramp engineer behind the platform, writes in the company’s engineering blog . In Tuesday’s post, Ramp detailed how Laminar brings agent execution, sandboxing, observability, and asynchronous workflows under a single platform. The architecture caught the attention of LangChain CEO Harrison Chase , who praised several design choices in his X post , while pointing to similar work underway in LangChain’s Deep Agents . Ramp and LangChain are approaching the problem from different directions, but both point to a bigger shift in agent infrastructure . As harnesses take on more responsibility, enterprises have to decide how much of that infrastructure they want to build and maintain themselves. Why Ramp built in-house Ramp didn’t want to be locked into one model provider. It needed the flexibility to switch models based on cost, speed, and performance, along with better visibility into how its agents behaved. Engineers were already digging through traces to find unnecessary tool calls, bloated context, and errors, but existing observability tools made that harder than it needed to be. So Ramp built its own debugging interface into Laminar. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes. Chase agreed with Ramp’s priorities, particularly model independence and observability, both of which LangChain has emphasized in its own work. And, there were other parts of Laminar’s architecture that caught his attention. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes. Sessions split from sandboxes Laminar runs everything from customer service agents to Ramp Inspect , the company’s cloud coding agent, and Glass, which handles longer-running, collaborative work. Supporting these products requires a harness that can manage persistent sessions, human approvals, and work across environments. Chase highlights Kronick’s observation that a production harness does far more than run a simple execution loop. “ +100 to this ,” he writes, pointing to LangChain’s investment in Deep Agents. Ramp keeps agent sessions separate from the sandboxes where code runs. Conversation history and execution state are stored independently, allowing sandboxes to spin up and shut down without disrupting a session. Chase sees the sandbox-as-a-tool approach as a growing trend, noting that Deep Agents uses a similar design. It also keeps credentials and orchestration outside the sandbox, an important consideration as developers work to isolate agents running untrusted code . Async agents by default Laminar lets agents keep working without waiting for every step to finish. Chase describes non-blocking asynchronous agents as the future and says LangChain is developing similar functionality for Deep Agents. Ramp’s Connectors Service also caught his attention. It centralizes authentication, credentials, access controls, and tool execution behind a shared API. Chase says LangChain is exploring comparable features for managed Deep Agents. Centralizing those functions also gives platform teams a consistent place to manage access and credential handling rather than implementing them separately for every agent. The harness is also where teams can trim inference costs, and LangChain has made that case directly. In an October 1 engineering post , it describes moving model selection into the harness of Open SWE , its open-source coding agent. A router examines the initial request and assigns one of three models based on expected task complexity, sending the simplest work to GLM-5.3-Flash, intermediate tasks to GPT-5.6 Sol, and the most demanding requests to GPT-6 Astra. Routing trims inference costs Across 973 agent threads, the router cut median LLM costs from $2.61 to $0.94 per thread, a 64 percent drop compared with using GPT-6 Astra for every task. The savings didn’t come with a measurable hit to performance. Merged pull request rates were 29.2 percent for routed threads and 27.3 percent for the control group, a difference that wasn’t statistically significant. Ninety percent of requests went to the two less expensive model tiers. LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway , where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. The harness already knows which prompts, tools, and domain context are involved, giving it more information to make that choice. LangChain uses model-selection middleware to pick a model at the start of each thread. The results don’t tell us whether building a custom harness is cheaper than using an existing framework. Ramp wasn’t part of the experiment. But they do show how much companies can save by making smarter model choices at the harness level, especially when their agents handle tasks with very different demands. The harness ownership dilemma Ramp’s decision also shows how coding agents have changed infrastructure costs. Kronick says agents generated all of Laminar’s initial code, with experienced engineers guiding the architecture and implementation. But building the first version in six weeks is one thing. Maintaining it is another. Ramp still needs engineers to handle incidents, update the platform, and support its product teams. The company also hasn’t published operating-cost comparisons or benchmarks against competing platforms, which makes it difficult to judge whether building in-house is cheaper. LangChain offers another option. Rather than building a harness from scratch, companies can use frameworks that handle much of the underlying infrastructure, an approach other vendors are also taking as they open-source their own harnesses . title: Bitcoin ETFs Erase October Losses With $1 Billion in Three Days
body:
Bitcoin ETF buyers have erased October’s losses in three trading days.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $524.8 million on Wednesday, according to Decrypt ’s ETF tracker , stretching an inflow streak that began Monday to three sessions and roughly $1.07 billion.
That’s enough to flip the month positive. After shedding about $615 million through last Friday, the funds are now up roughly $460 million for October.
Monday’s $526.7 million haul, the funds’ best day since Sept. 22, came entirely from BlackRock’s IBIT. The rebound follows two weeks in which the funds lost about $910 million. Cumulative net inflows since launch stand at $58.4 billion, with total net assets at $100.8 billion.
The return of buyers coincides with a fresh vote of long-term confidence from Wall Street. J.P. Morgan Asset Management this week projected a 10% compound annual return for Bitcoin over the next 10 to 15 years in its first long-term forecast for the asset, while cautioning about 55% volatility.
Ethereum ETFs, meanwhile, finally caught a break. The funds took in $14.9 million on Wednesday, snapping a five-day outflow streak that drained about $389 million. They remain deep in the red for October, though, down roughly $1.07 billion so far. Cumulative net inflows stand at $12.8 billion.
The inflows haven’t lifted prices. Bitcoin traded at about $81,470 on Thursday, down 2.4% over 24 hours but still up 2% on the week. It marks a sharp turn after Bitcoin hit a weekly high near $85,000 just yesterday.
Ethereum fell 2.6% to roughly $2,393, and the total crypto market cap slipped 2.9% to $2.84 trillion. Zcash was among the hardest hit in the top 10, dropping 5.6%, though it remains up nearly 14% over seven days.
Traders on Myriad, a prediction market developed by Decrypt’s parent company Dastan, aren’t betting on a breakout.
Myriad traders give Bitcoin just a 20% chance of topping $87,500 before October ends and 9% odds of reaching $90,000. On the downside, they put the odds of a drop to $77,500 at 35% ; Bitcoin already briefly slipped below $80,000 last week.
Sentiment on Ethereum is brighter, with Myriad users giving ETH a 61.3% chance of pumping to $3,000 before dumping to $1,500.
In terms of catalysts to watch, the Federal Reserve next meets on Oct. 27-28, with persistent inflation keeping another rate hike on the table.

title: Meet the a16z Ops Engineering Fellows
body: We’re excited to announce the fellows who will be part of the inaugural a16z Ops Engineering Fellowship, an 8-week cohort of leaders who are transforming their organizations with AI. We received thousands of applications from talented people around the world. Today, we’re thrilled to share more about the inaugural cohort of 50 fellows who are leading operations engineering at companies like Ramp, Decagon, Luma AI, Opendoor, and ElevenLabs. See a full list of the fellows here! Many sit at the intersection of operations and engineering, scaling operational rigor within and across teams. They’re leading the charge by building the internal tools that consolidate the tooling stack, designing the data and context layers that agents draw on, deploying agentic workflows with human checkpoints, and driving adoption. Folks like Ben Booi and Rushaabh Saliya at Opendoor, Chris Jones at Shopify, Dilan Shah from Cresta, Jordan Shapiro at Handshake, Kevin Chu from ElevenLabs, Saya Iwasaki at Notion, Christina Huang at Cognition, and Keith Gliksman at Tennr. Some are world-class COOs and chiefs of staff redefining how AI gets used across organizations. They’re deciding which workflows to automate first, the KPIs that prove it’s working, and are leading the teams that put it to work. Folks like Caroline Ingeborn at Luma AI, Gabriella Garcia at Warp, Brandon Gell at Every, Rohan Shah at Datavant (ex-Ramp), Matt Stehle at Formation Bio, and Meera Shah at Glean. title: Mining M&A wave set to lift juniors, investor predicts
body: Major and junior mining companies will be surfing in a big merger and acquisition wave (M&A) over the next several years as strong balance sheets give them more capital to pursue growth, founding partner and senior portfolio manager at Bastion Asset Management Michael Gentile said. Gentile said three of the 35 resource companies in his portfolio have been acquired over the past 12 months, reflecting growing interest from larger producers. He expects the trend to generate fresh investment in the junior mining sector and support higher valuations. “We’re seeing the major mining companies get a bit more aggressive on M&A because they can return capital to shareholders,” Gentile told MINING.COM host Devan Murugan on the latest episode of Top of Mine . “Their bounties are clean and still pay dividends and still have cash left over. That leaves them more firepower for growth.” Gentile believes that with more M&A activities, there will be more flow of capital that will also improve the financing picture of the ‘average junior, lifting the companies’ valuation too. As an investor focused more on long-term assets and strategies, Gentile sees that the markets became more open to junior mining companies in recent years. He warned that access to capital has tightened over the past three to five months, following a period when junior miners were generally able to fund their exploration programs. “Most of the companies I’ve invested in have healthy balance sheets,” he said, adding that the recent tightening of financing conditions could benefit disciplined companies. Golden Rule Gentile has one central piece of advice for the junior mining companies he invests in: raise capital before it is needed, rather than wait until their exploration budgets run dry. “When you have two years funded already, you have your drill program fully funded for the next two years and you have good results, the market is hungry to give you more capital,” he said. “My advice to companies, if it’s on good terms and less dilutive terms, no warrants, attractive financing, you take it because this is a cyclical business.” Gentile warned that companies often make the mistake of spending their available cash on drilling before seeking additional financing. That can leave them negotiating from a position of weakness, potentially disappointing shareholders through unfavourable financing terms. As a long-term investor, Gentile noticed that junior mining companies are a great opportunity for those that are willing to wait. “One of the key success factors for my companies is having sticky stable long-term capital,” he said. “So if it takes three to 10 years to go from a discovery to a producing mine or an exit or a sale to a major mining company, you need shareholders that are willing to sign up for a three to 10-year journey, not a three-week or three-month journey.” “It’s a business of making shareholders in the company significant returns along the way.” Watch the full episode here:

title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
body:
A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong. Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve. In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M , an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post. Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now. The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it. ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly. Solution overview This solution deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint: Q_max , the concurrency ceiling one instance serves inside the SLO, and T_total , how long a real scale-out takes. A synthesis request flows through four layers: a client, the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, a custom container on a GPU instance behind that endpoint, and the Kokoro-82M model inside the container. Figure 1: The Kokoro-82M request path, from client through the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint and custom container to the model The container supports two wire transports: response streaming ( InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream ), which streams audio back as it’s synthesized so playback starts before the utterance finishes, and bidirectional streaming ( InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream ), which holds one long-lived session open for multiple messages. Running Kokoro-82M in a custom container, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of this post possible. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal Amazon SageMaker AI already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn’t built for. The AWS CDK stacks that deploy this endpoint only attach auto scaling resources once a real, measured plan exists for the model, so a guessed configuration can never reach production silently. The rest of this post is that measurement. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need: An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon SageMaker AI resources. Note: the sample container pins an earlier PyTorch with a known advisory ( PYSEC-2026-2286 , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use. AWS CDK v2 , installed and bootstrapped in your target account and region. Python 3.11 or later, uv , and Docker to build the container image. A ml.g5.xlarge service quota with at least one spare slot above your baseline before running the scale-out measurement in this post. The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post. Walkthrough By the end of this walkthrough, you will have a live Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling policy for Kokoro-82M, derived entirely from two measurements taken against your own endpoint rather than from a guess. Deploy the endpoint stacks The endpoint deploys through three AWS CDK stacks, applied in order: SpeechFoundationStack creates the IAM roles and the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights, SpeechModelCacheStack syncs a model’s Hugging Face weights into that bucket once, and SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. Figure 2: The three AWS CDK stacks and the gate that decides whether auto scaling resources get synthesized The gate on the third stack keeps a default, unmeasured scaling configuration from reaching production. scaling_enabled is a static flag, true whenever max_instances is configured greater than min_instances , and it says nothing on its own about whether the numbers behind it were ever measured. The stack adds a second, independent check at synthesis time: does a real, feasible plan artifact exist for this model? Only when both conditions hold does the stack synthesize scaling resources: an EndpointAutoscaling construct that wires the scaling policy and alarms, and an EndpointObservability construct that adds the dashboards and alarms used to monitor it. A model with scaling_enabled=True but no measurement behind it gets the same no scaling resources output as one with scaling_enabled=False . The project’s CLI wraps the three stacks behind a single command, applying them in dependency order: uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m SpeechModelCacheStack runs an AWS CodeBuild project that syncs the model’s Hugging Face weights into the cached Amazon S3 bucket once. A cold endpoint start doesn’t need to pull them from the internet. Gated by the preceding scaling_enabled check, SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. The methodology packages as a command-line tool chain, run in a fixed order: Figure 3: The tool chain, run in order, each command handing an artifact to the next Step 1: Check for drift drift runs first, every time, before anything that costs money or holds an endpoint under load. It’s a read-only reconciliation between what’s actually deployed (scalable targets, scaling policies, alarm states) and what the config file says should be deployed. An orphaned policy from an earlier model, or a stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run, would otherwise silently move capacity mid-measurement and corrupt the numbers being measured. uv run tts-bench drift A clean result reports no mismatches and exits with a preflight-ok status, clearing the way for qmax . A stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run is the most common source of a reported mismatch, because it can leave auto scaling frozen on a single instance. uv run tts-bench thaw --endpoint speech-kokoro-82m restores the deployed policy before you proceed, since qmax and ttotal both assume the deployed state matches the config file exactly. Step 2: Measure Q_max, the concurrency ceiling Q_max is the largest concurrency, requests queued plus requests executing on one instance, at which a request still reaches first audio byte inside the SLO at the 95th percentile. It’s measured with a closed-loop load ladder: hold a fixed concurrency N exactly, and walk N upward one rung at a time until the SLO breaks. A closed loop avoids coordinated omission, the flaw in fixed-arrival-rate tests where a slowing server makes the client send fewer requests instead of surfacing real queueing delay. uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m --dry-run uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m --dry-run prints the schedule and a wall-clock estimate with zero AWS calls, so you can budget the roughly 36-minute cost of a live run first. The live command freezes auto scaling and pins capacity to one instance for the duration, restored automatically on exit, so the number it produces is a genuine per-instance ceiling. The load ladder recorded the following results: Concurrency p95 TTFAB (ms) Meets 3,000 ms SLO? 1 65.4 yes 5 286.2 yes 10 568.5 yes 20 1,129.3 yes 30 1,689.8 yes 40 2,245.0 yes 50 2,805.7 yes ( Q_max ) 60 3,374.8 no (breach) Figure 4: p95 time-to-first-audio-byte against concurrency, with the SLO line and the breach point at concurrency 60 Q_max = 50 , and it’s a bracketed result: rung 60 actually crossed the SLO, which makes 50 a real ceiling rather than a lower bound. The same run measured the uncontended service time, the time one request takes with no queueing at all: mean 61.3 ms, p95 66.1 ms. That number drives a second, independent alarm described later in this post. Step 3: Measure T_total, the real scale-out time T_total is how long it takes, wall clock, from the moment more capacity is requested to the moment that capacity serves healthy traffic. It’s measured by forcing a scale-out directly, bypassing the deployed policy’s own detection logic, then timestamping every distinguishable stage. uv run tts-bench ttotal --model kokoro-82m --qmax
ttotal requires the qmax artifact as input, since its recovery judgment reads off that ladder’s own measured rungs, and refuses to run against a ladder measured on a different wire transport. The forced scale-out broke down into eight measured stages: Stage Duration Share of T_total capacity requested to desired_set 30.0 s 9.4% desired_set to instance visible in logs 180.8 s 56.5% (dominant) instance visible to container started 3.7 s 1.2% container started to framework_init 0.0 s 0.0% framework_init to weights_ready 6.5 s 2.0% weights_ready to warmup_done 1.0 s 0.3% warmup_done to in_service 20.7 s 6.5% in_service to traffic recovered 47.4 s 14.8% measured total (t_total_s) 260.2 s + policy detection lag, bounded (not measured) 60.0 s T_total, planned against 320.2 s Figure 5: The eight measured stages of a real scale-out, from capacity request to recovered traffic The dominant stage is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance provisioning plus the container image pull, at 181 seconds, 56 percent of the planned-against total. The highest-impact way to reduce T_total isn’t application code, it’s reducing image size or using warm capacity pools. Everything downstream of “instance visible in logs” is a comparatively small 79 seconds combined. The 60-second addition on top of the measured 260.2 seconds isn’t measured in this run. It’s bounded from the policy’s own configuration (alarm evaluation period times evaluation periods, plus cooldown), because this run bypassed the policy’s detection logic on purpose to isolate pure provisioning time. plan sizes surge headroom against the full 320.2-second total, because that reaction time is a real part of any production scale-out even though this measurement excluded it. Step 4: Derive the deployed policy with plan plan is the only command that never touches AWS. It reads the qmax and ttotal artifacts, combines them with two operator-chosen inputs, an SLO of 3,000 ms p95 TTFAB and a surge ratio of 1.25x (the fleet tolerates traffic growing 25 percent within one scale-out cycle without breaching the SLO), and does the following arithmetic. It then prints a report with a verdict for each finding: ok , warn , or, for a genuinely infeasible plan, stop . uv run tts-bench plan --qmax
--ttotal
--peak-rps 5000 The --peak-rps flag (5,000 requests per second here, alongside an assumed trough of 10) sizes the fleet’s instance count. It doesn’t factor into the threshold arithmetic below. h = surge_ratio - 1 = 1.25 - 1 = 0.25 C_scale_max = (1 - h) x Q_max = 0.75 x 50 = 37.50 C_scale_min = (1 - 2h) x Q_max = 0.50 x 50 = 25.00 W_max = SLO - S_p95 = 3.000s - 0.066s = 2.934s C_scale_max is the concurrency at which one more instance is added, below Q_max by the surge fraction h , so the fleet still has queue headroom when it asks for more capacity. C_scale_min is the concurrency at or below which one instance is removed, set at (1 - 2h) of Q_max so scale-in triggers only once load has fallen well below where scale-out would trigger again. The final deployed configuration, exactly as produced by the tooling: "kokoro-82m": ModelEndpointConfig( model_name="kokoro-82m", instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge", min_instances=1, # trough 10 rps; 3 is the smallest safe floor for scale-in max_instances=9, # peak 5000 rps scaling_target_value=37.500, # C_scale_max, in Amazon CloudWatch units (ratio measured as 1.0) scale_in_threshold=25.000, # C_scale_min, in Amazon CloudWatch units ttfab_slo_ms=3000, queue_max_depth=50, # enforced by the container's own admission gate scale_out_cooldown_s=30, # short: one instance added at a time scale_in_cooldown_s=960, # long: see below ) The two cooldowns are asymmetric on purpose. Scaling out is cheap to be wrong about: worst case, you paid for one instance you didn’t need for thirty extra seconds. Scaling in isn’t symmetric in cost, since capacity removed and later needed again costs a full T_total (320 seconds) to replace. The scale-in cooldown is set to roughly three times T_total , so a scale-in decision only fires once load has genuinely, sustainedly dropped. The container’s own admission control separately enforces queue_max_depth=50 , equal to Q_max : past that depth, a request is refused immediately with a 503 queue_saturated response rather than left to queue past the point it could meet the SLO. A FirstChunkLatencyP95 alarm, thresholded at 65 ms (the measured p95 service time at concurrency 1), watches service time on an instance already serving, tighter than the end-to-end SLO, which includes queuing. Two findings from the Kokoro-82M run are worth including, because they’re the tool correctly surfacing a known, accepted trade-off rather than a defect: surge_survival (warn): Holding C_scale_max (37.5) against Q_max (50) puts one instance at 97.4% utilization the moment a scale-out triggers, and a replacement takes a full T_total to arrive. The surge ratio reserves extra queue slots, but surviving a real surge is about flow, how fast the queue drains, and there’s little flow headroom left at 97.4 percent utilization. scale_in_safety (warn): Removing one instance from a fleet of N multiplies every remaining instance’s concurrency by N / (N-1) . Scale-in stays stable only once that ratio holds under C_scale_max / C_scale_min (1.5 here), which requires N >= 3 . With a floor of 1 instance, a scale-in from 2 to 1 lands the survivor at exactly Q_max , right back at the ceiling that triggers another scale-out. The long cooldown damps this flapping without eliminating it. Raising the floor to 3 would remove it structurally, at the cost of standing capacity during low traffic. Every qmax or ttotal artifact’s file name encodes the configuration it was measured against, instance type and container image digest condensed into a slug (for example, g5xlarge-8b1b96bc ). ttotal and plan both refuse to pair artifacts whose fingerprints disagree. That’s downgradable to a warning with --allow-config-mismatch , but refusal is the default. Step 5: Confirm the deployed policy with validate validate is the last command in the chain, and the second one, alongside drift , that never mutates anything. It compares the scaling policy actually deployed against the values in the plan artifact, confirming the two match before you treat the configuration as live. uv run tts-bench validate --model kokoro-82m --plan
A clean result confirms scaling_target_value , scale_in_threshold , and both cooldowns on the deployed scalable target match what plan derived. Any mismatch means the deployed policy and the measured plan have drifted apart, and should be resolved before relying on the endpoint’s auto scaling behavior. Testing and validation Every qmax , ttotal , and plan artifact referenced in this post is a committed file in the repository, not a one-off local output. The preceding worked example, including every number, is independently reproducible by re-running plan against the two committed measurement files, with zero AWS calls and zero new spend: $ uv run tts-bench plan --qmax
--ttotal
--peak-rps 5000 scaling_target_value : 37.500 (C_scale_max) scale_in_threshold : 25.000 (C_scale_min) surge_survival : warn scale_in_safety : warn Clean up To remove the resources created in this walkthrough, tear down the stacks in reverse order with a single command: uv run speech-infra destroy kokoro-82m speech-infra destroy removes the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, endpoint, and any auto scaling or Amazon CloudWatch resources attached to it. It doesn’t empty the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or delete the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed. Conclusion Deploy Kokoro-82M as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint: Q_max , the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total , how long a real scale-out takes. You derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Scaling on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native, AWS-published metric, and measuring its unit conversion directly rather than assuming it, is what keeps this configuration tied to real concurrency. The result is an auto scaling policy where every number traces back to a real measurement against your own endpoint, not an assumption carried over from a different workload shape. That distinction is what turns a config-file guess, one that silently overpays or silently breaches its SLO, into a policy you can defend with a specific concurrency ceiling and a specific scale-out time, both measured, not asserted. Nothing about this four-number model, SLO and surge ratio chosen, Q_max and T_total measured, the rest derived, is specific to TTS. It generalizes to latency-sensitive, concurrency-bound, real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. For example, a real-time image-embedding endpoint that holds each request open through a GPU forward pass is bound by the same concurrency ceiling, not by a throughput metric. The same qmax / ttotal / plan chain applies unchanged. The real bottleneck there is concurrent in-flight requests rather than a throughput metric borrowed from a different workload shape. The specific numbers here, Q_max=50 and T_total=320s , are true for Kokoro-82M on ml.g5.xlarge . They will differ for a different model or instance type. The methodology and tooling that produce them don’t. The five-command tool chain, drift , qmax , ttotal , plan , and validate , carries over unchanged to the next model you deploy this way. Clone the sample repository , then run the five-command chain, drift , qmax , ttotal , plan , and validate , against your own endpoint to produce a measured policy. Review the Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling documentation to adapt the thresholds to your SLO, and open the SageMaker AI console to watch the policy react to live traffic. If you’d like help building a similar measurement-driven deployment, contact your AWS account team. About the author Joseph Cottingham Joseph is a Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he designs and delivers AI systems that move organizations from idea to production. His technical background spans firmware, software, and machine learning, with deep expertise in high-throughput, event-driven architectures that keep AI workloads performant at scale. Joseph focuses on the intersection of state-of-the-art research and operational reality, delivering solutions that materially transform organizations and the systems they operate.

title: Norway's $2.3 Trillion Oil Fund Loses $30 Billion in Third Quarter
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
The world’s biggest sovereign wealth fund, Norway’s $2.3-trillion Government Pension Fund Global, booked a loss of $30 billion for the third quarter as higher interest rates and market turbulence hit both its fixed-term and equity investments.
Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), which is commonly referred to as 'Norway's oil fund' because it was created with oil and gas revenues, is a shareholder in many large companies in the world, with more than half of the value of its equity investments in the U.S. market.
The Norwegian fund was created in the 1990s with the aim of ensuring long-term management of revenue from Norway’s oil and gas resources. Today the wealth fund holds, on average, 1.5% of all listed companies in the world.
Following a record-high profit of $185 billion for the first half of 2026, boosted by Asian tech stocks, the sovereign wealth fund booked a negative -0.5% return for the third quarter, the fund’s manager, Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), said on Thursday.
The negative return is a loss of 278 billion Norwegian crowns, or $29.69 billion, in accounting terms, for the world’s single largest investor in Q3.
“The fund’s return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments,” said Trond Grande, Deputy CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management.
“Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell,” the executive added.
As of September 30, 2026, the fund was valued at 22.014 trillion Norwegian crowns, or $2.35 trillion at today’s exchange rate. Of the total value, 72.1% was invested in equities, 25.8% in fixed income, 1.6% in unlisted real estate, and 0.5% in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure. Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft are the most valuable investments of the Norwegian wealth fund.

title: Utexo Opens Utexo Mint Early Access for USDT on Bitcoin Ahead of November 28 Launch
body: Bitcoin Magazine Utexo Opens Utexo Mint Early Access for USDT on Bitcoin Ahead of November 28 Launch Professional operators can now test USDT on Bitcoin and get their integrations ready for November’s public launch. Utexo has opened Utexo Mint, its dedicated platform for professional operators preparing to support and offer USDT on Bitcoin. The public launch is scheduled for November 28. The return of USDT creates an opportunity to bring dollar liquidity into the Bitcoin ecosystem, opening new markets for trading and BTC-backed lending. Operators who integrate early can be among the first to offer USDT on Bitcoin, “positioning themselves to capture initial demand and build market share as adoption grows,” according to a press release shared with Bitcoin Magazine. Utexo says existing partners are already preparing for the launch, as it is opening onboarding to exchanges, wallets, market makers, OTC desks, trading firms, and other professional operators interested in supporting USDT on Bitcoin. Utexo Mint Utexo Mint is a dedicated platform for verified operators to mint and redeem USDT on Bitcoin. Within its sandbox environment, operators can test how USDT works on Bitcoin via RGB , including “minting, confidential transfers, and redemption.” The testing period should give operators time to validate their transaction flows and finalize their integrations ahead of the launch. Utexo said they will also offer tools to manage USDT liquidity across supported networks and convert between fiat and USDT, giving operators greater flexibility in how they source and move funds. While Utxo Mint is not owned or operated by Tether, USDT on Bitcoin is nevertheless backed by USDT via Tether’s USDT0 protocol. Bringing USDT Back Home to Bitcoin USDT is returning to Bitcoin, where it first launched in 2014, bringing deep stablecoin liquidity to the ecosystem and expanding what businesses can do on the network. USDT on Bitcoin is launched by Utexo and not by Tether, the company clarified. USDT on Bitcoin will be “private by design,” said the press release, allowing individuals to hold and transfer funds without publicly exposing their transaction details . Among the various technology differences between its Bitcoin implementation and that on EVM blockchains, RGB’s USDT avoids address reuse, the worst privacy practice and one which may even expose holders to quantum computer risks . When it comes to compliance, the press release said businesses will be able to protect sensitive commercial activity while maintaining the controls required for regulatory compliance. When asked how privacy and compliance with sanctions and law enforcement can be offered as features at the same time, Utxo told Bitcoin Magazine, “We monitor all source USDT coming in, and check AML score + we monitor the risk on the RGB side too. We have a partnership with Crystal Intelligence for the AML” The rollout will take place in two phases. The first begins on November 28, when USDT becomes publicly available on the Bitcoin network via RGB. The launch will make it accessible through partner wallets and exchanges, introducing new liquidity for swap providers and lending platforms. The second phase, planned for Q1 2027, will extend USDT to the Lightning Network for payments, according to Utexo. This post Utexo Opens Utexo Mint Early Access for USDT on Bitcoin Ahead of November 28 Launch first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt .

title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
body: Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation. Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform. Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems. In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization. The challenge As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production. In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed. The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward. Why Rescale chose AI-DLC Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production. The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas: AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step. Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time. AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered the AI’s questions together and approved each plan before the AI moved on, so nothing was left to assumptions. Solution overview Rescale’s triage agent automates the classification and routing of nightly end-to-end test failures. It runs as a step within Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod. The agent performs the following steps: Invokes Claude Opus 4.8 on Amazon Bedrock to classify each failure into a root cause category: infrastructure issue, code bug, flaky test, or environment problem. Retrieves relevant historical failure patterns from a knowledge base for additional context. Queries pod logs through Model Context Protocol (MCP) for runtime evidence supporting the classification. Generates a structured remediation report with specific file references, function names, and recommended fixes for engineer review before any action is taken. The agent completes this workflow in seconds and outputs directly into the team’s existing reporting pipeline. The following diagram shows how these components fit together: Figure 1: Architecture for Rescale’s AI triage agent, running on Amazon EKS with Amazon Bedrock for classification, a knowledge base for historical failure patterns, and MCP-based log retrieval through Amazon CloudWatch integration The AI-DLC workshop experience The engagement was structured as a five-day, in-person workshop. AWS architects guided the build while Rescale engineers worked hands-on-keyboard, co-building in real time. Inception phase (days 1–2): From vision to validated requirements The team started by scoping requirements, capturing the intent in a vision document and a technical environment document that grounded the work before any building began. That intent began as a single statement, “We want AI-powered test triage that classifies failures and recommends remediation”. Working collaboratively in mob format, the team answered 20+ clarification questions generated by AI. This produced a scoped requirements document with Phase 1 boundaries explicitly defined and Phase 2 items deferred. Five user stories were consolidated into four units of work: Knowledge base for historical failure patterns. AI triage agent as the core classification and remediation engine. Argo Workflow Integration for trigger, infrastructure, and deployment. Evaluation Harness for accuracy measurement and regression gating. Human decisions drove the critical boundaries: what belongs in Phase 1 versus Phase 2, priority ordering, and deferred features like automated pull request (PR) generation. Construction phase (days 2–4): Architecture to running code The team defined interface contracts and data schemas, completed functional and non-functional design questions, and signed off on the architecture. Two architecture pivots emerged during the build, and the team validated each one before changing course. First, the team planned to host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then moved it to Amazon EKS, where Rescale already runs its Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline. Keeping the agent in the existing cluster meant no new runtime to operate and a direct trigger path from Argo. Second, in the early build the agent pulled log evidence from a third-party logging service through MCP. The team moved log retrieval to Amazon CloudWatch, which simplified the dependency chain. The MCP pattern stayed the same. Only the source behind it changed. Because AI-DLC keeps requirements and design decisions in shared documents, the team updated them in place and kept building without losing context. The agent was built using the Strands SDK, supporting concurrent failure analysis with structured output in JSON and HTML, containerized on Amazon EKS. By Day 4, the full pipeline was running in staging: Argo workflow trigger, triage agent pod, MCP log query, knowledge base retrieval, and structured triage output. Operations phase (day 5): Evaluation and handoff The team built a PyTest-based evaluation framework with live and stubbed test modes, establishing an initial classification-agreement baseline to measure the agent against and improve from. The agent was demoed live to Rescale’s CTO and VP of Engineering, correctly classifying both an infrastructure failure and a real code bug with specific file-level fix recommendations. How AI-DLC scaled rigor to complexity Not every unit of work gets the same treatment. The knowledge base needed minimal design and deployed using Terraform in hours. The Triage Agent got full rigor: architecture review, interface contracts, 12 design questions, and iterative code review. Argo Integration focused on infrastructure contracts and IAM. The Evaluation Harness used lightweight design but heavy implementation. AI-DLC matched depth to complexity automatically. By the end of Day 5, the agent was live in staging, processing real test failures with a measured accuracy baseline and a clear path to production. Production outcomes The triage agent has been running in production since the workshop. It automatically classifies nightly end-to-end test failures, replacing manual first-pass triage with an automated first pass that engineers validate. For each failure, the agent generates a structured remediation report with actionable next steps rather than raw logs. The agent’s classification agreement with human triage has risen from 44% at initial deployment to 68% today. It continues to improve as the team iterates on the golden dataset and prompt engineering. Since the triage agent entered production, the team has measured a 20% decrease in time blocking production deployment while test failures are analyzed. Because these tests gate Rescale’s weekly production releases, that reduction shows up directly in how quickly changes reach production. Engineers also spend less of the on-call rotation on repetitive classification. Life after the workshop: From one agent to an AI-first practice The workshop delivered one production agent, but its larger effect was on how Rescale approaches engineering work. The triage agent is part of a broader push at Rescale to deliver digital engineering capabilities for the AI era. Internally, Rescale is applying these same benefits realized from AI across its own engineering organization. AI-DLC gave Rescale’s engineers a structured, repeatable way to put that direction into practice. Scaling AI-DLC across the organization Rescale is evaluating an internal AI-DLC Center of Excellence , a small group that codifies best practices and helps other teams adopt the methodology independently. The engineers who participated are already applying what they learned. One of the engineers noted that the process “will be part of my workflow going forward,” not only for building agents, but for any complex development work where AI can contribute. Broader AI-native development Rescale is now incorporating AI-DLC into the standard software development lifecycle for new engineering simulation products. The framework brings simulation-domain expertise, product requirements, platform architecture, validation, and operations into one structured design process. Teams resolve key questions early, capture reviewed decisions in executable specifications, and give coding agents focused work with clear acceptance criteria. This shortens the path from product concept to validated implementation while engineers remain accountable for product correctness. The same approach is already being used in product-enabling platform work and agent systems: HPC simulation application catalog management. Container vulnerability tracking and remediation for government compliance requirements. Workflow-based cloud coding agents. Conclusion For the triage agent, the most useful output of AI-DLC was not the code itself. It was the structured path from an initial idea to a reviewed system design: clarifying questions, scoped requirements, and evaluation criteria. That specification gave coding agents a narrower, better-defined problem to solve. Instead of asking an agent to infer the architecture while implementing it, the team could use agents for focused construction against decisions that humans had already reviewed. The result was more focused, reviewable output that was easier to integrate and improve. For Rescale, that is the repeatable pattern: use AI-DLC to structure the design conversation, turn the decisions into a specification, and then use coding agents to accelerate implementation. Key takeaways Start with a real problem. Rescale’s triage agent succeeded because it solved an engineering challenge. The problem drove the solution, not the other way around. Human oversight accelerates, not decelerates. Every architecture pivot that improved the system came from human validation of AI proposals. The mob format, where AI generates and humans validate, is faster than working alone. The AWS stack provided each layer the agent needed. Amazon Bedrock supplied foundation-model access for classification in an environment Rescale was already using, so the team could build the triage workflow without taking on additional model-infrastructure overhead. The Strands SDK provided the agent framework, and Amazon EKS hosted the containerized agent within Rescale’s existing pipeline. Bitcoin extended daily losses to 3% as US stocks came under pressure from President Donald Trump’s comments on Iran military action.
Bitcoin (BTC) stayed below $82,000 around Thursday’s Wall Street open as Iran war headlines returned to pressure risk assets.
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD hitting $81,256 on Bitstamp, down 2.9% on the day.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Mixed reactions to Tesla earnings and capital expenditures combined with a risk-off mentality stoked by fresh comments from Trump that the US was “not negotiating” with the Iranian side.
“We are going to have something one way or the other that will happen fairly soon. Most people seem to think it’s after the election and we’ll see what happens,” he told reporters, referring to the US midterm elections on Nov. 3.
US stocks fell at the open, with the S&P 500 Index down 1.3% at the time of writing. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index was 2.3% lower.
