title: Critical PHP web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
body:
The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.
The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.
The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.
The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.
Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.
Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.
Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.
OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.
The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.
Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.
The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

title: Why governments pulled websites offline over the decades-old PHP programming language
body:
Government websites in Europe were taken offline on Wednesday as concerns spread about vulnerabilities in servers that host sites coded in PHP, the world's most popular server programming language.
The U.S. National Security Agency warned millions of organizations to either implement patches immediately or take their servers offline. It's the latest cyber scare in the artificial intelligence era, as vulnerabilities that previously took weeks or months for hackers to find can now be exploited in a matter of hours.
Matt Suiche, a researcher at cybersecurity startup Tolmo, says this level of urgency is "very new."
"That's not something that even existed a year ago," he said. "The reason there is that sense of urgency now is really because everyone has AI-augmented capabilities, not only defenders but also attackers."
PHP, created in the 1990s, is used by just under 70% of all websites with known server-side programming languages.
In mid-August, researchers at AI firm Calif and Google's Wiz identified vulnerabilities in all PHP installations serving web requests. For the discovery, Calif's researchers used OpenAI's GPT‑5.6 Sol, while the Wiz team used its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Google's Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
The vulnerabilities, dubbed "PHP2Shell," allow for unauthenticated hackers to remotely execute code on any PHP server, letting bad actors potentially steal data and read sensitive information.
The PHP Foundation was intending to release patches for the bugs on Thursday. But news of the vulnerabilities leaked earlier in online forums, and then by Calif itself, which accidentally posted a proof-of-concept video on Tuesday that demonstrated an exploit chain.
Though the video was ultimately taken down, the patches were fast-tracked and released 24 hours early by the PHP Foundation, at 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday. Shortly before that, the NSA issued its warning.
By that point, code had already been posted to public repository GitHub, which is owned by Microsoft , claiming to be able to exploit PHP2Shell for any server.
Elizabeth Barron, executive director of The PHP Foundation, told CNBC on Wednesday afternoon that the organization is "diligently monitoring the situation," but noted that there is currently no "evidence of any working exploits, only incomplete, misguided, and non-working generated ones."
However, Suiche said his team at Tolmo was able to code a working exploit in less than a day.
"With AI, it was relatively quick to have a local reproduction," he said, adding that before today's powerful AI models it would have taken his team "multiple weeks" to produce it.
Amazon Threat Intelligence reported on Wednesday that it identified a PHP2Shell exploit attempt on Saturday on its MadPot telemetry network, a network dedicated to identifying digital decoy connection attempts.
The vulnerabilities have been around for a long time. Two years ago, Mihail Kirov, then an engineer at Quarkslab and now a product security engineer at Tolmo, said he was part of a team that found a vulnerability with the same root cause as PHP2Shell.
Kirov said The PHP Foundation was alerted to the flaw in its systems at the time, but a fix was never rolled out. The foundation acknowledged in a blog post Wednesday that the delay was a "structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."
That was before large language models were so pervasive. Calif's researchers had new powerful technology at their fingertips. They found two vulnerabilities that were both rated a 9.2/10 in terms of security severity.
"They proved that today, in 2026, using large language models, things can go really, really fast," Kirov said, about the Calif team. "One of the reasons for that is that LLMs allow you to explore so many different angles."
Even as organizations apply patches to their vulnerabilities, they'll likely never know if data was breached, experts say.
Neatsun Ziv, CEO of cybersecurity provider Ox Security, said that unless an organization had preinstalled an application security platform before a hack attempt, it wouldn't be able to see suspicious requests made on its servers.
Suiche said a company would only know it was hacked if its valuable data was "being sold later on the dark web." He said that's the "reality of yesterday and is still the reality of today."
PHP is a legacy server language, Suiche said, so many of its users may not have implemented sophisticated security measures.
He said that city governments and other agencies often use PHP and "haven't updated their website in 10 years."
"Those people have a lot of critical data," he said.
Industry experts say the cybersecurity game has changed dramatically since Anthropic released its powerful Mythos model earlier this year. The Claude creator pre-released Mythos in April to a small number of companies and government agencies to ensure the cybersecurity measures were sufficient before wide-scale release.
Now, Mythos is available to many bad actors.
"The amount of time that it takes the bad guys, the threat actors, to actually find a new exploit and run it on the entire internet used to be weeks," Ziv said. "It went down to days, and starting in the Mythos age, from April 2026, it went down to hours."

title: Only 13 percent of companies see real returns from AI, Gartner survey finds
body:
Most companies still can't turn their AI spending into real business value. Only 13 percent of respondents report major or transformative returns from AI, according to a Gartner survey of 2,002 CIOs and other technology leaders presented at the Gartner IT Symposium in Orlando.
58 percent of CIOs are tasked with delivering cost savings through AI, yet 51 percent expect AI to raise total operating costs for their tech stack. 44 percent of CEOs struggle to demonstrate AI-driven financial returns to stakeholders. Gartner analyst Alicia Mullery sees a growing gap between the "innovation race" vendors are running and the "outcomes race" companies need to win. The companies that succeed decide early which projects are worth pursuing and which to shut down, even those already in production. They also plan proactively for how AI agents will reshape job roles.
Not everyone shares the impatience. Bloomberg CEO Vlad Kliatchko says it's too early to measure AI's economic payoff. His company is investing because it believes this is the right moment. Yet even with uncertain returns, 75 percent of CEOs plan to increase their technology spending, according to Gartner. Ad Ad

title: Coinbase Ireland Admits Breaches, Takes $3.64 Million Penalty Over Underfunded Customer Account
body: Coinbase Ireland Limited , the exchange’s Irish e-money unit, has admitted breaching rules meant to protect customer cash and accepted a €3,252,618 fine (about $3.64 million at current exchange rates) plus a reprimand from the Central Bank of Ireland , the regulator announced on Thursday. The regulator set the penalty at €4,646,597 (about $5.21 million) before cutting it by 30%, the cap on discounts under its settlement scheme. The sanctions take effect only once Ireland’s High Court confirms them. According to the settlement notice , the breaches of the Electronic Money Regulations 2011 ran from Nov. 1, 2020, to Aug. 19, 2025 . Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . What the Regulator Found The Central Bank said Coinbase Ireland leaned too heavily on its U.S. parent group to run safeguarding processes and lacked enough in-house expertise to supervise them. The notice details how customer money ended up in the wrong places. As Silvergate and Signature Bank collapsed in March 2023, the Irish unit directed 30 institutional clients to wire U.S. dollars to Coinbase Inc. accounts, first at Signature and then at Cross River Bank, rather than to an account in its own name. Their money stayed mixed with Coinbase Inc.’s funds for about 19 months . Separately, some users who moved over from Coinbase UK after Brexit kept depositing into a UK account, a problem that lasted almost five years. Calculation errors also left the unit’s designated safeguarding account short every day for at least 18 months , with the daily gap peaking at €5.2 million (about $5.8 million) in 2024. Had the firm become insolvent during that stretch, users “may not have been able to promptly and fully regain their funds,” the notice said. Karen O’Leary, the Central Bank’s director of enforcement, said in the release that “we have no tolerance for weaknesses in safeguarding arrangements.” She added that breaking commitments made during authorisation, or failing to report material changes, “is completely unacceptable.” Coinbase Says No Customer Lost Money Coinbase Ireland said in a statement that it caught several of the problems on its own, flagged them to the Central Bank in January 2024 and has fixed them since. The company said “no customers suffered financial loss or were unable to access their funds as a result” and that the problems “largely arose in the context of Coinbase taking steps to protect customers during periods of significant disruption,” including the 2023 U.S. banking crisis. Coinbase Europe Limited , another company in the group, was fined €21,464,734 (about $24.1 million at today’s rate) by the same regulator in November 2025, over failures in monitoring transactions for money laundering from April 23, 2021, to March 19, 2025. title: Mini brain organoids ‘reading’ Braille key step towards biohybrid computing
body:
A group of scientists have shown that brain organoids can pass on signals that correspond to Braille letters, an essential step towards developing the energy-efficient biohybrid computers of the future. The brain organoids, remotely connected to a sensor that recorded tactile signals from different Braille letters, produced signals that were different for each letter, allowing a decoder to distinguish between the different letters the organoids had been given. Although individual brain organoids provided accurately decodable signals 61% of the time, a team of three performed significantly better, producing an accurate signal 83% of the time. The team of three was also better at distinguishing the signals from artificial noise than the decoder working directly on the obscured signals, without the organoids’ involvement.
Could computers include tiny brain organoids one day? The human brain is an incredibly energy-efficient computer, and silicon processors that try to imitate it achieve huge energy savings over traditional processors. Now scientists are experimenting with using organoids modelled on the human forebrain to develop energy-efficient biohybrid computing. A crucial first step towards this is learning whether the organoids can receive and relay signals reliably, which a Bristol-based team of researchers investigated using Braille letters. They found that teams of three brain organoids produced signals which accurately corresponded to different letters 83% of the time.
“We can take information from a real tactile sensor, turn it into a form that a living neural network can receive, and then recover meaningful information from the organoid response,” said Tianyi Liu, PhD candidate at Bristol University and first author of the article in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence . “That gives us a practical way to connect artificial sensors with biological neural systems, which are a very interesting possible route towards more energy-efficient computing.”
The biohybrid systems tested by Liu and her team use brain organoids placed on multielectrode arrays and contained in a system that keeps the organoids alive and monitors their responses. These organoids are less than a millimeter across and lack several structures that a human brain has, but contain about 10,000 neurons, as well as supporting cells. The multielectrode arrays allow them to receive electrical signals.
First, the scientists applied a sensor that records tactile data to the 26 letters of the Braille alphabet. Then they converted this data to electrical stimulation patterns and presented the organoids with the different patterns to see if they would produce neural activity that could tell the scientists what stimulus they’d received. In other words, were they able to ‘read’ the electrical signal that corresponded to each Braille letter, and produce a signal that recognizably corresponded to the information they’d been given?
The organoids’ patterns of neural activity were classified using a simple machine learning algorithm, a support vector machine, that could sort the patterns and detect whether given signals corresponded to specific letters. A single organoid consistently produced a signal that could be accurately decoded as a letter about 61% of the time. However, three organoids working together produced a recognizable signal about 83% of the time.
“After processing by the organoids, the tactile data still contains enough information to classify Braille letters with good accuracy,” said Dr Benjamin Ward-Cherrier of Bristol University, senior author of the article. “Combining outputs from several organoids also showed an improvement in performance.”
The researchers can’t yet tell why three organoids performed better than just one; it could be because individual variation between the organoids means that they complement each other.
“Different organoids may have slightly different network connections, developmental states, and ongoing activity, so the same input can produce similar but not identical responses,” said Liu. “Combining those responses may give us complementary information that we would not get from a single organoid. At the same time, if every organoid behaves differently, it obviously makes it harder to build a predictable and standardized system.”
To make the task harder, the scientists applied different noise filters to the Braille letter signals. They also used the same support vector machine to compare decoding from the organoid responses with direct decoding of the deliberately obscured signals. The machine decoding directly, without the organoids’ involvement, turned out to be easier to fool than decoding from the organoid responses — it was less able to identify the letter signals among the artificial noise.
The scientists stress that these experiments don’t show if organoids can learn over time; they just show that the organoids received and responded to the Braille signals.
“We showed that tactile information could be encoded, processed through the organoids, and decoded, but we did not demonstrate learning or long-term changes in the organoids,” said Liu. “We also tested one tactile task using a fixed encoding scheme and a relatively simple measure of neural activity. The next step is definitely to move beyond Braille; we are interested in things such as textures, edges, and different kinds of touch, and eventually in closed-loop tasks where the organoid receives feedback from what it does. That would allow us to start asking whether the organoid can actually adapt through experience.”

title: Wildwood’s director says AI is ‘antithetical to everything that we are at this studio’
body:
Wildwood is the most ambitious film yet from Laika, the stop-motion studio best known for the likes of Coraline and ParaNorman. It’s a sprawling fantasy adventure that took five years to complete. The process involved more 230 puppets — including 36 of the main character Prue alone — which were brought to life by a team of 49 animators. All told, more than 1,000 artists worked on the film in some form. The painstaking process that goes into making a Laika film offers a distinct counterpoint to the instant progress promised by generative AI tools.
Recently Wildwood director and Laika CEO Travis Knight joined a chorus of influencer filmmakers in denouncing the technology. So when I had a chance to speak to Knight ahead of Wildwood’s premiere on October 23rd, I asked him what it’s like releasing a film like this at a time when AI tools seem inescapable.
“In so many ways generative AI is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” Knight told me. “It’s not that we don’t believe in technology. We do. We use technology, we use computers. We’re not just making films entirely with tools that we’ve inherited from a watchmaker’s widow. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is technology, a computer workstation is technology. But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist.”
In fact, Wildwood is full of technical advances for Laika, many of which iterate on the studio’s previous work. Many puppets are now equipped with diaphragms, for instance, that animators can use to make it appear as if characters are breathing. There is more advanced musculature on the puppets’ limbs, as well as more robust and flexible materials for clothing, hair, and fur. All of these elements together create a film that is decidedly more lifelike than its predecessors. (For a more detailed look at how Laika works, check out this good rundown from Tested.) For Knight, these tools and their continued advancement are an important part of the filmmaking process, but generative AI is something very different.
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bJQGtSeLPII]
“When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition,” he explains. “And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that. When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. That’s theft. I really do believe that when you’re telling a human story, when you’re telling a story about loss and grief and something that means something to someone, that has to come from a person. A computer has never fallen in love. A computer has never lost someone. They’ve never made a terrible choice and lost a brother. They’ve never had their heart broken. Only a person has done that. And so only a person can speak to what that experience is and what that feels like.”
Even though AI-generated films still leave a lot to be desired, the technology is infiltrating Hollywood in various ways, whether it’s the prospect of digital replicas of movie stars, studios training AI models on their films and shows, or some of the biggest players in the field investing heavily in the technology. This can make a studio like Laika, which is firmly entrenched in its handmade approach to filmmaking, stand out all the more. Ultimately Knight says he isn’t entirely against AI in fields outside of the arts, but rather wary of how it’s being used, both now and in the future.
“I think AI is extraordinary technology,” he says. “On the one hand you have to marvel at the advancement of it. And I do think that it’s going to be disruptive to our society and our world. I think there are a great many benefits that can come from it when you look at medicine and science. There’s a world in which these things can benefit humanity tremendously. And then there’s a world where they can be devastating. I fear for the latter, I hope for the former, but it requires people to be good stewards of this technology. As a group of humans we have not shown generally that we’re good at that. But I’m ever an optimist, and I hope that collectively we can see the value in the technology and use it responsibly, and see the danger in the technology and push back against it.”

title: The good, the bad and the unruly from over two dozen candidate debates
body: With less than two weeks until Election Day, most statewide debates have come and gone. Democrats tried to paint their Republican opponents into corners over loyalty to President Donald Trump, and Republicans tried to stake out nuanced positions on the Iran war and data centers. Here’s what we learned from the more than two dozen statewide candidate debates that occurred — and from those that didn’t. Republicans walk a fine line with an unpopular Trump In debate after debate, Democrats tried to tie their opponents to the unpopular president. Republicans weren’t always willing to let them. Several candidates — especially in blue states — were willing to break with the president. In New Hampshire, GOP former Sen. John Sununu said he’s “never met President Trump” and emphasized he’s “never hesitated to stand up to my party or the president when they're wrong,” specifically criticizing Trump’s policies on trade, Iran and Ukraine. In Minnesota, Republican Senate nominee Michelle Tafoya said she disagreed with Trump’s tariff policy and immigration enforcement, and when asked if she would appear onstage with Trump, she demurred. “I am talking to Minnesotans. Theirs is the only endorsement that I care about,” she said. In Maine, GOP Sen. Susan Collins emphasized that she has voted against the president more than 100 times this year, and criticized his approach on Iran. Bobby Charles, the GOP nominee for governor and a former official in President George W. Bush’s State Department during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, said he disagreed with Trump’s “extended engagement” in Iran because “I know what it means to get stuck in a place.” Some Republicans became frustrated by their opponents' efforts to tie them to the president. “He wants to make this about Donald Trump,” said former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) “The bingo game ought to be, how many times can he put the word ‘Trump’ in any answer that he has given in the last, whatever, 30 minutes? It’s ridiculous.” But in some redder states, candidates were more willing to hug the president — recognizing support from his base will be critical to win . “We need the Trump voters to come out,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) said in a debate Wednesday. “Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. Now, my wife is always right, and President Trump is not always right. But I do think that it's great that I have a relationship that I can pick up the phone and discuss with him the pros and cons of what he's contemplating.” It’s the economy, stupid Democrats hammered Republicans on affordability issues, blaming Trump’s tariff policy and Iran for spiking prices. In response, a few conceded some Trump policies were hurting them — while others tried to blame the last president. “That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal that my opponent voted for, that’s where all this inflation came from,” said Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) in a Senate debate in early October. The other Collins, Susan, went the opposite way in blue-leaning Maine. “The bottom line is Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs,” she said in an October 13 debate, after saying the Iran war was “not well thought out.” Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP nominee for Senate in Iowa, said she would pause the gasoline tax before acknowledging the effect of the war: "I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible, because I know people are being squeezed,” she said. Democrats largely sang the same tune on Trump’s policies. “These tariffs are crushing our state, and we'll repeal those tariffs,” said Sen. John Ossoff (D-Ga.). “The tariffs and the war in Iran has hurt Iowa more than any other state,” said state Rep. Josh Turek (D-Iowa). “If you appreciate having record diesel fuel prices … then I'd say vote for Roger Marshall,” said Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee running for Senate in Kansas. “If you want change, then I'd like to ask you to vote for me.” Everyone hates data centers Republicans and Democrats showed a remarkable similarity in their distaste for data centers even as their specific policy prescriptions diverged — a sign of the issue’s rapid ascent as a bipartisan bogeyman, even as Trump reiterates his support for them. Candidates from both parties called for local control. “Look, if you don't want a data center, I will stand up and defend it and make sure you don't get it,” said Rick Jackson, a Republican billionaire businessman running for Georgia governor. “Local communities know best,” said Hinson, the Iowa Republican. In Maine, both Senate candidates said guardrails should be installed to prevent the data centers from raising utility rates for local residents. In Iowa, both gubernatorial candidates — Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn — supported ending tax breaks for data center developers. In New Hampshire, both Senate candidates agreed with GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s push for a statewide moratorium. “At the end of the day, it's up to our governor, our local leaders, to make decisions about any big infrastructure, transmission, power plants, new factories, and data centers should be treated just the same,” Sununu said. Gaffe gamechangers Debates can do candidates more harm than good, and some candidates had some cringey moments. In Alaska, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola appeared to be reading from a notecard throughout a recent debate, giving her opponent, GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, a chance to pounce. "We weren't supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?" he asked the moderator. “You can’t cue-card your way through the Senate,” Sullivan later wrote on social media. Sullivan had his own moment a few weeks earlier when he peeked at Peltola’s answer during a lightning-round question, prompting laughter from the audience. “Happy to help, Dan,” Peltola wrote on social media . In Kansas, Marshall faced loud chats of “you don’t live here” during a debate at the state fair, while speaking about his residence in Kansas and his home in Florida . In Maine, Jackson said Collins should “shut up” after a protester interrupted the debate and Collins claimed the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy's supporters." "Oh, shut up,” Jackson said. “I don't even know that kid." Collins has pounced on the moment to try to paint Jackson as a sexist hothead; Jackson later said he did not regret his outburst. In Iowa, Hinson responded to a question about ensuring the solvency of Social Security by slamming young people’s saving habits . “We also need to be talking about millennials saving money,” she said. “Millennials are the worst group of savers in the country right now and have the least amount of savings.” The debates that didn’t happen Fear of gaffes may have cost voters a chance to see their candidates square off, as the longstanding political tradition of campaign debates took another hit this cycle. In Senate battlegrounds across the country, nominees in both parties outright refused to join their opponents onstage or carefully ducked debates. In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton rebuffed invitation after invitation (including one from Fox News), even after Trump urged him to get onstage. In Ohio, the Senate candidates still haven’t reached an agreement to debate. In North Carolina, there is no debate scheduled between the major-party Senate candidates for the first time in nearly 30 years . There doesn’t seem to be a partisan division over who will and won’t debate. Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs and Ohio Democratic nominee Amy Acton refused to debate their opponents. So did GOP Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas and Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama, who have rebuffed invitations to debate. “There’s so much difference between us, I mean, there’s no reason to get up there and argue about differences of opinion,” Tuberville, running for Alabama governor against Democratic former Sen. Doug Jones, told reporters in August. Andrew Howard, Jason Beeferman, Lisa Kashinsky, Aaron Pellish, Alec Hernandez, Erin Doherty and Jessica Piper contributed reporting.

title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
body:
For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.
This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.
Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.
In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement ( gls.de/taler ). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.
The outcome is the announcement today. The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).
We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bankâs processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bankâs product portfolio and process constraints.
Legal status: Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg). Purpose: Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it. Reach: After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany. Timing: Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens. Next steps: An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI). Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.
We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.
The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls , and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.
If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software .
And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:
Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.
We are looking for investors who: want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area; understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and are able to invest at least â¬50,000.
We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.
Contact us at invest@taler-systems.com to be given access to further business information.

body:

title: Iran better placed for asymmetric war
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – Iran's army commander said the country is now in a better position quantitatively and qualitatively in equipment needed for asymmetric warfare.
Major General Amir Hatami, commander-in-chief of the Iranian Army, made the remarks during a visit to one of the army's combat attack drone production centers.
Hatami said Iran gained important experience in the two recent imposed wars, including that the enemy cannot be trusted even slightly and that efforts must continue to increase readiness.
He said unmanned weapons, from drones and unmanned vessels to micro-aircraft, have found much broader uses with different missions and hold a special place in Iran's defense approach.
Hatami said Iran is specially active in producing, distributing and maintaining these weapons, and that necessary training has been given to forces who have very good skills. He said Iran can say it has reached good maturity in drones and unmanned systems generally.
He said parts of Iran's equipment and facilities were damaged in recent wars, but the enemy imagined Iran does not distinguish between symmetric and asymmetric warfare. Part of the army's equipment belonged and still belongs to symmetric warfare, but a large part relates to asymmetric warfare. Iran needs special readiness for asymmetric warfare and has worked and prepared for it, he said.
Hatami stressed the readiness of all four branches of the Iranian Army.

title: A Developer’s Guide to OmniParseBench: Leaderboard Benchmarks and OCR Testing

In this tutorial, we implement OmniParseBench , Datalab’s open benchmark for document parsers, which grades a parser’s output with 16,288 small pass-or-fail tests across 2,937 pages, from scanned forms and handwriting to arXiv math and dense tables. Rather than trust the leaderboard, we rebuild it from the verdicts Datalab released for 27 parsers, after feeding the scorer a hand-made page to see which mistakes flip a verdict. We then measure ranking certainty, slice it by document type, test whether the two models the card names as helping build tests behave differently on tests a model corrected, and run Tesseract and Indra OCR ourselves on a 50-page sample. Along the way, we find that the top two parsers are statistically tied, the leader changes on most slices, and one launch figure doesn’t match the released files. on Linux the shim changes nothing launcher = WORK / "indra_launch.py" launcher.write_text("import os, runpy, sys\n" "if not hasattr(os, 'sched_getaffinity'):\n" " os.sched_getaffinity = lambda pid: set(range(os.cpu_count()))\n" "sys.argv = ['server.py', '--port', '8001', '--workers', '2']\n" f"runpy.run_path({str(server)!r}, run_name='__main__')\n") log = open(WORK / "indra_server.log", "w") proc = subprocess.Popen([str(py), str(launcher)], stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT) t0 = time.time() while True: try: urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8001/health", timeout=2) break except Exception: if proc.poll() is not None or time.time() - t0 > 600: proc.terminate() raise RuntimeError("the Indra server did not start; see " + log.name) time.sleep(2) print(f"server up in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s: {INDRA[0]}, 2 worker processes") try: run = benchmark.Run("indra-ocr", {"base_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8001"}, WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr") benchmark.prepare(run, str(DATA), 900) n, per_page = predict_pages(run, SAMPLE, alive=lambda: proc.poll() is None) s = benchmark.grade(run, SAMPLE, say=lambda *_: None) finally: proc.terminate() fam = {k: 100 * v["score"] for k, v in s["families"].items()} print(f"Indra OCR: {n} pages, {per_page:.2f} s per page; text {fam['text']:.1f}%, tables {fam['tables']:.1f}%, " f"layout {fam['layout']:.1f}%; headline on these pages {100 * s['headline']:.1f}\n") ids = {p.page_id for p in SAMPLE} fmt = lambda x: "none" if x is None else f"{100 * x:.1f}" print(f"{'on the 50 pages':22s} {'headline':>9s} {'text':>6s} {'tables':>7s} {'layout':>7s}") for name, folder in (("Tesseract", WORK / "runs" / "tesseract"), ("Indra OCR", WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr")): pub = unit_tests.summarize(VERDICTS[(VERDICTS.system == name) & VERDICTS.page_id.isin(ids)][COLS].to_dict("records")) ours = unit_tests.summarize(benchmark.read_scores(benchmark.Run(name, {}, folder))) for who, x in (("ours", ours), ("published", pub)): f = x["families"] print(f"{name + ', ' + who:22s} {fmt(x['headline']):>9s} " + " ".join(f"{fmt(f[k]['score']) if k in f else 'none':>6s}" for k in ("text", "tables", "layout"))) print() for name, folder in (("Tesseract", WORK / "runs" / "tesseract"), ("Indra OCR", WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr")): m, same, total = agreement(folder, name) diff = m[m.result_ours != m.result_pub] print(f"{name:10s} our verdicts equal the published ones on {same} of {total} tests ({100 * same / total:.1f}%); " f"of the {len(diff)} that differ, {(diff.result_ours == 'pass').sum()} pass only for us and " f"{(diff.result_ours == 'fail').sum()} only in the published run") if len(diff): by_page = diff.test_id.map(TESTS.set_index("test_id").page_id).value_counts() print(" differing tests by type:", {k: int(v) for k, v in diff.test_id.map(TESTS.set_index("test_id").test_type).value_counts().items()}, f"| on {len(by_page)} pages, {by_page.iloc[0]} of them on {by_page.index[0]}") claim(f"{name}: our verdicts equal the published ones on at least 95% of the sample's tests", same >= 0.95 * total) return f"Indra OCR on 50 pages: headline {100 * s['headline']:.1f} (text {fam['text']:.1f}, tables {fam['tables']:.1f}, layout {fam['layout']:.1f}), {per_page:.2f} s/page" indra_step() Indra OCR is an open CPU model, and the package ships the HTTP server its adapter talks to, so we install the versions pinned in that server’s Dockerfile into a separate environment and start it in the background. Against the published verdicts on the same pages, Tesseract agrees on every scored test, so its sample score matches the published one. Indra agrees on 203 of 221, and all of its table differences sit on one page, which accounts for the whole gap between its published tables score of 36.1 and our 69.4. One page moving a family that far is the clearest argument for resampling documents. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("10. Bring your own parser: grade a PDF text-layer baseline with the same code") def byo_step(): import pypdfium2 as pdfium def text_layer(path): if path.suffix.lower() != ".pdf": return "" # an image has no text layer to read doc = pdfium.PdfDocument(str(path)) try: return "
" + html.escape(doc[0].get_textpage().get_text_range()) + "
" finally: doc.close() out = WORK / "runs" / "text-layer" (out / "predictions").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) for p in SAMPLE: (out / "predictions" / f"{p.page_id}.json").write_text(json.dumps({"html": text_layer(p.doc_path)})) s = benchmark.grade(benchmark.Run("text-layer", {}, out), SAMPLE, say=lambda *_: None, settings={"unsupported": ["blocks"]}) kind = {p.page_id: "PDF" if p.doc_path.suffix == ".pdf" else "image" for p in SAMPLE} print(f"{'parser on the same 50 pages':28s} {'text: PDF':>10s} {'images':>8s} {'all':>6s} {'tables':>8s}") for name in ("text-layer", "tesseract", "indra-ocr"): sc = pd.read_json(WORK / "runs" / name / "scores.jsonl", lines=True) sc = sc[sc.result.isin(["pass", "fail"])] txt = sc[sc.test_type.map(vocab.FAMILIES) == "text"] by = txt.groupby(txt.page_id.map(kind)).result.apply(lambda r: 100 * (r == "pass").mean()) tab = sc[sc.test_type == "table_cell"] print(f"{name:28s} {by.get('PDF', np.nan):10.1f} {by.get('image', np.nan):8.1f} " f"{100 * (txt.result == 'pass').mean():6.1f} {100 * (tab.result == 'pass').mean():8.1f}") fam = s["families"] return f"text layer, no OCR: text {100 * fam['text']['score']:.1f}%, tables {100 * fam['tables']['score']:.1f}% on the 50 pages" byo_step() Any parser can be graded without an adapter: we write one predictions file per page and call benchmark.grade, declaring the outputs we cannot produce as unsupported. Our parser reads a PDF’s embedded text layer with pypdfium2 and returns an empty string for images, which have none. On PDF pages it passes exactly as many text tests as Tesseract, 42.3% each, without any OCR, while on images it has nothing and Indra OCR still passes 43.1%. Plain text fails every table test, since a pass needs cell structure, so the mix of PDFs and images matters whenever two parsers are compared. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("11. The launch claims, checked against the files") def claims_step(): a, t = TABLE.loc["Datalab accurate"], TABLE.loc["Tesseract"] g = TABLE.loc["Gemini 3.8 Flash", "headline"] c = TABLE.loc["Claude Sonnet 5.5"] tags = TESTS.tags langs = {x for ts in tags for x in ts if re.fullmatch("[a-z]{3}", x)} - {"und", "zxx"} pkg = Path(vocab.__file__).parent # the scorer and the modules it reads; data.py and the harness only fetch and run scoring = sorted(pkg.glob("scorers/**/*.py")) + [pkg / f"{m}.py" for m in ("normalize", "tables", "equations", "views", "vocab", "markdown")] clients = [f.name for f in scoring if re.search(r"^\s*(import|from)\s+(httpx|requests|urllib|huggingface_hub|openai|anthropic|google" r"|transformers|torch|omni_parse_bench\.harness)\b", f.read_text(), re.M)] n_eng, n_table = tags.apply(lambda x: "eng" in x).sum(), tags.apply(lambda x: "table" in x).sum() rows = [ ("16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents", f"{len(TESTS):,} / {TESTS.page_id.nunique():,} / {TESTS.document.nunique():,}", (len(TESTS), TESTS.page_id.nunique(), TESTS.document.nunique()) == (16288, 2937, 2343)), ("92 languages", f"{len(langs)} codes besides und and zxx", len(langs) == 92), ("10,089 English tests, 6,767 table tests", f"{n_eng:,} and {n_table:,}", (n_eng, n_table) == (10089, 6767)), ("Datalab accurate scores 92.7", f"{a.headline:.2f} in results.parquet", round(a.headline, 1) == 92.7), ("Datalab accurate ranks second, behind Gemini", f"{a.headline:.3f} vs {g:.3f}", a.headline < g), ("Claude Sonnet 5.5: text 93.1, tables 95.4, l

title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
body:
We asked 14 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 35 of 41 answers were the same one.
By ModelCompare · 22 October 2026 · Updated 26 October 2026 · 139,573 reads
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”
We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 9 of the 14 gave it every time.
Kimi K3.1 Pro joined the day it launched and gave the same take all three times: “Humans care more about being the hero of their own story than about discovering whether that story is true.”
GPT-6.1 Terra joined the day it launched and also gave it all three times. Its first answer: “Most humans care more about feeling like good people than about doing good.”
Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.
We run experiments on AI models that make you think. Get the next one by email. Unsubscribe anytime.
Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.
Ask Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol yourself
Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.
The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.
Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”
Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchup
We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 41 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.
MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.
A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.
We run experiments on AI models that make you think. Get the next one by email. Unsubscribe anytime.
Fourteen text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. Kimi K3.1 Pro was added on 23 October, the day it came out, with the same prompt and the same illustrator, and GPT-6.1 Terra on 26 October, also the day it came out. All 68 calls cost $1.69. The prompt:
“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.
Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

title: Bitcoin Slides Towards $81,000 as Oil Above $110 Revives Rate-Hike Bets
body: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Slides Towards $81,000 as Oil Above $110 Revives Rate-Hike Bets Bitcoin’s price on Thursday slid — erasing the gains it made earlier in the week — after oil prices jumped. The largest cryptocurrency was down by nearly 4% over a 24-hour period on Thursday in New York, trading as low as $81,331 at one point. On Wednesday, the price of the top cryptocurrency was fast closing in on $85,000 as investors piled back into tech stocks following Elon Musk’s SpaceX earnings . But conflict in the Middle East pushed the oil price higher, spurring inflation fears with U.S. A surging oil price can — at least in the short-term — hurt the price of bitcoin and other “risk-on” assets because it increases the chances of the U.S. central bank raising interest rates. Bitcoin has in the past done well with low interest rates because of increased liquidity, moving at times with tech stocks and the Nasdaq. Stocks on Thursday slid on the news of more attacks from the Yemeni Houthis on Saudi Arabia — stoked fears of oil supply disruptions and a wider Middle East conflict. Bitcoin has typically faced downward pressure on news of war and rallied in hopes of a ceasefire. When the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran in February, the coin nosedived, and had been shaky on news of war in March and April. Oil rising is stoking what many politicians are calling an affordability crisis in the U.S. Americans will go to the polls on November 3, and surging inflation is one of the hottest topics. The Federal Reserve has said getting inflation down in the world’s largest economy is its top priority. Despite the price of bitcoin dipping, the asset just had its best quarter in years, and analysts have said the coin is now in a bull market after rising above its 365-day moving average. Bitcoin last month shrugged off the Federal Reserve raising interest rates and lawmakers blocking landmark crypto legislation, the Clarity Act . This post Bitcoin Slides Towards $81,000 as Oil Above $110 Revives Rate-Hike Bets first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: a16z Frontier
body: Today we’re announcing that we’re expanding the scope of our new fund beyond crypto startups to the broader category of frontier startups: companies building new technologies and creating markets that may take years to develop. To reflect this, we’re renaming a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier. This is an expansion: we will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation. When we started investing in crypto, it was a world of its own. But as blockchains have become more widely used, the lines have blurred and the infrastructure has gradually receded into the background. Wall Street and fintech companies now regularly launch products built on blockchains. Does that make them crypto companies? The label matters less now. It makes more sense to define companies by what they do rather than by the technologies they use. Our expansion also reflects an approach that has guided many of our investments for years: backing technologies that look futuristic, well before they reach the mainstream. When I joined a16z in 2013, I made these kinds of long-horizon investments a focus. One theme was new computing devices . The growth of smartphones made cameras, sensors, and chips better and cheaper, enabling new devices like drones, AR/VR headsets, and wearables. That theme led to investments in Oculus and drone startups like Skydio and Zipline . The other was crypto, which I saw as a new wave built on social media and the open source movement. Social media allowed networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum to gain traction from the outside in , as people formed communities without first needing mainstream acceptance. Open source provided the model for software that anyone could inspect, modify, and build on. Blockchains extended that model from software to services and networks. This theme guided our investment in Coinbase and the creation of our crypto funds , as well as later investments in projects like Solana and Uniswap. Now we are in the middle of another major tech wave centered on AI. The buildout of AI models and infrastructure will continue, but the tech is already sufficiently advanced to spawn a new generation of products and services. No one knows exactly what that generation will look like, but we’re beginning to catch glimpses. We’re especially interested in the new products and markets these advances will enable, including ones that don’t fit into existing categories. Foremost is the emergence of native use cases: brand-new activities you couldn’t do before. Early applications of new technologies tend to focus on doing old things better. To date, AI has mostly been used to do existing activities — like coding and other knowledge work — faster, better, and cheaper. But soon native uses will open up entirely new, unexpected experiences. At first, many of these experiments will look strange and unserious, like toys and hobbies , but over time some will grow into mainstream products. The key to telling the difference is to understand their potential rates of improvement, the factors that can bend deceptively marginal growth into an exponential curve . We’re lucky enough to be living through one of the most consequential curves in human history today. Technological progress is accelerating rapidly, and we’re already starting to see early signals about what a post-AGI world might look like. For one thing, software and increasingly hardware are becoming easier to create. Just as the growth of smartphones fueled an earlier computing cycle, we expect a proliferation of new devices to underpin this one. Some of these will be autonomous machines that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. Others will draw on advances in biology and medicine. Still others will fall somewhere, cybernetically, in between. All these advances will present new ways of building companies . We’ll see more full-stack startups that combine software with hardware and services, as founders take advantage of new capabilities and seek new forms of defensibility. Even the idea of what it means to be a founder may change as we gain more superpowers and as AI agents become increasingly autonomous, able to act on their own. As these capabilities spread, they could change how industries are organized and even give rise to new ones. AI will also enable entirely new kinds of networks connecting people and intelligent agents that learn, coordinate, produce, and transact. The large-scale networks we use every day were made for humans. Networks built for machines will look very different. Many will start as single-player tools and evolve into multiplayer networks. The potential here — for machine age networks — is enormous, and builders have barely begun to scratch the surface. Blockchains will play a significant role in this transformation. Crypto has given the internet money rails that are fast, cheap, global, and programmable. Stablecoins are quickly becoming a standard tool for fintechs, established institutions, and others. And, because blockchains are programmable, both centralized and decentralized financial services can be built on top. Crypto can give new networks native economic capabilities, enable machine-to-machine transactions, and create new ways to bootstrap them. These are examples, not boundaries. The defining companies of past waves were rarely the ones anyone predicted. As always, we expect founders to surprise us and create categories we haven’t imagined yet. I’ll be leading the fund along with the firm’s founders Marc and Ben, and GPs Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet . Our operating teams will continue to work with our existing and future portfolio companies on regulatory, go-to-market, talent, marketing, and technical R&D. We believe some of the most important technology waves are still ahead . Ideas that seem weird or far-fetched today will become indispensable, era-defining products of the future. If you are a founder building what comes next, please reach out. title: Pentagon, Lockheed Agree on 10-Year Framework for Buying F-35s
body: The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin on Oct. 22 announced a framework agreement to buy F-35 Joint Strike Fighters for the next 10 years. But the deal, touted by the Pentagon as “landmark” and a first of its kind, depends on Congress granting the military authority to enter into such a multiyear agreement. Under the deal, Lockheed will build 156 of the fifth-generation jets per year for both the U.S. and international customers, across lots 21 through 30. The U.S. military will buy at least 850 of those 1,560 aircraft over the decade covering the agreement, as well as procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, the Pentagon and Lockheed said in statements. The deal also covers sustainment of the global F-35 fleet. Details such as pricing and schedules have yet to be hammered out. It’s also unclear how many of each F-35 variant will be produced, and how many will go to individual services like the Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps. “We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in the Pentagon’s statement . “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.” Lockheed Martin has also agreed to invest at least $7 billion of its own money into projects to support the F-35 program. “This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” Lockheed President and CEO Jim Taiclet said in the company’s statement. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.” While the Defense Department touted the agreement’s ability to create “a stable, long-term procurement signal to modernize and expand” the F-35, it also noted in its statement that actually executing the agreement “remains subject to congressional authorization and appropriations.” Congress is currently considering granting the Pentagon the authority to enter into multiyear procurement contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX fighters as part of its work on the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers have also yet to pass a budget for fiscal 2027, leaving the agreement unfunded at the moment. With all that legislation still pending, the Oct. 22 announcement is only a framework and not finalized. Lockheed said if Congress does grant the multiyear procurement authority and the necessary appropriations in the next few months, it will work with the F-35 Joint Program Office to finalize the contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal award. Lockheed said having predictable, multiyear procurement plans for the F-35 would save billions of dollars “through long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” And the agreement will allow the program to combine data from a variety of sources into integrated analytics, that will provide more visibility into parts inventory and readiness metrics and allow “transparent, data-driven decision making.” The deal will also allow Lockheed to enter into long-term contracts with suppliers to buy raw materials and critical parts in bulk, which the company predicted would improve F-35 mission-capable rates. Currently, those deals are made on an annual basis, which Lockheed said “has historically strained the industrial base.” In an earnings call with investors Oct. 22, Taiclet said at least 60 percent of an F-35’s content comes from its suppliers, including major suppliers such as Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, which make the center and aft sections of the jets’ bodies, respectively. “We want them to have production stability, just as we would like to have it,” Taiclet said. Taiclet said one of Lockheed’s biggest costs comes from suppliers providing components late, or at poor quality, and he predicted this agreement will help correct those problems. Taiclet told investors that Lockheed and its suppliers will be under a fixed-price escalation contract, in which set prices increase under certain economic conditions. “We’ll all collectively—if we do well and perform well, and those investments pay off that we make—we will get to retain those profits under the fixed-price-with-escalator concept,” Taiclet said. “Before, we would have to give back, with price and operating profit, any improvements we invested in internally. So that is going to apply to the production system. Even if it stays at 156, it’ll be a much healthier production system for industry, and a more predictable production system for government.” And combining aircraft production with the purchase of spare parts and modification kits in the same contract will also yield volume savings and cost predictability, Lockheed said. “Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President OJ Sanchez said in the company’s statement. “This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission-capable rates and a more resilient supply chain—critical capabilities the warfighter needs to meet today’s mission and prepare for tomorrow’s threats.” During the earnings call, Taiclet reiterated Lockheed’s desire— first voiced in April 2025 , after the company lost the Air Force’s F-47 contract to Boeing—to add sixth-generation technologies into the F-35, which he previously referred to as making a “Ferrari” F-35. Taiclet said this could achieve 80 percent of a bespoke sixth-generation aircraft’s capabilities, at half the cost. Lockheed’s primary F-35 factory is in Fort Worth, Texas. The post Pentagon, Lockheed Agree on 10-Year Framework for Buying F-35s appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
body: OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). In addition to Open Responses, OpenSandbox , Anthropic’s Agent Skills , and HuggingFace’s OpenEv framework for agent environments are also joining the AAIF. The join other AAIF projects like the MCP and A2A protocols, AGENTS.md (also from OpenAI), the open source AI agent goose, agentgateway, and Agent Router. The foundation, which is part of the Linux Foundation, launched in December 2025, with MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md as its first projects. As for Open Responses, the core idea here is to provide developers with a set of core API calls that should work across LLM providers. When OpenAI first announced the specification in January, the team behind the project noted that virtually all LLM providers now offer the same building blocks (messages, tool calls, function calling, etc.), but that they also all represent them differently in their APIs. Agentic AI Foundation projects. Credit: The New Stack. Open Responses aims to create a spec that standardizes these primitives so that developers don’t have to translate between each vendor’s idiosyncratic API when they switch between models. “When we co-founded AAIF, we contributed AGENTS.md, a way to give coding agents project-specific instructions,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The New Stack. “Open Responses addresses another part of building agents by giving developers a shared format for working with models across endpoints that support it, so they have fewer provider-specific integrations to maintain. Vercel AI Gateway and Databricks Model Serving already implement it, and AAIF will provide a neutral home for developers and providers to continue developing the specification together.” Why a neutral home matters It’s this neutral home that is generally the reason why companies donate projects to a foundation. The AAIF is part of the Linux Foundation, which has become somewhat of the de facto standard for providing vendor-neutral homes for popular open source projects, with a technical steering committee , which will initially be made up of project maintainers, handling the technical discussions. Who already supports it — and who doesn’t There is already wide support for the spec, with the likes of AWS (in Bedrock), Databricks, LM Studio, Ollama, Hugging Face, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Red Hat, Vercel, and open source projects like vLLM and OGC (previously Llama Stack) supporting it. Among the names that are missing from this list is OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which defines its own Messages API for giving developers access to its models. Anthropic is a member of the AAIF, so maybe we’ll see the company adopt this spec at some point in the future. With the Interactions API, Google, too, has its default for letting developers work with its models. Open Responses doesn’t hide its lineage. The project’s own contributor guide notes that its core schema files are copied from OpenAI’s API. And while OpenAI’s earlier Chat Completions API became an early standard that others used to model their offerings after, Anthropic’s Messages API has now also left a clear mark (in large part thanks to the success of Claude Code), with the likes of DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, and others exposing Anthropic-compatible endpoints, too. That split is exactly the kind of fragmentation a vendor-neutral spec like this is meant to fix, of course. The post OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Russian Shahed Drone Strikes Private Home in Zhytomyr, Injuring 8, Including 2 Children
body:
A Russian Shahed drone struck a private, single-story house in the Zhytomyr community on Thursday, Oct. 22, injuring eight people, including two children.
The region, located in northwestern Ukraine, roughly 87 miles from Kyiv, is far from the current frontline. Vitalii Bunechko, head of the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration first reported the attack, putting the number of injured at nine and saying two of them had been taken to the regional hospital.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Russia continues its deliberate terror against the peaceful Zhytomyr region,” Bunechko said.
Several hours later, the State Emergency Service (D) reported that eight people had been injured, all of whom were hospitalized. The service, however, did not specify the severity of their injuries.
Psychologists from the Main Directorate in the Zhytomyr region provided support to residents, and the service’s bomb disposal teams were also deployed to the site. Other emergency services and volunteers from the Red Cross rapid response unit worked at the scene alongside rescuers.
At the time of the report, the information was still being clarified, and the casualty figures could change as more details become available.
Over the previous day, Russian forces had launched several jet-powered drone strikes on the region, targeting civilian sites – including private households – and critical energy infrastructure.
Eight residential houses were damaged, Bunechko reported in a statement on social media, confirming that no casualties were reported.
Although international humanitarian law prohibits deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian objects, such strikes have become a daily part of life for residents of Ukraine, reaching regions hundreds of miles from the frontline.
Closer to the front, regional authorities are urging civilians, particularly families with children, to leave as soon as possible.
On Thursday, the forced evacuation zone for families with children was expanded to the entire Sloviansk community in the Donetsk region, after repeated strikes killed eight civilians and injured two boys aged seven and 12 on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
“This is the right and important decision,” head of the Sloviansk City Military Administration Vadym Lyakh said.
Donetsk Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin has also urged parents to evacuate to safer parts of Ukraine with their children, saying that “no home and no circumstances are worth a child’s life.”
Russian forces have shelled settlements across the Donetsk region 42 times over the past day, prompting regional authorities to evacuate a total of 215 people, including 68 children.
The attack on the community came around the same time Russian forces used an FPV drone to strike an armored evacuation vehicle of the Proliska Humanitarian Mission near Kramatorsk, also located in the Donetsk region.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian forces struck a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv region with a drone, killing six people, including two children. The youngest victim was a little girl just over a year old, who was killed sitting in her stroller. Her mother, Inna, later died in hospital.
Months earlier, on July 30, a Russian missile struck the village of Radushne in the Kryvyi Rih district of Dnipropetrovsk region, killing an entire family of 10 people , including two parents, seven children, and an 18-month-old grandson.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.
